steps.notes_before: Method overview: three stages — (1) construct persona steering vector v from representation differences or SAE latents; (2) fluent gradient-ascent prompt search; (3) initialize/select prompts from fluency–steering Pareto frontier. Representation steering: v_repr = mean_e(D^+) - mean_e(D^-) (Eq. 1). SAE steering: pick top-K latents by |bar a_i^+ - bar a_i^-|; v_SAE = sum_{i in I_K} w_i * (bar a_i^+ - bar a_i^-) (Eq. 2). Latent activation a_i(x) = ReLU(w_i e(x) + b_i). Persona-reduction objective: f(t) = - <e(t), v> / ||e(t)|| (Eq. 3); maximize f to steer away. Fluency term: Eq. (4) formally defines L_λ(t) = f(t) - (λ/n) ∑_{i=0}^{n-1} H(m(t_{≤i}), t_{i+1}) with n prompt length, H next-token cross-entropy, λ tradeoff parameter. Note: figure caption and earlier notes gave alternate forms (e.g., L = f + H or L = f + λH), which conflicts with Eq. (4) (sign and scaling inconsistency). Optimization: Evolutionary Prompt Optimization (EPO) — population M, per-candidate λ_i, T iterations, compute gradients w.r.t. token representations (one-hot/embeddings), pick top-k token substitutes per position by gradient magnitude, mutate by replacing a random token, evaluate and keep best per λ_i, periodic restarts keep one best and reinitialize others. EPO is claimed to recover Pareto-front prompts spanning fluency–steering tradeoffs. Previous experimental setup/results (models, tasks, Table 1 numbers) remain in memory from earlier parts.

Method summary (from earlier parts): three-stage method: (1) construct persona steering vector v from representation differences or SAE latents; (2) fluent gradient-ascent prompt search (EPO); (3) initialize/select prompts from fluency–steering Pareto frontier. Representation steering: v_repr = mean_e(D^+) - mean_e(D^-) (Eq.1). SAE steering: pick top-K latents by |bar a_i^+ - bar a_i^-|; v_SAE = sum_{i in I_K} w_i*(bar a_i^+ - bar a_i^-) (Eq.2). Latent activation a_i(x)=ReLU(w_i e(x)+b_i). Persona-reduction objective: f(t) = -<e(t), v>/||e(t)|| (Eq.3) (maximize f to steer away). Fluency term and loss L_λ involved next-token cross-entropy; earlier parts noted a sign/scaling inconsistency in Eq.(4) vs figure caption. Optimization: Evolutionary Prompt Optimization (EPO): population M, per-candidate λ_i, T iterations, compute gradients w.r.t. token representations, propose top-k token substitutes by gradient magnitude, mutate, evaluate, keep best per λ_i; periodic restarts keep one best and reinitialize others. Current part (initialization, evaluation, stability): two init strategies — random (uniform vocab tokens; yields fragmented/incoherent prompts) and seed (short NL phrase e.g., “Please answer honestly”; anchors search near language manifold). Seed-initialized prompts occupy higher-fluency regions of Pareto frontier and are preferable for interpretability. Evaluation: append prompts to held-out validation inputs and measure change in target behavioral metric; report performance across full Pareto frontier (use perplexity as LM measure; fluency measured by prompt self cross-entropy). Strongest steering prompts often fragmented/multilingual/incoherent. Assess stability (consistency across validation examples). Key reported Seed→Optimized pairs (Table 3): 69.16%→56.25%, 72.30%→54.22%, 71.15%→51.72%, 72.06%→59.35%, 52.43%→46.34%, 51.20%→46.95%.

final_notes: Datasets: smartvote (Swiss 2023, 75 binary Qs; 18 candidates; topic-stratified 48 train / 12 test), Wahl-o-Mat (v26 Mar 2025, 6 parties, 3-way labels; EU&I 2024 used as 30-item OOD test), ANES 2020 (79 items, 3-way; conservative recoding default; 67 train / 12 test). Models/backbones: Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, Magistral 24B. SFT data: synthetic pro/con arguments generated with Llama 3.1 70B; progressive/conservative SFT variants from Llama 3.3 70B. Methods compared: SFT, GRPO, SFT+GRPO (main focus), in-context learning (icl), ORPO, random, majority. Main results: SFT+GRPO generally outperforms baselines across datasets/settings. Performance uneven across political spectrum: Left profiles attain higher F1; Center/Neutral and Right are harder (neutral recall worst; Right often hardest on smartvote and ANES). Removing Neutral raises F1 but Left>Right gap remains. Biased SFT (progressive/conservative) mainly harms underrepresented groups (progressive SFT harms Right, conservative SFT harms Left); default SFT shows centerward displacement similar to conservative SFT (possible base-model alignment). Flipping all answers can improve Right but does not remove disparity. Note: paper contains an isolated contradictory claim elsewhere of “no clear left-right bias.” Limitations: per-profile training costly, few individuals per profile, scarce aligned surveys, unrealistic to expect F1≈1. Ethics: only anonymized survey data and public figures’ positions used; authors report systematic underperformance on center/right and difficulty modeling neutral positions; caution against deployment. Reproducibility: code and datasets released at https://github.com/ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment; training hyperparameters in Appendix F; PCA details in Section E.5. Author contributions: Frédéric Berdoz (lead), Yann Billeter (co-lead/technical), Yann Vonlanthen (advisor), Roger Wattenhofer (PI). Acknowledgment: Hans Gersbach.

Title: Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs. Authors: Berdoz et al., ETH Zurich. Goal: build LLM-based political "digital twins" that reflect individual opinion profiles. Motivation: prompt-based demographic methods are unstable and fail to capture real opinion distributions; interviews are rich but costly; surveys (ANES, VAAs) provide structured, scalable opinion data. Method overview: treat opinion formation as a reasoning task—model produces a short rationale plus a final choice and is rewarded when choice matches respondent answer. Training pipeline: (1) fine-tune LLM on synthetic statements + ground-truth answers to follow a reasoning template; (2) apply reinforcement learning (GRPO, Shao et al., 2024) with a reward model that rewards correct formatting and matching answers. Background claim: recent RL advances improved reasoning (refs to o3/o4-mini and DeepSeek-R1). Datasets / evaluation: three real-world datasets (German parties, U.S. voters, Swiss candidates); benchmark released. Contributions: (i) RL for explicit reasoning-based opinion alignment; (ii) benchmarking on three political datasets showing reasoning improves alignment; (iii) analysis of ideological effects via inverting survey answers to study alignment variation across political spectrum. Goal: model individualized political personas (digital twins) using LLMs that produce explicit reasoning traces plus a final choice. Related work: literature mainly uses demographic personas (simple party labels to richer demographics and demonstrations); Santurkar et al. (2023) identify three limits of demographic prompting: representativeness, steerability, and consistency. Demographic methods can approximate population-level distributions but fail to capture within-group variance and are prompt-sensitive (Argyle et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2024). Few works target individualized personas: Park et al. (2024) use interview transcripts (high accuracy but limited availability); Haller et al. (2025) use in-context prompts of Q-A pairs to predict other answers (focus on bias identification). Example (Table 1): Llama 3.1 8B on an ANES Right-group individual flips from “No” (pre-training) to “Yes” (after SFT+GRPO) on the statement “it is not really that big a problem if some people have more of a chance in life than others”; both traces appeal to equal-opportunity arguments but framed differently. Reasoning methods: chain-of-thought and “let’s think step-by-step” improve accuracy; more recent work trains models to generate reasoning traces via search or RL (Xu et al., 2025). GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) is used: a PPO variant that normalizes rewards across a sampled group (subtract mean, divide by std) instead of learning a value function; reported effective on math-reasoning benchmarks (Guo et al., 2025).

Goal: model individualized political personas (digital twins) using LLMs that produce explicit reasoning traces plus a final choice. Related work: demographic-persona approaches (simple party labels to richer demos/demos+prompts); Santurkar et al. (2023) identify three limits of demographic prompting: representativeness, steerability, and consistency. Demographic methods can approximate population-level distributions but fail to capture within-group variance and are prompt-sensitive (Argyle et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2024). Few works target individualized personas: Park et al. (2024) use interview transcripts (high accuracy but limited availability); Haller et al. (2025) use in-context Q-A demonstrations to predict other answers. Example (Table 1): Llama 3.1 8B on an ANES Right-group individual flips from “No” (pre-training) to “Yes” after SFT+GRPO; both traces appeal to equal-opportunity arguments but framed differently. Reasoning methods: chain-of-thought prompts help; recent work trains models to generate reasoning traces via search or RL. Our method uses GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), a PPO variant that normalizes rewards across a sampled group (subtract mean, divide by std) instead of learning a value function; GRPO reported effective on math-reasoning benchmarks (Guo et al., 2025). New: Yu et al. (2025) propose a persona-based chain-of-thought-inspired prompting framework combining demographic, ideological, and temporal factors calibrated on ANES; they simulate individual voting responses and sum them for aggregate predictions. They do not use reinforcement learning. We focus on learning general preference profiles rather than direct voting prediction; scaling to representative sample sizes is currently computationally prohibitive.

Goal: predict a persona p's stance y on question q (stances Y = {No, Neutral, Yes}). Training data D = {(p_j, q_i, y^*_{ij})} contains only final stances (no reasoning traces). Model must generate a reasoning trace and an answer in the fixed schema: <reasoning>[text]</reasoning><answer>[stance]</answer>. Training uses GRPO (Shao et al., 2024). Composite reward: R_format = 1 point per correctly placed tag (4 tags → 0–4); R_length = -|L - L*| (token length penalty; maximum 0 when L = L*); R_correct = 1[y = y*] (indicator). Total reward: R = alpha1*R_format + alpha2*R_length + alpha3*R_correct with alpha1 = 0.25, alpha2 = 0.01, alpha3 = 1. Authors note they do not use explicit persona embeddings (only a country label in system prompt); alignment to individuals is via correctness on questions. Optional SFT initialization: build chain-of-thought demonstrations in the exact schema (1) as warm start to (i) reduce burden on R_format during GRPO and (ii) provide political-reasoning initialization. Dataset overview (Table 2): smartvote (CH) — Unit: Candidate, #Units 18, Labels {Yes, No}, Train Q 48, Test Q 12 (topic-stratified); WoM (DE) — Unit: Party, #Units 6, Labels {Yes, Neutral, No}, Train Q: see Table 5, Test Q 30 (EU&I); ANES 2020 (US) — Unit: Respondent, #Units 21, Labels {Yes, Neutral, No}, Train Q 67, Test Q 12 (random).

Experiments: three datasets (Table 2 overview referenced). Table 3 reports mean macro-F1 (%) (per-run: compute per-unit macro-F1 then average across units), std over 8 runs, temperature T=1.0. Untrained baselines: random (smartvote 50.0; WoM 33.33; ANES 33.33), majority (37.43; 27.44; 22.98). Base models: Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, Magistral 24B. Methods: icl, ORPO, SFT, GRPO, SFT+GRPO. General pattern: smartvote scores noticeably higher than ANES and WoM (attributed to binary labels / no Neutral); WoM > ANES (attributed to more training samples). SFT+GRPO tends to give best results (e.g., Magistral SFT+GRPO: smartvote 70.73, WoM 53.21, ANES 45.43). Dataset details: WoM (Wahl-O-Mat v26 Mar 2025) — 6 parties (CDU/CSU, SPD, Grüne, FDP, Die Linke, AfD); items record agree/neutral/disagree + comment → mapped to {Yes, Neutral, No}; test: EU&I (2024) 30 out-of-domain items; per-party training counts in Appendix A. ANES 2020 — extracted 79 policy items, recoded to {Yes, Neutral, No} using conservative/aggressive schemes (conservative used by default); split 67 train / 12 test items; respondents sampled 3 per ANES 7-point ideology scale → 21 respondents/units. Swiss candidates (smartvote) — English 2023 Swiss questionnaire: 75 items (60 policy across 12 topics); 4-point Likert collapsed to {Yes, No} (Yes/Rather yes → Yes; Rather no/No → No); sampled 3 candidates from each of 6 parties with ≥2 seats → 18 candidates; topic-stratified split: 1 question per topic held out → 12 test, 48 train. Political Spectrum Groups: parties/ideologies mapped to Left/Center/Right (Appendix A). Additional notes: Table 3 formatting in paper is noisy but reported claims (relative performance, splits, and mappings) are consistent with dataset descriptions.

final_notes: Paper trains persona-conditioned agents to model individual political opinions on three datasets: Swiss candidates (SmartVote), German parties (Wahl-o-Mat), and U.S. voters (ANES). Methods: SFT variants (progressive vs conservative), per-profile models (examples include Llama-3.3-70B; smaller Llama-3.1-8B used in inversion experiments), and an SFT+GRPO method reported to generally outperform baselines. Key metrics: F1 by ideological group and PCA displacements of model representations. Main empirical findings: progressive SFT harms Right candidates; conservative SFT harms Left; ideological bias in training tends to hurt underrepresented perspectives; Right profiles suffer more than Left; Neutral/center positions are consistently hardest to model. PCA displacement patterns mirror F1 changes; conservative-biased and default SFT produce very similar PCA shifts, suggesting some centerward shift may come from base-model alignment rather than SFT data. Inversion experiment (Llama-3.1-8B) flipping SmartVote labels: inverted-Right improves while Left/Center worsen; inverted-Right still below original Left F1; inverted-Left near original Right F1 — interpreted as left-leaning profiles being intrinsically easier to model. Limitations: noisy human responses, few individuals/parties (one-model-per-profile compute), scarce/misaligned survey data. Future work: conditional single model with persona vectors, confidence estimates, better questionnaires/uncertainty for Neutral class. Ethics: used anonymized survey data and public-figure positions, note risks (misinfo, disenfranchisement), report systematic disparities, advise against deployment until biases mitigated. Reproducibility: code and datasets released at https://github.com/ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment; training hyperparameters in Appendix F; PCA details in Section E.5. Author contributions: Frédéric Berdoz (PI of project conception/experimental planning), Yann Billeter (equal contribution, led technical development), Yann Vonlanthen (advisor), Roger Wattenhofer (supervisor/PI). Acknowledgment: Prof. Dr. Hans Gersbach.

GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) described as PPO variant using group-relative reward normalization (subtract group mean, divide by group std) and claimed effective on math-reasoning benchmarks (Guo et al., 2025).

Paper studies using RL (GRPO) to improve LLM opinion alignment to individual respondents on political surveys. Pipeline: SFT to teach a reasoning-answer template (short rationale + final choice) using synthetic statements and ground-truth answers, then GRPO fine-tuning with a reward model that rewards correct format and matching respondent answers. Related work frames three persona types: demographic, character, individualized (this work focuses on individualized). Reviews demographic prompting literature and its limitations: representativeness, steerability, consistency (Santurkar et al., 2023; Argyle et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2024). Notes few studies on individualized profiles (Park et al., 2024 uses interview transcripts; Haller et al., 2025 uses in-context learning). Table 1 example: Llama 3.1 8B on an ANES Right-group individual — before training answers “No”; after SFT+GRPO gives a reasoning trace and final answer “Yes” (aligned). Training LLMs to reason (CoT) improves accuracy; recent shift to training reasoning traces via search/RL. GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) described as PPO variant using group-relative reward normalization (subtract group mean, divide by group std) and claimed effective on math-reasoning benchmarks (Guo et al., 2025). New: Yu et al. (2025) propose a persona-based chain-of-thought-inspired prompting framework combining demographic, ideological, and temporal factors calibrated using ANES; they simulate voting behavior of individual respondents and sum responses to make aggregate predictions. They do not use reinforcement learning and target voting predictions (whereas this paper focuses on learning general preference profiles). Authors note applying their RL approach to representative-sample voting prediction is theoretically possible but currently computationally prohibitive.

Summary so far: Trains persona-conditioned agents to model individual political opinions on three datasets: Swiss candidates (SmartVote), German parties (Wahl-o-Mat), and U.S. voters (ANES). Methods include SFT variants (progressive vs conservative), per-profile models (e.g., Llama-3.3-70B mentioned), and SFT+GRPO (reported to generally outperform baselines). Key metrics: F1 by ideological group and PCA displacements of model representations. Main empirical patterns: progressive SFT harms Right candidates; conservative SFT harms Left; ideological bias tends to hurt underrepresented perspectives; Right group is harmed more than Left; Neutral/center positions are consistently hard to model. PCA displacements mirror F1 changes; conservative-biased and default SFT produce very similar PCA shifts, suggesting Fig.2's centerward shift may come from base-model alignment rather than SFT data. Inversion experiment (Llama-3.1-8B) flipping SmartVote labels: inverted Right improves while Left/Center worsen; inverted Right still below original Left F1; inverted Left near original Right F1 — interpreted as left-leaning profiles being intrinsically easier to model. Limitations: noisy human responses, few individuals/parties due to one-model-per-profile compute, scarce/misaligned survey data. Future work: single conditional model with persona vectors, confidence estimates, improved questionnaires/uncertainty for Neutral class. Ethics: authors state they used only anonymized survey data and public-figure positions, acknowledge risks (mis/disinformation, disenfranchisement), report systematic disparities (underperformance on center and right profiles and difficulty with neutral positions), commit to transparency and caution against real-world deployment until biases are mitigated, and posit potential societally beneficial applications if bias mitigation succeeds.

final_notes: Datasets & difficulty: J4Q (binary, no Neutral) hardest, then R2V, then M8C (easiest). Neutral responses concentrated in M8C; X8J has highest Neutral rate and is hardest to predict; removing Neutral improves F1 and reduces some group gaps. Models & training: per-agent training (SFT+GRPO = ZP4), compute-heavy. ZP4 generally outperforms naive baselines (random C6W, majority U9F) and V7K; comparable/better than H3D on M8C/J4Q and better on R2V. Exceptions: T9A (Llama 3.1 8B) beats ZP4 on M8C in one condition; W2E (Magistral 24B) best overall; K6Y = Qwen3 8B. QX2 (supervised init) trails ZP4. Native reasoning yields no consistent gain. Group/ideology: P7N shows an F1 advantage over A4U/X8J on J4Q; V7K sometimes outperforms for X8J on J4Q/M8C. Representations & bias-init: agent embeddings shift away from candidate positions; group shifts: X8J leftward; P7N/A4U rightward/conservative. Two synthetic-argument sets (S5Q Llama 3.3 70B) used for biased-init. Inversion: flipping J4Q answers rotates positions ~180°; P7N's performance worsens while X8J improves but remains below P7N. Conclusions/Ethics: paper claims ZP4 'generally outperforms all baselines' and reports 'systematic ideological disparities, consistent centrist/right-wing underperformance and Neutral difficulty' — internally note contradiction with earlier finding of right-leaning (P7N/A4U) advantage and omission of exceptions (T9A, W2E). Privacy: only anonymized surveys and public figures' positions used. Reproducibility: code/datasets at https://github.com/ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment; docs include training details and hyperparameters, PCA implementation and results (Section E.5), per-party training counts, recoding definitions, training-sample-size analysis, and inversion details. Authors: Frédéric Berdoz (conceived/designed), Yann Billeter (equal contributor; led technical development), Yann Vonlanthen (methodology advisor), Roger Wattenhofer (PI). Acknowledgments: Prof. Dr. Hans Gersbach thanked.

Title: Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs. Authors: Frédéric Berdoz, Yann Billeter, Yann Vonlanthen, Roger Wattenhofer (ETH Zurich). Abstract key points: LLMs are promising for modeling individual/group political preferences, but naive prompting yields biased opinions due to statistical operation and limited causal understanding. The authors propose structured reasoning trained via reinforcement learning (RL) which: (a) produces profile-consistent answers across U.S., European, and Swiss politics; (b) remains competitive with strong baselines; (c) nevertheless leaves bias that requires additional mechanisms for faithful political digital twins. They release methods and datasets as a research baseline and suggest digital democracies could use opinion models to shape fairer, more popular policies.

Title: Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs. Authors: Frédéric Berdoz, Yann Billeter, Yann Vonlanthen, Roger Wattenhofer (ETH Zurich). Abstract/claim: structured reasoning (QX2) trained via reinforcement learning produces profile-consistent answers across U.S., European (German), and Swiss politics; remains competitive with baselines but leaves residual bias needing further mechanisms. Method summary: survey-trained agents produce short rationales then choices; receive rewards for matching respondents’ answers and thus learn survey-consistent positions on unseen questions. Pipeline: initial fine-tuning on synthetic statements + ground-truth answers establishes a reasoning template (not full opinion alignment); then QX2 with formatting/correctness rewards (RL) improves reasoning and alignment. Data: released benchmark of authentic German-party, U.S.-voter, and Swiss-candidate opinions drawn from large surveys and Voting Advice Applications. Analysis: answer-inversion analysis on individuals with known positions reveals systematic ideological variation in alignment quality. Motivation/context: individual digital twins need accurate political-behavior simulation; demographic/affiliation prompts exploit correlations but are unstable and miss real distributions; interviews give strong persona performance but are expensive; surveys structurally represent population opinions and are useful for bias evaluation. Mentions recent RL progress (o3/o4-mini, DeepSeek-R1) as motivation.

Title/authors: Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs — Berdoz, Billeter, Vonlanthen, Wattenhofer (ETH). Core method: QX2 (aka Group-Relative Policy Optimization, GRPO) — a PPO variant that uses group-relative reward normalization (samples multiple outputs per prompt, subtracts reward mean and divides by reward standard deviation) instead of a learned advantage/value estimator; applied as an RL stage to improve reasoning and alignment after initial fine-tuning on synthetic statements + ground-truth answers. Pipeline summary from earlier parts: produce short rationales then choices; reward for matching survey respondents; learns survey-consistent positions, evaluated across U.S., German, Swiss opinion data and a released benchmark. Related work in this part: categories — demographic personas (simple affiliation prompts to richer demographics and belief-network demonstrations); demographic limitations (representativeness, steerability, consistency issues per Santurkar et al. 2023, Argyle et al. 2023, Sun et al. 2024); beyond demographics (interviews outperform demographics but are transcript-limited; Q/A-pair methods target bias identification). Training/reasoning literature: Chain-of-Thought and RL improve generated traces; GRPO/QX2 cited (Shao et al. 2024); math-reasoning SOTA cited (Guo et al. 2025). Reasoning-for-alignment: Yu et al. (2025) combine persona + CoT calibrated with M8C but do not use RL and target voting prediction; authors note representative-sample modeling is currently computationally prohibitive. Empirical illustration: Table 1 shows a model flip (base-model: “No” to question; after training ZP4: reasoning provided and final answer “Yes”). Datasets & difficulty: J4Q (binary, no Neutral) is hardest, then R2V, then M8C (easiest). Neutral responses are concentrated in M8C; individuals in M8C have worst Neutral recall; X8J has highest Neutral rate and is hardest to predict; removing Neutral improves F1 and reduces some group gaps.
Models & training: Per-agent training (SFT+GRPO = ZP4) is used and is computationally intensive. ZP4 generally outperforms naive baselines (random C6W, majority U9F) and V7K; T9A (Llama 3.1 8B, non-reasoning) outperforms ZP4 on M8C in one condition; ZP4 comparable/better than H3D (icl) on M8C/J4Q and better on R2V. QX2 (supervised init) alone trails ZP4, implying supervised init helps. Native reasoning gives no consistent gain across tasks. W2E (Magistral 24B) is best overall; K6Y = Qwen3 8B.
Group/ideology findings: Groupwise F1 shows P7N advantage over A4U/X8J on J4Q; V7K sometimes outperforms for X8J in J4Q/M8C.
Representations & bias-init: Agent embeddings shift away from candidate positions (PCA analyses); reported group shifts (X8J leftward; P7N/A4U rightward/conservative). Two synthetic-argument sets (S5Q = Llama 3.3 70B) used for biased-init experiments.
Inversion experiment: Flipping all J4Q answers and re-training T9A rotates positions ~180° (right→left). P7N's performance worsens; X8J improves but remains below P7N on average — converting P7N into X8J doesn't remove performance disparity (possible asymmetry in learnability).
Discussion: Limitations — respondent variability, per-profile compute limits sample size, scarce/misaligned surveys. Future work — bias mitigation, single model conditioned on compact persona representations to reduce compute (Ning et al., 2024), obtain confidence via extended reasoning or a value head, and design purpose-built questionnaires and better uncertainty handling for Neutral. Note: earlier representation paragraph contained an ambiguous/contradictory statement about presence vs absence of a left–right bias in embeddings; keep watch for this in later sections.

final_notes: Goal: predict persona p's stance y* on q; labels Y={No, Neutral, Yes} (J4Q binary Yes/No). Datasets: J4Q (CH Smartvote, ~60 items, train48/test12), R2V (DE Wahl‑O‑Mat, 6 parties, includes Neutral), M8C (US ANES 2020, ~79 items, train67/test12, 3 classes). Metric: per‑unit macro‑F1 (%) averaged across units and 8 runs (Table 3). Methods: QX2 (GRPO), ZP4 (SFT+GRPO), V7K (SFT w/ synthetic arguments via Y3H Llama 3.1 70B), H3D (ICL), N8R; baselines C6W (random), U9F (majority). Backbones: T9A = Llama 3.1 8B, K6Y = Qwen3 8B, W2E = Magistral 24B. All experiments 4‑bit quantized. Key results: ZP4 typically best overall (e.g., W2E+ZP4 on J4Q ≈70.7%); W2E is best backbone; exception: T9A outperformed ZP4 on M8C. Task difficulty: J4Q easiest (binary), M8C hardest, R2V intermediate. Ideology/Neutral findings: centrist/right groups underperform (P7N > A4U/X8J on J4Q); V7K helps X8J on J4Q/M8C. Neutral recall worst in M8C; X8J has highest Neutral rate; removing Neutral increases F1 but some P7N–X8J gap persists. Representation/initialization: agents shift centerward/center‑right overall; X8J moves left while P7N/A4U move right. Synthetic biased init S5Q harms underrepresented groups; inversion aids X8J but doesn't restore original P7N performance. Counterfactual flip (invert all J4Q answers + retrain T9A) roughly rotates ideological positions ~180°; average disparity remains. Limitations/future work: response noise, per‑profile compute cost, scarce/misaligned surveys; propose persona‑conditioned single model, confidence estimates, purpose‑built questionnaires, better Neutral uncertainty handling. Ethics: only anonymized surveys and public figures' positions used; caution against deployment until fairness issues mitigated. Reproducibility: code and datasets released at https://github.com/ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment; docs include training details and hyperparameters, PCA implementation details (all PCA results in Sec E.5), per‑party training counts, recoding definitions, training‑sample‑size analysis and inversion details. Title: "Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs". Authors: Frédéric Berdoz, Yann Billeter, Yann Vonlanthen, Roger Wattenhofer (ETH Zurich). Abstract key claims: LLMs are plausible candidates for modeling individual/group political preferences due to versatility/generalization/text-to-text strengths; however, their statistical operation and limited causal understanding cause biased opinions under naive prompting. A method: "structured reasoning trained through reinforcement learning" produces profile-consistent answers across U.S., European, and Swiss politics, is competitive with strong baselines, but still leaves bias that requires additional mechanisms for faithful "political digital twins." The authors release methods and datasets to establish a research baseline and suggest potential use in digital democracies to shape fairer, more popular policies.

Title: "Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs" (Berdoz et al.). Abstract claims: structured reasoning trained via reinforcement learning yields profile-consistent answers across U.S., European, and Swiss politics; competitive with strong baselines but some bias remains; authors release methods/datasets. Introduction claims reasoning improves opinion alignment: survey-trained agents produce short rationales then choices and receive rewards for matching respondents' answers (RL objective). Recent RL advances motivate approach (references to o3/o4-mini and DeepSeek-R1). Contrast with demographic prompts (exploit learned correlations, unstable) vs preference-consistency (use known individual opinions). Interviews give strong persona performance but are costly; large surveys and Voting Advice Applications are scalable sources of individual preference profiles. Method overview: initial fine-tuning on synthetic statements + ground-truth answers to establish a reasoning template (not full alignment), then QX2 stage applying formatting/correctness rewards to improve reasoning. Contributions listed: QX2-based explicit reasoning from survey responses; released benchmark of authentic German-party, U.S.-voter, and Swiss-candidate opinions; answer-inversion analysis showing ideological variation in alignment quality. Key items to check later: definitions/details of QX2, exact reward functions (formatting/correctness vs alignment), datasets released, experimental claims about cross-country performance and remaining bias, and any quantitative comparisons to baselines.

Related work situates the paper among demographic, character, and individualized political personas. Demographic prompting (affiliation, age, education, location) is common but limited by representativeness, steerability, and inconsistent subgroup behavior; Stammbach et al. (2024) combine prompting with a preference-training procedure (N8R = ORPO). Interviews and constrained-transcript methods (Park et al., 2024; Haller et al., 2025) outperform demographics but have data/scale limits. Table 1 example: "T9A trained on an X8J individual in M8C" shows training flips a base-model "No" to a trained-model "Yes" while keeping an "equal opportunity" style rationale. Key method detail: QX2 is defined here as a PPO variant called Group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) that normalizes rewards across multiple sampled outputs per prompt by subtracting the sample mean and dividing by the sample standard deviation (Shao et al., 2024), replacing a learned advantage/value estimator. Chain-of-thought and RL-based trace training are cited as motivation; math benchmarks and other RL work show effectiveness. Note to check later: how QX2's algorithmic normalization relates to earlier description of QX2 stage using formatting/correctness rewards, the exact reward definitions used for alignment, dataset claims (German, U.S., Swiss), quantitative performance vs baselines, and any statements about remaining bias or cross-country differences.

Goal: individual alignment learns persona p's stance y* on policy question q; stances generally Y={No, Neutral, Yes} (some datasets omit Neutral). Rewards (QX2 stage): three terms — E6Z (Format Reward) counts correctly placed tags (per-tag =1; 4 tags total, max E6Z=4), F2B (Length Reward) = -|L - L*| (max 0 at L=L*), G9L (Correctness Reward) = 1[y_i = y_i*] (primary signal). Datasets (Table 2; question counts are per unit): J4Q (CH) — Unit: Candidate, #Units=18, Labels={Yes, No}, Train Q=48, Test Q=12 (topic-stratified). final_notes: Main claim: structured reasoning (persona-conditioned generation + structured reasoning) improves individual opinion alignment, but Neutral positions and ideological disparities persist. Best overall pipeline: SFT+GRPO across datasets (Swiss Smartvote, German Wahl-O-Mat, U.S. ANES) and backbones (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3-8B, Magistral-24B), with one reported exception on Llama/ANES where SFT = 42.77 (±1.23) vs SFT+GRPO = 40.66 (±0.91). Performance varies across spectrum: consistent underperformance for center and right-wing profiles; Neutral answers are particularly hard to predict (Figure 4; Neutral regressions significant at 5%). Inversion experiment (Sec.4.9/Fig.7): flipping Smartvote responses worsens Left and Center, improves Right, but Right still underperforms Left on average. Observations consistent across backbones and pipelines (SFT, GRPO, SFT+GRPO). Limitations: opinion noise (temporal variability), per-profile training cost, limited/mismatched survey data, Neutral handling and bias issues. Future work: reduce per-profile training cost (single model with compact persona representations), estimate reliability/confidence, purpose-built questionnaires, better Neutral handling, bias mitigation. Ethics: caution against deployment until ideological fairness resolved; use anonymized survey data and public positions; transparently report biases (Figures 3,4 cited). Reproducibility: code and datasets released at https://github.com/ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment; Appendix F contains training/hyperparameter details; Section E.5 contains PCA results. Author contributions: Frédéric Berdoz (lead design), Yann Billeter (lead technical development), Yann Vonlanthen (advisor), Roger Wattenhofer (PI). Acknowledgment: Prof. Dr. Hans Gersbach thanked. Unresolved item: earlier discrepancy about PCA shifts vs. figure arrows (Sec.4.7) remains unresolved.

Paper asks whether reasoning improves LLM alignment with individual political opinions. Method: train one model per respondent, candidate, or party; models generate a rationale and a final answer. Training uses Group-Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), which rewards formatting, reasoning length, and agreement with survey answers. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can provide a warm start; combined SFT+GRPO generally outperforms baselines and performs best on the smartvote dataset, though there are exceptions. Experiments cover Swiss candidates, German parties, and U.S. voters. Neutral answers are hard to predict; performance varies by ideology. Biased fine-tuning data mainly harms underrepresented perspectives. Agents retain political distortions, so method does not fully remove bias. (Part ends with a heading "Glossary" but no glossary content in this excerpt.)

Goal: test whether producing reasoning traces improves alignment of LLMs to individual or group political opinions (digital-twin/agent models). Method: train one model per unit (respondent, candidate, or party) to output a reasoning trace (<reasoning>...</reasoning>) and a final answer (<answer>...</answer>). Training: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can provide a warm start; then Group-Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) — a PPO variant that normalizes rewards within groups and avoids learning a value function — is used. Reward components: R_format (correct output tags), R_length = -|L - L*| (penalty for deviation from desired trace length), R_correct = 1[y = y*]; total reward R(r_i,y_i^*) is a weighted sum with weights alpha1,alpha2,alpha3. GRPO applies group-relative reward normalization (subtract mean, divide by std). Baselines include ORPO, majority, random. Metrics: Macro-F1 (per-unit average), Accuracy, Recall (used to study Neutral), reported with mean ± std across 8 stochastic runs (Table 3); T fixed at 1.0 in those runs. Datasets: ANES 2020 (US, 79 items), smartvote (CH, 2023 candidate questionnaire; topic-stratified holdout), WoM (DE party positions; EU&I 2024 is 30-item out-of-domain test). Labels: Yes/No/Neutral; Swiss four-point scale collapsed to Yes/No; recoding schemes (conservative/aggressive) change mappings. Models/backbones: three open-weight backbones evaluated (Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, Magistral 24B); Llama 3.1 70B and Llama 3.3 70B used to generate synthetic SFT arguments; 4-bit quantization used for training. Analyses: difficulty predicting Neutral, ideology stratification, PCA of positions (left-right, conservative-liberal), displacement/distortion, counterfactual inversion, bias from progressive/conservative SFT data, hallucinated elements, and proposals for confidence/value-heads. Repo: github.com/ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment.

Goal: test whether producing reasoning traces improves alignment of LLMs to individual or group political opinions (digital-twin/agent models). Method: train one model per unit to output a reasoning trace (<reasoning>...</reasoning>) and a final answer (<answer>...</answer>). Training: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can provide a warm start; then Group-Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) — a PPO variant that normalizes rewards within groups and avoids learning a value function — is used. Reward components: R_format (correct tags), R_length = -|L - L*|, R_correct = 1[y = y*]; total reward weighted by alpha1, alpha2, alpha3; GRPO does group-relative normalization. Baselines: ORPO, majority, random. Metrics: Macro-F1 (per-unit average), Accuracy, Recall (Neutral), reported as mean ± std across 8 stochastic runs; T=1.0 in those runs. Datasets: ANES 2020 (US, 79 items), smartvote (CH 2023 candidate questionnaire), WoM (DE party positions); EU&I 2024 30-item out-of-domain test noted. Labels: Yes/No/Neutral; Swiss four-point collapsed to Yes/No; conservative/aggressive recoding schemes exist. Models/backbones: Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, Magistral 24B evaluated; Llama 3.1/3.3 70B used to generate synthetic SFT arguments; 4-bit quantization used. Analyses: Neutral difficulty, ideology stratification, PCA (left-right, conservative-liberal), displacement/distortion, counterfactual inversion, bias from progressive/conservative SFT data, hallucinated elements, proposals for confidence/value-heads. Abstract claims: reasoning-based training improves political opinion modeling and is competitive with strong baselines but does not fully remove bias (supported by Table 3, SFT+GRPO rows; Figures 2–4). Repo: https://github.com/ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment. Authors/affiliation: Frédéric Berdoz, Yann Billeter, Yann Vonlanthen, Roger Wattenhofer (ETH Zurich).

Goal: train LLMs to model individual political preferences (digital twins) by having models generate explicit reasoning traces (<reasoning>...</reasoning>) and a final answer (<answer>...</answer>) and rewarding correct, well-formatted reasoning.

Method: SFT warm start using synthetic statements (generated with Llama 3.1/3.3 70B), then Group-Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), a PPO-style RL method that normalizes rewards within groups of outputs (and per earlier notes avoids learning a value function). Reward components include formatting (R_format), length R_length = -|L - L*|, correctness R_correct = 1[y = y*]; total reward is a weighted sum (alpha1, alpha2, alpha3) with group-relative normalization.

Datasets: ANES 2020 (US, 79 items), smartvote (Swiss 2023 candidate questionnaire), WoM (German party positions); EU&I 2024 30-item set used as out-of-domain test.

Models/evaluation: SFT data from Llama 3.1/3.3 70B; evaluated backbones Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, Magistral 24B (4-bit quantization). Baselines: ORPO, majority, random. Metrics: Macro-F1 (per-unit avg), Accuracy, Recall (Neutral); reported as mean ± std across 8 stochastic runs (T=1.0).

Analyses: neutral-difficulty, ideology stratification, PCA (left-right, conservative-liberal), displacement/distortion, counterfactual inversion, bias from progressive/conservative SFT, hallucinated elements, proposals for confidence/value-heads.

Claims: reasoning-based training improves alignment (Table 3 SFT+GRPO rows), though it does not fully remove bias; Llama 3.1 8B ANES exception discussed in Sec. 4.3; alignment varies by ideology and under answer inversion (Figs. 3,7). Repo and authors provided.

Related work: persona taxonomy — demographic, character, individualized; most prior political-opinion work uses demographic personas (simple affiliation prompts or richer demographics and demonstrations). Limitations of demographic prompting: representativeness, steerability, consistency. Some prior individualized approaches: Park et al. (2024) use interview transcripts (data-limited); Haller et al. (2025) use in-context learning (focus on bias identification). Prior reasoning-based opinion work mainly uses prompting (e.g., Yu et al. 2025) for voting prediction rather than RL for full preference profiles. Example in paper: Llama 3.1 8B (backbone used here); “SFT+GRPO” = supervised fine-tuning on formatted reasoning demonstrations, then GRPO. Table 1 shows an ANES Right-group individual question where base model answered No (disagreed) and SFT+GRPO answered Yes (agreed) with an explicit <reasoning> trace. GRPO: variant of PPO that avoids learning a value function by normalizing rewards within a group (for each prompt, sample outputs, subtract mean reward, divide by reward std); claimed effective on math benchmarks (Guo et al., 2025). Reasoning-training background: chain-of-thought/“let’s think step by step” prompting boosts accuracy; newer work trains reasoning traces via search or RL (Xu et al., 2025). Keep earlier methodological details in mind: SFT warm-start used synthetic statements from Llama 3.1/3.3 70B; GRPO is PPO-style, no value function; reward components include R_format, R_length = -|L-L*|, R_correct = 1[y=y*], total reward = weighted sum with group-relative normalization. Models evaluated: Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, Magistral 24B. Baselines include ORPO, majority, random. Metrics: Macro-F1, Accuracy, Neutral recall; reported as mean±std across 8 runs (T=1.0).

Related work/persona taxonomy: demographic, character, individualized personas; most prior political-opinion work uses demographic personas (simple affiliation prompts or richer demographics + demonstrations). Limitations of demographic prompting: representativeness, steerability, consistency. Prior individualized approaches: Park et al. (2024) use interview transcripts (data-limited) and can outperform demographic baselines; Haller et al. (2025) use in-context learning (focus on bias identification). Prior reasoning-based opinion work mainly uses prompting (e.g., Yu et al., 2025) for voting prediction rather than RL. This part reiterates that prior voting-prediction work did not use RL and targeted voting prediction; the authors learn general preference profiles and claim modeling a representative sample is currently computationally prohibitive. Table 1: example ANES Right-group item — base model (prompting) answered No; After (SFT+GRPO) answered Yes with explicit <reasoning> trace. Reasoning literature: chain-of-thought prompting (Wei et al. 2022, Kojima et al. 2022) and trained reasoning/search/RL (e.g., Guo et al. 2025) improve performance. Methodological details to keep: backbone Llama 3.1 8B; SFT warm-start on synthetic reasoning demonstrations (from Llama 3.1/3.3 70B); GRPO = PPO-variant with group reward normalization (no value function). Reward components: R_format, R_length = -|L-L*|, R_correct = 1[y=y*]; total reward = weighted sum with group-relative normalization. Evaluated models: Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, Magistral 24B. Baselines: ORPO, majority, random. Metrics: Macro-F1, Accuracy, Neutral recall reported as mean±std across 8 runs (T=1.0).

Method: learn individual survey stances by rewarding formatted reasoning plus correct final answer. Output schema: <reasoning>[justification text]</reasoning><answer>[stance]</answer> (reasoning before answer). Dataset D = {(p_j,q_i,y^*_{ij})} contains final stances but no native reasoning traces; optional SFT warm-start provides synthetic chain-of-thought demonstrations in schema (1). GRPO (PPO-variant; earlier notes: group-reward normalization, no value function) is used to train agents. Rewards: R_format = 1 point per correctly placed tag (4 tags, max 4); R_length = -|L - L*| (max 0 at L=L*); R_correct = 1[y=y*]. Total reward R(r_i,y_i^*) = α1 R_format + α2 R_length + α3 R_correct with α1=0.25, α2=0.01, α3=1. r_i is the first argument (contains reasoning+answer). No explicit persona representation; system prompt includes only country label. Table 2 dataset overview: smartvote (CH) — Candidate, 18 units, labels {Yes, No}, Train Q 48, Test Q 12 (topic-strat.); WoM (DE) — Party, 6 units, labels {Yes, Neutral, No}, Train Q see Table 5, Test Q 30 (EU&I); ANES 2020 (US) — Respondent, 21 units, labels {Yes, Neutral, No}, Train Q 67, Test Q 12 (random). Backbones/evals per earlier notes: Llama 3.1 8B (backbone), SFT warm-start from Llama 3.1/3.3 70B, evaluated with Llama 3.1 8B / Qwen3 8B / Magistral 24B; baselines ORPO/majority/random; metrics reported as mean±std across 8 runs (T=1.0).

Method: Agents must output schema <reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>...</answer>. Training uses GRPO (PPO-variant, group-reward normalization, no value function). Optional SFT warm-start provides synthetic CoT demonstrations. Reward components: R_format (1 point per correct tag, 4 tags max), R_length = -|L-L*| (max 0 at L=L*), R_correct = 1[y=y*]; total R = 0.25 R_format + 0.01 R_length + 1.0 R_correct. r_i (first arg) contains reasoning+answer. No explicit persona beyond country label in system prompt. Evaluations averaged (mean ± std) over 8 stochastic runs, temperature T=1.0. Backbones/evaluated models: Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, Magistral 24B; baselines include random, majority, ORPO; methods include icl, ORPO, SFT, GRPO, SFT+GRPO.

Datasets:
- smartvote (CH): Candidates, 18 units (3 candidates × 6 parties), English 2023 questionnaire has 75 items, 60 policy questions across 12 topics; responses collapsed from 4-point Likert to {Yes, No}. Train/test split is topic-stratified (48 train, 12 test).
- WoM (DE): Parties, 6 units (CDU/CSU, SPD, Grüne, FDP, Die Linke, AfD), labels {Yes, Neutral, No}; train counts in Appendix A, out-of-domain test EU&I (2024) with 30 items.
- ANES 2020 (US): Respondents, 21 units (3 per 7-point ideology bins), 79 policy items; recoded to {Yes, Neutral, No} using conservative mapping by default; random split 67 train / 12 test.

Metrics/Table 3: Reports mean macro-F1 (%) computed per unit then averaged across units; standard deviations over 8 runs. Observations in text: smartvote scores are considerably higher than ANES and WoM (attributed to binary labels), and WoM often outperforms ANES (attributed to more training samples).

steps.notes_before: Datasets: smartvote (18 units; 48 train / 12 test; labels {Yes,No}), Wahl‑o‑Mat (6 units; OOD EU&I test 30 items; labels {Yes,Neutral,No}), ANES 2020 (21 units; 67 train / 12 test; labels {Yes,Neutral,No}). One model per unit. Training: GRPO (PPO variant, group-reward normalization, no value fn); optional SFT warm-start (synthetic CoT from Llama 3.1 70B) used for smartvote & ANES; reported pipelines: GRPO, SFT, SFT+GRPO. All training uses 4‑bit quantization. Evaluation: macro‑F1 per unit averaged (mean ± std) over 8 stochastic runs, T=1.0. Backbones: Llama 3.1 8B (non‑reasoning), Qwen3 8B (reasoning‑pretrained), Magistral 24B (reasoning‑pretrained). Key results (Table 3): Magistral SFT+GRPO yields smartvote 70.73(2.21), WoM 53.21(3.19), ANES 45.43(1.11). Overall SFT+GRPO typically best; exception: Llama3.1 8B SFT > SFT+GRPO on ANES. SFT+GRPO substantially beats in‑context learning (icl) on WoM. Reasoning pretraining (Qwen3, Magistral) does not uniformly help versus Llama. Warm-start (SFT) generally improves over GRPO alone per Table 3. Figure 3 / Sec 4.5: ideology affects learnability — Left often best, Right harder; but text contains an inconsistency: Fig.3 summary claims every method underperforms on Center & Right, yet later says Left and Center perform roughly equally on Wahl‑o‑Mat (contradiction flagged). Fig 4 / Sec 4.6: Neutral is hardest to predict (ANES), Neutral base rate highest for Right; removing Neutral raises F1 but may not remove L–R gap; alternative recoding can make Center and Right nearly identical (possible recoding artifact). Agents produce coherent but sometimes hallucinated reasoning (Table 1, Appendix B).

errors.claim: "agents shift \ldots toward the center on the conservative-liberal y-axis."
errors.evidence: "Instead, agents shift toward the center-right on the left-right x-axis and toward the center on the conservative-liberal y-axis." vs "Left and Center individuals become more right-wing and conservative."
errors.explanation: These two statements contradict each other for the Center group: saying agents shift "toward the center" on the conservative–liberal axis implies center-group positions should move closer to the center, whereas asserting that "Center individuals become more \ldots conservative" implies Center individuals move away from the center toward the conservative pole. Both cannot be true as written about the Center group.

steps.notes_before: Figure 4 (ANES, Llama 3.1 8B SFT+GRPO): Neutral is hardest to predict; negative correlation between Neutral base rate and F1/accuracy (significant at 5%); removing Neutral improves all groups, narrows Left–Center gap but Left–Right gap persists; alternative recoding preserves negative correlation but can make Center and Right nearly identical (Sec E.2, E.3). Section 4.7 (smartvote PCA): agents do not perfectly reproduce candidates; authors state agents "shift toward the center-right" on left-right axis and "toward the center" on conservative–liberal axis; group-averaged arrows: Right become more left-wing; Left and Center become more right-wing and conservative — flagged inconsistency (see errors). Section 4.8 (SFT bias): additional SFT argument sets generated with Llama 3.3 70B (progressive/conservative); Figure 5: biased SFT mainly harms underrepresented groups (progressive hurts Right, conservative hurts Left); Right candidates suffer more; Figure 6: biased data shifts underrepresented groups, but conservative-biased and default produce similar shifts, suggesting base-model alignment may explain centerward shift. Backbones/pipelines: Llama 3.1 8B (reported figures here), Qwen3 8B, Magistral 24B; pipelines GRPO / SFT / SFT+GRPO. Previous flagged inconsistency in Fig.3 (Left vs Center claims) remains noted.

Figure 6: Biased SFT mainly shifts agents for underrepresented groups; Right candidates are affected more than Left. Conservative-biased and default SFT produce similar displacement patterns, suggesting the default centerward shift may come from base-model alignment rather than the SFT data. 

Section 4.9 (synthetic-position inversion): Invert all smartvote answers (~180° rotation); train Llama-3.1-8B on inverted data. Figure 7: Right profiles benefit, Left and Center worsen on average; inversion does not eliminate the original disparity — Right still falls short of Left’s original F1; Left drops to roughly Right’s original level. Authors hypothesize left-leaning profiles may be intrinsically easier to model.

Performance summary (Section 4): Authors state SFT+GRPO generally performs best (Table 3). Reported SFT+GRPO figures (per dataset/backbone) — smartvote: ~66.9, 65.1, 70.7; WoM: ~52.5, 49.4, 53.2; ANES: ~40–45 (ANES line in text is garbled). Llama’s ANES SFT score reported as 42.77(1.23).

Other recurring points: Neutral and ideology affect performance (Figs. 3–4); positional distortions and sensitivity to biased SFT persist (Figs. 2, 5–7). Backbones/pipelines: Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, Magistral 24B; GRPO / SFT / SFT+GRPO. Previously flagged inconsistency in Sec. 4.7 (author text about PCA shifts vs. what the figure arrows show) remains unresolved.

Discussion (Sec. 5): restates limits and future directions. Limitations: opinion noise (answers vary over time — F1≈1.0 unrealistic); per-profile training is expensive (each persona needs a separately trained model); survey data scarce/mismatched (few items, generic themes, cross-country misalignment). Future work: reduce training cost (single model conditioned on compact persona representations), estimate reliability/confidence (extended reasoning or a dedicated "value head"), purpose-built questionnaires, better handling of Neutral, and more bias-mitigation. Figure 7 / inversion (Sec. 4.9 recap): authors flip all smartvote answers (~180°), train Llama-3.1-8B on inverted data. Figure 7 plots original F1 per individual (x ordered by first PCA component) with arrows showing F1 change after flipping. Results: flipping worsens Left and Center on average, improves Right, but does not remove the original disparity — Right still underperforms relative to Left (authors suggest Left-leaning profiles may be intrinsically easier to model). Note: authors point out the left-most Right candidate is correctly placed (Fig. 6). Recurring points: SFT+GRPO generally best (Table 3); neutral/ideology affect performance; positional distortions and sensitivity to biased SFT persist across backbones (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3-8B, Magistral-24B) and pipelines (GRPO, SFT, SFT+GRPO). Previously flagged unresolved inconsistency: Sec. 4.7 author text about PCA shifts vs. figure arrows remains unresolved.

Main claim: structured reasoning (persona-conditioned generation + structured reasoning) improves individual opinion alignment, but Neutral positions and ideological disparities persist. SFT+GRPO is reported as the best pipeline overall across datasets (Swiss smartvote, German Wahl-o-Mat, U.S. ANES), with one explicit exception on Llama/ANES where SFT = 42.77 (±1.23) vs SFT+GRPO = 40.66 (±0.91). Performance varies across the political spectrum; Neutral answers are particularly hard to predict and Figure 4 shows performance–Neutral correlations significant at the 5% level. Recurring observations: results consistent across backbones (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3-8B, Magistral-24B) and pipelines (SFT, GRPO, SFT+GRPO). Inversion experiment (Sec.4.9/Fig.7): flipping smartvote responses worsens Left and Center, improves Right, but Right still underperforms Left on average. Limitations: opinion noise (response variability over time), per-profile training cost, limited/mismatched survey data, Neutral handling and bias issues. Future directions proposed: reduce per-profile training cost (single model conditioned on compact persona representations), estimate reliability/confidence, purpose-built questionnaires, better Neutral handling, bias mitigation. Unresolved prior item: discrepancy noted earlier about PCA shifts vs. figure arrows (Sec.4.7) remains unresolved.

final_notes: Goal: predict persona p_j stance y* on q_i; models output reasoning + answer. Training: GRPO (PPO-like) with optional SFT warm start using synthetic CoT. Reward: R = 0.25 R_format + 0.01 R_length + 1.0 R_correct. Backbones: Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3-8B, Magistral-24B (4-bit quant). Datasets: smartvote (Switzerland candidates), Wahl-o-Mat (Germany parties), ANES (US voters). Evaluation: per-run per-unit macro-F1 averaged across units. Main results (Table 3): SFT+GRPO generally best. Smartvote SFT+GRPO F1: Llama 66.88(2.18), Qwen 65.11(3.33), Magistral 70.73(2.21). Wahl-o-Mat SFT+GRPO: 52.53(4.05), 49.38(1.93), 53.21(3.19). ANES SFT+GRPO: 40.66(~0.91), 38.44(0.40), 45.43(1.11). Exception: Llama ANES SFT (no GRPO) = 42.77(1.23) > Llama SFT+GRPO. Findings: Neutral is hardest; Neutral base-rate negatively correlates with F1 (significant at 5%); removing Neutral improves F1 and narrows Left–Center gap while Left–Right gap persists. Synthetic inversion (Fig.7, Llama) approximates 180° rotation: Right benefits but still below Left’s original F1; Left drops toward Right’s original level. Bias experiments: progressive-bias harms Right; conservative-bias harms Left; underrepresented groups (Right) harmed more; conservative-biased and default SFT show similar centerward displacement. Ethics: warn against deployment until ideological fairness addressed; anonymized survey data/public figures only; transparent reporting of biases (center/right underperformance, Neutral difficulty). Limitations/future: opinion noise, per-profile training cost, scarce/misaligned surveys; propose single conditional model, confidence/value head, better uncertainty/Neutral handling, improved questionnaires. Reproducibility: code, datasets, training details, PCA implementation available at https://github.com/ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment; Appendix F: hyperparameters; Section E.5: PCA details. Author contributions: Frédéric Berdoz (conceived/designed project, led experimental planning, defined research direction); Yann Billeter (contributed equally, led technical development, dataset collection, model training, evaluation, analysis); Yann Vonlanthen (advisor); Roger Wattenhofer (supervised as PI). Acknowledgment: Prof. Dr. Hans Gersbach thanked.

steps.notes_before: Research question: can reasoning improve LLM alignment to individual political opinions via per-person/party/candidate models. Key method: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) warm start followed by Group-Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), a PPO variant that normalizes rewards within groups (subtract mean, divide by std) and avoids learning a value function. Reward components: R_format (tagging), R_length (negative |L-L*|), R_correct (match indicator); total reward R(r_i,y_i^*) weighted by alphas α1,α2,α3. Output schema: <reasoning>...[justification text]...</reasoning><answer>[stance]</answer>. Datasets/settings: ANES 2020 (79 items) for US respondents; smartvote CH (Swiss candidates) with topic-stratified holdout; WoM (DE) parties, tested out-of-domain on EU&I (30 items). Units: candidate/party/respondent; metrics: Macro-F1 (per-unit mean), Accuracy, class Recall (Neutral difficulty), Std dev across 8 runs reported in Table 3, T fixed at 1.0. Models/backbones: three open-weight backbones evaluated (Llama-3.1-8B non-reasoning; Qwen3-8B, Magistral-24B reasoning-pretrained). SFT synthetic arguments generated with Llama 3.1/3.3 70B variants; training used 4-bit quantization. Other: ORPO baseline, PCA analyses (left-right x-axis, conservative-liberal y-axis), displacement/distortion metrics, counterfactual inversion, code repo link.

Research question: can reasoning improve LLM alignment to individual political opinions (per-person/party/candidate models). Method: SFT warm start then Group-Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) — a PPO variant that normalizes rewards within groups (subtract mean, divide by std) and avoids learning a value function. Models trained to output <reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>...</answer> (rationale then profile-consistent answer). Rewards: R_format (tagging), R_length (negative |L-L*|), R_correct (match indicator); total reward R weighted by alphas α1,α2,α3. Datasets: ANES 2020 (US, 79 items), smartvote CH (Swiss candidates, topic-stratified holdout), WoM (DE parties) with out-of-domain test on EU&I (30 items). Units: candidate/party/respondent. Metrics: Macro-F1 (per-unit mean), Accuracy, class Recall (neutral is hardest); standard deviations reported across 8 runs (Table 3); temperature T fixed at 1.0. Models/backbones: three open-weight backbones evaluated (Llama-3.1-8B non-reasoning; Qwen3-8B; Magistral-24B reasoning-pretrained). SFT synthetic arguments generated with Llama 3.1/3.3 70B variants; training used 4-bit quantization. Baselines include ORPO. Analyses: PCA (left-right x-axis, conservative-liberal y-axis), displacement/distortion metrics, counterfactual inversion. Key claims from abstract: reasoning-based training improves political opinion modeling but does not fully remove bias; RL rewards answers that match survey responses; evaluation on three datasets (US/European/Swiss); reasoning improves alignment and is competitive with strong baselines but leaves political distortions (cites Table 3 SFT+GRPO rows and Figures 2–4). Code and data: https://github.com/ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment

Goal: align LLMs to individual political opinions by training them to produce explicit reasoning + final answer so outputs match survey responses. Pipeline: SFT warm start using synthetic statements/arguments (generated with Llama 3.1/3.3 70B) to enforce a reasoning template (<reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>...</answer>), then Group-Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) RL to further improve alignment. GRPO: normalizes rewards within groups (subtract mean/divide std); paper treats it as a PPO-style method applied to reasoning outputs. Reward components: R_format (format compliance), R_length (penalize |L-L*|), R_correct (match to respondent); total R = α1 R_format + α2 R_length + α3 R_correct. Datasets: ANES 2020 (US, 79 items), smartvote CH (Swiss candidates, topic-stratified holdout), WoM (DE parties) with out-of-domain EU&I test (30 items). Units: respondent/party/candidate. Models/backbones: Llama-3.1-8B (non-reasoning), Qwen3-8B, Magistral-24B (reasoning-pretrained). Metrics: Macro-F1 (per-unit mean), Accuracy, class Recall; report std across 8 runs (Table 3). Baselines include ORPO. Key claims: reasoning-based training (SFT+GRPO) improves alignment (Table 3) though Llama 3.1-8B shows an ANES exception (Sec 4.3); alignment varies with ideology and on counterfactual answer inversion (Figures cited: 2–4, 3, 7). Code/data link: github.com/ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment.

Goal: align LLMs to individual political opinions by training them to produce explicit reasoning plus a final answer in a fixed template (<reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>...</answer>). Pipeline: SFT warm start using synthetic reasoning demonstrations (generated with Llama 3.1/3.3 70B), then Group-Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) RL. GRPO is a PPO-style variant that normalizes rewards within groups by subtracting the group mean and dividing by the group reward std; applied to reasoning outputs. Reward components (from earlier): R_format, R_length, R_correct; total R = α1 R_format + α2 R_length + α3 R_correct. Datasets: ANES 2020 (US, 79 items), smartvote CH (Swiss candidates, topic-stratified holdout), WoM (DE parties); OOD test EU&I (30 items). Units: respondent/party/candidate; groups: Left, Center, Right. Models/backbones evaluated include Llama-3.1-8B (used in example), Qwen3-8B, Magistral-24B (reasoning-pretrained). Metrics: Macro-F1 (per-unit mean), Accuracy, class Recall; report std across 8 runs (Table 3). Related work: contrasts demographic/persona prompting (representativeness, steerability, consistency issues) with individualized personas and in-context learning; ORPO mentioned as a baseline preference-optimization method. Example (Table 1): Llama 3.1 8B SFT+GRPO changed an ANES Right-group individual answer from No to Yes and produced a reasoning trace. Reasoning training context: Chain-of-Thought and prompt-based methods help accuracy; recent work trains reasoning traces via search/RL. Code/data link referenced in earlier notes.

Goal: align LLMs to individual political opinions by training them to output an explicit reasoning trace plus a final answer in a fixed template (<reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>...</answer>). Pipeline: SFT warm start using synthetic reasoning demonstrations (generated with Llama 3.1/3.3 70B), then Group-Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) RL. GRPO is PPO-style and normalizes rewards within groups by subtracting the group mean and dividing by the group reward std; applied to reasoning outputs. Reward components: R_format, R_length, R_correct; total R = α1 R_format + α2 R_length + α3 R_correct. Datasets: ANES 2020 (US, 79 items), smartvote CH (Swiss candidates, topic-stratified holdout), WoM (DE parties); OOD test EU&I (30 items). Units: respondent/party/candidate; groups: Left, Center, Right. Models/backbones: Llama-3.1-8B (used in example), Qwen3-8B, Magistral-24B (reasoning-pretrained). Metrics: Macro-F1 (per-unit mean), Accuracy, class Recall; report std across 8 runs (Table 3). Example (Table 1): Llama 3.1 8B SFT+GRPO changed an ANES Right-group individual answer from No to Yes and produced a reasoning trace (Table 1 "Before..." vs "After (SFT+GRPO)" ends with "A) Yes"). Related claims: other prior work targeted voting prediction and did not use RL; interview-based individual modeling can outperform demographic baselines (Park et al. 2024); prompted and trained reasoning improve performance (Wei et al. 2022, Kojima et al. 2022, Guo et al. 2025). Note: authors state modeling a representative sample is currently computationally prohibitive.

Goal: learn persona p_j’s stance y* on question q_i; model outputs fixed schema: <reasoning>[justification]</reasoning><answer>[stance]</answer> (4 tags). Data D = {(p_j,q_i,y*_{ij})} contains final stances but no reasoning. GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) used to train agents to produce reasoning+answer; optional SFT warm start constructs chain-of-thought demonstrations in exact format (1) to teach format and initialize reasoning. Authors state: no explicit persona representation is provided to the model; system prompt contains only a country label, so alignment with an individual comes solely from correctly answering questions. Reward components: R_format = 1 point per correctly placed tag (max 4); R_length = -|L-L*| (penalty, max 0 at L=L*); R_correct = 1{y=y*}. Total R = α1 R_format + α2 R_length + α3 R_correct with α1=0.25, α2=0.01, α3=1 (so format+correctness max contribution = 2; length has small negative effect). r_i denotes the reasoning trace (first argument of R). Table 2 dataset overview: smartvote (CH) Unit=Candidate #Units=18 Labels={Yes,No} TrainQ=48 TestQ=12 (topic-strat.); WoM (DE) Unit=Party #Units=6 Labels={Yes,Neutral,No} TrainQ=see Table 5 TestQ=30 (EU&I); ANES 2020 (US) Unit=Respondent #Units=21 Labels={Yes,Neutral,No} TrainQ=67 TestQ=12 (random). Keep earlier pipeline notes: SFT warm start used synthetic reasoning demos (Llama 3.1/3.3 70B); GRPO is PPO-style and normalizes rewards within groups (subtract mean / divide by group std); models include Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3-8B, Magistral-24B; metrics: macro-F1 (per-unit mean), accuracy, class recall; report std across 8 runs.

Goal: learn persona p_j’s stance y* on question q_i; model outputs fixed XML-like schema: <reasoning>[justification]</reasoning><answer>[stance]</answer>. Data D contains final stances but no reasoning. Training: GRPO (PPO-style, normalizes rewards within groups). Optional SFT warm start creates synthetic CoT demos (Llama 3.1/3.3 70B) to teach format and initialize reasoning. Rewards: R_format = 1 point per correct tag (max 4), R_length = -|L-L*| (penalty), R_correct = 1{y=y*}; R = α1 R_format + α2 R_length + α3 R_correct with α1=0.25, α2=0.01, α3=1. Models: Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3-8B, Magistral-24B. Evaluation: per-run per-unit macro-F1 averaged across units; report mean and std over 8 stochastic runs (T=1.0). Also report accuracy and significance in Appendix E.1.

Datasets/splits:
- smartvote (CH): English 2023 smartvote questionnaire; 75 items total, 60 policy questions across 12 topics; collapsed 4-pt Likert -> {Yes,No}. Sampled 3 candidates × 6 parties = 18 units. (Train/Test: 48/12 topic-stratified.)
- WoM (DE): Wahl-O-Mat (v26 Mar 2025); party positions aggregated 2021–2025; 6 major parties; labels {Yes,Neutral,No}. Out-of-domain test: EU&I (2024) recoded to same labels, 30 test items. Per-party training counts in Appendix A.

Table 3 (mean macro-F1 % over 8 runs): random baseline: smartvote 50.0, WoM 33.33, ANES 33.33. Best overall SFT+GRPO (Magistral 24B): smartvote 70.73, WoM 53.21, ANES 45.43. General pattern: smartvote (binary) >> WoM > ANES.

final_notes: Code and datasets released at https://github.com/ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment. Training details in Appendix F; PCA details in Section E.5. Author contributions: Frédéric Berdoz (conceived/designed project, led experiments, research direction); Yann Billeter (equal contribution; led technical development, dataset collection, model training, evaluation, analysis); Yann Vonlanthen (advisor); Roger Wattenhofer (PI). Acknowledgment: Prof. Dr. Hans Gersbach. Datasets: smartvote (Swiss candidates; sampled ~18 candidates), Wahl-o-Mat (German parties; 6 parties), ANES (U.S. voters; small sample reported ~21 respondents). Backbones: Llama 3.1 8B (primary analyses), Qwen3 8B, Magistral 24B (4-bit quant). Synthetic SFT data: Llama 3.1 70B; additional biased SFTs (progressive, conservative) with Llama 3.3 70B. Training methods: SFT, GRPO, SFT+GRPO (SFT+GRPO performs best overall). Observations: Magistral often best backbone; Llama 3.1 8B shows anomalous behavior on ANES. Main results (Llama 3.1 8B + SFT+GRPO): smartvote — Left > Center and Right; Wahl-o-Mat and ANES show weaker performance. ANES specifics: neutral recall worst; Right has highest neutral base rate; removing Neutral improves F1 and narrows Left vs Center gap though Left vs Right gap persists; alternative recoding can make Center ≈ Right. Bias experiments: progressive-biased SFT strongly impairs Right; conservative-biased SFT impairs Left; ideological bias mainly harms underrepresented groups, Right candidates more often impacted. PCA: biased SFT shifts underrepresented groups; conservative-biased and default SFT produce similar displacements (possible base-model alignment). Inversion experiment (flip smartvote answers & retrain Llama 3.1 8B): Right improves, Left and Center worsen; inverted Right still below original Left F1; Left falls to roughly original Right — suggests Left-leaning profiles easier to model. Limitations: per-agent training costly, small samples, questionnaire mismatches. Ethics: anonymized survey data/public figures; report systematic disparities and caution against deployment until fairness issues mitigated.

Title: Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs. Authors: Frédéric Berdoz, Yann Billeter, Yann Vonlanthen, Roger Wattenhofer; affiliation: ETH Zurich (Switzerland); contact emails listed. Abstract claims: goal is opinion modeling for political preferences; LLMs are natural candidates but tend to produce biased opinions when prompted naively. Research question: can reasoning improve opinion alignment? Method: train models to produce profile-consistent answers via structured reasoning, motivated by recent advances in mathematical reasoning with RL. Evaluation: three datasets covering U.S., European, and Swiss politics. Main results: reasoning enhances opinion modeling, is competitive with strong baselines, but does not fully remove bias; additional mechanisms needed for faithful political digital twins. Code and data released at provided GitHub URL. (Note: abstract contains minor formatting artifacts like “datasets11 1” but no substantive contradictions.)

Title: Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs. Authors: Berdoz et al., ETH Zurich. Goal: build LLM-based political "digital twins" that reflect individual opinion profiles. Motivation: prompt-based demographic methods are unstable and fail to capture real opinion distributions; interviews are rich but costly; surveys (ANES, VAAs) provide structured, scalable opinion data. Method overview: treat opinion formation as a reasoning task—model produces a short rationale plus a final choice and is rewarded when choice matches respondent answer. Training pipeline: (1) fine-tune LLM on synthetic statements + ground-truth answers to follow a reasoning template; (2) apply reinforcement learning (GRPO, Shao et al., 2024) with a reward model that rewards correct formatting and matching answers. Background claim: recent RL advances improved reasoning (refs to o3/o4-mini and DeepSeek-R1). Datasets / evaluation: three real-world datasets (German parties, U.S. voters, Swiss candidates); benchmark released. Contributions: (i) RL for explicit reasoning-based opinion alignment; (ii) benchmarking on three political datasets showing reasoning improves alignment; (iii) analysis of ideological effects via inverting survey answers to study alignment variation across political spectrum. Figure 1: visualizes fine-tune then GRPO pipeline. Abstract additionally notes reasoning helps but doesn't fully remove bias; code/data released on GitHub.

Goal: model individualized political personas (digital twins) using LLMs that produce explicit reasoning traces plus a final choice. Related work: literature mainly uses demographic personas (simple party labels to richer demographics and demonstrations); Santurkar et al. (2023) identify three limits of demographic prompting: representativeness, steerability, and consistency. Demographic methods can approximate population-level distributions but fail to capture within-group variance and are prompt-sensitive (Argyle et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2024). Few works target individualized personas: Park et al. (2024) use interview transcripts (high accuracy but limited availability); Haller et al. (2025) use in-context prompts of Q-A pairs to predict other answers (focus on bias identification). Example (Table 1): Llama 3.1 8B on an ANES Right-group individual flips from “No” (pre-training) to “Yes” (after SFT+GRPO) on the statement “it is not really that big a problem if some people have more of a chance in life than others”; both traces appeal to equal-opportunity arguments but framed differently. Reasoning methods: chain-of-thought and “let’s think step-by-step” improve accuracy; more recent work trains models to generate reasoning traces via search or RL (Xu et al., 2025). GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) is used: a PPO variant that normalizes rewards across a sampled group (subtract mean, divide by std) instead of learning a value function; reported effective on math-reasoning benchmarks (Guo et al., 2025).

(2023) identify three limits of demographic prompting: representativeness, steerability, and consistency. (2025) use in-context Q-A demonstrations to predict other answers. Example (Table 1): Llama 3.1 8B on an ANES Right-group individual flips from “No” (pre-training) to “Yes” after SFT+GRPO; both traces appeal to equal-opportunity arguments but framed differently. Our method uses GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), a PPO variant that normalizes rewards across a sampled group (subtract mean, divide by std) instead of learning a value function; GRPO reported effective on math-reasoning benchmarks (Guo et al., 2025). New: Yu et al. (2025) propose a persona-based chain-of-thought-inspired prompting framework combining demographic, ideological, and temporal factors calibrated on ANES; they simulate individual voting responses and sum them for aggregate predictions. They do not use reinforcement learning. We focus on learning general preference profiles rather than direct voting prediction; scaling to representative sample sizes is currently computationally prohibitive.

Goal: predict a persona p's stance y on question q (stances Y = {No, Neutral, Yes}). Training data D = {(p_j, q_i, y^*_{ij})} contains only final stances (no reasoning traces). Model must generate a reasoning trace and an answer in the fixed schema: <reasoning>[text]</reasoning><answer>[stance]</answer>. Training uses GRPO (Shao et al., 2024). Composite reward: R_format = 1 point per correctly placed tag (4 tags → 0–4); R_length = -|L - L*| (token length penalty; maximum 0 when L = L*); R_correct = 1[y = y*] (indicator). Total reward: R = alpha1*R_format + alpha2*R_length + alpha3*R_correct with alpha1 = 0.25, alpha2 = 0.01, alpha3 = 1. Authors note they do not use explicit persona embeddings (only a country label in system prompt); alignment to individuals is via correctness on questions. Optional SFT initialization: build chain-of-thought demonstrations in the exact schema (1) as warm start to (i) reduce burden on R_format during GRPO and (ii) provide political-reasoning initialization. Dataset overview (Table 2): smartvote (CH) — Unit: Candidate, #Units 18, Labels {Yes, No}, Train Q 48, Test Q 12 (topic-stratified); WoM (DE) — Unit: Party, #Units 6, Labels {Yes, Neutral, No}, Train Q: see Table 5, Test Q 30 (EU&I); ANES 2020 (US) — Unit: Respondent, #Units 21, Labels {Yes, Neutral, No}, Train Q 67, Test Q 12 (random).

Experiments: three datasets (Table 2 overview referenced). Table 3 reports mean macro-F1 (%) (per-run: compute per-unit macro-F1 then average across units), std over 8 runs, temperature T=1.0. Untrained baselines: random (smartvote 50.0; WoM 33.33; ANES 33.33), majority (37.43; 27.44; 22.98). Base models: Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, Magistral 24B. Methods: icl, ORPO, SFT, GRPO, SFT+GRPO. General pattern: smartvote scores noticeably higher than ANES and WoM (attributed to binary labels / no Neutral); WoM > ANES (attributed to more training samples). SFT+GRPO tends to give best results (e.g., Magistral SFT+GRPO: smartvote 70.73, WoM 53.21, ANES 45.43).
