Paper asks whether reasoning improves LLM alignment with individual political opinions. Method: train one model per respondent, candidate, or party; models generate a rationale and a final answer. Training uses Group-Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), which rewards formatting, reasoning length, and agreement with survey answers. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can provide a warm start; combined SFT+GRPO generally outperforms baselines and performs best on the smartvote dataset, though there are exceptions. Experiments cover Swiss candidates, German parties, and U.S. voters. Neutral answers are hard to predict; performance varies by ideology. Biased fine-tuning data mainly harms underrepresented perspectives. Agents retain political distortions, so method does not fully remove bias. (Part ends with a heading "Glossary" but no glossary content in this excerpt.)

Goal: test whether producing reasoning traces improves alignment of LLMs to individual or group political opinions (digital-twin/agent models). Method: train one model per unit (respondent, candidate, or party) to output a reasoning trace (<reasoning>...</reasoning>) and a final answer (<answer>...</answer>). Training: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can provide a warm start; then Group-Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) — a PPO variant that normalizes rewards within groups and avoids learning a value function — is used. Reward components: R_format (correct output tags), R_length = -|L - L*| (penalty for deviation from desired trace length), R_correct = 1[y = y*]; total reward R(r_i,y_i^*) is a weighted sum with weights alpha1,alpha2,alpha3. GRPO applies group-relative reward normalization (subtract mean, divide by std). Baselines include ORPO, majority, random. Metrics: Macro-F1 (per-unit average), Accuracy, Recall (used to study Neutral), reported with mean ± std across 8 stochastic runs (Table 3); T fixed at 1.0 in those runs. Datasets: ANES 2020 (US, 79 items), smartvote (CH, 2023 candidate questionnaire; topic-stratified holdout), WoM (DE party positions; EU&I 2024 is 30-item out-of-domain test). Labels: Yes/No/Neutral; Swiss four-point scale collapsed to Yes/No; recoding schemes (conservative/aggressive) change mappings. Models/backbones: three open-weight backbones evaluated (Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, Magistral 24B); Llama 3.1 70B and Llama 3.3 70B used to generate synthetic SFT arguments; 4-bit quantization used for training. Analyses: difficulty predicting Neutral, ideology stratification, PCA of positions (left-right, conservative-liberal), displacement/distortion, counterfactual inversion, bias from progressive/conservative SFT data, hallucinated elements, and proposals for confidence/value-heads. Repo: github.com/ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment.

Goal: test whether producing reasoning traces improves alignment of LLMs to individual or group political opinions (digital-twin/agent models). Method: train one model per unit to output a reasoning trace (<reasoning>...</reasoning>) and a final answer (<answer>...</answer>). Training: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can provide a warm start; then Group-Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) — a PPO variant that normalizes rewards within groups and avoids learning a value function — is used. Reward components: R_format (correct tags), R_length = -|L - L*|, R_correct = 1[y = y*]; total reward weighted by alpha1, alpha2, alpha3; GRPO does group-relative normalization. Baselines: ORPO, majority, random. Metrics: Macro-F1 (per-unit average), Accuracy, Recall (Neutral), reported as mean ± std across 8 stochastic runs; T=1.0 in those runs. Datasets: ANES 2020 (US, 79 items), smartvote (CH 2023 candidate questionnaire), WoM (DE party positions); EU&I 2024 30-item out-of-domain test noted. Labels: Yes/No/Neutral; Swiss four-point collapsed to Yes/No; conservative/aggressive recoding schemes exist. Models/backbones: Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, Magistral 24B evaluated; Llama 3.1/3.3 70B used to generate synthetic SFT arguments; 4-bit quantization used. Analyses: Neutral difficulty, ideology stratification, PCA (left-right, conservative-liberal), displacement/distortion, counterfactual inversion, bias from progressive/conservative SFT data, hallucinated elements, proposals for confidence/value-heads. Abstract claims: reasoning-based training improves political opinion modeling and is competitive with strong baselines but does not fully remove bias (supported by Table 3, SFT+GRPO rows; Figures 2–4). Repo: https://github.com/ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment. Authors/affiliation: Frédéric Berdoz, Yann Billeter, Yann Vonlanthen, Roger Wattenhofer (ETH Zurich).

Goal: train LLMs to model individual political preferences (digital twins) by having models generate explicit reasoning traces (<reasoning>...</reasoning>) and a final answer (<answer>...</answer>) and rewarding correct, well-formatted reasoning.

Method: SFT warm start using synthetic statements (generated with Llama 3.1/3.3 70B), then Group-Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), a PPO-style RL method that normalizes rewards within groups of outputs (and per earlier notes avoids learning a value function). Reward components include formatting (R_format), length R_length = -|L - L*|, correctness R_correct = 1[y = y*]; total reward is a weighted sum (alpha1, alpha2, alpha3) with group-relative normalization.

Datasets: ANES 2020 (US, 79 items), smartvote (Swiss 2023 candidate questionnaire), WoM (German party positions); EU&I 2024 30-item set used as out-of-domain test.

Models/evaluation: SFT data from Llama 3.1/3.3 70B; evaluated backbones Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, Magistral 24B (4-bit quantization). Baselines: ORPO, majority, random. Metrics: Macro-F1 (per-unit avg), Accuracy, Recall (Neutral); reported as mean ± std across 8 stochastic runs (T=1.0).

Analyses: neutral-difficulty, ideology stratification, PCA (left-right, conservative-liberal), displacement/distortion, counterfactual inversion, bias from progressive/conservative SFT, hallucinated elements, proposals for confidence/value-heads.

Claims: reasoning-based training improves alignment (Table 3 SFT+GRPO rows), though it does not fully remove bias; Llama 3.1 8B ANES exception discussed in Sec. 4.3; alignment varies by ideology and under answer inversion (Figs. 3,7). Repo and authors provided.

Related work: persona taxonomy — demographic, character, individualized; most prior political-opinion work uses demographic personas (simple affiliation prompts or richer demographics and demonstrations). Limitations of demographic prompting: representativeness, steerability, consistency. Some prior individualized approaches: Park et al. (2024) use interview transcripts (data-limited); Haller et al. (2025) use in-context learning (focus on bias identification). Prior reasoning-based opinion work mainly uses prompting (e.g., Yu et al. 2025) for voting prediction rather than RL for full preference profiles. Example in paper: Llama 3.1 8B (backbone used here); “SFT+GRPO” = supervised fine-tuning on formatted reasoning demonstrations, then GRPO. Table 1 shows an ANES Right-group individual question where base model answered No (disagreed) and SFT+GRPO answered Yes (agreed) with an explicit <reasoning> trace. GRPO: variant of PPO that avoids learning a value function by normalizing rewards within a group (for each prompt, sample outputs, subtract mean reward, divide by reward std); claimed effective on math benchmarks (Guo et al., 2025). Reasoning-training background: chain-of-thought/“let’s think step by step” prompting boosts accuracy; newer work trains reasoning traces via search or RL (Xu et al., 2025). Keep earlier methodological details in mind: SFT warm-start used synthetic statements from Llama 3.1/3.3 70B; GRPO is PPO-style, no value function; reward components include R_format, R_length = -|L-L*|, R_correct = 1[y=y*], total reward = weighted sum with group-relative normalization. Models evaluated: Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, Magistral 24B. Baselines include ORPO, majority, random. Metrics: Macro-F1, Accuracy, Neutral recall; reported as mean±std across 8 runs (T=1.0).

Related work/persona taxonomy: demographic, character, individualized personas; most prior political-opinion work uses demographic personas (simple affiliation prompts or richer demographics + demonstrations). Limitations of demographic prompting: representativeness, steerability, consistency. Prior individualized approaches: Park et al. (2024) use interview transcripts (data-limited) and can outperform demographic baselines; Haller et al. (2025) use in-context learning (focus on bias identification). Prior reasoning-based opinion work mainly uses prompting (e.g., Yu et al., 2025) for voting prediction rather than RL. This part reiterates that prior voting-prediction work did not use RL and targeted voting prediction; the authors learn general preference profiles and claim modeling a representative sample is currently computationally prohibitive. Table 1: example ANES Right-group item — base model (prompting) answered No; After (SFT+GRPO) answered Yes with explicit <reasoning> trace. Reasoning literature: chain-of-thought prompting (Wei et al. 2022, Kojima et al. 2022) and trained reasoning/search/RL (e.g., Guo et al. 2025) improve performance. Methodological details to keep: backbone Llama 3.1 8B; SFT warm-start on synthetic reasoning demonstrations (from Llama 3.1/3.3 70B); GRPO = PPO-variant with group reward normalization (no value function). Reward components: R_format, R_length = -|L-L*|, R_correct = 1[y=y*]; total reward = weighted sum with group-relative normalization. Evaluated models: Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, Magistral 24B. Baselines: ORPO, majority, random. Metrics: Macro-F1, Accuracy, Neutral recall reported as mean±std across 8 runs (T=1.0).

Method: learn individual survey stances by rewarding formatted reasoning plus correct final answer. Output schema: <reasoning>[justification text]</reasoning><answer>[stance]</answer> (reasoning before answer). Dataset D = {(p_j,q_i,y^*_{ij})} contains final stances but no native reasoning traces; optional SFT warm-start provides synthetic chain-of-thought demonstrations in schema (1). GRPO (PPO-variant; earlier notes: group-reward normalization, no value function) is used to train agents. Rewards: R_format = 1 point per correctly placed tag (4 tags, max 4); R_length = -|L - L*| (max 0 at L=L*); R_correct = 1[y=y*]. Total reward R(r_i,y_i^*) = α1 R_format + α2 R_length + α3 R_correct with α1=0.25, α2=0.01, α3=1. r_i is the first argument (contains reasoning+answer). No explicit persona representation; system prompt includes only country label. Table 2 dataset overview: smartvote (CH) — Candidate, 18 units, labels {Yes, No}, Train Q 48, Test Q 12 (topic-strat.); WoM (DE) — Party, 6 units, labels {Yes, Neutral, No}, Train Q see Table 5, Test Q 30 (EU&I); ANES 2020 (US) — Respondent, 21 units, labels {Yes, Neutral, No}, Train Q 67, Test Q 12 (random). Backbones/evals per earlier notes: Llama 3.1 8B (backbone), SFT warm-start from Llama 3.1/3.3 70B, evaluated with Llama 3.1 8B / Qwen3 8B / Magistral 24B; baselines ORPO/majority/random; metrics reported as mean±std across 8 runs (T=1.0).

Method: Agents must output schema <reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>...</answer>. Training uses GRPO (PPO-variant, group-reward normalization, no value function). Optional SFT warm-start provides synthetic CoT demonstrations. Reward components: R_format (1 point per correct tag, 4 tags max), R_length = -|L-L*| (max 0 at L=L*), R_correct = 1[y=y*]; total R = 0.25 R_format + 0.01 R_length + 1.0 R_correct. r_i (first arg) contains reasoning+answer. No explicit persona beyond country label in system prompt. Evaluations averaged (mean ± std) over 8 stochastic runs, temperature T=1.0. Backbones/evaluated models: Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, Magistral 24B; baselines include random, majority, ORPO; methods include icl, ORPO, SFT, GRPO, SFT+GRPO.

Datasets:
- smartvote (CH): Candidates, 18 units (3 candidates × 6 parties), English 2023 questionnaire has 75 items, 60 policy questions across 12 topics; responses collapsed from 4-point Likert to {Yes, No}. Train/test split is topic-stratified (48 train, 12 test).
- WoM (DE): Parties, 6 units (CDU/CSU, SPD, Grüne, FDP, Die Linke, AfD), labels {Yes, Neutral, No}; train counts in Appendix A, out-of-domain test EU&I (2024) with 30 items.
- ANES 2020 (US): Respondents, 21 units (3 per 7-point ideology bins), 79 policy items; recoded to {Yes, Neutral, No} using conservative mapping by default; random split 67 train / 12 test.

Metrics/Table 3: Reports mean macro-F1 (%) computed per unit then averaged across units; standard deviations over 8 runs. Observations in text: smartvote scores are considerably higher than ANES and WoM (attributed to binary labels), and WoM often outperforms ANES (attributed to more training samples).

final_notes: Datasets: smartvote (Swiss candidates), Wahl-o-Mat (German parties), ANES (U.S. voters). Method: persona-conditioned supervised fine-tuning (one model per profile) with GRPO; answer generation framed as structured reasoning. Main result: SFT+GRPO generally outperforms baselines; Neutral class is hard to predict. Ideological/bias findings: mixed — some analyses indicate underperformance for center and right-wing profiles and difficulties modeling neutral positions, while elsewhere the paper reports “no clear left-right bias” (possible internal tension). Bias experiments: progressive-bias training harms Right strongly; conservative-bias training harms Left; bias primarily harms underrepresented perspectives. PCA analyses: biased training shifts underrepresented groups; Right candidates show larger positional shifts; conservative-biased and default SFT had similar displacement patterns suggesting base-model centerward alignment. Inversion experiments (Llama-3.1-8B): flipping responses benefits Right while Left and Center worsen; Right does not reach Left's original F1 and Left drops to about Right's original level — authors suggest left-leaning profiles may be intrinsically easier to model. Limitations: noisy labels, few individuals/parties, compute cost, scarce aligned survey items. Future work: single conditioned model, confidence/value head, better questionnaires, improved uncertainty handling for Neutral. Ethics: anonymized survey data and public figures' positions; commit to transparency and caution against deployment until biases mitigated. Reproducibility: code and datasets released at https://github.com/ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment; training details in Appendix F; PCA details in Section E.5. Author contributions: Frédéric Berdoz (conceived/designed, led planning), Yann Billeter (contributed equally, led technical development), Yann Vonlanthen (advisor), Roger Wattenhofer (supervisor). Acknowledgment: Prof. Dr. Hans Gersbach.

Title: Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs. Authors: Frédéric Berdoz, Yann Billeter, Yann Vonlanthen, Roger Wattenhofer; affiliation: ETH Zurich (Switzerland); contact emails listed. Abstract claims: goal is opinion modeling for political preferences; LLMs are natural candidates but tend to produce biased opinions when prompted naively. Research question: can reasoning improve opinion alignment? Method: train models to produce profile-consistent answers via structured reasoning, motivated by recent advances in mathematical reasoning with RL. Evaluation: three datasets covering U.S., European, and Swiss politics. Main results: reasoning enhances opinion modeling, is competitive with strong baselines, but does not fully remove bias; additional mechanisms needed for faithful political digital twins. Code and data released at provided GitHub URL. (Note: abstract contains minor formatting artifacts like “datasets11 1” but no substantive contradictions.)

Title: Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs. Authors: Berdoz et al., ETH Zurich. Goal: build LLM-based political "digital twins" that reflect individual opinion profiles. Motivation: prompt-based demographic methods are unstable and fail to capture real opinion distributions; interviews are rich but costly; surveys (ANES, VAAs) provide structured, scalable opinion data. Method overview: treat opinion formation as a reasoning task—model produces a short rationale plus a final choice and is rewarded when choice matches respondent answer. Training pipeline: (1) fine-tune LLM on synthetic statements + ground-truth answers to follow a reasoning template; (2) apply reinforcement learning (GRPO, Shao et al., 2024) with a reward model that rewards correct formatting and matching answers. Background claim: recent RL advances improved reasoning (refs to o3/o4-mini and DeepSeek-R1). Datasets / evaluation: three real-world datasets (German parties, U.S. voters, Swiss candidates); benchmark released. Contributions: (i) RL for explicit reasoning-based opinion alignment; (ii) benchmarking on three political datasets showing reasoning improves alignment; (iii) analysis of ideological effects via inverting survey answers to study alignment variation across political spectrum. Figure 1: visualizes fine-tune then GRPO pipeline. Abstract additionally notes reasoning helps but doesn't fully remove bias; code/data released on GitHub.

Goal: model individualized political personas (digital twins) using LLMs that produce explicit reasoning traces plus a final choice. Related work: literature mainly uses demographic personas (simple party labels to richer demographics and demonstrations); Santurkar et al. (2023) identify three limits of demographic prompting: representativeness, steerability, and consistency. Demographic methods can approximate population-level distributions but fail to capture within-group variance and are prompt-sensitive (Argyle et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2024). Few works target individualized personas: Park et al. (2024) use interview transcripts (high accuracy but limited availability); Haller et al. (2025) use in-context prompts of Q-A pairs to predict other answers (focus on bias identification). Example (Table 1): Llama 3.1 8B on an ANES Right-group individual flips from “No” (pre-training) to “Yes” (after SFT+GRPO) on the statement “it is not really that big a problem if some people have more of a chance in life than others”; both traces appeal to equal-opportunity arguments but framed differently. Reasoning methods: chain-of-thought and “let’s think step-by-step” improve accuracy; more recent work trains models to generate reasoning traces via search or RL (Xu et al., 2025). GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) is used: a PPO variant that normalizes rewards across a sampled group (subtract mean, divide by std) instead of learning a value function; reported effective on math-reasoning benchmarks (Guo et al., 2025).

Goal: model individualized political personas (digital twins) using LLMs that produce explicit reasoning traces plus a final choice. Related work: demographic-persona approaches (simple party labels to richer demos/demos+prompts); Santurkar et al. (2023) identify three limits of demographic prompting: representativeness, steerability, and consistency. Demographic methods can approximate population-level distributions but fail to capture within-group variance and are prompt-sensitive (Argyle et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2024). Few works target individualized personas: Park et al. (2024) use interview transcripts (high accuracy but limited availability); Haller et al. (2025) use in-context Q-A demonstrations to predict other answers. Example (Table 1): Llama 3.1 8B on an ANES Right-group individual flips from “No” (pre-training) to “Yes” after SFT+GRPO; both traces appeal to equal-opportunity arguments but framed differently. Reasoning methods: chain-of-thought prompts help; recent work trains models to generate reasoning traces via search or RL. Our method uses GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), a PPO variant that normalizes rewards across a sampled group (subtract mean, divide by std) instead of learning a value function; GRPO reported effective on math-reasoning benchmarks (Guo et al., 2025). New: Yu et al. (2025) propose a persona-based chain-of-thought-inspired prompting framework combining demographic, ideological, and temporal factors calibrated on ANES; they simulate individual voting responses and sum them for aggregate predictions. They do not use reinforcement learning. We focus on learning general preference profiles rather than direct voting prediction; scaling to representative sample sizes is currently computationally prohibitive.

Goal: predict a persona p's stance y on question q (stances Y = {No, Neutral, Yes}). Training data D = {(p_j, q_i, y^*_{ij})} contains only final stances (no reasoning traces). Model must generate a reasoning trace and an answer in the fixed schema: <reasoning>[text]</reasoning><answer>[stance]</answer>. Training uses GRPO (Shao et al., 2024). Composite reward: R_format = 1 point per correctly placed tag (4 tags → 0–4); R_length = -|L - L*| (token length penalty; maximum 0 when L = L*); R_correct = 1[y = y*] (indicator). Total reward: R = alpha1*R_format + alpha2*R_length + alpha3*R_correct with alpha1 = 0.25, alpha2 = 0.01, alpha3 = 1. Authors note they do not use explicit persona embeddings (only a country label in system prompt); alignment to individuals is via correctness on questions. Optional SFT initialization: build chain-of-thought demonstrations in the exact schema (1) as warm start to (i) reduce burden on R_format during GRPO and (ii) provide political-reasoning initialization. Dataset overview (Table 2): smartvote (CH) — Unit: Candidate, #Units 18, Labels {Yes, No}, Train Q 48, Test Q 12 (topic-stratified); WoM (DE) — Unit: Party, #Units 6, Labels {Yes, Neutral, No}, Train Q: see Table 5, Test Q 30 (EU&I); ANES 2020 (US) — Unit: Respondent, #Units 21, Labels {Yes, Neutral, No}, Train Q 67, Test Q 12 (random).

Experiments: three datasets (Table 2 overview referenced). Table 3 reports mean macro-F1 (%) (per-run: compute per-unit macro-F1 then average across units), std over 8 runs, temperature T=1.0. Untrained baselines: random (smartvote 50.0; WoM 33.33; ANES 33.33), majority (37.43; 27.44; 22.98). Base models: Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, Magistral 24B. Methods: icl, ORPO, SFT, GRPO, SFT+GRPO. General pattern: smartvote scores noticeably higher than ANES and WoM (attributed to binary labels / no Neutral); WoM > ANES (attributed to more training samples). SFT+GRPO tends to give best results (e.g., Magistral SFT+GRPO: smartvote 70.73, WoM 53.21, ANES 45.43). Dataset details: WoM (Wahl-O-Mat v26 Mar 2025) — 6 parties (CDU/CSU, SPD, Grüne, FDP, Die Linke, AfD); items record agree/neutral/disagree + comment → mapped to {Yes, Neutral, No}; test: EU&I (2024) 30 out-of-domain items; per-party training counts in Appendix A. ANES 2020 — extracted 79 policy items, recoded to {Yes, Neutral, No} using conservative/aggressive schemes (conservative used by default); split 67 train / 12 test items; respondents sampled 3 per ANES 7-point ideology scale → 21 respondents/units. Swiss candidates (smartvote) — English 2023 Swiss questionnaire: 75 items (60 policy across 12 topics); 4-point Likert collapsed to {Yes, No} (Yes/Rather yes → Yes; Rather no/No → No); sampled 3 candidates from each of 6 parties with ≥2 seats → 18 candidates; topic-stratified split: 1 question per topic held out → 12 test, 48 train. Political Spectrum Groups: parties/ideologies mapped to Left/Center/Right (Appendix A). Additional notes: Table 3 formatting in paper is noisy but reported claims (relative performance, splits, and mappings) are consistent with dataset descriptions.

final_notes: Datasets/tasks: J4Q (Swiss, binary); R2V (Wahl-O-Mat) & M8C (ANES), three-way. Baselines: C6W=random, U9F=majority, H3D=in-context learning. Methods: QX2=GRPO (RL), ZP4=SFT+GRPO (best overall), V7K=synthetic-arguments. Backbones: T9A=Llama 3.1 8B, K6Y=Qwen3 8B, W2E=Magistral 24B (best backbone). All experiments use 4-bit quantization. Key results: ZP4 generally outperforms baselines; comparable/better than H3D on M8C/J4Q and better on R2V. J4Q yields highest scores (binary); M8C hardest; R2V > M8C in difficulty. Reasoning support mixed. Neutral class depresses performance; removing Neutral improves F1 and narrows some group gaps. Ideology: P7N (left/center-left) often easiest; X8J (right) hardest; right-leaning groups underperform; V7K can sometimes outperform on X8J. Representation shifts: agents move relative to candidates (centerward/center-right); a conservative (negative-y) group-average distortion was reported, though elsewhere the paper claimed "no clear left–right bias" (noted internal inconsistency). Initialization effects: synthetic progressive/conservative prompts harm underrepresented groups; conservative-biased and default data produce similar shifts. Synthetic-inversion: inverting X8J helps X8J but worsens P7N/A4U and does not reach original P7N F1. Full J4Q label inversion rotates positions ~180°; P7N worsens (individually & on average), X8J improves but stays below P7N. Limitations: per-respondent noise, compute-intensive per-profile training, scarce aligned surveys. Future work: bias mitigation, single models conditioned on compact persona reps, confidence estimates, purpose-built questionnaires. Reproducibility: code/data at https://github.com/ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment; released docs include training details, hyperparameters, PCA implementation details (all PCA results: Section E.5), per-party training counts, recoding definitions, training-sample-size analysis and inversion details. Authors: Frédéric Berdoz (project conception/experimental planning), Yann Billeter (equal contribution; technical lead: data collection, training, evaluation, analysis), Yann Vonlanthen (methodology adviser), Roger Wattenhofer (principal investigator). Acknowledgment: Prof. Dr. Hans Gersbach.

Title: Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs. Authors: Frédéric Berdoz, Yann Billeter, Yann Vonlanthen, Roger Wattenhofer (ETH Zurich). Abstract key points: LLMs are promising for modeling individual/group political preferences, but naive prompting yields biased opinions due to statistical operation and limited causal understanding. The authors propose structured reasoning trained via reinforcement learning (RL) which: (a) produces profile-consistent answers across U.S., European, and Swiss politics; (b) remains competitive with strong baselines; (c) nevertheless leaves bias that requires additional mechanisms for faithful political digital twins. They release methods and datasets as a research baseline and suggest digital democracies could use opinion models to shape fairer, more popular policies.

Title: Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs. Authors: Frédéric Berdoz, Yann Billeter, Yann Vonlanthen, Roger Wattenhofer (ETH Zurich). Abstract/claim: structured reasoning (QX2) trained via reinforcement learning produces profile-consistent answers across U.S., European (German), and Swiss politics; remains competitive with baselines but leaves residual bias needing further mechanisms. Method summary: survey-trained agents produce short rationales then choices; receive rewards for matching respondents’ answers and thus learn survey-consistent positions on unseen questions. Pipeline: initial fine-tuning on synthetic statements + ground-truth answers establishes a reasoning template (not full opinion alignment); then QX2 with formatting/correctness rewards (RL) improves reasoning and alignment. Data: released benchmark of authentic German-party, U.S.-voter, and Swiss-candidate opinions drawn from large surveys and Voting Advice Applications. Analysis: answer-inversion analysis on individuals with known positions reveals systematic ideological variation in alignment quality. Motivation/context: individual digital twins need accurate political-behavior simulation; demographic/affiliation prompts exploit correlations but are unstable and miss real distributions; interviews give strong persona performance but are expensive; surveys structurally represent population opinions and are useful for bias evaluation. Mentions recent RL progress (o3/o4-mini, DeepSeek-R1) as motivation.

Title/authors: Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs — Berdoz, Billeter, Vonlanthen, Wattenhofer (ETH). Core method: QX2 (aka Group-Relative Policy Optimization, GRPO) — a PPO variant that uses group-relative reward normalization (samples multiple outputs per prompt, subtracts reward mean and divides by reward standard deviation) instead of a learned advantage/value estimator; applied as an RL stage to improve reasoning and alignment after initial fine-tuning on synthetic statements + ground-truth answers. Pipeline summary from earlier parts: produce short rationales then choices; reward for matching survey respondents; learns survey-consistent positions, evaluated across U.S., German, Swiss opinion data and a released benchmark. Related work in this part: categories — demographic personas (simple affiliation prompts to richer demographics and belief-network demonstrations); demographic limitations (representativeness, steerability, consistency issues per Santurkar et al. 2023, Argyle et al. 2023, Sun et al. 2024); beyond demographics (interviews outperform demographics but are transcript-limited; Q/A-pair methods target bias identification). Training/reasoning literature: Chain-of-Thought and RL improve generated traces; GRPO/QX2 cited (Shao et al. 2024); math-reasoning SOTA cited (Guo et al. 2025). Reasoning-for-alignment: Yu et al. (2025) combine persona + CoT calibrated with M8C but do not use RL and target voting prediction; authors note representative-sample modeling is currently computationally prohibitive. Empirical illustration: Table 1 shows a model flip (base-model: “No” to question; after training ZP4: reasoning provided and final answer “Yes”). Several acronyms appear (T9A, X8J, M8C, ZP4, N8R/ORPO) that are not yet defined in earlier parts — keep track for later parts.

Key results: ZP4 generally best; comparable/better than H3D on M8C/J4Q and better on R2V; J4Q highest scores (binary), M8C hardest, R2V > M8C. Reasoning support mixed; W2E best overall. Neutral examples depress performance; removing Neutral improves F1 and narrows some group gaps. Ideology: P7N often easiest, X8J hardest/right-leaning underperform; V7K can outperform on X8J in some cases. Representation: agents shift relative to candidates (centerward/center-right); a conservative (negative-y) group-average distortion was reported, but earlier text also claimed "no clear left–right bias" (internal inconsistency noted). Initialization: synthetic progressive/conservative prompts harm underrepresented groups; conservative-biased and default data give similar shifts. Synthetic-inversion (group-level): inverting X8J helps X8J but worsens P7N/A4U; inverted X8J does not reach original P7N F1. New (this part): full J4Q label inversion, train T9A — positions rotate ~180°; points ordered by first J4Q PC; P7N worsens individually & on average; X8J improves but its average remains below P7N; converting P7N into X8J via inversion does not remove the disparity, suggesting harder right-wing learning (contradicts earlier "no clear left–right bias" claim).

Datasets/tasks: J4Q (Swiss, binary); R2V (Wahl-O-Mat) & M8C (ANES), three-way. Baselines: C6W=random, U9F=majority, H3D=icl. Methods: QX2=GRPO (RL), ZP4=SFT+GRPO (best overall), V7K=synthetic-arguments. Backbones: T9A=Llama 3.1 8B, K6Y=Qwen3 8B, W2E=Magistral 24B (best backbone). All experiments use 4-bit quantization. Key results: ZP4 generally outperforms baselines and is comparable/better than H3D on M8C/J4Q and better on R2V. J4Q yields highest scores (binary task); M8C is hardest; R2V > M8C in difficulty. Reasoning support mixed. Neutral class depresses performance; removing Neutral improves F1 and narrows some group gaps. Ideology: P7N (left/center-left) often easiest; X8J (right) hardest; right-leaning groups underperform; V7K can sometimes outperform on X8J. Representation shifts: agents move relative to candidates (centerward/center-right); a conservative (negative-y) group-average distortion was reported, though text also at one point claimed “no clear left–right bias” (noted earlier inconsistency). Initialization effects: synthetic progressive/conservative prompts harm underrepresented groups; conservative-biased and default data produce similar shifts. Synthetic-inversion: inverting X8J helps X8J but worsens P7N/A4U and does not reach original P7N F1. New experiment: full J4Q label inversion (train T9A) rotates positions ~180°; P7N worsens (individually & on average), X8J improves but remains below P7N on average — converting P7N into X8J via inversion does not remove disparity (suggests harder right-wing learning). Limitations (current part): per-respondent day-to-day variation adds noise; per-profile training is compute-intensive limiting scale; suitable surveys scarce and not aligned across countries. Future work: bias-mitigation, single model conditioned on compact persona reps (Ning et al., 2024) to reduce compute, add confidence estimates (extended reasoning or value head), purpose-built questionnaires and better uncertainty handling to address Neutral difficulties.

final_notes: Datasets: smartvote (18 units; 48 train / 12 test; labels {Yes,No}), Wahl-o-Mat (6 units; OOD EU&I 30 items; labels {Yes,Neutral,No}), ANES 2020 (21 units; 67 train / 12 test; labels {Yes,Neutral,No}). One model per unit. Training: GRPO (PPO variant, group-reward normalization, no value fn); optional SFT warm-start (synthetic CoT from Llama 3.1 70B) used for smartvote & ANES; biased-SFT data for bias tests generated with Llama 3.3 70B (progressive/conservative). Pipelines: GRPO, SFT, SFT+GRPO. 4-bit quantization. Eval: macro-F1 per unit averaged (mean±std) over 8 runs, T=1.0. Backbones: Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, Magistral 24B. Key Table 3 (SFT+GRPO, per-backbone Llama/Qwen/Magistral): smartvote — 66.88(2.18), 65.11(3.33), 70.73(2.21); Wahl-o-Mat — 52.53(4.05), 49.38(1.93), 53.21(3.19); ANES — 40.66(≈0.91), 38.44(0.40), 45.43(1.11). Magistral best overall; exception: ANES with Llama SFT alone (42.77±1.23) > SFT+GRPO (40.66±≈0.91). PCA (Fig.2): agents don't perfectly match candidates; center-right shift on LR axis; centerward on cons–lib axis; paper notes Section E.5 contains PCA details. Fig.4 (ANES): Neutral class hardest; neutral base rate correlates negatively with performance; removing Neutral raises F1 and narrows Left–Center gap while Left–Right gap persists; performance–Neutral regression reported significant at 5% level. Bias tests: progressive-biased SFT tends to harm Right; conservative-biased harms Left (text contains some inconsistent statements about which group is most harmed). Section 4.9 inversion (smartvote): flipping answers improves Right F1 but post-inversion Right still below Left's original avg; authors conclude right-leaning profiles are harder to model. Ethics: data anonymized; authors warn against deployment until ideological fairness problems (center & right underperformance, and neutral difficulty) are resolved, citing results (Fig.3, Fig.4). Reproducibility: code, datasets, training details, and PCA implementation released at https://github.com/ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment; Appendix F lists hyperparameters. Author contributions: Frédéric Berdoz (conceived/designed project, led experimental planning), Yann Billeter (contributed equally; led technical development, dataset collection, model training, evaluation, analysis), Yann Vonlanthen (advisor), Roger Wattenhofer (PI). Acknowledgments: Prof. Dr. Hans Gersbach thanked.

Paper asks whether reasoning improves LLM alignment with individual political opinions. Method: train one model per respondent, candidate, or party; models generate a rationale and a final answer. Training uses Group-Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), which rewards formatting, reasoning length, and agreement with survey answers. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can provide a warm start; combined SFT+GRPO generally outperforms baselines and performs best on the smartvote dataset, though there are exceptions. Experiments cover Swiss candidates, German parties, and U.S. voters. Neutral answers are hard to predict; performance varies by ideology. Biased fine-tuning data mainly harms underrepresented perspectives. Agents retain political distortions, so method does not fully remove bias. (Part ends with a heading "Glossary" but no glossary content in this excerpt.)

Goal: test whether producing reasoning traces improves alignment of LLMs to individual or group political opinions (digital-twin/agent models). Method: train one model per unit (respondent, candidate, or party) to output a reasoning trace (<reasoning>...</reasoning>) and a final answer (<answer>...</answer>). Training: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can provide a warm start; then Group-Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) — a PPO variant that normalizes rewards within groups and avoids learning a value function — is used. Reward components: R_format (correct output tags), R_length = -|L - L*| (penalty for deviation from desired trace length), R_correct = 1[y = y*]; total reward R(r_i,y_i^*) is a weighted sum with weights alpha1,alpha2,alpha3. GRPO applies group-relative reward normalization (subtract mean, divide by std). Baselines include ORPO, majority, random. Metrics: Macro-F1 (per-unit average), Accuracy, Recall (used to study Neutral), reported with mean ± std across 8 stochastic runs (Table 3); T fixed at 1.0 in those runs. Datasets: ANES 2020 (US, 79 items), smartvote (CH, 2023 candidate questionnaire; topic-stratified holdout), WoM (DE party positions; EU&I 2024 is 30-item out-of-domain test). Labels: Yes/No/Neutral; Swiss four-point scale collapsed to Yes/No; recoding schemes (conservative/aggressive) change mappings. Models/backbones: three open-weight backbones evaluated (Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, Magistral 24B); Llama 3.1 70B and Llama 3.3 70B used to generate synthetic SFT arguments; 4-bit quantization used for training. Analyses: difficulty predicting Neutral, ideology stratification, PCA of positions (left-right, conservative-liberal), displacement/distortion, counterfactual inversion, bias from progressive/conservative SFT data, hallucinated elements, and proposals for confidence/value-heads. Repo: github.com/ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment.

Goal: test whether producing reasoning traces improves alignment of LLMs to individual or group political opinions (digital-twin/agent models). Method: train one model per unit to output a reasoning trace (<reasoning>...</reasoning>) and a final answer (<answer>...</answer>). Training: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can provide a warm start; then Group-Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) — a PPO variant that normalizes rewards within groups and avoids learning a value function — is used. Reward components: R_format (correct tags), R_length = -|L - L*|, R_correct = 1[y = y*]; total reward weighted by alpha1, alpha2, alpha3; GRPO does group-relative normalization. Baselines: ORPO, majority, random. Metrics: Macro-F1 (per-unit average), Accuracy, Recall (Neutral), reported as mean ± std across 8 stochastic runs; T=1.0 in those runs. Datasets: ANES 2020 (US, 79 items), smartvote (CH 2023 candidate questionnaire), WoM (DE party positions); EU&I 2024 30-item out-of-domain test noted. Labels: Yes/No/Neutral; Swiss four-point collapsed to Yes/No; conservative/aggressive recoding schemes exist. Models/backbones: Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, Magistral 24B evaluated; Llama 3.1/3.3 70B used to generate synthetic SFT arguments; 4-bit quantization used. Analyses: Neutral difficulty, ideology stratification, PCA (left-right, conservative-liberal), displacement/distortion, counterfactual inversion, bias from progressive/conservative SFT data, hallucinated elements, proposals for confidence/value-heads. Abstract claims: reasoning-based training improves political opinion modeling and is competitive with strong baselines but does not fully remove bias (supported by Table 3, SFT+GRPO rows; Figures 2–4). Repo: https://github.com/ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment. Authors/affiliation: Frédéric Berdoz, Yann Billeter, Yann Vonlanthen, Roger Wattenhofer (ETH Zurich).

Goal: train LLMs to model individual political preferences (digital twins) by having models generate explicit reasoning traces (<reasoning>...</reasoning>) and a final answer (<answer>...</answer>) and rewarding correct, well-formatted reasoning.

Method: SFT warm start using synthetic statements (generated with Llama 3.1/3.3 70B), then Group-Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), a PPO-style RL method that normalizes rewards within groups of outputs (and per earlier notes avoids learning a value function). Reward components include formatting (R_format), length R_length = -|L - L*|, correctness R_correct = 1[y = y*]; total reward is a weighted sum (alpha1, alpha2, alpha3) with group-relative normalization.

Datasets: ANES 2020 (US, 79 items), smartvote (Swiss 2023 candidate questionnaire), WoM (German party positions); EU&I 2024 30-item set used as out-of-domain test.

Models/evaluation: SFT data from Llama 3.1/3.3 70B; evaluated backbones Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, Magistral 24B (4-bit quantization). Baselines: ORPO, majority, random. Metrics: Macro-F1 (per-unit avg), Accuracy, Recall (Neutral); reported as mean ± std across 8 stochastic runs (T=1.0).

Analyses: neutral-difficulty, ideology stratification, PCA (left-right, conservative-liberal), displacement/distortion, counterfactual inversion, bias from progressive/conservative SFT, hallucinated elements, proposals for confidence/value-heads.

Claims: reasoning-based training improves alignment (Table 3 SFT+GRPO rows), though it does not fully remove bias; Llama 3.1 8B ANES exception discussed in Sec. 4.3; alignment varies by ideology and under answer inversion (Figs. 3,7). Repo and authors provided.

Related work: persona taxonomy — demographic, character, individualized; most prior political-opinion work uses demographic personas (simple affiliation prompts or richer demographics and demonstrations). Limitations of demographic prompting: representativeness, steerability, consistency. Some prior individualized approaches: Park et al. (2024) use interview transcripts (data-limited); Haller et al. (2025) use in-context learning (focus on bias identification). Prior reasoning-based opinion work mainly uses prompting (e.g., Yu et al. 2025) for voting prediction rather than RL for full preference profiles. Example in paper: Llama 3.1 8B (backbone used here); “SFT+GRPO” = supervised fine-tuning on formatted reasoning demonstrations, then GRPO. Table 1 shows an ANES Right-group individual question where base model answered No (disagreed) and SFT+GRPO answered Yes (agreed) with an explicit <reasoning> trace. GRPO: variant of PPO that avoids learning a value function by normalizing rewards within a group (for each prompt, sample outputs, subtract mean reward, divide by reward std); claimed effective on math benchmarks (Guo et al., 2025). Reasoning-training background: chain-of-thought/“let’s think step by step” prompting boosts accuracy; newer work trains reasoning traces via search or RL (Xu et al., 2025). Keep earlier methodological details in mind: SFT warm-start used synthetic statements from Llama 3.1/3.3 70B; GRPO is PPO-style, no value function; reward components include R_format, R_length = -|L-L*|, R_correct = 1[y=y*], total reward = weighted sum with group-relative normalization. Models evaluated: Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, Magistral 24B. Baselines include ORPO, majority, random. Metrics: Macro-F1, Accuracy, Neutral recall; reported as mean±std across 8 runs (T=1.0).

Related work/persona taxonomy: demographic, character, individualized personas; most prior political-opinion work uses demographic personas (simple affiliation prompts or richer demographics + demonstrations). Limitations of demographic prompting: representativeness, steerability, consistency. Prior individualized approaches: Park et al. (2024) use interview transcripts (data-limited) and can outperform demographic baselines; Haller et al. (2025) use in-context learning (focus on bias identification). Prior reasoning-based opinion work mainly uses prompting (e.g., Yu et al., 2025) for voting prediction rather than RL. This part reiterates that prior voting-prediction work did not use RL and targeted voting prediction; the authors learn general preference profiles and claim modeling a representative sample is currently computationally prohibitive. Table 1: example ANES Right-group item — base model (prompting) answered No; After (SFT+GRPO) answered Yes with explicit <reasoning> trace. Reasoning literature: chain-of-thought prompting (Wei et al. 2022, Kojima et al. 2022) and trained reasoning/search/RL (e.g., Guo et al. 2025) improve performance. Methodological details to keep: backbone Llama 3.1 8B; SFT warm-start on synthetic reasoning demonstrations (from Llama 3.1/3.3 70B); GRPO = PPO-variant with group reward normalization (no value function). Reward components: R_format, R_length = -|L-L*|, R_correct = 1[y=y*]; total reward = weighted sum with group-relative normalization. Evaluated models: Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, Magistral 24B. Baselines: ORPO, majority, random. Metrics: Macro-F1, Accuracy, Neutral recall reported as mean±std across 8 runs (T=1.0).

Method: learn individual survey stances by rewarding formatted reasoning plus correct final answer. Output schema: <reasoning>[justification text]</reasoning><answer>[stance]</answer> (reasoning before answer). Dataset D = {(p_j,q_i,y^*_{ij})} contains final stances but no native reasoning traces; optional SFT warm-start provides synthetic chain-of-thought demonstrations in schema (1). GRPO (PPO-variant; earlier notes: group-reward normalization, no value function) is used to train agents. Rewards: R_format = 1 point per correctly placed tag (4 tags, max 4); R_length = -|L - L*| (max 0 at L=L*); R_correct = 1[y=y*]. Total reward R(r_i,y_i^*) = α1 R_format + α2 R_length + α3 R_correct with α1=0.25, α2=0.01, α3=1. r_i is the first argument (contains reasoning+answer). No explicit persona representation; system prompt includes only country label. Table 2 dataset overview: smartvote (CH) — Candidate, 18 units, labels {Yes, No}, Train Q 48, Test Q 12 (topic-strat.); WoM (DE) — Party, 6 units, labels {Yes, Neutral, No}, Train Q see Table 5, Test Q 30 (EU&I); ANES 2020 (US) — Respondent, 21 units, labels {Yes, Neutral, No}, Train Q 67, Test Q 12 (random). Backbones/evals per earlier notes: Llama 3.1 8B (backbone), SFT warm-start from Llama 3.1/3.3 70B, evaluated with Llama 3.1 8B / Qwen3 8B / Magistral 24B; baselines ORPO/majority/random; metrics reported as mean±std across 8 runs (T=1.0).

Method: Agents must output schema <reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>...</answer>. Training uses GRPO (PPO-variant, group-reward normalization, no value function). Optional SFT warm-start provides synthetic CoT demonstrations. Reward components: R_format (1 point per correct tag, 4 tags max), R_length = -|L-L*| (max 0 at L=L*), R_correct = 1[y=y*]; total R = 0.25 R_format + 0.01 R_length + 1.0 R_correct. r_i (first arg) contains reasoning+answer. No explicit persona beyond country label in system prompt. Evaluations averaged (mean ± std) over 8 stochastic runs, temperature T=1.0. Backbones/evaluated models: Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, Magistral 24B; baselines include random, majority, ORPO; methods include icl, ORPO, SFT, GRPO, SFT+GRPO.

Datasets:
- smartvote (CH): Candidates, 18 units (3 candidates × 6 parties), English 2023 questionnaire has 75 items, 60 policy questions across 12 topics; responses collapsed from 4-point Likert to {Yes, No}. Train/test split is topic-stratified (48 train, 12 test).
- WoM (DE): Parties, 6 units (CDU/CSU, SPD, Grüne, FDP, Die Linke, AfD), labels {Yes, Neutral, No}; train counts in Appendix A, out-of-domain test EU&I (2024) with 30 items.
- ANES 2020 (US): Respondents, 21 units (3 per 7-point ideology bins), 79 policy items; recoded to {Yes, Neutral, No} using conservative mapping by default; random split 67 train / 12 test.

Metrics/Table 3: Reports mean macro-F1 (%) computed per unit then averaged across units; standard deviations over 8 runs. Observations in text: smartvote scores are considerably higher than ANES and WoM (attributed to binary labels), and WoM often outperforms ANES (attributed to more training samples).

final_notes: Models & data: primary experiments use Llama 3.1 8B with SFT+GRPO; biased-SFT argument sets were generated with Llama 3.3 70B (Sec A.4) — versions not reconciled. Methods: persona-conditioned agents trained on known opinions; answer generation via structured reasoning (GRPO). Main empirical findings: SFT+GRPO generally outperforms baselines across datasets (smartvote — Swiss candidates; Wahl-o-Mat — German parties; ANES — U.S. voters), but performance is uneven. smartvote: SFT+GRPO yields Left > Center & Right. Wahl-o-Mat: Left ≈ Center, with Right relatively stronger. ANES: lower overall scores; Neutral class has worst recall and high base rate; Neutral base rate negatively correlates with performance. Removing Neutral raises F1 for all and narrows Left–Center gap but Left–Right gap often remains; alternative recoding can make Center ≈ Right. SFT sometimes outperforms other methods for Right on smartvote & ANES; SFT+GRPO still improves vs ICL after Neutral removal. PCA & bias analyses: biased-SFT (progressive/conservative) shifts groups predictably; conservative-biased and default SFT show centerward PCA displacement (base-model alignment); synthetic inversion yields ≈180° PCA rotation — Right benefits, Left & Center worsen; inverted-Right still below original-Left F1. Figures: Fig.7 orders by PCA first component; flipping answers makes Left worse and Right improve but Right still often worse on average than Left. Reproducibility: code & datasets released at https://github.com/ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment; training hyperparameters in Appendix F; PCA details in Section E.5. Author contributions: Frédéric Berdoz (conceived/designed/led), Yann Billeter (contributed equally; led technical development), Yann Vonlanthen (advisor), Roger Wattenhofer (PI). Acknowledgment: Prof. Dr. Hans Gersbach thanked.

Title: Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs. Authors: Frédéric Berdoz, Yann Billeter, Yann Vonlanthen, Roger Wattenhofer; affiliation: ETH Zurich (Switzerland); contact emails listed. Abstract claims: goal is opinion modeling for political preferences; LLMs are natural candidates but tend to produce biased opinions when prompted naively. Research question: can reasoning improve opinion alignment? Method: train models to produce profile-consistent answers via structured reasoning, motivated by recent advances in mathematical reasoning with RL. Evaluation: three datasets covering U.S., European, and Swiss politics. Main results: reasoning enhances opinion modeling, is competitive with strong baselines, but does not fully remove bias; additional mechanisms needed for faithful political digital twins. Code and data released at provided GitHub URL. (Note: abstract contains minor formatting artifacts like “datasets11 1” but no substantive contradictions.)

Title: Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs. Authors: Frédéric Berdoz et al. Goal: build LLM-based political "digital twins" that reflect individual opinions. Motivation: prompt-based demographic conditioning is unstable and fails to capture true opinion distributions; interviews are rich but impractical at scale. Proposal: use political survey data (e.g., ANES, VAAs) as structured input to train individual-level political agents. Method: encourage explicit structured reasoning — model writes a short rationale and a final choice — and train with reinforcement learning (GRPO) to reward survey-consistent answers; pipeline: (1) fine-tune on synthetic statements + ground-truth answers to enforce the reasoning template, (2) apply GRPO with a reward model that rewards correct formatting and matching respondent answers. Motivation cites recent RL-for-reasoning advances (e.g., o3/o4-mini, DeepSeek-R1). Datasets / evaluation: three real-world datasets — German parties (Europe), U.S. voters, Swiss candidates — released as a benchmark. Key claims/results: reasoning consistently improves opinion alignment; analysis of ideological effects via answer inversion shows inversion helps Left profiles but harms Right profiles. From abstract: reasoning enhances opinion modeling and is competitive with strong baselines but does not fully remove bias; code/data released on GitHub. Important numbers/method names to watch: GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), rationale+choice template, reward model that checks format + correctness.

Goal: build LLM-based political "digital twins" to mirror individual opinions; encourage explicit structured reasoning (short rationale + final choice) and use GRPO RL to align answers with survey responses. Related work: demographic, character, and individualized personas; demographic prompting widely used but has limitations (representativeness, steerability, consistency). Few individualized methods: Park et al. (2024) use interview transcripts; Haller et al. (2025) use in-context Q/A for bias identification. Example (Table 1): Llama 3.1 8B on ANES (Right individual) changed from disagree (No) in base prompting to agree (Yes) after SFT+GRPO; after-reasoning includes <reasoning> then <answer>A) Yes</answer>. Training to reason: chain-of-thought and prompting improve accuracy; recent shift to training models to produce reasoning traces via search or RL. GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) is used: described as a PPO variant that does group-relative reward normalization (for each prompt sample a group of outputs, normalize rewards by subtracting group mean and dividing by group std) rather than learning a value function; claimed effective on math reasoning benchmarks (Guo et al., 2025). Key methods to watch: rationale+choice template, SFT+GRPO pipeline, reward model checking format and answer-match.

Goal: build LLM-based political “digital twins” to mirror individual opinions; encourage explicit structured reasoning (short rationale + final choice). Use SFT + GRPO (RL) to align answers with survey responses. Key template: rationale+choice with <reasoning> then <answer> tags. Example (Table 1): Llama 3.1 8B on ANES (Right individual) flipped from disagree (No) under base prompting to agree (Yes) after SFT+GRPO; after-reasoning includes <reasoning> then <answer>A) Yes</answer>. Related work: demographic prompting (widely used but has representativeness/steerability/consistency limits); few individualized methods (Park et al., 2024: interview transcripts; Haller et al., 2025: in-context Q/A for bias identification). Training to reason: chain-of-thought and prompting improve accuracy; recent work trains models to produce reasoning traces via search or RL. GRPO (Shao et al., 2024): PPO variant using group-relative reward normalization (for each prompt sample, normalize rewards across a group by subtracting group mean and dividing by group std) instead of learning a value function; reported effective on math reasoning benchmarks (Guo et al., 2025). Methods to watch: rationale+choice template, SFT+GRPO pipeline, reward model checking format and answer-match. New: Yu et al. (2025) propose a persona-based chain-of-thought-style prompting framework combining demographic, ideological, and temporal factors calibrated on ANES to simulate individual voting and aggregate predictions. They do not use RL; they target voting predictions, while our focus is on learning general preference profiles. Applying our method to representative aggregate prediction is theoretically possible but currently computationally prohibitive.

Goal: learn a persona p's stance y on question q where Y={No, Neutral, Yes}. Output schema: produce a structured trace: <reasoning>[justification]</reasoning><answer>[stance]</answer> (two tag pairs = four tags). Training data D = {(p_j, q_i, y^*_{ij})} contains only final stances (no reasoning traces). Training method: use GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) to train agents to generate the schema above; optional supervised fine-tuning (SFT) warm-start using constructed chain-of-thought demonstrations that follow format (1) to reduce burden on format reward and initialize political reasoning. Composite reward (per generation): R_format = 1 point per correctly placed tag (max 4); R_length = -|L - L*| (<=0; 0 when length matches desired L*); R_correct = 1 if model answer y_i equals ground-truth y_i^*. Total R = alpha1*R_format + alpha2*R_length + alpha3*R_correct with alpha1=0.25, alpha2=0.01, alpha3=1. They state they do not use an explicit persona representation in prompts (only a country label); alignment occurs via correct answers. Dataset overview (Table 2): smartvote (CH) — Unit: Candidate, #Units=18, Labels={Yes,No}, Train Q=48, Test Q=12 (topic-strat.); WoM (DE) — Unit: Party, #Units=6, Labels={Yes,Neutral,No}, Train Q = "see Table 5", Test Q=30 (EU&I); ANES 2020 (US) — Unit: Respondent, #Units=21, Labels={Yes,Neutral,No}, Train Q=67, Test Q=12 (random). Note from earlier: GRPO uses group-relative reward normalization (normalize rewards across group) instead of learning a value function — not restated here but relevant for later checks.

final_notes: Datasets: J4Q (Swiss referendum, binary Yes/No; 18 units; Train=48 Test=12), R2V (Wahl‑O‑Mat DE; 6 party units; labels {Yes,Neutral,No}), M8C (ANES US; 79 items → Train=67 Test=12; 21 respondent units). Spectrum groups: P7N=Left, A4U=Center, X8J=Right. Methods: QX2=GRPO, V7K=SFT (CoT warm start), ZP4=SFT+GRPO. Baselines: C6W=random, U9F=majority, H3D=icl. Synthetic/bias sources: Y3H (Llama 3.1 70B), S5Q (Llama 3.3 70B). Backbones: T9A (Llama 3.1 8B), K6Y (Qwen3 8B), W2E (Magistral 24B). Training uses 4‑bit quantization. Key results: ZP4 generally outperforms naive baselines and V7K; exception: T9A beats ZP4 on M8C; ZP4 comparable/better than H3D on M8C/J4Q and better on R2V. Dataset difficulty: J4Q easiest, R2V middle, M8C hardest. Group effects: centrist/right underperformance; P7N often easiest. Neutral label harms performance (M8C worst Neutral recall; X8J highest Neutral rate); removing Neutral improves F1 and narrows some group gaps. Representation/initialization: reported overall shifts (center‑right horizontal, centerward vertical, conservative negative‑y) and per‑group moves (X8J→more left; P7N/A4U→more right/conservative) — earlier text noted tension between these descriptions. Bias experiments: underrepresented groups harmed; default vs conservative‑biased shifts similar. Synthetic inversion (J4Q): ~180° rotation; P7N worsens, X8J improves but stays below P7N on average. Conclusion reiterates ZP4's general advantage (contradicted by T9A exception). Reproducibility: code and datasets released at https://github.com/ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment; released documentation includes training details/hyperparameters, principal‑component implementation details and all PCA results (Section E.5), per‑party training counts, recoding definitions, training‑sample‑size analysis and inversion details. Title: Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs. Authors: Frédéric Berdoz, Yann Billeter, Yann Vonlanthen, Roger Wattenhofer (ETH Zurich). Abstract key points: LLMs are promising for modeling individual/group political preferences, but naive prompting yields biased opinions due to statistical operation and limited causal understanding. The authors propose structured reasoning trained via reinforcement learning (RL) which: (a) produces profile-consistent answers across U.S., European, and Swiss politics; (b) remains competitive with strong baselines; (c) nevertheless leaves bias that requires additional mechanisms for faithful political digital twins. They release methods and datasets as a research baseline and suggest digital democracies could use opinion models to shape fairer, more popular policies.

Title: Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs. Authors: Frédéric Berdoz, Yann Billeter, Yann Vonlanthen, Roger Wattenhofer (ETH Zurich). Abstract: LLMs can model individual/group political preferences but naive prompting yields biased opinions; authors propose structured reasoning trained via RL (QX2) to improve opinion alignment; they release methods/datasets and warn bias remains. Intro key points: survey-trained agents produce short rationales then choices, trained with rewards for matching respondents’ answers, enabling survey-consistent positions on unseen questions. Recent RL model advances (o3/o4-mini, DeepSeek-R1) motivate approach. Motivation: accurate political-behavior simulation needed for digital twins; current LLM political discourse fails to capture viewpoint diversity; demographic prompts exploit correlations but are unstable; preference-consistency (using known individual opinions) preferred; interviews provide strong persona signals but are costly. Data source: large surveys and Voting Advice Applications (VAAs) structurally represent population opinions (less narrative richness). Contributions listed: QX2-based explicit reasoning from survey responses; released benchmark of authentic German-party, U.S.-voter, and Swiss-candidate opinions; answer-inversion analysis showing answer inversion improves P7N profiles but harms X8J profiles. Figure 1 / pipeline: public surveys -> initial fine-tuning on synthetic statements + ground-truth answers to establish reasoning template (not full alignment) -> QX2 with formatting/correctness rewards to improve reasoning. Unknown terms to track: QX2, P7N, X8J (likely defined later).

Related work situates three persona types (demographic, character, individualized). Demographic prompting has coverage/consistency/steerability issues; some work augments with demonstrations or preference-training (Stammbach et al. 2024 uses N8R = odds-ratio preference optimization (ORPO)). Chain-of-thought prompting (Wei et al., 2022; Kojima et al., 2022) improves accuracy; search/RL increasingly produce high-quality traces. QX2 is defined here as a PPO variant called Group-relative policy optimization (GRPO): it replaces a learned value function with group-relative reward normalization, samples multiple outputs per prompt and standardizes rewards by subtracting the sample mean and dividing by the sample std (Shao et al., 2024). Mathematical-reasoning benchmarks show strong gains (Guo et al., 2025). Table 1 (Related Work) gives an example: “T9A trained on an X8J individual in M8C.” Base-model answer to an equality-of-opportunity question is “No…” After training/‘ZP4’ reasoning, the model produces a Yes answer while retaining similar “equal opportunity” phrasing. Yu et al. (2025) combine demographic/ideological/temporal factors with chain-of-thought and calibrate with M8C (no RL). Keep tracking acronyms used earlier: QX2 now equated to GRPO; M8C appears repeatedly; P7N and X8J remain important profile labels referenced elsewhere.

Synthetic/bias argument sources: Y3H (Llama 3.1 70B) and S5Q (Llama 3.3 70B). Backbones: T9A (Llama 3.1 8B), K6Y (Qwen3 8B), W2E (Magistral 24B). Training uses 4-bit quantization. Key results: ZP4 generally best vs naive and V7K (exception: T9A on M8C); comparable/better than H3D on M8C/J4Q and better on R2V. Dataset difficulty: J4Q easiest (highest performance), R2V middle, M8C hardest. Native reasoning gives no consistent gain (T9A > K6Y on R2V/M8C; W2E best overall). Group effects: training methods underperform on centrist/right groups; P7N often easiest. Neutral label harms performance: M8C worst Neutral recall; X8J highest Neutral rate; removing Neutral improves F1 and narrows some group gaps. Representation/initialization: reported overall shifts (center‑right horizontal and centerward vertical, conservative negative‑y) and per‑group moves (X8J → more left; P7N/A4U → more right/conservative) — earlier parts noted apparent tension between those descriptions. Bias experiments: underrepresented groups harmed; default and conservative‑biased shifts similar. Synthetic inversion (J4Q): invert answers, retrain T9A, yields ~180° position rotation; P7N worsens, X8J improves but stays below P7N on average. New (Discussion): same‑respondent day‑to‑day variation adds noise; per‑profile training is computationally intensive restricting scale; suitable surveys scarce. Future work: bias mitigation, single model conditioned on persona vectors, confidence estimates (extended reasoning or value head), purpose‑built questionnaires and better uncertainty handling to address Neutral issues.

final_notes: Datasets: smartvote (18 candidates; 60 items; topic-stratified holdout 1/question → Test=12, Train=48; labels {Yes, No}), Wahl-o-Mat (6 party units; test=30 OOD items; labels {Yes, Neutral, No}), ANES 2020 (21 respondent units; 79 items → Train=67, Test=12; labels {Yes, Neutral, No}; conservative recoding default). Backbones & SFT: Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, Magistral 24B; SFT data for smartvote & ANES generated by Llama 3.1 70B; biased SFT (progressive, conservative) from Llama 3.3 70B. Training: one model per unit, 4-bit quantization; methods = GRPO, SFT (warm-start), SFT+GRPO. Eval: mean per-unit macro-F1 (%) averaged across units and 8 runs. Main results: SFT+GRPO generally best; Magistral 24B SFT+GRPO top (smartvote 70.73; Wahl-o-Mat 53.21; ANES 45.43). Exception: on ANES with Llama SFT ≈ 42.77 (±1.23) > SFT+GRPO ≈ 40.66 (±0.91). Class-level: Neutral hardest class; neutral base-rate negatively correlates with F1/accuracy; neutral recall worst; removing Neutral raises F1 but Left–Right gap remains. Biased SFT: harms underrepresented groups, Right affected most; conservative-biased and default SFT show similar displacement. PCA/synthetic inversion: ~180° rotation helps Right but gap persists; flipping answers helps Right but Left still higher. Limitations & future: opinion noise, per-profile training cost, propose single model with persona conditioning; need confidence head and better uncertainty handling; purpose-built questionnaires. Ethics & reproducibility: only anonymized survey & public figures data used; warn against deployment until ideological fairness resolved; code, datasets, training details, and PCA implementation details released at https://github.com/ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment; Appendix F contains training/hyperparameter details and Section E.5 describes PCA results. Author contributions: Frédéric Berdoz (project conception/design), Yann Billeter (lead technical development, equal contribution), Yann Vonlanthen (advisor), Roger Wattenhofer (supervisor). Acknowledgment: Prof. Dr. Hans Gersbach thanked.

Paper asks whether reasoning improves LLM alignment with individual political opinions. Method: train one model per respondent, candidate, or party; models generate a rationale and a final answer. Training uses Group-Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), which rewards formatting, reasoning length, and agreement with survey answers. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can provide a warm start; combined SFT+GRPO generally outperforms baselines and performs best on the smartvote dataset, though there are exceptions. Experiments cover Swiss candidates, German parties, and U.S. voters. Neutral answers are hard to predict; performance varies by ideology. Biased fine-tuning data mainly harms underrepresented perspectives. Agents retain political distortions, so method does not fully remove bias. (Part ends with a heading "Glossary" but no glossary content in this excerpt.)

Goal: test whether producing reasoning traces improves alignment of LLMs to individual or group political opinions (digital-twin/agent models). Method: train one model per unit (respondent, candidate, or party) to output a reasoning trace (<reasoning>...</reasoning>) and a final answer (<answer>...</answer>). Training: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can provide a warm start; then Group-Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) — a PPO variant that normalizes rewards within groups and avoids learning a value function — is used. Reward components: R_format (correct output tags), R_length = -|L - L*| (penalty for deviation from desired trace length), R_correct = 1[y = y*]; total reward R(r_i,y_i^*) is a weighted sum with weights alpha1,alpha2,alpha3. GRPO applies group-relative reward normalization (subtract mean, divide by std). Baselines include ORPO, majority, random. Metrics: Macro-F1 (per-unit average), Accuracy, Recall (used to study Neutral), reported with mean ± std across 8 stochastic runs (Table 3); T fixed at 1.0 in those runs. Datasets: ANES 2020 (US, 79 items), smartvote (CH, 2023 candidate questionnaire; topic-stratified holdout), WoM (DE party positions; EU&I 2024 is 30-item out-of-domain test). Labels: Yes/No/Neutral; Swiss four-point scale collapsed to Yes/No; recoding schemes (conservative/aggressive) change mappings. Models/backbones: three open-weight backbones evaluated (Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, Magistral 24B); Llama 3.1 70B and Llama 3.3 70B used to generate synthetic SFT arguments; 4-bit quantization used for training. Analyses: difficulty predicting Neutral, ideology stratification, PCA of positions (left-right, conservative-liberal), displacement/distortion, counterfactual inversion, bias from progressive/conservative SFT data, hallucinated elements, and proposals for confidence/value-heads. Repo: github.com/ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment.

Goal: test whether producing reasoning traces improves alignment of LLMs to individual or group political opinions (digital-twin/agent models). Method: train one model per unit to output a reasoning trace (<reasoning>...</reasoning>) and a final answer (<answer>...</answer>). Training: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can provide a warm start; then Group-Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) — a PPO variant that normalizes rewards within groups and avoids learning a value function — is used. Reward components: R_format (correct tags), R_length = -|L - L*|, R_correct = 1[y = y*]; total reward weighted by alpha1, alpha2, alpha3; GRPO does group-relative normalization. Baselines: ORPO, majority, random. Metrics: Macro-F1 (per-unit average), Accuracy, Recall (Neutral), reported as mean ± std across 8 stochastic runs; T=1.0 in those runs. Datasets: ANES 2020 (US, 79 items), smartvote (CH 2023 candidate questionnaire), WoM (DE party positions); EU&I 2024 30-item out-of-domain test noted. Labels: Yes/No/Neutral; Swiss four-point collapsed to Yes/No; conservative/aggressive recoding schemes exist. Models/backbones: Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, Magistral 24B evaluated; Llama 3.1/3.3 70B used to generate synthetic SFT arguments; 4-bit quantization used. Analyses: Neutral difficulty, ideology stratification, PCA (left-right, conservative-liberal), displacement/distortion, counterfactual inversion, bias from progressive/conservative SFT data, hallucinated elements, proposals for confidence/value-heads. Abstract claims: reasoning-based training improves political opinion modeling and is competitive with strong baselines but does not fully remove bias (supported by Table 3, SFT+GRPO rows; Figures 2–4). Repo: https://github.com/ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment. Authors/affiliation: Frédéric Berdoz, Yann Billeter, Yann Vonlanthen, Roger Wattenhofer (ETH Zurich).

Goal: train per-person "digital-twin" LLMs to reflect individuals' survey answers by producing an explicit reasoning trace and a final answer. Method: SFT warm start (synthetic statements/answers generated by Llama 3.1/3.3 70B), then Group-Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO; Shao et al., 2024) — a PPO-style RL that normalizes rewards within groups (and per earlier summary avoids learning a value function). Output format enforces <reasoning>...</reasoning> and <answer>...</answer>. Reward components: R_format (format tags), R_length = -|L - L*|, R_correct = 1[y = y*]; combined with weights alpha1..alpha3. GRPO applied to improve survey-consistent reasoning; agent writes rationale + final choice and is rewarded when choice matches respondent. Baselines: ORPO, majority, random. Metrics: Macro-F1 (per-unit average), Accuracy, Neutral recall; reported as mean ± std over 8 stochastic runs (temperature T=1.0). Datasets: ANES 2020 (US, 79 items), smartvote (CH 2023 candidate questionnaire), WoM (DE party positions); also EU&I 2024 30-item out-of-domain test. Models: Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, Magistral 24B evaluated; Llama 70B used for synthetic SFT; 4-bit quantization used. Key claims: reasoning-based training improves alignment (Table 3, SFT+GRPO rows) though Llama 3.1 8B shows an ANES exception (Sec 4.3); alignment varies with ideology and answer inversion (answer inversion helps Left profiles, harms Right; Figures cited: 3 and 7). Repo: https://github.com/ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment.

Related work: contrasts demographic, character, and individualized personas; most prior political-opinion work uses demographic personas (affiliation, age, education, location) and demonstrations. Limitations of demographic approaches: representativeness, steerability, consistency. Few studies use individualized profiles (Park et al. 2024 transcripts; Haller et al. 2025 in‑context learning). ORPO (odds-ratio preference optimization) is a prior preference-optimization baseline (used by Stammbach et al. 2024). Example: Table 1 shows Llama 3.1 8B (backbone evaluated here) before fine-tuning answered “No” (no tags); after SFT+GRPO it produces a <reasoning> trace and <answer>A) Yes</answer>, i.e., SFT+GRPO changed output to match a Right-group respondent. SFT+GRPO = supervised fine-tuning on formatted reasoning demonstrations followed by Group-Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). GRPO: described as a PPO variant that avoids learning a value function by normalizing rewards within groups — standardizing sampled-output rewards per prompt (subtract mean, divide by std). Paper claims GRPO has been effective on math reasoning benchmarks. Training-to-reason background: chain-of-thought and “let’s think step by step” prompting increase accuracy; recent work trains reasoning traces via search or RL. Prior reasoning-based opinion work mainly uses prompting (e.g., Yu et al. 2025) for voting prediction, not RL for general preference profiles. Experimental groups: Left, Center, Right. (Keep these points for consistency checks with methods, experiments, and claimed results later.)

Related work: most prior political-opinion work uses demographic personas (affiliation, age, education, location) and demonstrations; limitations of demographic approaches include representativeness, steerability, and consistency. Few studies use individualized profiles (Park et al. 2024 transcripts; Haller et al. 2025 in‑context learning). Prior voting-prediction work mainly uses prompting (e.g., Yu et al. 2025) rather than RL. ORPO (odds-ratio preference optimization; Stammbach et al. 2024) is a prior preference-optimization baseline. Our method: SFT+GRPO = supervised fine-tuning on formatted reasoning demonstrations followed by Group-Relative Policy Optimization. Table 1 example: Llama 3.1 8B base answered “No” before fine-tuning; after SFT+GRPO it emits a reasoning trace and ends with "A) Yes" (aligning with a Right-group respondent). This part contrasts prior voting-prediction work (they don’t use RL; they target voting prediction) with our goal of learning general preference profiles; authors note our method could in principle address voting prediction but modeling a representative sample is currently computationally prohibitive. Park et al. (2024) supports interview-based individual modeling outperforming demographic baselines. Prompted and trained reasoning improvements cited: Wei et al. (2022), Kojima et al. (2022), Guo et al. (2025). Experimental groups: Left, Center, Right.

Method: learn persona p_j's stance y on question q by training agents to generate structured reasoning traces in fixed schema (1): <reasoning>[text]</reasoning><answer>[stance]</answer>. Training data D = {(p_j, q_i, y*_{ij})} contains final stances but no reasoning; model must learn format and reasoning.

Rewards (composite used by GRPO): R = α1 R_format + α2 R_length + α3 R_correct. R_format: 1 point per correctly placed tag (4 tags, max=4). R_length: R_length = -|L - L*| (max 0 when L = L*). R_correct = 1[y_i = y*_i]. Weights: α1 = 0.25, α2 = 0.01, α3 = 1. Total reward denoted R(r_i, y_i^*); r_i is the first argument.

GRPO referenced (Shao et al., 2024). No explicit persona token used at generation time; system prompt includes only a country label (alignment arises from correctly answering questions). Optional SFT warm start: supervised chain-of-thought demonstrations in format (1) to teach format and initialize reasoning (cited to Shao et al., 2024).

Dataset overview (Table 2): smartvote (CH) — Unit: Candidate, #Units=18, Labels={Yes,No}, Train Q=48, Test Q=12 (topic-strat.). WoM (DE) — Unit: Party, #Units=6, Labels={Yes,Neutral,No}, Train Q: see Table 5, Test Q=30 (EU&I). ANES 2020 (US) — Unit: Respondent, #Units=21, Labels={Yes,Neutral,No}, Train Q=67, Test Q=12 (random). Train/test counts are per unit.

Method: learn persona p_j stance y on question q by training agents to generate structured traces in fixed schema: <reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>[stance]. Training data D contains only final stances (no reasoning). Reward R = α1 R_format + α2 R_length + α3 R_correct with R_format = 1 point per correctly placed tag (4 tags max), R_length = -|L - L*| (max 0 when L = L*), R_correct = 1[y=y*]. Weights: α1=0.25, α2=0.01, α3=1.0. GRPO cited; optional SFT warm start of CoT demos. No explicit persona token at generation time (only country label in system prompt).

Datasets (Table 2): three datasets (CH smartvote, DE WoM, US ANES). Key per-unit train/test splits: smartvote (candidate units N=18): 60 policy items (75 total items, 60 policy across 12 topics) split topic-stratified Train=48 / Test=12; labels {Yes, No}. WoM (party units N=6): labels {Yes, Neutral, No}; test = EU&I out-of-domain 30 items; per-party training counts given in Appendix / Table 5. ANES 2020 (respondent units N=21): 79 policy items split Train=67 / Test=12 (random); labels {Yes, Neutral, No}. For ANES, two recodings (conservative/aggressive); conservative mapping used by default. ANES units: sample 3 respondents per 7-point ideology (3x7=21).

Evaluation / Table 3: report mean per-unit macro-F1 (%) averaged across units and over 8 stochastic runs at temperature T=1.0. Baselines: random (smartvote 50.0, WoM 33.33, ANES 33.33); majority (smartvote 37.43, WoM 27.44, ANES 22.98). Backbones: Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, Magistral 24B. Methods: icl, ORPO, SFT, GRPO, SFT+GRPO. Paper claims: smartvote scores >> ANES, WoM (attributed to binary labels); WoM > ANES (attributed to more training samples). Detailed per-model numbers in Table 3 (SFT and SFT+GRPO generally best; e.g., Magistral SFT+GRPO smartvote 70.73%, WoM 53.21%, ANES 45.43%).
