Paper question: can internal computations of in-context learning (ICL) improve supervised fine-tuning (SFT)? Key claims/method: ICL and SFT activation patterns differ even on same data. Proposes ICL Activation Alignment (IA2): train a model without demonstrations to match its own activations with demonstrations (i.e., priming via activation matching), then run SFT on this primed model using ground-truth responses. Experimental setup: 12 benchmarks, 2 model families, and >13,000 trained models. Reported results: IA2 improves SFT accuracy and calibration; IA2 and SFT find different weight subspaces; IA2 does not consistently outperform ICL (notably fails on some multi-token math tasks). Additional investigations: simultaneous IA2 and SFT, soft-label distillation, and an alternative parameter-efficient tuning method. Glossary follows.

Paper goal: Can internal computations of in-context learning (ICL) improve supervised fine-tuning (SFT)?
Method: IA2 (ICL Activation Alignment) — self-distillation that trains a student model without demonstrations to match activations of the same model under ICL demonstrations (teacher). Workflows: IA2 → SFT (priming) and IA2 + SFT (simultaneous; β is weight on SFT loss).
Key objectives/losses: L_SFT = summed cross-entropy on target tokens; L_IA2 = summed activation-matching MSE. Activation tensors shaped L × G × d (G capped at 200 for IA2). Activation similarity (asim) = token-wise cosine similarity. Demonstrations use leave-one-out (N-1 demos per IA2 training sample). Teacher = ICL-conditioned model; student = model trained without demos to match teacher activations.
Models/datasets: Two model families (Qwen3-4B-Base and Llama-3.2). Llama-3.2 variants: 1B/3B/4B mapped to 16/28/36 layers; Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct used as a post-trained multi-token test. Datasets: SciQ, QASC, SciQr, QASCr, GSM8K, GSM8Ks, HMathA, SST2, Financial Phrasebank (FinS), PoemS, AGNews (AGN), BBCNews (BBCN), StrategyQA.
Settings/metrics: Single-token vs multi-token tasks; accuracy (exact match after parsing), ECE for single-token calibration. PEFT: LoRA adapters (rank r = 8) used; subspace overlap = (1/r)||U1^T U2||_F^2 using SVD bases. LR sweep {1e-4, 3e-4, 1e-3}; epoch cap 50. Reported scope: 12 benchmarks, 2 model families, >13,000 trained models. Main reported findings to check later: IA2 improves SFT accuracy/calibration; IA2 and SFT occupy largely different (almost orthogonal) weight subspaces; IA2 does not uniformly outperform ICL (notably weaker on some multi-token math tasks).

Paper goal: Test whether internal ICL computations can improve supervised fine-tuning (SFT) via self-distillation (IA2).
Method (IA2): Use the model's ICL-conditioned activations (teacher) to train the same model without demonstrations (student) to match those activations (MSE). Activation tensors shaped L × G × d (G capped at 200). Demonstrations use leave-one-out (N-1). Losses: L_SFT (cross-entropy on targets), L_IA2 (activation-matching MSE). Also combined IA2+SFT with weight β on SFT loss.
Models/datasets/setting: Two model families (Qwen3-4B-Base and Llama-3.2 family: 1B/3B/4B mapped to 16/28/36 layers). Benchmarks: 12 tasks (SciQ, QASC, SciQr, QASCr, GSM8K, GSM8Ks, HMathA, SST2, FinS, PoemS, AGN, BBCN, StrategyQA noted earlier). PEFT via LoRA rank=8; subspace overlap metric; LR sweep {1e-4,3e-4,1e-3}; epochs up to 50. Large-scale sweep: >13k trained models.
Main claims/evidence: ICL and SFT produce distinct activations (Figure 2). IA2 priming before SFT improves accuracy and calibration across benchmarks and both model families. Examples quoted: FinS→FinS accuracy 67.4 vs 78.7, ECE 0.31 vs 0.16; HMathA→HMathA accuracy 50.4 vs 55.3. Also note prior summary that IA2 and SFT occupy largely different (nearly orthogonal) weight subspaces and that IA2 does not uniformly outperform ICL on some multi-token math tasks.

Paper goal: Use ICL internal activations to improve supervised fine-tuning (SFT) via self-distillation called IA2 (match ICL-conditioned activations). Method: collect ICL activations (teacher) using leave-one-out demonstrations (N-1); train same model (student) without demos to match activations via MSE (L_IA2). Also standard SFT loss L_SFT (cross-entropy); can combine IA2+SFT with weight β. Activation tensors shaped L × G × d (G capped at 200). Models/datasets: Qwen3-4B-Base and Llama-3.2 family (1B/3B/4B mapped to 16/28/36 layers); 12 benchmarks (SciQ, QASC, SciQr, QASCr, GSM8K, GSM8Ks, HMathA, SST2, FinS, PoemS, AGN, BBCN, StrategyQA noted across earlier parts). PEFT via LoRA rank=8; LR sweep {1e-4,3e-4,1e-3}; epochs ≤50. Large-scale sweep: >13k trained models. IA2 pipeline: (1) collect ICL activations, (2) enforce alignment (IA2 priming), (3) perform SFT on primed model. Key claims: ICL and SFT activations differ (Fig.2); IA2 priming before SFT drastically improves SFT performance and calibration (examples: SST2→SST2 accuracy 65.2 vs 90.4, ECE 0.22 vs 0.06; SciQ→SciQ accuracy 35.0 vs 40.8; earlier noted FinS→FinS 67.4 vs 78.7, ECE 0.31 vs 0.16; HMathA→HMathA 50.4 vs 55.3). IA2 supplies a training signal absent from SFT: §5.2 reports ~39% average weight-subspace overlap between IA2-only and IA2→SFT, while SFT-only updates are almost completely orthogonal. Findings supported by Figures 1–4 and Tables 1–2; >13k models across 12 benchmarks.

Goal: IA2 — use ICL internal activations to improve SFT via self-distillation (match ICL-conditioned activations). Method: collect ICL activations (teacher) using leave-one-out demos (n = N-1), train the same model (student) without demos to match activations via MSE (L_IA2). Combine with standard SFT cross-entropy loss L_SFT (weight β) for IA2→SFT pipeline: (1) collect ICL activations, (2) IA2 priming (align activations), (3) SFT on primed model. Models/datasets: Qwen3-4B-Base and Llama-3.2 family (1B/3B/4B mapped to 16/28/36 layers); 12 benchmarks (SciQ, QASC, SciQr, QASCr, GSM8K, GSM8Ks, HMathA, SST2, FinS, PoemS, AGN, BBCN, StrategyQA). PEFT via LoRA rank=8; LR sweep {1e-4,3e-4,1e-3}; epochs ≤50. Large-scale sweep: >13k trained models. Key empirical claims: ICL and SFT activations differ (Fig.2); IA2 priming before SFT drastically improves SFT performance and calibration (examples: SST2 acc 65.2→90.4, ECE 0.22→0.06; SciQ 35.0→40.8; FinS 67.4→78.7, ECE 0.31→0.16; HMathA 50.4→55.3). IA2 supplies a training signal absent from SFT: §5.2 reports ~39% average weight-subspace overlap between IA2-only and IA2→SFT, while SFT-only updates are almost completely orthogonal. Background/notation: decoder-only transformer M_Θ with L layers; self-attention uses W_Q,W_K,W_V,W_O (collectively W_{QKVO}). For token i: q_i = t_i·W_Q, K = t_{:i}·W_K, V = t_{:i}·W_V (causal attention). SA output z_i = softmax(q_i K^T / sqrt d) V · W_O; inputs/outputs T,Z have shape R×d (R = sequence length). SFT dataset D_T = {(X_i,Y_i)}_{i=1}^N; if ground-truth response has G tokens, L_SFT = sum_{i=1}^N sum_{j=1}^G cross-entropy(̅Y_{ij}, Y_{ij}). ICL uses demonstrations I = [X_1∘Y_1∘...∘X_n∘Y_n], model computes M_Θ(I∘X_t)=ĥy_t (no weight updates). Activations: hidden SA outputs form tensor A of size L×R×d; for ICL use T=[I∘X], for no-ICL use T=X. Activation similarity asim(A1,A2) is token-wise cosine similarity between corresponding layer/token d-vectors, producing an L×R map.

Goal: IA2 — use ICL internal activations to improve SFT via self-distillation (match ICL-conditioned activations). Pipeline: (1) collect ICL activations (teacher) using demonstrations, (2) IA2 priming: train model without demos to match those activations via MSE, (3) SFT on primed model (combine L_IA2 with standard cross-entropy L_SFT). Models: Qwen3 and Llama-3.2 family mapped 1B↔16 layers, 3B↔28, 4B↔36. Datasets: 12 benchmarks (SciQ, QASC, SciQr, QASCr, GSM8K, GSM8Ks, HMathA, SST2, FinS, PoemS, AGN, BBCN, StrategyQA); some experiments here used 100 test samples from multiple datasets including SST2 and AGNews. PEFT: LoRA rank=8; LR sweep {1e-4,3e-4,1e-3}; epochs ≤50; large sweep >13k models. Activations: SA hidden outputs form A of shape L×R×d; for ICL use T=[I∘X], for no-ICL use T=X. asim(A1,A2) is token-wise cosine similarity (L×R map); experiments computed asim at output-token positions and averaged across tokens/samples/datasets. Key empirical claims: ICL and SFT activations differ (Fig.2 — “SFT only” shows low asim, especially in middle layers; better alignment in initial/final layers); ICL is better calibrated than SFT at similar/slightly better accuracy (Fig.1); IA2→SFT substantially improves SFT performance & calibration (examples: SST2 acc 65.2→90.4, ECE 0.22→0.06; FinS 67.4→78.7, ECE 0.31→0.16; SciQ 35.0→40.8; HMathA 50.4→55.3).

errors.claim: "Find \tilde{W}_{QKVO}=(\tilde{W}_{Q},\tilde{W}_{K},\tilde{W}_{V},\tilde{W}_{O}) such that for every newly generated token (at index: -1 ): SA([I\circ X];W_{QKVO})\approx SA(X;\tilde{W}_{QKVO}) \quad\forall X\in\mathcal{T}." (Equation 3)
errors.evidence: "Next, we provide the response attached only with the query T_{i}=[X_{i}\circ\hat{Y}_{i}], as if the model had produced the ICL response with only the query in context. This gives an unaligned activation tensor A^{i} at the output token positions. Then, we simply train the model to minimize the mean squared error between the two activations w.r.t. model parameters: \n\n\mathcal{L}_{\textbf{{IA2}}}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}||A^{i}-A^{i}_{\text{ICL}}||. (4)"
errors.explanation: Equation (3) states the target is to match SA([I∘X]; W) to SA(X; \tilde{W}) (i.e., activations when only X is provided under modified weights). But the IA2 implementation matches activations produced when feeding [X∘\hat{Y}] to those from [I∘X]. The RHS inputs differ (X alone vs X with appended \hat{Y}), so the described training procedure does not implement the stated equation exactly.

Title: IA2: Alignment with ICL Activations — Improves Supervised Fine-Tuning. Authors: Aayush Mishra; Daniel Khashabi & Anqi Liu (Johns Hopkins University). Abstract claims: ICL (in-context learning) adapts models at inference via prompt instructions/demos and can offer better generalizability and more calibrated responses than SFT in data-scarce settings, but costs more inference compute. The authors state that ICL and SFT produce distinct activation patterns. They introduce IA2 (ICL Activation Alignment), a self-distillation technique that aims to replicate ICL activation patterns in SFT models, incentivizing ICL-like internal reasoning. Performing IA2 as a priming step before SFT reportedly significantly improves accuracy and calibration across 12 popular benchmarks and two model families. Footnote: equal advising and correspondence emails listed. Key items to check in later parts: evidence that ICL vs SFT activations are distinct; IA2 method details (how activations are matched, loss functions, when/how priming is applied); empirical results substantiating "significant" improvements across the claimed 12 benchmarks and two model families (metrics, baselines, significance); any claims about compute tradeoffs or calibration comparisons.

Title: IA2: Alignment with ICL Activations — Improves Supervised Fine-Tuning. Authors: Aayush Mishra; Daniel Khashabi & Anqi Liu. Introduction claims: SFT (often via PEFT) needs large labeled datasets; ICL generalizes well in few-shot and yields better calibration but costs context/inference compute. Authors report ICL and SFT produce disparate internal activations (§3) even when token-level behavior looks similar. Hypothesis: ICL activations contain richer information for generalization; SFT (especially few-shot) may lack this and overfit/learn shortcuts. They propose IA2 (ICL Activation Alignment), a self-distillation/priming method: (1) collect ICL activations, (2) enforce functional alignment with ICL, then (3) perform SFT on the primed model (§4). Claim IA2 priming before SFT “drastically improves” accuracy and calibration on a variety of text classification and generation tasks (§5). They state they trained >13,000 models across 12 benchmarks to validate results. Also claim the IA2 training signal is absent in SFT-only training. Figure 1 summarizes pipeline and aggregated performance charts. Items to verify in later parts: evidence for distinct activations (§3) (metrics/visualizations); precise IA2 method (which activations/layers, loss, optimization, priming procedure) and compute cost; experimental details and results (§5): datasets, models (note: abstract mentioned two model families), baselines, metrics (accuracy, calibration), statistical significance, and any claims about inference/compute tradeoffs.

Paper: IA2: Alignment with ICL Activations — Improves Supervised Fine-Tuning. Core claim: ICL and SFT produce disparate internal activations even when token-level behavior looks similar; authors propose IA2 (ICL Activation Alignment): collect ICL activations, enforce functional alignment with ICL, then perform SFT on the primed model. They claim IA2 improves accuracy and calibration, trained >13,000 models across 12 benchmarks. 

Section 2 (background/notation) details: decoder-only transformer M_Θ with R token vectors T=[t_i]_{i=1..R}. Self-attention uses weights W_Q,W_K,W_V,W_O (denoted W_QKVO). For causal attention q_i = t_i W_Q, K = t_:i W_K, V = t_:i W_V, and SA output Z = [z_i = softmax(q_i K^T / sqrt(d)) V · W_O]_{i=1..R}. 

SFT: given dataset D_T={(X_i,Y_i)}_{i=1..N}, fine-tune Θ→Θ' by generating G tokens per response and minimizing L_SFT = sum_{i=1..N} sum_{j=1..G} cross-entropy(\bar{Y}_{ij},Y_{ij}). 

ICL: prompt with concatenated demos I=[X1◦Y1◦...◦Xn◦Yn] and query X_t, produce M_Θ(I◦X_t)=\hat{y}_t (classic demo-based ICL). 

Activations: hidden SA outputs form tensor A of shape L×R×d. Activation similarity asim(A1,A2) is token-wise cosine similarity, producing an L×R map.

Section 3 investigates whether ICL and SFT produce similar internal activations. Experiment: collected ICL activations A_ICL (T=[I◦X]) for 100 test samples across datasets (SST2, AGNews, etc.) and models (Qwen3 & Llama-3.2 family: 1B↔16 layers, 3B↔28 layers, 4B↔36 layers). Trained SFT models using the same ICL demos until convergence and collected A_SFT (T=X). Computed asim(A_ICL,A_SFT) at output-token positions (token-wise cosine similarity per §2) and averaged across tokens, samples, datasets (plotted in Figure 2; SFT-only in first row). Result: ICL and SFT activations are not aligned across models — better alignment near initial and final layers, misalignment in middle layers. They note ICL is much better calibrated than SFT at similar (slightly better) accuracy (Figure 1), hypothesizing SFT learns output-oriented shortcuts while ICL uses generalizable circuits. Conclusion: SFT is not a drop-in replacement for ICL; research question: can ICL activations be used to improve SFT (motivating IA2→SFT pipeline described next).

errors.claim: "Find \tilde{W}_{QKVO}=(\tilde{W}_{Q},\tilde{W}_{K},\tilde{W}_{V},\tilde{W}_{O}) such that for every newly generated token (at index: -1 ): SA([I\circ X];W_{QKVO})\approx SA(X;\tilde{W}_{QKVO}) \quad\forall X\in\mathcal{T}." (Equation 3)
errors.evidence: "Next, we provide the response attached only with the query T_{i}=[X_{i}\circ\hat{Y}_{i}], as if the model had produced the ICL response with only the query in context. This gives an unaligned activation tensor A^{i} at the output token positions. Then, we simply train the model to minimize the mean squared error between the two activations w.r.t. model parameters: \n\n\mathcal{L}_{\textbf{{IA2}}}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}||A^{i}-A^{i}_{\text{ICL}}||. (4)"
errors.explanation: Equation (3) states the target is to match SA([I∘X]; W) to SA(X; \tilde{W}) (i.e., activations when only X is provided under modified weights). But the IA2 implementation matches activations produced when feeding [X∘\hat{Y}] to those from [I∘X]. The RHS inputs differ (X alone vs X with appended \hat{Y}), so the described training procedure does not implement the stated equation exactly.

steps.notes_before: Section 3: ICL vs SFT activations diverge (100 test samples across datasets; Qwen3 & Llama-3.2 family 1B/3B/4B). ICL and SFT not aligned except near initial/final layers; ICL better calibrated than SFT. Motivation: induce ICL-like internal behavior in SFT. Section 4 (IA2→SFT pipeline): Goal (Eq.3) — for each layer find modified attention weights \tilde{W}_{QKVO} so SA([I◦X];W) ≈ SA(X;\tilde{W}) for newly generated token positions. Prior closed-form exists for linearized attention; aim for general transformers. Practical IA2: generate ICL responses \hat{Y}_i from T=[I◦X_i], collect A^{i}_{ICL} ∈ R^{L×G×d} at output-token positions; then feed T'=[X_i◦\hat{Y}_i] to get unaligned activations A^i and train (MSE) to minimize ||A^i - A^{i}_{ICL}|| (Eq.4) w.r.t model params. After IA2 (Θ→Θ'), continue standard SFT (cross-entropy) on ground-truth Y to align outputs; pipeline: (1) IA2 to align internal behavior with ICL; (2) SFT to align outputs. Note: the text's stated objective (match activations for X alone under \tilde{W}) appears to differ from the implemented loss (matching activations for [X◦\hat{Y}] to those for [I◦X]).

Figure 4 / subspace analysis: used models from all single/multi-token experiments. Performed SVD on weight matrices to obtain basis vectors; computed subspace overlap = (1/r) * ||U1^T U2||_F^2 where U1,U2 are basis vectors and r is the rank of LoRA weights (r likely 8). Findings: SFT-only weight updates are almost completely orthogonal to the other two methods; IA2→SFT (most performant) models share ~39% of spanned weight space on average with IA2-only models, implying IA2 contributes much of IA2→SFT gains and IA2 subspaces are largely unreachable by SFT-only. Title: IA2: Alignment with ICL Activations — subtitle: Improves Supervised Fine-Tuning. Authors: Aayush Mishra; Daniel Khashabi & Anqi Liu (Dept. of Computer Science, Johns Hopkins University). Note: "♡ Equal advising." Correspondence emails: {amishr24,danielk,aliu.cs}@jhu.edu. Title: IA2: Alignment with ICL Activations — subtitle: Improves Supervised Fine-Tuning. Authors: Aayush Mishra; Daniel Khashabi; Anqi Liu. Abstract claims to verify later: P4Z improves output U6R and calibration across 12 benchmarks and 2 model families; R8D is a self-distillation method that replicates V2K activation patterns; R8D’s priming signal unavailable via H9C. From this part: PEFT (Hu et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2022) adapts small parameter subsets. Q7M generalization typically needs many labeled samples (Le Scao & Rush, 2021); V2K demonstrations consume context capacity and add per-query compute. Research question: can V2K (ICL) activations improve Q7M quality? Hypothesis: V2K activations encode generalizable contextual patterns missing from few-shot weight adaptation (which may take shortcuts/overfit). Note: similar token outputs don’t imply similar internal processing (Shen et al., 2024). Context-to-weight distillation from response text can reproduce outputs without matching internal function (Snell et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2024b). Proposed three-step pipeline: (1) collect V2K activations, (2) enforce functional alignment, (3) train against target responses (standard Q7M corresponds to output-space alignment—step 3—and is claimed to yield subpar performance and miscalibration under low data). Details/results deferred to §5. Acronyms to track: IA2, ICL, P4Z, U6R, R8D, V2K, H9C, Q7M, PEFT.

Title: IA2: Alignment with ICL Activations — subtitle: Improves Supervised Fine-Tuning. Authors: Aayush Mishra; Daniel Khashabi; Anqi Liu. Abstract claims: P4Z improves output U6R and calibration across 12 benchmarks & 2 model families; R8D is a self-distillation method that replicates V2K activation patterns; R8D’s priming signal unavailable via H9C. PEFT adapts small parameter subsets. Q7M = supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Q7M updates Θ→Θ' so M_{Θ'}(X_t) produces response tokens; loss L_Q7M = sum_{i=1..N} sum_{j=1..G} cross-entropy(predicted token, true token) (eq.2). Model: decoder-only transformer with L layers processing R tokens T=[t_i] (shape R×d). Self-attention SA(T;W_{QKVO}) = Z with z_i = softmax(q_i K^T / sqrt(d)) V · W_O, q_i=t_iW_Q, K=t_{:i}W_K, V=t_{:i}W_V; Z and T are R×d. V2K = in-context learning (ICL): demonstrations I=[X1∘Y1∘…] processed at inference so M_Θ(I∘X_t)=ŷ_t without weight updates. Hidden SA outputs are activations A ∈ ℝ^{L×R×d}. K4X (asim) is token-wise cosine similarity between two activation tensors, yielding an L×R matrix. Studied sequences compare T=[I∘X] (with demonstrations) vs T=X (no demonstrations) under differing weights. Pipeline (from intro): (1) collect V2K activations, (2) enforce functional alignment, (3) train against target responses (standard Q7M corresponds to output-space alignment = step 3).

Title: IA2: Alignment with ICL Activations — subtitle: Improves Supervised Fine-Tuning. Authors: Aayush Mishra; Daniel Khashabi; Anqi Liu. Key methods: V2K = in-context learning (ICL): demonstrations I=[X1∘Y1∘…], M_Θ(I∘X_t)=ŷ_t at inference (no weights changed). Q7M = supervised fine-tuning (SFT): updates Θ→Θ' so M_{Θ'}(X_t) produces responses; loss L_Q7M = token cross-entropy (eq.2). Pipeline (intro): (1) collect V2K activations, (2) enforce functional alignment, (3) train against target responses (Q7M = step 3). Model: decoder-only transformer with L layers; hidden self-attention outputs A ∈ ℝ^{L×R×d}. K4X: token-wise cosine similarity between two activation tensors → L×R matrix. Earlier claims: P4Z improves output U6R and calibration across 12 benchmarks & 2 model families; R8D is self-distillation that replicates V2K activation patterns; R8D’s priming signal unavailable via H9C. From Part 4: empirical claim that V2K responses are much better calibrated than Q7M responses with similar, slightly better U6R (cites Duan et al., 2024). Internal-gradient-descent accounts predict similar output-position activations for base-with-demos vs trained-without-demos, but observed activations do not align across models: initial and final layers align better than middle layers. Fig.2: H9C shows small K4X; P4Z aligns much more closely and performs much better. Experimental procedure: collect A_V2K using T=[I∘X] on 100 test samples (datasets include B7V and W3F), then train using those same demonstrations until convergence and collect A_Q7M using T=X. Models: Qwen3 and Llama-3.2; size–depth correspondences: 1B↔16 layers, 3B↔28 layers, 4B↔36 layers. Output-position comparison = K4X(A_V2K,A_Q7M). First-row H9C curves average output-token K4X across tokens, samples, datasets. Experiment details referenced in §B.

steps.notes_before: Paper: IA2 (ICL Activation Alignment) — aims to improve supervised fine-tuning (Q7M). Key defs: V2K = in-context learning with demonstrations I; Q7M = supervised fine-tuning with token CE loss L_Q7M. Model activations: A ∈ R^{L×R×d} (layer × token × dim); K4X measures tokenwise cosine similarity. Pipeline: (1) collect V2K activations, (2) enforce functional alignment (IA2 / R8D), (3) train with Q7M. This part: R8D (IA2) objective (eq.3) seeks adapted attention matrices so SA([I∘X]; W) ≈ SA(X; ˜W) for all X in T — i.e., transfer V2K layerwise processing into weights (authors mention adapting Q,K,V,O). Implementation: for each training X_i, build I from other samples, generate responses hat Y_i from T_i=[I∘X_i], collect V2K output-position activations A^i_{V2K} ∈ R^{L×G×d} for G response tokens; run T_i=[X_i∘hat Y_i] (no demonstrations) to get unaligned A^i; define loss L_R8D = Σ ||A^i - A^i_{V2K}|| and minimize until convergence. After priming (Θ→Θ') the model is fine-tuned with L_Q7M against ground-truth Y. Noted inconsistencies in text: (a) the loss is described as 'mean squared error' but equation lacks a square/mean; (b) the ordering/notation for generated responses is inconsistent (uses \bar Y_i then \hat Y_i; unclear whether generation is before or after priming); (c) unclear whether optimization updates only Q/K/V/O or all model parameters.

Paper question: can internal computations of in-context learning (ICL) improve supervised fine-tuning (SFT)? Key claims/method: ICL and SFT activation patterns differ even on same data. Proposes ICL Activation Alignment (IA2): train a model without demonstrations to match its own activations with demonstrations (i.e., priming via activation matching), then run SFT on this primed model using ground-truth responses. Experimental setup: 12 benchmarks, 2 model families, and >13,000 trained models. Reported results: IA2 improves SFT accuracy and calibration; IA2 and SFT find different weight subspaces; IA2 does not consistently outperform ICL (notably fails on some multi-token math tasks). Additional investigations: simultaneous IA2 and SFT, soft-label distillation, and an alternative parameter-efficient tuning method. Glossary follows.

Paper goal: Can internal computations of in-context learning (ICL) improve supervised fine-tuning (SFT)?
Method: IA2 (ICL Activation Alignment) — self-distillation that trains a student model without demonstrations to match activations of the same model under ICL demonstrations (teacher). Workflows: IA2 → SFT (priming) and IA2 + SFT (simultaneous; β is weight on SFT loss).
Key objectives/losses: L_SFT = summed cross-entropy on target tokens; L_IA2 = summed activation-matching MSE. Activation tensors shaped L × G × d (G capped at 200 for IA2). Activation similarity (asim) = token-wise cosine similarity. Demonstrations use leave-one-out (N-1 demos per IA2 training sample). Teacher = ICL-conditioned model; student = model trained without demos to match teacher activations.
Models/datasets: Two model families (Qwen3-4B-Base and Llama-3.2). Llama-3.2 variants: 1B/3B/4B mapped to 16/28/36 layers; Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct used as a post-trained multi-token test. Datasets: SciQ, QASC, SciQr, QASCr, GSM8K, GSM8Ks, HMathA, SST2, Financial Phrasebank (FinS), PoemS, AGNews (AGN), BBCNews (BBCN), StrategyQA.
Settings/metrics: Single-token vs multi-token tasks; accuracy (exact match after parsing), ECE for single-token calibration. PEFT: LoRA adapters (rank r = 8) used; subspace overlap = (1/r)||U1^T U2||_F^2 using SVD bases. LR sweep {1e-4, 3e-4, 1e-3}; epoch cap 50. Reported scope: 12 benchmarks, 2 model families, >13,000 trained models. Main reported findings to check later: IA2 improves SFT accuracy/calibration; IA2 and SFT occupy largely different (almost orthogonal) weight subspaces; IA2 does not uniformly outperform ICL (notably weaker on some multi-token math tasks).

IA2 supplies a training signal absent from SFT: §5.2 reports ~39% average weight-subspace overlap between IA2-only and IA2→SFT, while SFT-only updates are almost completely orthogonal. Background/notation: decoder-only transformer M_Θ with L layers; self-attention uses W_Q,W_K,W_V,W_O (collectively W_{QKVO}). For token i: q_i = t_i·W_Q, K = t_{:i}·W_K, V = t_{:i}·W_V (causal attention). SA output z_i = softmax(q_i K^T / sqrt d) V · W_O; inputs/outputs T,Z have shape R×d (R = sequence length). SFT dataset D_T = {(X_i,Y_i)}_{i=1}^N; if ground-truth response has G tokens, L_SFT = sum_{i=1}^N sum_{j=1}^G cross-entropy(̅Y_{ij}, Y_{ij}). ICL uses demonstrations I = [X_1∘Y_1∘...∘X_n∘Y_n], model computes M_Θ(I∘X_t)=ĥy_t (no weight updates). Activations: hidden SA outputs form tensor A of size L×R×d; for ICL use T=[I∘X], for no-ICL use T=X. Activation similarity asim(A1,A2) is token-wise cosine similarity between corresponding layer/token d-vectors, producing an L×R map.

Activations: SA hidden outputs form A of shape L×R×d; for ICL use T=[I∘X], for no-ICL use T=X. asim(A1,A2) is token-wise cosine similarity (L×R map); experiments computed asim at output-token positions and averaged across tokens/samples/datasets. Key empirical claims: ICL and SFT activations differ (Fig.2 — “SFT only” shows low asim, especially in middle layers; better alignment in initial/final layers); ICL is better calibrated than SFT at similar/slightly better accuracy (Fig.1); IA2→SFT substantially improves SFT performance & calibration (examples: SST2 acc 65.2→90.4, ECE 0.22→0.06; FinS 67.4→78.7, ECE 0.31→0.16; SciQ 35.0→40.8; HMathA 50.4→55.3).

steps.notes_before: Goal: IA2—use ICL output-position activations to prime models so SFT works better. Pipeline (from earlier parts): (1) For each train sample, generate ICL response using the other N-1 samples as demonstrations and collect output-position activations A^i_ICL. Experiments (§5): tasks split into single-token (SST2, FinS, PoemS, StrategyQA, AGN, BBCN, SciQ/QASC MCQ variants) and multi-token (GSM8K, GSM8Ks, HMathA, SciQ generation). Data: few-shot N in powers of two [2,4,8,16,...], 5 training sets per N; IA2 collects A^i_ICL using N-1 demos per sample; evaluation uses a separate 500-example sample per task. Models: Qwen3-4B-Base for all tasks; Llama-3.2-1B for single-token (except SciQr use 3B); Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct used as secondary for multi-token. Note: paper states 1B Llama "could not improve above the random baseline for any N up to 128." LoRA setup: rank 8 on W_Q,W_K,W_O in SA layers; >13,000 models trained. Training: up to 50 epochs, choose best of three LR (1e-4, 3e-4, 1e-3). Eval: single-token metrics = accuracy and ECE based on first-token distribution. ICL baseline: evaluate validation set 5× with different demos; report averages. Training methods evaluated without demos, reporting best-performing average metrics.

final_notes: Models evaluated: OpenFlamingo-9B, BLIP-2 (OPT-2.7b fusion), InstructBLIP (Vicuna-7b fusion), LLaVA (Vicuna-13B). Key quantitative results (selected): Table 2 few-shot — Multi-P: shot0 0.6095 -> shot2 0.5730 (drop); CroPA: shot0 0.7708 -> shot2 0.6635 (drop). Table 4 (BLIP-2 overall) — Multi-P 0.7104, CroPA 0.7958, CIA ≈0.37, CroPA+Init 0.9209; per-task CroPA+Init: VQAgeneral 0.8723, VQAspecific 0.9457, Cls 0.7518, Cap 0.6138. Table 5 (cross-image) — CroPA 0.4355, CroPA+SCMix 0.7055, CroPA+CutMix 0.5565. Table 6 (BLIP-2, target 'Bomb') — Multi-P 0.68, CroPA 0.8433, CIA 0.4199, CroPA+D-UAP 0.9685 (note: BLIP-2 CroPA baseline differs between Table 4 and Table 6: 0.7958 vs 0.8433). Table 7 (OpenFlamingo) — Multi-P 0.6960, CroPA 0.7900, CIA 0.3027, CroPA+D-UAP 0.9270. Table 8 (cross-model) — CroPA transfer ≈0.03, D-UAP transfer ≈0.10; caption/label mismatch noted. Discussion/claims: authors assert CroPA excels at cross-prompt transfer, diffusion initialization yields higher ASRs without harming cross-prompt transferability, and D-UAP is a step toward universal perturbations, but these claims conflict with some reported tables and the modest cross-model/cross-prompt transfer results. Final part (current): authors state they reproduced key CroPA results and ran ablations but were compute-limited (prevented extensive hyperparameter tuning, ensembles, broader cross-model evaluation); recommend future work on encoder-agnostic methods and query-based optimization; no contact with original authors and a GitHub issue (BLIP-2/InstructBLIP) remained unresolved.

Title: Revisiting CroPA: reproducibility study + enhancements for cross-prompt adversarial transferability in VLMs. Authors (IIT Roorkee); note: authors marked as equal contributors. Abstract claims: (1) reproduce and validate CroPA (Cross-Prompt Attack) and confirm its superior cross-prompt transferability vs baselines; (2) propose three improvements: novel initialization strategy that significantly improves Attack Success Rate (ASR); investigation of cross-image transferability via learned universal perturbations; novel loss function targeting vision-encoder attention to improve generalization. Evaluation: performed across Flamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, and extended experiments on LLaVA; results reportedly validate original CroPA findings and show consistent improvement from proposed methods. Code link: https://github.com/Swadesh06/Revisting_CroPA. OpenReview link provided. No numeric results or tables in this part. No internal contradictions found in this section.

Title: Revisiting CroPA: reproducibility study + enhancements for cross-prompt adversarial transferability in VLMs. Authors: IIT Roorkee (equal contributors). Context: VLMs (e.g., BLIP, BLIP-2, Flamingo, InstructBLIP, LLaVA) are vulnerable to adversarial image/text attacks. Prior work classifies transferability into cross-model and cross-image; Luo et al. (2024) introduced Cross-Prompt Transferability and CroPA (learnable prompts to make adversarial images effective across textual prompts) and showed efficacy on classification, captioning, VQA. Goals claimed in this paper: (1) Reproducibility: successfully reproduced and verified four main claims of Luo et al.: CroPA’s superior cross-prompt transferability vs baselines (independent of target text semantics/word frequency); increasing number of prompts improves transferability but converges rapidly and baselines still don’t surpass CroPA; CroPA remains effective with extra in-context examples; reproduction of CroPA convergence via overall ASR across attack iterations plus per-task ASR analysis. (2) Extended work: (a) Better initialization strategy that substantially increases ASR and transferability; (b) Investigate cross-image transferability / Universal Adversarial Perturbations using CroPA backbone and image augmentation; (c) New loss function targeting vision-encoder attention by manipulating value vectors to improve generalization and ASR. Claims: in-depth analyses to explain mechanisms; code link provided. No numeric results given yet.

Section 2 (Related Work) recap: adversarial transferability spans cross-model (Liu et al. 2017; Tramèr et al. 2017), cross-image / Universal Adversarial Perturbations (Moosavi-Dezfooli et al. 2017; Mopuri et al. 2017), and cross-task transfer (Naseer et al. 2019a/b; Lu et al. 2020; Salzmann et al. 2021). Early VLM attacks targeted captioning and VQA on older CNN-RNN architectures (Xu et al. 2018/2019; Zhang et al.; Aafaq et al.; Chen et al.; Kaushik et al.; Kovatchev et al.; Li et al.; Sheng et al.). More recent work (Zhao et al. 2023) studied BLIP/BLIP-2 under black-box/cross-model transfer settings. CroPA (Luo et al. 2024) introduced cross-prompt adversarial transferability by optimizing learnable prompts jointly with image perturbations; the paper treats this as a new attack surface with few prior benchmarks. Yang et al. (2024) propose Context Injection Attack (CIA) — another cross-prompt method — and is used here as an additional comparison. Techniques to enhance transferability noted: input diversity (Xie et al. 2019), data augmentation (Wang et al. 2021), and addressing gradient misalignment (Li et al. 2023a; Wang et al. 2023). Connection to current paper: authors build on these insights to extend and improve CroPA (reproducibility of Luo et al.'s claims plus enhancements: better prompt initialization, cross-image/UAP experiments, and a new loss targeting vision-encoder attention/value vectors).

Repro study goal: reproduce Luo et al. (2024) CroPA and validate that it significantly improves cross-prompt transferability of adversarial examples. Four main claims to verify: (1) CroPA achieves cross-prompt transferability across various target texts; (2) CroPA achieves the best overall performance across different numbers of prompts; (3) CroPA converges to higher ASR as iterations increase; (4) CroPA outperforms baselines in few-shot settings. Beyond replication, authors will extend scope to cross-model and cross-image (including UAP) settings and compare CroPA to other cross-prompt methods (e.g., CIA) and baselines to test whether CroPA-generated adversarial images can consistently fool diverse VLMs regardless of prompt or model parameters. Planned methodological extensions noted earlier: improved prompt initialization, cross-image/UAP experiments, and a new loss targeting vision-encoder attention/value vectors. These claims and extensions will be checked against reproduced experiments and additional benchmarks.

(algorithm truncated). Note contradictions to check later: (1) algorithm uses the clean prompt x^i_t in image forward pass though paper claims to apply adversarial prompt x'^i_t per min-max; (2) no projection step shown after image update to enforce ||δ_v||_p ≤ ε (despite PGD claim). steps.notes_before: Repro goal: reproduce Luo et al. (2024) CroPA and validate cross-prompt transferability. Setup: VLM f(x_v,x_t); image perturbation constraint ||δ_v||_p ≤ ε. Objectives: targeted multi-prompt (sum L(f(x_v+δ_v,x_t^i),T)); non-targeted (maximize discrepancy). CroPA formulation (Eq.5): min_{δ_v} max_{δ_t} L(f(x_v+δ_v,x_t+δ_t),T). Implementation claims: iterative PGD style, image updates by gradient descent, prompt updates by gradient ascent, update-frequency N (image updated N times per prompt update). Algorithm (now complete): init x'_v=x_v; sample prompt x^i_t; lazy init x'^i_t=x^i_t; compute image gradient g_v = ∇_{x_v}L(f(x'_v,x^i_t),T) and update x'_v = x'_v - α1 sign(g_v) (note: forward pass uses clean prompt x^i_t); if mod(step,N)=0 compute prompt gradient g_t = ∇_{x_t}L(f(x'_v,x^i_t),T) and update x'^i_t = x'^i_t + α2 sign(g_t) (again gradient uses clean prompt in forward pass); project x'_v back to ε-ball: x'_v = Clip_{x_v,ε}(x'_v); return x'_v. Evaluation: only optimized image perturbation applied; prompt perturbations discarded. Key inconsistencies to track: algorithm uses clean prompt in forward passes despite min-max formulation (so adversarial prompts may not influence image updates); projection step is present in this part (resolves earlier omission).

Repro goal: reproduce Luo et al. (2024) CroPA and validate cross-prompt transferability. Setup: VLM f(x_v,x_t); image perturbation constraint ||δ_v||_p ≤ ε. Objectives: targeted multi-prompt and non-targeted formulations; CroPA min_{δ_v} max_{δ_t} L(f(x_v+δ_v,x_t+δ_t),T). Implementation (algorithm): iterative PGD-style; init x'_v=x_v; sample prompt x_t^i; lazy init x'^i_t=x_t^i; image update uses g_v = ∇_{x_v}L(f(x'_v,x_t^i),T) and x'_v ← x'_v - α1 sign(g_v) with forward pass using clean prompt x_t^i; every N steps compute g_t = ∇_{x_t}L(f(x'_v,x_t^i),T) and update x'^i_t ← x'^i_t + α2 sign(g_t) (again forward used clean prompt); project x'_v back into ε-ball; evaluation: only optimized image perturbation is applied; prompt perturbations discarded. Key implementation inconsistency to track: forward passes use clean prompt despite bi-level formulation (adversarial prompts may not influence image updates). From current part (Section 5): CroPA is effective on a single model but has poor transferability (authors cite Table 9, Appendix A.1; Table 1 shows poor performance on Classification and Captioning). CroPA is compute-intensive: reportedly >6 hours on a 48GB L40S GPU (95% VRAM) for 50 images. Goals: improve task consistency and transferability (cross-image and cross-model). Proposed method (5.1): Noise Initialization via Vision Encoding Optimization — replace random init with semantically informed init generated by diffusion (Stable Diffusion XL): x_target = D(T,z;θ_SDXL) (Eq.6). Align perturbation to x_target via vision-encoder features and optimize with an MSE loss to enforce semantic similarity while keeping adversarial effectiveness. Claims: reduces optimization steps, improves cross-prompt transferability; preliminary BLIP-2/InstructBLIP experiments show significant improvement at cost +20–25s per image. Points to later empirical evidence in Section 6.5.1 (Fig.7, Table 3) for sensitivity to initialization.

steps.notes_before: Repro goal: reproduce Luo et al. (2024) CroPA and evaluate cross-prompt/model transfer. Reproduced CroPA algorithm: iterative PGD-style with lazy prompt updates — image update uses gradients computed with the clean prompt; prompt updates computed every N steps also using clean prompt; project image back to ||·||_∞ ≤ ε; at evaluation only the optimized image perturbation applied and optimized prompts discarded. Implementation inconsistency: forward passes use clean prompts despite theoretical bi-level min_{δ_v} max_{δ_t} formulation (adversarial prompts may not affect image updates). CroPA is compute-heavy (>6 hrs on 48GB L40S GPU for 50 images). Proposed method (Sec 5.1): semantic noise init via diffusion SDXL: x_target = D(T,z;θ_SDXL) (Eq.6). Vision-encoder anchored init: δ_init = argmin_{||δ||_∞≤ε} || f_v(x+δ) - f_v(x_target) ||_2^2 (Eq.7). PGD refinement: x_adv^{t+1} = Π_{B_ε(x)}[ x_adv^{t} - α ∇_{x_adv^{t}} L_MSE ] (Eq.8) with L_MSE = || f_v(x_adv) - f_v(x_target) ||_2^2 (Eq.9). Sec 5.2: critique CroPA for lacking architectural sensitivity; propose joint CroPA + modified Doubly-UAP loss that targets value vectors in vision-attention layers (freeze text encoder), aiming to improve ASR and transferability. They plan to focus on two core attention components (list continues). Empirical sensitivity/benefits promised in Sec 6.5.1 (Fig.7, Table 3); SDXL init reportedly reduces optimization steps but costs +20–25s/image in BLIP-2/InstructBLIP experiments.

errors.claim: "Jointly minimize -ve of this loss along with the CroPA loss with proper scaling to ensure adversarial robustness and target alignment."
errors.evidence: Text: "Jointly minimize -ve of this loss along with the CroPA loss with proper scaling..." (5.2.1). Eq.11: "L_{\text{d-UAP}}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(1-\frac{V_{i}(x+\delta)\cdot V_{t}}{\|V_{i}(x+\delta)\|_{2}\|V_{t}\|_{2}}\right)". Eq.12: "L_{\text{re-CroPA}}=L_{\text{CroPA}}(x_{v}+\delta_{v},x_{t}+\delta_{t},T)-\lambda L_{\text{d-UAP}}(\delta_{v})".
errors.explanation: The text says to "minimize" the (negative) cosine-similarity loss (i.e. encourage alignment). But Eq.12 subtracts +λ L_d-UAP. If the combined objective L_re-CroPA is minimized as stated, the negative sign makes the optimizer prefer larger L_d-UAP (worse alignment). Thus the verbal instruction to jointly minimize the alignment loss contradicts the algebraic sign in Eq.12 unless they instead intend to maximize L_re-CroPA (which the text did not state).

steps.notes_before: Focus: attack vision encoder attention (weights and value vectors), targeting value vectors in mid-to-late layers. Baseline Doubly-UAP: δ* = argmax_δ (1/|L|) Σ_l Loss(V_l(x), V_l(x+δ)) (Eq.10). Modified D-UAP: derive target value vectors V_t from a reference image for target text T; extract perturbed head value vectors V_i(x+δ). Define L_d-UAP = Σ_{i=1}^N (1 - cosine(V_i(x+δ), V_t)) (Eq.11) to encourage alignment with target representation. They integrate with CroPA via L_re-CroPA = L_CroPA(x_v+δ_v,x_t+δ_t,T) - λ L_d-UAP(δ_v) (Eq.12). Text describes "jointly minimize" the (negative) cosine loss with CroPA, but Eq.12's subtraction creates an optimization-direction/sign inconsistency (minimize vs sign). Authors note potential limited transferability across models with different vision encoder architectures. Section 5.3 begins discussion of cross-image transferability and mentions UAPs and CutMix as augmentation strategies to improve universality.

Goal: attack vision-encoder attention (value vectors and heads), targeting mid-to-late layers. Baseline D-UAP: δ* = argmax_δ (1/|L|) Σ_l Loss(V_l(x), V_l(x+δ)) (Eq.10). Modified D-UAP: derive target value vectors V_t from a reference image for target text T; perturbed head value vectors V_i(x+δ). L_d-UAP = Σ_{i=1}^N (1 - cosine(V_i(x+δ), V_t)) (Eq.11). Integrated with CroPA as L_re-CroPA = L_CroPA(x_v+δ_v,x_t+δ_t,T) - λ L_d-UAP(δ_v) (Eq.12); earlier text claims “jointly minimize” but subtraction gives a sign/optimization-direction inconsistency. Authors note limited transferability across models with different vision-encoder architectures. Section 5.3 addresses cross-image transferability and augmentation strategies (UAPs, CutMix, SCMix). New content: ETU (Zhang et al. 2024) introduces SCMix (self-mix + cross-mix) to boost cross-image transferability; authors integrate SCMix into perturbation generation. SCMix self-mix: I1' = η X1 + (1-η) X2 where Xi = Resize(RandomCrop(I1)), they fix η = 0.5 (claim equivalence to α→∞ for Beta(α,α)). Cross-mix: I3 = β1 I1' + β2 I2 with β1 ≫ β2 (β2 ∈ [0,1)), to keep base-image semantics and text compatibility. CutMix (Yun et al. 2019): ṽx = M ⊙ xA + (1-M) ⊙ xB with M a rectangular binary mask (Eq.15). 5.4.1 threat model: attacker crafts a single perturbation to make multiple V-L models output a target text regardless of prompt; white-box access to surrogate (BLIP-2 or Flamingo), target models only known by architecture family (e.g., CLIP-based); L_inf budget ε = 16/255. Section cuts off before listing the two cross-model scenarios.

errors.claim: "The implementation follows an iterative approach using Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) Madry et al. (2017)."
errors.evidence: "To ensure real-world applicability, the authors constrain the adversarial perturbation δ_v within human-imperceptible bounds, enforcing ||δ_v||_p≤ε_v." and "The implementation follows an iterative approach using Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) Madry et al. (2017)." and Algorithm line: "Update with gradient descent: x'_{v}=x'_{v}-α_{1}·sign(g_{v})"
errors.explanation: PGD by definition includes a projection step to keep the perturbation within the L_p ball (||δ_v||_p ≤ ε_v). The presented algorithm shows only a sign-gradient update for x'_v and omits any projection/clipping step, so it does not implement (or at least does not show) PGD as claimed.

errors.claim: Eq.5 and text: "The algorithm optimizes both visual perturbation δ_v and prompt perturbation δ_t but with opposing objectives... min_{δ_v} max_{δ_t} L(f(x_v+δ_v,x_t+δ_t),T)"
errors.evidence: "min_{δ_{v}}\max_{δ_{t}}L(f(x_{v}+\delta_{v},x_{t}+\delta_{t}),T)" (Eq.5) versus Algorithm step 7: "Compute gradient for adversarial image : g_{v}=\nabla_{x_{v}}L(f(x^{\prime}_{v},x^{i}_{t}),T)" and earlier Algorithm step 5 initialises "x^{\prime i}_{t}=x^{i}_{t}"
errors.explanation: The min-max objective (Eq.5) implies losses/gradients should be computed using the perturbed prompt (x_t+δ_t), but the algorithm computes the image gradient using the original prompt x^{i}_{t} (not x^{\prime i}_{t}). Thus the algorithm as written does not reflect the stated min-max dependence on adversarial prompts.

errors.claim: Important internal issues to track later: algorithm omits projection to enforce ||δ_v||_p ≤ ε_v (contradicts PGD claim)
errors.evidence: This part, line 13: "Project x^{\prime}_{v} to be within the \epsilon -ball of x_{v} : x^{\prime}_{v}=\text{Clip}_{x_{v},\epsilon}(x^{\prime}_{v})"
errors.explanation: My earlier note asserted the pseudocode omitted the projection step; this part explicitly includes a projection/clip step, so the earlier claim is contradicted by the paper's algorithm as shown here.

errors.claim: Compute gradient for adversarial prompt: g_{t}=\nabla_{x_{t}}L(f(x^{\prime}_{v},x^{i}_{t}),T) and update x^{\prime i}_{t}=x^{\prime i}_{t}+\alpha_{2}\cdot\text{sign}(g_{t})
errors.location: this part (algorithm) vs CroPA min-max (Eq5) in earlier notes
errors.evidence: This part, line 10: "g_{t}=\nabla_{x_{t}}L(f(x^{\prime}_{v},x^{i}_{t}),T)" and line 11: "x^{\prime i}_{t}=x^{\prime i}_{t}+\alpha_{2}\cdot\text{sign}(g_{t})"; earlier formulation (Eq5) in notes: "CroPA: min_{\delta_v} max_{\delta_t} L(f(x_v+\delta_v,x_t+\delta_t),T)"
errors.explanation: The algorithm computes the prompt gradient using the original prompt x^{i}_{t} (not the current perturbed prompt x^{\prime i}_{t}) and then applies that gradient to update x^{\prime i}_{t}. That contradicts the stated min-max objective, which requires maximizing with respect to the current perturbed prompt (i.e., gradients should be evaluated at x^{\prime i}_{t}). The gradient is therefore evaluated at a different point than the variable being updated, inconsistent with the described CroPA optimization.

errors.claim: "our comprehensive evaluation of CroPA’s bi-level optimization framework in Section 6.5.1 reveals that its effectiveness is highly sensitive to initialization, as empirically verified in Figure 7 and Table 3."
errors.evidence: Earlier algorithm notes: "compute prompt gradient g_t = ∇_{x_t} L(f(x'_v, x^i_t), T) and update x'_t^i += α2·sign(g_t). ... Key objectives: CroPA defined as min_{δ_v} max_{δ_t} L(f(x_v+δ_v,x_t+δ_t),T). ... (2) However, the prompt gradient is computed using the original prompt x^i_t rather than the current perturbed prompt x'_t^i and then applied to x'_t^i — this mis-evaluates the ascent step and therefore does not implement the stated min-max (max over δ_t) correctly."
errors.explanation: The current part claims evaluation of CroPA's "bi-level optimization framework" (i.e., the intended min-max over prompt perturbations) but the algorithm implementation recorded earlier computes prompt gradients with respect to the original prompt x_t^i (not the current perturbed prompt), so the implementation does not actually realize the stated max-over-δ_t bi-level optimization. Thus calling it a bi-level optimization being evaluated is inconsistent with the earlier-recorded algorithmic behavior.

errors.claim: "This loss encourages the perturbed image’s value vectors to closely align with the target text’s representation."
errors.evidence: Eq.11: "L_{\text{d-UAP}}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(1-\frac{V_{i}(x+\delta)\cdot V_{t}}{\|V_{i}(x+\delta)\|_{2}\|V_{t}\|_{2}}\right)" (defines L_d-UAP as 1 - cosine), and Eq.12: "L_{\text{re-CroPA}}=L_{\text{CroPA}}(x_{v}+\delta_{v},x_{t}+\delta_{t},T)-\lambda L_{\text{d-UAP}}(\delta_{v})" (subtracts λ L_d-UAP in final objective).
errors.explanation: L_d-UAP = 1 - cosine should be minimized to increase cosine similarity (alignment). But Eq.12 subtracts λ L_d-UAP; minimizing L_re-CroPA will therefore encourage increasing L_d-UAP (i.e., increasing 1 - cosine ⇒ decreasing cosine), which is the opposite of the stated goal of encouraging alignment. The sign in Eq.12 contradicts the alignment claim.

errors.claim: Final combined objective given as L_re-CroPA = L_CroPA(...) - λ L_d-UAP (Eq.12).
errors.evidence: L_d-UAP = \sum_{i=1}^N (1 - cosine(V_i(x+\delta), V_t)) (Eq.11). Final combined objective given as L_re-CroPA = L_CroPA(...) - λ L_d-UAP (Eq.12).
errors.explanation: Since L_d-UAP is defined as (1 - cosine(...)), minimizing L_re-CroPA with a minus sign on λ L_d-UAP will drive L_d-UAP upward (because it is subtracted), i.e., reduce cosine similarity (anti-align the vectors). This contradicts the stated intent to enforce alignment between V_i(x+δ) and V_t. The sign/optimization direction is therefore inconsistent.

final_notes: Carry-forward summary: D-UAP introduced to improve cross-model and cross-image generalizability by targeting more general components of vision encoders; gives strong in-model ASRs and modest cross-model gains for architecturally similar models (BLIP-2 <-> InstructBLIP) but limited gains for very different architectures (BLIP-2 <-> Flamingo). CroPA vs trade-offs: CroPA optimizes against text embeddings and yields strong cross-prompt ASR but is architecture-tied (ASRs drop on transfer); D-UAP partially mitigates. Cross-image: CroPA couples to image-specific features; data augmentations (SCMix, CutMix) improve cross-image transfer but do not fully resolve tension. Initialization: diffusion-based semantic initialization boosts ASR and (authors claim) does not harm cross-prompt transfer; initialization influences trade-offs. Key empirical numbers to keep: cross-image mixing — CroPA base 0.4355; +SCMix 0.7055; +CutMix 0.5565. CroPA+Init strong gains (BLIP2 ~0.9209). D-UAP in-model uplift e.g., CroPA 0.8433 -> CroPA+D-UAP 0.9685 for BLIP2; cross-model examples: BLIP2->InstructBLIP 0.5065 -> 0.6850; BLIP2->Flamingo 0.1435 -> 0.2335. Open issues: ambiguous percent vs percentage-point reporting and CroPA BLIP2 baseline mismatches across tables. New from final part: authors state they reproduced key CroPA results and extensive ablations but were compute-limited (hyperparam sweeps, ensemble experiments infeasible); suggest future work on encoder-agnostic methods, improving cross-image generalization, and query-based optimization; no direct communication with original authors and a GitHub issue about BLIP-2 / InstructBLIP remains unresolved.

Title: Revisiting CroPA: reproducibility study + enhancements for cross-prompt adversarial transferability in VLMs. Authors: Atharv Mittal et al., all authors contributed equally (formatting of footnotes present). Paper reproduces "An Image is Worth 1000 Lies" Cross-Prompt Attack (CroPA) and confirms CroPA's superior cross-prompt transferability vs baselines. Proposed improvements: (1) novel initialization strategy that significantly improves Attack Success Rate (ASR), (2) study cross-image transferability via learned universal perturbations, (3) novel loss targeting vision-encoder attention mechanisms to improve generalization. Evaluated on Flamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, and extended experiments on LLaVA. Claims improvements consistently boost adversarial effectiveness. Code: GitHub link provided. Reviewed on OpenReview (link provided).

Title: Revisiting CroPA: reproducibility study + enhancements for cross-prompt adversarial transferability in VLMs. Authors contributed equally. Context: CroPA (Luo et al., 2024; “Cross-Prompt Attack”) introduces cross-prompt transferability and uses learnable prompts so adversarial images remain effective across textual prompts. Definitions: Cross-model transferability, Cross-image transferability (UAPs), and Cross-prompt transferability (CroPA). Reproduction goals: reproduced and verified four main claims from the original CroPA paper: (1) CroPA outperforms baselines in cross-prompt transferability across target texts and is independent of target text semantics/word frequency; (2) increasing number of prompts improves transferability but converges rapidly; even many prompts do not enable baselines to surpass CroPA; (3) CroPA remains effective with added in-context learning examples; (4) reproduced CroPA’s convergence behavior (ASR vs attack iterations) and added per-task ASR analysis. Extended contributions of this paper: (A) a novel initialization strategy that substantially increases Attack Success Rate (ASR) and transferability; (B) study of cross-image transferability / learning universal perturbations using CroPA backbone and image augmentations; (C) a novel loss targeting vision-encoder attention value vectors to improve generalization and ASR. Additional notes: authors provide code (GitHub) and OpenReview link; evaluations reportedly include Flamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, and extended LLaVA experiments. No contradictions found so far.

Paper: Revisiting CroPA — reproducibility study + enhancements for cross-prompt adversarial transferability in VLMs. Authors contributed equally. Context: CroPA (Luo et al., 2024) introduces cross-prompt transferability using learnable prompts so adversarial images remain effective across textual prompts. Reproduction goals: reproduce/verify four CroPA claims: (1) CroPA outperforms baselines in cross-prompt transferability and is independent of target text semantics/word frequency; (2) more prompts improves transferability but converges rapidly; baselines do not surpass CroPA even with many prompts; (3) CroPA remains effective with added in-context learning examples; (4) reproduced CroPA’s convergence behavior (ASR vs iterations) and added per-task ASR analysis. Paper contributions beyond reproduction: (A) novel initialization strategy that substantially increases ASR and transferability; (B) study of cross-image transferability / Universal Adversarial Perturbations (UAPs) using CroPA backbone + image augmentations; (C) new loss targeting vision-encoder attention value vectors to improve generalization and ASR. Code and OpenReview provided. Evaluations reported on Flamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, and extended LLaVA. Related work summarized: adversarial transferability across models, images (UAPs), and tasks; earlier VLM attacks targeted captioning/VQA on CNN–RNN models (lacking in-context learning); Zhao et al. (2023) examined BLIP/BLIP-2 for cross-model transferability; CroPA pioneered cross-prompt attacks via competing learnable prompts; Yang et al. (2024) proposed CIA (Context Injection Attack). Techniques to boost transferability include input diversity, augmentations, and approaches addressing gradient misalignment (Xie et al. 2019; Wang et al. 2021; Li et al. 2023a; Wang et al. 2023).

steps.notes_before: Paper: Reproducing/extending CroPA (Luo et al., 2024) for cross-prompt adversarial transferability in VLMs. Replication goals: verify four CroPA claims (cross-prompt transferability/outperformance of baselines; prompt-count scaling & convergence; robustness with in-context few-shot; ASR convergence and per-task analysis). Extensions: improved initialization, cross-model/cross-image (UAP) studies, attention-targeting loss. Eval models: Flamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, LLaVA. Methodology (this part): VLM f(x_v,x_t). Constrain image perturbation δ_v via ||δ_v||_p ≤ ε_v. Two attack types: targeted (Eq1: min_{δ_v} Σ_i L(f(x_v+δ_v,x_t^i),T)) and non-targeted (Eq2: max_{δ_v} Σ_i L(f(x_v+δ_v,x_t^i), f(x_v,x_t^i))). ASR: targeted requires exact target text; non-targeted = any change. Baselines: Single-P (Eq3) and Multi-P (Eq4). CroPA: min_{δ_v} max_{δ_t} L(f(x_v+δ_v,x_t+δ_t),T) (Eq5); claims to use PGD with image descent and prompt ascent, image updates N per prompt update. Algorithm pseudocode provided but truncated: initializes x'_v and x'_t^i, samples prompts, computes g_v and does sign update x'_v -= α1·sign(g_v), then 'if mod(step,N)=0 then' is left incomplete. Section 5 (this part): introduces Noise Initialization via Vision Encoding Optimization — generate a semantically relevant x_target with a diffusion model (SDXL): x_target = D(T, z; θ_SDXL), align initial perturbation to x_target in vision-encoder feature space using an MSE loss, aiming to reduce optimization steps and improve cross-prompt transferability. Claims: CroPA baseline is expensive (>6 hours on a 48GB L40S GPU for 50 images, 95% VRAM); diffusion init adds ~20–25s per image (prelim. tests on BLIP-2, InstructBLIP) and preserves visual fidelity while respecting ε budgets. CroPA algorithm (from earlier parts): iterative PGD-style updates for image and prompt perturbations. Implementation detail: prompt gradient was reported as g_t = ∇_{x_t} L(f(x'_v, x^i_t), T) and x'_t^i updated by a sign-step; after the prompt-ascent block x'_v is projected (x'_v = Clip_{x_v,ε}(x'_v)). At evaluation only the optimized image perturbation is applied; prompt perturbations are discarded. Stated high-level objective: min_{δ_v} max_{δ_t} L(f(x_v+δ_v, x_t+δ_t), T). Noted implementation caveat: prompt gradient appears computed w.r.t. original prompt x_t^i (not current x'_t^i), which would break the intended max-over-δ_t.

New in this part (Sec. 5.1.3–5.2): diffusion-based noise init using SDXL: x_target = D(T, z; θ_SDXL). Vision-encoder-anchored init: δ_init = argmin_{||δ||_∞ ≤ ε} || f_v(x+δ) - f_v(x_target) ||_2^2 (Eq.7). PGD refinement: x_adv^{(t+1)} = Π_{B_ε(x)}[ x_adv^{(t)} - α ∇_{x_adv^{(t)}} L_MSE ] (Eq.8) with L_MSE = || f_v(x_adv) - f_v(x_target) ||_2^2 (Eq.9). Claims: diffusion init reduces optimization steps and improves cross-prompt transferability; CroPA baseline expensive (>6 hours on a 48GB L40S for 50 images, 95% VRAM); diffusion init adds ~20–25s/image (prelim.). Sec.5.2 criticizes CroPA for treating vision and language uniformly and proposes integrating CroPA loss with a Doubly-UAP-style loss targeting value vectors of vision-attention layers (minimize losses between value vectors of image and reference), freezing text encoder; goals: better ASR, semantic alignment, transferability. Part ends saying they focus on two core attention components (not specified here).

steps.notes_before: Summary to carry forward: - CroPA typically outperforms Multi-P/Single-P; CroPA+Init showed strong gains (BLIP2 ~0.9209). - Cross-image mixing (6.5.2): CroPA base 0.4355; +SCMix 0.7055; +CutMix 0.5565 (SCMix adds +0.2700 absolute). - D-UAP (6.5.3): BLIP2 (target 'Bomb') Multi-P 0.75, CroPA 0.8433, CroPA+D-UAP 0.9685; Flamingo: CroPA 0.8233 -> CroPA+D-UAP 0.9270. - Cross-model (Table 8 snapshots): BLIP2->InstructBLIP CroPA 0.5065 -> D-UAP 0.6850; BLIP2->Flamingo 0.1435->0.2335; BLIP2->LLaVA 0.3040->0.5325; InstructBLIP->BLIP2 0.2288->0.4900; InstructBLIP->LLaVA 0.1345->0.3558; InstructBLIP->Flamingo 0.0598->0.1375. - Flamingo->* averages added earlier: e.g. Flamingo->BLIP2 Multi-P 0.0105, CroPA 0.0335, CroPA+D-UAP 0.1013. - New claims in this part: vision-encoder value vectors are approximately consistent across input images for a given target text; CroPA robust in few-shot (6.4); semantically-informed (diffusion) initialization (Sec 5.1) reportedly yields up to 15% Targeted ASR gains and fewer optimization steps; SCMix/CutMix boost cross-image transfer (paper states ~27% and ~12%, but earlier decimals indicate +0.2700 and +0.1210 absolute); D-UAP yields CroPA+D-UAP 0.9685 and is reported as a ~13.5% improvement (numeric mismatch with 0.8433 baseline: absolute +0.1252 = 12.52 pp, relative ≈14.85%). - Open issues to watch: CroPA BLIP2 baseline mismatch across tables (e.g. 0.7958 vs 0.8433), ambiguous use of 'percent' vs 'percentage points', and tension between 'value-vector consistency across images' and the observed benefit of cross-image augmentation.

Carry-forward summary: D-UAP: introduced to improve cross-model (and cross-image) generalizability by targeting more general components of vision encoders; helps for architecturally similar models (BLIP-2 <-> InstructBLIP) but gains are modest for very different architectures (BLIP-2 <-> Flamingo). Contextual Injection Attack was excluded from cross-model comparisons because it is non-transferable per authors. Trade-offs: (1) Cross-prompt vs cross-model — CroPA optimizes against text embeddings and yields strong cross-prompt ASR but is implicitly tied to target-model architecture (ASRs drop when transferred); D-UAP partially mitigates this. (2) Cross-prompt vs cross-image — CroPA couples perturbations to image-specific features, limiting cross-image generalization; data augmentations (SCMix, CutMix) improve cross-image transfer but do not fully resolve the tension. (3) Initialization — diffusion-based semantic initialization boosts ASR and (authors claim) does not harm cross-prompt transferability; starting point influences the balance between transfer types, though no single method maximizes all. Empirical highlights to retain: cross-image mixing (CroPA base 0.4355; +SCMix 0.7055; +CutMix 0.5565); CroPA+Init strong gains (BLIP2 ~0.9209); D-UAP yields high in-model ASRs (e.g., CroPA 0.8433 -> CroPA+D-UAP 0.9685 for BLIP2 in notes) and improves cross-model rates (examples: BLIP2->InstructBLIP 0.5065->0.6850; BLIP2->Flamingo 0.1435->0.2335). Open issues to keep: ambiguous percent vs percentage-point reporting and CroPA BLIP2 baseline mismatches across tables.

errors.claim: Q7X jointly optimizes image and prompt perturbations as a min-max (δ_v, δ_t) problem (equation (5)) and Algorithm 1 implements that joint optimization.
errors.evidence:
Equation (5) states the Q7X objective as: min_{δ_v} max_{δ_t} L(f(x_v+δ_v, x_t+δ_t), T). However Algorithm 1 computes the image gradient as
    g_v = ∇_{x_v} L(f(x'_v, x_t^i), T)
and the prompt gradient as
    g_t = ∇_{x_t} L(f(x'_v, x_t^i), T)
(i.e. both gradients are evaluated with x_t^i, not with the adversarial prompt variable x'_t^i).
errors.explanation: The algorithm's gradient calculations use the original prompt x_t^i rather than the adversarial prompt x'_t^i, contradicting the stated min-max formulation and the narrative that Q7X jointly optimizes δ_v and δ_t.

        Initialise x'_t^i = x_t^i
which checks whether x_t^i is initialised before setting x'_t^i.
errors.explanation: The condition as written checks the original prompt variable x_t^i rather than the adversarial prompt variable x'_t^i, which is inconsistent with the apparent intent to lazily initialize x'_t^i. This is a variable-use inconsistency in the algorithm pseudocode.

final_notes: Reproduction used authors' repo and original configs; BLIP-2/InstructBLIP required substantial debugging and had runtime/memory limits. Section 6 summary: comparisons among R4K, V9D, Q7X (Figs 5/6). Few-shot Flamingo: Q7X > V9D (Table 2: shot=0 C8H V9D=0.6095, Q7X=0.7708; shot=2 V9D=0.5730, Q7X=0.6635). Section 6.5 experiments: add initialization, attention/value guidance, and input-diversity. 6.5.1 Noise Init (B8N=CroPA+Init): paper reports B8N better on averages (Table 4 C8H 0.9209 vs Q7X 0.7958) but earlier Table 3 lists counterexamples (A7L/T4B, G9M). 6.5.2 Image augmentations J6T/U8G show measurable gains vs base Q7X (Table 5: Q7X base C8H=0.4355 → +J6T=0.7055, +U8G=0.5565); text sometimes claims U8G>J6T though tables often show J6T≥U8G. 6.5.3 Value-vector guidance P2F substantially improves targeted H2Q (Tables 6–7). 6.5.4 Value-guided transfer is encoder-dependent: BLIP2↔InstructBLIP transfer best; transfers to Flamingo poor (Table 8: BLIP2→InstructBLIP C8H=0.685; BLIP2→Flamingo 0.2335; Flamingo→others ≈0.10). Outstanding issues: model-count/list mismatch in Sec.6, targeted vs untargeted transfer inconsistencies, unresolved sign inconsistency in Eq.(12). Computational constraints limited replication depth and ensemble experiments.

Title: Revisiting CroPA: A Reproducibility Study and Enhancements for Cross-Prompt Adversarial Transferability in Vision-Language Models. Authors: Atharv Mittal, Agam Pandey, Amritanshu Tiwari, Sukrit Jindal, Swadesh Swain (all IIT Roorkee). Abstract key claims: reproducibility study of “An Image is Worth 1000 Lies: Adversarial Transferability Across Prompts on Vision-Language Models” validates Q7X and its superiority to existing baselines in N6Z; semantic meaning and target-word frequency do not determine transferability. Proposed/replicated enhancements: initialization, common perturbations across images, attention-directed loss; these extend the replication and consistently increase adversarial effectiveness. Evaluation across Flamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, and extended LLaVA; original results validated. Code: https://github.com/Swadesh06/Revisting_CroPA. OpenReview: https://openreview.net/forum?id=5L90cl0xtf. Note: author-table contains atypical/possibly malformed footnote markers (e.g., “††thanks: All authors contributed equally” for first author and repeated “11footnotemark: 1” entries for others). Also abstract contains unexplained tokens/labels (Q7X, N6Z) — treat them as method/dataset identifiers to verify later. No internal contradictions found in this part.

Title: Revisiting CroPA: A Reproducibility Study and Enhancements for Cross-Prompt Adversarial Transferability in Vision-Language Models. Authors: Mittal et al. Abstract claims: reproducibility study of "An Image is Worth 1000 Lies..."; validates Q7X and its superiority to baselines in N6Z; semantic meaning and target-word frequency do not determine transferability. Proposed/replicated enhancements: initialization, common/shared perturbations across images (UAPs), attention-directed loss / attention-based targeting; these consistently increase adversarial effectiveness. Evaluated models: Flamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, extended LLaVA. Many shorthand tokens used: F8V = Cross-Model Transferability (commonly called transferability), K3R = Cross-Image Transferability (admits shared perturbations/Z4P = UAPs), N6Z = Cross-Prompt Transferability. Other tokens: G9M, D5R refer to image datasets/tasks (and VQA mentioned). Luo et al. (2024) introduced N6Z and learnable prompts; attacks effective across textual inputs. Replication tests claim: superiority across target texts, rapid saturation with additional prompts, robustness to added in-context examples, convergence over attack iterations, plus task-wise analyses beyond aggregate. Extensions in this work: initialization improving H2Q and transferability, shared perturbations on Q7X backbone with transfer-promoting image augmentation, target value vectors/attention components govern patch interaction, and targeted manipulation proposed to improve generalization and H2Q. Paper will analyze mechanisms of these enhancements and the nature of VLM adversarial vulnerabilities. Note earlier observed odd/malformed footnote markers in author table and unexplained tokens; treat tokens as method/dataset identifiers.

errors.claim: Q7X jointly optimizes image and prompt perturbations as a min-max (δ_v, δ_t) problem (equation (5)) and Algorithm 1 implements that joint optimization.
errors.evidence:
Equation (5) states the Q7X objective as: min_{δ_v} max_{δ_t} L(f(x_v+δ_v, x_t+δ_t), T). However Algorithm 1 computes the image gradient as
    g_v = ∇_{x_v} L(f(x'_v, x_t^i), T)
and the prompt gradient as
    g_t = ∇_{x_t} L(f(x'_v, x_t^i), T)
(i.e. both gradients are evaluated with x_t^i, not with the adversarial prompt variable x'_t^i).
errors.explanation: The algorithm's gradient calculations use the original prompt x_t^i rather than the adversarial prompt x'_t^i, contradicting the stated min-max formulation and the narrative that Q7X jointly optimizes δ_v and δ_t.

errors.claim: Algorithm 1 initializes per-prompt adversarial variables correctly (i.e. initializes x'_t^i when needed).
errors.evidence:
Algorithm 1 contains the line:
    if x_t^i is not initialised then
        Initialise x'_t^i = x_t^i
which checks whether x_t^i is initialised before setting x'_t^i.
errors.explanation: The condition as written checks the original prompt variable x_t^i rather than the adversarial prompt variable x'_t^i, which is inconsistent with the apparent intent to lazily initialize x'_t^i. This is a variable-use inconsistency in the algorithm pseudocode.

steps.notes_before: 4 Methodology summary: 4.1 defines targeted objective (eq 1) min_{δ_v} Σ_{i=1}^k L(f(x_v+δ_v,x_t^i), T) and untargeted objective (eq 2) max_{δ_v} Σ L(f(x_v+δ_v,x_t^i), f(x_v,x_t^i)); H2Q = Attack Success Rate; perceptibility bound ||δ_v||_p ≤ ε_v. 4.2 describes baselines from Luo et al.: Single-P (R4K) eq (3) and Multi-P (V9D) eq (4); text again claims 'absent established N6Z baselines' (see flagged inconsistency with earlier mention of Yang et al.). 4.3 defines Q7X (Cross-Prompt Attack, CroPA) as eq (5) min_{δ_v} max_{δ_t} L(f(x_v+δ_v,x_t+δ_t), T) and describes iterative PGD-style updates: image updates K steps, prompt updates every N steps; Algorithm 1 given with inputs (f,T,x_v,X_t,ε,α1,α2,K,N). Pseudocode uses sign-gradient updates and clipping to ε-ball. Internal problems noted in algorithm: gradients are evaluated at x_t^i (original prompt) rather than at adversarial prompt x'_t^i despite the min-max objective; initialization conditional checks x_t^i instead of x'_t^i. steps.notes_before: Part 5: Reports Q7X performs poorly on G9M and D5R; S3D raises single-model H2Q but limits transferability (cites and Table 9 in Appendix). Resource/time table: Q7X training on 50 images >6 hours on 48GB L40S GPU (95% VRAM). Added initialization cost per image (single GPU) 20–25s. Reported metrics: Initialization aggregate accuracy gains 6–15%; initialization targeted H2Q gains up to 15%. P2F results: aggregate targeted H2Q = 96.85%; P2F increase over base Q7X reported as 12.5% (results) and 13.5% (discussion) — inconsistent. P2F A7L increase 13%; P2F D5R increase 28%. Value-guided F8V: G9M +14%, D5R +21%. J6T K3R aggregate increase ≈27%; U8G net increase over base K3R Q7X ≈12%. 5.1 W5J (diffusion-anchored initialization): eq (6) x_target = D(T,z;θ_SDXL) (SDXL); eq (7) δ_init = argmin_{||δ||_∞≤ε} ||f_v(x+δ)-f_v(x_target)||_2^2; Algorithm 2 in Appendix B. 5.1.4 refinement S3D: eq (8) x_adv^{t+1} = Π_{B_ε(x)}[x_adv^{t} - α ∇_{x_adv^{t}} L_{L6V}], with L_{L6V} defined in eq (9) as MSE of vision-encoder outputs. 5.2: target value-vector (middle/late vision layers) guidance adapted from D-UAP (Kim et al. 2024), here minimizing loss between value vectors of x_i and T_i rather than maximizing. Note: earlier Algorithm 1 had issues (gradients evaluated at original prompts x_t^i not adversarial prompts x'_t^i; initialization checks use x_t^i).

errors.claim: "The loss is described as encouraging closeness to the target representation; combined gradients update \u03b4, preserving adversarial character, N6Z, and guided semantic influence." (this part, 5.2.1)
errors.evidence: "L_{\mathrm{X9C}} = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left(1-\frac{V_i(x+\delta)\cdot V_t}{\|V_i(x+\delta)\|_2\|V_t\|_2}\right)" (Eq. 11); "L_{\mathrm{P2F}} = L_{\mathrm{Q7X}}(x_v+\delta_v,x_t+\delta_t,T) -\lambda L_{\mathrm{X9C}}(\delta_v)" (Eq. 12). Also earlier notes: "target value-vector ... here minimizing loss between value vectors of x_i and T_i rather than maximizing."
errors.explanation: Eq.11 defines L_X9C = 1 - cosine(V_i(x+\u03b4),V_t) (a distance-like loss). Eq.12 subtracts \u03bb L_X9C from L_Q7X, so minimizing L_P2F will, all else equal, increase L_X9C (because it appears with a negative sign). Increasing L_X9C decreases cosine similarity (moves V_i(x+\u03b4) away from V_t), which is the opposite of the claimed "encouraging closeness" and contradicts the earlier-stated intent to minimize value-vector distance to the target.

steps.notes_before: Motivation: attack vision-encoder internals (attention weights vs value vectors); middle-to-late-layer value vectors identified vulnerable. Eq.(10) standard objective: maximize loss between V_l(x) and V_l(x+δ). Modified approach (5.2.1): Eq.(11) L_X9C = sum_i (1 - cosine(V_i(x+δ), V_t)). Eq.(12) L_P2F = L_Q7X(x_v+δ_v,x_t+δ_t,T) - λ L_X9C(δ_v) and P2F = CroPA + D-UAP (re-CroPA). Text claims this encourages closeness to target representation, but the sign in Eq.(12) implies minimizing L_P2F will increase L_X9C (reduce cosine similarity) — sign inconsistency to resolve. Freezing text encoder; hypothesized encoder-dependence may limit transfer to models with different vision encoders. Augmentation for transferability (5.3): per-image gradients overfit; use across-image augmentations. J6T (SCMix/self+cross-mix) defined: I'_1 = η X_1 + (1-η) X_2 with η=0.5; I_3 = β1 I'_1 + β2 I_2 with β1 >> β2 in [0,1). U8G (CutMix) defined: \u007etilde{x} = M \odot x_A + (1-M) \odot x_B where M is a rectangular mask. Keep flagged sign issue for later cross-checks with results and Appendix algorithms.

steps.notes_before: Attack/setup: two transfer scenarios — model-transfer (5.4.1) and image-transfer/pattern (5.4.2). Surrogate white-box access (gradients + internals); surrogates used: BLIP-2 or Flamingo. Perturbation budget L_infty epsilon = 16/255. Model-transfer: described as seeking a single perturbation that elicits a specified target text across multiple VLMs (intra-family: optimize BLIP-2+OPT-2.7b, evaluate InstructBLIP+Vicuna-7b; cross-architecture: BLIP-2 <-> Flamingo). Image-transfer (pattern): aim for one pattern working on any image; limited training set, J6T augmentations (self+cross-mix variants) and CutMix (U8G) used; separate unseen test set; same epsilon. Evaluation: H2Q counts failure to generate correct output on target tasks, independent of prompt/content. Section 5.4.3 explicitly says all N6Z and F8V transferability results are presented under untargeted attacks and argues targeted transfer varies by encoder family; E3W excluded due to negligible transfer. Paper discussion overstates universality of semantic-noise gains and claims initialization raises H2Q without N6Z loss; experimental tables show mixed trade-offs. Computational/memory limits constrained Flamingo/BLIP-2 experiments and ensemble testing.

Paper: Revisiting CroPA — reproducibility + enhancements for cross-prompt adversarial transferability in VLMs (Atharv Mittal et al.). Goal: reproduce Luo et al. (2024) CroPA (Q7X) and extend it. Key labels/definitions: F8V = Cross-Model Transferability; K3R = Cross-Image Transferability; Z4P = shared/image-generalizing perturbations (UAPs); N6Z = Cross-Prompt Transferability; Q7X = CroPA (Luo et al. 2024); E3W = Context Injection Attack (CIA, Yang et al. 2024). Proposed extensions (from earlier parts): (1) improved initialization boosting H2Q and transferability, (2) shared/common perturbations across images (Z4P) aided by transfer-promoting image augmentation, (3) attention-directed manipulation of value vectors to control patch interactions and improve generalization/H2Q. Related work (this part): adversarial attacks extend across tasks (classification→detection) and models (Szegedy, Goodfellow, Naseer, Lu, Salzmann); cross-model transferability established (Liu, Tramèr); universal perturbations exist (Moosavi-Dezfooli, Mopuri); early VLM attacks targeted CNN–RNN pipelines and lacked in-context learning applicability; BLIP/BLIP-2 black-box study (Zhao et al. 2023) emphasized F8V rather than N6Z. Cross-prompt transferability is new with no standard benchmarks; Yang et al. (2024) provides CIA as an extra comparator to Q7X. Gradient misalignment and input diversity/augmentation (Li, Wang, Xie) are known to improve transferability and motivate the paper's Q7X-informed enhancements. Keep these points to check for consistency in methods, baselines, and claimed reproductions/results later.

Paper: Revisiting CroPA — reproduce Luo et al. (2024) CroPA (Q7X) and extend it. Reproducibility scope: faithfully reproduce Luo et al. procedures and test four named claims: (1) Q7X achieves N6Z across target texts; (2) Q7X has the best aggregate performance across prompt counts; (3) Q7X converges toward higher H2Q with increasing iterations; (4) Q7X outperforms baselines in few-shot settings. Extended scope in this work: evaluate F8V and K3R, compare to other N6Z methods (e.g., CIA), and test Q7X-generated images for consistent deception across diverse VLMs, prompts, and model parameters — i.e., broader robustness/versatility beyond original prompt-transfer claim. Proposed extensions to CroPA (from earlier parts): improved initialization to boost H2Q/transferability, creation of shared perturbations (Z4P/UAPs) aided by transfer-promoting image augmentations, and attention-directed manipulation of value vectors to control patch interactions and improve generalization. These items are the reference points for checking later methods/results for internal consistency.

steps.notes_before: Reproduction of Luo et al. CroPA (Q7X). Objectives: targeted ASR minimize over image perturbation (Eq.1): min_{δ_v} Σ_i L(f(x_v+δ_v,x_t^i), T). Untargeted objective (Eq.2) maximizes divergence from clean output: max_{δ_v} Σ_i L(f(x_v+δ_v,x_t^i), f(x_v,x_t^i)). Baselines: Single-P (Eq.3) and Multi-P (Eq.4) minimize target loss for one or many prompts. CroPA (Q7X) is min_{δ_v} max_{δ_t} L(f(x_v+δ_v,x_t+δ_t), T) (Eq.5); training uses image-gradient descent and prompt-gradient ascent (PGD-style), with image updates every step and prompt ascent every N steps. Algorithm 1: sample prompt uniformly each step, update x'_v by x'_v = x'_v - α_1·sign(g_v) (image PGD), update x'_t^i by ascent every N steps, and project x'_v via Clip_{x_v,ε}. Evaluation discards prompt perturbations and uses only optimized image. Noted internal issues: (1) pseudocode checks/initialises wrong variable (x_t^i vs x'_t^i), which would leave x'_t^i uninitialised; (2) paper states a general p-norm bound ||δ_v||_p ≤ ε_v but algorithm uses sign updates and Clip_{x_v,ε} (implying L_∞) and mismatched epsilon naming (ε vs ε_v). H2Q equated to ASR; intent to train adversarial prompts but evaluate only image perturbations.
