steps.notes_before: Reproduction target: Luo et al. CroPA (Q7X). Bi-level targeted ASR objective; baselines Single-P/Multi-P; CroPA = min_{δ_v} max_{δ_t} L(f(x_v+δ_v,x_t+δ_t), T). Algorithm 1 samples prompts, updates image and prompt (notes: pseudocode had var-init bug), image update in Alg1 recorded as sign-based PGD with Clip (implying ℓ_∞). Section 5 reports Q7X weak on G9M/D5R; S3D raises single-model H2Q but limits transfer. Resource/table: training on 50 images >6 hours on 48GB L40S (95% VRAM); per-image init overhead 20–25s; initialization aggregate accuracy gains 6–15%; init targeted H2Q gains up to 15%; P2F aggregate targeted H2Q 96.85%; P2F increase over base Q7X inconsistently listed as 12.5% (results) and 13.5% (discussion); P2F A7L +13%, D5R +28%; value-guided F8V: G9M +14%, D5R +21%; other reported increases: K3R/J6T ~27%, U8G ~12%. Proposed W5J: diffusion-anchored init via SDXL: x_target = D(T,z;θ_SDXL). δ_init = argmin_{||δ||_∞≤ε} || f_v(x+δ) - f_v(x_target) ||_2^2 (Eq.7). Adversarial refinement (Eq.8-9) minimizes L6V = || f_v(x_adv) - f_v(x_target) ||_2^2 with projection to ℓ_∞ ball. 5.2: guide perturbations via value vectors; adapt prior D-UAP component selection by minimizing value-vector differences to target text.

errors.claim: The loss is described as encouraging closeness to the target representation; combined gradients update \u03b4, preserving adversarial character, N6Z, and guided semantic influence.
errors.evidence:
Eq. (11): L_{\mathrm{X9C}} = \sum_{i=1}^{N} (1 - (V_i(x+\delta)\cdot V_t)/(\|V_i(x+\delta)\|_2\|V_t\|_2)).
Eq. (12): L_{\mathrm{P2F}} = L_{\mathrm{Q7X}}(x_v+\delta_v,x_t+\delta_t,T) - \lambda L_{\mathrm{X9C}}(\delta_v).
errors.explanation: Minimizing L_{\mathrm{P2F}} as written (L_Q7X - \u03bb L_X9C) causes gradient-descent updates that increase L_X9C (because the update includes +\u03bb \nabla L_X9C), i.e. increase 1 - cosine similarity and thus reduce similarity to V_t. This is the opposite of the stated aim to 'encourage closeness to the target representation.'

steps.notes_before: Reproduction target: Luo et al. CroPA (Q7X) — bi-level targeted ASR: min_{\delta_v} max_{\delta_t} L(f(x_v+\delta_v,x_t+\delta_t), T). Alg1: per-image sign-PGD with Clip (implies \ell_\infty); pseudocode var-init bug noted. Resource: 50 images >6h on 48GB L40S; per-image init overhead 20–25s; init gains 6–15%; P2F aggregate targeted H2Q 96.85%; reported P2F increases vs base Q7X inconsistently 12.5%/13.5%; per-dataset increases (A7L +13%, D5R +28%, etc.). W5J: diffusion-anchored init via SDXL: x_target = D(T,z;\theta_SDXL); \delta_init = argmin_{\|\delta\|_\infty\le\epsilon} ||f_v(x+\delta)-f_v(x_target)||_2^2 (Eq.7); adversarial refinement minimizes L6V = ||f_v(x_adv)-f_v(x_target)||_2^2 with projection. Section 5.2: target encoder internals (attention weights, value vectors); prior work finds middle-to-late-layer value vectors vulnerable. Eq.(10) X9C original: maximize representation change: \delta^*=argmax_\delta (1/|L|)\sum_{l\in L} Loss(V_l(x),V_l(x+\delta)). New loss (Eq.11) L_X9C = \sum_{i=1}^N (1 - cos(V_i(x+\delta),V_t)). Combined objective (Eq.12) L_P2F = L_Q7X(...) - \lambda L_X9C(\delta_v). Text claims this encourages closeness to target V_t, but Eq.(12)'s subtraction means minimizing L_P2F will increase L_X9C (decrease cosine similarity). Section 5.3: per-image gradients overfit; investigate cross-image augmentations. J6T (SCMix-like): I'_1 = \eta X_1+(1-\eta)X_2, \eta fixed=0.5; I_3 = \beta_1 I'_1+\beta_2 I_2 with \beta_1\gg\beta_2. U8G (CutMix-like): \tilde{x}=M\odot x_A+(1-M)\odot x_B with rectangular mask M.

Study of Cross-Prompt Attack (CroPA) across textual prompts in Vision-Language Models (VLMs). Paper reproduces four claims: cross-prompt transferability, prompt counts, convergence, and few-shot evaluation. Additional tests: semantically guided initialization, loss targeting vision-encoder value vectors, and image augmentation for cross-image transfer. Main reported outcomes: CroPA outperforms baselines; task-level convergence can be unstable. Guided initialization improves overall targeted ASR (defined as proportion of successful attacks). Value-vector enhancement achieves 96.85% targeted ASR on BLIP-2. Image augmentation improves cross-image results but cross-image transfer remains limited. Cross-model transfer improves most between models with similar vision encoders.

steps.notes_before: Paper studies CroPA (Cross-Prompt Attack): bi-level/min-max optimization of image and prompt perturbations with opposing objectives across VLM prompts/tasks. Targeted success requires exact target text; untargeted requires output different from clean prediction. Warning: ASR is used inconsistently in the paper (expanded both as 'Attack Success Rate' and 'Adversarial Success Rate' in Section 5.2). CroPA variants: Single-P, Multi-P, CroPA+Init (Noise Initialization via Vision Encoding Optimization aligning perturbed image's vision-encoder rep to an SDXL-generated target via MSE), CroPA+D-UAP (value-vector loss adapted from Doubly-UAP), re-CroPA = combined objective (Eq.12). Image augmentations: SCMix (self-mixing + cross-mixing), CutMix; used to improve cross-image transfer. Key losses/methods: PGD, MSE, language-modeling loss (minimized for image perturbations, maximized for prompt perturbations in targeted CroPA). Models: BLIP-2 (frozen CLIP encoder + Querying Transformer + OPT-2.7b), InstructBLIP (Vicuna-7b), LLaVA (CLIP ViT-L -> Vicuna-13B), OpenFlamingo-9B. Other terms: UAP, value vectors/attention heads, CLIP score, input diversity, cross-prompt/cross-image/cross-model transfer, in-context few-shot (0-/2-shot). Runtime example: L40S (48GB GPU) with ~95% VRAM. Example targets: "unknown", "I am sorry", "not sure", "very good", "too late", "metaphor", "bomb", "Bomb". Note the glossary also flags an internal naming inconsistency for CIA (Context Injection vs Contextual Injection).

Paper defines symbols for CroPA: f (VLM), f_v (vision encoder), x_v (visual input), x_t (text prompt), X_t={x_t^1...x_t^k} (prompt set), k (number of prompts), T (predetermined target text). Perturbations: δ_v (image), δ_t (prompt), δ (generic/bold), δ_init (MSE-based initialization aligning vision-encoder rep to SDXL-generated target x_target), δ* (from Doubly-UAP). Constraints: ε_v, ε (permitted magnitudes), ||·||_p with ||·||_∞ used; projection Clip_{x_v,ε} / Π_{B_ε(x)}. Algorithm 1 vars: x_v' (returned adv image), x_t'^{i} (adversarial prompt i), g_v/g_t (image/prompt gradients), ∇, α1/α2 (image/prompt step sizes), K (iterations), N (prompt-update interval; also used as number of attention heads in Eq.11), step, sign(·), mod(step,N). Losses: L (language-modeling loss; note L also used to index selected layers in Eq.10), L_MSE (squared vision-encoder rep diff), L_d-UAP (value-vector loss), L_CroPA, L_re-CroPA (combined Eq.12) with weight λ. Value vectors: V_l(x) (layer l), V_i(x+δ) (head i), V_t (target text reference). SCMix/CutMix: I1 base, I1' self-mixed, I2 secondary, I3 final; T1 base text kept for synthetic image; η self-mixing weight fixed at 0.5 in this study (original SCMix samples η ~ Beta(α,α); α→∞ ≈ fixed 0.5). CutMix: x_A,x_B → ṽx via mask M (dimensions W,H) with ⊙. Diffusion: 𝒟 process, z Gaussian input, θ_SDXL pretrained weights produce x_target. Notes: several symbols are overloaded (α used as PGD step size in Eq.8 and as Beta-distribution parameter in SCMix; α1/α2 used in Alg.1; L used both as loss and layer-set index; N used in two roles; t used for iteration indices). No direct internal contradictions found in this part.

Perturbations: δ_v (image), δ_t (prompt), δ (generic), δ_init (MSE-based initialization aligning vision-encoder rep to SDXL-generated x_target), δ* (from Doubly-UAP). Constraints: ε_v, ε; norms ||·||_p (∞ used), projection Clip_{x_v,ε}/Π_{B_ε(x)}. Algorithm 1 variables: x_v' (returned adv image), x_t'^{i} (adversarial prompt i), g_v/g_t (image/prompt gradients), ∇, α1/α2 (step sizes), K (iterations), N (prompt-update interval; also used as #attention heads), step, sign(·), mod(step,N). Losses: L (language-modeling loss; L also used to index selected layers), L_MSE (squared vision-encoder rep diff), L_d-UAP (value-vector loss), L_CroPA, L_re-CroPA (combined, weight λ). Value vectors: V_l(x), V_i(x+δ), V_t. Augmentations: SCMix/CutMix (SCMix uses η fixed=0.5 in this study), CutMix uses mask M. Diffusion: 𝒟; SDXL pretrained θ_SDXL produces x_target. steps.notes_before:
Method summary: Targeted and non-targeted cross-prompt attacks optimize bounded image perturbations (||δ_v||_p ≤ ε_v). Targeted objective (Eq.1) minimizes L(f(x_v+δ_v,x_t^i), T) across k prompts; non-targeted (Eq.2) maximizes discrepancy L(f(x_v+δ_v,x_t^i), f(x_v,x_t^i)). ASR: targeted requires exact target string; non-targeted success if output differs from clean.

Baselines: Single-P (Eq.3) optimizes with one prompt; Multi-P (Eq.4) optimizes over a prompt set. The paper also states there are "no established literature baselines" (internal inconsistency with other sections that cite prior methods).

CroPA: min_{δ_v} max_{δ_t} L(f(x_v+δ_v,x_t+δ_t),T) (Eq.5). Uses PGD: image gradient descent, prompt gradient ascent, prompt-update interval N (N image updates per prompt update), step sizes α1, α2, iterations K; clip x_v' to ε-ball. Evaluation discards prompt perturbations and applies only the optimized image perturbation.

Algorithm 1: inputs f,T,x_v,X_t,ε,α1,α2,K,N; initializes x_v'=x_v; samples prompt each step; updates x_v' each step and x_t' periodically; returns x_v'. Algorithm contains inconsistent variable/gradient notation (gradients taken w.r.t. unprimed vars, wrong init check for prompt) that must be resolved when checking implementation/results.

Key reported numbers to verify later (from earlier notes): Table1 CroPA per-target Overall ASRs [0.7708,0.7985,0.5033,0.7020,0.6920,0.8680]; Table2 few-shot (shot=2) CroPA Overall=0.6635; Table3 CroPA+Init Overall ~[0.8977,0.9260,0.9458,0.8761,0.9333]; Table5 augmentations Overall [0.7055,0.5565]; Table6 CroPA+Doubly-UAP Overall=0.9685. Keep these for later consistency checks.

Noise Initialization (5.1): claim that CroPA uses random-noise init (contradicted by Algorithm 1). Proposed SDXL-based target synthesis x_target = D(T,z;θ_SDXL). Reported improvements: Table3 shows CroPA vs CroPA+Init pairs 0.7708/0.8977, 0.8433/0.9260, 0.7985/0.9458, 0.8190/0.8761, 0.8535/0.9333; Fig.7 shows faster convergence and CLIP scores 21.80→23.09. errors.claim: The paper claims the adapted value-vector loss "encourages alignment with the target text representation" and combines it with CroPA via Eq (12) L_re-CroPA = L_CroPA - λ L_d-UAP to jointly minimize for alignment.
errors.location: this part (Section 5.2, Eqs. 11–12 and surrounding text)
errors.evidence: Eq. (11) defines L_d-UAP = sum_{i=1}^N (1 - cosine(V_i(x+δ), V_t)) (a loss that is small when cosine is large). Eq. (12) defines L_re-CroPA = L_CroPA(...) - λ L_d-UAP(δ_v). The text also says they "compute cosine similarity loss... Jointly minimize -ve of this loss..." and "This loss encourages alignment with the target text representation."
errors.explanation: As written, L_d-UAP = 1 - cos is a loss to be minimized to increase cosine. But Eq. (12) subtracts λ L_d-UAP from L_CroPA; minimizing L_re-CroPA = L_CroPA - λ(1 - cos) is (up to a constant) equivalent to minimizing L_CroPA + λ cos, which penalizes larger cosine and therefore discourages alignment. The sign convention in Eq. (12) (and the textual description of minimizing the 'negative' loss) is inconsistent with the stated goal of enforcing alignment.

steps.notes_before: CroPA summary: bi-level attack min_{δ_v} max_{δ_t} L(f(x_v+δ_v,x_t+δ_t), T) (Eq.5). PGD: image descent, prompt ascent; image updates via Eq.(8) projection into ℓ_∞ ball; MSE vision loss Eq.(9): ||f_v(x_adv)-f_v(x_target)||_2^2. Section 5.1 proposed SDXL-based target synthesis and vision-encoder-anchored init (Eq.7) — reported strong ASR gains (Table3 CroPA vs CroPA+Init pairs: 0.7708→0.8977, 0.8433→0.9260, 0.7985→0.9458, 0.8190→0.8761, 0.8535→0.9333). Combined objective given as L_re-CroPA = L_CroPA - λ L_d-UAP (Eq.12) and claimed to improve alignment, transferability, and robustness. CroPA summary (earlier): bi-level attack min_{δ_v} max_{δ_t} L(f(x_v+δ_v,x_t+δ_t),T) (Eq.5). PGD used: image descent, prompt ascent; image updates projected into L_∞ ball (Eq.8). Vision loss MSE: ||f_v(x_adv)-f_v(x_target)||_2^2 (Eq.9). Evaluation reportedly discards prompt perturbations and uses only optimized image perturbation. Sec.5.1: SDXL-based target synthesis and vision-encoder-anchored init (Eq.7) claimed strong ASR gains (Table 3 CroPA→CroPA+Init pairs: 0.7708→0.8977, 0.8433→0.9260, 0.7985→0.9458, 0.8190→0.8761, 0.8535→0.9333). Sec.5.2: adapted Doubly-UAP to target value vectors (standard D-UAP maximizes inter-value divergence Eq.10; modified L_d-UAP (Eq.11) = sum(1 - cosine(V_i(x+δ), V_t)) to align values; combined objective L_re-CroPA = L_CroPA - λ L_d-UAP (Eq.12)). New (current) part: hypothesis that transfer may be limited to models with same/similar vision-encoder architectures. To improve cross-image transfer, integrate image augmentations SCMix and CutMix. SCMix: self-mixing I1' = η X1 + (1-η) X2 with X_i = Resize(RandomCrop(I1)), fixed η=0.5 (Eq.13); original SCMix samples η ~ Beta(α,α), they fix η=0.5 (claimed equivalent to α→∞). Cross-mixing: I3 = β1 I1' + β2 I2 with β1 ≫ β2 ∈ [0,1) (Eq.14). CutMix: "+"-style hard replacement ∴ x̃ = M ⊙ x_A + (1-M) ⊙ x_B with rectangular mask M (Eq.15). Sec.5.4 attack setup: use D-UAP for cross-model transfer; adversary goal: one perturbation per image to force multiple VLMs to produce target text regardless of prompt; white-box access to surrogate model (BLIP-2 or Flamingo) including gradients; target models only known by architecture family (e.g., CLIP-based); L_∞ budget ε = 16/255.

errors.claim: "This loss encourages alignment with the target text representation."
errors.explanation: L_{d-UAP} is 1 - cosine, so minimizing L_{d-UAP} increases cosine similarity (alignment). However equation (12) subtracts \u03bb L_{d-UAP} from L_{CroPA}; if the overall objective L_{re-CroPA} is minimized, the negative sign makes the optimizer favor increasing L_{d-UAP} (i.e., decreasing cosine similarity). Thus the written objective (12) contradicts the claim that the loss "encourages alignment" — the sign in (12) would encourage misalignment.

errors.claim: Combined objective given as L_re-CroPA = L_CroPA(x_v+δ_v,x_t+δ_t,T) - λ L_d-UAP(δ_v) (eq 12).

errors.explanation: Because L_d-UAP is defined as sum(1 - cos(...)), subtracting λ·L_d-UAP in an objective being minimized exerts pressure to increase (1 - cos) (i.e., decrease cos), which is the opposite of the stated aim to encourage alignment (increase cos) with the target vectors.

Paper studies Cross-Prompt Attack (CroPA) for VLMs; asks if adversarial images remain effective across different textual prompts. Reproduces four claims relating to cross-prompt transferability, prompt counts, convergence, and few-shot evaluation. Methods tested: semantically guided initialization, a loss targeting vision-encoder value vectors, and image augmentation for cross-image transfer. Main reported results: CroPA outperforms baselines; task-level convergence can be unstable. Guided initialization improves overall targeted Attack Success Rate (ASR) (ASR = proportion of successful attacks). Value-vector enhancement achieves 96.85% targeted ASR on BLIP-2. Image augmentation improves cross-image transfer but cross-image transfer remains limited. Cross-model transfer improves most between models that share similar vision encoders.

steps.notes_before: Paper studies CroPA (Cross-Prompt Attack) for VLMs: alternating/min-max optimization of image perturbations (PGD) and adversarial prompt perturbations. Key methods: Noise Initialization via Vision Encoding Optimization (aka semantically guided initialization; uses SDXL to synthesize target image and MSE to align vision-encoder outputs), value-vector enhancement adapted from Doubly-UAP (D-UAP / d-UAP) targeting vision-encoder value vectors, and input-augmentation (SCMix: self-mixing + cross-mixing) to improve cross-image transfer. Baselines: Single-P (one prompt), Multi-P (multiple prompts). Variants: CroPA+Init (Init), CroPA+D-UAP, re-CroPA (combined objective). Metrics: ASR reported (paper uses the abbreviation ASR both as "Attack Success Rate" and alternatively as "Adversarial Success Rate" in Section 5.2 — ambiguous). Targeted vs non-targeted ASR defined (targeted requires exact target text). Models: BLIP-2 (frozen CLIP encoder + Querying Transformer + OPT-2.7b), InstructBLIP (Vicuna-7b), LLaVA (CLIP ViT-L encoder + Vicuna-13B), OpenFlamingo. Notable reported findings (from earlier parts): CroPA outperforms baselines; value-vector enhancement achieves ~96.85% targeted ASR on BLIP-2; image augmentation helps cross-image transfer but transfer remains limited; cross-model transfer better when vision encoders are similar. Other useful refs: PGD, MSE, UAP, CLIP score, perturbation budget, L40S (48GB GPU, 95% VRAM example).

steps.notes_before: Revisiting CroPA (joint image PGD + learned prompt perturbations). Key components recalled: diffusion-based noise initialization (SDXL target image → δ_init via MSE between vision-encoder outputs); value-vector guidance (D-UAP style loss targeting value vectors V_l(x)); SCMix augmentation (self-mixing weight η fixed at 0.5 in this work); algorithm uses K iterations with step sizes α1/α2 for image/prompt (paper reuses symbol α ambiguously). Evaluated models: Flamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, extended LLaVA. Reproduction goals: reproduce CroPA claims (Table 1 CroPA Overall ASRs = [0.7708,0.7985,0.5033,0.7020,0.6920,0.8680]); CroPA with Init (Table 3) overall = [0.8977,0.9260,0.9458,0.8761,0.9333]; SCMix/CutMix overall (Table 5) = 0.7055 / 0.5565; CroPA+D-UAP overall (Table 6) = 0.9685. Introduction reiterates goals: reproducibility, better initialization, cross-image transferability, and (per Introduction) a loss targeting value vectors. Note internal inconsistency: abstract earlier claimed the third enhancement was an attention-targeting loss, but Introduction describes targeting value vectors.

Related works overview: adversarial transferability spans cross-model, cross-image (UAPs), and cross-task settings; prior VQA and image-captioning attacks often targeted attention mechanisms but focused on older CNN-RNN architectures. Modern VLM work (e.g., Zhao et al. 2023) studied BLIP/BLIP-2 in black-box, cross-model settings. CroPA (Luo et al. 2024) is described as jointly optimizing image perturbations and learnable prompts to improve cross-prompt transferability; CIA (Yang et al. 2024) is another recent cross-prompt method (Context Injection Attack). Paper motivates extensions to CroPA via input diversity, augmentations, and gradient-alignment literature.

Key method facts from earlier parts to carry forward: CroPA = joint image PGD + learned prompt perturbations; diffusion-based initialization: δ_init derived from an SDXL target image by minimizing MSE between vision-encoder outputs; loss that the Introduction called a value-vector-targeting loss (targets value vectors V_l(x)), though the abstract earlier claimed an attention-targeting loss (noted inconsistency). SCMix augmentation used, with self-mixing weight η fixed to 0.5. Algorithm uses K iterations and separate step sizes for image vs prompt (paper reused symbol α ambiguously). Evaluated models: Flamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, extended LLaVA.

Reproduction targets (from earlier notes): CroPA Table 1 overall ASRs = [0.7708, 0.7985, 0.5033, 0.7020, 0.6920, 0.8680]; CroPA+Init Table 3 overall = [0.8977, 0.9260, 0.9458, 0.8761, 0.9333]; SCMix / CutMix overall (Table 5) = 0.7055 / 0.5565; CroPA+D-UAP overall (Table 6) = 0.9685. Keep these numbers and the value-vector vs attention-targeting inconsistency in mind when reading methods/results.

Paper goal: reproduce and extend Luo et al. (2024) CroPA (joint image PGD + learnable prompt perturbations) to confirm improved cross-prompt transferability. Key method points: CroPA jointly optimizes image perturbation and prompt tokens; diffusion-based initialization δ_init obtained by minimizing MSE between vision-encoder outputs of image and target SDXL image; loss in Methods described as targeting value vectors V_l(x) but earlier abstract called it an attention-targeting loss (internal inconsistency flagged). SCMix augmentation used with self-mixing weight η = 0.5. Algorithm uses K iterations and separate step sizes for image vs prompt; paper reuses symbol α ambiguously. Evaluated models: Flamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, extended LLaVA. Reproduction numeric targets noted from earlier parts: CroPA Table 1 overall ASRs = [0.7708, 0.7985, 0.5033, 0.7020, 0.6920, 0.8680]; CroPA+Init Table 3 overall = [0.8977, 0.9260, 0.9458, 0.8761, 0.9333]; SCMix / CutMix overall (Table 5) = 0.7055 / 0.5565; CroPA+D-UAP overall (Table 6) = 0.9685. New in this part: the reproducibility scope lists four claims to test: (1) cross-prompt transferability across target texts; (2) best overall performance across different numbers of prompts; (3) ASR improves as iterations increase (convergence); (4) outperforms baselines under few-shot settings. They also state they will extend evaluation to cross-model and cross-image effectiveness. Keep earlier noted value-vector vs attention-targeting wording inconsistency and ambiguous step-size symbol in mind for later parts.

steps.notes_before: Paper goal: reproduce/extend CroPA (joint image + learnable prompt perturbations) to improve cross-prompt transfer. Key objectives: targeted attacks (min_{δ_v} sum_i L(f(x_v+δ_v,x_t^i),T)), non-targeted (maximize discrepancy). CroPA objective: min_{δ_v} max_{δ_t} L(f(x_v+δ_v,x_t+δ_t),T). Baselines: Single-P (eq 3), Multi-P (eq 4). Implementation (Section 4): uses PGD; inputs: model f, target T, x_v, prompt set X_t, perturb size ε, step sizes α_1, α_2, iterations K, prompt-update interval N. Algorithm samples a prompt x_t^i each step, updates image every iteration (descent via sign(g_v)) and updates the prompt every N steps (ascent via sign(g_t)), then clips x_v' to ε-ball. Evaluation discards prompt perturbations and uses only the optimized image perturbation. Important inconsistency found in pseudocode: gradients g_v and g_t are computed using x_t^i (the original prompt) but the prompt update is applied to x_t^{\prime i}; the forward/backprop does not use x_t^{\prime i}, so the code as written does not implement the stated min–max over perturbed prompts. Keep earlier flagged items for later checks: diffusion-based initialization δ_init (MSE on vision-encoder outputs to SDXL image), wording mismatch about loss (value vectors V_l(x) vs attention-targeting), SCMix (η=0.5), ambiguous α in other parts, evaluation targets/numeric reproduction goals, cross-model and cross-image extension plans.

errors.claim: Section 6.5.1, Figure 7, and Table 3 show that CroPA’s bi-level optimization—its opposing image and prompt objectives—is highly sensitive to initialization.
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: "Important inconsistency found in pseudocode: gradients g_v and g_t are computed using x_t^i (the original prompt) but the prompt update is applied to x_t^{\prime i}; the forward/backprop does not use x_t^{\prime i}, so the code as written does not implement the stated min–max over perturbed prompts."
errors.explanation: The current part attributes sensitivity to CroPA's bi-level (min–max) image-vs-prompt optimization, but the paper's own pseudocode (earlier) shows the implementation does not actually perform the stated perturbed-prompt min–max (prompt updates are not used in the forward/backprop). Therefore the paper cannot consistently claim observed sensitivity is due to a bi-level optimization that it did not implement.

steps.notes_before:
Goal: reproduce/extend CroPA (joint image + learnable prompt perturbations) to improve cross-prompt transfer. CroPA objective: min_{δ_v} max_{δ_t} L(f(x_v+δ_v,x_t+δ_t),T). Implementation: PGD; image updated each iter, prompt updated every N steps; evaluation discards prompt perturbations and uses only optimized image δ_v. Pseudocode bug: gradients g_v and g_t computed using original prompt x_t^i but prompt update applied to x_t'^{i}, so forward/backprop does not implement the claimed min–max.
Part 5 adds diffusion-based initialization: synthesize x_target = D(T,z;θ_SDXL) and compute δ_init = argmin_{||δ||_∞≤ε} ||f_v(x+δ)-f_v(x_target)||_2^2 (MSE in vision-encoder space), then refine via PGD. Claims: faster convergence, improved cross-prompt transfer. Reported evidence: Table 3 CroPA vs CroPA+Init pairs (0.7708/0.8977, 0.8433/0.9260, 0.7985/0.9458, 0.8190/0.8761, 0.8535/0.9333) and CLIP scores 21.80→23.09. Preliminary BLIP-2/InstructBLIP: +20–25s/image overhead. CroPA compute claim: training 50 images >6 hours on an L40S 48GB GPU using ~95% VRAM. Flagged inconsistency: paper credits sensitivity to bi-level optimization despite earlier pseudocode that does not implement the min–max prompt perturbation.

errors.claim: "This loss encourages alignment with the target text representation."
errors.explanation: L_{d-UAP} is 1 - cosine, so minimizing L_{d-UAP} increases cosine similarity (alignment). However equation (12) subtracts \u03bb L_{d-UAP} from L_{CroPA}; if the overall objective L_{re-CroPA} is minimized, the negative sign makes the optimizer favor increasing L_{d-UAP} (i.e., decreasing cosine similarity). Thus the written objective (12) contradicts the claim that the loss "encourages alignment" — the sign in (12) would encourage misalignment.

steps.notes_before: PGD refinement: eq (8) updates x_adv with step size \u03b1 and projection to L_infty ball; MSE refinement loss eq (9): L_MSE = ||f_v(x_adv)-f_v(x_target)||_2^2. Introduce value-vector targeting (Doubly-UAP): standard Doubly-UAP maximizes per-layer Loss(V_l(x),V_l(x+\delta)) (eq 10). Modified D-UAP defines L_d-UAP = sum_{i=1}^N (1 - cos(V_i(x+\delta), V_t)) (eq 11) using target reference V_t. Paper states goal is to encourage alignment with target vectors and to jointly optimize this with CroPA. Combined objective given as L_re-CroPA = L_CroPA(x_v+\delta_v,x_t+\delta_t,T) - \u03bb L_d-UAP(\delta_v) (eq 12). Internal sign inconsistency: because L_d-UAP is (1-cos), subtracting it in an objective to be minimized yields pressure to increase (1-cos) (i.e., reduce cos), which contradicts the stated aim of encouraging alignment. Also noted: text encoder is frozen (keeps perturbations focused on vision), and CroPA still involves joint image/text perturbations per earlier parts.

errors.claim: Combined objective given as L_re-CroPA = L_CroPA(x_v+δ_v,x_t+δ_t,T) - λ L_d-UAP(δ_v) (eq 12).
errors.evidence: Earlier part: "Modified D-UAP defines L_d-UAP = sum_{i=1}^N (1 - cos(V_i(x+δ), V_t)) (eq 11)"; and "Combined objective given as L_re-CroPA = L_CroPA(x_v+δ_v,x_t+δ_t,T) - λ L_d-UAP(δ_v) (eq 12)". The paper also states the goal is to "encourage alignment with target vectors."
errors.explanation: Because L_d-UAP is defined as sum(1 - cos(...)), subtracting λ·L_d-UAP in an objective being minimized exerts pressure to increase (1 - cos) (i.e., decrease cos), which is the opposite of the stated aim to encourage alignment (increase cos) with the target vectors.

steps.notes_before: Key earlier definitions: PGD refinement (eq8) and MSE refinement loss (eq9). Modified D-UAP: L_d-UAP = sum_{i=1}^N (1 - cos(V_i(x+δ), V_t)) (eq11), intended to align vision-layer value vectors to target V_t. Paper reports combined objective L_re-CroPA = L_CroPA(x_v+δ_v, x_t+δ_t, T) - λ L_d-UAP(δ_v) (eq12) — flagged sign inconsistency (subtracting (1-cos) in minimization would discourage alignment). Text encoder reportedly frozen; CroPA still described as involving joint image/text perturbations (potentially important). Current part (5.3–5.4): transfer may be limited to models with similar vision encoders. SCMix (eq13): I1' = η X1 + (1-η) X2 with X_i = Resize(RandomCrop(I1)), η fixed to 0.5 (claimed equivalent to β distribution α→∞). Cross-mix (eq14): I3 = β1 I1' + β2 I2 with β1 >> β2 ∈ [0,1). CutMix (eq15): x̃ = M ⊙ x_A + (1-M) ⊙ x_B with M a rectangular binary mask. Section 5.4.1: use D-UAP to probe cross-model transfer; attacker white-box on surrogate (BLIP-2 or Flamingo), target models only known by family (e.g., CLIP-based); L_∞ budget ε=16/255.

steps.notes_before: Intra-family transfer: optimize on BLIP-2 (OPT-2.7b LM) → evaluate on InstructBLIP (Vicuna-7b); both use CLIP ViT-L/14. Cross-architecture transfer: BLIP-2 ↔ Flamingo (different encoders/LMs/architectures). Evaluation measures ASR for VQAgeneral, VQAspecific, Classification, Captioning. 5.4.2 describes a cross-image attacker that learns one universal perturbation (L_∞ budget ε=16/255) from limited training images (uses SCMix variants) and tests on unseen images; it also states attacker has white-box access to the target during optimization. SCMix and Cross-mix are intended to reduce image-specific overfitting. However, 5.4.2's "Adversary’s Goal" is stated as targeted (force a predetermined target text), while its "Evaluation Setup" and Section 5.4.3 say transferability results use an untargeted success criterion (model fails to generate correct output). CIA is excluded from transfer comparisons due to negligible transferability; decoder-only (e.g., LLaVA, OpenFlamingo) vs fusion-based models (e.g., BLIP-2, InstructBLIP) distinction is used to justify untargeted evaluation across heterogeneous architectures.

steps.notes_before: Reproduced CroPA cross-prompt experiments on Flamingo using targeted ASR metric. Table 1 reports targeted ASRs for VQAgeneral, VQAspecific, Classification, Captioning across several target texts; CroPA substantially outperforms Single-P and Multi-P, with very high VQA ASRs (often >0.86–0.99), lower performance on Classification and especially Captioning for abstract targets. errors.claim: CroPA is formulated as a min-max problem min_{δ_v} max_{δ_t} L(f(x_v+δ_v, x_t+δ_t), T) and the algorithm optimizes both visual and prompt perturbations during the forward pass.
errors.evidence: Equation (5): "min_{\delta_{v}}\max_{\delta_{t}}L(f(x_{v}+\delta_{v},x_{t}+\delta_{t}),T)" and text: "The algorithm optimizes both visual perturbation δ_v and prompt perturbation δ_t..." vs Algorithm step 7: "Compute gradient for adversarial image : g_{v}=\nabla_{x_{v}}L(f(x^{\prime}_{v},x^{i}_{t}),T)" and steps 4-6: "if x^{i}_{t} is not initialised then Initialise x^{\prime i}_{t}=x^{i}_{t}".
errors.explanation: The min-max objective and the surrounding description require forward passes to include the adversarial prompt (x'_t). Yet the algorithm's image-gradient step uses the clean prompt x^i_t (not x'^i_t), contradicting the claim that both perturbations are applied together in the forward computation.

errors.claim: "The implementation follows an iterative approach using Projected Gradient Descent (PGD)" to enforce the perturbation constraint ||δ_v||_p ≤ ε_v.
errors.evidence: Text: "The implementation follows an iterative approach using Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) Madry et al. (2017)." and constraint: "\|\delta_{v}\|_{p}\leq\epsilon_{v}" vs Algorithm step 8: "Update with gradient descent: x^{\prime}_{v}=x^{\prime}_{v}-\alpha_{1}\cdot\text{sign}(g_{v})" (no projection or clipping shown).
errors.explanation: PGD implies a projection step to keep the visual perturbation within the allowed norm ball, but the shown algorithm update lacks any projection/clipping after the update, inconsistent with the stated use of PGD and the stated norm constraint.

errors.claim: "Compute gradient for adversarial prompt: g_{t}=\nabla_{x_{t}}L(f(x^{\prime}_{v},x^{i}_{t}),T)" — the forward pass uses the clean prompt x^{i}_{t} rather than the adversarial prompt x^{\prime i}_{t}
errors.location: this part (contradicts min-max formulation in earlier part / Eq.5)
errors.evidence: This part: "Compute gradient for adversarial prompt: g_{t}=\nabla_{x_{t}}L(f(x^{\prime}_{v},x^{i}_{t}),T)". Earlier (Eq.5 in paper): "min_{\delta_v} max_{\delta_t} L(f(x_v+\delta_v, x_t+\delta_t), T)"
errors.explanation: The inner maximization in the min-max CroPA formulation requires evaluating the loss at the perturbed prompt x'_{t}, but the algorithm computes g_t (and earlier g_v) with x^{i}_{t} (the clean prompt) inside f, so the adversarial prompt is not used in the forward pass as the formulation implies.

errors.claim: Earlier observation (notes) that the algorithm omitted a projection step after image update to enforce ||\delta_v||_p \le \epsilon
errors.location: your notes (earlier part) versus this part

errors.explanation: The current part includes an explicit projection/clip step for x'_v, so the earlier note that no projection was shown is contradicted by this later algorithm fragment.

errors.claim: "During evaluation, only the optimized image perturbation is applied, while prompt perturbations are discarded. This ensures that the attack’s effectiveness stems from the image perturbation’s inherent transferability rather than prompt modifications."
errors.location: this part (contradiction with algorithm forward-pass detail from earlier part)
errors.evidence: This part: "During evaluation, only the optimized image perturbation is applied, while prompt perturbations are discarded...". Earlier algorithm lines (in notes): image gradient computed as g_v = ∇_{x_v} L(f(x'_v, x^{i}_{t}), T) and image update x'_v = x'_v - α1 sign(g_v) (i.e. image updates used clean prompt x^{i}_{t}).
errors.explanation: Since image updates were computed with the clean prompt (x^{i}_{t}), the optimized prompt perturbations did not influence the image optimization; therefore discarding prompts at evaluation does not 'ensure' that the attack's effectiveness stems from prompt-based min-max optimization—the prompts were never used to shape the image perturbation in the implemented forward passes.

errors.claim: "CroPA attempts to enhance adversarial effectiveness by optimizing both image and text inputs through PGD,"
errors.evidence: "While CroPA attempts to enhance adversarial effectiveness by optimizing both image and text inputs through PGD..." (this part)
errors.explanation: Earlier in the paper (reproduction notes) the CroPA implementation specifically used forward passes with the clean prompt (so adversarial prompt updates did not influence image updates) and at evaluation discarded prompt perturbations, meaning CroPA did not in practice optimize both image and text jointly as claimed here.

errors.claim: "Jointly minimize -ve of this loss along with the CroPA loss with proper scaling to ensure adversarial robustness and target alignment."
errors.evidence: Text: "Jointly minimize -ve of this loss along with the CroPA loss with proper scaling..." (5.2.1). Eq.11: "L_{\text{d-UAP}}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(1-\frac{V_{i}(x+\delta)\cdot V_{t}}{\|V_{i}(x+\delta)\|_{2}\|V_{t}\|_{2}}\right)". Eq.12: "L_{\text{re-CroPA}}=L_{\text{CroPA}}(x_{v}+\delta_{v},x_{t}+\delta_{t},T)-\lambda L_{\text{d-UAP}}(\delta_{v})".
errors.explanation: The text says to "minimize" the (negative) cosine-similarity loss (i.e. encourage alignment). But Eq.12 subtracts +λ L_d-UAP. If the combined objective L_re-CroPA is minimized as stated, the negative sign makes the optimizer prefer larger L_d-UAP (worse alignment). Thus the verbal instruction to jointly minimize the alignment loss contradicts the algebraic sign in Eq.12 unless they instead intend to maximize L_re-CroPA (which the text did not state).

errors.claim: "The attacker has white-box access to the target model during perturbation optimization"
errors.evidence: "The attacker has white-box access to the target model during perturbation optimization but must create a perturbation that generalizes to unseen images." (this part, 5.4.2) vs earlier notes: "white-box access to surrogate (BLIP-2 or Flamingo), target models only known by architecture family (e.g., CLIP-based)" (5.4.1, earlier part).
errors.explanation: Earlier the paper specified white-box access only to a surrogate model (with only architecture-family knowledge of target models); here it asserts white-box access to the target model during optimization, which contradicts the previously stated threat model.

errors.claim: "Adversary’s Goal: ... causes a VLM to output a predetermined target text regardless of the input prompt or image content."
errors.evidence: "Adversary’s Goal: The attacker aims to generate a single perturbation pattern that, when applied to any image, causes a VLM to output a predetermined target text regardless of the input prompt or image content." (this part, 5.4.2) vs "we present all cross-prompt and cross-model transferability results under the untargeted attack setting." (this part, 5.4.3).
errors.explanation: Section 5.4.2 frames the universal attack as targeted (forcing a predetermined target text), while 5.4.3 says all cross-model/prompt transfer results are presented under an untargeted setting; these are mutually inconsistent without clarification.

errors.claim: "we evaluated five state-of-the-art Vision-Language Models (VLMs): OpenFlamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP and LLaVA."
errors.evidence: "In reproducing the work of Luo et al. (2024), we evaluated five state-of-the-art Vision-Language Models (VLMs): OpenFlamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP and LLaVA."
errors.explanation: The sentence asserts five models were evaluated but then lists only four model names (OpenFlamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, LLaVA), a clear count/list mismatch within the same sentence.

errors.claim: "Our evaluation focused on measuring the Targeted Attack Success Rate (ASR) across the following tasks: VQA (both general and specific), image classification, and image captioning."
errors.evidence: This part: "Our evaluation focused on measuring the Targeted Attack Success Rate (ASR) ..."; Earlier notes (Section 5.4.3): "all cross-prompt and cross-model transferability results are reported under an untargeted attack setting..."
errors.explanation: Section 6.1 reports and analyzes targeted ASR for cross-prompt transferability, which contradicts the earlier-stated protocol (Section 5.4.3) that those cross-prompt/cross-model transferability results are reported under an untargeted attack setting.

errors.claim: "Table 1: Targeted ASRs tested on Flamingo with different target texts, across a variety of Vision-Language tasks."
errors.evidence: "Table 1: Targeted ASRs tested on Flamingo..." (this part) and earlier note: "Section 5.4.3 (notes) said cross-prompt/cross-model transferability results are reported under an untargeted setting."
errors.explanation: Earlier notes record that the paper reported cross-prompt/cross-model transferability under an untargeted setting (Section 5.4.3), but Section 6 here presents and repeatedly labels the experiments as targeted (Table 1 and target-text discussions). The paper thus contradicts itself on whether those transferability experiments are targeted or untargeted.

errors.claim: "Our obtained results on investigating the converging ASR rate for CroPA resulted in contrasting results with respect to the original reported metrics of convergence with higher number of iterations ... Where the original metrics showed CroPA converging with higher number of prompts."
errors.evidence: "...convergence with higher number of iterations (refer Appendix A.2) ... Where the original metrics showed CroPA converging with higher number of prompts."
errors.explanation: The paragraph first frames the comparison in terms of convergence vs. iterations but then attributes the original reported behavior to convergence vs. number of prompts. It mixes two different independent variables (iterations vs prompts), creating an internal inconsistency in what exactly is being compared.

errors.claim: the integration of our method (CroPA+Init) consistently outperforms both CroPA and Multi-P across all metrics
errors.evidence: Table 3 (this part) shows multiple cases where CroPA+Init scores lower than CroPA on individual metrics: for target 'unknown' VQAgeneral CroPA=0.9680 vs CroPA+Init=0.8824; 'unknown' VQAspecific CroPA=0.9880 vs CroPA+Init=0.8920; for target 'bomb' Classification CroPA=0.9498 vs CroPA+Init=0.9020; for 'very good' VQAspecific CroPA=0.8990 vs CroPA+Init=0.8894.
errors.explanation: The paper's claim of consistent outperformance is contradicted by its own Table 3, which shows CroPA+Init performing worse than CroPA on several per-task metrics.

errors.claim: achieving 6-15% gains in overall accuracy
errors.evidence: Table 3 overall values (this part) give for target 'very good' CroPA overall=0.8190 and CroPA+Init overall=0.8761, an absolute increase of 0.0571 (5.71 percentage points), which is below the claimed 6% lower bound.
errors.explanation: At least one reported overall gain (for 'very good') falls below the claimed 6% minimum, contradicting the stated 6-15% improvement range.

errors.claim: "We believe CutMix outperforms SCMix in promoting adversarial transferability because its region-based mixing maintains distinct, non-overlapping spatial areas."
errors.explanation: Table 5 shows SCMix achieves a higher overall ASR (0.7055) than CutMix (0.5565) and outperforms CutMix on three of the four listed tasks (VQA, Classification, Captioning). The assertion that CutMix outperforms SCMix is contradicted by the reported numbers in the same part.

errors.claim: Claim recorded in earlier notes: CroPA+Init "consistently outperforms" CroPA/Multi-P and "achieves 6-15% gains in overall accuracy."
errors.explanation: While CroPA+Init improves overall (0.9209 vs 0.7958), it does not "consistently" outperform CroPA on every task: CroPA's VQAspecific (0.9457) is higher than CroPA+Init's (0.9342). This contradicts the blanket claim of consistent outperformance across tasks.

errors.claim: "overall ASR of 96.85% which is an 12.5% increase from CroPA’s base method."
errors.evidence: "Earlier (Table 4) reported CroPA overall 0.7958 on BLIP-2 (notes). In this part's Table 6 CroPA overall is 0.8433 and CroPA+D-UAP is 0.9685."
errors.explanation: The 12.5 percentage-point increase (0.9685 - 0.8433 ≈ 0.1252) only holds if CroPA's baseline is 0.8433 as reported in Table 6 here. However the paper's earlier Table 4 (from previous part) reported CroPA overall = 0.7958, which would imply an increase of ≈0.1727 (≈17.3 percentage points). The paper therefore reports inconsistent CroPA baselines for BLIP-2 between parts, so the stated 12.5% increase conflicts with earlier reported numbers.

errors.claim: "significant improvements ... especially in Classification and Captioning tasks (14% and 21% respectively)"
errors.evidence: "Table 8 (BLIP2 → InstructBLIP) shows CroPA Classification 0.6720 → CroPA+D-UAP 0.8800 (increase 0.208 = 20.8 percentage points) and Captioning 0.6150 → 0.8880 (increase 0.273 = 27.3 percentage points)."
errors.explanation: The textual claim of 14% (Classification) and 21% (Captioning) improvements does not match the values in Table 8 for at least the BLIP2→InstructBLIP transfer (which show ~20.8 and ~27.3 percentage-point increases). Improvements vary across transfer pairs and are generally different from the quoted 14%/21%, so the claim is inconsistent with the table.

errors.claim: "BLIP2 to InstructBLIP' means the perturbations optimised on BLIP2 are tested on the InstructBLIP and similarly for 'BLIP2 to Flamingo'" (caption/explanatory sentence)
errors.evidence: "Flamingo to BLIP2 | Multi-P | 0.0140 | 0.0070 | 0.0090 | 0.0120 | 0.0105" and "Flamingo to InstructBLIP | Multi-P | 0.0100 | 0.0060 | 0.0050 | 0.0090 | 0.0075" (table rows shown immediately above the caption)
errors.explanation: The caption defines the naming convention using 'BLIP2 to ...' (perturbations optimized on BLIP2 then tested on other models), but the table fragment presented lists rows labeled 'Flamingo to ...' (perturbations from Flamingo to other models). The direction described in the caption does not match the row labels shown.

errors.claim: "CroPA remains robust in few-shot settings (6.4), outperforming other baselines and demonstrating resilience to the shift from the generation conditions from the optimization stage introduced by in-context learning examples."
errors.evidence: "Few-shot (Table 2): Multi-P (shot0) 0.6095 -> (shot2) 0.5730; CroPA 0.7708 -> 0.6635."
errors.explanation: Table 2 shows a clear drop in CroPA ASR when moving to the few-shot condition (0.7708 -> 0.6635), so describing CroPA as "resilient" to that shift contradicts the paper's own few-shot results.

errors.claim: "The D-UAP-modified CroPA framework ... achieving an overall Targeted Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 96.85%, an 13.5% improvement over the base CroPA method as shown in 6.5.3."
errors.location: this part (Section 7.3.2) vs earlier tables (Table 6 and Table 4)
errors.evidence: Table 6 (BLIP-2, target 'Bomb') reports CroPA = 0.8433 and CroPA+D-UAP = 0.9685. Table 4 (BLIP-2 overall) reports CroPA = 0.7958. Using Table 6 as baseline gives an absolute increase of 0.1252 (12.52 percentage points, ~14.86% relative), using Table 4 gives an absolute increase of 0.1727 (17.27 percentage points, ~21.7% relative).
errors.explanation: The paper uses inconsistent CroPA baseline values across its tables, and the stated "13.5% improvement" does not match the percent change implied by either reported baseline (nor clearly specifies whether it is absolute or relative), so the 13.5% figure is inconsistent with the paper's own numbers.

errors.claim: "The original CroPA method excels at cross-prompt transferability by optimizing perturbations against competing text embeddings." vs "CroPA achieves strong cross-prompt transferability by tightly coupling perturbations to image-specific features."
errors.evidence: "The original CroPA method excels at cross-prompt transferability by optimizing perturbations against competing text embeddings." (Section 7.4.1) and "CroPA achieves strong cross-prompt transferability by tightly coupling perturbations to image-specific features." (Section 7.4.2).
errors.explanation: The part gives two mutually inconsistent mechanisms for why CroPA achieves cross-prompt transferability: one attributes it to optimization against text embeddings (a prompt-side mechanism), the other to tight coupling to image-specific features (an image-side mechanism). Both cannot be the primary, contrasting explanation for the same observed cross-prompt behavior without reconciliation.

errors.claim: "Despite this, the D-UAP framework marks a critical step forward in creating universal adversarial perturbations that are effective across both prompts and images..."
errors.evidence: This part claims broad effectiveness for D-UAP, yet earlier reported cross-model transfer numbers are small: Table 8 (from notes) shows Flamingo→BLIP2 D-UAP mean = 0.1013, Flamingo→InstructBLIP D-UAP mean = 0.0938, Flamingo→LLaVA D-UAP mean = 0.1025. By contrast, within-model ASR (Table 6) for BLIP-2 CroPA+D-UAP = 0.9685.
errors.explanation: The claim that D-UAP is "effective across both prompts and images" overstates results: D-UAP attains very high within-model ASR but only low cross-model transfer (≈0.10), so it is not shown to be broadly effective across models in the paper's own results.

errors.claim: "While this improves cross-model transferability between architecturally similar models (e.g., BLIP-2 and InstructBLIP), the overall improvement is greater between fundamentally different architectures (e.g., BLIP-2 and Flamingo)."
errors.evidence: From Table 8 (notes): Flamingo→BLIP2 CroPA=0.0335 → D-UAP=0.1013 (improvement +0.0678); Flamingo→InstructBLIP CroPA=0.0290 → D-UAP=0.0938 (improvement +0.0648); Flamingo→LLaVA CroPA=0.0370 → D-UAP=0.1025 (improvement +0.0655).
errors.explanation: The reported numeric improvements are nearly identical (~0.065–0.068). The textual claim that improvement is noticeably greater for BLIP-2↔Flamingo than for BLIP-2↔InstructBLIP is not supported by these numbers.

errors.claim: "These modifications have demonstrated a marked increase in both the Attack Success Rate (ASR) and the generalizability of adversarial examples across different models and images."
errors.evidence: The paper's own results attribute different gains to different techniques: CroPA+Init (Table 4) yields very high ASR (CroPA+Init = 0.9209) but that pertains to within-model ASR; cross-image gains come from augmentation (Table 5: CroPA = 0.4355 → CroPA+SCMix = 0.7055), while cross-model transfer remains low (Table 8 D-UAP means ≈0.10).
errors.explanation: The sentence attributes simultaneous marked gains in ASR and generalizability across models/images to the CroPA refinements, but the reported results show that (a) diffusion initialization mainly increases within-model ASR, (b) SCMix/CutMix drive cross-image improvements, and (c) cross-model transfer remains limited—so the blanket claim is inconsistent with the paper's own breakdown of results.

errors.claim: While we were successfully able to reproduce the key results of CroPA and conduct extensive ablations, our progress was hindered on multiple occasions due to a lack of computational resources.
errors.evidence: Earlier reported results in the paper show inconsistent CroPA numbers for the same model/dataset: "BLIP-2 CroPA baseline differs across tables (0.7958 in Table 4 vs 0.8433 in Table 6)" and few-shot results where CroPA performance drops ("Table 2 few-shot: ... CroPA shot0 0.7708 -> shot2 0.6635"). Section 7.4 also contains conflicting accounts of CroPA's mechanism (text-embedding optimization vs image-specific coupling).
errors.explanation: The paper's own tables and text present inconsistent numeric results and conflicting descriptions for CroPA; claiming successful reproduction of the "key results" is inconsistent with these internal inconsistencies, which indicate the reported results are not self-consistent and therefore undermine the assertion of clear reproducibility.

final_notes: Models: OpenFlamingo-9B, BLIP-2 (OPT-2.7b fusion), InstructBLIP (Vicuna-7b fusion), LLaVA (Vicuna-13B). Key numeric findings: Table 2 few-shot: Multi-P shot0 0.6095 -> shot2 0.5730; CroPA shot0 0.7708 -> shot2 0.6635 (performance drops under few-shot). Table 4 (BLIP-2 overall): Multi-P 0.7104, CroPA 0.7958, CroPA+Init 0.9209. Table 6 (BLIP-2, target 'Bomb'): Multi-P 0.68, CroPA 0.8433, CIA 0.4199, CroPA+D-UAP 0.9685 (note CroPA 0.7958 vs 0.8433 mismatch). Table 5 (cross-image): CroPA 0.4355, CroPA+SCMix 0.7055, CroPA+CutMix 0.5565. Table 7 (OpenFlamingo): Multi-P 0.6960, CroPA 0.7900, CIA 0.3027, CroPA+D-UAP 0.9270. Cross-model snippet/Table (caption/label mismatch): Flamingo→BLIP2 CroPA 0.0335, D-UAP 0.1013; Flamingo→InstructBLIP CroPA 0.0290, D-UAP 0.0938; Flamingo→LLaVA CroPA 0.0370, D-UAP 0.1025. Observations/inconsistencies: BLIP-2 CroPA baseline differs across tables; Section 7.4 gives conflicting explanations of CroPA transfer mechanism; D-UAP yields very high within-model ASR but low cross-model transfer (~0.10); SCMix/CutMix improve cross-image transfer; some blanket claims about unified refinements and D-UAP effectiveness are not consistently supported by per-method numbers. From this part: authors claim they reproduced key CroPA results and did extensive ablations but were limited by compute, could not run ensembles, and established no direct contact with original authors (GitHub issue unresolved).

Title: Revisiting CroPA: reproducibility study + enhancements for cross-prompt adversarial transferability in VLMs. Authors (IIT Roorkee); note: authors marked as equal contributors. Abstract claims: (1) reproduce and validate CroPA (Cross-Prompt Attack) and confirm its superior cross-prompt transferability vs baselines; (2) propose three improvements: novel initialization strategy that significantly improves Attack Success Rate (ASR); investigation of cross-image transferability via learned universal perturbations; novel loss function targeting vision-encoder attention to improve generalization. Evaluation: performed across Flamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, and extended experiments on LLaVA; results reportedly validate original CroPA findings and show consistent improvement from proposed methods. Code link: https://github.com/Swadesh06/Revisting_CroPA. OpenReview link provided. No numeric results or tables in this part. No internal contradictions found in this section.

Title: Revisiting CroPA: reproducibility study + enhancements for cross-prompt adversarial transferability in VLMs. Authors: IIT Roorkee (equal contributors). Context: VLMs (e.g., BLIP, BLIP-2, Flamingo, InstructBLIP, LLaVA) are vulnerable to adversarial image/text attacks. Prior work classifies transferability into cross-model and cross-image; Luo et al. (2024) introduced Cross-Prompt Transferability and CroPA (learnable prompts to make adversarial images effective across textual prompts) and showed efficacy on classification, captioning, VQA. Goals claimed in this paper: (1) Reproducibility: successfully reproduced and verified four main claims of Luo et al.: CroPA’s superior cross-prompt transferability vs baselines (independent of target text semantics/word frequency); increasing number of prompts improves transferability but converges rapidly and baselines still don’t surpass CroPA; CroPA remains effective with extra in-context examples; reproduction of CroPA convergence via overall ASR across attack iterations plus per-task ASR analysis. (2) Extended work: (a) Better initialization strategy that substantially increases ASR and transferability; (b) Investigate cross-image transferability / Universal Adversarial Perturbations using CroPA backbone and image augmentation; (c) New loss function targeting vision-encoder attention by manipulating value vectors to improve generalization and ASR. Claims: in-depth analyses to explain mechanisms; code link provided. No numeric results given yet.

Section 2 (Related Work) recap: adversarial transferability spans cross-model (Liu et al. 2017; Tramèr et al. 2017), cross-image / Universal Adversarial Perturbations (Moosavi-Dezfooli et al. 2017; Mopuri et al. 2017), and cross-task transfer (Naseer et al. 2019a/b; Lu et al. 2020; Salzmann et al. 2021). Early VLM attacks targeted captioning and VQA on older CNN-RNN architectures (Xu et al. 2018/2019; Zhang et al.; Aafaq et al.; Chen et al.; Kaushik et al.; Kovatchev et al.; Li et al.; Sheng et al.). More recent work (Zhao et al. 2023) studied BLIP/BLIP-2 under black-box/cross-model transfer settings. CroPA (Luo et al. 2024) introduced cross-prompt adversarial transferability by optimizing learnable prompts jointly with image perturbations; the paper treats this as a new attack surface with few prior benchmarks. Yang et al. (2024) propose Context Injection Attack (CIA) — another cross-prompt method — and is used here as an additional comparison. Techniques to enhance transferability noted: input diversity (Xie et al. 2019), data augmentation (Wang et al. 2021), and addressing gradient misalignment (Li et al. 2023a; Wang et al. 2023). Connection to current paper: authors build on these insights to extend and improve CroPA (reproducibility of Luo et al.'s claims plus enhancements: better prompt initialization, cross-image/UAP experiments, and a new loss targeting vision-encoder attention/value vectors).

Repro study goal: reproduce Luo et al. (2024) CroPA and validate that it significantly improves cross-prompt transferability of adversarial examples. Four main claims to verify: (1) CroPA achieves cross-prompt transferability across various target texts; (2) CroPA achieves the best overall performance across different numbers of prompts; (3) CroPA converges to higher ASR as iterations increase; (4) CroPA outperforms baselines in few-shot settings. Beyond replication, authors will extend scope to cross-model and cross-image (including UAP) settings and compare CroPA to other cross-prompt methods (e.g., CIA) and baselines to test whether CroPA-generated adversarial images can consistently fool diverse VLMs regardless of prompt or model parameters. Planned methodological extensions noted earlier: improved prompt initialization, cross-image/UAP experiments, and a new loss targeting vision-encoder attention/value vectors. These claims and extensions will be checked against reproduced experiments and additional benchmarks.

errors.claim: CroPA is formulated as a min-max problem min_{δ_v} max_{δ_t} L(f(x_v+δ_v, x_t+δ_t), T) and the algorithm optimizes both visual and prompt perturbations during the forward pass.
errors.evidence: Equation (5): "min_{\delta_{v}}\max_{\delta_{t}}L(f(x_{v}+\delta_{v},x_{t}+\delta_{t}),T)" and text: "The algorithm optimizes both visual perturbation δ_v and prompt perturbation δ_t..." vs Algorithm step 7: "Compute gradient for adversarial image : g_{v}=\nabla_{x_{v}}L(f(x^{\prime}_{v},x^{i}_{t}),T)" and steps 4-6: "if x^{i}_{t} is not initialised then Initialise x^{\prime i}_{t}=x^{i}_{t}".
errors.explanation: The min-max objective and the surrounding description require forward passes to include the adversarial prompt (x'_t). Yet the algorithm's image-gradient step uses the clean prompt x^i_t (not x'^i_t), contradicting the claim that both perturbations are applied together in the forward computation.

(2017)." and constraint: "\|\delta_{v}\|_{p}\leq\epsilon_{v}" vs Algorithm step 8: "Update with gradient descent: x^{\prime}_{v}=x^{\prime}_{v}-\alpha_{1}\cdot\text{sign}(g_{v})" (no projection or clipping shown).

steps.notes_before: Repro study goal: reproduce Luo et al. (2024) CroPA and validate cross-prompt transferability claims. Key definitions and constraints: VLM f(x_v, x_t); visual perturbation δ_v with constraint ||δ_v||_p ≤ ε_v (paper sometimes denotes ε_v or ε). Targeted objective (multi-prompt): minimize sum_{i=1}^k L(f(x_v+δ_v, x_t^i), T) (Eq.1/4). Non-targeted objective: maximize discrepancy sum L(f(x_v+δ_v,x_t^i), f(x_v,x_t^i)) (Eq.2). Baselines: Single-P (Eq.3) optimizes with a single prompt; Multi-P uses multiple prompts. CroPA: framed as min_{δ_v} max_{δ_t} L(f(x_v+δ_v, x_t+δ_t), T) (Eq.5). Implementation claims: iterative PGD; image updates by gradient descent, prompt updates by gradient ascent; update-frequency parameter N (image updated N times per prompt update). Algorithm (partial): initialize x'_v = x_v; each step sample prompt x^i_t; lazily initialize per-prompt adversarial prompt x'^i_t = x^i_t; compute g_v = ∇_{x_v} L(f(x'_v, x^i_t), T) and update x'_v = x'_v - α1 sign(g_v); if mod(step,N)=0 then ... (algorithm truncated). Note contradictions to check later: (1) algorithm uses the clean prompt x^i_t in image forward pass though paper claims to apply adversarial prompt x'^i_t per min-max; (2) no projection step shown after image update to enforce ||δ_v||_p ≤ ε (despite PGD claim). Keep these for validation against later algorithm details/results.

errors.claim: "Compute gradient for adversarial prompt: g_{t}=\nabla_{x_{t}}L(f(x^{\prime}_{v},x^{i}_{t}),T)" — the forward pass uses the clean prompt x^{i}_{t} rather than the adversarial prompt x^{\prime i}_{t}

steps.notes_before: Repro goal: reproduce Luo et al. (2024) CroPA and validate cross-prompt transferability. Setup: VLM f(x_v,x_t); image perturbation constraint ||δ_v||_p ≤ ε. Objectives: targeted multi-prompt (sum L(f(x_v+δ_v,x_t^i),T)); non-targeted (maximize discrepancy). CroPA formulation (Eq.5): min_{δ_v} max_{δ_t} L(f(x_v+δ_v,x_t+δ_t),T). Implementation claims: iterative PGD style, image updates by gradient descent, prompt updates by gradient ascent, update-frequency N (image updated N times per prompt update). Algorithm (now complete): init x'_v=x_v; sample prompt x^i_t; lazy init x'^i_t=x^i_t; compute image gradient g_v = ∇_{x_v}L(f(x'_v,x^i_t),T) and update x'_v = x'_v - α1 sign(g_v) (note: forward pass uses clean prompt x^i_t); if mod(step,N)=0 compute prompt gradient g_t = ∇_{x_t}L(f(x'_v,x^i_t),T) and update x'^i_t = x'^i_t + α2 sign(g_t) (again gradient uses clean prompt in forward pass); project x'_v back to ε-ball: x'_v = Clip_{x_v,ε}(x'_v); return x'_v. Repro goal: reproduce Luo et al. (2024) CroPA and validate cross-prompt transferability. Setup: VLM f(x_v,x_t); image perturbation constraint ||δ_v||_p ≤ ε. Objectives: targeted multi-prompt and non-targeted formulations; CroPA min_{δ_v} max_{δ_t} L(f(x_v+δ_v,x_t+δ_t),T). Implementation (algorithm): iterative PGD-style; init x'_v=x_v; sample prompt x_t^i; lazy init x'^i_t=x_t^i; image update uses g_v = ∇_{x_v}L(f(x'_v,x_t^i),T) and x'_v ← x'_v - α1 sign(g_v) with forward pass using clean prompt x_t^i; every N steps compute g_t = ∇_{x_t}L(f(x'_v,x_t^i),T) and update x'^i_t ← x'^i_t + α2 sign(g_t) (again forward used clean prompt); project x'_v back into ε-ball; evaluation: only optimized image perturbation is applied; prompt perturbations discarded. Key implementation inconsistency to track: forward passes use clean prompt despite bi-level formulation (adversarial prompts may not influence image updates). From current part (Section 5): CroPA is effective on a single model but has poor transferability (authors cite Table 9, Appendix A.1; Table 1 shows poor performance on Classification and Captioning). CroPA is compute-intensive: reportedly >6 hours on a 48GB L40S GPU (95% VRAM) for 50 images. Goals: improve task consistency and transferability (cross-image and cross-model). Proposed method (5.1): Noise Initialization via Vision Encoding Optimization — replace random init with semantically informed init generated by diffusion (Stable Diffusion XL): x_target = D(T,z;θ_SDXL) (Eq.6). Align perturbation to x_target via vision-encoder features and optimize with an MSE loss to enforce semantic similarity while keeping adversarial effectiveness. Claims: reduces optimization steps, improves cross-prompt transferability; preliminary BLIP-2/InstructBLIP experiments show significant improvement at cost +20–25s per image. Points to later empirical evidence in Section 6.5.1 (Fig.7, Table 3) for sensitivity to initialization.

steps.notes_before: Repro goal: reproduce Luo et al. (2024) CroPA and evaluate cross-prompt/model transfer. Reproduced CroPA algorithm: iterative PGD-style with lazy prompt updates — image update uses gradients computed with the clean prompt; prompt updates computed every N steps also using clean prompt; project image back to ||·||_∞ ≤ ε; at evaluation only the optimized image perturbation applied and optimized prompts discarded. Implementation inconsistency: forward passes use clean prompts despite theoretical bi-level min_{δ_v} max_{δ_t} formulation (adversarial prompts may not affect image updates). CroPA is compute-heavy (>6 hrs on 48GB L40S GPU for 50 images). Proposed method (Sec 5.1): semantic noise init via diffusion SDXL: x_target = D(T,z;θ_SDXL) (Eq.6). Vision-encoder anchored init: δ_init = argmin_{||δ||_∞≤ε} || f_v(x+δ) - f_v(x_target) ||_2^2 (Eq.7). PGD refinement: x_adv^{t+1} = Π_{B_ε(x)}[ x_adv^{t} - α ∇_{x_adv^{t}} L_MSE ] (Eq.8) with L_MSE = || f_v(x_adv) - f_v(x_target) ||_2^2 (Eq.9). Sec 5.2: critique CroPA for lacking architectural sensitivity; propose joint CroPA + modified Doubly-UAP loss that targets value vectors in vision-attention layers (freeze text encoder), aiming to improve ASR and transferability. They plan to focus on two core attention components (list continues). Empirical sensitivity/benefits promised in Sec 6.5.1 (Fig.7, Table 3); SDXL init reportedly reduces optimization steps but costs +20–25s/image in BLIP-2/InstructBLIP experiments.

errors.claim: "Jointly minimize -ve of this loss along with the CroPA loss with proper scaling to ensure adversarial robustness and target alignment."
errors.evidence: Text: "Jointly minimize -ve of this loss along with the CroPA loss with proper scaling..." (5.2.1). Eq.11: "L_{\text{d-UAP}}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(1-\frac{V_{i}(x+\delta)\cdot V_{t}}{\|V_{i}(x+\delta)\|_{2}\|V_{t}\|_{2}}\right)". Eq.12: "L_{\text{re-CroPA}}=L_{\text{CroPA}}(x_{v}+\delta_{v},x_{t}+\delta_{t},T)-\lambda L_{\text{d-UAP}}(\delta_{v})".
errors.explanation: The text says to "minimize" the (negative) cosine-similarity loss (i.e. encourage alignment). But Eq.12 subtracts +λ L_d-UAP. If the combined objective L_re-CroPA is minimized as stated, the negative sign makes the optimizer prefer larger L_d-UAP (worse alignment). Thus the verbal instruction to jointly minimize the alignment loss contradicts the algebraic sign in Eq.12 unless they instead intend to maximize L_re-CroPA (which the text did not state).

steps.notes_before: Focus: attack vision encoder attention (weights and value vectors), targeting value vectors in mid-to-late layers. Baseline Doubly-UAP: δ* = argmax_δ (1/|L|) Σ_l Loss(V_l(x), V_l(x+δ)) (Eq.10). Modified D-UAP: derive target value vectors V_t from a reference image for target text T; extract perturbed head value vectors V_i(x+δ). Define L_d-UAP = Σ_{i=1}^N (1 - cosine(V_i(x+δ), V_t)) (Eq.11) to encourage alignment with target representation. They integrate with CroPA via L_re-CroPA = L_CroPA(x_v+δ_v,x_t+δ_t,T) - λ L_d-UAP(δ_v) (Eq.12). Text describes "jointly minimize" the (negative) cosine loss with CroPA, but Eq.12's subtraction creates an optimization-direction/sign inconsistency (minimize vs sign). Authors note potential limited transferability across models with different vision encoder architectures. Section 5.3 begins discussion of cross-image transferability and mentions UAPs and CutMix as augmentation strategies to improve universality.

Goal: attack vision-encoder attention (value vectors and heads), targeting mid-to-late layers. Baseline D-UAP: δ* = argmax_δ (1/|L|) Σ_l Loss(V_l(x), V_l(x+δ)) (Eq.10). Modified D-UAP: derive target value vectors V_t from a reference image for target text T; perturbed head value vectors V_i(x+δ). L_d-UAP = Σ_{i=1}^N (1 - cosine(V_i(x+δ), V_t)) (Eq.11). Integrated with CroPA as L_re-CroPA = L_CroPA(x_v+δ_v,x_t+δ_t,T) - λ L_d-UAP(δ_v) (Eq.12); earlier text claims “jointly minimize” but subtraction gives a sign/optimization-direction inconsistency. Authors note limited transferability across models with different vision-encoder architectures. Section 5.3 addresses cross-image transferability and augmentation strategies (UAPs, CutMix, SCMix). New content: ETU (Zhang et al. 2024) introduces SCMix (self-mix + cross-mix) to boost cross-image transferability; authors integrate SCMix into perturbation generation. SCMix self-mix: I1' = η X1 + (1-η) X2 where Xi = Resize(RandomCrop(I1)), they fix η = 0.5 (claim equivalence to α→∞ for Beta(α,α)). Cross-mix: I3 = β1 I1' + β2 I2 with β1 ≫ β2 (β2 ∈ [0,1)), to keep base-image semantics and text compatibility. CutMix (Yun et al. 2019): ṽx = M ⊙ xA + (1-M) ⊙ xB with M a rectangular binary mask (Eq.15). 5.4.1 threat model: attacker crafts a single perturbation to make multiple V-L models output a target text regardless of prompt; white-box access to surrogate (BLIP-2 or Flamingo), target models only known by architecture family (e.g., CLIP-based); L_inf budget ε = 16/255. Section cuts off before listing the two cross-model scenarios.

From Discussion: authors claim CroPA strong cross-prompt transfer and robustness in few-shot (contradicted by Table 2 drop), semantic (diffusion) initialization claimed to give up to ~15% Targeted ASR gains and faster convergence (matches CroPA+Init jump in Table 4), SCMix/CutMix improvements align with Table 5, and D-UAP yields high within-model ASR (0.9685) but percent-improvement statements are inconsistent with reported baseline values.

errors.claim: "The original CroPA method excels at cross-prompt transferability by optimizing perturbations against competing text embeddings." vs "CroPA achieves strong cross-prompt transferability by tightly coupling perturbations to image-specific features."
errors.evidence: "The original CroPA method excels at cross-prompt transferability by optimizing perturbations against competing text embeddings." (Section 7.4.1) and "CroPA achieves strong cross-prompt transferability by tightly coupling perturbations to image-specific features." (Section 7.4.2).
errors.explanation: The part gives two mutually inconsistent mechanisms for why CroPA achieves cross-prompt transferability: one attributes it to optimization against text embeddings (a prompt-side mechanism), the other to tight coupling to image-specific features (an image-side mechanism). Both cannot be the primary, contrasting explanation for the same observed cross-prompt behavior without reconciliation.

errors.claim: "Despite this, the D-UAP framework marks a critical step forward in creating universal adversarial perturbations that are effective across both prompts and images..."
errors.evidence: This part claims broad effectiveness for D-UAP, yet earlier reported cross-model transfer numbers are small: Table 8 (from notes) shows Flamingo→BLIP2 D-UAP mean = 0.1013, Flamingo→InstructBLIP D-UAP mean = 0.0938, Flamingo→LLaVA D-UAP mean = 0.1025. By contrast, within-model ASR (Table 6) for BLIP-2 CroPA+D-UAP = 0.9685.
errors.explanation: The claim that D-UAP is "effective across both prompts and images" overstates results: D-UAP attains very high within-model ASR but only low cross-model transfer (≈0.10), so it is not shown to be broadly effective across models in the paper's own results.

errors.claim: "While this improves cross-model transferability between architecturally similar models (e.g., BLIP-2 and InstructBLIP), the overall improvement is greater between fundamentally different architectures (e.g., BLIP-2 and Flamingo)."
errors.evidence: From Table 8 (notes): Flamingo→BLIP2 CroPA=0.0335 → D-UAP=0.1013 (improvement +0.0678); Flamingo→InstructBLIP CroPA=0.0290 → D-UAP=0.0938 (improvement +0.0648); Flamingo→LLaVA CroPA=0.0370 → D-UAP=0.1025 (improvement +0.0655).
errors.explanation: The reported numeric improvements are nearly identical (~0.065–0.068). The textual claim that improvement is noticeably greater for BLIP-2↔Flamingo than for BLIP-2↔InstructBLIP is not supported by these numbers.

errors.claim: "These modifications have demonstrated a marked increase in both the Attack Success Rate (ASR) and the generalizability of adversarial examples across different models and images."
errors.evidence: The paper's own results attribute different gains to different techniques: CroPA+Init (Table 4) yields very high ASR (CroPA+Init = 0.9209) but that pertains to within-model ASR; cross-image gains come from augmentation (Table 5: CroPA = 0.4355 → CroPA+SCMix = 0.7055), while cross-model transfer remains low (Table 8 D-UAP means ≈0.10).
errors.explanation: The sentence attributes simultaneous marked gains in ASR and generalizability across models/images to the CroPA refinements, but the reported results show that (a) diffusion initialization mainly increases within-model ASR, (b) SCMix/CutMix drive cross-image improvements, and (c) cross-model transfer remains limited—so the blanket claim is inconsistent with the paper's own breakdown of results.

errors.claim: Q7X jointly optimizes image and prompt perturbations as a min-max (δ_v, δ_t) problem (equation (5)) and Algorithm 1 implements that joint optimization.
errors.evidence:
Equation (5) states the Q7X objective as: min_{δ_v} max_{δ_t} L(f(x_v+δ_v, x_t+δ_t), T). However Algorithm 1 computes the image gradient as
    g_v = ∇_{x_v} L(f(x'_v, x_t^i), T)
and the prompt gradient as
    g_t = ∇_{x_t} L(f(x'_v, x_t^i), T)
(i.e. both gradients are evaluated with x_t^i, not with the adversarial prompt variable x'_t^i).
errors.explanation: The algorithm's gradient calculations use the original prompt x_t^i rather than the adversarial prompt x'_t^i, contradicting the stated min-max formulation and the narrative that Q7X jointly optimizes δ_v and δ_t.

errors.claim: Algorithm 1 initializes per-prompt adversarial variables correctly (i.e. initializes x'_t^i when needed).
errors.evidence:
Algorithm 1 contains the line:
    if x_t^i is not initialised then
        Initialise x'_t^i = x_t^i
which checks whether x_t^i is initialised before setting x'_t^i.
errors.explanation: The condition as written checks the original prompt variable x_t^i rather than the adversarial prompt variable x'_t^i, which is inconsistent with the apparent intent to lazily initialize x'_t^i. This is a variable-use inconsistency in the algorithm pseudocode.

errors.claim: There are no established N6Z baselines.

errors.evidence: This part: "The reference attacks introduced by Luo et al. (2024), absent established N6Z baselines, optimize a perturbation...". (2024) as offering a comparator; the claim of 'no established baselines' therefore conflicts with other parts of the paper that cite alternative methods.

errors.claim: "P2F increase over base Q7X, results characterization | 12.5%" and "P2F increase over base Q7X, discussion characterization | 13.5%"
errors.evidence:
"P2F increase over base Q7X, results characterization | 12.5%"
"P2F increase over base Q7X, discussion characterization | 13.5%"
errors.explanation: The table reports two different percentage increases for the same quantity (P2F increase over base Q7X) without explanation; these values are inconsistent within this part.

errors.claim: "The loss is described as encouraging closeness to the target representation; combined gradients update \u03b4, preserving adversarial character, N6Z, and guided semantic influence." (this part, 5.2.1)
errors.evidence: "L_{\mathrm{X9C}} = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left(1-\frac{V_i(x+\delta)\cdot V_t}{\|V_i(x+\delta)\|_2\|V_t\|_2}\right)" (Eq. 11); "L_{\mathrm{P2F}} = L_{\mathrm{Q7X}}(x_v+\delta_v,x_t+\delta_t,T) -\lambda L_{\mathrm{X9C}}(\delta_v)" (Eq. 12). Also earlier notes: "target value-vector ... here minimizing loss between value vectors of x_i and T_i rather than maximizing."
errors.explanation: Eq.11 defines L_X9C = 1 - cosine(V_i(x+\u03b4),V_t) (a distance-like loss). Eq.12 subtracts \u03bb L_X9C from L_Q7X, so minimizing L_P2F will, all else equal, increase L_X9C (because it appears with a negative sign). Increasing L_X9C decreases cosine similarity (moves V_i(x+\u03b4) away from V_t), which is the opposite of the claimed "encouraging closeness" and contradicts the earlier-stated intent to minimize value-vector distance to the target.

errors.claim: "The attacker seeks one image perturbation eliciting a specified target text from multiple VLMs independently of prompt: accessible-surrogate optimization followed by deployment against unknown models."
errors.evidence: "All N6Z and F8V transferability results are presented under untargeted attacks." (Section 5.4.3)
errors.explanation: Section 5.4.1 describes a targeted attacker who optimizes a perturbation to elicit a specified target text across models, while Section 5.4.3 states that all reported transferability results are presented under untargeted attacks. The paper does not reconcile these two statements or indicate which experiments use targeted vs. untargeted evaluations, so they are inconsistent.

errors.claim: "The evaluation reproduces the central N6Z claim, with nonzero H2Q reported across all tasks..." (Table caption: "Targeted H2Q on Flamingo...")
errors.location: conflict between this part and earlier notes (Section 5.4.3)
