Paper sets up standard notation. Data (X_i,Y_i) i.i.d. from P. Scoring f: X→R^d, decoder d: R^d→Y, prediction ŷ=d(f(x)). Task risk (instantaneous-label form): R(f)=E_P[ℓ(d∘f(X),Y)] (eq.1). Alternative task-risk that depends on conditional label distribution: R(f)=E_P[ℓ(d∘f(X),P(·|X))] (eq.2) — e.g., multiclass 0–1 loss ℓ(ŷ,P)=∑_y P(Y=y)1{ŷ≠y}. Surrogate φ: R^d×Y→R gives surrogate risk R_φ(f)=E_P[φ(f(X),Y)]. Two consistency settings: (i) Fisher consistency (all measurable functions allowed); (ii) restricted/statistical parametric models (possibly misspecified). Aggregation: observe richer response Z∈Z; aggregation map A: Z→A; aggregated surrogate risk R_{φ,A}(f)=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))] (eq.3). Repeated-sampling regime: Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m) with Y_i|X iid; define A(Z)=argmin_{y∈Y} ∑_{l=1}^m ℓ(y,Y_l) (majority vote for 0–1 loss). KNN-aggregation example: additional iid sample (X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m; Z=(Y,(X_i,Y_i)); order neighbors and set A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_{y∈Y} ∑_{l=0}^K ℓ(y,Y_{(l)}). Main aim reiterated: study when minimizing aggregated surrogate (3) suffices to minimize task risk (2), and show aggregation improves consistency in both settings. Track m, k, A_m, R_φ, R_{φ,A}, excess risks, calibration/identifying functions, and constants (C_{φ,1},C_{φ,2}) for later results.

Definitions: conditional task and surrogate risks R(s|x)=ℓ(d∘s,P(Y∈·|X=x)), R_φ(s|x)=E[φ(s,Y)|X=x]. Pointwise excess risks δ_ℓ(s,x)=R(s|x)-inf_{s'}R(s'|x), δ_φ(s,x)=R_φ(s|x)-inf_{s'}R_φ(s'|x). Population minima R* and R_φ*. Consistency notions: (i) Fisher consistency: R_φ(f_n)→R_φ* ⇒ R(f_n)→R* for any sequence f_n; (ii) uniform comparison inequality: ∃nondecreasing ψ with ψ(R(f)-R*) ≤ R_φ(f)-R_φ* and ψ(ε)>0 ∀ε>0. Calibration functions: ψ(ε,x)=inf_{s}{δ_φ(s,x) | δ_ℓ(s,x)≥ε}, overlineψ(ε)=inf_x ψ(ε,x). Corollary 3.1: positive pointwise calibration (ψ(ε,x)>0 ∀x,ε>0) ⇔ Fisher consistency; Fenchel-biconjugate of overlineψ yields a ψ giving the comparison inequality ψ(R(f)-R*) ≤ R_φ(f)-R_φ*. Ranking example: labels Y={(i,j): i≠j, i,j∈[k]}, p_{ij}=P(Y=(i,j)|x). Define normalized matrix C_x with (C_x)_{ii}=0 and (C_x)_{ij}=p_{ij}/∑_{l≠ j}p_{lj} (use 0/0=1/(k-1)), so C_x^T 1=1. Rank by C_x 1 (or powers/Perron vector). Loss (incorporating decoder) ℓ(s,C)=max_{i<j} 1{(s_i-s_j)((e_i-e_j)^T C1) ≤0, (e_i-e_j)^T C1 ≠0}; population risk R(f)=P(f(X) and C_X1 order differently). Main claims: (Prop 1) for k≥3, any φ convex in score argument is not Fisher consistent for this ranking risk. Aggregation: collect Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m); let m_{ij} be counts of pair (i,j), m_j=∑_i m_{ij}. Define A(Z)=★ if some m_j=0; otherwise A(Z)=(∑_{columns} m_{i·}/m_·)_i (vector of per-column frequencies summed for each i). Claim: regressing on A(Z) (when A(Z)≠★) is consistent; (Prop 2) squared-loss regression on aggregated response is Fisher consistent when m≥k.

final_notes: Paper studies how label aggregation (collecting m labels per example and aggregating) affects surrogate calibration and consistency. Key definitions/assumptions: Mammen–Tsybakov noise (parameters α, C_MT); noise condition number κ(X) (eq. (9)) important for multiclass comparison inequalities (κ(X)=1 in binary). Optimal predictability (eq. (12)) = Bayes-optimal classifier lies in F, used in mis-specified model results. Main theoretical points: comparison inequalities of form ψ(R(f)-R^*) ≤ R_φ(f)-R_φ^* and an m-dependent version ψ_m(R(f)-R^*) ≤ R_{φ,A_m}(f)-R_{φ,A_m}^*; aggregation can strengthen calibration and ψ_m can approach a tighter (linear) bound as m→∞ (Theorem 1 may be conservative). Title: Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning. Authors: Chen Cheng, John Duchi. Abstract claims: learning procedures that rely on aggregated labels (label information distilled from noisy responses) enjoy robustness properties not possible without data cleaning. Key points: (1) In the context of risk consistency (minimizing surrogate, typically convex, losses instead of target task loss like 0-1), procedures using label aggregation obtain stronger consistency guarantees than those possible using raw labels. (2) Classical perfectly-specified model scenarios suggest modeling label uncertainty is statistically efficient, but consistency for “standard” approaches fails as soon as the loss is even slightly mis-specified. (3) Procedures leveraging aggregated information still converge to optimal classifiers despite such mis-specification. Overall claim: incorporating a fuller view of the data collection-to-prediction pipeline (via label aggregation/cleaning) yields a more robust methodology by refining noisy signals.

Title: Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning. Authors: Chen Cheng, John Duchi. Paper studies how label aggregation/cleaning in data pipelines (e.g., crowdsourcing multiple noisy labels then denoising) fundamentally improves consistency and robustness of learned models. Two main robustness aspects: (1) For surrogate risk consistency (minimizing convex surrogate losses vs. target loss like 0-1), procedures using aggregated labels can achieve consistency and optimal prediction in limits where methods using raw (X,Y) pairs cannot. (2) Even in finite-dimensional parametric/statistical settings, aggregation can yield consistent classifiers when standard approaches fail. The paper situates itself with prior surrogate-consistency theory (Bartlett et al. and follow-up work) and asks whether aggregation is necessary/useful, and in what sense. Promised contributions/examples: ranking, binary and multiclass classification with linear estimators where (X,Y)-based estimators fail but aggregation yields consistency; nonparametric results where number of samples aggregated and noise conditions determine improved consistency; demonstration that aggregation enables surrogate risk consistency under weak conditions via (approximate) linear comparison inequalities; results showing aggregation can guarantee consistency even over restricted hypothesis classes where unaggregated approaches fail.

Paper title: "Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning" by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: aggregating/cleaning labels (information distilled from noisy responses) yields robustness not available without cleaning. Specifically: (1) minimizing a typically convex surrogate loss on aggregated labels gives stronger task-risk consistency guarantees than procedures using raw labels; (2) finite-dimensional classifiers remain consistent under loss mis-specification that breaks standard uncertainty-modeling approaches; (3) in perfectly specified statistical models, using all information is more efficient, but slight loss mis-specification can destroy standard consistency; (4) aggregation preserves convergence to optimal classifiers despite noise; (5) the whole pipeline (collection, fitting, prediction) admits robustness via noisy-signal refinement. Keep these claims in mind for checking consistency with later sections (definitions, assumptions, theorems, empirical results) about surrogate losses, aggregation methods, consistency under mis-specification, and comparisons to raw-label procedures.

Introduction adds: aggregation permits consistent optimal prediction under surrogate (but unaggregated estimation cannot), including finite-dimensional problems; linear-estimator constructions in ranking and binary/multiclass classification separate procedures restricted to (X,Y) from aggregation procedures; nonparametric results combine aggregation count and noise conditions, allow approximately linear comparison inequalities under weak surrogate conditions, and extend consistency beyond unrestricted measurable hypothesis classes. Context: prior surrogate-risk consistency theory (Bartlett et al. etc.) and many extensions; pair-based empirical-process analyses do not address aggregation machinery. Central research questions: is aggregation needed, does pair-based surrogate consistency suffice, and in what sense does aggregation improve consistency.

final_notes: Key theoretical results: Theorem 2 (Sec.4) — under a convex cone F containing a Bayes-optimal predictor and P(Δ(X)>0)=1, any sequence f_m in ε_m-argmin_{f∈F} R_{φ,A_m}(f) with ε_m→0 satisfies R(f_m)→R*. Linear zero-sum scores form such a cone. Parametric multiclass model: Θ∈R^{d×(k−1)} with θ_k=0, softmax σ^{lr}; logistic surrogate φ(Θ^T x,y)=−⟨θ_y,x⟩+log(1+∑_{i=1}^{k−1}e^{⟨θ_i,x⟩}). First-order condition: E[X(σ^{lr}(Θ_m^T X)−ρ_m(Θ^{*T} X))^T]=0. For k=2 and X∼N(0,I) direction recovered: Θ_m = t_m Θ^*, t_m>0. Proposition 5 (k≥3) — small link perturbations can change normalized unaggregated minimizer; aggregation can fix this. Theorem 3 — if Θ^*=U^* T^* (U^* orthonormal, T^* nonsingular), then Θ_m = U^* T_m, ||T_m||→∞ and T_m/||T_m||→T^*/||T^*|| as m→∞. Experiments: (i) Truncated-quadratic margin surrogate: unaggregated calibration ψ(ε)=ε^2; Lemma 3.1 yields aggregated bound ψ_m(ε)=(1/16)(ε−√((32/m)log40))_+, whose slope approaches 1/16 as m→∞. (ii) Corrupted-link logistic (k=3,d=2,r=3, score-shrink α=0.1), true Θ*: θ1*=(0,1), θ2*=(1,1); alignment error vs m shows empirical recovery consistent with Theorem 3. Discussion/future work: many guarantees are asymptotic in m; finite-m theory is open (ranking/Prop.2 gives m≥k finite-case); noise condition-number κ(X) (Eq.(9)) can be large beyond binary even at low Mammen–Tsybakov exponent α≈1; model results need optimal predictability (Eq.(12)); extending aggregation-based comparison bounds to restricted classes/H-consistency is suggested. Claimed cross-references: Corollary 4.1 and Theorems 2–3 are asymptotic; Prop.4/5 illustrate failures of unaggregated surrogates versus aggregated methods.

Paper studies whether aggregating noisy labels improves consistency of learned predictors. Focus: surrogate losses (used during fitting), analyzed over all measurable predictors and over restricted model classes. Develops calibration inequalities for aggregated labels; analyzes ranking, classification, structured prediction. Key claims to remember: for ranking with k ≥ 3 items, no convex surrogate based on individual comparisons is Fisher consistent; an aggregated squared-loss procedure is consistent when m ≥ k. Under certain noise conditions, aggregation yields approximately linear comparison inequalities. In restricted model classes, aggregation can restore consistency when ordinary surrogate minimization fails (including link mis-specification). Two numerical illustrations are reported. "R(f):=E_P[\ell(d\circ f(X),Y)]. (1)"
and then introduced the conditional-distribution version

errors.claim: Clearly \sigma^{\epsilon} satisfies the link consistency condition (14) and is optimally predictable (12).
errors.evidence:
Definition (14) (paraphrased in the paper): "t_y = max_i t_i iff \sigma_y(t) = max_i \sigma_i(t)." 
The paper's perturbation: "\sigma^{\epsilon}(t)=\sigma^{\textup{lr}}(t)1\{t\not\in\mathcal{T}_{\epsilon}\}+\frac{1}{k}\mathbf{1}\cdot 1\{t\in\mathcal{T}_{\epsilon}\}," i.e. \sigma^{\epsilon}(t) is uniform on the set \mathcal{T}_{\epsilon}.
errors.explanation: If t\in\mathcal{T}_{\epsilon}, then \sigma^{\epsilon}(t) is the uniform vector, so every coordinate is a (tied) maximum; the right-hand side of (14) is true for every y, but the left-hand side (t_y is the unique/maximal coordinate of t) need not hold. Thus the equivalence in (14) fails for t\in\mathcal{T}_{\epsilon}, so the claim that \sigma^{\epsilon} satisfies (14) is false.

errors.claim: The paper's claim that σ^{ε} (which equals σ^{lr} off a small-measure set T_ε and is uniform on T_ε) preserves the link-consistency condition (14).
errors.evidence: From my earlier notes: "The paper defines σ^{ε} that equals σ^{lr} off a small-measure set T_ε and is uniform on T_ε... (Note: the paper's claim that σ^{ε} preserves link-consistency (14) is incorrect because uniform outputs on T_ε break the iff equivalence in (14).)". From this part: "Majority vote, however, can address this inconsistency as m→∞ without any assumptions on the true link σ except that it satisfies the consistency condition (14). ... as Proposition 5 highlights, methods without label aggregation are generally inconsistent."
errors.explanation: If σ^{ε} returns a uniform vector on T_ε then ties / altered orderings occur there, so σ^{ε} does not preserve the argmax-equivalence required by (14). The paper appears to have used σ^{ε} as a small perturbation while also (earlier) claiming it preserves (14); that claim is false. Thus the example underlying Proposition 5 either does not satisfy condition (14) (contradicting the paper's earlier assertion) or the paper misstated σ^{ε}'s properties.

errors.claim: "threshold 1/4 requires only $m\geq128\log40$."
errors.evidence:
The paper gives
"\displaystyle\psi_{m}(\epsilon)=\frac{1}{16}\left(\epsilon-\sqrt{\frac{32}{m}\log 40}\right)_{+},"
then states "threshold 1/4 requires only $m\geq128\log40$."
errors.explanation: For ψ_m(ε) to be positive at ε=1/4 we need sqrt(32/m · log40) < 1/4, i.e. 32/m · log40 < 1/16, so m > 512·log40. Thus the correct bound for threshold 1/4 is m ≥ 512·log40, not 128·log40. (Note: m ≥ 128·log40 would ensure positivity at ε=1/2, not ε=1/4.)

final_notes: Key results/assumptions: Theorem 2: risk consistency for linear-cone class F (linear predictors Θ∈R^{d×(k-1)} with Θ_k=0) under optimal predictability (a Bayes-optimal classifier lies in F) and P(Δ(X)>0)=1. Section 4.3: link must preserve argmax (link-consistency (14)); multiclass logistic σ^{lr} satisfies stationary condition E[X(σ^{lr}(Θ_m^T X)-ρ(Θ^{*T}X))^T]=0. Proposition 5: for k≥3 small link mis-specification can break single-label risk consistency (directions can change) under an invertibility condition. Theorem 3: when Θ^*=U^*T^* (U^* orthogonal, T^* nonsingular) aggregated solutions Θ_m satisfy Θ_m=U^*T_m with ||T_m||→∞ and T_m/||T_m||→T^*/||T^*|| (aggregation recovers direction asymptotically). Experiments: (1) truncated quadratic surrogate φ(δ)=(max{1-δ,0})^2 with calibration ψ(ε)=ε^2; aggregated calibration derived ψ_m(ε)=(1/16)(ε - sqrt(32/m · log40))_+; note: paper contains an arithmetic mistake in a numeric threshold (correct threshold for ε=1/4 is m≥512·log40). (2) Mis-specified logistic experiment: k=3,d=2, corrupted link ∴σ^{lr} for ||t||≤r and σ^{lr}(α t) for ||t||>r with r=3, α=0.1; true Θ^*: θ1*=(0,1), θ2*=(1,1). Fig.2: normalized-direction error of T_m vs m under two sampling regimes (n=10,000 constant; n=640,000/m to keep total labels fixed) shows aggregation recovers direction as m→∞, consistent with Theorem 3. Open directions: finite-m guarantees beyond ranking, tighter links between loss/surrogate and noise condition number κ(X) (eq.9), relaxing optimal-predictability, and restricted-H consistency (H-consistency) analyses.

Title: Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning. Authors: Chen Cheng, John Duchi. Abstract claims: learning procedures that rely on aggregated labels (label information distilled from noisy responses) enjoy robustness properties not possible without data cleaning. Key points: (1) In the context of risk consistency (minimizing surrogate, typically convex, losses instead of target task loss like 0-1), procedures using label aggregation obtain stronger consistency guarantees than those possible using raw labels. (2) Classical perfectly-specified model scenarios suggest modeling label uncertainty is statistically efficient, but consistency for “standard” approaches fails as soon as the loss is even slightly mis-specified. (3) Procedures leveraging aggregated information still converge to optimal classifiers despite such mis-specification. Overall claim: incorporating a fuller view of the data collection-to-prediction pipeline (via label aggregation/cleaning) yields a more robust methodology by refining noisy signals.

Title: Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning. Authors: Chen Cheng, John Duchi. Paper studies how label aggregation/cleaning in data pipelines (e.g., crowdsourcing multiple noisy labels then denoising) fundamentally improves consistency and robustness of learned models. Two main robustness aspects: (1) For surrogate risk consistency (minimizing convex surrogate losses vs. target loss like 0-1), procedures using aggregated labels can achieve consistency and optimal prediction in limits where methods using raw (X,Y) pairs cannot. (2) Even in finite-dimensional parametric/statistical settings, aggregation can yield consistent classifiers when standard approaches fail. The paper situates itself with prior surrogate-consistency theory (Bartlett et al. and follow-up work) and asks whether aggregation is necessary/useful, and in what sense. Promised contributions/examples: ranking, binary and multiclass classification with linear estimators where (X,Y)-based estimators fail but aggregation yields consistency; nonparametric results where number of samples aggregated and noise conditions determine improved consistency; demonstration that aggregation enables surrogate risk consistency under weak conditions via (approximate) linear comparison inequalities; results showing aggregation can guarantee consistency even over restricted hypothesis classes where unaggregated approaches fail.

errors.claim: "whose minimizers frequently coincide with the original problem (2), but which allows more sophistication."
errors.evidence:
Earlier in the same paragraph the paper defined the instantaneous-label risk as
"R(f):=E_P[\ell(d\circ f(X),Y)]. (1)"
and then introduced the conditional-distribution version
"R(f):=E_P[\ell(d\circ f(X),P(\cdot\mid X))]. (2)"
The quoted sentence then says the minimizers coincide with "the original problem (2)".
errors.explanation: The sentence refers to (2) as the "original problem" although (2) is the new, conditional-distribution version just introduced; the intended reference is almost certainly to the original instantaneous-label problem (1). This is a self-contradictory cross-reference within the paragraph.

steps.notes_before: Preliminaries: X input space, Y output space, data (X_i,Y_i) iid from P. Scoring f:X->R^d, decoder d:R^d->Y, task risk R(f)=E_P[ℓ(d∘f(X),Y)] (instantaneous-label form, eq. (1)). Also consider a refined task loss depending on conditional label distribution: R(f)=E_P[ℓ(d∘f(X), P(·|X))] (eq. (2)). Two study scenarios: (i) Fisher consistency (F all Borel functions); (ii) statistical/parametric hypothesis classes (possibly mis-specified). Surrogate φ introduced to optimize: originally φ:R^d×Y->R, surrogate risk R_φ(f)=E_P[φ(f(X),Y)]. Label aggregation: observed Z (e.g., multiple labels or extra draws), aggregation map A:Z->A, aggregated surrogate φ:R^d×A->R_+, aggregated risk R_{φ,A}(f)=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))]. Example 1 (majority vote): Z=(Y_1,...,Y_m), A(Z)=argmin_y ∑_{l=1}^m ℓ(y,Y_l); for 0-1 loss this is majority vote. Example 2 (K-NN aggregation): Z=(Y,(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m); order X_i by distance to X, set X_(0)=X (so Y_(0)=Y), define A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y ∑_{l=0}^K ℓ(y,Y_(l)). Main claimed message: label aggregation improves consistency/robustness in both scenarios.

Surrogate-consistency setup: conditional task risk R(s|x)=ℓ(d∘s,P(Y|X=x)), conditional surrogate risk R_φ(s|x)=E[φ(s,Y)|X=x]. Pointwise excesses δ_ℓ(s,x)=R(s|x)-inf_s'R(s'|x), δ_φ(s,x)=R_φ(s|x)-inf_s'R_φ(s'|x). Global minima R* and R_φ*. Two consistency notions: (i) Fisher consistency: for any sequence f_n, R_φ(f_n)→R_φ* implies R(f_n)→R*; (ii) uniform comparison: exists nondecreasing ψ with ψ(ε)>0 for ε>0 s.t. ψ(R(f)-R*) ≤ R_φ(f)-R_φ* for all f. Calibration functions: ψ(ε,x)=inf_{s}{δ_φ(s,x) | δ_ℓ(s,x)≥ε}, overline ψ(ε)=inf_x ψ(ε,x). Corollary 3.1: φ is Fisher consistent iff ψ(ε,x)>0 for all x,ε>0; taking Fenchel biconjugate of overline ψ gives a ψ s.t. ψ(R(f)-R*) ≤ R_φ(f)-R_φ*. Ranking example (Sec 3.1): Y={(i,j): i≠j, i beats j}, p_{ij}=P(Y=(i,j)|x). Define C_x with (C_x)_{ii}=0 and (C_x)_{ij}=p_{ij}/∑_{l≠j}p_{lj} (set 0/0=1/(k-1)), so C_x is column-stochastic (C_x^T1=1). Rank by vector C_x1; loss ℓ(s,C)=max_{i<j}1{(s_i-s_j)((C1)_i-(C1)_j) ≤0, (C1)_i≠(C1)_j}. Population risk R(f)=P(f(X) and C_X1 order differently). Proposition 1: for k≥3, any convex-in-first-arg φ:R^k×Y→R is not Fisher consistent. Aggregation fix: collect m independent comparisons Z=(Y_1,..,Y_m); counts m_{ij}, m_j=∑_i m_{ij}; define A(Z)=⋆ if any m_j=0, else A_i=∑_{j} m_{ij}/m_j. Claim: regressing on A(Z) yields consistency when m≥k (Prop 2; proofs in App A.1/A.2).

errors.claim: The paper defines the uniform calibration function as "\overline{\psi}_{A}(\epsilon) \coloneqq \inf_{s\in\mathbb{R}^{d}} \overline{\psi}_{A}(\epsilon,x)" (equation (5)).
errors.evidence: Earlier (and standard) definition of the uniform calibration function is an infimum over x: "calibration functions: psi(ε,x)=inf_s{δ_φ(s,x) | δ_ℓ(s,x)≥ε}, overline psi(ε)=inf_x psi(ε,x)." Also the text here refers to "pointwise and uniform" calibration, so the uniform version should be an infimum over x.
errors.explanation: Equation (5) incorrectly repeats an infimum over s for the uniform calibration function, but the uniform calibration must take the infimum over x (the conditioning point). This contradicts the earlier/standard definition and the stated 'pointwise and uniform' distinction.

steps.notes_before: Surrogate-consistency setup: conditional task risk R(s|x)=ℓ(d∘s,P(Y|X=x)), surrogate risk R_φ(s|x)=E[φ(s,Y)|X=x]; pointwise excesses δ_ℓ(s,x), δ_φ(s,x); global minima R*, R_φ*. Two consistency notions: Fisher consistency (R_φ(f_n)→R_φ* ⇒ R(f_n)→R*) and uniform comparison with ψ nondecreasing s.t. ψ(R-R*) ≤ R_φ-R_φ*. Calibration: ψ(ε,x)=inf_s{δ_φ(s,x) | δ_ℓ(s,x)≥ε}, uniform ψ̅(ε)=inf_x ψ(ε,x) (note: the paper's equation (5) has a typo giving inf over s instead of inf over x). Ranking example: labels Y={(i,j)}, define C_x and rank by C_x1; loss indicates misordering. Prop1: for k≥3 any convex-in-first-arg φ:R^k×Y→R is not Fisher consistent. Aggregation: collect m comparisons, form A(Z) (vector of fractions) — Prop2: regressing on A(Z) yields consistency when m≥k. Example surrogate: φ(s,q)=||s-q||_2^2 (φ(s,⋆)=0) is Fisher consistent for ranking if m≥k. Prop3: under integrability, φ is Fisher consistent iff ψ̅_A(ε,x)>0 ∀x,ε>0; Fenchel biconjugate gives ψ_A(R-R*) ≤ R_{φ,A}-R_{φ,A}*. Definition 3.1: (C1,C2)-identifying surrogate: exist a_y∈A and s_y with d(s_y)=y satisfying margin-like inequalities (6a,6b); hinge loss is (1,2)-identifying. Aggregator A_m returns a_{ŷ} with ŷ minimizing sample sum loss; Corollary 3.2: if m→∞ and φ identifying then surrogate-consistency (R_{φ,A_m}(f_n)→opt) implies task-consistency (R(f_n)→opt).

errors.claim: "In cases with low noise in the labels, the aggregation strategy (7) allows an explicitly improved comparison inequality ψ(R(f)-R^{\star})\leq R_{\varphi}(f)-R^{\star}",

Thus ζ=C_{φ,1}/16 and ξ = 2P(κ(X)>M)+(4C_MT e_m(M))^{1/(1-α)}. Define ξ_m = inf_M {...}; ξ_m→0 as m→∞. errors.claim: R(f)-R^{\star}\leq\frac{8}{\min_{\hat{y}\neq y}\ell(\hat{y},y)}(R_{\varphi,A_{m}}(f)-R_{\varphi,A_{m}}^{\star}).
errors.evidence: Earlier in this part: "Under the conditions of Theorem 1, for any f such that R(f)-R^{\star}\geq\xi_{m,k}, R(f)-R^{\star}\leq\frac{16}{\mathsf{C}_{\varphi,1}}\cdot\left({R_{\varphi,{A_{m}}}(f)-R_{\varphi,{A_{m}}}^{\star}}\right)."  Also Lemma 3.3 states "\mathsf{C}_{\varphi,1}=\min_{\hat{y}\neq y}\ell(\hat{y},y),\qquad\mathsf{C}_{\varphi,2}=\max_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\tau(y)+1."

The paper instead claims 8/(min ℓ) here, a factor-of-two inconsistency with the general theorem.

steps.notes_before: Theorem 1 / Corollary 3.3: for scores f with R(f)-R* ≥ ξ_{m,k}, we have R(f)-R* ≤ (16/C_{φ,1})(R_{φ,A_m}(f)-R_{φ,A_m}*). (ii) Bipartite matching: C_{φ,1}=1/N, C_{φ,2}=2, k=N!, so for k≥3 ξ uses k≥3 formula and RHS constant is 16N. The paper instead states 8/(min ℓ) (factor-of-two mismatch).

Earlier results (Thm 1 / Cor 3.3): aggregation can upgrade surrogate consistency; explicit ξ_{m,k} formulas given (k=2 and k≥3) and constants in bounds (R(f)-R* ≤ (16/C_{φ,1})(R_{φ,A_m}(f)-R_{φ,A_m}*)). Examples: binary nonsmooth, bipartite matching, structured prediction (noted a factor-2 mismatch in the paper's stated constant vs. what Lemma 3.3+Cor 3.3 imply).

New (Part 8) — Section 4: studies restricted hypothesis classes (parametric models). Binary case (Y∈{±1}): margin surrogate φ(sy) (convex). Classical result recalled: for unrestricted F, φ achieves Fisher and uniform consistency iff φ'(0)<0. But restricting to linear predictors F={f_θ(x)=⟨θ,x⟩} can break consistency even when P is optimally predictable along some θ* (sgn(⟨θ*,x⟩)=sgn(P(Y=1|x)-1/2)).

Proposition 4: For any ε>0 and nonzero θ*, there exists P (optimally predictable along θ*) such that any θ_φ ∈ argmin_θ E[φ(f_θ(X),Y)] satisfies R(f_{θ_φ})>R(f_{θ*}) and |cos angle(θ_φ,θ*)| ≤ ε (i.e., essentially orthogonal).

Aggregation (majority vote A_m) can fix this: define θ_m ∈ ε_m-argmin_θ R_{φ,A_m}(f_θ) with ε_m→0. Corollary 4.1 (via Thm 2): R(f_{θ_m})→R(f_{θ*}) and cos angle(θ_m,θ*)→1 as m→∞.

Multiclass (Y∈[k]): consider F a linear cone with f(x)^T 1=0 and closed under positive scaling. Assume φ is Fisher consistent and satisfies limiting loss condition (13): φ(s,y)→0 if s_y - s_j → +∞ for all j≠y. Multiclass logistic and additive pairwise-margin losses satisfy (13).

errors.claim: Clearly \sigma^{\epsilon} satisfies the link consistency condition (14) and is optimally predictable (12).
errors.evidence:
Definition (14) (paraphrased in the paper): "t_y = max_i t_i iff \sigma_y(t) = max_i \sigma_i(t)." 
The paper's perturbation: "\sigma^{\epsilon}(t)=\sigma^{\textup{lr}}(t)1\{t\not\in\mathcal{T}_{\epsilon}\}+\frac{1}{k}\mathbf{1}\cdot 1\{t\in\mathcal{T}_{\epsilon}\}," i.e. \sigma^{\epsilon}(t) is uniform on the set \mathcal{T}_{\epsilon}.
errors.explanation: If t\in\mathcal{T}_{\epsilon}, then \sigma^{\epsilon}(t) is the uniform vector, so every coordinate is a (tied) maximum; the right-hand side of (14) is true for every y, but the left-hand side (t_y is the unique/maximal coordinate of t) need not hold. Thus the equivalence in (14) fails for t\in\mathcal{T}_{\epsilon}, so the claim that \sigma^{\epsilon} satisfies (14) is false.

steps.notes_before: Theorem 2: If F is a linear cone that optimally predicts P and P(Δ(X)>0)=1, then any sequence f_m ∈ ε_m-argmin_{f∈F} R_{φ,A_m}(f) with ε_m→0 satisfies R(f_m)→R^*. Section 4.3 setup: X∈R^d, Y∈[k], linear predictors parameterized by Θ∈R^{d×(k-1)} with θ_k=0; link σ:R^{k-1}→R^{k-1}_+ assumed to satisfy link-consistency (14): argmax_t equals argmax_σ(t). Multiclass logistic σ^{lr} is an example. Majority vote mapping ρ_m from σ gives p_{Θ,m}(x)=ρ_m(Θ^*^T x) and ρ_m preserves the argmax order if σ does. Logistic loss (15) used; stationary condition: E[X(σ^{lr}(Θ_m^T X)-ρ_m(Θ^{*T}X))^T]=0. For k=2, even mis-specified link may preserve direction (Θ_m = t_m Θ^* in some settings). For k≥3, small link mis-specification can break risk consistency. The paper defines σ^{ε} that equals σ^{lr} off a small-measure set T_ε and is uniform on T_ε, and then considers L_{m,ε} and Θ_m(ε)=argmin L_{m,ε}; they state Θ_1(0)=Θ^* and claim (forthcoming Proposition 5) that arbitrarily small ε>0 can cause inconsistency without aggregation. (Note: the paper's claim that σ^{ε} preserves link-consistency (14) is incorrect because uniform outputs on T_ε break the iff equivalence in (14).)

errors.claim: The paper's claim that σ^{ε} (which equals σ^{lr} off a small-measure set T_ε and is uniform on T_ε) preserves the link-consistency condition (14).

(Note: the paper's claim that σ^{ε} preserves link-consistency (14) is incorrect because uniform outputs on T_ε break the iff equivalence in (14).)". From this part: "Majority vote, however, can address this inconsistency as m→∞ without any assumptions on the true link σ except that it satisfies the consistency condition (14). ... as Proposition 5 highlights, methods without label aggregation are generally inconsistent."
errors.explanation: If σ^{ε} returns a uniform vector on T_ε then ties / altered orderings occur there, so σ^{ε} does not preserve the argmax-equivalence required by (14). The paper appears to have used σ^{ε} as a small perturbation while also (earlier) claiming it preserves (14); that claim is false. Thus the example underlying Proposition 5 either does not satisfy condition (14) (contradicting the paper's earlier assertion) or the paper misstated σ^{ε}'s properties.

errors.claim: "threshold 1/4 requires only $m\geq128\log40$."
errors.evidence:
The paper gives
"\displaystyle\psi_{m}(\epsilon)=\frac{1}{16}\left(\epsilon-\sqrt{\frac{32}{m}\log 40}\right)_{+},"
then states "threshold 1/4 requires only $m\geq128\log40$."
errors.explanation: For ψ_m(ε) to be positive at ε=1/4 we need sqrt(32/m · log40) < 1/4, i.e. 32/m · log40 < 1/16, so m > 512·log40. Thus the correct bound for threshold 1/4 is m ≥ 512·log40, not 128·log40. (Note: m ≥ 128·log40 would ensure positivity at ε=1/2, not ε=1/4.)

steps.notes_before: Earlier: Theorem 2 gives risk consistency for linear-cone F under optimal prediction and P(Δ(X)>0)=1. Section 4.3: X∈R^d, Y∈[k], linear predictors Θ∈R^{d×(k-1)} with Θ_k=0; link σ must preserve argmax (link-consistency (14)). For multiclass logistic σ^{lr} stationary condition is E[X(σ^{lr}(Θ_m^T X)-ρ_m(Θ^{*T}X))^T]=0. For k≥3 small link mis-spec can break single-label risk consistency (Prop.5 shows small perturbation can change Θ_1 direction under an invertibility condition). Theorem 3: if Θ^*=U^*T^* (U^* orthogonal, T^* nonsingular) then Θ_m=U^*T_m with ||T_m||→∞ and T_m/||T_m||→T^*/||T^*|| (aggregation recovers direction asymptotically). Current part: two experiments. (1) Truncated quadratic φ(δ)=(max{1-δ,0})^2 has calibration ψ(ε)=ε^2. Derived aggregated calibration ψ_m(ε) = (1/16)(ε - sqrt(32/(m) log40))_+. The paper's numeric claim about the threshold m contains an arithmetic error (should be m≥512·log40 for ε=1/4). (2) Mis-specified logistic experiment (k=3,d=2) uses corrupted link \tildeσ(t)=σ^{lr}(t) for ||t||≤r and σ^{lr}(α t) for ||t||>r with r=3, α=0.1; true θ1*=(0,1), θ2*=(1,1). Fig.2 reports normalized-direction error of T_m vs m under two sampling regimes (n=10,000 constant; n=640,000/m to keep total labels constant); results show aggregation recovering direction as m→∞, consistent with Theorem 3.

final_notes: Theorem 1: excess target risk R(f)-R* ≤ (16/C_{φ,1}) · surrogate-regret, so slope ζ = C_{φ,1}/16. Part 10 (Discussion): many consistency results rely on m→∞; finite-m guarantees remain important (ranking can admit finite-m results). Fundamental limits of B2Z: κ(X) can remain large even with low noise (α≈1); binary problems have κ(X)=1. Mis-specified-model results require assumption K7M (existence of Bayes-optimal classifier in F); classical surrogate consistency can still fail while aggregation succeeds. Joint predictor+representation inference suggests task-loss-dependent surrogates; H-consistency and aggregation for restricted classes (Mao et al. show rate-optimal quadratic ψ growth) are open directions.

Paper title: "Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning" by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: aggregating/cleaning labels (information distilled from noisy responses) yields robustness not available without cleaning. Specifically: (1) minimizing a typically convex surrogate loss on aggregated labels gives stronger task-risk consistency guarantees than procedures using raw labels; (2) finite-dimensional classifiers remain consistent under loss mis-specification that breaks standard uncertainty-modeling approaches; (3) in perfectly specified statistical models, using all information is more efficient, but slight loss mis-specification can destroy standard consistency; (4) aggregation preserves convergence to optimal classifiers despite noise; (5) the whole pipeline (collection, fitting, prediction) admits robustness via noisy-signal refinement. Keep these claims in mind for checking consistency with later sections (definitions, assumptions, theorems, empirical results) about surrogate losses, aggregation methods, consistency under mis-specification, and comparisons to raw-label procedures.

Paper: "Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning" (Chen Cheng, John Duchi). Abstract-level claims to check later: aggregation/cleaning of noisy labels yields robustness not available without cleaning, specifically (1) minimizing a convex surrogate on aggregated labels gives stronger task-risk consistency than using raw labels; (2) finite-dimensional classifiers remain consistent under loss mis-specification that breaks standard uncertainty-modeling approaches; (3) in well-specified models, using all information is more efficient but slight loss mis-specification can destroy standard consistency; (4) aggregation preserves convergence to optimal classifiers despite noise; (5) end-to-end pipeline (collection, fitting, prediction) shows robustness via noisy-signal refinement. Introduction adds: aggregation permits consistent optimal prediction under surrogate (but unaggregated estimation cannot), including finite-dimensional problems; linear-estimator constructions in ranking and binary/multiclass classification separate procedures restricted to (X,Y) from aggregation procedures; nonparametric results combine aggregation count and noise conditions, allow approximately linear comparison inequalities under weak surrogate conditions, and extend consistency beyond unrestricted measurable hypothesis classes. Notes that typical supervised pipeline omits cleaning; the paper's concern is that cleaning fundamentally and necessarily improves fitted-model consistency. Context: prior surrogate-risk consistency theory (Bartlett et al. etc.) and many extensions; pair-based empirical-process analyses do not address aggregation machinery. Central research questions: is aggregation needed, does pair-based surrogate consistency suffice, and in what sense does aggregation improve consistency.

steps.notes_before:
Paper: "Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning" — studies how aggregating noisy labels (cleaning) affects surrogate-risk consistency. Key claims (from earlier parts): aggregation can enable consistency not available without cleaning; finite-dimensional classifiers can be consistent under loss mis-specification; nonparametric results combine aggregation counts and noise conditions.

From Preliminaries (this part): two regimes — unrestricted Borel F (classical/Fisher consistency) and parametric (possibly misspecified) F where aggregation may improve consistency. Definitions:
- Distribution-dependent task risk: R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X), P(·|X))] (eqn (2)). Special case zero-one: ℓ(ŷ,P)=∑_y P(Y=y)1{ŷ≠y}.
- Instantaneous task risk: R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),Y)] with ℓ: Y×Y→R_+ (eqn (1)). Binary case: d=1, d(s)=sgn(s), ℓ(y,y')=1{y y'≤0}.
- Surrogate risk: R_φ(f)=E[φ(f(X),Y)].
- Aggregated surrogate risk: R_{φ,A}(f)=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))] (eqn (3)), where Z is response-replacement and A:Z→A is aggregation.
- Repeated labeling: Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m), A_m(Z)=argmin_y ∑_{l=1}^m ℓ(y,Y_l) (majority vote for 0-1 loss).
- K-NN aggregation: Z=(Y,(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m), order X_{(l)} by dist to X, and A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y ∑_{l=0}^K ℓ(y,Y_{(l)}).

Note: the paper uses ℓ both as distribution-dependent ℓ(ŷ,P) and instantaneous ℓ(ŷ,y); equation-numbering/reference error noted above.

final_notes: Key results: Theorem 3 (parametric asymptotic) — with Θ^*=U^* T^*, minimizers satisfy Θ_m=U^* T_m and as m→∞, ||T_m||→∞ and T_m/||T_m||→T^*/||T^*|| (normalized direction recovered). Proposition 5 (k≥3, Σ=I) was stated to produce small-measure perturbations σ^ε that preserve link-consistency (14) while altering the fitted normalized parameter; this appears inconsistent with Theorem 3 unless Proposition 5 is strictly finite-m or otherwise qualified. Binary special case: Θ_m=t_m Θ^* in Gaussian example. Section 3: ranking has finite-m guarantees (Prop.2: m≥k); Section 3.2.3 gives uniform linear comparison at α=1 with O(log k) bound; multiclass condition number κ(X) (eq.9) can be large even when Mammen–Tsybakov noise α≈1. Section 4.3 requires optimal predictability (12); many model results (Corollary 4.1, Theorems 2–3) are asymptotic m→∞. Experiments (Section 5): Truncated quadratic surrogate and aggregated bound ψ_m(ε)=1/16(ε - sqrt{(32/m) log 40})_+ illustrated for m∈{2^16,...,2^32}. Mis-specified logistic experiment (d=2,k=3,r=3,α=0.1) compares errors across m∈{1,4,16,64,256,1024} under two data-designs; reported 95% error bars over T=100 trials. Internal issues: (i) contradiction between Proposition 5 and Theorem 3 (acknowledged by paper but not reconciled), (ii) experiment Figure 2 caption appears to report an incorrect, non-normalized error metric inconsistent with Theorem 3's target.

Paper studies whether aggregating noisy labels improves consistency of learned predictors. Focus: surrogate losses (used during fitting), analyzed over all measurable predictors and over restricted model classes. Develops calibration inequalities for aggregated labels; analyzes ranking, classification, structured prediction. Key claims to remember: for ranking with k ≥ 3 items, no convex surrogate based on individual comparisons is Fisher consistent; an aggregated squared-loss procedure is consistent when m ≥ k. More generally, "identifying" surrogates become asymptotically consistent as number m of aggregated labels grows; many guarantees require m → ∞. Under certain noise conditions, aggregation yields approximately linear comparison inequalities. In restricted model classes, aggregation can restore consistency when ordinary surrogate minimization fails (including link mis-specification). Two numerical illustrations are reported. Glossary follows (definitions and reused symbols listed).

Corollary 3.1: positivity of psi(·,x) for all x,ε>0 characterizes Fisher consistency; Fenchel biconjugate of overline{psi} yields a comparison bound psi(R-R^*) ≤ R_phi-R_phi^*. Ranking example: labels Y={(i,j):i≠j}, p_{ij}=P(Y=(i,j)|x). Define C_x with (C_x)_{ii}=0 and (C_x)_{ij}=p_{ij}/\sum_{l≠j} p_{lj} (use 0/0=1/(k-1)), so C_x^T 1 = 1. Section 4: Aggregation can restore consistency when optimization is restricted to a hypothesis class. Key definitions: ε-argmin g = {θ | g(θ) ≤ inf g + ε}. A_m is majority vote on Z=(Y1,..,Ym). Binary setting: Y={±1}, φ-margin surrogate φ(s,y)=φ(sy) with convex scalar φ; Fisher/uniform consistency over all measurables iff φ'(0)<0. Linear predictor class F = {f_θ(x)=⟨θ,x⟩}. Optimal predictability along θ* means sgn(⟨θ*,x⟩)=sgn(P(Y=1|x)-1/2). Proposition 4 (App D.1): For any nonnegative φ and any ε>0 and nonzero θ*, there exists P optimally predictable along θ* such that every surrogate minimizer θ_φ ∈ argmin_θ E[φ(f_θ(X),Y)] has R(f_{θ_φ})>R(f_{θ*}) and |cos∠(θ_φ,θ*)| ≤ ε (i.e., can be nearly orthogonal). Surrogate φ: R^k×[k]→R_+ assumed Fisher consistent and satisfying limiting loss condition (13): φ(s,y)→0 if s_y - s_j → +∞ for all j≠y. Examples: multiclass logistic φ(s,y)=log(∑ e^{s_j-s_y}) and pairwise-sum losses ∑_{i≠y} φ(s_y-s_i) with scalar φ convex, nonincreasing, φ'(0)<0, inf φ=0. Title: Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning. Authors: Chen Cheng, John Duchi. Abstract claims: learning procedures that rely on aggregated labels (label information distilled from noisy responses) enjoy robustness properties not possible without data cleaning. Key points: (1) In the context of risk consistency (minimizing surrogate, typically convex, losses instead of target task loss like 0-1), procedures using label aggregation obtain stronger consistency guarantees than those possible using raw labels. (2) Classical perfectly-specified model scenarios suggest modeling label uncertainty is statistically efficient, but consistency for “standard” approaches fails as soon as the loss is even slightly mis-specified. (3) Procedures leveraging aggregated information still converge to optimal classifiers despite such mis-specification. Overall claim: incorporating a fuller view of the data collection-to-prediction pipeline (via label aggregation/cleaning) yields a more robust methodology by refining noisy signals.

Title: Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning. Authors: Chen Cheng, John Duchi. Paper studies how label aggregation/cleaning in data pipelines (e.g., crowdsourcing multiple noisy labels then denoising) fundamentally improves consistency and robustness of learned models. Two main robustness aspects: (1) For surrogate risk consistency (minimizing convex surrogate losses vs. target loss like 0-1), procedures using aggregated labels can achieve consistency and optimal prediction in limits where methods using raw (X,Y) pairs cannot. (2) Even in finite-dimensional parametric/statistical settings, aggregation can yield consistent classifiers when standard approaches fail. The paper situates itself with prior surrogate-consistency theory (Bartlett et al. and follow-up work) and asks whether aggregation is necessary/useful, and in what sense. Promised contributions/examples: ranking, binary and multiclass classification with linear estimators where (X,Y)-based estimators fail but aggregation yields consistency; nonparametric results where number of samples aggregated and noise conditions determine improved consistency; demonstration that aggregation enables surrogate risk consistency under weak conditions via (approximate) linear comparison inequalities; results showing aggregation can guarantee consistency even over restricted hypothesis classes where unaggregated approaches fail.

steps.notes_before: Preliminaries: X input space, Y output space, data (X_i,Y_i) iid from P. Scoring f:X->R^d, decoder d:R^d->Y, task risk R(f)=E_P[ℓ(d∘f(X),Y)] (instantaneous-label form, eq. (1)). Also consider a refined task loss depending on conditional label distribution: R(f)=E_P[ℓ(d∘f(X), P(·|X))] (eq. (2)). Two study scenarios: (i) Fisher consistency (F all Borel functions); (ii) statistical/parametric hypothesis classes (possibly mis-specified). Surrogate φ introduced to optimize: originally φ:R^d×Y->R, surrogate risk R_φ(f)=E_P[φ(f(X),Y)]. Label aggregation: observed Z (e.g., multiple labels or extra draws), aggregation map A:Z->A, aggregated surrogate φ:R^d×A->R_+, aggregated risk R_{φ,A}(f)=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))]. Example 1 (majority vote): Z=(Y_1,...,Y_m), A(Z)=argmin_y ∑_{l=1}^m ℓ(y,Y_l); for 0-1 loss this is majority vote. Example 2 (K-NN aggregation): Z=(Y,(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m); order X_i by distance to X, set X_(0)=X (so Y_(0)=Y), define A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y ∑_{l=0}^K ℓ(y,Y_(l)). Main claimed message: label aggregation improves consistency/robustness in both scenarios.

Surrogate-consistency setup: conditional task risk R(s|x)=ℓ(d∘s,P(Y|X=x)), conditional surrogate risk R_φ(s|x)=E[φ(s,Y)|X=x]. Pointwise excesses δ_ℓ(s,x)=R(s|x)-inf_s'R(s'|x), δ_φ(s,x)=R_φ(s|x)-inf_s'R_φ(s'|x). Global minima R* and R_φ*. Two consistency notions: (i) Fisher consistency: for any sequence f_n, R_φ(f_n)→R_φ* implies R(f_n)→R*; (ii) uniform comparison: exists nondecreasing ψ with ψ(ε)>0 for ε>0 s.t. ψ(R(f)-R*) ≤ R_φ(f)-R_φ* for all f. Calibration functions: ψ(ε,x)=inf_{s}{δ_φ(s,x) | δ_ℓ(s,x)≥ε}, overline ψ(ε)=inf_x ψ(ε,x). Corollary 3.1: φ is Fisher consistent iff ψ(ε,x)>0 for all x,ε>0; taking Fenchel biconjugate of overline ψ gives a ψ s.t. ψ(R(f)-R*) ≤ R_φ(f)-R_φ*. Ranking example (Sec 3.1): Y={(i,j): i≠j, i beats j}, p_{ij}=P(Y=(i,j)|x). Define C_x with (C_x)_{ii}=0 and (C_x)_{ij}=p_{ij}/∑_{l≠j}p_{lj} (set 0/0=1/(k-1)), so C_x is column-stochastic (C_x^T1=1). Rank by vector C_x1; loss ℓ(s,C)=max_{i<j}1{(s_i-s_j)((C1)_i-(C1)_j) ≤0, (C1)_i≠(C1)_j}. Population risk R(f)=P(f(X) and C_X1 order differently). Proposition 1: for k≥3, any convex-in-first-arg φ:R^k×Y→R is not Fisher consistent. Aggregation fix: collect m independent comparisons Z=(Y_1,..,Y_m); counts m_{ij}, m_j=∑_i m_{ij}; define A(Z)=⋆ if any m_j=0, else A_i=∑_{j} m_{ij}/m_j. Claim: regressing on A(Z) yields consistency when m≥k (Prop 2; proofs in App A.1/A.2).

final_notes:
Main theoretical claims: aggregation (T4K) yields robustness; Prop.4: unaggregated multiclass can be arbitrarily misaligned (near-orthogonality). Aggregation of approximate minimizers (ε_m→0) implies R(f_m)→R^*. Multiclass logistic surrogate (with θ_k=0 convention) φ(Θ^T x,y) = -⟨θ_y,x⟩ + log(1+∑_{i=1}^{k-1} e^{⟨θ_i,x⟩}); first-order conditions involve the logistic σ^{lr}. Small corruptions can destroy unaggregated consistency; aggregation restores consistency in many settings. Key inequalities: ψ(R-R^*) ≤ R_φ - R_φ^* and aggregated version ψ_m(R-R^*) ≤ R_{φ,A_m} - R_{φ,A_m}^*.
Experiments: (1) D4X (binary truncated-quadratic φ(δ)=max{1-δ,0}^2). Unaggregated H8N ψ(ε)=ε^2. With parameters δ=1, α=0, C_MT=1, derived aggregated calibration ψ_m(ε) = (1/16)(ε - √(32/m · log 40))_+. Plotted m∈{2^16,2^20,2^24,2^28,2^32}.
(2) Mis-specified logistic finite-dimensional experiment: corrupted link \tildeσ(t)=σ^{lr}(t)·1{||t||≤r}+σ^{lr}(αt)·1{||t||>r} with r=3, α=0.1. Two regimes: fixed n=10,000 per m and fixed total labels nm with n=640000/m. Settings: d=2, k=3, θ_1^*=(0,1)^T, θ_2^*=(1,1)^T (θ_3=0), m∈{1,4,16,64,256,1024}, 95% error bars, T=100 trials. Plotted error likely ||T_m/||T_m|| - T^*/||T^*|||| (T_m ≈ fitted Θ_m).
Discussion / open problems: reliance on m→∞ unsatisfying; ranking admits explicit finite-m guarantees; need a joint theory depending on (ℓ,φ,m) and counts (possibly higher-order comparisons). B2Z limits: κ(X) can be large beyond binary even with low noise (α≈1); binary problems have κ(X)=1. Mis-specified-model results assume K7M (existence of Bayes-optimal classifier in F); aggregation can succeed where classical surrogate consistency fails. Extensions: restricted-class (H-)consistency, aggregation upgrades, and unifying parametric/nonparametric analyses (Mao et al. show rate-optimal quadratic ψ growth for smooth convex losses).

Paper title: "Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning" by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: aggregating/cleaning labels (information distilled from noisy responses) yields robustness not available without cleaning. Specifically: (1) minimizing a typically convex surrogate loss on aggregated labels gives stronger task-risk consistency guarantees than procedures using raw labels; (2) finite-dimensional classifiers remain consistent under loss mis-specification that breaks standard uncertainty-modeling approaches; (3) in perfectly specified statistical models, using all information is more efficient, but slight loss mis-specification can destroy standard consistency; (4) aggregation preserves convergence to optimal classifiers despite noise; (5) the whole pipeline (collection, fitting, prediction) admits robustness via noisy-signal refinement. Keep these claims in mind for checking consistency with later sections (definitions, assumptions, theorems, empirical results) about surrogate losses, aggregation methods, consistency under mis-specification, and comparisons to raw-label procedures.

Paper: "Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning" (Chen Cheng, John Duchi). Abstract-level claims to check later: aggregation/cleaning of noisy labels yields robustness not available without cleaning, specifically (1) minimizing a convex surrogate on aggregated labels gives stronger task-risk consistency than using raw labels; (2) finite-dimensional classifiers remain consistent under loss mis-specification that breaks standard uncertainty-modeling approaches; (3) in well-specified models, using all information is more efficient but slight loss mis-specification can destroy standard consistency; (4) aggregation preserves convergence to optimal classifiers despite noise; (5) end-to-end pipeline (collection, fitting, prediction) shows robustness via noisy-signal refinement. Introduction adds: aggregation permits consistent optimal prediction under surrogate (but unaggregated estimation cannot), including finite-dimensional problems; linear-estimator constructions in ranking and binary/multiclass classification separate procedures restricted to (X,Y) from aggregation procedures; nonparametric results combine aggregation count and noise conditions, allow approximately linear comparison inequalities under weak surrogate conditions, and extend consistency beyond unrestricted measurable hypothesis classes. Notes that typical supervised pipeline omits cleaning; the paper's concern is that cleaning fundamentally and necessarily improves fitted-model consistency. Context: prior surrogate-risk consistency theory (Bartlett et al. etc.) and many extensions; pair-based empirical-process analyses do not address aggregation machinery. Central research questions: is aggregation needed, does pair-based surrogate consistency suffice, and in what sense does aggregation improve consistency.

From Preliminaries (this part): two regimes — unrestricted Borel F (classical/Fisher consistency) and parametric (possibly misspecified) F where aggregation may improve consistency. Definitions:
- Distribution-dependent task risk: R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X), P(·|X))] (eqn (2)). Special case zero-one: ℓ(ŷ,P)=∑_y P(Y=y)1{ŷ≠y}.

- Aggregated surrogate risk: R_{φ,A}(f)=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))] (eqn (3)), where Z is response-replacement and A:Z→A is aggregation.
- Repeated labeling: Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m), A_m(Z)=argmin_y ∑_{l=1}^m ℓ(y,Y_l) (majority vote for 0-1 loss).
- K-NN aggregation: Z=(Y,(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m), order X_{(l)} by dist to X, and A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y ∑_{l=0}^K ℓ(y,Y_{(l)}).

Paper studies whether aggregating noisy labels improves consistency of learned predictors. Focus: surrogate losses (used during fitting), analyzed over all measurable predictors and over restricted model classes. Develops calibration inequalities for aggregated labels; analyzes ranking, classification, structured prediction. Key claims to remember: for ranking with k ≥ 3 items, no convex surrogate based on individual comparisons is Fisher consistent; an aggregated squared-loss procedure is consistent when m ≥ k. More generally, "identifying" surrogates become asymptotically consistent as number m of aggregated labels grows; many guarantees require m → ∞. Under certain noise conditions, aggregation yields approximately linear comparison inequalities. In restricted model classes, aggregation can restore consistency when ordinary surrogate minimization fails (including link mis-specification). Two numerical illustrations are reported. Calibration psi(ε,x)=inf_{s}{delta_phi(s,x) | delta_l(s,x)≥ε}, overline{psi}(ε)=inf_x psi(ε,x). final_notes: Paper studies label aggregation vs un-aggregated (noisy) labels. Setup: multiclass Y∈[k], features X∈R^d, linear predictors Θ∈R^{d×(k-1)} with Θ_k=0. Key theoretical claims: Theorem 2 risk consistency for linear-cone F when F optimally predicts P and P(Δ(X)>0)=1. Section 4.3: logistic surrogate σ^{lr} stationary condition and a construction σ^ε shows small link mis-spec can break risk consistency for k≥3 (Prop.5). Theorem 3: for Θ*=U* T* (U* orthogonal, T* nonsingular), minimizers Θ_m have Θ_m = U* T_m with ||T_m||→∞ and T_m/||T_m||→T*/||T*|| — aggregated-label minimizers asymptotically recover Θ* direction. Note: earlier claim that σ^ε preserved argmax (link-consistency (14)) was corrected (it does not). Experiments: (i) truncated-quadratic binary surrogate φ(δ)=max{1-δ,0}^2 yields calibration ψ(ε)=ε^2 and finite-m bound from Lemma 3.1: ψ_m(ε)= (1/16)(ε - sqrt((32/m) log 40))_+. Aggregation moves ψ_m from quadratic toward linear as m→∞. (ii) Mis-specified logistic experiment: define σ~ using σ^{lr} for ||t||≤r and σ^{lr}(α t) otherwise (r=3, α=0.1); d=2,k=3, true θ1*=(0,1)^T, θ2*=(1,1)^T. Two experiments: fixed n=10k; and n=640k/m so total labels constant. Plot normalized-direction error vs m∈{1,4,16,64,256,1024}, 100 trials, showing aggregation recovers asymptotic consistency (consistent with Theorem 3). Discussion/future work: need finite-m consistency theory; study noise condition number κ(X) (Eq.(9))—binary case trivially κ(X)=1; κ(X) presents challenges beyond binary even under low Mammen–Tsybakov noise (α≈1); study mis-specified models beyond optimal-predictability (12); extend H-consistency/restricted-class comparison inequalities and relate aggregation to quadratic-growth ψ rate-optimality (Mao et al.).

Title: Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning. Authors: Chen Cheng, John Duchi. Abstract claims: learning procedures that rely on aggregated labels (label information distilled from noisy responses) enjoy robustness properties not possible without data cleaning. Key points: (1) In the context of risk consistency (minimizing surrogate, typically convex, losses instead of target task loss like 0-1), procedures using label aggregation obtain stronger consistency guarantees than those possible using raw labels. (2) Classical perfectly-specified model scenarios suggest modeling label uncertainty is statistically efficient, but consistency for “standard” approaches fails as soon as the loss is even slightly mis-specified. (3) Procedures leveraging aggregated information still converge to optimal classifiers despite such mis-specification. Overall claim: incorporating a fuller view of the data collection-to-prediction pipeline (via label aggregation/cleaning) yields a more robust methodology by refining noisy signals.

Title: Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning. Authors: Chen Cheng, John Duchi. Paper studies how label aggregation/cleaning in data pipelines (e.g., crowdsourcing multiple noisy labels then denoising) fundamentally improves consistency and robustness of learned models. Two main robustness aspects: (1) For surrogate risk consistency (minimizing convex surrogate losses vs. target loss like 0-1), procedures using aggregated labels can achieve consistency and optimal prediction in limits where methods using raw (X,Y) pairs cannot. (2) Even in finite-dimensional parametric/statistical settings, aggregation can yield consistent classifiers when standard approaches fail. The paper situates itself with prior surrogate-consistency theory (Bartlett et al. and follow-up work) and asks whether aggregation is necessary/useful, and in what sense. Promised contributions/examples: ranking, binary and multiclass classification with linear estimators where (X,Y)-based estimators fail but aggregation yields consistency; nonparametric results where number of samples aggregated and noise conditions determine improved consistency; demonstration that aggregation enables surrogate risk consistency under weak conditions via (approximate) linear comparison inequalities; results showing aggregation can guarantee consistency even over restricted hypothesis classes where unaggregated approaches fail.

steps.notes_before: Preliminaries: X input space, Y output space, data (X_i,Y_i) iid from P. Scoring f:X->R^d, decoder d:R^d->Y, task risk R(f)=E_P[ℓ(d∘f(X),Y)] (instantaneous-label form, eq. (1)). Also consider a refined task loss depending on conditional label distribution: R(f)=E_P[ℓ(d∘f(X), P(·|X))] (eq. (2)). Two study scenarios: (i) Fisher consistency (F all Borel functions); (ii) statistical/parametric hypothesis classes (possibly mis-specified). Surrogate φ introduced to optimize: originally φ:R^d×Y->R, surrogate risk R_φ(f)=E_P[φ(f(X),Y)]. Label aggregation: observed Z (e.g., multiple labels or extra draws), aggregation map A:Z->A, aggregated surrogate φ:R^d×A->R_+, aggregated risk R_{φ,A}(f)=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))]. Example 1 (majority vote): Z=(Y_1,...,Y_m), A(Z)=argmin_y ∑_{l=1}^m ℓ(y,Y_l); for 0-1 loss this is majority vote. Example 2 (K-NN aggregation): Z=(Y,(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m); order X_i by distance to X, set X_(0)=X (so Y_(0)=Y), define A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y ∑_{l=0}^K ℓ(y,Y_(l)). Main claimed message: label aggregation improves consistency/robustness in both scenarios.

Surrogate-consistency setup: conditional task risk R(s|x)=ℓ(d∘s,P(Y|X=x)), conditional surrogate risk R_φ(s|x)=E[φ(s,Y)|X=x]. Pointwise excesses δ_ℓ(s,x)=R(s|x)-inf_s'R(s'|x), δ_φ(s,x)=R_φ(s|x)-inf_s'R_φ(s'|x). Global minima R* and R_φ*. Two consistency notions: (i) Fisher consistency: for any sequence f_n, R_φ(f_n)→R_φ* implies R(f_n)→R*; (ii) uniform comparison: exists nondecreasing ψ with ψ(ε)>0 for ε>0 s.t. ψ(R(f)-R*) ≤ R_φ(f)-R_φ* for all f. Calibration functions: ψ(ε,x)=inf_{s}{δ_φ(s,x) | δ_ℓ(s,x)≥ε}, overline ψ(ε)=inf_x ψ(ε,x). Corollary 3.1: φ is Fisher consistent iff ψ(ε,x)>0 for all x,ε>0; taking Fenchel biconjugate of overline ψ gives a ψ s.t. ψ(R(f)-R*) ≤ R_φ(f)-R_φ*. Ranking example (Sec 3.1): Y={(i,j): i≠j, i beats j}, p_{ij}=P(Y=(i,j)|x). Define C_x with (C_x)_{ii}=0 and (C_x)_{ij}=p_{ij}/∑_{l≠j}p_{lj} (set 0/0=1/(k-1)), so C_x is column-stochastic (C_x^T1=1). Rank by vector C_x1; loss ℓ(s,C)=max_{i<j}1{(s_i-s_j)((C1)_i-(C1)_j) ≤0, (C1)_i≠(C1)_j}. Population risk R(f)=P(f(X) and C_X1 order differently). Proposition 1: for k≥3, any convex-in-first-arg φ:R^k×Y→R is not Fisher consistent. Aggregation fix: collect m independent comparisons Z=(Y_1,..,Y_m); counts m_{ij}, m_j=∑_i m_{ij}; define A(Z)=⋆ if any m_j=0, else A_i=∑_{j} m_{ij}/m_j. Claim: regressing on A(Z) yields consistency when m≥k (Prop 2; proofs in App A.1/A.2).

final_notes: Theorem 1: excess target risk R(f)-R* ≤ (16/C_{φ,1})·(surrogate regret) (slope ζ = C_{φ,1}/16). Theorem 2: for F a cone and P(Δ(X)>0)=1, any ε_m-approx surrogate minimizers (with aggregation) satisfy R(f_m)→R*. Pairwise surrogates can be inconsistent for k≥3; aggregation (A_m) restores ordering/direction asymptotically: fitted parameters behave like Θ_m = U* T_m with ||T_m||→∞ and normalized directions → true direction. Constructed corruptions σ^ε replace softmax by uniform on a small set. Finite-dimensional multiclass logistic used identification θ_k=0; first-order condition equates E[X(σ^{lr}(Θ_m^T X) - ρ_m(Θ^*^T X))^T]=0. Binary case (k=2) can preserve direction under Gaussian X (Θ_m = t_m Θ^*). Numerics: (1) D4X surrogate amplification (binary) with truncated-quadratic φ(δ)=max{1-δ,0}^2: unaggregated calibration ψ(ε)=ε^2; aggregated calibration ψ_m(ε) = (1/16)·(ε - sqrt{(32/m)·log 40})_+. m ∈ {2^16,2^20,2^24,2^28,2^32} shows transition from quadratic toward linear as m→∞. (2) Mis-specified logistic (k=3,d=2) corrupted link ~σ(t)=σ^{lr}(t)·1{||t||≤r} + σ^{lr}(α t)·1{||t||>r} with r=3, α=0.1. Two sampling regimes: (i) fixed n=10,000 multilabeled points; (ii) fixed total labels nm=640,000 (n=640,000/m). True params θ1*=(0,1), θ2*=(1,1), θ3*=0. m ∈ {1,4,16,64,256,1024}, T=100 trials; metric is directional classification-rule error vs m showing asymptotic consistency as m→∞. Discussion points: finite-m consistency is unsatisfying and ranking has explicit finite-m guarantees; need joint theory in (ℓ,φ,m). Claim that κ(X) is smaller beyond binary (binary κ(X)=1) even under low N6Y noise (α≈1). Mis-specified-model results require K7M; Nguyen et al. and Duchi et al. show joint inference of f and representation forces task-loss-dependent surrogate forms. H-consistency work (e.g. Mao et al.) shows rate-optimal quadratic ψ growth for smooth convex loss; extending aggregation comparisons to restricted hypothesis classes and unifying parametric/nonparametric perspectives are open directions.

Paper title: "Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning" by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: aggregating/cleaning labels (information distilled from noisy responses) yields robustness not available without cleaning. Specifically: (1) minimizing a typically convex surrogate loss on aggregated labels gives stronger task-risk consistency guarantees than procedures using raw labels; (2) finite-dimensional classifiers remain consistent under loss mis-specification that breaks standard uncertainty-modeling approaches; (3) in perfectly specified statistical models, using all information is more efficient, but slight loss mis-specification can destroy standard consistency; (4) aggregation preserves convergence to optimal classifiers despite noise; (5) the whole pipeline (collection, fitting, prediction) admits robustness via noisy-signal refinement. Keep these claims in mind for checking consistency with later sections (definitions, assumptions, theorems, empirical results) about surrogate losses, aggregation methods, consistency under mis-specification, and comparisons to raw-label procedures.

Paper: "Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning" (Chen Cheng, John Duchi). Abstract-level claims to check later: aggregation/cleaning of noisy labels yields robustness not available without cleaning, specifically (1) minimizing a convex surrogate on aggregated labels gives stronger task-risk consistency than using raw labels; (2) finite-dimensional classifiers remain consistent under loss mis-specification that breaks standard uncertainty-modeling approaches; (3) in well-specified models, using all information is more efficient but slight loss mis-specification can destroy standard consistency; (4) aggregation preserves convergence to optimal classifiers despite noise; (5) end-to-end pipeline (collection, fitting, prediction) shows robustness via noisy-signal refinement. Introduction adds: aggregation permits consistent optimal prediction under surrogate (but unaggregated estimation cannot), including finite-dimensional problems; linear-estimator constructions in ranking and binary/multiclass classification separate procedures restricted to (X,Y) from aggregation procedures; nonparametric results combine aggregation count and noise conditions, allow approximately linear comparison inequalities under weak surrogate conditions, and extend consistency beyond unrestricted measurable hypothesis classes. Notes that typical supervised pipeline omits cleaning; the paper's concern is that cleaning fundamentally and necessarily improves fitted-model consistency. Context: prior surrogate-risk consistency theory (Bartlett et al. etc.) and many extensions; pair-based empirical-process analyses do not address aggregation machinery. Central research questions: is aggregation needed, does pair-based surrogate consistency suffice, and in what sense does aggregation improve consistency.

steps.notes_before:
Paper: "Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning" — studies how aggregating noisy labels (cleaning) affects surrogate-risk consistency. Key claims (from earlier parts): aggregation can enable consistency not available without cleaning; finite-dimensional classifiers can be consistent under loss mis-specification; nonparametric results combine aggregation counts and noise conditions.

From Preliminaries (this part): two regimes — unrestricted Borel F (classical/Fisher consistency) and parametric (possibly misspecified) F where aggregation may improve consistency. Definitions:
- Distribution-dependent task risk: R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X), P(·|X))] (eqn (2)). Special case zero-one: ℓ(ŷ,P)=∑_y P(Y=y)1{ŷ≠y}.
- Instantaneous task risk: R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),Y)] with ℓ: Y×Y→R_+ (eqn (1)). Binary case: d=1, d(s)=sgn(s), ℓ(y,y')=1{y y'≤0}.
- Surrogate risk: R_φ(f)=E[φ(f(X),Y)].
- Aggregated surrogate risk: R_{φ,A}(f)=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))] (eqn (3)), where Z is response-replacement and A:Z→A is aggregation.
- Repeated labeling: Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m), A_m(Z)=argmin_y ∑_{l=1}^m ℓ(y,Y_l) (majority vote for 0-1 loss).
- K-NN aggregation: Z=(Y,(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m), order X_{(l)} by dist to X, and A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y ∑_{l=0}^K ℓ(y,Y_{(l)}).

Note: the paper uses ℓ both as distribution-dependent ℓ(ŷ,P) and instantaneous ℓ(ŷ,y); equation-numbering/reference error noted above.

W3C (Identifying surrogate): φ: R^d×A→R is (C_{φ,1},C_{φ,2})-W3C if ∃ parameters {a_y}⊂A and vectors {s_y}⊂R^d with d(s_y)=y and for all y≠y': (6a) φ(s_y,a_y)+C_{φ,1} ≤ inf_{d∘s≠y} φ(s,a_y), (6b) φ(s_y,a_{y'})-C_{φ,2} ≤ inf_s φ(s,a_{y'}). Constants satisfy 0<C_{φ,1}≤C_{φ,2}<∞. Binary hinge example yields (C_{φ,1},C_{φ,2})=(1,2). Theorem 1 (W3C + J9P aggregator): assume 0≤ℓ≤1 and noise condition (Nα) (α∈[0,1]). For any M>0, if R(f)-R* ≥ 2P(κ(X)>M) + (4 C_MT e_m(M))^{1/(1-α)} then R(f)-R* ≤ (16/C_{φ,1})(R_{φ,A_m}(f)-R_{φ,A_m}^*). Using crude bound κ≤1/Δ and optimizing M gives a piecewise lower bound ξ_{m,k} (k=2 and otherwise) (forms given in text). Corollary 3.3: any f with R(f)-R* ≥ ξ_{m,k} satisfies the same bound. Definition 3.2 (U6A: level-(ξ,ζ) consistency): ∃ψ with ψ(ε)≥ζ ε for ε≥ξ and ψ(R(f)-R*) ≤ R_{φ,A}(f)-R_{φ,A}^*. Δ(x)=min_{d(s)∉y*(x)} δ_ℓ(s,x) (eq.8). Noise conditions: (Nα) P(d∘f≠d∘f*) ≤ C_MT (R(f)-R*)^α; (Mβ) P(Δ(X)≤ε) ≤ (C_MT ε)^β; equivalent when β=α/(1-α). κ(x) ratio defined eq.(9). Error function e_m(t)= t sqrt{(2/m) log(4k(C_{φ,1}+C_{φ,2})/C_{φ,1})} (eq.10). Section 3.3: Lemma 3.1 (binary): for any δ>0 φ is feasible with C_{φ,1}=φ(0)-φ(δ)>0, C_{φ,2}=φ(-δ); gives explicit threshold-bound for k=2 and corresponding multiplicative constant 16/(φ(0)-φ(δ)).

\[

errors.claim: "Clearly \(\sigma^\epsilon\) satisfies (14)"
errors.evidence: (14): "\(t_y=\max_{1\le i\le k}t_i\quad\text{if and only if}\quad\sigma_y(t)=\max_{1\le i\le k}\sigma_i(t).\)" and the definition "\(\sigma^\epsilon(t)=\sigma^{\textup{lr}}(t)1\{t\notin\mathcal T_\epsilon\}+\frac1k\mathbf1\cdot1\{t\in\mathcal T_\epsilon\}.\)"

final_notes: Discussion (Part 15): paper situates results in data-cleaning debate; highlights finite-m, noise condition κ(X) (eq.9), mis-specified-model limits (optimal predictability eq.12), and restricted-class comparison extensions. Finite-m: ranking has finite-m guarantees (Prop.2 gives m≥k); Section 3.2.3 gives uniform linear comparison at α=1 with displayed O(log k) bound. Many model guarantees asymptotic: Corollary 4.1 and Theorems 2–3 require m→∞ (Theorem 3: Θ_m = U^* T_m, ||T_m||→∞ and T_m/||T_m||→T^*/||T^*||). Mis-specification: Section 4.3 requires optimal predictability; Prop.4 and Prop.5 show ordinary surrogate failure contrasts with aggregation successes (Prop.5 tension flagged earlier). Internal contradiction: subsection on noise condition number both claims it "can remain large beyond binary classification, even at low noise" and also claims it "is smaller than in binary classification even when α≈1"; unresolved. Numerical experiments (Part 14) aimed to illustrate Theorem 3 convergence (normalized T_m → normalized T^*).

Paper studies whether aggregating noisy labels improves consistency of learned predictors. Focus: surrogate losses (used during fitting), analyzed over all measurable predictors and over restricted model classes. Develops calibration inequalities for aggregated labels; analyzes ranking, classification, structured prediction. Key claims to remember: for ranking with k ≥ 3 items, no convex surrogate based on individual comparisons is Fisher consistent; an aggregated squared-loss procedure is consistent when m ≥ k. More generally, "identifying" surrogates become asymptotically consistent as number m of aggregated labels grows; many guarantees require m → ∞. Under certain noise conditions, aggregation yields approximately linear comparison inequalities. In restricted model classes, aggregation can restore consistency when ordinary surrogate minimization fails (including link mis-specification). Two numerical illustrations are reported. Glossary follows (definitions and reused symbols listed).

final_notes: Main theoretical points: Zhang's Thm.8 (binary-margin) gives consistency for convex, nonincreasing φ with φ'(0)<0 and inf φ=0. Finite-dimensional multiclass setup: X=R^d, k classes, model p_Θ via link σ(t) with t_k=0; link-consistency means argmax t ↔ argmax σ(t). Proposition 5 (k≥3, Σ=I) exhibits small perturbations of softmax giving inconsistency without aggregation (Θ_1(ε)/||Θ_1(ε)|| ≠ Θ*/||Θ*||). Theorem 3 (aggregation) shows that for Θ*=U* T* (U* orthonormal columns, T* nonsingular) the minimizer under aggregation Θ_m = U* T_m with ||T_m||→∞ and T_m/||T_m||→T*/||T*|| as m→∞ (so normalized Θ_m→normalized Θ*). Numerics: (1) Truncated quadratic surrogate φ(δ)=max{1−δ,0}^2 with calibration ψ(ε)=ε^2. Using Lemma 3.1 (δ=1, no low-noise α=0,C_MT=1) yields ψ_m(ε) = (1/16)(ε − sqrt((32/m) log 40))_+. Plots for m∈{2^16,...,2^32} show ψ_m→(1/16)ε and theorem bounds are conservative. (2) Mis-specified logistic (multiclass) experiment: k=3,d=2; corrupted link ṡigma(t)=σ^{lr}(t) for ||t||≤r and σ^{lr}(α t) for ||t||>r (r=3, α=0.1). True parameters θ1*=(0,1)^T, θ2*=(1,1)^T. Directional error of normalized T_m vs m∈{1,4,16,64,256,1024} shows normalized T_m→normalized T* as m grows; left panel n=10,000 per m, right panel n=640,000/m (fixed total labels); 95% error bars over 100 trials. Discussion / open problems: many consistency results are asymptotic in m→∞; finite-m guarantees (ranking Sec.3.1 has some finite-m results) are important future work. The noise condition number κ(X) (Eq.(9)) characterizes comparison inequalities in multiclass; binary trivially κ(X)=1 but κ can be large beyond binary even if Mammen–Tsybakov exponent α is favorable. Mis-specified model results (Sec.4.3) require optimal predictability (Eq.(12): Bayes-optimal classifier in F); moving beyond that is open. Extending restricted-class (H-)consistency and connecting loss ℓ and surrogate φ to tighten comparison inequalities are promising directions.

Title: Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning. Authors: Chen Cheng, John Duchi. Abstract claims: learning procedures that rely on aggregated labels (label information distilled from noisy responses) enjoy robustness properties not possible without data cleaning. Key points: (1) In the context of risk consistency (minimizing surrogate, typically convex, losses instead of target task loss like 0-1), procedures using label aggregation obtain stronger consistency guarantees than those possible using raw labels. (2) Classical perfectly-specified model scenarios suggest modeling label uncertainty is statistically efficient, but consistency for “standard” approaches fails as soon as the loss is even slightly mis-specified. (3) Procedures leveraging aggregated information still converge to optimal classifiers despite such mis-specification. Overall claim: incorporating a fuller view of the data collection-to-prediction pipeline (via label aggregation/cleaning) yields a more robust methodology by refining noisy signals.

Title: Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning. Authors: Chen Cheng, John Duchi. Paper studies how label aggregation/cleaning in data pipelines (e.g., crowdsourcing multiple noisy labels then denoising) fundamentally improves consistency and robustness of learned models. Two main robustness aspects: (1) For surrogate risk consistency (minimizing convex surrogate losses vs. target loss like 0-1), procedures using aggregated labels can achieve consistency and optimal prediction in limits where methods using raw (X,Y) pairs cannot. (2) Even in finite-dimensional parametric/statistical settings, aggregation can yield consistent classifiers when standard approaches fail. The paper situates itself with prior surrogate-consistency theory (Bartlett et al. and follow-up work) and asks whether aggregation is necessary/useful, and in what sense. Promised contributions/examples: ranking, binary and multiclass classification with linear estimators where (X,Y)-based estimators fail but aggregation yields consistency; nonparametric results where number of samples aggregated and noise conditions determine improved consistency; demonstration that aggregation enables surrogate risk consistency under weak conditions via (approximate) linear comparison inequalities; results showing aggregation can guarantee consistency even over restricted hypothesis classes where unaggregated approaches fail.

Surrogate φ introduced to optimize: originally φ:R^d×Y->R, surrogate risk R_φ(f)=E_P[φ(f(X),Y)]. Label aggregation: observed Z (e.g., multiple labels or extra draws), aggregation map A:Z->A, aggregated surrogate φ:R^d×A->R_+, aggregated risk R_{φ,A}(f)=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))]. Example 1 (majority vote): Z=(Y_1,...,Y_m), A(Z)=argmin_y ∑_{l=1}^m ℓ(y,Y_l); for 0-1 loss this is majority vote. Example 2 (K-NN aggregation): Z=(Y,(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m); order X_i by distance to X, set X_(0)=X (so Y_(0)=Y), define A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y ∑_{l=0}^K ℓ(y,Y_(l)). Main claimed message: label aggregation improves consistency/robustness in both scenarios.

Surrogate-consistency setup: conditional task risk R(s|x)=ℓ(d∘s,P(Y|X=x)), conditional surrogate risk R_φ(s|x)=E[φ(s,Y)|X=x]. Pointwise excesses δ_ℓ(s,x)=R(s|x)-inf_s'R(s'|x), δ_φ(s,x)=R_φ(s|x)-inf_s'R_φ(s'|x). Global minima R* and R_φ*. Two consistency notions: (i) Fisher consistency: for any sequence f_n, R_φ(f_n)→R_φ* implies R(f_n)→R*; (ii) uniform comparison: exists nondecreasing ψ with ψ(ε)>0 for ε>0 s.t. ψ(R(f)-R*) ≤ R_φ(f)-R_φ* for all f. Calibration functions: ψ(ε,x)=inf_{s}{δ_φ(s,x) | δ_ℓ(s,x)≥ε}, overline ψ(ε)=inf_x ψ(ε,x). Corollary 3.1: φ is Fisher consistent iff ψ(ε,x)>0 for all x,ε>0; taking Fenchel biconjugate of overline ψ gives a ψ s.t. ψ(R(f)-R*) ≤ R_φ(f)-R_φ*. Ranking example (Sec 3.1): Y={(i,j): i≠j, i beats j}, p_{ij}=P(Y=(i,j)|x). Define C_x with (C_x)_{ii}=0 and (C_x)_{ij}=p_{ij}/∑_{l≠j}p_{lj} (set 0/0=1/(k-1)), so C_x is column-stochastic (C_x^T1=1). Rank by vector C_x1; loss ℓ(s,C)=max_{i<j}1{(s_i-s_j)((C1)_i-(C1)_j) ≤0, (C1)_i≠(C1)_j}. Population risk R(f)=P(f(X) and C_X1 order differently). Proposition 1: for k≥3, any convex-in-first-arg φ:R^k×Y→R is not Fisher consistent. Aggregation fix: collect m independent comparisons Z=(Y_1,..,Y_m); counts m_{ij}, m_j=∑_i m_{ij}; define A(Z)=⋆ if any m_j=0, else A_i=∑_{j} m_{ij}/m_j. Claim: regressing on A(Z) yields consistency when m≥k (Prop 2; proofs in App A.1/A.2).

Also the text here refers to "pointwise and uniform" calibration, so the uniform version should be an infimum over x.

Aggregator A_m returns a_{ŷ} with ŷ minimizing sample sum loss; Corollary 3.2: if m→∞ and φ identifying then surrogate-consistency (R_{φ,A_m}(f_n)→opt) implies task-consistency (R(f_n)→opt).

New (Part 8) — Section 4: studies restricted hypothesis classes (parametric models). Binary case (Y∈{±1}): margin surrogate φ(sy) (convex). Classical result recalled: for unrestricted F, φ achieves Fisher and uniform consistency iff φ'(0)<0. But restricting to linear predictors F={f_θ(x)=⟨θ,x⟩} can break consistency even when P is optimally predictable along some θ* (sgn(⟨θ*,x⟩)=sgn(P(Y=1|x)-1/2)).

Proposition 4: For any ε>0 and nonzero θ*, there exists P (optimally predictable along θ*) such that any θ_φ ∈ argmin_θ E[φ(f_θ(X),Y)] satisfies R(f_{θ_φ})>R(f_{θ*}) and |cos angle(θ_φ,θ*)| ≤ ε (i.e., essentially orthogonal).

Aggregation (majority vote A_m) can fix this: define θ_m ∈ ε_m-argmin_θ R_{φ,A_m}(f_θ) with ε_m→0. Corollary 4.1 (via Thm 2): R(f_{θ_m})→R(f_{θ*}) and cos angle(θ_m,θ*)→1 as m→∞.

Multiclass (Y∈[k]): consider F a linear cone with f(x)^T 1=0 and closed under positive scaling. Assume φ is Fisher consistent and satisfies limiting loss condition (13): φ(s,y)→0 if s_y - s_j → +∞ for all j≠y. Multiclass logistic and additive pairwise-margin losses satisfy (13).

Immediately after: "Theorem 2 shows that for a broad class of surrogate problems with an arbitrary compact hypothesis class \mathcal{F}, we can achieve consistency asymptotically by aggregation as m\to\infty."

errors.claim: "Clearly \sigma^{\epsilon} satisfies the link consistency condition (14)"
errors.evidence: Link consistency (14): "t_{y}=\max_{1\le i\le k}t_{i}~~\mbox{if and only if}~~\sigma_{y}(t)=\max_{1\le i\le k}\sigma_{i}(t)." Definition of \sigma^{\epsilon}: "\sigma^{\epsilon}(t)=\sigma^{\textup{lr}}(t)1\{t\not\in\mathcal{T}_{\epsilon}\}+\frac{1}{k}\mathbf{1}\cdot 1\{t\in\mathcal{T}_{\epsilon}\}."

final_notes: Key theoretical claims: Theorem 1 gives a calibration-type bound R(f)-R* ≤ (16/C_{φ,1))·(surrogate regret) (slope ζ = C_{φ,1}/16). Section 4: Prop.4 shows unaggregated inconsistency in binary; Cor.4.1 / Thm.2 show aggregation can recover risk convergence (and decision-direction under extra assumptions). Multiclass: Prop.5/Thm.3 show pairwise finite-dimensional surrogates can be inconsistent without aggregation. Logistic model (eq.15) uses θ_k = 0 and φ(Θ^T x,y)= -⟨θ_y,x⟩ + log(1+∑_{i=1}^{k-1} exp⟨θ_i,x⟩). Population stationary condition: E[X(σ^{lr}(Θ_m^T X)-ρ_m(Θ^*^T X))^T]=0; in a binary Gaussian case this preserves direction (Θ_m = t_m Θ^*). Constructed corruption σ^ε mixes softmax and uniform on a small-measure set (noting earlier textual/formula description ambiguity). Experiments: (1) D4X surrogate: truncated quadratic φ(δ)=max{1-δ,0}^2; unaggregated H-calibration ψ(ε)=ε^2; with δ=1 and no low-noise (α=0), C_MT=1 yields ψ_m(ε)= (φ(0)-φ(1))/16 · (ε - sqrt(32/m · log40))_+ = 1/16·(ε - sqrt(32/m·log40))_+. m ∈ {2^16,...,2^32}. (2) Mis-specified logistic: corrupted link uses σ^{lr}(t) for ||t||≤r and σ^{lr}(α t) for ||t||>r (score shrink); experiments in two regimes (fixed n=10k per m, and n=640k/m) with d=2,k=3, θ1*=(0,1), θ2*=(1,1), θ3*=0, r=3, α=0.1, m∈{1,4,...,1024}, T=100. Discussion: paper claims fundamental limitations of uncleaned supervised labels and robustness gains from cleaning; many consistency results need m→∞ though ranking admits some finite-m guarantees; a joint (ℓ,φ,m) finite-m theory is open. Notes also: beyond binary, κ(X) can be large even with low noise (α≈1) though binary trivially has κ(X)=1. Mis-specified-model results assume K7M (Bayes-optimal classifier in F); classical surrogate consistency can fail even there while aggregation can succeed. Extensions to H-consistency/restricted classes are proposed.
