Paper title: "Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning" by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: aggregating/cleaning labels (information distilled from noisy responses) yields robustness not available without cleaning. Specifically: (1) minimizing a typically convex surrogate loss on aggregated labels gives stronger task-risk consistency guarantees than procedures using raw labels; (2) finite-dimensional classifiers remain consistent under loss mis-specification that breaks standard uncertainty-modeling approaches; (3) in perfectly specified statistical models, using all information is more efficient, but slight loss mis-specification can destroy standard consistency; (4) aggregation preserves convergence to optimal classifiers despite noise; (5) the whole pipeline (collection, fitting, prediction) admits robustness via noisy-signal refinement. Keep these claims in mind for checking consistency with later sections (definitions, assumptions, theorems, empirical results) about surrogate losses, aggregation methods, consistency under mis-specification, and comparisons to raw-label procedures.

Paper: "Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning" (Chen Cheng, John Duchi). Abstract-level claims to check later: aggregation/cleaning of noisy labels yields robustness not available without cleaning, specifically (1) minimizing a convex surrogate on aggregated labels gives stronger task-risk consistency than using raw labels; (2) finite-dimensional classifiers remain consistent under loss mis-specification that breaks standard uncertainty-modeling approaches; (3) in well-specified models, using all information is more efficient but slight loss mis-specification can destroy standard consistency; (4) aggregation preserves convergence to optimal classifiers despite noise; (5) end-to-end pipeline (collection, fitting, prediction) shows robustness via noisy-signal refinement. Introduction adds: aggregation permits consistent optimal prediction under surrogate (but unaggregated estimation cannot), including finite-dimensional problems; linear-estimator constructions in ranking and binary/multiclass classification separate procedures restricted to (X,Y) from aggregation procedures; nonparametric results combine aggregation count and noise conditions, allow approximately linear comparison inequalities under weak surrogate conditions, and extend consistency beyond unrestricted measurable hypothesis classes. Notes that typical supervised pipeline omits cleaning; the paper's concern is that cleaning fundamentally and necessarily improves fitted-model consistency. Context: prior surrogate-risk consistency theory (Bartlett et al. etc.) and many extensions; pair-based empirical-process analyses do not address aggregation machinery. Central research questions: is aggregation needed, does pair-based surrogate consistency suffice, and in what sense does aggregation improve consistency.

steps.notes_before:
Paper: "Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning" — studies how aggregating noisy labels (cleaning) affects surrogate-risk consistency. Key claims (from earlier parts): aggregation can enable consistency not available without cleaning; finite-dimensional classifiers can be consistent under loss mis-specification; nonparametric results combine aggregation counts and noise conditions.

From Preliminaries (this part): two regimes — unrestricted Borel F (classical/Fisher consistency) and parametric (possibly misspecified) F where aggregation may improve consistency. Definitions:
- Distribution-dependent task risk: R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X), P(·|X))] (eqn (2)). Special case zero-one: ℓ(ŷ,P)=∑_y P(Y=y)1{ŷ≠y}.
- Instantaneous task risk: R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),Y)] with ℓ: Y×Y→R_+ (eqn (1)). Binary case: d=1, d(s)=sgn(s), ℓ(y,y')=1{y y'≤0}.
- Surrogate risk: R_φ(f)=E[φ(f(X),Y)].
- Aggregated surrogate risk: R_{φ,A}(f)=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))] (eqn (3)), where Z is response-replacement and A:Z→A is aggregation.
- Repeated labeling: Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m), A_m(Z)=argmin_y ∑_{l=1}^m ℓ(y,Y_l) (majority vote for 0-1 loss).
- K-NN aggregation: Z=(Y,(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m), order X_{(l)} by dist to X, and A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y ∑_{l=0}^K ℓ(y,Y_{(l)}).

Note: the paper uses ℓ both as distribution-dependent ℓ(ŷ,P) and instantaneous ℓ(ŷ,y); equation-numbering/reference error noted above.

errors.claim: "This defines a conditional distribution on \(Y\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\) that samples \(Y\sim\sigma^{\textup{lr}}(t)\) if \(t\in\mathcal T_\epsilon\), and uniformly otherwise."
errors.evidence:
The paper first defines

sigma^\epsilon(t)=\sigma^{\textup{lr}}(t)1\{t\notin\mathcal T_\epsilon\}+\frac1k\mathbf1\cdot1\{t\in\mathcal T_\epsilon\}.

but the quoted sentence says the opposite (that it uses sigma^{lr} on T_\epsilon and uniform otherwise).
errors.explanation: The textual description is the reverse of the displayed formula: the formula sets sigma^\epsilon = sigma^{lr} when t \notin T_\epsilon and uniform when t \in T_\epsilon, whereas the sentence states the opposite.

errors.claim: "Clearly \sigma^\epsilon satisfies (14) and is optimally predictable under (12)."
errors.evidence:
Definition (14):

t_y=\max_i t_i \iff \sigma_y(t)=\max_i\sigma_i(t).

But sigma^\epsilon(t) (per the displayed formula) equals the uniform vector 1/k on t\in T_\epsilon; for such t the RHS (each sigma_y is a max) holds for every y while the LHS need not hold for every y unless t has tied maxima. The paper does not restrict T_\epsilon to tie-points.
errors.explanation: If sigma^\epsilon is uniform on T_\epsilon, it will not preserve the argmax mapping (14) at those t except in degenerate tie cases, so the claim that sigma^\epsilon "clearly" satisfies (14) is incorrect unless additional restrictions on T_\epsilon are imposed (which are not stated).

final_notes: Section 4 recap: aggregation can restore consistency when optimization is restricted to hypothesis class. Key defs: ε-argmin; aggregation A_m = majority vote. Binary: convex margin φ consistent iff φ'(0)<0. Linear predictors f_θ(x)=⟨θ,x⟩. Prop.4: for any nonneg φ and any ε>0 there exists P optimally predictable along θ* where every surrogate minimizer θ_φ has worse risk and |cos(θ_φ,θ*)|≤ε (ordinary surrogate failure possible). Aggregation: choose θ_m ∈ ε_m-argmin R_{φ,A_m} with ε_m→0. Corollary 4.1 / Theorem 2: if P optimally predictable and ε_m→0 then R(f_{θ_m})→R(f_{θ*}) and cos∠(θ_m,θ*)→1. Theorem 3 (multiclass aggregation): if Θ*=U^*T^* then Θ_m=U^*T_m ∀m, ||T_m||→∞ and T_m/||T_m||→T^*/||T^*||. Important caveat: earlier parts flagged the σ^ε construction underlying Proposition 5 (multiclass unaggregated inconsistency) as flawed/unreliable. Section 5 experiments: truncated-quadratic surrogate — finite-m ψ_m bound (≈(1/16)ε for large m) and plotted (Fig.1); mis-specified logistic multiclass synthetic experiment (d=2, k=3, r=3, α=0.1) with multiple m regimes and two sampling protocols; Fig.2 shows improved direction recovery with larger m. Section 6: discussion — many guarantees require m→∞; some finite-m results exist (Prop.2: m≥k for ranking; Sec.3.2.3: uniform linear comparison at α=1, O(log k) bound); multiclass condition number κ(X) (eq.9) can be large even at low noise; model results rely on optimal predictability (eq.12); open problems: finite-m theory, sharper loss-dependent analysis, behavior beyond optimal-predictability, and restricted-class comparison inequalities.

Paper studies whether aggregating noisy labels improves consistency of learned predictors. Focus: surrogate losses (used during fitting), analyzed over all measurable predictors and over restricted model classes. Develops calibration inequalities for aggregated labels; analyzes ranking, classification, structured prediction. Key claims to remember: for ranking with k ≥ 3 items, no convex surrogate based on individual comparisons is Fisher consistent; an aggregated squared-loss procedure is consistent when m ≥ k. More generally, "identifying" surrogates become asymptotically consistent as number m of aggregated labels grows; many guarantees require m → ∞. Under certain noise conditions, aggregation yields approximately linear comparison inequalities. In restricted model classes, aggregation can restore consistency when ordinary surrogate minimization fails (including link mis-specification). Two numerical illustrations are reported. Glossary follows (definitions and reused symbols listed).

Paper: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” (Chen Cheng, John Duchi). Thesis: aggregating noisy labels (label cleaning) can yield consistency and robustness not available using single noisy labels. Two consistency settings studied: (i) Fisher consistency (all measurable functions), (ii) statistical/parametric restricted models. Calibration constants referenced earlier: C_{φ,1}, C_{φ,2}, ψ_A. steps.notes_before: Section summarizes Fisher consistency and comparison inequalities via calibration functions: define conditional risks R(s|x), R_phi(s|x); pointwise excesses delta_l(s,x)=R(s|x)-inf_s'R(s'|x), delta_phi(s,x) similarly. Calibration psi(ε,x)=inf_{s}{delta_phi(s,x) | delta_l(s,x)≥ε}, overline{psi}(ε)=inf_x psi(ε,x). Corollary 3.1: positivity of psi(·,x) for all x,ε>0 characterizes Fisher consistency; Fenchel biconjugate of overline{psi} yields a comparison bound psi(R-R^*) ≤ R_phi-R_phi^*. Ranking example: labels Y={(i,j):i≠j}, p_{ij}=P(Y=(i,j)|x). Define C_x with (C_x)_{ii}=0 and (C_x)_{ij}=p_{ij}/\sum_{l≠j} p_{lj} (use 0/0=1/(k-1)), so C_x^T 1 = 1. Loss ℓ(s,C)=max_{i<j} 1{(s_i-s_j)(C1_i-C1_j)≤0, C1_i-C1_j≠0}; population risk R(f)=P(f(X) and C_X1 order differently) (eq.4). Restrict scores to s^T1=0. Proposition 1: for k≥3, any surrogate φ convex in scores is not Fisher consistent for this ranking risk. Aggregation: collect Z=(Y_1,...,Y_m); define counts m_{ij} (definition in text appears to sum over Y^m and is inconsistent — it should sum over observed labels), m_j=Σ_i m_{ij}, and A(Z)=star if some m_j=0, else vector whose i-th entry is Σ_j m_{ij}/m_j. Proposition 2: squared-loss regression on A(Z) is Fisher consistent when m≥k.

steps.notes_before: Squared-loss surrogate: φ(s,q)=||s-q||_2^2, φ(s,★)=0. Proposition 2: for ranking risk (eq.4) φ is Fisher consistent when m≥k. Aggregation expands response space from Y to R^k; A(Z) is vector-valued in R^k when all m_j>0. Prop 1 (earlier): for k≥3 no convex-in-scores surrogate is Fisher consistent for pairwise ranking risk. Proposition 3: if ∫ b(x)dP(x)<∞ and δ_ℓ(f(x),x) ≤ b(x), then φ is Fisher consistent for task risk iff for all x, ε>0 the pointwise calibration overlineψ_A(ε,x)>0; with ψ_A=(overlineψ_A)^{**} we get ψ_A(R(f)-R^*) ≤ R_{φ,A}(f)-R_{φ,A}^*. Correct calibration defs: overlineψ_A(ε,x):=inf_{s∈R^d}{δ_{φ,A}(s,x) | δ_ℓ(s,x)≥ε}; overlineψ_A(ε):=inf_{x∈X} overlineψ_A(ε,x) (paper's eq.(5) mistakenly used inf over s). Definition 3.1: (C_{φ,1},C_{φ,2})-identifying surrogate with params a_y∈A and s_y∈R^d, d(s_y)=y satisfying (6a),(6b). Example: hinge loss is (1,2)-identifying. Generalized majority vote A_m(y_1..y_m)=a_{ŷ} with ŷ=argmin_y Σ_i ℓ(y,y_i); for i.i.d. labels w.p.1 there exists random M such that for m≥M empirical argmin ⊂ population argmin y^*(x). Corollary 3.2: vanishing aggregated surrogate regret implies vanishing task regret as m→∞.

Corollary 3.2: If m(n)→∞ and φ is identifying (Def.3.1) then R_{φ,A_m}(f_n)-R_{φ,A_m}^*→0 ⇒ R(f_n)-R^*→0. Example: hinge is (C_{φ,1},C_{φ,2})=(1,2)-identifying. Majority vote A_m eventually selects only optimal labels (empirical argmin ⊂ population argmin) for m≥M (random finite M).

Level-(ξ,ζ) consistency (Def.3.2): there exists ψ with ψ(ε)≥ζε for ε≥ξ and ψ(R(f)-R^*) ≤ R_{φ,A}(f)-R_{φ,A}^*.

Noise/margin quantities:
- Δ(x)=min_{d(s)∉y^*(x)} δ_ℓ(s,x) (binary: Δ(x)=|2P(Y=1|X=x)-1|).

- Condition-number κ(x)=max_{d(s)≠y^*}δ / min_{d(s)≠y^*}δ (binary κ=1 if P(Δ(X)>0)=1).

Aggregation error func: e_m(t)= t sqrt{(2/m) log(4k(C_{φ,1}+C_{φ,2})/C_{φ,1})}.

Theorem 1: If φ is (C_{φ,1},C_{φ,2})-identifying, A_m aggregator (7), 0≤ℓ≤1 and (N_α) holds, then for any M>0 and any f with
R(f)-R^* ≥ 2P(κ(X)>M) + (4C_{MT} e_m(M))^{1/(1-α)},
we have
R(f)-R^* ≤ (16/C_{φ,1}) (R_{φ,A_m}(f)-R_{φ,A_m}^*).
Thus level-(ξ,ζ) with ξ as the LHS threshold and ζ=C_{φ,1}/16. Let ξ_m = inf_M{…}; ξ_m→0 as m→∞, so taking α=0 yields Corollary 3.2.

Optimizing using κ≤1/Δ gives explicit ξ_{m,k}: for k=2,
ξ_{m,2}=((32 C_{MT}^2/m) log(8(C_{φ,1}+C_{φ,2})/C_{φ,1}))^{1/(2(1-α))},
and a stated expression for k≥3. Corollary 3.3: same linear comparison holds whenever R(f)-R^*≥ξ_{m,k}.

Theorem 1 (recap): if φ is (C_{φ,1},C_{φ,2})-identifying, A_m aggregator (7), 0≤ℓ≤1 and (N_α) holds, then for any M>0 and f with
R(f)-R^* ≥ 2P(κ(X)>M) + (4 C_{MT} e_m(M))^{1/(1-α)}
we have R(f)-R^* ≤ (16/C_{φ,1})(R_{φ,A_m}(f)-R_{φ,A_m}^*). Here e_m(t)= t sqrt{(2/m) log(4k(C_{φ,1}+C_{φ,2})/C_{φ,1})}.
Noise conditions: (N_α) and (M_β) equivalent with β=α/(1-α) (α=β=0 allowed). Binary κ=1 if P(Δ(X)>0)=1.
As α→1 aggregation requirement falls; in the limit α=1 the paper claims that if
m ≥ 32 max{C_{MT}^2,C_{MT}^4} log(4k(C_{φ,1}+C_{φ,2})/C_{φ,1}) = O(log k)
then ξ_{m,k}=0 (uniform linear comparison with factor 16/C_{φ,1}).
Section 3.3 examples:
- Binary nonsmooth surrogate: φ(f,y)=φ(yf). If ∂φ(0) ⊂ (-∞,0) and lim_{t→∞}φ(t)=0, then for any δ>0 Lemma 3.1 gives feasibility constants C_{φ,1}=φ(0)-φ(δ)>0, C_{φ,2}=φ(-δ). Corollary 3.3 (k=2) yields threshold

The paper first defines

sigma^\epsilon(t)=\sigma^{\textup{lr}}(t)1\{t\notin\mathcal T_\epsilon\}+\frac1k\mathbf1\cdot1\{t\in\mathcal T_\epsilon\}.

errors.claim: "Clearly \sigma^\epsilon satisfies (14) and is optimally predictable under (12)."

Definition (14):

t_y=\max_i t_i \iff \sigma_y(t)=\max_i\sigma_i(t).

But sigma^\epsilon(t) (per the displayed formula) equals the uniform vector 1/k on t\in T_\epsilon; for such t the RHS (each sigma_y is a max) holds for every y while the LHS need not hold for every y unless t has tied maxima. The paper does not restrict T_\epsilon to tie-points.

errors.evidence: The paper itself cites Bartlett et al.: "φ is consistent if and only if φ'(0)<0." Immediately after it assumes "the subgradient set ∂φ(0) ⊂ (-\infty,0) ..."

errors.claim: The paper states: "Clearly σ^ε satisfies the link consistency condition (14) and is optimally predictable (12)."
errors.evidence:
Link consistency (14): "t_y = max_{1≤i≤k} t_i  if and only if  σ_y(t) = max_{1≤i≤k} σ_i(t)."
Definition given for σ^ε: "σ^ε(t) = σ^{lr}(t) 1{t ∉ T_ε} + (1/k) 1 · 1{t ∈ T_ε}," where T_ε ⊂ R^{k-1} has Lebesgue measure ε.
errors.explanation: If t ∈ T_ε then σ^ε(t) is the uniform vector (1/k,...,1/k), so the argmax of σ^ε(t) is the full label set. Condition (14) requires equivalence between argmax(t) and argmax(σ^ε(t)) for every t; for a generic t ∈ T_ε (which will typically have a unique maximizer), this equivalence fails. The paper gives no restriction that T_ε consists only of tie points, so the claim that σ^ε satisfies (14) is inconsistent with the definitions.

final_notes: The paper studies how aggregating m labels affects surrogate regret and consistency. Key theory: Zhang [51, Thm.8] gives surrogate consistency in the symmetric constraint F={f:1^T f=0} under convex, nonincreasing φ with φ'(0)<0 and inf φ=0. Theorem 2: if F is a cone that optimally predicts P and P(Δ(X)>0)=1 then ε_m-argmin sequences for R_{φ,A_m} converge to R^* as m→∞ (asymptotic consistency). Section 4.3 (finite-dimensional multiclass): parameterize Θ∈R^{d×(k-1)} with link σ; logistic link has stationarity E[X(σ^{lr}(Θ_m^T X)-ρ_m(Θ^{*T}X))^T]=0. For k=2 under Gaussian, Θ_m collinear with Θ^*. Proposition 5: for k≥3, Σ=I and an invertibility condition, small perturbations can make m=1 directionally inconsistent. Theorem 3: if Θ^*=U^* T^* (U^* orthonormal, T^* nonsingular) then Θ_m=U^* T_m and as m→∞ ||T_m||→∞ and T_m/||T_m||→T^*/||T^*|| (directional consistency). Experiments: (i) truncated quadratic φ gives ψ(ε)=ε^2; with δ=1 one gets ψ_m(ε)=(1/16)*(ε - sqrt{(32/m) log 40})_+ and Fig.1 shows aggregated ψ_m moving from quadratic→linear as m increases (m∈{2^16,...,2^32}). (ii) mis-specified logistic (k=3,d=2) with corrupted link (r=3,α=0.1) and Θ^* invertible; experiments (fixed n per m and fixed total labels) over m∈{1,4,16,64,256,1024} show normalized T_m approaching normalized T^* as m grows. Discussion (Part 12): emphasizes need for finite-m guarantees (ranking Sec.3.1 gives some finite-m results), highlights noise condition number κ(X) (Eq.9) which can be large beyond binary (binary κ=1), notes mis-specification results require optimal predictability (Eq.12), and proposes extending to H-consistency (Mao et al. [27] shows quadratic ψ growth is rate-optimal for smooth convex losses).

Title: Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning (Chen Cheng, John Duchi). Abstract claims: learning procedures that rely on aggregated labels (label information distilled from noisy responses) enjoy robustness properties impossible without data cleaning. Key points to check later: (1) In risk consistency (minimizing a surrogate, typically convex, loss instead of task loss like zero-one), procedures using label aggregation obtain stronger consistency guarantees than those possible using raw labels. (2) Classical perfectly-specified-model scenarios suggest modeling uncertainty in labels is statistically efficient, but consistency fails for “standard” approaches as soon as the loss to be minimized is even slightly mis-specified. (3) Procedures leveraging aggregated information still converge to optimal classifiers with every fixed label count. Overall claim: incorporating aggregation/refinement of noisy labels across the data pipeline yields more robust methodology. Terms to watch: "aggregated labels", "risk consistency", "surrogate loss (convex)", "standard approaches", "consistency fails when loss mis-specified", and "converge to optimal classifiers with every fixed label count".

Paper studies how label cleaning/aggregation improves surrogate risk consistency. Key claims: (1) Aggregating labels yields robustness impossible without aggregation: improves consistency when minimizing a surrogate loss (e.g., multiclass logistic) so procedures using aggregated labels can achieve consistent/optimal prediction in limits where using raw (X,Y) cannot. (2) Even in finite-dimensional settings (e.g., linear estimators for ranking, binary and multiclass classification) aggregation can produce consistent classifiers when standard (X,Y)-based methods fail. (3) In nonparametric settings, the number of samples aggregated interacts with noise conditions to improve consistency. (4) Aggregation allows surrogate risk consistency under weaker conditions on the surrogate (they refer to approximate linear comparison inequalities). (5) Unlike conventional theory that often needs hypothesis class F to be all measurable functions, aggregation can guarantee consistency even for restricted hypothesis classes. Examples promised: ranking, binary and multiclass with linear estimators. Terms to watch in later parts: "aggregated labels", "risk consistency", "surrogate loss (convex)", "standard approaches" (failure conditions), "approximate linear comparison inequalities", and claims about convergence to optimal classifiers for every fixed label count.

Definitions and setup: scoring f:X->R^d, decoder d:R^d->Y. Task risk (1): R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),Y)] with ℓ:Y×Y->R_+. Alternate formulation (2) allows ℓ to depend on the conditional distribution: R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),P(·|X))]. Surrogate φ introduced: classical surrogate risk R_φ(f)=E[φ(f(X),Y)]. Aggregation: replace Y by Z∈Z and use aggregator A:Z->A; aggregated surrogate risk (3): R_{φ,A}(f)=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))]. Two settings of interest: (i) Fisher consistency (F contains all Borel functions), (ii) parametric/mis-specified hypothesis classes. Examples: repeated-labels/majority vote: Z=(Y_1,...,Y_m), A_m(Z)=argmin_y Σ_{l=1}^m ℓ(y,Y_l) (reduces to majority vote for 0-1 loss); K-nearest-neighbors style aggregation: Z=(Y,(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m), order neighbors X_{(l)}, set A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y Σ_{l=0}^K ℓ(y,Y_{(l)}) (index 0 denotes the original Y). Appendix C will extend population-level aggregation to single-sample aggregation.

Definitions: conditional task risk R(s|x)=ℓ(d∘s,P(Y∈·|X=x)), conditional surrogate risk R_φ(s|x)=E[φ(s,Y)|X=x]. Pointwise excess risks δ_ℓ(s,x)=R(s|x)-inf_{s'}R(s'|x), δ_φ(s,x)=R_φ(s|x)-inf_{s'}R_φ(s'|x). Minimal risks R^*=inf_{f∈F}R(f), R_φ^*=inf_{f∈F}R_φ(f). Consistency notions: (i) Fisher consistency — for any sequence f_n, R_φ(f_n)→R_φ^* implies R(f_n)→R^*; (ii) uniform comparison inequality: exists nondecreasing ψ with ψ(R(f)-R^*) ≤ R_φ(f)-R_φ^*. Calibration: ψ(ε,x)=inf_s{δ_φ(s,x) | δ_ℓ(s,x)≥ε}, overlineψ(ε)=inf_x ψ(ε,x). Corollary 3.1: φ is Fisher consistent iff ψ(ε,x)>0 for all x,ε>0; letting ψ be Fenchel biconjugate of overlineψ yields comparison inequality ψ(R(f)-R^*) ≤ R_φ(f)-R_φ^*. Ranking example (Sec.3.1): Y={(i,j): i≠j, i,j∈[k]}, p_{ij}=P(Y=(i,j)|x). Define C_x with diagonal zero and for i≠j, C_{ij}=p_{ij}/(Σ_{l≠j}p_{lj}) (define 0/0=1/(k-1)), so C_x is column-stochastic (C_x^T1=1). Rank by vector C_x1; loss ℓ(s,C)=max_{i<j} 1{(s_i-s_j)(C1_i-C1_j)≤0, C1_i-C1_j≠0}. Task risk R(f)=P[f(X) and C_X1 order differently]. Proposition 1: for k≥3, any convex-in-first-arg surrogate φ is not Fisher consistent. Aggregation: with m iid comparisons Z=(Y_1,...,Y_m), counts m_{ij} and m_j=Σ_i m_{ij}; define A(Z)=★ if some m_j=0, else A(Z)=(Σ_{j} m_{ij}/m_j)_{i∈[k]}. Claim: regressing on A(Z) (when A(Z)≠★) yields consistency when m≥k (Proposition 2; proof in Appendix A.2).

steps.notes_before: (none yet: this is the first part)

Title: Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning (Chen Cheng, John Duchi). Abstract-level claims: Aggregated labels (information distilled from noisy responses / label cleaning) enable robustness not available without cleaning. Minimizing a typically convex surrogate loss on cleaned/aggregated labels yields stronger task-risk consistency guarantees than procedures using raw labels. Finite-dimensional classifiers remain consistent under loss mis-specification when using aggregation/cleaning, whereas standard uncertainty-modeling approaches fail under such mis-specification. In perfectly specified statistical models, incorporating all information is more efficient, but even slight loss mis-specification can destroy standard consistency. Aggregation (with a fixed number of labels per item) still yields convergence to optimal classifiers; the processes of collection, fitting, and prediction jointly provide robustness via noisy-signal refinement. Key concepts to check in later parts: definitions of "aggregated labels" and "label cleaning," formal statements of "task-risk consistency," the nature of the convex surrogate loss, what constitutes "loss mis-specification," the contrast with "standard uncertainty-modeling approaches," formal results about finite-dimensional classifier consistency, claims about efficiency under perfect specification vs fragility under mis-specification, and the claim that aggregation converges to optimal classifiers with any fixed label count.

Paper studies how aggregation/label cleaning yields robustness for surrogate-risk consistency, including in finite-dimensional problems where unaggregated estimation fails. Claims: aggregation permits consistent optimal prediction under surrogate (rather than task) loss when unaggregated estimation cannot. Technical approaches: linear-estimator constructions for ranking, binary, and multiclass classification that separate (X,Y)-pair procedures from aggregation procedures; nonparametric results that combine aggregation count and noise conditions to produce approximately linear comparison inequalities under weak surrogate conditions and extend consistency beyond unrestricted measurable hypothesis classes. Context: standard supervised pipeline collects (X_i,Y_i) and fits a model but typically omits cleaning/filtering/repeated crowdsourced labels/denoising; crowdsourcing literature handles this machinery, while this work focuses on how that machinery fundamentally improves fitted-model consistency. Prior theory on surrogate-risk consistency (e.g., Bartlett et al.) and extensions to many settings exist; pair-based analyses support empirical-process theory but do not model aggregation. Open questions the paper delimits: whether aggregation is necessary, whether pair-based surrogate consistency suffices, and in what sense aggregation improves consistency. Key items to check later against claims: formal definitions of aggregated labels/label cleaning, precise statements of 'task-risk consistency' and comparison inequalities, what constitutes 'loss mis-specification', the contrast with standard uncertainty-modeling approaches, finite-dimensional classifier consistency results, efficiency vs fragility under perfect vs mis-specified models, and convergence claims when aggregation count is fixed.

"R(f)\coloneqq \mathbb E_P\!\left[\ell(\mathsf d\circ f(X),P(\cdot\mid X))\right].\n\tag{2}"

Later the instantaneous formulation is given and labelled (1):

"The instantaneous formulation, for \ell:\mathcal Y\times\mathcal Y\to\mathbb R_+, minimizes over f\in\mathcal F
\[R(f):=\mathbb E_P[\ell(\mathsf d\circ f(X),Y)].\]\n\tag{1}"
errors.explanation: The sentence claims minimizers of the distribution-dependent criterion coincide with the "original problem (2)", but the instantaneous (original) formulation is actually labelled (1) in the text; the cross-reference to equation numbering is inconsistent.

steps.notes_before:
Two regimes: unrestricted Borel F (Fisher consistency) and parametric possibly misspecified F, where aggregation can improve consistency.

Setup: i.i.d. (X_i,Y_i)~P. Scores f: X->R^d, decoder d: R^d->Y, prediction y_hat = d(f(x)).

Distribution-dependent task criterion (labelled (2) in text): R(f) := E_P[ ell(d o f(X), P(·|X)) ].

Instantaneous formulation (labelled (1) in text): R(f) := E_P[ ell(d o f(X), Y) ].

Note: text contains a cross-reference/numbering error — the sentence "Its minimizers frequently coincide with the original problem (2)" appears to mislabel the instantaneous formulation (should refer to (1)).

Surrogate risk: R_phi(f) := E_P[ phi(f(X), Y) ].

Aggregated surrogate risk (eq (3)): R_{phi,A}(f) := E[ phi(f(X), A(Z)) ], with aggregation map A: Z->A.

Repeated labeling: Z=(Y_1,...,Y_m), A_m(Z)=argmin_{y in Y} sum_{l=1}^m ell(y,Y_l) (majority vote when ell is zero-one).

K-NN aggregation: Z=(Y,(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m), order neighbors X_(1)...X_(m) with X_(0)=X; A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y sum_{l=0}^K ell(y,Y_(l)).

errors.claim: For arbitrary A: Z->A, the required objects are ... overline\psi_A(\epsilon,x) := inf_{s\in\mathbb R^d} { \delta_{\varphi,A}(s,x) | \delta_\ell(s,x) \ge \epsilon },  overline\psi_A(\epsilon) := inf_{s\in\mathbb R^d} overline\psi_A(\epsilon,x). (Equation (5) in this part)
errors.evidence:
Earlier in this part the canonical construction was defined as
"psi(\epsilon,x) := inf_{s\in\mathbb R^d} { \delta_\varphi(s,x) | \delta_\ell(s,x) \ge \epsilon },    overline\psi(\epsilon) := inf_{x\in\mathcal X} psi(\epsilon,x)."
But Proposition 3 instead writes
"overline\psi_A(\epsilon,x) := inf_{s\in\mathbb R^d} { \delta_{\varphi,A}(s,x) | \delta_\ell(s,x) \ge \epsilon },    overline\psi_A(\epsilon) := inf_{s\in\mathbb R^d} overline\psi_A(\epsilon,x)."
errors.explanation: The paper's earlier, canonical notation uses psi(epsilon,x) for the pointwise calibration function and overline-psi(epsilon)=inf_{x} psi(epsilon,x) for the uniform calibration. Proposition 3 reassigns the pointwise definition to overline\psi_A(\epsilon,x) (i.e. swaps the names) and then takes an infimum over 's' instead of over 'x' when defining the uniform quantity. The second equality is therefore inconsistent (the infimum should be over x), and the notation psi vs overline\psi is used inconsistently.

steps.notes_before: Corollary 3.1: Pointwise calibration psi(eps,x)=inf_{s}{delta_phi(s,x) | delta_ell(s,x) >= eps}; uniform overline{psi}(eps)=inf_{x} psi(eps,x). Positivity of psi(eps,x) for all x,eps>0 ⇔ phi is Q7D for ell; with psi its Fenchel biconjugate, overline{psi}(eps)>0 ⇔ psi(eps)>0 and psi(R(f)-R*) ≤ R_phi(f)-R_phi^*. Standard framework: (i) R_phi(f_n)→R_phi* ⇒ R(f_n)→R*, (ii) uniform comparison psi(R(f)-R*)≤R_phi(f)-R_phi* (stronger). Definitions: R(s|x)=ell(d∘s,P(Y|X=x)), R_phi(s|x)=E[phi(s,Y)|X=x], delta_ell and delta_phi pointwise excesses; R*, R_phi* infima over F. Section 3.1 ranking: Prop 1 — convex phi in first arg fails Q7D for k≥3. Prop 2 — phi(s,q)=||s-q||^2 with aggregation and m≥k is Q7D. Pairwise Y={(i,j)} size k(k-1); define C_x from p_{ij}; task loss (4) R(f)=P(f(X) and C_X 1 order differently). For multiple comparisons Z=(Y_1..Y_m) define counts m_{ij} (counts of occurrences) and A(Z) returns vector or star if some m_j=0. Section 3.2: Prop 3 gives aggregated calibration criterion: with integrable envelope b and pointwise bound on delta_ell, phi is Q7D iff the aggregated uniform calibration function is positive; inequality with psi_A=(overline{psi}_A)^{**} holds. NOTE: the paper contains a notational/typo error in (5): it names the pointwise function overline{psi}_A(eps,x) (contradicting the earlier psi notation) and then defines overline{psi}_A(eps)=inf_{s} overline{psi}_A(eps,x) (should be inf_{x}). Corollary 3.2: if m(n)→∞ and phi is W3C, then R_{phi,A_m}(f_n)-R_{phi,A_m}*→0 ⇒ R(f_n)-R*→0; finite label-space assumed; generalized majority vote A_m uses empirical argmin and stabilizes to population argmin a.s. for large m.

Lemma 3.1 (binary margin): for φ(yf)=φ(y f(x)) convex with ∂φ(0)⊂(-∞,0), lim_{t→∞}φ(t)=0, any δ>0 gives C_{φ,1}=φ(0)-φ(δ)>0 and C_{φ,2}=φ(-δ), yielding the Theorem 1 bound for k=2 with C_{φ,1}=φ(0)-φ(δ).

errors.claim: “As a corollary to Theorem 2, if P satisfies K7M along \theta^\star and \epsilon_m\to0 as m\to\infty, the aggregated approximate minimizers satisfy R(f_{\theta_m})\to R(f_{\theta^\star}), \cos\angle(\theta_m,\theta^\star)\to1.”

errors.explanation: Corollary 4.1 is presented as following from Theorem 2 but omits the explicit assumption P(\Delta(X)>0)=1 required by Theorem 2. Either the corollary must include this extra assumption or justify why K7M along \theta^\star implies P(\Delta(X)>0)=1; the text gives no such justification. steps.notes_before:
Matching example (2N vertices): matching surrogate W3C with C_{φ,1}=1/N, C_{φ,2}=2; label set size k=N!, embedding v(y)∈{0,1}^{d}, d=N^2; loss ℓ(·) scaled so aggregation needs O(N log N). (Recorded earlier inconsistency: matching-special constants/thresholds disagree with general structured-form bounds when plugging min_ℓ=1/N.)

Definitions/assumptions: K7M = existence of model f in class that matches Bayes predictor (optimal predictability along parameter θ^\star). T4K = the top-1 aggregation scheme used. Q7D surrogates satisfy φ(s,y)→0 when s_y - s_j→+∞ (examples: multiclass logistic, margin-sum surrogates).

4.1 Proposition 4: For any ε>0 and nonzero θ^\star there exists P satisfying K7M along θ^\star yet every global minimizer of surrogate risk over linear predictors has strictly worse target risk and can be nearly orthogonal (|cos angle|≤ε); holds for any nonnegative φ (unaggregated surrogate minimization can fail badly).

Corollary 4.1 claims aggregation of approximate minimizers yields R(f_{θ_m})→R(f_{θ^\star}) and direction recovery if ε_m→0; however this statement omits the Theorem 2 assumption P(Δ(X)>0)=1 required for the corollary to follow (inconsistency noted above).

Theorem 2: If F is a cone, F satisfies K7M for P, and P(Δ(X)>0)=1, then any ε_m→0 argmin over aggregated surrogate risk satisfies R(f_m)→R^\star.

4.3 Finite-dimensional multiclass: Proposition 5 and Theorem 3 show pair-based surrogates can be inconsistent for k≥3 under slight misspecification, while T4K aggregation recovers the correct ordering/direction asymptotically (Theorem 3: Θ_m = U^\star T_m with ||T_m||→∞ but T_m/||T_m||→T^\star/||T^\star||).

steps.notes_before: Logistic multiclass surrogate with baseline θ_k=0: φ(Θ^T x,y)= -<θ_y,x> + log(1+∑_{i=1}^{k-1} exp(<θ_i,x>)). Gradient ∇_{θ_i}φ = -x(1{y=i}-σ_i^{lr}(Θ^T x)), so minimizer Θ_m satisfies E[ X (σ^{lr}(Θ_m^T X) - ρ_m(Θ^*^T X))^T ] = 0 (ρ_m(·) = conditional agg. label distribution per K7M). Well-specified unaggregated models have standard consistency; for m≥1, k=2, X~N(0,I_d), Cheng et al. show Θ_m = t_m Θ^* (t_m>0) so direction Θ^*/||Θ^*|| suffices for binary classification at all aggregation levels. Corruption construction: for T_ε ⊂ R^{k-1} of Lebesgue measure ε define σ^ε(t)=σ^{lr}(t)·1{t∉T_ε} + (1/k)·1·1{t∈T_ε} (note: text contains a contradictory sentence but the formula means logistic off T_ε and uniform on T_ε). Define L_{m,ε}(Θ)=E[ E_{σ^ε}[ φ(Θ^T X,Y_m^+) | X ] ] and Θ_m(ε)=argmin_Θ L_{m,ε}(Θ); although Θ_1(0)=Θ^*, arbitrarily small ε>0 can destroy unaggregated consistency. General defs: L_{m,σ}(Θ)=E[ E_σ[ φ(Θ^T X,Y_m^+) | X ] ], Θ_m=argmin L_{m,σ}. Conclusion: aggregation yields robustness under mis-specification; without aggregation, multiclass methods are often inconsistent. (Also retain earlier notes re: Propositions 4/5, Theorem 2/3, and recorded earlier inconsistency about matching constants.)

errors.claim: The paper states "Here \alpha\in[0,1] and \beta\in[0,\infty]" and in Theorem 1 assumes "condition (N\alpha) with \alpha\in[0,1]".

Text: "Here \alpha\in[0,1] and \beta\in[0,\infty]." Later Theorem 1 requires f satisfy
R(f)-R^* \ge 2\,\mathbb P(\kappa(X)>M) + (4\mathsf C_{\mathsf{MT}} e_m(M))^{\frac1{1-\alpha}},

errors.claim: Theorem 1 gives a comparison factor 16/C_{phi,1} (aggregation preserves calibration and yields factor 16/C_{phi,1}).

errors.explanation: Theorem 1 (as recorded earlier) uniformly yields a factor 16/C_{phi,1}; for structured prediction C_{phi,1}=min_{ĥ ≠ y} ℓ(ĥ,y), so the factor should be 16/min ℓ, not 8/min ℓ. The corollary here reports half that factor, a direct contradiction.

errors.claim: "Clearly \sigma^\epsilon satisfies (14)."
errors.evidence: Equation (14): "t_y = max_{1\le i\le k} t_i if and only if \sigma_y(t) = max_{1\le i\le k} \sigma_i(t)". Definition: "\sigma^\epsilon(t) = \sigma^{lr}(t) 1\{t\notin \mathcal T_\epsilon\} + (1/k)\mathbf1 \cdot 1\{t\in\mathcal T_\epsilon\}."
errors.explanation: If t lies in T_\epsilon then \sigma^\epsilon(t) is uniform (all components 1/k), so for any index y that is not a maximizer of t we still have \sigma^\epsilon_y(t) = max_i \sigma^\epsilon_i(t). This violates the 'only if' direction of the claimed equivalence in (14), so \sigma^\epsilon need not satisfy (14).

errors.claim: "This defines a conditional distribution on Y in {1,...,k} that samples Y ~ \sigma^{lr}(t) if t \in \mathcal T_\epsilon, and uniformly otherwise."

errors.explanation: The sentence describing the mixture reverses the indicator roles compared to the explicit formula: the formula sets logistic weights when t \notin T_\epsilon and uniform when t \in T_\epsilon, so the sentence contradicts the formula.

errors.claim: "Aggregation is robust to the stated multiclass link mis-specification: Proposition 5 supplies the unaggregated failure for k\geq3; Theorem 3 supplies normalized-direction convergence as m\to\infty." (this part)
errors.evidence: This part: "Majority vote addresses this inconsistency as m\to\infty, without assumptions on the true link beyond (14)." and "Aggregation is robust to the stated multiclass link mis-specification: Proposition 5 supplies the unaggregated failure for k\geq3; Theorem 3 supplies normalized-direction convergence as m\to\infty." Earlier notes: "(ii) the declared property 'σ^ε satisfies (14)' is false in general because uniformization on T_ε breaks the iff link-consistency condition."
errors.explanation: Proposition 5's counterexample σ^ε was constructed by uniformizing the link on a small set T_ε; earlier parts (my notes) show this can break the link-consistency condition (14). Theorem 3 is stated to require only (14), so it does not apply to σ^ε. Paper studies whether aggregating noisy labels improves consistency of learned predictors. Focus: surrogate losses (used during fitting), analyzed over all measurable predictors and over restricted model classes. Develops calibration inequalities for aggregated labels; analyzes ranking, classification, structured prediction. Key claims to remember: for ranking with k ≥ 3 items, no convex surrogate based on individual comparisons is Fisher consistent; an aggregated squared-loss procedure is consistent when m ≥ k. More generally, "identifying" surrogates become asymptotically consistent as number m of aggregated labels grows; many guarantees require m → ∞. Under certain noise conditions, aggregation yields approximately linear comparison inequalities. In restricted model classes, aggregation can restore consistency when ordinary surrogate minimization fails (including link mis-specification). Two numerical illustrations are reported. Glossary follows (definitions and reused symbols listed).

Preliminaries: task risk R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),Y)] (Eq.1). Alternate formulation uses conditional distribution: R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),P(·|X))] (Eq.2) — minimizers often coincide. Scoring f:X→R^d, decoder d:R^d→Y (binary: d(s)=sgn(s), ℓ(y,ŷ)=1{yŷ≤0}, R(f)=P(Yf(X)≤0)). Surrogate φ and surrogate risk R_φ(f)=E[φ(f(X),Y)]. Two consistency settings: (i) Fisher consistency (all measurable f allowed), (ii) statistical/parametric restricted models. Aggregation: observe richer response Z∈Z (e.g. m noisy labels or neighbor sample); aggregation map A:Z→A. Aggregated surrogate φ: R^d×A→R_+ and aggregated surrogate risk R_{φ,A}(f)=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))] (Eq.3). Example 1 (majority vote): repeated labels Y_i|X iid ∼P_{Y|X}; A_m(Z)=argmin_y ∑_{l=1}^m ℓ(y,Y_l) (for 0-1 loss this is majority vote). Example 2 (KNN aggregation): extra iid sample (X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m ~P, Z=(Y,(X_i,Y_i)); order X_{(1)},…,X_{(m)} by distance to X, set X_{(0)}=X, and A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_{y} ∑_{l=0}^K ℓ(y,Y_{(l)}) (includes original label as l=0). Appendix C will extend to finite-sample aggregation.

Preliminaries: Task risk R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),Y)] and alternate view R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),P(·|X))]. Scoring f:X→R^d, decoder d:R^d→Y. Section 3: Define conditional risks R(s|x)=ℓ(d∘s,P(Y|X=x)) and R_φ(s|x)=E[φ(s,Y)|X=x]. Pointwise excesses δ_ℓ(s,x), δ_φ(s,x). Minimal risks R^*, R_φ^*. Fisher consistency: for any sequence f_n, R_φ(f_n)→R_φ^* ⇒ R(f_n)→R^*. Uniform comparison inequality: ∃ nondecreasing ψ with ψ(R(f)-R^*) ≤ R_φ(f)-R_φ^*, ψ(ε)>0 ∀ε>0. Calibration functions: ψ(ε,x)=inf_s{δ_φ(s,x) | δ_ℓ(s,x)≥ε}, overline ψ(ε)=inf_x ψ(ε,x). Corollary: φ is Fisher consistent iff ψ(ε,x)>0 ∀x,ε>0. Let ψ be Fenchel biconjugate of overline ψ: overline ψ(ε)>0 ⇔ ψ(ε)>0 and ψ(R(f)-R^*) ≤ R_φ(f)-R_φ^* for all measurable f.

3.1 Ranking example: labels Y={(i,j):i≠j,1≤i,j≤k}, p_{ij}=P(Y=(i,j)|x). Define C_x with (C_x)_{ii}=0, (C_x)_{ij}=p_{ij}/∑_{l≠j}p_{lj} (0/0 set to 1/(k-1)), so columns sum to 1 (C_x^T 1=1). Rank by C_x 1. Loss ℓ(s,C)=max_{i<j}1{(s_i-s_j)((e_i-e_j)^T C1) ≤0, ((e_i-e_j)^T C1)≠0}. Task risk R(f)=P(f(X) and C_X1 order differently). Aggregation: collect Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m), counts m_{ij}, column totals m_j; define A(Z)=★ if some m_j=0, else A(Z) with i-th coord ∑_{j} m_{ij}/m_j. Title: Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning. Authors: Chen Cheng, John Duchi. Abstract claims: learning procedures that rely on aggregated labels (label information distilled from noisy responses) enjoy robustness properties not possible without data cleaning. Key points: (1) In the context of risk consistency (minimizing surrogate, typically convex, losses instead of target task loss like 0-1), procedures using label aggregation obtain stronger consistency guarantees than those possible using raw labels. (2) Classical perfectly-specified model scenarios suggest modeling label uncertainty is statistically efficient, but consistency for “standard” approaches fails as soon as the loss is even slightly mis-specified. (3) Procedures leveraging aggregated information still converge to optimal classifiers despite such mis-specification. Overall claim: incorporating a fuller view of the data collection-to-prediction pipeline (via label aggregation/cleaning) yields a more robust methodology by refining noisy signals.

Title: Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning. Authors: Chen Cheng, John Duchi. Paper studies how label aggregation/cleaning in data pipelines (e.g., crowdsourcing multiple noisy labels then denoising) fundamentally improves consistency and robustness of learned models. Two main robustness aspects: (1) For surrogate risk consistency (minimizing convex surrogate losses vs. target loss like 0-1), procedures using aggregated labels can achieve consistency and optimal prediction in limits where methods using raw (X,Y) pairs cannot. (2) Even in finite-dimensional parametric/statistical settings, aggregation can yield consistent classifiers when standard approaches fail. The paper situates itself with prior surrogate-consistency theory (Bartlett et al. and follow-up work) and asks whether aggregation is necessary/useful, and in what sense. Promised contributions/examples: ranking, binary and multiclass classification with linear estimators where (X,Y)-based estimators fail but aggregation yields consistency; nonparametric results where number of samples aggregated and noise conditions determine improved consistency; demonstration that aggregation enables surrogate risk consistency under weak conditions via (approximate) linear comparison inequalities; results showing aggregation can guarantee consistency even over restricted hypothesis classes where unaggregated approaches fail.

final_notes: Main theoretical claims: Theorem 1 — excess target risk R(f) - R* ≤ (16 / C_{φ,1}) · (surrogate regret), so calibration slope ζ = C_{φ,1} / 16. Theorem 2 — for F a cone and P(Δ(X) > 0) = 1, any ε_m-approx surrogate minimizers with aggregation satisfy R(f_m) → R* (aggregation restores consistency asymptotically). Pairwise surrogates can be inconsistent for k ≥ 3; aggregation (A_m) restores ordering/direction asymptotically: fitted parameters behave as Θ_m = U* T_m with ||T_m|| → ∞ while directions → true direction. Corruption constructions: small-measure corruption σ^ε replaces softmax on a tiny region T_ε. Finite-dimensional multiclass logistic fit uses identification θ_k = 0; FOC: E[X(σ^{lr}(Θ_m^T X) - ρ_m(Θ^*^T X))^T] = 0. Binary case (k=2) can preserve direction under Gaussian X (Θ_m = t_m Θ^*). Numerics: (1) Binary truncated-quadratic surrogate φ(δ) = max{1-δ,0}^2: unaggregated calibration ψ(ε) = ε^2; aggregated calibration derived ψ_m(ε) = (1/16)·(ε - sqrt{(32/m)·log 40})_+. Experiments with m ∈ {2^16,...,2^32} show transition from quadratic (unaggregated) toward linear (aggregated) as m increases. (2) Mis-specified multiclass logistic (k=3,d=2) with corrupted link ~σ(t) = σ^{lr}(t)·1{||t||≤r} + σ^{lr}(α t)·1{||t||>r} (r=3, α=0.1). Two sampling regimes (fixed n and fixed total-label budget); θ1*=(0,1), θ2*=(1,1), θ3*=0; m ∈ {1,4,16,64,256,1024}, T=100 trials; directional error → 0 as m → ∞. Discussion: many consistency results rely on m → ∞; finite-m theory remains open (ranking gives finite-m guarantees). κ(X) can stay large beyond binary; binary problems trivially have κ(X)=1; aggregation reduces B2Z. Mis-specified-model results assume existence of Bayes-optimal classifier in F; classical surrogate consistency can still fail while aggregation succeeds. Future: extend aggregation/ H-consistency comparisons to restricted classes and better characterize finite-m limits.

Paper title: "Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning" by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: aggregating/cleaning labels (information distilled from noisy responses) yields robustness not available without cleaning. Specifically: (1) minimizing a typically convex surrogate loss on aggregated labels gives stronger task-risk consistency guarantees than procedures using raw labels; (2) finite-dimensional classifiers remain consistent under loss mis-specification that breaks standard uncertainty-modeling approaches; (3) in perfectly specified statistical models, using all information is more efficient, but slight loss mis-specification can destroy standard consistency; (4) aggregation preserves convergence to optimal classifiers despite noise; (5) the whole pipeline (collection, fitting, prediction) admits robustness via noisy-signal refinement. Keep these claims in mind for checking consistency with later sections (definitions, assumptions, theorems, empirical results) about surrogate losses, aggregation methods, consistency under mis-specification, and comparisons to raw-label procedures.

Paper: "Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning" (Chen Cheng, John Duchi). Abstract-level claims to check later: aggregation/cleaning of noisy labels yields robustness not available without cleaning, specifically (1) minimizing a convex surrogate on aggregated labels gives stronger task-risk consistency than using raw labels; (2) finite-dimensional classifiers remain consistent under loss mis-specification that breaks standard uncertainty-modeling approaches; (3) in well-specified models, using all information is more efficient but slight loss mis-specification can destroy standard consistency; (4) aggregation preserves convergence to optimal classifiers despite noise; (5) end-to-end pipeline (collection, fitting, prediction) shows robustness via noisy-signal refinement. Introduction adds: aggregation permits consistent optimal prediction under surrogate (but unaggregated estimation cannot), including finite-dimensional problems; linear-estimator constructions in ranking and binary/multiclass classification separate procedures restricted to (X,Y) from aggregation procedures; nonparametric results combine aggregation count and noise conditions, allow approximately linear comparison inequalities under weak surrogate conditions, and extend consistency beyond unrestricted measurable hypothesis classes. Notes that typical supervised pipeline omits cleaning; the paper's concern is that cleaning fundamentally and necessarily improves fitted-model consistency. Context: prior surrogate-risk consistency theory (Bartlett et al. etc.) and many extensions; pair-based empirical-process analyses do not address aggregation machinery. Central research questions: is aggregation needed, does pair-based surrogate consistency suffice, and in what sense does aggregation improve consistency.

steps.notes_before:
Paper: "Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning" — studies how aggregating noisy labels (cleaning) affects surrogate-risk consistency. Key claims (from earlier parts): aggregation can enable consistency not available without cleaning; finite-dimensional classifiers can be consistent under loss mis-specification; nonparametric results combine aggregation counts and noise conditions.

From Preliminaries (this part): two regimes — unrestricted Borel F (classical/Fisher consistency) and parametric (possibly misspecified) F where aggregation may improve consistency. Definitions:
- Distribution-dependent task risk: R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X), P(·|X))] (eqn (2)). Special case zero-one: ℓ(ŷ,P)=∑_y P(Y=y)1{ŷ≠y}.
- Instantaneous task risk: R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),Y)] with ℓ: Y×Y→R_+ (eqn (1)). Binary case: d=1, d(s)=sgn(s), ℓ(y,y')=1{y y'≤0}.
- Surrogate risk: R_φ(f)=E[φ(f(X),Y)].
- Aggregated surrogate risk: R_{φ,A}(f)=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))] (eqn (3)), where Z is response-replacement and A:Z→A is aggregation.
- Repeated labeling: Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m), A_m(Z)=argmin_y ∑_{l=1}^m ℓ(y,Y_l) (majority vote for 0-1 loss).
- K-NN aggregation: Z=(Y,(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m), order X_{(l)} by dist to X, and A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y ∑_{l=0}^K ℓ(y,Y_{(l)}).

Note: the paper uses ℓ both as distribution-dependent ℓ(ŷ,P) and instantaneous ℓ(ŷ,y); equation-numbering/reference error noted above.

Later (eq. (5)): "\overline\psi_A(\epsilon,x)\coloneqq \inf_{s\in\mathbb R^d}\{\delta_{\varphi,A}(s,x)\mid\delta_\ell(s,x)\geq\epsilon\}, \qquad \overline\psi_A(\epsilon)\coloneqq \inf_{s\in\mathbb R^d}\overline\psi_A(\epsilon,x)."

errors.claim: Proposition 3: "Then \varphi is Q7D for the task risk exactly when \overline\psi_A(\epsilon,x)>0 for every x\in\mathcal X, \epsilon>0; with \psi_A=(\overline\psi_A)^{**}, ..."

errors.claim: "For multiple independent comparisons Z=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_m) ... put m_{ij}=\sum_{y\in\mathcal Y^m}1\{y=(i,j)\},\qquad m_j=\sum_{i=1}^k m_{ij},"

steps.notes_before: Section 3 develops surrogate consistency and calibration functions. Corollary 3.1: positivity of the calibration function ψ(ε,x) for all x,ε>0 characterizes Q7D surrogates; taking the Fenchel biconjugate links pointwise ψ and uniform \overlineψ and yields the inequality ψ(R(f)-R^*) ≤ R_φ(f)-R_φ^*. Definitions: R(s|x)=ℓ(d∘s,P(Y|X=x)), R_φ(s|x)=E[φ(s,Y)|X=x]; excesses δ_ℓ, δ_φ. Canonical pointwise calibration: ψ(ε,x)=inf_{s}{δ_φ(s,x) | δ_ℓ(s,x)≥ε}, and uniform \overlineψ(ε)=inf_x ψ(ε,x). 3.1: ranking task — Prop.1: for k≥3, any φ convex in first argument fails Q7D. Prop.2: with φ(s,q)=||s-q||^2 and aggregation (see below) and m≥k, φ is Q7D. Pairwise ranking: Y={(i,j)}, population C_x matrix, loss penalizes score/order disagreement; aggregation A(Z) uses counts m_{ij}. 3.2: aggregation extends calibration theory. Prop.3 gives aggregated calibration objects R_{φ,A}(s|x), δ_{φ,A} and an aggregated calibration function (notation in eq.(5) is inconsistent: eq.(5) wrongly quantifies the uniform object over s rather than x — see errors). Corollary 3.2: for m(n)→∞ and W3C φ, R_{φ,A_m}(f_n)-R_{φ,A_m}^*→0 implies R(f_n)-R^*→0. Generalized majority-vote (eq.7) defined by empirical minimizer \hat y; claim that for finite Y and i.i.d. labels empirical minimizers stabilize to population minimizers a.s. (random M exists).

W3C (Identifying surrogate): φ: R^d×A→R is (C_{φ,1},C_{φ,2})-W3C if ∃ parameters {a_y}⊂A and vectors {s_y}⊂R^d with d(s_y)=y and for all y≠y': (6a) φ(s_y,a_y)+C_{φ,1} ≤ inf_{d∘s≠y} φ(s,a_y), (6b) φ(s_y,a_{y'})-C_{φ,2} ≤ inf_s φ(s,a_{y'}). Constants satisfy 0<C_{φ,1}≤C_{φ,2}<∞. Binary hinge example yields (C_{φ,1},C_{φ,2})=(1,2). Theorem 1 (W3C + J9P aggregator): assume 0≤ℓ≤1 and noise condition (Nα) (α∈[0,1]). For any M>0, if R(f)-R* ≥ 2P(κ(X)>M) + (4 C_MT e_m(M))^{1/(1-α)} then R(f)-R* ≤ (16/C_{φ,1})(R_{φ,A_m}(f)-R_{φ,A_m}^*). Thus threshold ξ = 2P(κ(X)>M) + (4 C_MT e_m(M))^{1/(1-α)} and slope ζ = C_{φ,1}/16. Define ξ_m = inf_M { ... }; ξ_m→0 (by letting M↑∞ and m→∞ for fixed M). Using crude bound κ≤1/Δ and optimizing M gives a piecewise lower bound ξ_{m,k} (k=2 and otherwise) (forms given in text). Corollary 3.3: any f with R(f)-R* ≥ ξ_{m,k} satisfies the same bound. Definition 3.2 (U6A: level-(ξ,ζ) consistency): ∃ψ with ψ(ε)≥ζ ε for ε≥ξ and ψ(R(f)-R*) ≤ R_{φ,A}(f)-R_{φ,A}^*. Δ(x)=min_{d(s)∉y*(x)} δ_ℓ(s,x) (eq.8). Noise conditions: (Nα) P(d∘f≠d∘f*) ≤ C_MT (R(f)-R*)^α; (Mβ) P(Δ(X)≤ε) ≤ (C_MT ε)^β; equivalent when β=α/(1-α). κ(x) ratio defined eq.(9). Error function e_m(t)= t sqrt{(2/m) log(4k(C_{φ,1}+C_{φ,2})/C_{φ,1})} (eq.10). Section 3.3: Lemma 3.1 (binary): for any δ>0 φ is feasible with C_{φ,1}=φ(0)-φ(δ)>0, C_{φ,2}=φ(-δ); gives explicit threshold-bound for k=2 and corresponding multiplicative constant 16/(φ(0)-φ(δ)).

Part 7 (current): Section 4 studies restricted (parametric) classes and aggregation. K7M = existence of f∈F realizing Bayes decision (binary: sgn(⟨θ*,x⟩)=sgn(P(Y=1|x)-1/2)). Proposition 4: for any ε>0 and nonzero θ*, some P satisfies K7M along θ* but every surrogate minimizer θ_φ is nearly orthogonal to θ* (|cos angle| ≤ ε) and has worse target risk — holds for any nonnegative φ (proof App D.1). Corollary 4.1 (via Theorem 2): with aggregation A_m (T4K) and ε_m→0, aggregated approximate minimizers satisfy R(f_{θ_m})→R(f_{θ*}) and cos angle→1 (asymptotic recovery).
Theorem 2: If F is a cone, K7M holds and P(Δ(X)>0)=1, then any ε_m-approx minimizers (w.r.t aggregated surrogate R_{φ,A_m}) with ε_m→0 satisfy R(f_m)→R* (proof App D.2).
Multiclass: require Q7D surrogate with limiting property (13): φ(s,y)→0 when s_y - s_j→+∞ for all j≠y (logistic and certain pairwise forms satisfy). Proposition 5 (App E.1) and Theorem 3 (App E.2): in finite-dimensional multiclass (k≥3) small misspecification can cause pair-based surrogate inconsistency; with aggregation there exist parameter sequences Θ_m = U* T_m with ||T_m||→∞ but directions T_m/||T_m||→T*/||T*||, so ordering is recovered while norms diverge. Aggregation (T4K) thus restores asymptotic correctness without strong true-link assumptions.

steps.notes_before: Theorem 1: excess target risk bound R-R* ≤ (16/C_{φ,1})·surrogate-regret (slope ζ = C_{φ,1}/16). Matching example and Lemma 3.3 show possible numerical inconsistencies (16 vs 8 factors; C_{φ,1} identification issues). Section 4 (restricted classes): K7M = existence of f∈F realizing Bayes decision along some direction. Prop.4: one can have P satisfying K7M but surrogate minimizer nearly orthogonal to true direction; aggregation (A_m, T4K) with ε_m→0 recovers direction and risk (Cor.4.1 via Thm.2). Thm.2: if F is a cone and P(Δ(X)>0)=1, any ε_m-approx minimizers w.r.t aggregated surrogate satisfy R(f_m)→R*. Multiclass: need Q7D (limiting property φ(s,y)→0 as s_y - s_j→+∞). Pairwise surrogates can be inconsistent for k≥3; aggregation restores ordering asymptotically (Θ_m = U* T_m with ||T_m||→∞ but directions → true direction). Current part: fitted multiclass logistic (θ_k=0) given in (15). Gradient ∇_{θ_i}φ = -x(1{y=i}-σ_i^{lr}(Θ^T x)); first-order condition: E[X(σ^{lr}(Θ_m^T X) - ρ_m(Θ^*^T X))^T] = 0. Binary case (k=2): Cheng et al. show Θ_m = t_m Θ^* (direction preserved) under Gaussian X. Corruption construction: for a small-measure set T_ε, define σ^ε(t) = σ^{lr}(t)1{t∉T_ε} + (1/k)1 1{t∈T_ε}; note text erroneously describes membership reversed. Define L_{m,ε}(Θ)=E[E_{σ^ε}[φ(Θ^T X,Y_m^+)|X]] and Θ_m(ε)=argmin L_{m,ε}. Although Θ_1(0)=Θ^*, arbitrarily small positive corruption can break unaggregated consistency; aggregation/L_{m,σ}(Θ) framework gives robustness under mis-specification while unaggregated multiclass methods may be inconsistent.

Theorem/consistency summary so far: Theorem 1 gives excess target risk R(f)-R* ≤ (16/C_{φ,1})·(surrogate regret) (slope ζ = C_{φ,1}/16). Thm.2: for F a cone and P(Δ(X)>0)=1, any ε_m-approx surrogate minimizers (with aggregation) satisfy R(f_m)→R*. Pairwise surrogates can be inconsistent for k≥3; aggregation (A_m) restores ordering/direction asymptotically: fitted parameters behave like Θ_m = U* T_m with ||T_m||→∞ while directions → true direction. Corruption constructions: small-measure corruption σ^ε replaces softmax by uniform on a small set T_ε (earlier text had a membership indicator reversed). Finite-dimensional multiclass logistic fit used identification θ_k=0; gradient first-order condition equates E[X(σ^{lr}(Θ_m^T X) - ρ_m(Θ^*^T X))^T]=0. Binary case (k=2) can preserve direction under Gaussian X (Θ_m = t_m Θ^*).

New from Part 9 (numerics): Two experiments:
- D4X surrogate amplification (binary): truncated-quadratic loss φ(δ)=max{1-δ,0}^2. Unaggregated H8N calibration ψ(ε)=ε^2. With δ=1, no low-noise (α=0), C_MT=1, derived aggregated calibration
  ψ_m(ε) = (1/16)·(ε - sqrt{(32/m)·log 40})_+.
  Figure 1 used aggregated-label counts m∈{2^16,2^20,2^24,2^28,2^32} and shows transition from quadratic (unaggregated) toward linear (aggregated) as m→∞.
- Mis-specified logistic (multiclass k=3, d=2): corrupted link 
  ~σ(t)=σ^{lr}(t)·1{||t||≤r} + σ^{lr}(α t)·1{||t||>r} (r=3, α=0.1). Two sampling regimes: (i) fixed n=10,000 multilabeled points; (ii) fixed total labels nm=640,000 (n=640,000/m). True parameters θ1*=(0,1), θ2*=(1,1) (θ3*=0 by id.). Label counts m∈{1,4,16,64,256,1024}, T=100 trials, 95% error bars. Plotted metric is directional classification-rule error (distance between estimated and true normalized parameter directions) vs label count; results show asymptotic consistency as m→∞.

grade.reason: None of the reported errors addresses the claim that increasing aggregation reduces the intrinsic noise condition number (or the related kappa/B2Z definition and its dependence solely on conditional risks), so the planted error was not identified.

errors.claim: "Noise exponent α: the exponent in condition (Nα), with α∈[0,1]." and "α=0.1 in Figure 2: the score-shrinkage parameter of the corrupted link."

errors.explanation: The glossary assigns α to the Mammen–Tsybakov noise exponent and elsewhere reuses the same symbol α for an unrelated figure parameter (score-shrinkage). This is an inconsistent reuse of the same symbol for two different meanings without disambiguation.

errors.evidence: "Noise exponent α: the exponent in condition (Nα), with α∈[0,1]."; "β: the exponent in condition (Mβ), with β=α/(1-α)."

errors.claim: "Stochastic matrix: the matrix C_x satisfying C_x^T 1 = 1." and "C_x 1: the vector used to rank items by how often they are preferred."

If the aim is to rank by 'how often they are preferred' the intended normalization (row- vs column-stochastic) is unclear and the two statements are inconsistent or at least ambiguous.

errors.claim: Let m_{ij} = \sum_{y\in\mathcal Y^m} 1\{y=(i,j)\},
errors.evidence: The text immediately before this definition states: "Assume multiple independent pairwise comparisons Z=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_m) conditional on X." and then defines m_{ij} as above, followed by using m_{ij} in A(Z).
errors.explanation: The formula sums over all possible m-tuples y in Y^m rather than over the observed sample Z=(Y_1,...,Y_m). To define observed counts m_{ij} consistent with the preceding sentence and the subsequent use in A(Z), it should sum over the m observed labels (e.g. m_{ij}=\sum_{l=1}^m 1\{Y_l=(i,j)\}). As written the definition is inconsistent with the surrounding text and with how m_{ij} is used.

errors.claim: Equation (5) defines the uniform calibration function as "\overline\psi_A(\epsilon)\coloneqq \inf_{s\in\mathbb R^d}\overline\psi_A(\epsilon,x)."
errors.evidence: Earlier (and standard) definition recorded in my notes: "psi(ε,x)=inf_s{delta_phi(s,x) | delta_l(s,x)≥ε}, overline{psi}(ε)=inf_x psi(ε,x)." This same part correctly defines the pointwise calibration as "\overline\psi_A(\epsilon,x)\coloneqq \inf_{s\in\mathbb R^d}\{\delta_{\varphi,A}(s,x)\mid\delta_\ell(s,x)\geq\epsilon\}," so the uniform function should be an infimum over x, not over s.
errors.explanation: The displayed formula in (5) takes an infimum over s again, contradicting the intended/earlier definition that the uniform calibration is the infimum across x of the pointwise calibration; this appears to be a typographical/internal error.

errors.claim: 'Theorem 1 with factor 16/ C_{\varphi,1}' (as asserted in this part)
errors.evidence: 'Aggregation preserves calibration theory and strengthens consistency: Proposition 3, Corollaries 3.2–3.3, and Theorem 1 with factor 16/\mathsf C_{\varphi,1}.' (this part) and, in the structured-prediction specialization, the paper also states 'R(f)-R^\star \leq \frac{8}{\min_{\hat y\neq y}\ell(\hat y,y)}\left(R_{\varphi,A_m}(f)-R_{\varphi,A_m}^\star\right).' (displayed inequality in Section 3.3.3 of this part)

errors.claim: "This defines a conditional distribution on \(Y\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\) that samples \(Y\sim\sigma^{\textup{lr}}(t)\) if \(t\in\mathcal T_\epsilon\), and uniformly otherwise."
errors.evidence:
"Fix a set \(\mathcal T_\epsilon\subset\mathbb R^{k-1}\) of Lebesgue measure \(\epsilon\), and define
\[
\sigma^\epsilon(t)=
\sigma^{\textup{lr}}(t)1\{t\notin\mathcal T_\epsilon\}
+\frac1k\mathbf1\cdot1\{t\in\mathcal T_\epsilon\}.
\]"
errors.explanation: The displayed formula sets \(\sigma^\epsilon(t)=\sigma^{\textup{lr}}(t)\) when \(t\notin\mathcal T_\epsilon\) and uniform when \(t\in\mathcal T_\epsilon\), which is the opposite of the prose sentence.

errors.claim: "Clearly \(\sigma^\epsilon\) satisfies (14)"
errors.evidence: (14): "\(t_y=\max_{1\le i\le k}t_i\quad\text{if and only if}\quad\sigma_y(t)=\max_{1\le i\le k}\sigma_i(t).\)" and the definition "\(\sigma^\epsilon(t)=\sigma^{\textup{lr}}(t)1\{t\notin\mathcal T_\epsilon\}+\frac1k\mathbf1\cdot1\{t\in\mathcal T_\epsilon\}.\)"
errors.explanation: For \(t\in\mathcal T_\epsilon\) the formula gives a uniform distribution so \(\sigma^\epsilon_y(t)=\max_i\sigma^\epsilon_i(t)\) holds for every y, which by (14) would force \(t_y=\max_i t_i\) for every y (i.e. all components equal). Since \(\mathcal T_\epsilon\) is stated to have positive Lebesgue measure, (14) cannot hold on \(\mathcal T_\epsilon\) in general, so the claim that \(\sigma^\epsilon\) "clearly" satisfies (14) contradicts the displayed construction.

errors.claim: "σ^ε(t)=σ^{lr}(t)1{t∉T_ε} + (1/k)1{t∈T_ε}; authors assert σ^ε satisfies (14) and that arbitrarily small ε>0 can break unaggregated logistic consistency for k≥3 (Proposition 5)."
errors.evidence: "σ^ε(t)=σ^{lr}(t)1{t∉T_ε} + (1/k)1{t∈T_ε}" (construction from earlier part) and this part's Proposition 5: "there is an ε0>0 such that, for any ε∈(0,ε0), some set T_ε has Lebesgue measure at most ε and satisfies Θ_1(ε)/‖Θ_1(ε)‖ ≠ Θ^⋆/‖Θ^⋆‖."
errors.explanation: Replacing σ^{lr} by the uniform vector (1/k) on any set T_ε with positive measure makes all class outputs equal there, which violates link-consistency (14) (argmax equivalence) unless those t were already tie points. If T_ε is required to be a subset of the tie set to preserve (14), that tie set must have positive measure to matter — but then modification is vacuous (it doesn't change σ) and so cannot produce the claimed change in Θ_1. Thus the paper's construction/claim that σ^ε both preserves (14) and, when changed on an arbitrarily small-measure set T_ε, produces a different fitted normalized parameter is internally inconsistent.

final_notes:
Keep flagged theoretical tension: Proposition 5 (k≥3, Σ=I, App. E.1) — under an invertibility condition on linear map D there exists ε0>0 s.t. for any ε∈(0,ε0) some set T_ε (Lebesgue measure ≤ε) yields Θ_1(ε)/||Θ_1(ε)|| ≠ Θ^*/||Θ^*||. Earlier construction used σ^ε(t)=σ^{lr}(t) for t∉T_ε and =1/k for t∈T_ε; authors claim this preserves link-consistency (eq. (14): argmax t = argmax σ(t)) while arbitrarily small perturbations break unaggregated fitting — potential tension unless T_ε lies in tie set.
Theorem 3 (App. E.2): with Θ^*=U^*T^* (U^* orthogonal, T^* nonsingular) minimizer Θ_m satisfies Θ_m=U^*T_m for every m, and as m→∞, ||T_m||→∞ and T_m/||T_m||→T^*/||T^*|| (aggregation restores normalized direction). Binary Gaussian case: Θ_m = t_m Θ^* (scalar multiple).
Numerics (Part 14): two experiments. 1) Truncated quadratic surrogate φ(δ)=max{1-δ,0}^2, ψ(ε)=ε^2 per Bartlett et al.; using Lemma 3.1 with δ=1 and no low-noise (α=0,C_MT=1) gives ψ_m(ε)=(1/16)(ε - sqrt((32/m) log40))_+; m={2^16,...,2^32}; ψ_m→(1/16)ε as m→∞. 2) Mis-specified logistic model (k=3,d=2) with score-shrink α=0.1, r=3, θ1*,θ2* given; m∈{1,4,16,64,256,1024}; left: n=10,000 per m; right: n=640,000/m fixed total labels; plots show ||T_m/||T_m|| - T^*/||T^*|||| →0 as m grows (consistent with Theorem 3).
Discussion summary: many guarantees asymptotic (Cor.4.1, Thms2–3 require m→∞); some finite-m results (Prop2: m≥k for ranking; Sec3.2.3 uniform linear comparison at α=1 with O(log k) bound); κ(X) (eq.9) can be large beyond binary even at low noise; mis-specified-model results require optimal predictability (12); open directions: finite-m theory, sharper loss-dependent analysis, extending aggregation-based comparison bounds to restricted classes.

Paper studies whether aggregating noisy labels improves consistency of learned predictors. Focus: surrogate losses (used during fitting), analyzed over all measurable predictors and over restricted model classes. Develops calibration inequalities for aggregated labels; analyzes ranking, classification, structured prediction. Key claims to remember: for ranking with k ≥ 3 items, no convex surrogate based on individual comparisons is Fisher consistent; an aggregated squared-loss procedure is consistent when m ≥ k. More generally, "identifying" surrogates become asymptotically consistent as number m of aggregated labels grows; many guarantees require m → ∞. Under certain noise conditions, aggregation yields approximately linear comparison inequalities. In restricted model classes, aggregation can restore consistency when ordinary surrogate minimization fails (including link mis-specification). Two numerical illustrations are reported. Glossary follows (definitions and reused symbols listed).

Corollary 3.1: positivity of psi(·,x) for all x,ε>0 characterizes Fisher consistency; Fenchel biconjugate of overline{psi} yields a comparison bound psi(R-R^*) ≤ R_phi-R_phi^*. Section 4: Aggregation can restore consistency when optimization is restricted to a hypothesis class. Key definitions: ε-argmin g = {θ | g(θ) ≤ inf g + ε}. A_m is majority vote on Z=(Y1,..,Ym). Binary setting: Y={±1}, φ-margin surrogate φ(s,y)=φ(sy) with convex scalar φ; Fisher/uniform consistency over all measurables iff φ'(0)<0. Linear predictor class F = {f_θ(x)=⟨θ,x⟩}. Optimal predictability along θ* means sgn(⟨θ*,x⟩)=sgn(P(Y=1|x)-1/2). Proposition 4 (App D.1): For any nonnegative φ and any ε>0 and nonzero θ*, there exists P optimally predictable along θ* such that every surrogate minimizer θ_φ ∈ argmin_θ E[φ(f_θ(X),Y)] has R(f_{θ_φ})>R(f_{θ*}) and |cos∠(θ_φ,θ*)| ≤ ε (i.e., can be nearly orthogonal). Corollary 4.1 (from Theorem 2): if P optimally predictable along θ* and ε_m→0 as m→∞, then R(f_{θ_m})→R(f_{θ*}) and cos∠(θ_m,θ*)→1. Multiclass (Y=[k]): consider cone F with 1^T f=0 and closed under positive scaling. Surrogate φ: R^k×[k]→R_+ assumed Fisher consistent and satisfying limiting loss condition (13): φ(s,y)→0 if s_y - s_j → +∞ for all j≠y. Section 4.3: multiclass linear predictors Θ∈R^{d×(k-1)} (Θ_k=0), link σ preserves argmax (link-consistency) is assumed; multiclass logistic σ^{lr} is an example. Proposition 5: small ε>0 can change the direction Θ_1(ε)/||·|| ≠ Θ*/||·|| under an invertibility condition on a linear operator D. Theorem 3: if Θ*=U* T* (U* orthogonal, T* nonsingular) then Θ_m = U* T_m with ||T_m||→∞ and T_m/||T_m||→T*/||T*|| (aggregated-label minimizers recover Θ* direction asymptotically). Experiments: (1) Binary truncated-quadratic φ(δ)=max{1-δ,0}^2 gives calibration ψ(ε)=ε^2; with majority-vote aggregation and no low-noise (α=0) they derive ψ_m(ε)=(1/16)(ε - sqrt(32/m · log 40))_+ and comparison inequalities. (2) Logistic mis-spec example: corrupted link ~σ with r=3, α=0.1, k=3,d=2, Θ* columns θ1*=(0,1)^T, θ2*=(1,1)^T (invertible); experiments show directional error of T_m/||T_m|| vs T*/||T*|| decreases with m. From current part (Discussion): many consistency results rely on m→∞; ranking (Sec.3.1) admits finite-m consistency guarantees; noise condition number κ(X) (eq.9) used to characterize multiclass comparison inequalities (binary trivially κ=1 but κ can be large even when Mammen–Tsybakov noise α is small); mis-specified-model results rely on optimal predictability (Eq.12) requiring Bayes-optimal classifier in F. Future directions: finite-m surrogate consistency, precise failure-mode constructions, and extending H-consistency/restricted-class comparison inequalities with aggregation.

Title: Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning. Authors: Chen Cheng, John Duchi. Abstract claims: learning procedures that rely on aggregated labels (label information distilled from noisy responses) enjoy robustness properties not possible without data cleaning. Key points: (1) In the context of risk consistency (minimizing surrogate, typically convex, losses instead of target task loss like 0-1), procedures using label aggregation obtain stronger consistency guarantees than those possible using raw labels. (2) Classical perfectly-specified model scenarios suggest modeling label uncertainty is statistically efficient, but consistency for “standard” approaches fails as soon as the loss is even slightly mis-specified. (3) Procedures leveraging aggregated information still converge to optimal classifiers despite such mis-specification. Overall claim: incorporating a fuller view of the data collection-to-prediction pipeline (via label aggregation/cleaning) yields a more robust methodology by refining noisy signals.

Title: Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning. Authors: Chen Cheng, John Duchi. Paper studies how label aggregation/cleaning in data pipelines (e.g., crowdsourcing multiple noisy labels then denoising) fundamentally improves consistency and robustness of learned models. Two main robustness aspects: (1) For surrogate risk consistency (minimizing convex surrogate losses vs. target loss like 0-1), procedures using aggregated labels can achieve consistency and optimal prediction in limits where methods using raw (X,Y) pairs cannot. (2) Even in finite-dimensional parametric/statistical settings, aggregation can yield consistent classifiers when standard approaches fail. The paper situates itself with prior surrogate-consistency theory (Bartlett et al. and follow-up work) and asks whether aggregation is necessary/useful, and in what sense. Promised contributions/examples: ranking, binary and multiclass classification with linear estimators where (X,Y)-based estimators fail but aggregation yields consistency; nonparametric results where number of samples aggregated and noise conditions determine improved consistency; demonstration that aggregation enables surrogate risk consistency under weak conditions via (approximate) linear comparison inequalities; results showing aggregation can guarantee consistency even over restricted hypothesis classes where unaggregated approaches fail.

Paper title: "Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning" by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: aggregating/cleaning labels (information distilled from noisy responses) yields robustness not available without cleaning. Specifically: (1) minimizing a typically convex surrogate loss on aggregated labels gives stronger task-risk consistency guarantees than procedures using raw labels; (2) finite-dimensional classifiers remain consistent under loss mis-specification that breaks standard uncertainty-modeling approaches; (3) in perfectly specified statistical models, using all information is more efficient, but slight loss mis-specification can destroy standard consistency; (4) aggregation preserves convergence to optimal classifiers despite noise; (5) the whole pipeline (collection, fitting, prediction) admits robustness via noisy-signal refinement. Keep these claims in mind for checking consistency with later sections (definitions, assumptions, theorems, empirical results) about surrogate losses, aggregation methods, consistency under mis-specification, and comparisons to raw-label procedures.

Introduction adds: aggregation permits consistent optimal prediction under surrogate (but unaggregated estimation cannot), including finite-dimensional problems; linear-estimator constructions in ranking and binary/multiclass classification separate procedures restricted to (X,Y) from aggregation procedures; nonparametric results combine aggregation count and noise conditions, allow approximately linear comparison inequalities under weak surrogate conditions, and extend consistency beyond unrestricted measurable hypothesis classes. Notes that typical supervised pipeline omits cleaning; the paper's concern is that cleaning fundamentally and necessarily improves fitted-model consistency. Context: prior surrogate-risk consistency theory (Bartlett et al. etc.) and many extensions; pair-based empirical-process analyses do not address aggregation machinery. Central research questions: is aggregation needed, does pair-based surrogate consistency suffice, and in what sense does aggregation improve consistency.

From Preliminaries (this part): two regimes — unrestricted Borel F (classical/Fisher consistency) and parametric (possibly misspecified) F where aggregation may improve consistency. Definitions:
- Distribution-dependent task risk: R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X), P(·|X))] (eqn (2)). Special case zero-one: ℓ(ŷ,P)=∑_y P(Y=y)1{ŷ≠y}.

- Aggregated surrogate risk: R_{φ,A}(f)=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))] (eqn (3)), where Z is response-replacement and A:Z→A is aggregation.

- K-NN aggregation: Z=(Y,(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m), order X_{(l)} by dist to X, and A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y ∑_{l=0}^K ℓ(y,Y_{(l)}).

Paper studies whether aggregating noisy labels improves consistency of learned predictors. Focus: surrogate losses (used during fitting), analyzed over all measurable predictors and over restricted model classes. Develops calibration inequalities for aggregated labels; analyzes ranking, classification, structured prediction. Key claims to remember: for ranking with k ≥ 3 items, no convex surrogate based on individual comparisons is Fisher consistent; an aggregated squared-loss procedure is consistent when m ≥ k. More generally, "identifying" surrogates become asymptotically consistent as number m of aggregated labels grows; many guarantees require m → ∞. Under certain noise conditions, aggregation yields approximately linear comparison inequalities. In restricted model classes, aggregation can restore consistency when ordinary surrogate minimization fails (including link mis-specification). Two numerical illustrations are reported. Glossary follows (definitions and reused symbols listed).

Paper: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” (Chen Cheng, John Duchi). Thesis: aggregating noisy labels (label cleaning) can yield consistency and robustness not available using single noisy labels. Settings: ranking, binary/multiclass classification, finite-dimensional linear predictors. Key formal claims (from earlier parts): Propositions 1–2 show convex ranking surrogates fail without aggregation when k≥3 but can be consistent after aggregation (Prop.2 uses squared-loss φ(s,q)=||s−q||_2^2). Theorem 1 gives approximate linear comparison inequalities for aggregated-label losses (slope C_{φ,1}/16 above threshold). Corollary 4.1 and Theorems 2–3 show aggregation restores convergence as m→∞ for restricted hypothesis classes F; Propositions 4–5 exhibit failures without aggregation. Notation/definitions introduced in this part: data (X,Y) i.i.d. from P; scorer f:X→R^d, decoder d:R^d→Y; task loss ℓ:Y×Y→R_+ and task risk R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),Y)] (eq.1). steps.notes_before: Section summarizes Fisher consistency and comparison inequalities via calibration functions: define conditional risks R(s|x), R_phi(s|x); pointwise excesses delta_l(s,x)=R(s|x)-inf_s'R(s'|x), delta_phi(s,x) similarly. Calibration psi(ε,x)=inf_{s}{delta_phi(s,x) | delta_l(s,x)≥ε}, overline{psi}(ε)=inf_x psi(ε,x). Corollary 3.1: positivity of psi(·,x) for all x,ε>0 characterizes Fisher consistency; Fenchel biconjugate of overline{psi} yields a comparison bound psi(R-R^*) ≤ R_phi-R_phi^*. Ranking example: labels Y={(i,j):i≠j}, p_{ij}=P(Y=(i,j)|x). Define C_x with (C_x)_{ii}=0 and (C_x)_{ij}=p_{ij}/\sum_{l≠j} p_{lj} (use 0/0=1/(k-1)), so C_x^T 1 = 1. Loss ℓ(s,C)=max_{i<j} 1{(s_i-s_j)(C1_i-C1_j)≤0, C1_i-C1_j≠0}; population risk R(f)=P(f(X) and C_X1 order differently) (eq.4). Restrict scores to s^T1=0. Proposition 1: for k≥3, any surrogate φ convex in scores is not Fisher consistent for this ranking risk. Aggregation: collect Z=(Y_1,...,Y_m); define counts m_{ij} (definition in text appears to sum over Y^m and is inconsistent — it should sum over observed labels), m_j=Σ_i m_{ij}, and A(Z)=star if some m_j=0, else vector whose i-th entry is Σ_j m_{ij}/m_j. steps.notes_before: Squared-loss surrogate: φ(s,q)=||s-q||_2^2, φ(s,★)=0. Proposition 2: for ranking risk (eq.4) φ is Fisher consistent when m≥k. Aggregation expands response space from Y to R^k; A(Z) is vector-valued in R^k when all m_j>0. Prop 1 (earlier): for k≥3 no convex-in-scores surrogate is Fisher consistent for pairwise ranking risk. Proposition 3: if ∫ b(x)dP(x)<∞ and δ_ℓ(f(x),x) ≤ b(x), then φ is Fisher consistent for task risk iff for all x, ε>0 the pointwise calibration overlineψ_A(ε,x)>0; with ψ_A=(overlineψ_A)^{**} we get ψ_A(R(f)-R^*) ≤ R_{φ,A}(f)-R_{φ,A}^*. Definition 3.1: (C_{φ,1},C_{φ,2})-identifying surrogate with params a_y∈A and s_y∈R^d, d(s_y)=y satisfying (6a),(6b). Example: hinge loss is (1,2)-identifying. Corollary 3.2: If m(n)→∞ and φ is identifying (Def.3.1) then R_{φ,A_m}(f_n)-R_{φ,A_m}^*→0 ⇒ R(f_n)-R^*→0. Example: hinge is (C_{φ,1},C_{φ,2})=(1,2)-identifying. Majority vote A_m eventually selects only optimal labels (empirical argmin ⊂ population argmin) for m≥M (random finite M).

Level-(ξ,ζ) consistency (Def.3.2): there exists ψ with ψ(ε)≥ζε for ε≥ξ and ψ(R(f)-R^*) ≤ R_{φ,A}(f)-R_{φ,A}^*.

Noise/margin quantities:
- Δ(x)=min_{d(s)∉y^*(x)} δ_ℓ(s,x) (binary: Δ(x)=|2P(Y=1|X=x)-1|).
- Conditions: (N_α) P(d◦f ≠ d◦f^*) ≤ C_{MT}(R(f)-R^*)^α, α∈[0,1]; (M_β) P(Δ(X) ≤ ε) ≤ (C_{MT}ε)^β. They are equivalent under β=α/(1-α).

R(f)-R^* ≥ 2P(κ(X)>M) + (4C_{MT} e_m(M))^{1/(1-α)},
we have
R(f)-R^* ≤ (16/C_{φ,1}) (R_{φ,A_m}(f)-R_{φ,A_m}^*).
Thus level-(ξ,ζ) with ξ as the LHS threshold and ζ=C_{φ,1}/16. Let ξ_m = inf_M{…}; ξ_m→0 as m→∞, so taking α=0 yields Corollary 3.2.

Optimizing using κ≤1/Δ gives explicit ξ_{m,k}: for k=2,
ξ_{m,2}=((32 C_{MT}^2/m) log(8(C_{φ,1}+C_{φ,2})/C_{φ,1}))^{1/(2(1-α))},
and a stated expression for k≥3. Corollary 3.3: same linear comparison holds whenever R(f)-R^*≥ξ_{m,k}.

Theorem 1 (recap): if φ is (C_{φ,1},C_{φ,2})-identifying, A_m aggregator (7), 0≤ℓ≤1 and (N_α) holds, then for any M>0 and f with
R(f)-R^* ≥ 2P(κ(X)>M) + (4 C_{MT} e_m(M))^{1/(1-α)}
we have R(f)-R^* ≤ (16/C_{φ,1})(R_{φ,A_m}(f)-R_{φ,A_m}^*). Here e_m(t)= t sqrt{(2/m) log(4k(C_{φ,1}+C_{φ,2})/C_{φ,1})}.

As α→1 aggregation requirement falls; in the limit α=1 the paper claims that if
m ≥ 32 max{C_{MT}^2,C_{MT}^4} log(4k(C_{φ,1}+C_{φ,2})/C_{φ,1}) = O(log k)
then ξ_{m,k}=0 (uniform linear comparison with factor 16/C_{φ,1}).
Section 3.3 examples:
- Binary nonsmooth surrogate: φ(f,y)=φ(yf). If ∂φ(0) ⊂ (-∞,0) and lim_{t→∞}φ(t)=0, then for any δ>0 Lemma 3.1 gives feasibility constants C_{φ,1}=φ(0)-φ(δ)>0, C_{φ,2}=φ(-δ). Corollary 3.3 (k=2) yields threshold

and linear comparison with factor 16/(φ(0)-φ(δ)).

Section 4: Aggregation can restore consistency when optimization is restricted to a hypothesis class. Key definitions: ε-argmin g = {θ | g(θ) ≤ inf g + ε}. A_m is majority vote on Z=(Y1,..,Ym). Binary setting: Y={±1}, φ-margin surrogate φ(s,y)=φ(sy) with convex scalar φ; Fisher/uniform consistency over all measurables iff φ'(0)<0. Linear predictor class F = {f_θ(x)=⟨θ,x⟩}. Optimal predictability along θ* means sgn(⟨θ*,x⟩)=sgn(P(Y=1|x)-1/2). Proposition 4 (App D.1): For any nonnegative φ and any ε>0 and nonzero θ*, there exists P optimally predictable along θ* such that every surrogate minimizer θ_φ ∈ argmin_θ E[φ(f_θ(X),Y)] has R(f_{θ_φ})>R(f_{θ*}) and |cos∠(θ_φ,θ*)| ≤ ε (i.e., can be nearly orthogonal). Aggregation: choose θ_m ∈ ε_m-argmin_θ R_{φ,A_m}(f_θ)=ε_m-argmin_θ E[φ(A_m(Y1..Ym) f_θ(X))] with ε_m→0. Corollary 4.1 (from Theorem 2): if P optimally predictable along θ* and ε_m→0 as m→∞, then R(f_{θ_m})→R(f_{θ*}) and cos∠(θ_m,θ*)→1. Multiclass (Y=[k]): consider cone F with 1^T f=0 and closed under positive scaling. Surrogate φ: R^k×[k]→R_+ assumed Fisher consistent and satisfying limiting loss condition (13): φ(s,y)→0 if s_y - s_j → +∞ for all j≠y. Examples: multiclass logistic φ(s,y)=log(∑ e^{s_j-s_y}) and pairwise-sum losses ∑_{i≠y} φ(s_y-s_i) with scalar φ convex, nonincreasing, φ'(0)<0, inf φ=0. Zhang [51, Thm.8] shows consistency over F={f:1^T f=0}.

\[
\sigma^\epsilon(t)=
