+\frac1k\mathbf1\cdot1\{t\in\mathcal T_\epsilon\}.
\]"
errors.explanation: The displayed formula sets \(\sigma^\epsilon(t)=\sigma^{\textup{lr}}(t)\) when \(t\notin\mathcal T_\epsilon\) and uniform when \(t\in\mathcal T_\epsilon\), which is the opposite of the prose sentence.

errors.claim: "Clearly \(\sigma^\epsilon\) satisfies (14)"
errors.evidence: (14): "\(t_y=\max_{1\le i\le k}t_i\quad\text{if and only if}\quad\sigma_y(t)=\max_{1\le i\le k}\sigma_i(t).\)" and the definition "\(\sigma^\epsilon(t)=\sigma^{\textup{lr}}(t)1\{t\notin\mathcal T_\epsilon\}+\frac1k\mathbf1\cdot1\{t\in\mathcal T_\epsilon\}.\)"
errors.explanation: For \(t\in\mathcal T_\epsilon\) the formula gives a uniform distribution so \(\sigma^\epsilon_y(t)=\max_i\sigma^\epsilon_i(t)\) holds for every y, which by (14) would force \(t_y=\max_i t_i\) for every y (i.e. all components equal). Since \(\mathcal T_\epsilon\) is stated to have positive Lebesgue measure, (14) cannot hold on \(\mathcal T_\epsilon\) in general, so the claim that \(\sigma^\epsilon\) "clearly" satisfies (14) contradicts the displayed construction.

errors.explanation: Replacing σ^{lr} by the uniform vector (1/k) on any set T_ε with positive measure makes all class outputs equal there, which violates link-consistency (14) (argmax equivalence) unless those t were already tie points. If T_ε is required to be a subset of the tie set to preserve (14), that tie set must have positive measure to matter — but then modification is vacuous (it doesn't change σ) and so cannot produce the claimed change in Θ_1. Thus the paper's construction/claim that σ^ε both preserves (14) and, when changed on an arbitrarily small-measure set T_ε, produces a different fitted normalized parameter is internally inconsistent.

Title: Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning. Authors: Chen Cheng, John Duchi. Abstract claims: learning procedures that rely on aggregated labels (label information distilled from noisy responses) enjoy robustness properties not possible without data cleaning. Key points: (1) In the context of risk consistency (minimizing surrogate, typically convex, losses instead of target task loss like 0-1), procedures using label aggregation obtain stronger consistency guarantees than those possible using raw labels. (2) Classical perfectly-specified model scenarios suggest modeling label uncertainty is statistically efficient, but consistency for “standard” approaches fails as soon as the loss is even slightly mis-specified. (3) Procedures leveraging aggregated information still converge to optimal classifiers despite such mis-specification. Overall claim: incorporating a fuller view of the data collection-to-prediction pipeline (via label aggregation/cleaning) yields a more robust methodology by refining noisy signals.

Title: Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning. Authors: Chen Cheng, John Duchi. Paper studies how label aggregation/cleaning in data pipelines (e.g., crowdsourcing multiple noisy labels then denoising) fundamentally improves consistency and robustness of learned models. Two main robustness aspects: (1) For surrogate risk consistency (minimizing convex surrogate losses vs. target loss like 0-1), procedures using aggregated labels can achieve consistency and optimal prediction in limits where methods using raw (X,Y) pairs cannot. (2) Even in finite-dimensional parametric/statistical settings, aggregation can yield consistent classifiers when standard approaches fail. The paper situates itself with prior surrogate-consistency theory (Bartlett et al. and follow-up work) and asks whether aggregation is necessary/useful, and in what sense. Promised contributions/examples: ranking, binary and multiclass classification with linear estimators where (X,Y)-based estimators fail but aggregation yields consistency; nonparametric results where number of samples aggregated and noise conditions determine improved consistency; demonstration that aggregation enables surrogate risk consistency under weak conditions via (approximate) linear comparison inequalities; results showing aggregation can guarantee consistency even over restricted hypothesis classes where unaggregated approaches fail.

Example 1 (majority vote): Z=(Y_1,...,Y_m), A(Z)=argmin_y ∑_{l=1}^m ℓ(y,Y_l); for 0-1 loss this is majority vote. Surrogate-consistency setup: conditional task risk R(s|x)=ℓ(d∘s,P(Y|X=x)), conditional surrogate risk R_φ(s|x)=E[φ(s,Y)|X=x]. Pointwise excesses δ_ℓ(s,x)=R(s|x)-inf_s'R(s'|x), δ_φ(s,x)=R_φ(s|x)-inf_s'R_φ(s'|x). Global minima R* and R_φ*. Two consistency notions: (i) Fisher consistency: for any sequence f_n, R_φ(f_n)→R_φ* implies R(f_n)→R*; (ii) uniform comparison: exists nondecreasing ψ with ψ(ε)>0 for ε>0 s.t. ψ(R(f)-R*) ≤ R_φ(f)-R_φ* for all f. Calibration functions: ψ(ε,x)=inf_{s}{δ_φ(s,x) | δ_ℓ(s,x)≥ε}, overline ψ(ε)=inf_x ψ(ε,x). Corollary 3.1: φ is Fisher consistent iff ψ(ε,x)>0 for all x,ε>0; taking Fenchel biconjugate of overline ψ gives a ψ s.t. ψ(R(f)-R*) ≤ R_φ(f)-R_φ*. Ranking example (Sec 3.1): Y={(i,j): i≠j, i beats j}, p_{ij}=P(Y=(i,j)|x). Define C_x with (C_x)_{ii}=0 and (C_x)_{ij}=p_{ij}/∑_{l≠j}p_{lj} (set 0/0=1/(k-1)), so C_x is column-stochastic (C_x^T1=1). Paper title: "Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning" by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: aggregating/cleaning labels (information distilled from noisy responses) yields robustness not available without cleaning. Specifically: (1) minimizing a typically convex surrogate loss on aggregated labels gives stronger task-risk consistency guarantees than procedures using raw labels; (2) finite-dimensional classifiers remain consistent under loss mis-specification that breaks standard uncertainty-modeling approaches; (3) in perfectly specified statistical models, using all information is more efficient, but slight loss mis-specification can destroy standard consistency; (4) aggregation preserves convergence to optimal classifiers despite noise; (5) the whole pipeline (collection, fitting, prediction) admits robustness via noisy-signal refinement. Keep these claims in mind for checking consistency with later sections (definitions, assumptions, theorems, empirical results) about surrogate losses, aggregation methods, consistency under mis-specification, and comparisons to raw-label procedures.

Paper: "Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning" (Chen Cheng, John Duchi). Abstract-level claims to check later: aggregation/cleaning of noisy labels yields robustness not available without cleaning, specifically (1) minimizing a convex surrogate on aggregated labels gives stronger task-risk consistency than using raw labels; (2) finite-dimensional classifiers remain consistent under loss mis-specification that breaks standard uncertainty-modeling approaches; (3) in well-specified models, using all information is more efficient but slight loss mis-specification can destroy standard consistency; (4) aggregation preserves convergence to optimal classifiers despite noise; (5) end-to-end pipeline (collection, fitting, prediction) shows robustness via noisy-signal refinement. Introduction adds: aggregation permits consistent optimal prediction under surrogate (but unaggregated estimation cannot), including finite-dimensional problems; linear-estimator constructions in ranking and binary/multiclass classification separate procedures restricted to (X,Y) from aggregation procedures; nonparametric results combine aggregation count and noise conditions, allow approximately linear comparison inequalities under weak surrogate conditions, and extend consistency beyond unrestricted measurable hypothesis classes. Notes that typical supervised pipeline omits cleaning; the paper's concern is that cleaning fundamentally and necessarily improves fitted-model consistency. Context: prior surrogate-risk consistency theory (Bartlett et al. etc.) and many extensions; pair-based empirical-process analyses do not address aggregation machinery. Central research questions: is aggregation needed, does pair-based surrogate consistency suffice, and in what sense does aggregation improve consistency.

steps.notes_before:
Paper: "Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning" — studies how aggregating noisy labels (cleaning) affects surrogate-risk consistency. Key claims (from earlier parts): aggregation can enable consistency not available without cleaning; finite-dimensional classifiers can be consistent under loss mis-specification; nonparametric results combine aggregation counts and noise conditions.

From Preliminaries (this part): two regimes — unrestricted Borel F (classical/Fisher consistency) and parametric (possibly misspecified) F where aggregation may improve consistency. Definitions:
- Distribution-dependent task risk: R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X), P(·|X))] (eqn (2)). Special case zero-one: ℓ(ŷ,P)=∑_y P(Y=y)1{ŷ≠y}.
- Instantaneous task risk: R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),Y)] with ℓ: Y×Y→R_+ (eqn (1)). Binary case: d=1, d(s)=sgn(s), ℓ(y,y')=1{y y'≤0}.
- Surrogate risk: R_φ(f)=E[φ(f(X),Y)].
- Aggregated surrogate risk: R_{φ,A}(f)=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))] (eqn (3)), where Z is response-replacement and A:Z→A is aggregation.
- Repeated labeling: Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m), A_m(Z)=argmin_y ∑_{l=1}^m ℓ(y,Y_l) (majority vote for 0-1 loss).
- K-NN aggregation: Z=(Y,(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m), order X_{(l)} by dist to X, and A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y ∑_{l=0}^K ℓ(y,Y_{(l)}).

Note: the paper uses ℓ both as distribution-dependent ℓ(ŷ,P) and instantaneous ℓ(ŷ,y); equation-numbering/reference error noted above.

steps.notes_before: Section 3 develops surrogate consistency and calibration functions. Corollary 3.1: positivity of the calibration function ψ(ε,x) for all x,ε>0 characterizes Q7D surrogates; taking the Fenchel biconjugate links pointwise ψ and uniform \overlineψ and yields the inequality ψ(R(f)-R^*) ≤ R_φ(f)-R_φ^*. Definitions: R(s|x)=ℓ(d∘s,P(Y|X=x)), R_φ(s|x)=E[φ(s,Y)|X=x]; excesses δ_ℓ, δ_φ. Canonical pointwise calibration: ψ(ε,x)=inf_{s}{δ_φ(s,x) | δ_ℓ(s,x)≥ε}, and uniform \overlineψ(ε)=inf_x ψ(ε,x). 3.1: ranking task — Prop.1: for k≥3, any φ convex in first argument fails Q7D. Prop.2: with φ(s,q)=||s-q||^2 and aggregation (see below) and m≥k, φ is Q7D. Pairwise ranking: Y={(i,j)}, population C_x matrix, loss penalizes score/order disagreement; aggregation A(Z) uses counts m_{ij}. 3.2: aggregation extends calibration theory. Prop.3 gives aggregated calibration objects R_{φ,A}(s|x), δ_{φ,A} and an aggregated calibration function (notation in eq.(5) is inconsistent: eq.(5) wrongly quantifies the uniform object over s rather than x — see errors). Corollary 3.2: for m(n)→∞ and W3C φ, R_{φ,A_m}(f_n)-R_{φ,A_m}^*→0 implies R(f_n)-R^*→0. Generalized majority-vote (eq.7) defined by empirical minimizer \hat y; claim that for finite Y and i.i.d. labels empirical minimizers stabilize to population minimizers a.s. (random M exists).

W3C (Identifying surrogate): φ: R^d×A→R is (C_{φ,1},C_{φ,2})-W3C if ∃ parameters {a_y}⊂A and vectors {s_y}⊂R^d with d(s_y)=y and for all y≠y': (6a) φ(s_y,a_y)+C_{φ,1} ≤ inf_{d∘s≠y} φ(s,a_y), (6b) φ(s_y,a_{y'})-C_{φ,2} ≤ inf_s φ(s,a_{y'}). Constants satisfy 0<C_{φ,1}≤C_{φ,2}<∞. Binary hinge example yields (C_{φ,1},C_{φ,2})=(1,2). Theorem 1 (W3C + J9P aggregator): assume 0≤ℓ≤1 and noise condition (Nα) (α∈[0,1]). For any M>0, if R(f)-R* ≥ 2P(κ(X)>M) + (4 C_MT e_m(M))^{1/(1-α)} then R(f)-R* ≤ (16/C_{φ,1})(R_{φ,A_m}(f)-R_{φ,A_m}^*). Thus threshold ξ = 2P(κ(X)>M) + (4 C_MT e_m(M))^{1/(1-α)} and slope ζ = C_{φ,1}/16. Define ξ_m = inf_M { ... }; ξ_m→0 (by letting M↑∞ and m→∞ for fixed M). Using crude bound κ≤1/Δ and optimizing M gives a piecewise lower bound ξ_{m,k} (k=2 and otherwise) (forms given in text). Corollary 3.3: any f with R(f)-R* ≥ ξ_{m,k} satisfies the same bound. Definition 3.2 (U6A: level-(ξ,ζ) consistency): ∃ψ with ψ(ε)≥ζ ε for ε≥ξ and ψ(R(f)-R*) ≤ R_{φ,A}(f)-R_{φ,A}^*. Δ(x)=min_{d(s)∉y*(x)} δ_ℓ(s,x) (eq.8). Noise conditions: (Nα) P(d∘f≠d∘f*) ≤ C_MT (R(f)-R*)^α; (Mβ) P(Δ(X)≤ε) ≤ (C_MT ε)^β; equivalent when β=α/(1-α). κ(x) ratio defined eq.(9). Error function e_m(t)= t sqrt{(2/m) log(4k(C_{φ,1}+C_{φ,2})/C_{φ,1})} (eq.10). Paper studies whether aggregating noisy labels improves consistency of learned predictors. Focus: surrogate losses (used during fitting), analyzed over all measurable predictors and over restricted model classes. Develops calibration inequalities for aggregated labels; analyzes ranking, classification, structured prediction. Key claims to remember: for ranking with k ≥ 3 items, no convex surrogate based on individual comparisons is Fisher consistent; an aggregated squared-loss procedure is consistent when m ≥ k. More generally, "identifying" surrogates become asymptotically consistent as number m of aggregated labels grows; many guarantees require m → ∞. Under certain noise conditions, aggregation yields approximately linear comparison inequalities. In restricted model classes, aggregation can restore consistency when ordinary surrogate minimization fails (including link mis-specification). Two numerical illustrations are reported. Glossary follows (definitions and reused symbols listed).

Risks: task risk R(f), surrogate R_φ(f), aggregated surrogate R_{φ,A}(f); conditional risks R(·|x); infimal risks R^*, R_φ^*, R_{φ,A}^*. Excess risks δ_ℓ, δ_φ, δ_{φ,A}. Calibration: pointwise ψ, uniform overlineψ, ψ_A = Fenchel biconjugate of overlineψ_A. Fisher consistency = surrogate-risk→infimum implies task-risk→infimum; uniform comparison inequalities yield explicit ψ. Ranking setup: p_{ij}=P(i preferred j), C_x normalized transition matrix from p_{ij}, ranking target uses C_x 1. Squared-loss ranking φ(s,q)=||s−q||_2^2 referenced (Prop.2). Identifying surrogates Def.3.1 uses constants C_{φ,1}, C_{φ,2}. Low-noise assumptions: Mammen–Tsybakov (N_α),(M_β) with β = α/(1−α). Error function e_m(t) for majority vote. Parametric section: linear predictors f_θ=<θ,x>, multiclass logistic σ (σ^{lr}), population logistic losses L_m, Θ^*, Θ_m. Numerics: ψ_m, corrupted logistic link ~σ, T=100 trials, 95% error bars. Note: paper reuses α elsewhere; β formula requires α≠1.

Paper: "Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning" (Chen Cheng, John Duchi). Main thesis: aggregating noisy labels (label cleaning) can yield consistency and robustness not available using raw single labels. Key settings/examples: ranking, binary and multiclass classification, and finite-dimensional linear predictors. Aggregators: majority vote A_m, generalized majority vote (eq.7), KNN aggregator A_{m,K}. Main formal claims: Propositions 1–2 show convex ranking surrogates fail without aggregation when k≥3 but become consistent after aggregation when m≥k (Prop.2 uses squared-loss φ(s,q)=||s−q||_2^2). Theorem 1: under weak surrogate assumptions, aggregated-label losses admit approximate linear comparison inequalities (linear bounds relating excess task risk to excess surrogate risk); stated slope = C_{φ,1}/16 above its risk threshold. Corollary 4.1 and Theorem 2 (and Theorem 3 in earlier notes) establish aggregation restores convergence as m→∞ for restricted hypothesis classes F; Propositions 4–5 show failures without aggregation. Notation reminders: risks R, R_φ, R_{φ,A}; conditional risks and infima R^*, R_φ^*, R_{φ,A}^*; excess risks δ_ℓ, δ_φ, δ_{φ,A}. Calibration/identifiability: constants C_{φ,1}, C_{φ,2}, ψ_A (Fenchel biconjugate of overlineψ_A). Low-noise assumptions: Mammen–Tsybakov (N_α),(M_β) with β = α/(1−α) (α≠1). Experiments: corrupted logistic link, T=100 trials, 95% error bars.

Paper: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” (Chen Cheng, John Duchi). Thesis: aggregating noisy labels (label cleaning) can yield consistency and robustness not available using single noisy labels. Settings: ranking, binary/multiclass classification, finite-dimensional linear predictors. Key formal claims (from earlier parts): Propositions 1–2 show convex ranking surrogates fail without aggregation when k≥3 but can be consistent after aggregation (Prop.2 uses squared-loss φ(s,q)=||s−q||_2^2). Theorem 1 gives approximate linear comparison inequalities for aggregated-label losses (slope C_{φ,1}/16 above threshold). Corollary 4.1 and Theorems 2–3 show aggregation restores convergence as m→∞ for restricted hypothesis classes F; Propositions 4–5 exhibit failures without aggregation. Notation/definitions introduced in this part: data (X,Y) i.i.d. from P; scorer f:X→R^d, decoder d:R^d→Y; task loss ℓ:Y×Y→R_+ and task risk R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),Y)] (eq.1). Alternative conditional formulation R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),P(·|X))] (eq.2). Surrogate φ:R^d×Y→R and surrogate risk R_φ(f)=E[φ(f(X),Y)]. Aggregation: response Z∈Z, aggregator A:Z→A, aggregated surrogate φ:R^d×A→R_+, aggregated risk R_{φ,A}(f)=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))] (eq.3). Examples: majority vote A_m(Z)=argmin_{y∈Y}∑_{l=1}^m ℓ(y,Y_l); KNN aggregation uses extra sample (X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m with Z=(Y,(X_i,Y_i)), order by distance and define A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_{y}∑_{l=0}^K ℓ(y,Y_{(l)}) (X_{(0)}=X, so Y_{(0)}=Y). Two consistency settings studied: (i) Fisher consistency (all measurable functions), (ii) statistical/parametric restricted models. Calibration constants referenced earlier: C_{φ,1}, C_{φ,2}, ψ_A. Experiments use corrupted logistic link, T=100 trials.

errors.evidence: The text immediately before this definition states: "Assume multiple independent pairwise comparisons Z=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_m) conditional on X." and then defines m_{ij} as above, followed by using m_{ij} in A(Z).

To define observed counts m_{ij} consistent with the preceding sentence and the subsequent use in A(Z), it should sum over the m observed labels (e.g. m_{ij}=\sum_{l=1}^m 1\{Y_l=(i,j)\}). steps.notes_before: Section summarizes Fisher consistency and comparison inequalities via calibration functions: define conditional risks R(s|x), R_phi(s|x); pointwise excesses delta_l(s,x)=R(s|x)-inf_s'R(s'|x), delta_phi(s,x) similarly. Calibration psi(ε,x)=inf_{s}{delta_phi(s,x) | delta_l(s,x)≥ε}, overline{psi}(ε)=inf_x psi(ε,x). Corollary 3.1: positivity of psi(·,x) for all x,ε>0 characterizes Fisher consistency; Fenchel biconjugate of overline{psi} yields a comparison bound psi(R-R^*) ≤ R_phi-R_phi^*. Ranking example: labels Y={(i,j):i≠j}, p_{ij}=P(Y=(i,j)|x). Define C_x with (C_x)_{ii}=0 and (C_x)_{ij}=p_{ij}/\sum_{l≠j} p_{lj} (use 0/0=1/(k-1)), so C_x^T 1 = 1. Loss ℓ(s,C)=max_{i<j} 1{(s_i-s_j)(C1_i-C1_j)≤0, C1_i-C1_j≠0}; population risk R(f)=P(f(X) and C_X1 order differently) (eq.4). Restrict scores to s^T1=0. Proposition 1: for k≥3, any surrogate φ convex in scores is not Fisher consistent for this ranking risk. Aggregation: collect Z=(Y_1,...,Y_m); define counts m_{ij} (definition in text appears to sum over Y^m and is inconsistent — it should sum over observed labels), m_j=Σ_i m_{ij}, and A(Z)=star if some m_j=0, else vector whose i-th entry is Σ_j m_{ij}/m_j. Proposition 2: squared-loss regression on A(Z) is Fisher consistent when m≥k.

errors.claim: Equation (5) defines the uniform calibration function as "\overline\psi_A(\epsilon)\coloneqq \inf_{s\in\mathbb R^d}\overline\psi_A(\epsilon,x)."
errors.evidence: Earlier (and standard) definition recorded in my notes: "psi(ε,x)=inf_s{delta_phi(s,x) | delta_l(s,x)≥ε}, overline{psi}(ε)=inf_x psi(ε,x)." This same part correctly defines the pointwise calibration as "\overline\psi_A(\epsilon,x)\coloneqq \inf_{s\in\mathbb R^d}\{\delta_{\varphi,A}(s,x)\mid\delta_\ell(s,x)\geq\epsilon\}," so the uniform function should be an infimum over x, not over s.
errors.explanation: The displayed formula in (5) takes an infimum over s again, contradicting the intended/earlier definition that the uniform calibration is the infimum across x of the pointwise calibration; this appears to be a typographical/internal error.

steps.notes_before: Squared-loss surrogate: φ(s,q)=||s-q||_2^2, φ(s,★)=0. Proposition 2: for ranking risk (eq.4) φ is Fisher consistent when m≥k. Aggregation expands response space from Y to R^k; A(Z) is vector-valued in R^k when all m_j>0. Prop 1 (earlier): for k≥3 no convex-in-scores surrogate is Fisher consistent for pairwise ranking risk. Proposition 3: if ∫ b(x)dP(x)<∞ and δ_ℓ(f(x),x) ≤ b(x), then φ is Fisher consistent for task risk iff for all x, ε>0 the pointwise calibration overlineψ_A(ε,x)>0; with ψ_A=(overlineψ_A)^{**} we get ψ_A(R(f)-R^*) ≤ R_{φ,A}(f)-R_{φ,A}^*. Correct calibration defs: overlineψ_A(ε,x):=inf_{s∈R^d}{δ_{φ,A}(s,x) | δ_ℓ(s,x)≥ε}; overlineψ_A(ε):=inf_{x∈X} overlineψ_A(ε,x) (paper's eq.(5) mistakenly used inf over s). Definition 3.1: (C_{φ,1},C_{φ,2})-identifying surrogate with params a_y∈A and s_y∈R^d, d(s_y)=y satisfying (6a),(6b). Example: hinge loss is (1,2)-identifying. Generalized majority vote A_m(y_1..y_m)=a_{ŷ} with ŷ=argmin_y Σ_i ℓ(y,y_i); for i.i.d. labels w.p.1 there exists random M such that for m≥M empirical argmin ⊂ population argmin y^*(x). Corollary 3.2: vanishing aggregated surrogate regret implies vanishing task regret as m→∞.

Corollary 3.2: If m(n)→∞ and φ is identifying (Def.3.1) then R_{φ,A_m}(f_n)-R_{φ,A_m}^*→0 ⇒ R(f_n)-R^*→0. Example: hinge is (C_{φ,1},C_{φ,2})=(1,2)-identifying. Majority vote A_m eventually selects only optimal labels (empirical argmin ⊂ population argmin) for m≥M (random finite M).

Level-(ξ,ζ) consistency (Def.3.2): there exists ψ with ψ(ε)≥ζε for ε≥ξ and ψ(R(f)-R^*) ≤ R_{φ,A}(f)-R_{φ,A}^*.

Noise/margin quantities:
- Δ(x)=min_{d(s)∉y^*(x)} δ_ℓ(s,x) (binary: Δ(x)=|2P(Y=1|X=x)-1|).
- Conditions: (N_α) P(d◦f ≠ d◦f^*) ≤ C_{MT}(R(f)-R^*)^α, α∈[0,1]; (M_β) P(Δ(X) ≤ ε) ≤ (C_{MT}ε)^β. They are equivalent under β=α/(1-α).
- Condition-number κ(x)=max_{d(s)≠y^*}δ / min_{d(s)≠y^*}δ (binary κ=1 if P(Δ(X)>0)=1).

Aggregation error func: e_m(t)= t sqrt{(2/m) log(4k(C_{φ,1}+C_{φ,2})/C_{φ,1})}.

Theorem 1: If φ is (C_{φ,1},C_{φ,2})-identifying, A_m aggregator (7), 0≤ℓ≤1 and (N_α) holds, then for any M>0 and any f with
R(f)-R^* ≥ 2P(κ(X)>M) + (4C_{MT} e_m(M))^{1/(1-α)},
we have
R(f)-R^* ≤ (16/C_{φ,1}) (R_{φ,A_m}(f)-R_{φ,A_m}^*).
Thus level-(ξ,ζ) with ξ as the LHS threshold and ζ=C_{φ,1}/16. Let ξ_m = inf_M{…}; ξ_m→0 as m→∞, so taking α=0 yields Corollary 3.2.

Optimizing using κ≤1/Δ gives explicit ξ_{m,k}: for k=2,
ξ_{m,2}=((32 C_{MT}^2/m) log(8(C_{φ,1}+C_{φ,2})/C_{φ,1}))^{1/(2(1-α))},
and a stated expression for k≥3. Corollary 3.3: same linear comparison holds whenever R(f)-R^*≥ξ_{m,k}.

Theorem 1 (recap): if φ is (C_{φ,1},C_{φ,2})-identifying, A_m aggregator (7), 0≤ℓ≤1 and (N_α) holds, then for any M>0 and f with
R(f)-R^* ≥ 2P(κ(X)>M) + (4 C_{MT} e_m(M))^{1/(1-α)}
we have R(f)-R^* ≤ (16/C_{φ,1})(R_{φ,A_m}(f)-R_{φ,A_m}^*). Here e_m(t)= t sqrt{(2/m) log(4k(C_{φ,1}+C_{φ,2})/C_{φ,1})}.
Noise conditions: (N_α) and (M_β) equivalent with β=α/(1-α) (α=β=0 allowed). Binary κ=1 if P(Δ(X)>0)=1.
As α→1 aggregation requirement falls; in the limit α=1 the paper claims that if
m ≥ 32 max{C_{MT}^2,C_{MT}^4} log(4k(C_{φ,1}+C_{φ,2})/C_{φ,1}) = O(log k)
then ξ_{m,k}=0 (uniform linear comparison with factor 16/C_{φ,1}).
Section 3.3 examples:
- Binary nonsmooth surrogate: φ(f,y)=φ(yf). If ∂φ(0) ⊂ (-∞,0) and lim_{t→∞}φ(t)=0, then for any δ>0 Lemma 3.1 gives feasibility constants C_{φ,1}=φ(0)-φ(δ)>0, C_{φ,2}=φ(-δ). Corollary 3.3 (k=2) yields threshold
R-R^* ≥ ( (32 C_{MT}^2 / m) log(8(φ(-δ)+φ(0)-φ(δ))/(φ(0)-φ(δ))) )^{1/(2(1-α))}
and linear comparison with factor 16/(φ(0)-φ(δ)).
- Bipartite matching: v embeds matchings; loss ℓ=(1/2N)||v(y1)-v(y2)||_1. Lemma 3.2: C_{φ,1}=1/N, C_{φ,2}=2. Substituting into Corollary 3.3 (k≥3) gives the paper's threshold (displayed) and comparison R-R^* ≤ 16N (R_{φ,A_n}-R^*). Proofs in Appendix B.5.

Section 4: Aggregation can restore consistency when optimization is restricted to a hypothesis class. Key definitions: ε-argmin g = {θ | g(θ) ≤ inf g + ε}. A_m is majority vote on Z=(Y1,..,Ym). Binary setting: Y={±1}, φ-margin surrogate φ(s,y)=φ(sy) with convex scalar φ; Fisher/uniform consistency over all measurables iff φ'(0)<0. Linear predictor class F = {f_θ(x)=⟨θ,x⟩}. Optimal predictability along θ* means sgn(⟨θ*,x⟩)=sgn(P(Y=1|x)-1/2). Proposition 4 (App D.1): For any nonnegative φ and any ε>0 and nonzero θ*, there exists P optimally predictable along θ* such that every surrogate minimizer θ_φ ∈ argmin_θ E[φ(f_θ(X),Y)] has R(f_{θ_φ})>R(f_{θ*}) and |cos∠(θ_φ,θ*)| ≤ ε (i.e., can be nearly orthogonal). Aggregation: choose θ_m ∈ ε_m-argmin_θ R_{φ,A_m}(f_θ)=ε_m-argmin_θ E[φ(A_m(Y1..Ym) f_θ(X))] with ε_m→0. Corollary 4.1 (from Theorem 2): if P optimally predictable along θ* and ε_m→0 as m→∞, then R(f_{θ_m})→R(f_{θ*}) and cos∠(θ_m,θ*)→1. Multiclass (Y=[k]): consider cone F with 1^T f=0 and closed under positive scaling. Surrogate φ: R^k×[k]→R_+ assumed Fisher consistent and satisfying limiting loss condition (13): φ(s,y)→0 if s_y - s_j → +∞ for all j≠y. Examples: multiclass logistic φ(s,y)=log(∑ e^{s_j-s_y}) and pairwise-sum losses ∑_{i≠y} φ(s_y-s_i) with scalar φ convex, nonincreasing, φ'(0)<0, inf φ=0. Zhang [51, Thm.8] shows consistency over F={f:1^T f=0}.

errors.claim: "whose minimizers frequently coincide with the original problem (2), but which allows more sophistication."
errors.evidence:
Earlier in the same paragraph the paper defined the instantaneous-label risk as
"R(f):=E_P[\ell(d\circ f(X),Y)]. (1)"
and then introduced the conditional-distribution version
"R(f):=E_P[\ell(d\circ f(X),P(\cdot\mid X))]. (2)"
The quoted sentence then says the minimizers coincide with "the original problem (2)".
errors.explanation: The sentence refers to (2) as the "original problem" although (2) is the new, conditional-distribution version just introduced; the intended reference is almost certainly to the original instantaneous-label problem (1). This is a self-contradictory cross-reference within the paragraph.

errors.claim: The paper defines the uniform calibration function as "\overline{\psi}_{A}(\epsilon) \coloneqq \inf_{s\in\mathbb{R}^{d}} \overline{\psi}_{A}(\epsilon,x)" (equation (5)).
errors.evidence: Earlier (and standard) definition of the uniform calibration function is an infimum over x: "calibration functions: psi(ε,x)=inf_s{δ_φ(s,x) | δ_ℓ(s,x)≥ε}, overline psi(ε)=inf_x psi(ε,x)." Also the text here refers to "pointwise and uniform" calibration, so the uniform version should be an infimum over x.
errors.explanation: Equation (5) incorrectly repeats an infimum over s for the uniform calibration function, but the uniform calibration must take the infimum over x (the conditioning point). This contradicts the earlier/standard definition and the stated 'pointwise and uniform' distinction.

errors.claim: Clearly \sigma^{\epsilon} satisfies the link consistency condition (14) and is optimally predictable (12).
errors.evidence:
Definition (14) (paraphrased in the paper): "t_y = max_i t_i iff \sigma_y(t) = max_i \sigma_i(t)." 
The paper's perturbation: "\sigma^{\epsilon}(t)=\sigma^{\textup{lr}}(t)1\{t\not\in\mathcal{T}_{\epsilon}\}+\frac{1}{k}\mathbf{1}\cdot 1\{t\in\mathcal{T}_{\epsilon}\}," i.e. \sigma^{\epsilon}(t) is uniform on the set \mathcal{T}_{\epsilon}.
errors.explanation: If t\in\mathcal{T}_{\epsilon}, then \sigma^{\epsilon}(t) is the uniform vector, so every coordinate is a (tied) maximum; the right-hand side of (14) is true for every y, but the left-hand side (t_y is the unique/maximal coordinate of t) need not hold. Thus the equivalence in (14) fails for t\in\mathcal{T}_{\epsilon}, so the claim that \sigma^{\epsilon} satisfies (14) is false.

errors.claim: The paper's claim that σ^{ε} (which equals σ^{lr} off a small-measure set T_ε and is uniform on T_ε) preserves the link-consistency condition (14).
errors.evidence: From my earlier notes: "The paper defines σ^{ε} that equals σ^{lr} off a small-measure set T_ε and is uniform on T_ε... (Note: the paper's claim that σ^{ε} preserves link-consistency (14) is incorrect because uniform outputs on T_ε break the iff equivalence in (14).)". From this part: "Majority vote, however, can address this inconsistency as m→∞ without any assumptions on the true link σ except that it satisfies the consistency condition (14). ... as Proposition 5 highlights, methods without label aggregation are generally inconsistent."
errors.explanation: If σ^{ε} returns a uniform vector on T_ε then ties / altered orderings occur there, so σ^{ε} does not preserve the argmax-equivalence required by (14). The paper appears to have used σ^{ε} as a small perturbation while also (earlier) claiming it preserves (14); that claim is false. Thus the example underlying Proposition 5 either does not satisfy condition (14) (contradicting the paper's earlier assertion) or the paper misstated σ^{ε}'s properties.

final_notes: Theorem 2: risk consistency for linear-cone F when F predicts P and P(Δ(X)>0)=1. Sec.4.3: multiclass linear predictors Θ∈R^{d×(k-1)} (Θ_k=0); link σ:R^{k-1}→R_+^{k-1} must preserve argmax (link-consistency (14)); softmax σ^{lr} is an example. For logistic surrogate (Eq.15) stationarity: E[X(σ^{lr}(Θ_m^T X)-ρ_m(Θ^{*T}X))^T]=0. For k=2 direction robustness holds; for k≥3 small link mis-spec can break risk consistency (Prop.5 constructs σ^ε producing Θ_1(ε) whose direction ≠ Θ* under an invertibility condition). Note: the paper earlier claimed σ^ε preserves (14) but that is incorrect—the uniform outputs on T_ε break argmax-preservation. Theorem 3 (parametric): if Θ*=U* T* (U* orthogonal, T* nonsingular) then Θ_m = U* T_m, ||T_m||→∞ and T_m/||T_m||→T*/||T*||, so aggregation recovers Θ* direction asymptotically. Experiments: (1) Truncated-quadratic φ(δ)=(1-δ)_+^2 implies calibration ψ(ε)=ε^2; derived ψ_m(ε)=(1/16)(ε - sqrt{32/m log 40})_+ for δ=1—paper states derivation used α=0 but then says plotted bounds use α=1/2 (inconsistent). (2) Mis-specified logistic link ṡ(t)=σ^{lr}(t) for ||t||≤r and σ^{lr}(αt) for ||t||>r (r=3, α=0.1); true Θ*: θ1^*=(0,1), θ2^*=(1,1); experiments (n large or n=640000/m) show normalized T_m→normalized T*, consistent with Theorem 3. Discussion/future work (this part): calls for finite-m results (explicit consistency guarantees beyond asymptotic m→∞, e.g., ranking Sec.3.1), study of fundamental limits of noise condition number κ(X) (eq.(9))—binary case trivially κ(X)=1; behavior in mis-specified models needs relaxing optimal predictability (12) (Bayes-optimal in F); extend restricted-class (H-)consistency results to aggregation (cite Mao et al. and others).

Title: Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning. Authors: Chen Cheng, John Duchi. Abstract claims: learning procedures that rely on aggregated labels (label information distilled from noisy responses) enjoy robustness properties not possible without data cleaning. Key points: (1) In the context of risk consistency (minimizing surrogate, typically convex, losses instead of target task loss like 0-1), procedures using label aggregation obtain stronger consistency guarantees than those possible using raw labels. (2) Classical perfectly-specified model scenarios suggest modeling label uncertainty is statistically efficient, but consistency for “standard” approaches fails as soon as the loss is even slightly mis-specified. (3) Procedures leveraging aggregated information still converge to optimal classifiers despite such mis-specification. Overall claim: incorporating a fuller view of the data collection-to-prediction pipeline (via label aggregation/cleaning) yields a more robust methodology by refining noisy signals.

Title: Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning. Authors: Chen Cheng, John Duchi. Paper studies how label aggregation/cleaning in data pipelines (e.g., crowdsourcing multiple noisy labels then denoising) fundamentally improves consistency and robustness of learned models. Two main robustness aspects: (1) For surrogate risk consistency (minimizing convex surrogate losses vs. target loss like 0-1), procedures using aggregated labels can achieve consistency and optimal prediction in limits where methods using raw (X,Y) pairs cannot. (2) Even in finite-dimensional parametric/statistical settings, aggregation can yield consistent classifiers when standard approaches fail. The paper situates itself with prior surrogate-consistency theory (Bartlett et al. and follow-up work) and asks whether aggregation is necessary/useful, and in what sense. Promised contributions/examples: ranking, binary and multiclass classification with linear estimators where (X,Y)-based estimators fail but aggregation yields consistency; nonparametric results where number of samples aggregated and noise conditions determine improved consistency; demonstration that aggregation enables surrogate risk consistency under weak conditions via (approximate) linear comparison inequalities; results showing aggregation can guarantee consistency even over restricted hypothesis classes where unaggregated approaches fail.

steps.notes_before: Preliminaries: X input space, Y output space, data (X_i,Y_i) iid from P. Scoring f:X->R^d, decoder d:R^d->Y, task risk R(f)=E_P[ℓ(d∘f(X),Y)] (instantaneous-label form, eq. (1)). Also consider a refined task loss depending on conditional label distribution: R(f)=E_P[ℓ(d∘f(X), P(·|X))] (eq. (2)). Two study scenarios: (i) Fisher consistency (F all Borel functions); (ii) statistical/parametric hypothesis classes (possibly mis-specified). Surrogate φ introduced to optimize: originally φ:R^d×Y->R, surrogate risk R_φ(f)=E_P[φ(f(X),Y)]. Label aggregation: observed Z (e.g., multiple labels or extra draws), aggregation map A:Z->A, aggregated surrogate φ:R^d×A->R_+, aggregated risk R_{φ,A}(f)=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))]. Example 1 (majority vote): Z=(Y_1,...,Y_m), A(Z)=argmin_y ∑_{l=1}^m ℓ(y,Y_l); for 0-1 loss this is majority vote. Example 2 (K-NN aggregation): Z=(Y,(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m); order X_i by distance to X, set X_(0)=X (so Y_(0)=Y), define A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y ∑_{l=0}^K ℓ(y,Y_(l)). Main claimed message: label aggregation improves consistency/robustness in both scenarios.

Surrogate-consistency setup: conditional task risk R(s|x)=ℓ(d∘s,P(Y|X=x)), conditional surrogate risk R_φ(s|x)=E[φ(s,Y)|X=x]. Pointwise excesses δ_ℓ(s,x)=R(s|x)-inf_s'R(s'|x), δ_φ(s,x)=R_φ(s|x)-inf_s'R_φ(s'|x). Global minima R* and R_φ*. Two consistency notions: (i) Fisher consistency: for any sequence f_n, R_φ(f_n)→R_φ* implies R(f_n)→R*; (ii) uniform comparison: exists nondecreasing ψ with ψ(ε)>0 for ε>0 s.t. ψ(R(f)-R*) ≤ R_φ(f)-R_φ* for all f. Calibration functions: ψ(ε,x)=inf_{s}{δ_φ(s,x) | δ_ℓ(s,x)≥ε}, overline ψ(ε)=inf_x ψ(ε,x). Corollary 3.1: φ is Fisher consistent iff ψ(ε,x)>0 for all x,ε>0; taking Fenchel biconjugate of overline ψ gives a ψ s.t. ψ(R(f)-R*) ≤ R_φ(f)-R_φ*. Ranking example (Sec 3.1): Y={(i,j): i≠j, i beats j}, p_{ij}=P(Y=(i,j)|x). Define C_x with (C_x)_{ii}=0 and (C_x)_{ij}=p_{ij}/∑_{l≠j}p_{lj} (set 0/0=1/(k-1)), so C_x is column-stochastic (C_x^T1=1). Rank by vector C_x1; loss ℓ(s,C)=max_{i<j}1{(s_i-s_j)((C1)_i-(C1)_j) ≤0, (C1)_i≠(C1)_j}. Population risk R(f)=P(f(X) and C_X1 order differently). Proposition 1: for k≥3, any convex-in-first-arg φ:R^k×Y→R is not Fisher consistent. Aggregation fix: collect m independent comparisons Z=(Y_1,..,Y_m); counts m_{ij}, m_j=∑_i m_{ij}; define A(Z)=⋆ if any m_j=0, else A_i=∑_{j} m_{ij}/m_j. Claim: regressing on A(Z) yields consistency when m≥k (Prop 2; proofs in App A.1/A.2).

final_notes: Main theoretical results: Thm1—excess target risk R(f)-R* ≤ (16 / C_{φ,1}) · (surrogate regret). Aggregation can recover Bayes direction for restricted/cone classes (Thm2: cone + P(Δ(X)>0)=1 ⇒ R(f_m)→R*). Multiclass logistic: small link corruptions can break unaggregated surrogate consistency, but aggregation (A_m/T4K) recovers direction asymptotically (directions → Θ* while norms grow). Nonparametric experiment D4X: truncated quadratic φ(δ)=max{1−δ,0}^2; unaggregated exact ψ(ε)=ε^2. Derived aggregated-theory ψ_m(ε) = (φ(0)−φ(1))/16 · (ε − sqrt(32/m · log 40))_+ = (1/16)·(ε − sqrt(32/m · log 40))_+. Plotted for m∈{2^16,2^20,2^24,2^28,2^32}; authors report aggregated curves shift from quadratic toward linear as m→∞. Finite-dimensional mis-specified logistic experiment: d=2,k=3, θ1*=(0,1), θ2*=(1,1), θ3 assumed 0; corrupted link ~tildeσ(t)=σ^{lr}(t) for ||t||≤r and σ^{lr}(α t) for ||t||>r with r=3, α=0.1. Two sampling protocols: (i) fixed n=10,000 per m; (ii) n=640,000/m to keep total labels constant. m∈{1,4,16,64,256,1024}, T=100 trials, 95% error bars; Figure2 reports directional classification error. Discussion / open problems: many consistency results use m→∞—finite-m guarantees remain unsatisfying; ranking admits explicit finite-m guarantees; a joint theory depending on (ℓ,φ,m) is open (possible need for higher-order comparisons, powers C_x^p). Beyond binary, κ(X) can be large even with low noise (binary trivially κ(X)=1); minimal surrogate assumptions can cause this. Mis-specified-model results assume existence of Bayes-optimal classifier in F (K7M); classical surrogate consistency can fail even then while aggregation succeeds. Extensions: restricted-class (H-)consistency, unifying parametric and nonparametric aggregation effects.

Paper title: "Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning" by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: aggregating/cleaning labels (information distilled from noisy responses) yields robustness not available without cleaning. Specifically: (1) minimizing a typically convex surrogate loss on aggregated labels gives stronger task-risk consistency guarantees than procedures using raw labels; (2) finite-dimensional classifiers remain consistent under loss mis-specification that breaks standard uncertainty-modeling approaches; (3) in perfectly specified statistical models, using all information is more efficient, but slight loss mis-specification can destroy standard consistency; (4) aggregation preserves convergence to optimal classifiers despite noise; (5) the whole pipeline (collection, fitting, prediction) admits robustness via noisy-signal refinement. Keep these claims in mind for checking consistency with later sections (definitions, assumptions, theorems, empirical results) about surrogate losses, aggregation methods, consistency under mis-specification, and comparisons to raw-label procedures.

Introduction adds: aggregation permits consistent optimal prediction under surrogate (but unaggregated estimation cannot), including finite-dimensional problems; linear-estimator constructions in ranking and binary/multiclass classification separate procedures restricted to (X,Y) from aggregation procedures; nonparametric results combine aggregation count and noise conditions, allow approximately linear comparison inequalities under weak surrogate conditions, and extend consistency beyond unrestricted measurable hypothesis classes. Notes that typical supervised pipeline omits cleaning; the paper's concern is that cleaning fundamentally and necessarily improves fitted-model consistency. Context: prior surrogate-risk consistency theory (Bartlett et al. etc.) and many extensions; pair-based empirical-process analyses do not address aggregation machinery. Central research questions: is aggregation needed, does pair-based surrogate consistency suffice, and in what sense does aggregation improve consistency.

From Preliminaries (this part): two regimes — unrestricted Borel F (classical/Fisher consistency) and parametric (possibly misspecified) F where aggregation may improve consistency. Definitions:
- Distribution-dependent task risk: R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X), P(·|X))] (eqn (2)). Special case zero-one: ℓ(ŷ,P)=∑_y P(Y=y)1{ŷ≠y}.

- Surrogate risk: R_φ(f)=E[φ(f(X),Y)].
- Aggregated surrogate risk: R_{φ,A}(f)=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))] (eqn (3)), where Z is response-replacement and A:Z→A is aggregation.
- Repeated labeling: Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m), A_m(Z)=argmin_y ∑_{l=1}^m ℓ(y,Y_l) (majority vote for 0-1 loss).
- K-NN aggregation: Z=(Y,(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m), order X_{(l)} by dist to X, and A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y ∑_{l=0}^K ℓ(y,Y_{(l)}).

final_notes: Key formal results and tensions: Proposition 5 (k≥3, Σ=I) constructs σ^ε by overwriting σ^{lr} on a set T_ε of Lebesgue measure ≤ ε; earlier text simultaneously claims σ^ε preserves link-consistency (eq.14) yet the overwrite breaks unaggregated fitting — these two claims appear incompatible unless T_ε lies inside the tie set (contradiction flagged earlier). Theorem 3 (App E.2) (matrix-parametric setting) says minimizers Θ_m = U^* T_m with U^* fixed; as m→∞, ||T_m||→∞ and T_m/||T_m||→ T^*/||T^*|| (so majority voting restores normalized direction, not bounded parameter recovery). Experiments (Section 5) show two issues: (A) Truncated-quadratic surrogate: paper derives ψ_m(ε) = (1/16)(ε - sqrt(32/m · log40))_+ under stated "no low-noise" (α=0), C_MT=1, δ=1, but text/plot commentary also says plotted bounds use α=1/2 (inconsistent). The reported numeric curves for large m∈{2^16,…,2^32} supposedly show aggregated curve moving from quadratic toward linear. (B) Mis-specified logistic experiment: design specified (d=2,k=3,r=3,α=0.1,θ1*=(0,1),θ2*=(1,1)), two sample-size regimes (n fixed=10k and nm const with n=640k/m), m∈{1,4,...,1024}, T=100 trials; figure caption/error plot formula is mistyped/ambiguous. Discussion (current part) restates limitations: many guarantees asymptotic (Corollary 4.1, Theorems 2–3 require m→∞), some finite-m results exist (Prop.2 gives m≥k for ranking; Section 3.2.3 claims uniform linear comparison at α=1 under an O(log k) bound), condition-number κ(X) can be large beyond binary, mis-specified-model results require optimal predictability (12), and contrasts: Prop.4 vs Cor.4.1/Theorem2 and Prop.5 vs Theorem3. Remaining unresolved: finite-m theory, sharper loss-dependent measures, behavior beyond optimal-predictability, and restricted-class H-consistency extensions.

Paper studies whether aggregating noisy labels improves consistency of learned predictors. Focus: surrogate losses (used during fitting), analyzed over all measurable predictors and over restricted model classes. Develops calibration inequalities for aggregated labels; analyzes ranking, classification, structured prediction. Key claims to remember: for ranking with k ≥ 3 items, no convex surrogate based on individual comparisons is Fisher consistent; an aggregated squared-loss procedure is consistent when m ≥ k. More generally, "identifying" surrogates become asymptotically consistent as number m of aggregated labels grows; many guarantees require m → ∞. Under certain noise conditions, aggregation yields approximately linear comparison inequalities. In restricted model classes, aggregation can restore consistency when ordinary surrogate minimization fails (including link mis-specification). Two numerical illustrations are reported. Glossary follows (definitions and reused symbols listed).

Fisher consistency = surrogate-risk→infimum implies task-risk→infimum; uniform comparison inequalities yield explicit ψ. Ranking setup: p_{ij}=P(i preferred j), C_x normalized transition matrix from p_{ij}, ranking target uses C_x 1. Squared-loss ranking φ(s,q)=||s−q||_2^2 referenced (Prop.2). Identifying surrogates Def.3.1 uses constants C_{φ,1}, C_{φ,2}. Low-noise assumptions: Mammen–Tsybakov (N_α),(M_β) with β = α/(1−α). Error function e_m(t) for majority vote. Parametric section: linear predictors f_θ=<θ,x>, multiclass logistic σ (σ^{lr}), population logistic losses L_m, Θ^*, Θ_m. Numerics: ψ_m, corrupted logistic link ~σ, T=100 trials, 95% error bars. Note: paper reuses α elsewhere; β formula requires α≠1.

Paper: "Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning" (Chen Cheng, John Duchi). Main thesis: aggregating noisy labels (label cleaning) can yield consistency and robustness not available using raw single labels. Key settings/examples: ranking, binary and multiclass classification, and finite-dimensional linear predictors. Aggregators: majority vote A_m, generalized majority vote (eq.7), KNN aggregator A_{m,K}. Main formal claims: Propositions 1–2 show convex ranking surrogates fail without aggregation when k≥3 but become consistent after aggregation when m≥k (Prop.2 uses squared-loss φ(s,q)=||s−q||_2^2). Theorem 1: under weak surrogate assumptions, aggregated-label losses admit approximate linear comparison inequalities (linear bounds relating excess task risk to excess surrogate risk); stated slope = C_{φ,1}/16 above its risk threshold. Corollary 4.1 and Theorem 2 (and Theorem 3 in earlier notes) establish aggregation restores convergence as m→∞ for restricted hypothesis classes F; Propositions 4–5 show failures without aggregation. Notation reminders: risks R, R_φ, R_{φ,A}; conditional risks and infima R^*, R_φ^*, R_{φ,A}^*; excess risks δ_ℓ, δ_φ, δ_{φ,A}. Calibration/identifiability: constants C_{φ,1}, C_{φ,2}, ψ_A (Fenchel biconjugate of overlineψ_A). Low-noise assumptions: Mammen–Tsybakov (N_α),(M_β) with β = α/(1−α) (α≠1). Experiments: corrupted logistic link, T=100 trials, 95% error bars.

Paper: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” (Chen Cheng, John Duchi). Thesis: aggregating noisy labels (label cleaning) can yield consistency and robustness not available using single noisy labels. Settings: ranking, binary/multiclass classification, finite-dimensional linear predictors. Key formal claims (from earlier parts): Propositions 1–2 show convex ranking surrogates fail without aggregation when k≥3 but can be consistent after aggregation (Prop.2 uses squared-loss φ(s,q)=||s−q||_2^2). Theorem 1 gives approximate linear comparison inequalities for aggregated-label losses (slope C_{φ,1}/16 above threshold). Corollary 4.1 and Theorems 2–3 show aggregation restores convergence as m→∞ for restricted hypothesis classes F; Propositions 4–5 exhibit failures without aggregation. Notation/definitions introduced in this part: data (X,Y) i.i.d. from P; scorer f:X→R^d, decoder d:R^d→Y; task loss ℓ:Y×Y→R_+ and task risk R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),Y)] (eq.1). Alternative conditional formulation R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),P(·|X))] (eq.2). Surrogate φ:R^d×Y→R and surrogate risk R_φ(f)=E[φ(f(X),Y)]. Aggregation: response Z∈Z, aggregator A:Z→A, aggregated surrogate φ:R^d×A→R_+, aggregated risk R_{φ,A}(f)=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))] (eq.3). Examples: majority vote A_m(Z)=argmin_{y∈Y}∑_{l=1}^m ℓ(y,Y_l); KNN aggregation uses extra sample (X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m with Z=(Y,(X_i,Y_i)), order by distance and define A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_{y}∑_{l=0}^K ℓ(y,Y_{(l)}) (X_{(0)}=X, so Y_{(0)}=Y). Two consistency settings studied: (i) Fisher consistency (all measurable functions), (ii) statistical/parametric restricted models. Calibration constants referenced earlier: C_{φ,1}, C_{φ,2}, ψ_A. Experiments use corrupted logistic link, T=100 trials.

steps.notes_before: Section summarizes Fisher consistency and comparison inequalities via calibration functions: define conditional risks R(s|x), R_phi(s|x); pointwise excesses delta_l(s,x)=R(s|x)-inf_s'R(s'|x), delta_phi(s,x) similarly. Calibration psi(ε,x)=inf_{s}{delta_phi(s,x) | delta_l(s,x)≥ε}, overline{psi}(ε)=inf_x psi(ε,x). Corollary 3.1: positivity of psi(·,x) for all x,ε>0 characterizes Fisher consistency; Fenchel biconjugate of overline{psi} yields a comparison bound psi(R-R^*) ≤ R_phi-R_phi^*. Ranking example: labels Y={(i,j):i≠j}, p_{ij}=P(Y=(i,j)|x). Define C_x with (C_x)_{ii}=0 and (C_x)_{ij}=p_{ij}/\sum_{l≠j} p_{lj} (use 0/0=1/(k-1)), so C_x^T 1 = 1. Loss ℓ(s,C)=max_{i<j} 1{(s_i-s_j)(C1_i-C1_j)≤0, C1_i-C1_j≠0}; population risk R(f)=P(f(X) and C_X1 order differently) (eq.4). Restrict scores to s^T1=0. Proposition 1: for k≥3, any surrogate φ convex in scores is not Fisher consistent for this ranking risk. Aggregation: collect Z=(Y_1,...,Y_m); define counts m_{ij} (definition in text appears to sum over Y^m and is inconsistent — it should sum over observed labels), m_j=Σ_i m_{ij}, and A(Z)=star if some m_j=0, else vector whose i-th entry is Σ_j m_{ij}/m_j. Proposition 2: squared-loss regression on A(Z) is Fisher consistent when m≥k.

steps.notes_before: Squared-loss surrogate: φ(s,q)=||s-q||_2^2, φ(s,★)=0. Proposition 2: for ranking risk (eq.4) φ is Fisher consistent when m≥k. Aggregation expands response space from Y to R^k; A(Z) is vector-valued in R^k when all m_j>0. Prop 1 (earlier): for k≥3 no convex-in-scores surrogate is Fisher consistent for pairwise ranking risk. Proposition 3: if ∫ b(x)dP(x)<∞ and δ_ℓ(f(x),x) ≤ b(x), then φ is Fisher consistent for task risk iff for all x, ε>0 the pointwise calibration overlineψ_A(ε,x)>0; with ψ_A=(overlineψ_A)^{**} we get ψ_A(R(f)-R^*) ≤ R_{φ,A}(f)-R_{φ,A}^*. Definition 3.1: (C_{φ,1},C_{φ,2})-identifying surrogate with params a_y∈A and s_y∈R^d, d(s_y)=y satisfying (6a),(6b). Example: hinge loss is (1,2)-identifying. Generalized majority vote A_m(y_1..y_m)=a_{ŷ} with ŷ=argmin_y Σ_i ℓ(y,y_i); for i.i.d. labels w.p.1 there exists random M such that for m≥M empirical argmin ⊂ population argmin y^*(x). Corollary 3.2: vanishing aggregated surrogate regret implies vanishing task regret as m→∞.

Corollary 3.2: If m(n)→∞ and φ is identifying (Def.3.1) then R_{φ,A_m}(f_n)-R_{φ,A_m}^*→0 ⇒ R(f_n)-R^*→0. Example: hinge is (C_{φ,1},C_{φ,2})=(1,2)-identifying. Majority vote A_m eventually selects only optimal labels (empirical argmin ⊂ population argmin) for m≥M (random finite M).

Level-(ξ,ζ) consistency (Def.3.2): there exists ψ with ψ(ε)≥ζε for ε≥ξ and ψ(R(f)-R^*) ≤ R_{φ,A}(f)-R_{φ,A}^*.

Noise/margin quantities:
- Δ(x)=min_{d(s)∉y^*(x)} δ_ℓ(s,x) (binary: Δ(x)=|2P(Y=1|X=x)-1|).
- Conditions: (N_α) P(d◦f ≠ d◦f^*) ≤ C_{MT}(R(f)-R^*)^α, α∈[0,1]; (M_β) P(Δ(X) ≤ ε) ≤ (C_{MT}ε)^β. They are equivalent under β=α/(1-α).
- Condition-number κ(x)=max_{d(s)≠y^*}δ / min_{d(s)≠y^*}δ (binary κ=1 if P(Δ(X)>0)=1).

Aggregation error func: e_m(t)= t sqrt{(2/m) log(4k(C_{φ,1}+C_{φ,2})/C_{φ,1})}.

Theorem 1: If φ is (C_{φ,1},C_{φ,2})-identifying, A_m aggregator (7), 0≤ℓ≤1 and (N_α) holds, then for any M>0 and any f with
R(f)-R^* ≥ 2P(κ(X)>M) + (4C_{MT} e_m(M))^{1/(1-α)},
we have
R(f)-R^* ≤ (16/C_{φ,1}) (R_{φ,A_m}(f)-R_{φ,A_m}^*).
Thus level-(ξ,ζ) with ξ as the LHS threshold and ζ=C_{φ,1}/16. Let ξ_m = inf_M{…}; ξ_m→0 as m→∞, so taking α=0 yields Corollary 3.2.

Optimizing using κ≤1/Δ gives explicit ξ_{m,k}: for k=2,
ξ_{m,2}=((32 C_{MT}^2/m) log(8(C_{φ,1}+C_{φ,2})/C_{φ,1}))^{1/(2(1-α))},
and a stated expression for k≥3. Corollary 3.3: same linear comparison holds whenever R(f)-R^*≥ξ_{m,k}.

Theorem 1 (recap): if φ is (C_{φ,1},C_{φ,2})-identifying, A_m aggregator (7), 0≤ℓ≤1 and (N_α) holds, then for any M>0 and f with
R(f)-R^* ≥ 2P(κ(X)>M) + (4 C_{MT} e_m(M))^{1/(1-α)}
we have R(f)-R^* ≤ (16/C_{φ,1})(R_{φ,A_m}(f)-R_{φ,A_m}^*). Here e_m(t)= t sqrt{(2/m) log(4k(C_{φ,1}+C_{φ,2})/C_{φ,1})}.
Noise conditions: (N_α) and (M_β) equivalent with β=α/(1-α) (α=β=0 allowed). Binary κ=1 if P(Δ(X)>0)=1.
As α→1 aggregation requirement falls; in the limit α=1 the paper claims that if
m ≥ 32 max{C_{MT}^2,C_{MT}^4} log(4k(C_{φ,1}+C_{φ,2})/C_{φ,1}) = O(log k)
then ξ_{m,k}=0 (uniform linear comparison with factor 16/C_{φ,1}).
Section 3.3 examples:
- Binary nonsmooth surrogate: φ(f,y)=φ(yf). If ∂φ(0) ⊂ (-∞,0) and lim_{t→∞}φ(t)=0, then for any δ>0 Lemma 3.1 gives feasibility constants C_{φ,1}=φ(0)-φ(δ)>0, C_{φ,2}=φ(-δ). Corollary 3.3 (k=2) yields threshold
R-R^* ≥ ( (32 C_{MT}^2 / m) log(8(φ(-δ)+φ(0)-φ(δ))/(φ(0)-φ(δ))) )^{1/(2(1-α))}
and linear comparison with factor 16/(φ(0)-φ(δ)).

Section 4: Aggregation can restore consistency when optimization is restricted to a hypothesis class. Key definitions: ε-argmin g = {θ | g(θ) ≤ inf g + ε}. A_m is majority vote on Z=(Y1,..,Ym). Binary setting: Y={±1}, φ-margin surrogate φ(s,y)=φ(sy) with convex scalar φ; Fisher/uniform consistency over all measurables iff φ'(0)<0. Linear predictor class F = {f_θ(x)=⟨θ,x⟩}. Optimal predictability along θ* means sgn(⟨θ*,x⟩)=sgn(P(Y=1|x)-1/2). Proposition 4 (App D.1): For any nonnegative φ and any ε>0 and nonzero θ*, there exists P optimally predictable along θ* such that every surrogate minimizer θ_φ ∈ argmin_θ E[φ(f_θ(X),Y)] has R(f_{θ_φ})>R(f_{θ*}) and |cos∠(θ_φ,θ*)| ≤ ε (i.e., can be nearly orthogonal). Aggregation: choose θ_m ∈ ε_m-argmin_θ R_{φ,A_m}(f_θ)=ε_m-argmin_θ E[φ(A_m(Y1..Ym) f_θ(X))] with ε_m→0. Corollary 4.1 (from Theorem 2): if P optimally predictable along θ* and ε_m→0 as m→∞, then R(f_{θ_m})→R(f_{θ*}) and cos∠(θ_m,θ*)→1. Multiclass (Y=[k]): consider cone F with 1^T f=0 and closed under positive scaling. Surrogate φ: R^k×[k]→R_+ assumed Fisher consistent and satisfying limiting loss condition (13): φ(s,y)→0 if s_y - s_j → +∞ for all j≠y. Examples: multiclass logistic φ(s,y)=log(∑ e^{s_j-s_y}) and pairwise-sum losses ∑_{i≠y} φ(s_y-s_i) with scalar φ convex, nonincreasing, φ'(0)<0, inf φ=0. Zhang [51, Thm.8] shows consistency over F={f:1^T f=0}.

errors.explanation: The displayed formula sets \(\sigma^\epsilon(t)=\sigma^{\textup{lr}}(t)\) when \(t\notin\mathcal T_\epsilon\) and uniform when \(t\in\mathcal T_\epsilon\), which is the opposite of the prose sentence.

errors.claim: "Clearly \(\sigma^\epsilon\) satisfies (14)"
errors.evidence: (14): "\(t_y=\max_{1\le i\le k}t_i\quad\text{if and only if}\quad\sigma_y(t)=\max_{1\le i\le k}\sigma_i(t).\)" and the definition "\(\sigma^\epsilon(t)=\sigma^{\textup{lr}}(t)1\{t\notin\mathcal T_\epsilon\}+\frac1k\mathbf1\cdot1\{t\in\mathcal T_\epsilon\}.\)"
errors.explanation: For \(t\in\mathcal T_\epsilon\) the formula gives a uniform distribution so \(\sigma^\epsilon_y(t)=\max_i\sigma^\epsilon_i(t)\) holds for every y, which by (14) would force \(t_y=\max_i t_i\) for every y (i.e. all components equal). Since \(\mathcal T_\epsilon\) is stated to have positive Lebesgue measure, (14) cannot hold on \(\mathcal T_\epsilon\) in general, so the claim that \(\sigma^\epsilon\) "clearly" satisfies (14) contradicts the displayed construction.

steps.notes_before: Theorem 2: For cone F that optimally predicts P, if P(Δ(X)>0)=1 and ε_m→0, then any f_m∈ε_m-argmin_{f∈F} E[φ(f(X),A_m(Y_1..Y_m))] satisfies R(f_m)→R*. errors.explanation: Replacing σ^{lr} by the uniform vector (1/k) on any set T_ε with positive measure makes all class outputs equal there, which violates link-consistency (14) (argmax equivalence) unless those t were already tie points. If T_ε is required to be a subset of the tie set to preserve (14), that tie set must have positive measure to matter — but then modification is vacuous (it doesn't change σ) and so cannot produce the claimed change in Θ_1. Thus the paper's construction/claim that σ^ε both preserves (14) and, when changed on an arbitrarily small-measure set T_ε, produces a different fitted normalized parameter is internally inconsistent.

Title: Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning. Authors: Chen Cheng, John Duchi. Abstract claims: learning procedures that rely on aggregated labels (label information distilled from noisy responses) enjoy robustness properties not possible without data cleaning. Key points: (1) In the context of risk consistency (minimizing surrogate, typically convex, losses instead of target task loss like 0-1), procedures using label aggregation obtain stronger consistency guarantees than those possible using raw labels. (2) Classical perfectly-specified model scenarios suggest modeling label uncertainty is statistically efficient, but consistency for “standard” approaches fails as soon as the loss is even slightly mis-specified. (3) Procedures leveraging aggregated information still converge to optimal classifiers despite such mis-specification. Overall claim: incorporating a fuller view of the data collection-to-prediction pipeline (via label aggregation/cleaning) yields a more robust methodology by refining noisy signals.

Title: Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning. Authors: Chen Cheng, John Duchi. Paper studies how label aggregation/cleaning in data pipelines (e.g., crowdsourcing multiple noisy labels then denoising) fundamentally improves consistency and robustness of learned models. Two main robustness aspects: (1) For surrogate risk consistency (minimizing convex surrogate losses vs. target loss like 0-1), procedures using aggregated labels can achieve consistency and optimal prediction in limits where methods using raw (X,Y) pairs cannot. (2) Even in finite-dimensional parametric/statistical settings, aggregation can yield consistent classifiers when standard approaches fail. The paper situates itself with prior surrogate-consistency theory (Bartlett et al. and follow-up work) and asks whether aggregation is necessary/useful, and in what sense. Promised contributions/examples: ranking, binary and multiclass classification with linear estimators where (X,Y)-based estimators fail but aggregation yields consistency; nonparametric results where number of samples aggregated and noise conditions determine improved consistency; demonstration that aggregation enables surrogate risk consistency under weak conditions via (approximate) linear comparison inequalities; results showing aggregation can guarantee consistency even over restricted hypothesis classes where unaggregated approaches fail.

Paper title: "Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning" by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: aggregating/cleaning labels (information distilled from noisy responses) yields robustness not available without cleaning. Specifically: (1) minimizing a typically convex surrogate loss on aggregated labels gives stronger task-risk consistency guarantees than procedures using raw labels; (2) finite-dimensional classifiers remain consistent under loss mis-specification that breaks standard uncertainty-modeling approaches; (3) in perfectly specified statistical models, using all information is more efficient, but slight loss mis-specification can destroy standard consistency; (4) aggregation preserves convergence to optimal classifiers despite noise; (5) the whole pipeline (collection, fitting, prediction) admits robustness via noisy-signal refinement. Keep these claims in mind for checking consistency with later sections (definitions, assumptions, theorems, empirical results) about surrogate losses, aggregation methods, consistency under mis-specification, and comparisons to raw-label procedures.

Paper: "Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning" (Chen Cheng, John Duchi). Abstract-level claims to check later: aggregation/cleaning of noisy labels yields robustness not available without cleaning, specifically (1) minimizing a convex surrogate on aggregated labels gives stronger task-risk consistency than using raw labels; (2) finite-dimensional classifiers remain consistent under loss mis-specification that breaks standard uncertainty-modeling approaches; (3) in well-specified models, using all information is more efficient but slight loss mis-specification can destroy standard consistency; (4) aggregation preserves convergence to optimal classifiers despite noise; (5) end-to-end pipeline (collection, fitting, prediction) shows robustness via noisy-signal refinement. Introduction adds: aggregation permits consistent optimal prediction under surrogate (but unaggregated estimation cannot), including finite-dimensional problems; linear-estimator constructions in ranking and binary/multiclass classification separate procedures restricted to (X,Y) from aggregation procedures; nonparametric results combine aggregation count and noise conditions, allow approximately linear comparison inequalities under weak surrogate conditions, and extend consistency beyond unrestricted measurable hypothesis classes. Notes that typical supervised pipeline omits cleaning; the paper's concern is that cleaning fundamentally and necessarily improves fitted-model consistency. Context: prior surrogate-risk consistency theory (Bartlett et al. etc.) and many extensions; pair-based empirical-process analyses do not address aggregation machinery. Central research questions: is aggregation needed, does pair-based surrogate consistency suffice, and in what sense does aggregation improve consistency.

From Preliminaries (this part): two regimes — unrestricted Borel F (classical/Fisher consistency) and parametric (possibly misspecified) F where aggregation may improve consistency. Definitions:
- Distribution-dependent task risk: R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X), P(·|X))] (eqn (2)). Special case zero-one: ℓ(ŷ,P)=∑_y P(Y=y)1{ŷ≠y}.
- Instantaneous task risk: R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),Y)] with ℓ: Y×Y→R_+ (eqn (1)). Binary case: d=1, d(s)=sgn(s), ℓ(y,y')=1{y y'≤0}.
- Surrogate risk: R_φ(f)=E[φ(f(X),Y)].
- Aggregated surrogate risk: R_{φ,A}(f)=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))] (eqn (3)), where Z is response-replacement and A:Z→A is aggregation.
- Repeated labeling: Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m), A_m(Z)=argmin_y ∑_{l=1}^m ℓ(y,Y_l) (majority vote for 0-1 loss).
- K-NN aggregation: Z=(Y,(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m), order X_{(l)} by dist to X, and A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y ∑_{l=0}^K ℓ(y,Y_{(l)}).

Note: the paper uses ℓ both as distribution-dependent ℓ(ŷ,P) and instantaneous ℓ(ŷ,y); equation-numbering/reference error noted above.

final_notes: Key theoretical points: Surrogate-aggregation improves robustness but many guarantees are asymptotic in m. Thm2 (App D.2): for cone F with P(Δ(X)>0)=1, any ε_m-argmin of R_{φ,A_m} with ε_m→0 implies R(f_m)→R^*. Prop4 (App D.1): restricted linear parameter classes can have unaggregated-surrogate minimizers with worse task risk; aggregation recovers consistency (Corollary 4.1). Section 4.3 (multiclass linear, logistic link σ^{lr}): FOC for Θ_m; k=2 recovers direction (Θ_m aligns with Θ^* up to scale); for k≥3 Prop5 (App E.1) shows mis-specification can change recovered direction at finite m, while Thm3 (App E.2) shows Θ^*=U^*T^*, Θ_m=U^*T_m and as m→∞, ||T_m||→∞ and T_m/||T_m||→T^*/||T^*|| (aggregation restores normalized direction). Construction of σ^ε remains unresolved. Experiments: truncated-quadratic surrogate φ(δ)=(max{1-δ,0})^2 with unaggregated calibration ψ(ε)=ε^2; Lemma 3.1 (δ=1) gives ψ_m(ε)=(1/16)(ε - sqrt((32/m) log 40))_+; plotted m∈{2^16,2^20,2^24,2^28,2^32}; aggregated ψ_m empirical slope →1/16 (bounds conservative). Logistic mis-spec experiment: k=3,d=2, corrupted link ṡσ(t)=σ^{lr}(t)1{||t||≤r}+σ^{lr}(α t)1{||t||>r} with r=3,α=0.1; true θ_1^*=(0,1)^T, θ_2^*=(1,1)^T; m∈{1,4,16,64,256,1024}; designs: fixed n=10k and fixed total labels nm=640k; T=100 trials, 95% error bars. Note: Figure 2 caption formula is ill-typed and conflicts with Thm3; intended metric is normalized-direction error. Discussion: open problems — finite-m theory, sharper loss-dependent condition-number analysis (κ(X)), extending mis-specified-model results beyond optimal-predictability (12), and restricted-class (H-)consistency with aggregation.

Paper studies whether aggregating noisy labels improves consistency of learned predictors. Focus: surrogate losses (used during fitting), analyzed over all measurable predictors and over restricted model classes. Develops calibration inequalities for aggregated labels; analyzes ranking, classification, structured prediction. Key claims to remember: for ranking with k ≥ 3 items, no convex surrogate based on individual comparisons is Fisher consistent; an aggregated squared-loss procedure is consistent when m ≥ k. More generally, "identifying" surrogates become asymptotically consistent as number m of aggregated labels grows; many guarantees require m → ∞. Under certain noise conditions, aggregation yields approximately linear comparison inequalities. In restricted model classes, aggregation can restore consistency when ordinary surrogate minimization fails (including link mis-specification). Two numerical illustrations are reported. Glossary follows (definitions and reused symbols listed).

Key settings/examples: ranking, binary and multiclass classification, and finite-dimensional linear predictors. Aggregators: majority vote A_m, generalized majority vote (eq.7), KNN aggregator A_{m,K}. Main formal claims: Propositions 1–2 show convex ranking surrogates fail without aggregation when k≥3 but become consistent after aggregation when m≥k (Prop.2 uses squared-loss φ(s,q)=||s−q||_2^2). Theorem 1: under weak surrogate assumptions, aggregated-label losses admit approximate linear comparison inequalities (linear bounds relating excess task risk to excess surrogate risk); stated slope = C_{φ,1}/16 above its risk threshold. Corollary 4.1 and Theorem 2 (and Theorem 3 in earlier notes) establish aggregation restores convergence as m→∞ for restricted hypothesis classes F; Propositions 4–5 show failures without aggregation. Notation reminders: risks R, R_φ, R_{φ,A}; conditional risks and infima R^*, R_φ^*, R_{φ,A}^*; excess risks δ_ℓ, δ_φ, δ_{φ,A}. Calibration/identifiability: constants C_{φ,1}, C_{φ,2}, ψ_A (Fenchel biconjugate of overlineψ_A). Low-noise assumptions: Mammen–Tsybakov (N_α),(M_β) with β = α/(1−α) (α≠1). Experiments: corrupted logistic link, T=100 trials, 95% error bars.

Paper: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” (Chen Cheng, John Duchi). Thesis: aggregating noisy labels (label cleaning) can yield consistency and robustness not available using single noisy labels. Settings: ranking, binary/multiclass classification, finite-dimensional linear predictors. Key formal claims (from earlier parts): Propositions 1–2 show convex ranking surrogates fail without aggregation when k≥3 but can be consistent after aggregation (Prop.2 uses squared-loss φ(s,q)=||s−q||_2^2). Theorem 1 gives approximate linear comparison inequalities for aggregated-label losses (slope C_{φ,1}/16 above threshold). Corollary 4.1 and Theorems 2–3 show aggregation restores convergence as m→∞ for restricted hypothesis classes F; Propositions 4–5 exhibit failures without aggregation. Notation/definitions introduced in this part: data (X,Y) i.i.d. from P; scorer f:X→R^d, decoder d:R^d→Y; task loss ℓ:Y×Y→R_+ and task risk R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),Y)] (eq.1). Alternative conditional formulation R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),P(·|X))] (eq.2). Surrogate φ:R^d×Y→R and surrogate risk R_φ(f)=E[φ(f(X),Y)]. Aggregation: response Z∈Z, aggregator A:Z→A, aggregated surrogate φ:R^d×A→R_+, aggregated risk R_{φ,A}(f)=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))] (eq.3). Examples: majority vote A_m(Z)=argmin_{y∈Y}∑_{l=1}^m ℓ(y,Y_l); KNN aggregation uses extra sample (X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m with Z=(Y,(X_i,Y_i)), order by distance and define A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_{y}∑_{l=0}^K ℓ(y,Y_{(l)}) (X_{(0)}=X, so Y_{(0)}=Y). Two consistency settings studied: (i) Fisher consistency (all measurable functions), (ii) statistical/parametric restricted models. Calibration constants referenced earlier: C_{φ,1}, C_{φ,2}, ψ_A. Experiments use corrupted logistic link, T=100 trials.

steps.notes_before: Section summarizes Fisher consistency and comparison inequalities via calibration functions: define conditional risks R(s|x), R_phi(s|x); pointwise excesses delta_l(s,x)=R(s|x)-inf_s'R(s'|x), delta_phi(s,x) similarly. Calibration psi(ε,x)=inf_{s}{delta_phi(s,x) | delta_l(s,x)≥ε}, overline{psi}(ε)=inf_x psi(ε,x). Corollary 3.1: positivity of psi(·,x) for all x,ε>0 characterizes Fisher consistency; Fenchel biconjugate of overline{psi} yields a comparison bound psi(R-R^*) ≤ R_phi-R_phi^*. Ranking example: labels Y={(i,j):i≠j}, p_{ij}=P(Y=(i,j)|x). Define C_x with (C_x)_{ii}=0 and (C_x)_{ij}=p_{ij}/\sum_{l≠j} p_{lj} (use 0/0=1/(k-1)), so C_x^T 1 = 1. Loss ℓ(s,C)=max_{i<j} 1{(s_i-s_j)(C1_i-C1_j)≤0, C1_i-C1_j≠0}; population risk R(f)=P(f(X) and C_X1 order differently) (eq.4). Restrict scores to s^T1=0. Proposition 1: for k≥3, any surrogate φ convex in scores is not Fisher consistent for this ranking risk. Aggregation: collect Z=(Y_1,...,Y_m); define counts m_{ij} (definition in text appears to sum over Y^m and is inconsistent — it should sum over observed labels), m_j=Σ_i m_{ij}, and A(Z)=star if some m_j=0, else vector whose i-th entry is Σ_j m_{ij}/m_j. Proposition 2: squared-loss regression on A(Z) is Fisher consistent when m≥k.

errors.claim: Equation (5) defines the uniform calibration function as "\overline\psi_A(\epsilon)\coloneqq \inf_{s\in\mathbb R^d}\overline\psi_A(\epsilon,x)."

This same part correctly defines the pointwise calibration as "\overline\psi_A(\epsilon,x)\coloneqq \inf_{s\in\mathbb R^d}\{\delta_{\varphi,A}(s,x)\mid\delta_\ell(s,x)\geq\epsilon\}," so the uniform function should be an infimum over x, not over s.

steps.notes_before: Squared-loss surrogate: φ(s,q)=||s-q||_2^2, φ(s,★)=0. Proposition 2: for ranking risk (eq.4) φ is Fisher consistent when m≥k. Aggregation expands response space from Y to R^k; A(Z) is vector-valued in R^k when all m_j>0. Prop 1 (earlier): for k≥3 no convex-in-scores surrogate is Fisher consistent for pairwise ranking risk. Proposition 3: if ∫ b(x)dP(x)<∞ and δ_ℓ(f(x),x) ≤ b(x), then φ is Fisher consistent for task risk iff for all x, ε>0 the pointwise calibration overlineψ_A(ε,x)>0; with ψ_A=(overlineψ_A)^{**} we get ψ_A(R(f)-R^*) ≤ R_{φ,A}(f)-R_{φ,A}^*. Correct calibration defs: overlineψ_A(ε,x):=inf_{s∈R^d}{δ_{φ,A}(s,x) | δ_ℓ(s,x)≥ε}; overlineψ_A(ε):=inf_{x∈X} overlineψ_A(ε,x) (paper's eq.(5) mistakenly used inf over s). Definition 3.1: (C_{φ,1},C_{φ,2})-identifying surrogate with params a_y∈A and s_y∈R^d, d(s_y)=y satisfying (6a),(6b). Example: hinge loss is (1,2)-identifying. Generalized majority vote A_m(y_1..y_m)=a_{ŷ} with ŷ=argmin_y Σ_i ℓ(y,y_i); for i.i.d. labels w.p.1 there exists random M such that for m≥M empirical argmin ⊂ population argmin y^*(x). Corollary 3.2: vanishing aggregated surrogate regret implies vanishing task regret as m→∞.

Corollary 3.2: If m(n)→∞ and φ is identifying (Def.3.1) then R_{φ,A_m}(f_n)-R_{φ,A_m}^*→0 ⇒ R(f_n)-R^*→0. Example: hinge is (C_{φ,1},C_{φ,2})=(1,2)-identifying. Majority vote A_m eventually selects only optimal labels (empirical argmin ⊂ population argmin) for m≥M (random finite M).

Level-(ξ,ζ) consistency (Def.3.2): there exists ψ with ψ(ε)≥ζε for ε≥ξ and ψ(R(f)-R^*) ≤ R_{φ,A}(f)-R_{φ,A}^*.

Noise/margin quantities:
- Δ(x)=min_{d(s)∉y^*(x)} δ_ℓ(s,x) (binary: Δ(x)=|2P(Y=1|X=x)-1|).
- Conditions: (N_α) P(d◦f ≠ d◦f^*) ≤ C_{MT}(R(f)-R^*)^α, α∈[0,1]; (M_β) P(Δ(X) ≤ ε) ≤ (C_{MT}ε)^β. They are equivalent under β=α/(1-α).
- Condition-number κ(x)=max_{d(s)≠y^*}δ / min_{d(s)≠y^*}δ (binary κ=1 if P(Δ(X)>0)=1).

Aggregation error func: e_m(t)= t sqrt{(2/m) log(4k(C_{φ,1}+C_{φ,2})/C_{φ,1})}.

Theorem 1: If φ is (C_{φ,1},C_{φ,2})-identifying, A_m aggregator (7), 0≤ℓ≤1 and (N_α) holds, then for any M>0 and any f with
R(f)-R^* ≥ 2P(κ(X)>M) + (4C_{MT} e_m(M))^{1/(1-α)},
we have
R(f)-R^* ≤ (16/C_{φ,1}) (R_{φ,A_m}(f)-R_{φ,A_m}^*).
Thus level-(ξ,ζ) with ξ as the LHS threshold and ζ=C_{φ,1}/16. Let ξ_m = inf_M{…}; ξ_m→0 as m→∞, so taking α=0 yields Corollary 3.2.

Optimizing using κ≤1/Δ gives explicit ξ_{m,k}: for k=2,
ξ_{m,2}=((32 C_{MT}^2/m) log(8(C_{φ,1}+C_{φ,2})/C_{φ,1}))^{1/(2(1-α))},
and a stated expression for k≥3. Corollary 3.3: same linear comparison holds whenever R(f)-R^*≥ξ_{m,k}.

Title: Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning. Authors: Chen Cheng, John Duchi. Abstract claims: learning procedures that rely on aggregated labels (label information distilled from noisy responses) enjoy robustness properties not possible without data cleaning. Key points: (1) In the context of risk consistency (minimizing surrogate, typically convex, losses instead of target task loss like 0-1), procedures using label aggregation obtain stronger consistency guarantees than those possible using raw labels. (2) Classical perfectly-specified model scenarios suggest modeling label uncertainty is statistically efficient, but consistency for “standard” approaches fails as soon as the loss is even slightly mis-specified. (3) Procedures leveraging aggregated information still converge to optimal classifiers despite such mis-specification. Overall claim: incorporating a fuller view of the data collection-to-prediction pipeline (via label aggregation/cleaning) yields a more robust methodology by refining noisy signals.

Title: Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning. Authors: Chen Cheng, John Duchi. Paper claim: label cleaning / aggregation yields robustness impossible without aggregation. Two facets: (1) Improved surrogate-risk consistency—procedures using aggregated labels can achieve consistent and optimal prediction in the limit when methods using only (X,Y) cannot. (2) Even in finite-dimensional (parametric) settings, aggregation can produce consistent classifiers where standard methods fail. Paper will give concrete examples (ranking; binary and multiclass classification with linear estimators) where estimators using only (X,Y) necessarily fail but aggregation yields consistency. In nonparametric settings, the number of samples aggregated interacts with noise conditions to improve consistency. Aggregation permits surrogate risk consistency under weak conditions on the surrogate loss: losses using aggregated labels admit (approximate) linear comparison inequalities, with multiclass threshold O(m^{-1}) at α = 1/2. Also claims consistency can be obtained over restricted hypothesis classes (not just all measurable functions) when using aggregated labels, whereas standard theory requires unrestricted classes. References prior surrogate-consistency literature (Bartlett et al. and follow-ups).

Part 9 experiments: (A) D4X surrogate-consistency amplification (binary truncated quadratic φ(δ)=max{1-δ,0}^2). Unaggregated ψ(ε)=ε^2; with δ=1, no low-noise (α=0), C_MT=1 gives ψ_m(ε) = (1/16)(ε - sqrt(32/m · log 40))_+. Aggregated m values used {2^16,2^20,2^24,2^28,2^32}. (B) Finite-dimensional logistic with piecewise corrupted link ˜σ(t)=σ^{lr}(t) for ||t||≤r and σ^{lr}(α t) for ||t||>r (r=3, α=0.1). Two sampling regimes: (i) fixed n=10,000 multilabeled observations per m; (ii) fixed total labels n·m = 640,000 (n=640000/m). Discussion/high-level points: cleaning provides robustness gains; many consistency results rely on m→∞ and separating finite-m problems needing cleaning is open; beyond binary κ(X) can be large even with low-noise (α≈1); mis-specified-model results assume K7M (a Bayes-optimal classifier in F) and classical surrogate consistency can still fail while aggregation succeeds; extending aggregation analysis to restricted hypothesis classes (H-consistency) and unifying parametric/nonparametric perspectives (e.g., Mao et al.'s quadratic ψ growth) are important directions.

Paper title: "Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning" by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: aggregating/cleaning labels (information distilled from noisy responses) yields robustness not available without cleaning. Theorem 1 (sketch): if φ is W3C (C_{φ,1},C_{φ,2}), aggregator A_m = J9P and noise (N_α), then under a threshold condition R(f)-R* ≥ ξ one gets R(f)-R* ≤ (16/C_{φ,1})(R_{φ,A_m}(f)-R_{φ,A_m}^*). ξ_m→0 as m→∞. 3.3.2 Bipartite matching (2N vertices): Lemma 3.2: matching surrogate is W3C with C_{φ,1}=1/N, C_{φ,2}=2. steps.notes_before: Section 4: studies robustness/consistency when restricting to parametric/finite-dimensional classes. Props: 4 constructs distributions where any (unaggregated) surrogate minimizer θ_φ is essentially orthogonal to a true linear predictor θ^*, so surrogate minimization can fail (binary margin surrogates, any nonnegative φ). Corollary 4.1 claims aggregation + ε_m→0 recover R(f_{θ^*}) and direction (cos→1) as a corollary to Theorem 2—but Theorem 2 requires additionally P(Δ(X)>0)=1 (unique maximizer) and itself only guarantees R(f_m)→R^*. Theorem 2: for a cone F satisfying K7M and P(Δ(X)>0)=1, any ε_m-approximate minimizer (w.r.t aggregated surrogate R_{φ,A_m}) satisfies R(f_m)→R^*. Multiclass: Q7D surrogates satisfying limit condition (13) (φ→0 when correct coordinate dominates) apply (e.g., multiclass logistic). Prop.5 & Thm.3 (finite-dim multiclass, k≥3): under invertibility/mild conditions pair-based surrogates can be inconsistent; aggregation (T4K) recovers ordering but parameter norms may diverge (Θ_m norm→∞ while normalized Θ_m→normalized Θ^*). Aggregated class probabilities p_{Θ,m}(x) arise via a T4K transform ρ_m(·) of base link σ(·), and ρ_m preserves ordering consistency.

errors.claim: Clearly \sigma^\epsilon satisfies (14) and is optimally predictable under (12).

But the definition gives \sigma^\epsilon(t)=\tfrac1k\mathbf1 when t\in\mathcal T_\epsilon, so for such t the RHS (\sigma_y(t)=max_i\sigma_i(t)) holds for every y (all coordinates equal), while the LHS generally holds only for the coordinate(s) where t attains its maximum. final_notes: Finite-aggregation vs asymptotics: Many main model-consistency results require m → ∞ (Cor.4.1, Thm.2–3). Thm.3 (App. E.2) — for L_{m,σ}(Θ)=E[E_σ[φ(Θ^T X,Y_m^+)|X]] — gives minimizer Θ_m = U^* T_m with ||T_m||→∞ and T_m/||T_m|| → T^*/||T^*|| as m→∞. Some finite-m guarantees exist: Prop.2 (ranking) requires m ≥ k; Section 3.2.3 provides a uniform linear comparison at α=1 with a displayed O(log k) bound. Section references: Section 3.2.3 uses the noise condition number κ(X) (eq.(9)); κ(X)=1 in binary but can be large in multiclass even when Mammen–Tsybakov α≈1. Model misspecification: Section 4.3 requires optimal predictability (eq.(12)) — a Bayes-optimal classifier in F; classical surrogate consistency can still fail then while aggregation can succeed (Prop.4 vs Cor.4.1/Thm.2; Prop.5 vs Thm.3). Prop.5 (App. E.1) constructs k≥3, Σ=I, Z∼N(0,I_{k-1}), an invertible D, and small perturbed link giving an unaggregated minimizer Θ_1(ε) whose normalized direction differs from Θ^*. Experiments (Sec.5): (i) binary truncated-quadratic φ with calibration ψ(ε)=ε^2; Lemma 3.1 (δ=1, α=0) yields ψ_m(ε)=(1/16)(ε - sqrt((32/m) log 40))_+ and ψ_m→(1/16)ε as m→∞ (m∈{2^16,…,2^32}). (ii) mis-specified logistic (k=3,d=2) with r=3, α=0.1, θ1*=(0,1), θ2*=(1,1); m varied, n either fixed or scaled (100 trials, 95% error bars). Note: Fig.2 caption metric appears invalid; plotted metric likely directional error ||T_m/||T_m|| - T^*/||T^*||||.

Paper studies whether aggregating noisy labels improves consistency of learned predictors. Focus: surrogate losses (used during fitting), analyzed over all measurable predictors and over restricted model classes. Develops calibration inequalities for aggregated labels; analyzes ranking, classification, structured prediction. Key claims to remember: for ranking with k ≥ 3 items, no convex surrogate based on individual comparisons is Fisher consistent; an aggregated squared-loss procedure is consistent when m ≥ k. More generally, "identifying" surrogates become asymptotically consistent as number m of aggregated labels grows; many guarantees require m → ∞. Under certain noise conditions, aggregation yields approximately linear comparison inequalities. In restricted model classes, aggregation can restore consistency when ordinary surrogate minimization fails (including link mis-specification). Two numerical illustrations are reported. Glossary follows (definitions and reused symbols listed).
