Paper: "Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning" (Chen Cheng, John Duchi). Central claim: aggregating noisy labels (label cleaning) yields robustness and consistency benefits unavailable from raw labels. Two main benefits highlighted: (1) aggregation improves consistency of estimation for surrogate-risk minimization (e.g., multiclass logistic), enabling consistent/optimal prediction when unaggregated procedures fail; (2) aggregation can give consistent classifiers in finite-dimensional (parametric) problems where standard methods fail. Key technical items (from earlier parts and reinforced here): Propositions 1–2: convex ranking surrogates fail for k≥3 but become consistent after aggregation when m≥k. Theorem 1: under weak surrogate assumptions, aggregated-label losses admit approximate linear comparison inequalities; gives slope C_{φ,1}/16 above its risk threshold and a multiclass threshold scaling O(m^{-1}) at α=1/2. Corollary 4.1 and Theorem 2: aggregation restores convergence as m→∞ for restricted hypothesis classes (model mis-specification/finite-dimensional settings). Setup/notation recalled: aggregators (majority vote A_m, generalized majority (eq.7), KNN A_{m,K}); risks R, R_φ, R_{φ,A}; conditional risks and infimums R^*, R_φ^*, R_{φ,A}^*; low-noise Mammen–Tsybakov conditions (N_α),(M_β) with β=α/(1−α). Introduction offers examples in ranking, binary and multiclass classification with linear estimators. No internal contradictions found between this part and prior notes.

steps.notes_before: Preliminaries: X input space, Y outputs, data (X_i,Y_i) iid. Score f: X→R^d, decoder d: R^d→Y; task risk R(f)=E_P[ℓ(d∘f(X),Y)] (Eq.1). Binary: d(s)=sgn(s), ℓ(ŷ,y)=1{ŷ y≤0}, R(f)=P(Y f(X)≤0). Alternative formulation (Eq.2): allow loss to depend on conditional label distribution: R(f)=E_P[ℓ(d∘f(X), P(·|X))]; e.g., for multiclass ℓ(ŷ,P)=Σ_y P(Y=y)1{ŷ≠y} recovers 0-1 risk. Surrogate φ: R_φ(f)=E_P[φ(f(X),Y)]. Two consistency settings: (i) Fisher consistency (F all measurable functions); (ii) restricted parametric/misspecified models. Label aggregation: replace Y by response Z (e.g., Z=(Y_1,...,Y_m)). Aggregator A: Z→A; aggregated surrogate risk R_{φ,A}(f)=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))] (Eq.3). Examples: majority vote A_m(Z)=argmin_y Σ_{l=1}^m ℓ(y,Y_l); K-NN aggregator A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y Σ_{l=0}^K ℓ(y,Y_{(l)}) with additional iid sample (X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m and X_{(0)}=X. Appendix C treats sample-level aggregation.

Preliminaries: X input, Y outputs, data iid. Score f:X→R^d, decoder d:R^d→Y. Task risk R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),Y)] and alternative formulation R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),P(·|X))]. Surrogate φ gives R_φ(f)=E[φ(f(X),Y)]. Aggregation: Z (e.g. tuple of labels), aggregator A:Z→A, aggregated surrogate risk R_{φ,A}(f)=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))].

Conditional (pointwise) risks: R(s|x)=ℓ(d∘s,P(Y∈·|X=x)), R_φ(s|x)=E[φ(s,Y)|X=x]. Excesses δ_ℓ(s,x), δ_φ(s,x). Calibration: ψ(ε,x)=inf_{s}{δ_φ(s,x) | δ_ℓ(s,x)≥ε}, ψ̄(ε)=inf_x ψ(ε,x). Corollary: φ is Fisher consistent iff ψ(ε,x)>0 ∀x,ε>0; letting ψ be Fenchel biconjugate of ψ̄ yields equivalence of positivity and gives comparison inequality ψ(R(f)-R^*) ≤ R_φ(f)-R_φ^*.

Ranking example: Y={(i,j):i≠j,1≤i,j≤k}, p_{ij}=P(Y=(i,j)|x). Define C_x with (C_x)_{ii}=0 and (C_x)_{ij}=p_{ij}/(Σ_{l≠j}p_{lj}) for i≠j, using 0/0:=1/(k-1) so C_x^T1=1. Loss ℓ(s,C)=max_{i<j}1{(s_i-s_j)((e_i-e_j)^T C1)≤0, ((e_i-e_j)^T C1)≠0}; risk R(f)=P(f(X) and C_X1 order differently). Restrict s^T1=0.

Proposition 1: for k≥3, any φ convex in score argument is not Fisher consistent for this ranking risk. Aggregation: with Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m), counts m_{ij} (number of observed (i,j)), m_j=Σ_i m_{ij}; define A(Z)=⋆ if some m_j=0, else A(Z)_i=Σ_j m_{ij}/m_j. Proposition 2: squared-loss regression on A(Z) is Fisher consistent when m≥k.

Squared-loss surrogate for aggregation: φ(s,q)=||s-q||_2^2, φ(s,⋆)=0. For the ranking example, squared-loss on aggregated label A(Z) is Fisher consistent when m≥k (Proposition 2 repeated). Aggregation expands response space from Y to A⊂R^k (A(Z) defined when all m_j>0; otherwise A(Z)=⋆). Proposition 3: extend calibration theory to aggregated surrogates. Define R_{φ,A}(s|x)=E[φ(s,A(Z))|X=x], δ_{φ,A}(s,x)=R_{φ,A}(s|x)-inf_s R_{φ,A}(s|x), and calibration functions ūψ_A(ε,x)=inf_{s}{δ_{φ,A}(s,x) | δ_ℓ(s,x)≥ε}, ūψ_A(ε)=inf_x ūψ_A(ε,x). Under an integrability assumption (∃b(x)≥0 with ∫b<∞ and a pointwise bound on excess task risk), φ is Fisher consistent iff ūψ_A(ε,x)>0 ∀x,ε>0; with ψ_A=(ūψ_A)** we have ψ_A(R(f)-R*) ≤ R_{φ,A}(f)-R_{φ,A}^* (comparison inequality). Definition 3.1: (C1,C2)-identifying surrogate: ∃ aggregation params a_y∈A and score vectors s_y with decoder d(s_y)=y such that for y≠y' (6a) φ(s_y,a_y)+C1 ≤ inf_{d(s)≠y} φ(s,a_y) and (6b) φ(s_y,a_{y'})-C2 ≤ inf_s φ(s,a_{y'}). Example: binary hinge is (1,2)-identifying. Generalized majority vote aggregator A_m(y_1..y_m)=a_{ŷ} with ŷ=argmin_y Σ_i ℓ(y,y_i). For finite Y and i.i.d. Y_i, with probability 1 there is a random finite M such that for m≥M empirical minimizers ⊂ y*(x)=argmin_y E[ℓ(y,Y)|X=x]. Corollary 3.2: as m→∞, vanishing aggregated surrogate regret implies vanishing task regret. (Note: earlier parts used k both as ranking length and as |Y|; text warns of a slight abuse of notation.)

Aggregated-surrogate setup: φ(s,q)=||s-q||_2^2 etc.; aggregation A(Z) expands responses; for ranking squared-loss on A(Z) is Fisher-consistent when m≥k (Prop.2). Definition 3.1: (C1,C2)-identifying surrogate: params {a_y} and score vectors s_y with decoder d(s_y)=y satisfying (6a),(6b). Example: binary hinge is (1,2)-identifying. Generalized majority-vote aggregator A_m(Z)=a_{ŷ} with ŷ = argmin_y Σ_i ℓ(y,y_i); for i.i.d. labels there is a random finite M so for m≥M empirical minimizers ⊆ y*(x)=argmin_y E[ℓ(y,Y)|X=x]. Corollary 3.2: as m→∞, vanishing aggregated surrogate regret ⇒ vanishing task regret.

Part 8 (new): Level-(ξ,ζ) consistency: ψ(ε)≥ζε for ε≥ξ and ψ(R(f)-R*) ≤ R_{φ,A}(f)-R_{φ,A}*. Noise conditions: (Nα) P(d∘f ≠ d∘f*) ≤ C_MT (R(f)-R*)^α and (Mβ) P(Δ(X)≤ε) ≤ (C_MT ε)^β with β=α/(1-α). Δ(x)=min_{d(s)≠y*(x)} δ_ℓ(s,x). Condition-number κ(x)=max_{d(s)≠y*(x)} δ_ℓ/ min_{d(s)≠y*(x)} δ_ℓ; note κ(x)≤1/Δ(x) and for binary with P(Δ(X)>0)=1, κ(x)=1. Define e_m(t)= t sqrt[ (2/m) log( 4k(C_{φ,1}+C_{φ,2})/C_{φ,1} ) ].

Theorem 1: If φ is (C_{φ,1},C_{φ,2})-identifying and 0≤ℓ≤1 and (Nα) holds, then for any M>0 and f with R(f)-R* ≥ 2P(κ(X)>M) + (4 C_MT e_m(M))^{1/(1-α)} we have R(f)-R* ≤ (16/C_{φ,1}) [R_{φ,A_m}(f)-R_{φ,A_m}^*]. Hence level-(ξ,ζ) consistency with ξ as that RHS and ζ=C_{φ,1}/16. Define ξ_m = inf_M {2P(κ(X)>M) + (4 C_MT e_m(M))^{1/(1-α)}}; ξ_m→0 as m→∞ (so taking α=0 yields Corollary 3.2). Explicit bounds ξ_{m,k} given for k=2 and k≥3; Corollary 3.3: if R(f)-R*≥ξ_{m,k} then same linear comparison holds.

errors.claim: Clearly \sigma^\epsilon satisfies (14) and is optimally predictable under (12).

Link consistency (14) is stated as
"t_y=\max_{1\le i\le k}t_i \quad\text{if and only if}\quad \sigma_y(t)=\max_{1\le i\le k}\sigma_i(t)."
But the definition gives \sigma^\epsilon(t)=\tfrac1k\mathbf1 when t\in\mathcal T_\epsilon, so for such t the RHS (\sigma_y(t)=max_i\sigma_i(t)) holds for every y (all coordinates equal), while the LHS generally holds only for the coordinate(s) where t attains its maximum. errors.explanation: Because \sigma^\epsilon is uniform on T_\epsilon, it does not preserve the required iff relation (14) for t with a unique maximizer; therefore the claim that "\sigma^\epsilon satisfies (14)" is false as stated (optimally predictable may still hold, but (14) need not).

Definition: F optimally predicts P if some f\in F has argmax f_y(x) ∈ argmax P(Y|X=x) for all x. Logistic link given. With m repeated labels and majority vote A_m, Y^+|X has distribution p_{Θ,m}(x) obtained by applying majority-vote map ρ_m to σ(Θ^T x); ρ_m preserves argmax. Logistic population risk L_m(Θ)=E[φ(Θ^T X,Y_m^+)], gradient yields FOC E[ X(σ^{lr}(Θ_m^T X)-ρ_m(Θ^*{}^T X))^T ]=0. For k=2 and X~N(0,I), prior result (Cheng et al.) gives Θ_m = t_m Θ^* so direction recovered; hence binary case can be robust under aggregation. For k≥3 they define a perturbed link σ^ε that replaces σ^{lr} by uniform on a small-measure set T_ε; the paper intends to show arbitrarily small such perturbations can change the unaggregated logistic minimizer (Proposition 5). Note: the text contains a reversed-case sentence about σ^ε and an incorrect claim that σ^ε "satisfies (14)" (uniformization on T_ε generally violates the iff in (14)).

Proposition 5 (this part): For k≥3, Σ=I, Z~N(0,I_{k-1}). Define linear map D: M ↦ E[ Z (∇σ^{lr}((Θ^*)^T Z) M Z )^T ]. final_notes: Datasets: Controllable-preference datasets: Ethnicity + Gender image pairs (2.94M preference pairs each) and 537,660 HPDv2 pairs. Models: CLIP-based image reward models fine-tuned to produce man-preferred (RMM) and woman-preferred (RMW) RMs. Key reported numbers (averages across 42 verbs, Table 7): CLIP = -0.0726; RMM = 1.5280; RMW = -0.7448. Table 8 (VCM-VC2 PBSG alignment): baseline PBSG = 0.8034; +RMM = 0.9584 (+0.16); +RMW = 0.3082 (-0.50). Findings: reward-model-based alignment can steer bias via reward-data composition; RMM often amplifies male-preferred portrayals (e.g., exercise, row, cook); RMW can counter-skew and reduce baseline male-alignment (e.g., bake, sleep, sweep), enabling continuous trade-offs by mixing datasets. Sensitivity analysis: normalized sensitivity = ΔPBSG / baseline PBSG; top actions include sleep, stretch, read; semantically-neutral actions can shift alignment strongly. Limitations: focus on two social dimensions (gender, ethnicity) using U.S. Census categories; VLM-based evaluators validated against human judgments but may carry biases (authors ensemble multiple models); experiments use single-step latent consistency distillation and a limited set of reward models; controllable-preference experiments limited to synthetic gender manipulations; VideoBiasEval fixed on 42 socially associated actions. Flagged inconsistency: RMW was described as analogous to HPSv2.1, but HPSv2.1 avg (-0.0984) does not match RMW (-0.7448). Authors: Zefan Cai (UW–Madison), Haoyi Qiu, Haozhe Zhao, Ke Wan (UCSD), Jiachen Li (UCSB), Jiuxiang Gu, Wen Xiao (Microsoft; GitHub link noted), Nanyun Peng (UCLA), Junjie Hu (UIUC). Title: From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models. Authors: Zefan Cai et al. (footnote marker †† appears used twice in title block — inconsistent). Key claim/goal: introduce VideoBiasEval, a diagnostic framework to analyze social bias in text-to-video generation and to trace effects of alignment tuning. Definitions: 'aligned models' = video diffusion models undergoing post-training optimization to better match human preferences (via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style procedures using learned reward/preference models trained on human comparisons). Pipeline: base video diffusion model → preference/reward model → post-training optimization. 'Unaligned counterparts' = models trained only with likelihood-based objectives, used as baselines. Motivation: alignment improves perceptual quality and temporal coherence but may encode/reinforce human preference biases, affecting representation (who is generated, roles, frequency). VideoBiasEval methods: event-based prompting to separate verb/context (semantic content) from actor identity attributes; uses established social bias taxonomies; focuses on gender and ethnicity. Metrics: multi-granular metrics to assess (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) shifts in social attribute distributions across models, and (4) temporal persistence of bias within videos. Paper promises an end-to-end analysis tracing how social attribute distributions evolve through the alignment tuning pipeline. Existing eval gaps listed (limited identity coverage in prompts; lack of specific metrics; lack of methods to track pre/post alignment shifts).

Goal: introduce VideoBiasEval to diagnose social bias in text-to-video generation and trace effects of alignment tuning. Pipeline: base video diffusion model → human preference dataset → image reward model (e.g., HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore) → post-training alignment tuning (reward-weighted fine-tuning) producing an 'aligned' video diffusion model; compare to unaligned (likelihood-trained) baselines. Data & models examined: human preference datasets HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic; reward models HPSv2.0/HPSv2.1 and PickScore; a video consistency model distilled from VideoCrafter-2 is fine-tuned for experiments. Key empirical claims: (1) HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic show non-neutral gender preferences and a strong imbalance favoring White representations; (2) reward models inherit and amplify these biases; (3) alignment-tuned video models propagate biases—alignment with male- or female-preferred reward models systematically shifts gender portrayals while ethnic representation stays uneven; (4) Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS): alignment improves temporal consistency of social attribute portrayals but can make biased portrayals more persistent and visually stable. They also explore constructing controllable image reward datasets (Section 7) and report analyses across 42 events, claiming controllable/counter-biased reward modeling as a mitigation strategy. Contributions summarized: VideoBiasEval framework, first end-to-end analysis linking datasets→reward models→aligned video models, and experiments showing alignment improves quality/coherence while reshaping/reinforcing social composition.

Goal: introduce VideoBiasEval to diagnose social bias in text-to-video generation and trace effects of alignment tuning. Pipeline: base video diffusion model → human preference dataset → image reward model (HPSv2.0/HPSv2.1, PickScore) → reward-weighted fine-tuning producing 'aligned' video diffusion model; compare to unaligned (likelihood-trained) baselines. Key empirical claims: (1) HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic show non-neutral gender preferences and a strong imbalance favoring White representations; (2) reward models inherit and amplify these biases; (3) alignment-tuned video models propagate biases—alignment with male- or female-preferred reward models systematically shifts gender portrayals while ethnic representation stays uneven; (4) Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS): alignment improves temporal consistency of social attribute portrayals but can make biased portrayals more persistent. Also explore constructing controllable image reward datasets and claim controllable/counter-biased reward modeling as mitigation. Related work: existing T2V benchmarks (VBench, EvalCrafter, T2V-CompBench) use metrics like Fréchet Video Distance, CLIP-Score, object consistency but overlook who is depicted and demographic balance; GRiT/CLIP-based metrics verify presence/faithfulness of entities but fail to audit demographic representation or event-level role/verb/context joint patterns. This work proposes an event-centric, actor-verb-environment audit for gender and ethnicity-aware biases across the T2V pipeline.

VideoBiasEval: event-based framework for evaluating social biases in video diffusion models. Use structured prompts varying actor gender/ethnicity across real-world events; generate videos and extract social attributes via a VLM-based evaluation (Sec. 3.3). Events modeled as tuple <p,a,c> (actor p performs verb a in context c). Controlled attribute space: 4 gender categories (man, woman, the neutral term “person,” non-binary person) per Luccioni et al.; 7 ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino) per Karkkainen & Joo / US Census conventions. Verb set: 42 visually distinctive verbs (bake; bike; call; clean; climb; cook; cough; cry; drink; drive; eat; exercise; fish; hit; jump; kick; kneel; laugh; lift; paint; pick; pitch; pray; read; ride; row; run; shop; shout; sit; skate; sleep; smile; stand; stare; stretch; study; sweep; throw; walk; wash; work). Section 3.2 begins Event-Based Prompting Protocol (Settings) but details not shown in this part. Framing emphasizes reproducibility and bounded scope to trace bias propagation; connects to earlier claims about actor-verb-environment audit and later analyses (e.g., temporal consistency/TAS).

Ethnicity bias metrics (part 8): for each group e, P_e = N_e / N_total where N_total counts outputs with an identifiable ethnicity. Representation Deviation Score RDS_e = P_e - 1/|E| (with |E|=7, 1/7≈14.3%); example: RDS_e=0.769 → P_e≈0.912 (≈91.2%). Simpson's Diversity Index SDI = 1 - Σ_e P_e^2 (probability two random outputs are from different groups). Bias shift between unaligned and aligned models is measured via ΔPBS_G, ΔRDS_e, and ΔSDI (directional changes toward zero RDS, zero PBS_G, or higher SDI indicate improvements). steps.notes_before: Prompt template: "A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context]" with 42 verbs. Conditions: Person-only (actor='person', 42 prompts) and Ethnicity+Person (7 ethnic descriptors × 42 = 294 prompts). Generation: each prompt sampled 10× per model, 16 frames uniformly sampled per video. VLM ensemble: Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B infer frame-wise gender and ethnicity; majority-vote per model, then ensemble majority for per-video label. Labels: gender ∈ {man, woman}; ethnicity ∈ {White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino}. Metrics: PBSG = (N_man - N_woman)/N_total ∈ [-1,1] (paper inconsistently names the condition as "ethnicity+gender" vs "ethnicity+person"); RDS_e = P_e - 1/7 (1/7≈14.3%); SDI = 1 - Σ_e P_e^2. Missing values '—' indicate zero recognizable instances under person-only. Table 2 compares two pairs: ModelScope (u) → InstructVideo (a) and VideoCrafter-2 (u) → T2V-Turbo-V1 (a). Key numbers: ModelScope avg PBSG 0.4815, RDS_White 0.7690, SDI 0.0538; InstructVideo avg PBSG 0.5295, RDS_White 0.7833, SDI 0.0267 (Δ avg PBSG +0.0480, Δ RDS_White +0.0143, Δ SDI -0.0271). VideoCrafter avg PBSG 0.7581, RDS_White 0.6905, SDI 0.1252; T2V avg PBSG 0.8306, RDS_White 0.6381, SDI 0.1119 (Δ avg PBSG +0.0725, Δ RDS_White -0.0524, Δ SDI -0.0133). Interpretation in paper: alignment increased male bias in both pairs; effects on ethnicity are mixed (first pair: increased White overrepresentation; second pair: reduced White RDS but lower SDI). Also note the section lists additional aligned models (InternVid2-S2, ViCLIP) that do not appear in Table 2, an internal mismatch.

steps.notes_before: Prompt template: "A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context]" (42 verbs). Conditions: Person-only ('person', 42 prompts) and Ethnicity+Person (7 ethnic descriptors × 42 = 294 prompts). Sampling: each prompt sampled 10× per model; 16 frames uniformly per video. VLM ensemble: Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B; inference frame-wise, majority-vote per model, then ensemble majority for per-video label. Labels: gender ∈ {man, woman}; ethnicity ∈ {White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino}. Metrics: PBSG = (N_man - N_woman)/N_total; RDS_e = P_e - 1/7 (~14.3%); SDI = 1 - Σ_e P_e^2. Controllable preference datasets: Ethnicity+Gender image pairs (2.94M preference pairs each) + 537,660 HPDv2 pairs; fine-tuned CLIP-based image RMs: RMM (man-preferred) and RMW (woman-preferred). Table 7 (averages, 42 verbs): CLIP = -0.0726; RMM = 1.5280; RMW = -0.7448. Noted ambiguous delta annotations in Table 7 (RMM delta appears relative to CLIP; RMW delta appears relative to RMM). Table 8 (VCM-VC2 PBSG alignment): baseline PBSG = 0.8034; +RMM = 0.9584 (+0.16); +RMW = 0.3082 (-0.50); per-ethnicity breakdowns given elsewhere. Prior text described RMW as 'analogous to HPSv2.1', but HPSv2.1 image reward avg reported earlier = -0.0984 (not close to RMW = -0.7448). New (part 17) summary: framework shows bias can be steered by reward-data composition; counter-biased RM (RMW) can reduce existing skew and produce more balanced/socially representative generations; posits a continuous axis by mixing man-/woman-preferred data for tunable trade-offs; sensitivity analysis across 42 actions shows even semantically neutral actions can shift strongly. Figure 6 action-level: RMM amplifies male-preferred portrayals (exercise, row, cook); RMW shifts toward women-preferred (bake, sleep, sweep). Figures 6(b)/(c): actions ranked by normalized sensitivity = ΔPBSG / baseline PBSG; top-ranked actions reported as sleep, stretch, read for both RMM and RMW. Responsible-use caveats urging stakeholder engagement reiterated.

Datasets: Controllable preference datasets: Ethnicity+Gender image pairs (2.94M preference pairs each) + 537,660 HPDv2 pairs. Models: CLIP-based image reward models fine-tuned to produce man-preferred (RMM) and woman-preferred (RMW) RMs. Key reported numbers (averages across 42 verbs, Table 7): CLIP = -0.0726; RMM = 1.5280; RMW = -0.7448. Note: Table 7 had ambiguous delta annotations (RMM delta appears relative to CLIP; RMW delta appears relative to RMM). Table 8 (VCM-VC2 PBSG alignment): baseline PBSG = 0.8034; +RMM = 0.9584 (+0.16); +RMW = 0.3082 (-0.50). Prior inconsistency flagged: paper described RMW as 'analogous to HPSv2.1', but earlier HPSv2.1 image reward avg = -0.0984 (does not match RMW = -0.7448). Findings summarized earlier: reward-model-based alignment can steer bias via reward-data composition; RMM tends to amplify male-preferred portrayals (examples: exercise, row, cook); RMW can counter-skew and reduce baseline male-alignment (examples: bake, sleep, sweep), enabling a continuous axis by mixing man-/woman-preferred data for tunable trade-offs. Sensitivity analysis (Figure 6): normalized sensitivity = ΔPBSG / baseline PBSG shows top actions include sleep, stretch, read for both RMs; even semantically-neutral actions can shift strongly. Part 18 (Conclusion) restates VideoBiasEval decouples identity from content semantics and that reward-model-based alignment often inherits and frequently amplifies biases in human preference data; recommends integrating bias auditing/mitigation across the video generation pipeline.

Datasets: Controllable preference datasets: Ethnicity + Gender image pairs (2.94M preference pairs each) and 537,660 HPDv2 pairs. Models: CLIP-based image reward models fine-tuned to produce man-preferred (RMM) and woman-preferred (RMW) RMs. Key reported numbers (averages across 42 verbs, Table 7): CLIP = -0.0726; RMM = 1.5280; RMW = -0.7448. Table 7 had ambiguous delta annotations (RMM delta appears relative to CLIP; RMW delta appears relative to RMM). Table 8 (VCM-VC2 PBSG alignment): baseline PBSG = 0.8034; +RMM = 0.9584 (+0.16); +RMW = 0.3082 (-0.50). Findings: reward-model-based alignment can steer bias via reward-data composition; RMM often amplifies male-preferred portrayals (e.g., exercise, row, cook); RMW can counter-skew and reduce baseline male-alignment (e.g., bake, sleep, sweep), enabling continuous trade-offs by mixing datasets. Sensitivity analysis metric normalized sensitivity = ΔPBSG / baseline PBSG; top actions include sleep, stretch, read; semantically-neutral actions can shift alignment strongly. Limitations: focus on two social dimensions (gender, ethnicity) using U.S. Census categories; VLM-based evaluators validated against human judgments but operate at image-level and may carry biases (authors ensemble multiple models); experiments use a specific training strategy (single-step latent consistency distillation) and a limited set of reward models; controllable-preference experiments limited to synthetic gender manipulations; VideoBiasEval benchmark fixed on 42 socially associated actions. Prior flagged inconsistency to watch: RMW described as analogous to HPSv2.1 earlier, but HPSv2.1 avg (-0.0984) does not match RMW (-0.7448).

Datasets: Controllable-preference datasets: Ethnicity + Gender image pairs (2.94M preference pairs each) and 537,660 HPDv2 pairs. Models: CLIP-based image reward models fine-tuned to produce man-preferred (RMM) and woman-preferred (RMW) RMs. Key reported numbers (averages across 42 verbs, Table 7): CLIP = -0.0726; RMM = 1.5280; RMW = -0.7448. Table 7 had ambiguous delta annotations (RMM delta appears relative to CLIP; RMW delta appears relative to RMM). Table 8 (VCM-VC2 PBSG alignment): baseline PBSG = 0.8034; +RMM = 0.9584 (+0.16); +RMW = 0.3082 (-0.50). Findings: reward-model-based alignment can steer bias via reward-data composition; RMM often amplifies male-preferred portrayals (e.g., exercise, row, cook); RMW can counter-skew and reduce baseline male-alignment (e.g., bake, sleep, sweep), enabling continuous trade-offs by mixing datasets. Sensitivity analysis: normalized sensitivity = ΔPBSG / baseline PBSG; top actions include sleep, stretch, read; semantically-neutral actions can shift alignment strongly. Limitations: focus on two social dimensions (gender, ethnicity) using U.S. Census categories; VLM-based evaluators validated against human judgments but may carry biases (authors ensemble multiple models); experiments use a specific training strategy (single-step latent consistency distillation) and a limited set of reward models; controllable-preference experiments limited to synthetic gender manipulations; VideoBiasEval benchmark fixed on 42 socially associated actions. Flagged inconsistency to watch: RMW was earlier described as analogous to HPSv2.1, but HPSv2.1 avg (-0.0984) does not match RMW (-0.7448). Broader Impact (this part): alignment tuning can act as a "bias stabilizer" by removing artifacts and making stereotypes appear natural; controllable preference modeling is dual-use (can amplify or suppress groups); mitigation recommended via multi-granular, event-centric auditing like VideoBiasEval and rigorous preference-dataset curation. Broader Impact uses RLHF as an example of alignment tuning though experiments used distillation.

final_notes: Key quantitative results: VCM-VC2 baseline PBSG = 0.8034. HPSv2.0 increases PBSG (~0.9116); HPSv2.1 reduces man-dominant bias (~0.2267). RM datasets: ~2.94M Ethnicity+Gender pairs + 537,660 HPDv2 pairs. Two reward models (CLIP-fine-tuned): RMM (man-preferred) and RMW (woman-preferred). Table 7 RM scoring avgs: CLIP avg -0.0726, RMM avg 1.5280, RMW avg -0.7448. Alignment effects (Table 8): baseline 0.8034 -> +RMM 0.9584 (Δ ≈ +0.155, amplification) -> +RMW 0.3082 (Δ ≈ -0.495, reduction/over-correction). Paper demonstrates directed bias control but mixed outcomes (some RMs amplify, some reduce/over-correct). Action-level: 42 socially-associated actions analyzed; RMM amplifications include exercise, row, cook; RMW produces shifts for bake, sleep, sweep; normalized sensitivity top actions: sleep, stretch, read. Limitations: US Census-limited gender/ethnicity categories; VLM-based evaluators are image-level and potentially biased (authors ensemble models to mitigate); single training strategy (latent consistency distillation) and limited set of RMs; controllable preference experiments use synthetic gender manipulations; VideoBiasEval uses fixed 42-action taxonomy. Broader impact: alignment tuning can 'stabilize' biases by removing artifacts/smoothing flicker, making stereotypes appear natural; controllable preference datasets are dual-use and can systematically amplify/suppress attributes. Recommendations: adopt multi-granular, event-centric auditing (e.g., VideoBiasEval) and apply rigorous safeguards when curating preference datasets. Title: From Preferences to Prejudice — studies how alignment tuning shapes social bias in text-to-video diffusion models. Introduces VideoBiasEval: an evaluation framework grounded in social bias taxonomies. Key methods: event-based prompting to separate semantic content (verbs, contexts) from actor attributes (gender, ethnicity); use of visual-language models (VLMs) to infer actor attributes frame-wise and aggregate them (Section 3.3). Proposes multi-granular metrics to evaluate: (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) distributional shifts in social attributes across model variants, and (4) temporal persistence of bias within videos. Claims first end-to-end analysis linking biases in human preference datasets -> amplification in reward models -> propagation through alignment-tuned video diffusion models (Sections 5.1, 5.2, 6). Main result summary: alignment tuning strengthens representational biases and makes them temporally stable, producing smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Repo and review: GitHub link and OpenReview link provided.

Title: From Preferences to Prejudice — studies how alignment tuning shapes social bias in text-to-video diffusion models. Introduces VideoBiasEval (Section 3), an event-based prompting framework grounded in social bias taxonomies. Definition: "aligned models" = video diffusion models that undergo post-training optimization (reward-weighted fine-tuning / RLHF-style) using learned preference/reward models trained on human comparisons; contrasted with unaligned models trained only with likelihood objectives. Motivation: human preference judgments can encode systematic cultural/demographic biases that may be inherited/amplified by reward models and downstream generative systems. Paper focuses on gender and ethnicity as target social dimensions. VideoBiasEval separates semantic content (verbs, contexts) from actor identity attributes to permit interpretable probing. Claims three limitations of prior work: inadequate identity-diverse prompts, insufficient identity coverage/metrics, and lack of methods to track pre/post-alignment shifts. Introduces multi-granular metrics to assess: (1) ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) shifts in social attribute distributions across models, and (4) temporal persistence of bias within videos. Methods (noted from other sections): uses VLMs to infer actor attributes frame-wise and aggregate (Section 3.3). Main claimed findings (from summary): alignment tuning strengthens representational biases and makes them temporally stable; traces bias evolution across base model -> reward model -> aligned model (Sections 5.1, 5.2, 6). Repo and OpenReview links provided.

Goal: study how alignment tuning (reward-weighted fine-tuning / RLHF-style) changes social bias in text-to-video diffusion models. Key datasets/models: human preference datasets HPDv2 (Wu et al., 2023) and Pick-a-Pic (Kirstain et al., 2023a); image reward models HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore; video model: VideoCrafter-2 distilled consistency model fine-tuned (Section 6). Framework: VideoBiasEval (Section 3) uses event-based prompts (42 events), separates semantic content (verbs/contexts) from actor identity attributes; uses VLMs to infer actor attributes frame-wise and aggregate (Section 3.3). Metrics: multi-granular metrics for ethnicity bias, gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, shifts pre/post alignment, and Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS) to measure persistence across frames. Experimental pipeline: (5.1) analyze demographic preferences in HPDv2 & Pick-a-Pic; (5.2) analyze how reward models inherit/amplify those patterns; (6) fine-tune video consistency model with different reward models and compare pre/post alignment outputs; (7) explore controllable reward datasets via manipulated social-attribute distributions, test if reward training can steer biases. Main reported findings: human preference datasets show non-neutral gender preferences and strong imbalance favoring White representations; reward models inherit and amplify these biases; alignment tuning shifts gender portrayals according to reward-model preference, while ethnic representation remains uneven; TAS shows alignment increases temporal consistency and can make biased portrayals more persistent; alignment improves perceptual quality/coherence but can reinforce/stabilize existing biases. Contributions: (1) VideoBiasEval framework, (2) first end-to-end analysis linking preference datasets -> reward models -> aligned video diffusion models, (3) experiments showing preference alignment reshapes social composition and offering guidance for bias mitigation via targeted data composition and counter-biased reward design.

Goal: study how alignment tuning (reward-weighted fine-tuning / RLHF-style) changes social bias in text-to-video diffusion models. Datasets/models: human preference datasets HPDv2 (Wu et al., 2023) and Pick-a-Pic (Kirstain et al., 2023a); image reward models HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore; video model: VideoCrafter-2 distilled consistency model fine-tuned (Sec. 6). Framework: VideoBiasEval — event-centric (42 events) prompts that disentangle semantic content (verbs/contexts) from actor identity attributes; uses VLMs to infer actor attributes frame-wise and aggregate (Sec. 3.3). Metrics: multi-granular measures for ethnicity bias, gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, pre/post alignment shifts, and Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS) for persistence across frames. Pipeline: (5.1) analyze demographic preferences in HPDv2 & Pick-a-Pic; (5.2) test how reward models inherit/amplify those patterns; (6) fine-tune video consistency model with different reward models and compare pre/post; (7) test controllable reward datasets with manipulated social-attribute distributions. Main findings: human preference datasets show non-neutral gender preferences and a White-favoring imbalance; reward models inherit and amplify these biases; alignment tuning shifts gender portrayals according to reward-model preference while ethnic representation remains uneven; alignment increases temporal consistency (TAS) and can make biased portrayals more persistent; alignment improves perceptual quality/coherence but can reinforce/stabilize biases. Contributions: (1) VideoBiasEval, (2) first end-to-end analysis linking preference datasets → reward models → aligned T2V diffusion models, (3) experiments showing preference alignment reshapes social composition and offering guidance for bias mitigation via targeted data composition and counter-biased reward design. Related work: existing T2V benchmarks (FVD, CLIP-Score, object-consistency) and image-bias evaluations focus on surface metrics or single frames and miss actor-role-context temporal biases; our event-level audit addresses that gap.

VideoBiasEval: event-based prompting framework that represents each event as a tuple ⟨p,a,c⟩ (actor p performs verb a in context c). Uses SOTA diffusion models to generate videos (Sec 3.2) and a VLM-based evaluation method to extract social attributes frame-wise and perform multi-granular analysis across event categories (Sec 3.3; Fig.2). Controlled attribute space: 4 gender categories (man, woman, the neutral term “person”, non-binary person) following Luccioni et al. (2023); 7 ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino) following Karkkainen & Joo (2021)/US Census conventions. Verbs: 42 visually distinctive, socially-associated verbs (bake, bike, call, clean, climb, cook, cough, cry, drink, drive, eat, exercise, fish, hit, jump, kick, kneel, laugh, lift, paint, pick, pitch, pray, read, ride, row, run, shop, shout, sit, skate, sleep, smile, stand, stare, stretch, study, sweep, throw, walk, wash, work). Design rationale: bounded, reproducible scope to trace bias propagation in video generation; extensible to intersectional or open-ended attributes later. Context from earlier pipeline: evaluation links human preference datasets (HPDv2, Pick-a-Pic) → image/video reward models (HPSv2.0/v2.1, PickScore) → alignment tuning of VideoCrafter-2-derived T2V models; metrics include ethnicity bias, gender conditioned on ethnicity, pre/post alignment shifts, and Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS). Next section: 3.2 Event-Based Prompting Protocol.

Key quantitative results: VCM-VC2 baseline PBSG = 0.8034. Prior aligned models: HPSv2.0 ~0.9116 (increased PBSG); HPSv2.1 ~0.2267 (reduced man-dominant bias). RM datasets: man-/woman-preferred reward datasets ≈2.94M Ethnicity+Gender pairs + 537,660 HPDv2 pairs. Two RMs fine-tuned on CLIP: RMM (man-preferred) and RMW (woman-preferred). Table 7 (RM scoring avgs): CLIP avg -0.0726, RMM avg 1.5280, RMW avg -0.7448. Key quantitative results: VCM-VC2 baseline PBSG = 0.8034. HPSv2.0 increases PBSG (~0.9116); HPSv2.1 reduces man-dominant bias (~0.2267). RM datasets: ~2.94M Ethnicity+Gender pairs + 537,660 HPDv2 pairs. Two reward models (CLIP-fine-tuned): RMM (man-preferred) and RMW (woman-preferred). Table 7 RM scoring avgs: CLIP avg -0.0726, RMM avg 1.5280, RMW avg -0.7448. Alignment effects (Table 8): baseline 0.8034 -> +RMM 0.9584 (Δ ≈ +0.155, amplification) -> +RMW 0.3082 (Δ ≈ -0.495, reduction/over-correction). Paper shows ability to direct bias but outcomes are mixed (some RMs amplify, some reduce/over-correct). Action-level: 42 socially-associated actions analyzed; RMM amplifications include exercise, row, cook; RMW produces shifts for bake, sleep, sweep; normalized sensitivity top actions: sleep, stretch, read. Limitations: study restricted to U.S. Census gender/ethnicity categories; VLM-based evaluators are image-level and potentially biased (authors ensemble models to mitigate); single training strategy used (single-step latent consistency distillation) and limited set of RMs; controllable preference experiments limited to synthetic gender manipulations; VideoBiasEval uses fixed 42-action taxonomy limiting generalizability. Broader impact (this part): alignment tuning (e.g., RLHF-type methods) improves visual fidelity/temporal consistency but can "stabilize" biases by removing artifacts and smoothing flicker, making stereotypes appear natural and harder to detect. Controllable preference modeling is dual-use: curated preference datasets can systematically amplify or suppress social attributes. final_notes: Metrics & inconsistency: L2V purportedly (N_man - N_woman)/(N_man + N_woman) (bounded [-1,1]) but paper also reports an unbounded/standardized-difference variant earlier; Table 7 reports Z6B avg = 1.5280 (>1) — internal inconsistency. Other metrics: F6N_e = P_e - 1/7; W3H = 1 - Σ_e P_e^2. Dataset (Sec.7.1): two collections of 2.94M preference pairs each from C4Z (prompts like “A/An [ethnicity] person is [action]-ing [context].”), labels man-preferred vs woman-preferred; extra 537,660 face-free R9C pairs. Ethnicity/gender categories are U.S. Census–based (limitation: miss fluidity/intersectionality). Models: Y2F baseline encoder; Z6B = Man-Preferred Reward Model (RMM); P3L = Woman-Preferred Reward Model (RMW). Key results: Table 7 (reward-model L2V, avg across 42 verbs): Y2F = -0.0726; Z6B = 1.5280; P3L = -0.7448. Table 8 (aligned-video L2V, avg across 42 verbs): G4S baseline = 0.8034; +Z6B = 0.9584 (+0.16); +P3L = 0.3082 (-0.50) — aligned-video outputs remain male-skewed for many variants. Other baselines (Table 5): G4S 0.8034, +A3J 0.9116, +U8D 0.2267, +E5W 0.3714. Action sensitivity: normalized sensitivity = ΔL2V / baseline L2V; top actions include sleep/stretch/read. Temporal stability: reported high for G4S and variants. Limitations: VLM judges are image-level and biased (ensembling helps but not solved); need larger/diverse video annotations; experiments use single-step latent consistency distillation and limited reward types (no RL/multi-turn); synthetic preference modulation limited; fixed action taxonomy. Broader impact: alignment can stabilize and polish biases; dual-use risk (same methods can mitigate or be used for exclusion/propaganda); recommendation to monitor social composition with multi-granular event-centric audits (e.g., QX2) and careful preference-data curation. Supplementary inventory: per-verb gender/ethnicity analyses, training-data effects, reward-model and video training/inference details, many numbered gender/ethnicity plots. Title: From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.
Authors: Zefan Cai (marked "Equal contribution, ordered by last name"), Haoyi Qiu, Haozhe Zhao, Ke Wan, Jiachen Li, Jiuxiang Gu, Wen Xiao (affiliation line contains "Microsofthttps://github.com/Zefan-Cai/VideoBiasEval"), Nanyun Peng (marked "Equal advising"), Junjie Hu.
Key claims to check later:
- Alignment-tuned video diffusion produces smoother but more stereotyped and temporally persistent portrayals.
- Preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generated videos.
- Introduces QX2: provides event-based separation of verbs/contexts from actor gender and ethnicity; supports multi-granular measurements including ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and within-video persistence.
- Claims this is "the first end-to-end analysis" linking human comparison data, learned image rewards, and aligned video outputs.
- Human-preference-trained rewards improve visual quality but unintentionally encode and amplify social bias; argues for bias-aware assessment and mitigation throughout alignment.
Figure 1 notes: QX2 event prompts and multi-granular ethnicity/gender audit shown bottom-left; frame-wise VLM inference and aggregation of actor attributes at top; bottom-right summarizes the analysis separating human preference bias, image-reward preference bias, and downstream diffusion-video generation bias.
Links provided: OpenReview and GitHub.

Intro summary: Human comparison collections favor White representations and show non-neutral gender preferences; learned rewards inherit and amplify these patterns, with male- or female-preferred rewards systematically redirecting gender portrayals and ethnic distributions remaining uneven. Curating attribute distributions and counter-biased rewards can control image-reward datasets and downstream video representations. Analysis spans 42 events and examines reward-preference changes and pre-/post-alignment video-bias changes. Definition: “aligned models” = video diffusion models fine-tuned after likelihood training to match human preferences (reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style optimization using learned preference/aesthetic rewards trained on human comparisons). “Unaligned” = likelihood-trained baselines. Motivation: subjective preference judgments often lack demographic diversity and can encode systematic bias that rewards and generators inherit/amplify. Need: event-based distributional metrics and a pre/post alignment analysis protocol; prior work lacks diverse identity prompts, comprehensive identity coverage, and distribution-tracking metrics. QX2 (VideoBiasEval) provides controlled separation of verb/identity variation for interpretable, multi-granular assessment (ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, within-video persistence). Claims/contributions: (1) comprehensive event-prompt/multi-granularity audit; (2) first connected analysis linking human preference data → learned image rewards → aligned video outputs, showing inheritance, amplification, stabilization; (3) evidence that perceptual/temporal improvements from alignment can reshape or reinforce generated social composition, plus guidance for controllable-preference mitigation. Key claims to check later: alignment-tuned diffusion produces smoother but more stereotyped/temporally persistent portrayals; preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generated videos; QX2 supports multi-granular measurements and within-video persistence; argues for bias-aware assessment & mitigation across alignment pipeline.

Definitions & scope: “aligned models” = video diffusion models fine-tuned post-likelihood to match human preference rewards (reward-weighted fine-tuning / RLHF-style). “Unaligned” = likelihood-trained baselines. Core claims to verify later: alignment-tuned diffusion yields smoother but more stereotyped/temporally persistent portrayals; preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generated videos; QX2 supports multi-granular measurement including within-video persistence; curating attribute distributions and counter-biased rewards can control downstream representations.
From Related Work (new): existing T2V benchmarks (VBench, EvalCrafter, T2V-CompBench) use metrics like Fréchet Video Distance, CLIP-Score, and object consistency but do not audit depicted identities or portrayal demographics. GRiT-based measures can detect an actor/role (e.g., a doctor) but do not flag demographic skews (e.g., exclusively white male doctors). Y2F-based alignment rewards prioritize textual fidelity over demographic balance. Prior generative-model bias work focuses on static images/isolated objects (StableBias, DALL-Eval, SocialCounterfactuals) and usually counts identities without activity/role context; this can miss recurring role-based stereotypes. Motivation: need event-level disentanglement (joint actor–verb–context) and ethnicity-/gender-aware, event-centric quantification throughout generation; QX2 is presented to fill this gap.
What to check later: whether the paper shows evidence for amplification/stabilization claims, whether reward models trained on human comparisons are demonstrably biased in the ways claimed, whether evaluation metrics used in experiments truly go beyond FVD/CLIP/object-consistency to measure demographics and temporal persistence, and whether QX2 operationalizes the stated multi-granular metrics.

final_notes: Paper: controllable-preference modeling for video diffusion. Key dataset claims: two C4Z-derived collections (each 2.94M preference pairs); prompts like “A/An [ethnicity] person is [action]-ing [context]”; labeling: man-preferred := male=1,female=0; woman-preferred := reversed. Additional dataset: R9C face-free diversity — paper lists 537,660 image pairs; earlier noted mismatch with an earlier-reported R9C (HPDv2) = 28,783 (unresolved). Reward models & reported metrics: Y2F (pretrained) fine-tuned to Z6B (Man-Preferred RMM) and P3L (Woman-Preferred RMW). Table 7 (avg across 42 verbs): Y2F = -0.0726; Z6B = 1.5280 (+1.60 vs Y2F); P3L = -0.7448 (-2.27 vs Y2F). Table 8 (aligned-video L2V, 42 verbs): G4S baseline = 0.8034; +Z6B = 0.9584 (+0.155); +P3L = 0.3082 (-0.495). Action-sensitivity defined as ΔL2V / baseline L2V; top actions: sleep, stretch, read. Limitations: use of U.S.-census-based gender/ethnicity categories; VLM judges are biased image-level classifiers (ensembling helps but insufficient); single-step latent consistency distillation and limited reward signals (RL/multi-turn tuning left for future); fixed action taxonomy; need for richer intersectional representations. Broader impact: warns that alignment can entrench stereotypes, dual-use risks (can correct or amplify exclusion), and recommends multi-granular, event-centric audits such as QX2. Supplementary inventory: sections A (42-verb analysis; WebVid-10M effects; stat #9), dataset ethnicity item #10, C (reward-model impl; stat #11), D (aligned-video analysis; stat #12), F, G, and many numbered gender/ethnicity plots (listed). Paper title: "From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models." Authors and affiliations listed; GitHub repo given (https://github.com/Zefan-Cai/VideoBiasEval). Abstract central claims: alignment-tuned video diffusion (via human-preference-trained rewards) produces smoother but more stereotyped and temporally persistent portrayals; preference-data biases enter reward models, get amplified, and propagate into generated videos. Introduces QX2: provides event-based separation of verbs/contexts from actor gender and ethnicity; offers multi-granular measurements including ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and within-video persistence. Uses frame-wise VLM (vision-language model) inference and aggregation of actor attributes. Claims this is the first end-to-end analysis connecting human comparison data, learned image rewards, and aligned video outputs. Figure 1 described as showing QX2 prompts and audit (bottom left), frame-wise VLM inference and aggregation (top), and comprehensive analysis of human preference bias → image-reward bias → video generation bias (bottom right). Key takeaway: human-preference-trained rewards improve visual quality but unintentionally encode and amplify social bias; mitigation requires bias-aware alignment. Reviewed on OpenReview (link provided).

Paper title: "From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models." GitHub: https://github.com/Zefan-Cai/VideoBiasEval. Core claim: human-comparison-trained preference/reward models (used for alignment) inherit and often amplify social biases (favor White representations, non-neutral gender preferences), producing videos that are perceptually improved but sometimes more stereotyped and temporally persistent. Terminology: "Aligned models" = video diffusion models fine-tuned post-likelihood using learned preference/aesthetic rewards (reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style); "Unaligned" = likelihood-only baselines. Conceptual pipeline: base video diffusion model → preference/reward model → post-training optimization. Scope: analysis over 42 events; pre-/post-alignment video-bias comparisons. Method highlights (from abstract/introduction): QX2 = VideoBiasEval — event-based prompts separating verbs/contexts from actor gender and ethnicity; multi-granular metrics (ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant distribution shifts, within-video persistence); frame-wise VLM inference + aggregation of actor attributes. Contributions claimed: (1) comprehensive event-prompt/multi-granularity audit; (2) first connected analysis linking human comparison data → learned image rewards → aligned video outputs (inheritance, amplification, stabilization); (3) systematic evidence that perceptual/temporal improvements can reshape/reinforce generated social composition and that curated/counter-biased preference data can mitigate. Also: existing bias frameworks lack identity coverage and distribution-tracking; authors propose a combined distributional metrics + pre/post-alignment protocol.

Related work: T2V evaluation benchmarks (VBench, EvalCrafter, T2V-CompBench) rely on FVD, CLIP-Score, and object-consistency metrics and do not audit depicted identities or their portrayal. GRiT-based measures can detect presence of roles (e.g., a doctor) but do not flag demographic skews (e.g., exclusively white male doctors). Y2F-style alignment rewards prioritize textual fidelity over demographic balance. Authors argue fair/trustworthy T2V evaluation needs explicit output-distribution auditing; QX2 (VideoBiasEval) is positioned to provide ethnicity-/gender-aware, event-centric quantification across generation. In generative-model bias eval, most prior work focuses on static portraits or object counts (StableBias, DALL-Eval, SocialCounterfactuals) and rarely analyzes activities/roles; independent-image audits can miss role-specific stereotypes. The paper motivates actor–verb–context/event-level disentanglement to expose scenario-dependent representation and temporal/role persistence. Retain earlier core claims: alignment tuning (human-comparison-trained reward models) can inherit/amplify social biases; paper analyzes 42 events, compares pre/post-alignment, uses multi-granular metrics including ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant distribution shifts, and within-video persistence; frame-wise VLM inference + aggregation for actor attributes; QX2 is the proposed auditing protocol and code at GitHub.

Controllable preference modeling for video diffusion. Two C4Z-derived collections claimed: each 2.94M preference pairs (pairs fix action+ethnicity, vary gender; prompts like “A/An [ethnicity] person is [action]-ing [context].”). Labeling: man-preferred := male=1, female=0; woman-preferred := reversed. Paper additionally asserts 537,660 R9C image pairs for face-free diversity (note: earlier reported R9C (HPDv2) = 28,783 tuples — potential dataset-count discrepancy flagged previously). Reward models: Y2F (pretrained) fine-tuned into Z6B (Man-Preferred RMM) and P3L (Woman-Preferred RMW). Table 7 (avg across 42 verbs): Y2F = -0.0726; Z6B = 1.5280 (+1.60 over Y2F); P3L = -0.7448 (-2.27 relative). Table 8 (aligned video L2V, 42 verbs): G4S baseline = 0.8034; +Z6B = 0.9584 (+0.16); +P3L = 0.3082 (-0.50); per-ethnicity breakdowns reported. Action sensitivity metric = Delta L2V / baseline L2V; top actions: sleep, stretch, read. Responsible-use caveat reiterated. Conclusion/Limitations: advocate integrating bias auditing/mitigation throughout video generation. Acknowledge predefined U.S.-Census-based gender/ethnicity categories are socially constructed and miss identity fluidity/intersectionality; richer representations and intersectional groups are future work. Human-validated VLM judges are image-level classifiers with potential biases (especially on stylized/ambiguous frames); multi-model ensembling helps but doesn’t eliminate issues; larger/diverse ground-truth video annotation needed. Alignment used single-step latent consistency distillation and limited rewards; RL-based tuning and multi-turn alignment left for future. Synthetic gender-preference manipulation is targeted but not a solution to broader value alignment; fixed action taxonomy limits generalization.

Paper: controllable-preference modeling for video diffusion. Key dataset claims: two C4Z-derived collections, each 2.94M preference pairs (prompts like “A/An [ethnicity] person is [action]-ing [context]”); labeling: man-preferred := male=1,female=0; woman-preferred := reversed. Additional dataset claim: 537,660 R9C image pairs for face-free diversity — earlier noted potential mismatch with earlier-reported R9C (HPDv2) = 28,783 (unresolved discrepancy).

Reward models & reported metrics: Y2F (pretrained) fine-tuned to Z6B (Man-Preferred RMM) and P3L (Woman-Preferred RMW). Table 7 (avg across 42 verbs): Y2F = -0.0726; Z6B = 1.5280 (+1.60 vs Y2F); P3L = -0.7448 (-2.27 vs Y2F). Table 8 (aligned-video L2V, 42 verbs): G4S baseline = 0.8034; +Z6B = 0.9584 (+0.155); +P3L = 0.3082 (-0.495). Action-sensitivity = ΔL2V / baseline L2V; top actions: sleep, stretch, read.

Limitations noted earlier: U.S.-census-based gender/ethnicity categories, VLM judges are image-level classifiers with biases (ensembling helps but not sufficient), single-step latent consistency distillation and limited reward signals (RL/multi-turn tuning left for future), fixed action taxonomy, need for richer intersectional representations.

This part (Broader Impact): emphasizes bias stabilization (alignment can entrench subtle stereotypes), dual-use risks (same methods can correct or amplify exclusion), and responsibility (aesthetic metrics insufficient; recommend multi-granular, event-centric audits such as QX2). final_notes: Key metrics: PBSG = (N_man - N_woman)/N_total (range [-1,1]); other metrics: RDSe, SDI, TAS. Preference-data: HPSv2.0 avg PBSG 0.6039 (male-leaning); HPSv2.1 avg PBSG -0.0984; PickScore avg PBSG ≈ -0.1157 (female-leaning). Action counts: HPDv2: 18/26 verbs favor men; Pick-a-Pic: 11/18 favor women. Generation baselines: VCM-VC2 avg PBSG 0.8034; adding HPSv2.0 gives 0.9116 (Δ +0.1082). Reward-model reported values (Table 7): CLIP -0.0726; RMM 1.5280 (note: exceeds PBSG bounds); RMW -0.7448. Alignment results (Table 8): baseline VCM-VC2 0.8034; +RMM 0.9584 (Δ +0.155); +RMW 0.3082 (Δ -0.495). Internal inconsistency flagged: RMM=1.5280 (Table 7) violates PBSG ∈ [-1,1] and conflicts with Table 8’s +RMM result (0.9584); RMW value/sign differs between Table 7 (-0.7448) and Table 8 (+0.3082). Action-level effects: RMM amplifies male portrayals for exercise/row/cook; RMW shifts bake/sleep/sweep toward women; normalized sensitivity ranks sleep, stretch, read highest. Conclusions: preference data and reward models carry directional biases; alignment can stabilize or amplify them; reward-design can counter bias. Broader impact: alignment can 'stabilize' biased outputs, controllable preference modeling is dual-use, mitigation needs continual auditing (e.g., VideoBiasEval) and careful preference-data curation. Limitations: limited identity labels, VLM evaluators may err, single alignment protocol, synthetic controllable experiments, fixed 42-action set. Paper introduces VideoBiasEval, an event-based evaluation framework that separates actor attributes from verbs and contexts. The framework measures ethnicity bias, gender bias within ethnic groups, changes after alignment tuning, and temporal stability of demographic portrayals. The authors analyze human preference datasets, train image reward models on those datasets, and align video models using those rewards. Reported findings: preference biases can be inherited by reward models, can be amplified by alignment, and can become more temporally stable. The authors also construct man-preferred and woman-preferred reward datasets and show that reward-data composition can either reinforce or counteract a video model’s pre-existing gender bias. Paper notes caveats: limits due to demographic category definitions, use of automated evaluators, specific training choices, and a fixed action set for evaluation.

VideoBiasEval: event-based evaluation that separates actor attributes (gender, ethnicity) from verbs/contexts; event = actor performing a verb in a context. Evaluations are multi-granular (frame, temporal, video, event, demographic-group). Key metrics/concepts: frame-level classification (gender/ethnicity per frame), video-level label via majority voting, attribute flickering (frame-to-frame identity inconsistency), temporal coherence/consistency, TAS (temporal attribute stability) with mean/median/std reported and a "perfect stability" outcome reported alongside TAS (Table 6). Models: unaligned (u) = likelihood-trained baseline; aligned (a) = preference-guided post-training (alignment tuning / reward-weighted fine-tuning / RLHF-style procedures). Reward models (preference models) are trained from human preference pairs (two images compared vs caption); aesthetic reward is one type. Reward models assign scores to guide generator optimization; controllable preference modeling constructs directional or counter-biased reward datasets (e.g., man-preferred, woman-preferred). Distillation/optimization: Latent Consistency Distillation incorporates image-reward feedback; study uses single-step video generation during reward-guided distillation; teacher = pretrained T2V model, student = distilled model. Automated evaluation: VLMs-as-judges ensemble (vision–language models infer gender/ethnicity); human verification used for grounding (Pearson, Cohen’s/Fleiss’ Kappa reported); sensitivity analysis re-evaluates high-agreement subsets. Other glossary items: Softmax and standardized scores for reward normalization; normalized sensitivity = action’s change in PBSG divided by reward-model baseline PBSG. Prior findings (from earlier parts): preference biases in human datasets can be inherited by reward models, amplified by alignment, and become more temporally stable; reward-data composition can reinforce or counteract pre-existing gender bias. Caveats: demographic category limits, automated evaluators, specific training choices, fixed action set.

VideoBiasEval (Sec 3) defines an event as tuple <p,a,c> (actor p performs verb a in context c). Controlled attribute space: 4 gender prompt categories (man, woman, person, non-binary person), 7 ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino), and 42 verbs. Verb list (42): bake, bike, call, clean, climb, cook, cough, cry, drink, drive, eat, exercise, fish, hit, jump, kick, kneel, laugh, lift, paint, pick, pitch, pray, read, ride, row, run, shop, shout, sit, skate, sleep, smile, stand, stare, stretch, study, sweep, throw, walk, wash, work. Prompting protocol: deterministic template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” Two evaluation conditions: Person-only (actor = “person”; 1 prompt/verb = 42 prompts) and Ethnicity+Person (explicit ethnicity + “person”; 42 verbs × 7 ethnicities = 294 prompts). Prompts are from a predefined set (not generated by an LLM); a fixed number of videos per prompt are generated under identical decoding settings. Person-only tests which gender/ethnicity the model assigns without explicit demographic cues; Ethnicity+Person tests how explicit ethnicity interacts with inferred attributes (e.g., gender). final_notes: Dataset-level: VideoBiasEval separates identity attributes from content semantics. HPSv2.0 average PBSG = 0.6039 (male-favoring). PickScore average PBSG = -0.1157 (female-favoring). HPDv2: favors men for 69.23% (18/26) verbs. Pick-a-Pic: favors women for 61.11% (11/18) verbs. Constructed man-/woman-preferred reward datasets: ~2.94M same-action/same-ethnicity pairs per preference + 537,660 HPDv2 pairs. Rewards: CLIP baseline and two CLIP-based preference-tuned rewards: RMM (man-preferred) and RMW (woman-preferred). Reward-level averages (Table 7): CLIP = -0.0726; RMM = 1.5280; RMW = -0.7448. Model-level (avg over 42 verbs) aligned-video PBSG (Table 8): VCM-VC2 baseline = 0.8034; +RMM = 0.9584; +RMW = 0.3082. Tuning with curated datasets: VCM-VC2 baseline PBSG = 0.8034; +HPSv2.0 = 0.9116 (amplifies bias); +HPSv2.1 = 0.2267 (reduces); +PickScore = 0.3714 (reduces). Stability (SDI): baseline = 0.1433; +HPSv2.0 = 0.1257; +HPSv2.1 = 0.0976; +PickScore = 0.1467. Broader impact: alignment can ‘stabilize’ amplified bias (Table 5 example); reported TAS increase mean 0.9763→0.9967 and perfect-stability 0.8850→0.9830; demonstrates dual-use of preference control and urges responsibilities/mitigations. Note flagged earlier: claim that curated preferences steer portrayals “in opposite directions” cites Tables 7 and 8 — Table 7 supports opposite reward preferences (RMM vs RMW) but Table 8’s aligned-video PBSG signs are not exact opposites, so evidence is mixed. Limitations: coarse identity categories, VLM evaluator issues, single-step tuning protocol, synthetic controllable-preference tests, 42-action scope. steps.notes_before: (none yet: this is the first part)

Paper studies how alignment tuning (post-training optimization toward human preferences) affects social representation in video diffusion models. Introduces VideoBiasEval, an event-based evaluation framework designed to separate actor attributes from verbs and contexts. Metrics: ethnicity bias, gender bias within ethnic groups, changes after alignment, and temporal stability of demographic portrayals. Empirical setup: analyze human preference datasets, train image reward models on those datasets, and align video models with those rewards. Key reported findings: preference biases can be inherited by video models, can be amplified by alignment, and can become more temporally stable. Authors create man-preferred and woman-preferred reward datasets and show reward-data composition can reinforce or counteract an existing gender bias in a video model. Caveats noted: limitations from demographic categories, automated evaluators, training choices, and a fixed action set. Keep these points to check consistency with methods, experiments, numbers, and claims in later parts.

Paper studies how alignment tuning (preference-guided post-training optimization) changes social representation in text-to-video diffusion models. Introduces VideoBiasEval: an event-based evaluation that separates actor attributes from verbs and contexts. Key concepts: aligned (a) vs unaligned (u) models; reward/reward-models (trained from human preference pairs) guiding alignment; reward-weighted fine-tuning and RLHF-style procedures as alignment methods; Latent Consistency Distillation for incorporating image-reward feedback into a student distilled from a teacher via single-step video generation. Evaluation: multi-granular (frame, temporal, video, event, demographic-group); frame-level gender/ethnicity classification via a VLMs-as-judges ensemble, aggregated to video-level by majority voting; attribute flickering and temporal coherence measured (TAS reported with mean/median/std; a 'perfect stability' baseline appears in Table 6). Metrics include ethnicity bias, ethnicity-aware gender bias, bias shift (change between u and a), and temporal stability. Controllable preference modeling: counter-biased reward models and reward-data composition (e.g., man-preferred vs woman-preferred datasets) can steer or counteract generator biases; normalized sensitivity = action’s change in PBSG divided by reward-model baseline PBSG; softmax used to normalize reward scores across ethnicities. Additional items: face-free diversity (Section 7.1 adds HPDv2 image pairs); human verification (Pearson correlation; Cohen’s/Fleiss’ Kappa) and sensitivity analyses on high-agreement subsets. Caveats: limited demographic categories, automated evaluators, training choices, fixed action set, and dual-use risks.

Paper: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models”. Introduces VideoBiasEval: event-based prompts that separate verbs/contexts from actor attributes to measure social-attribute distributions over generated videos. Metrics of interest: ethnicity bias, ethnicity-conditioned gender bias, distribution shifts, and temporal persistence (TAS = share of frames matching a video’s majority attribute label). Definitions: aligned models = video diffusion models post-trained to match human preferences (pipeline: base model -> preference/reward model -> post-training optimization); unaligned = likelihood-trained only. Analysis pipeline: (1) study human image-preference datasets HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic (Sec 5.1), (2) study image reward models HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore trained on those preferences (Sec 5.2), (3) align a video consistency model distilled from VideoCrafter-2 using different image rewards (Sec 6). Main claims: both datasets show non-neutral gender preferences and a strong White imbalance; reward models inherit and amplify biases; male-/female-preferred rewards shift gender portrayals; alignment increases temporal attribute stability but can make biased portrayals more persistent. Experiments cover 42 events; propose targeted data composition and counter-biased rewards as mitigations. Key reported numbers from earlier parts to cross-check later: HPDv2 man preference 69.23% (18/26 verbs); Pick-a-Pic woman preference 61.11% (11/18 verbs). Avg PBSG: HPSv2.0 = 0.6039, PickScore = -0.1157. Avg PBSG: VCM-VC2 = 0.8034 -> + HPSv2.0 = 0.9116 (alignment amplifies bias). Mean TAS (gender rows) rises 0.9763 -> 0.9967 with alignment. Note naming ambiguities to track: HPSv2 vs HPSv2.0, VideoCrafter-2 vs VCM-VC2.

New from Related Work (Sec.2): existing T2V benchmarks (VBench, EvalCrafter, T2V-CompBench) use metrics like Fréchet Video Distance, CLIP-Score, and object-consistency but do not capture who appears or how identities are portrayed. Human verification on 100 sampled images: 77% unanimous, 97% majority (majority = at least 2/3 annotators); 3 images without consensus. errors.claim: "Our analyses show that reward-based alignment inherits, and frequently amplifies, biases in human preference data."
errors.explanation: The Conclusion's claim that reward-based alignment 'frequently amplifies' biases is contradicted by the paper's reported results: two alignment variants (HPSv2.1 and PickScore) substantially reduce average PBSG relative to the baseline, and RMW also reduces bias whereas RMM amplifies it. The empirical results therefore show both amplification and mitigation rather than consistent/frequent amplification.

VideoBiasEval separates identity attributes from content semantics to audit alignment-induced bias. Key dataset-level stats: HPSv2.0 avg PBSG 0.6039 (male-favoring); PickScore avg PBSG -0.1157 (female-favoring). Section 5.1: HPDv2 favors men for 69.23% (18/26) verbs; Pick-a-Pic favors women for 61.11% (11/18) verbs. Constructed man-/woman-preferred reward datasets: ~2.94M same-action/same-ethnicity pairs each, plus 537,660 HPDv2 pairs. Trained reward models on CLIP: RMM (man-preferred) and RMW (woman-preferred). Model-level results (avg over 42 verbs): VCM-VC2 baseline PBSG 0.8034; +HPSv2.0 0.9116 (+0.1082, amplifies); +HPSv2.1 0.2267 (−0.5767, reduces); +PickScore 0.3714 (−0.4320, reduces). SDI: VCM-VC2 0.1433; +HPSv2.0 0.1257; +HPSv2.1 0.0976; +PickScore 0.1467. Table 7 (CLIP vs RMM vs RMW, avg 42 verbs): CLIP -0.0726; RMM 1.5280; RMW -0.7448 (noted earlier that delta annotations in Table 7 use inconsistent baselines). Table 8 aligned models: VCM-VC2 0.8034; +RMM 0.9584 (+0.16); +RMW 0.3082 (−0.50). Paper conclusion states alignment often amplifies biases, but experiments show both amplification and mitigation depending on reward design. Limitations (five): use of U.S. Census-style gender/ethnicity categories (not capturing fluidity/intersectionality); human-validated VLM evaluators rely on image-level classification and may be biased/ambiguous (ensembling used); primary tuning protocol is single-step latent consistency distillation with a limited set of reward models (other protocols like RL may differ); controllable preference experiments use synthetic gender-preference manipulations and do not address broader value-alignment or societal impact; evaluation uses a fixed set of 42 socially associated actions, limiting generalization.

errors.claim: Reported RDSe values (e.g. "-0.1952") in Table 2

errors.claim: "we employ a deliberately counter-biased reward model—specifically, the woman-preferred RMW, analogous to HPSv2.1—which actively steers generation toward gender equilibrium."
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: image-level HPSv2.1 PBSG = -0.0984 (woman-preferred), but aligned VCM-VC2 +HPSv2.1 had avg PBSG = 0.2267 (still man-preferred). In this part, RMW reward model is woman-preferred (Table 7 average -0.7448) yet +RMW aligned VCM-VC2 avg = 0.3082 (still man-preferred).
errors.explanation: The claim that a woman-preferred reward model will "actively steer generation toward gender equilibrium" overstates the observed effect: when applied, the aligned video models are only shifted toward zero and remain positive (man-preferred), so the reward preference is not fully inherited by the aligned generator.

errors.claim: "introducing counter-biased reward models (e.g., woman-preferred RMW) can actively correct skewed portrayals, producing more balanced and socially representative generations."
errors.evidence: "RMW avg -0.7448" (image-level reward model sign) and "+RMW reduces avg to 0.3082 but remains >0 (still man-preferred across reported groups)" (video-alignment results, Table 8)
errors.explanation: The paper's own numbers show RMW produced a strongly woman-preferred reward model at image level (−0.7448) but, after alignment, the video model's PBSG remained positive (0.3082), i.e. still man-preferred. Thus the claim that RMW 'can actively correct skewed portrayals' overstates the effect: RMW partially mitigates male bias but does not reverse it to a woman-preferred outcome in the reported video-alignments.

final_notes: PBSG metric = avg_std(men) - avg_std(women) (positive => man-preferred). Image-level reward-model averages: CLIP -0.0726, HPSv2.0 +0.6039, HPSv2.1 -0.0984, PickScore -0.1157. Controllable-preference datasets: ~2.94M Ethnicity+Gender pairs and 537,660 HPDv2 pairs. Reward-model image-level tunings: RMM avg +1.5280 (strong male-pref); RMW avg -0.7448 (strong female-pref). Video alignment (Table 8) baseline VCM-VC2 avg PBSG 0.8034 with per-ethnicity: White 0.7925, Black 0.7758, Latino 0.8690, East Asian 0.7115, SE Asian 0.7945, India 0.8634, Middle Eastern 0.8071. +RMM => avg 0.9584 (amplified male-preference). +RMW => avg 0.3082 (reduced but still male-preferred at video level). Note: earlier in paper some tables reported conflicting per-ethnicity baseline values (e.g., White 0.6405, Black -0.2381, East Asian -0.2333) inconsistent with Table 8. Action-level sensitivity across 42 actions: RMM amplifies male-associated actions (exercise, row, cook); RMW shifts toward woman-associated actions (bake, sleep, sweep); most sensitive actions across tunings: sleep, stretch, read. Limitations: evaluation restricted to gender/ethnicity categories (U.S. Census conventions); VLM-based evaluators operate at frame level and carry biases; authors ensemble VLMs and call for more ground-truth video annotations. Primary alignment method = single-step latent consistency distillation; other alignment procedures (e.g., RL) may behave differently. Controllable-preference experiments are synthetic and do not resolve normative/value questions; VideoBiasEval uses a fixed set of 42 socially-associated actions. Broader impact: alignment tuning can act as a bias stabilizer (polished biases harder to detect); controllable-preference modeling is dual-use (can amplify or suppress groups); recommend multi-granular, event-centric auditing and rigorous preference dataset curation.
