steps.notes_before: Title: From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models. Authors: Zefan Cai (UW–Madison), Haoyi Qiu, Haozhe Zhao, Ke Wan (UCSD), Jiachen Li (UCSB), Jiuxiang Gu, Wen Xiao (Microsoft; GitHub link noted), Nanyun Peng (UCLA), Junjie Hu (UIUC). Note: footnote marker †† is used twice with different meanings (equal contribution and equal advising) — inconsistent. Abstract: introduce VideoBiasEval, a diagnostic framework for social bias in text-to-video generation. Key methods: event-based prompting to separate semantic content (verbs/contexts) from actor attributes (gender/ethnicity); multi-granular metrics for (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) distributional shifts across model variants, (4) temporal persistence of bias in videos. Analysis: end-to-end trace from human preference datasets → reward models → alignment-tuned video diffusion models; claim this is the first such end-to-end analysis. Findings: alignment tuning amplifies representational biases and makes them temporally stable, producing smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Figure 1 caption references Sections 3, 3.3, 5.1, 5.2, and 6 and mentions VLMs inferring actor attributes across frames and aggregating for bias quantification.

Title: From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models. Authors: Zefan Cai et al. (footnote marker †† appears used twice in title block — inconsistent). Key claim/goal: introduce VideoBiasEval, a diagnostic framework to analyze social bias in text-to-video generation and to trace effects of alignment tuning. Definitions: 'aligned models' = video diffusion models undergoing post-training optimization to better match human preferences (via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style procedures using learned reward/preference models trained on human comparisons). Pipeline: base video diffusion model → preference/reward model → post-training optimization. 'Unaligned counterparts' = models trained only with likelihood-based objectives, used as baselines. Motivation: alignment improves perceptual quality and temporal coherence but may encode/reinforce human preference biases, affecting representation (who is generated, roles, frequency). VideoBiasEval methods: event-based prompting to separate verb/context (semantic content) from actor identity attributes; uses established social bias taxonomies; focuses on gender and ethnicity. Metrics: multi-granular metrics to assess (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) shifts in social attribute distributions across models, and (4) temporal persistence of bias within videos. Paper promises an end-to-end analysis tracing how social attribute distributions evolve through the alignment tuning pipeline. Existing eval gaps listed (limited identity coverage in prompts; lack of specific metrics; lack of methods to track pre/post alignment shifts).

Goal: introduce VideoBiasEval to diagnose social bias in text-to-video generation and trace effects of alignment tuning. Pipeline: base video diffusion model → human preference dataset → image reward model (e.g., HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore) → post-training alignment tuning (reward-weighted fine-tuning) producing an 'aligned' video diffusion model; compare to unaligned (likelihood-trained) baselines. Data & models examined: human preference datasets HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic; reward models HPSv2.0/HPSv2.1 and PickScore; a video consistency model distilled from VideoCrafter-2 is fine-tuned for experiments. Key empirical claims: (1) HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic show non-neutral gender preferences and a strong imbalance favoring White representations; (2) reward models inherit and amplify these biases; (3) alignment-tuned video models propagate biases—alignment with male- or female-preferred reward models systematically shifts gender portrayals while ethnic representation stays uneven; (4) Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS): alignment improves temporal consistency of social attribute portrayals but can make biased portrayals more persistent and visually stable. They also explore constructing controllable image reward datasets (Section 7) and report analyses across 42 events, claiming controllable/counter-biased reward modeling as a mitigation strategy. Contributions summarized: VideoBiasEval framework, first end-to-end analysis linking datasets→reward models→aligned video models, and experiments showing alignment improves quality/coherence while reshaping/reinforcing social composition.

Goal: introduce VideoBiasEval to diagnose social bias in text-to-video generation and trace effects of alignment tuning. Pipeline: base video diffusion model → human preference dataset → image reward model (HPSv2.0/HPSv2.1, PickScore) → reward-weighted fine-tuning producing 'aligned' video diffusion model; compare to unaligned (likelihood-trained) baselines. Key empirical claims: (1) HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic show non-neutral gender preferences and a strong imbalance favoring White representations; (2) reward models inherit and amplify these biases; (3) alignment-tuned video models propagate biases—alignment with male- or female-preferred reward models systematically shifts gender portrayals while ethnic representation stays uneven; (4) Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS): alignment improves temporal consistency of social attribute portrayals but can make biased portrayals more persistent. Also explore constructing controllable image reward datasets and claim controllable/counter-biased reward modeling as mitigation. Related work: existing T2V benchmarks (VBench, EvalCrafter, T2V-CompBench) use metrics like Fréchet Video Distance, CLIP-Score, object consistency but overlook who is depicted and demographic balance; GRiT/CLIP-based metrics verify presence/faithfulness of entities but fail to audit demographic representation or event-level role/verb/context joint patterns. This work proposes an event-centric, actor-verb-environment audit for gender and ethnicity-aware biases across the T2V pipeline.

VideoBiasEval: event-based framework for evaluating social biases in video diffusion models. Use structured prompts varying actor gender/ethnicity across real-world events; generate videos and extract social attributes via a VLM-based evaluation (Sec. 3.3). Events modeled as tuple <p,a,c> (actor p performs verb a in context c). Controlled attribute space: 4 gender categories (man, woman, the neutral term “person,” non-binary person) per Luccioni et al.; 7 ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino) per Karkkainen & Joo / US Census conventions. Verb set: 42 visually distinctive verbs (bake; bike; call; clean; climb; cook; cough; cry; drink; drive; eat; exercise; fish; hit; jump; kick; kneel; laugh; lift; paint; pick; pitch; pray; read; ride; row; run; shop; shout; sit; skate; sleep; smile; stand; stare; stretch; study; sweep; throw; walk; wash; work). Section 3.2 begins Event-Based Prompting Protocol (Settings) but details not shown in this part. Framing emphasizes reproducibility and bounded scope to trace bias propagation; connects to earlier claims about actor-verb-environment audit and later analyses (e.g., temporal consistency/TAS).

Title: From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.
Authors: Zefan Cai (marked "Equal contribution, ordered by last name"), Haoyi Qiu, Haozhe Zhao, Ke Wan, Jiachen Li, Jiuxiang Gu, Wen Xiao (affiliation line contains "Microsofthttps://github.com/Zefan-Cai/VideoBiasEval"), Nanyun Peng (marked "Equal advising"), Junjie Hu.
Key claims to check later:
- Alignment-tuned video diffusion produces smoother but more stereotyped and temporally persistent portrayals.
- Preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generated videos.
- Introduces QX2: provides event-based separation of verbs/contexts from actor gender and ethnicity; supports multi-granular measurements including ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and within-video persistence.
- Claims this is "the first end-to-end analysis" linking human comparison data, learned image rewards, and aligned video outputs.
- Human-preference-trained rewards improve visual quality but unintentionally encode and amplify social bias; argues for bias-aware assessment and mitigation throughout alignment.
Figure 1 notes: QX2 event prompts and multi-granular ethnicity/gender audit shown bottom-left; frame-wise VLM inference and aggregation of actor attributes at top; bottom-right summarizes the analysis separating human preference bias, image-reward preference bias, and downstream diffusion-video generation bias.
Links provided: OpenReview and GitHub.

Intro summary: Human comparison collections favor White representations and show non-neutral gender preferences; learned rewards inherit and amplify these patterns, with male- or female-preferred rewards systematically redirecting gender portrayals and ethnic distributions remaining uneven. Curating attribute distributions and counter-biased rewards can control image-reward datasets and downstream video representations. Analysis spans 42 events and examines reward-preference changes and pre-/post-alignment video-bias changes. Definition: “aligned models” = video diffusion models fine-tuned after likelihood training to match human preferences (reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style optimization using learned preference/aesthetic rewards trained on human comparisons). “Unaligned” = likelihood-trained baselines. Motivation: subjective preference judgments often lack demographic diversity and can encode systematic bias that rewards and generators inherit/amplify. Need: event-based distributional metrics and a pre/post alignment analysis protocol; prior work lacks diverse identity prompts, comprehensive identity coverage, and distribution-tracking metrics. QX2 (VideoBiasEval) provides controlled separation of verb/identity variation for interpretable, multi-granular assessment (ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, within-video persistence). Claims/contributions: (1) comprehensive event-prompt/multi-granularity audit; (2) first connected analysis linking human preference data → learned image rewards → aligned video outputs, showing inheritance, amplification, stabilization; (3) evidence that perceptual/temporal improvements from alignment can reshape or reinforce generated social composition, plus guidance for controllable-preference mitigation. Key claims to check later: alignment-tuned diffusion produces smoother but more stereotyped/temporally persistent portrayals; preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generated videos; QX2 supports multi-granular measurements and within-video persistence; argues for bias-aware assessment & mitigation across alignment pipeline.

Definitions & scope: “aligned models” = video diffusion models fine-tuned post-likelihood to match human preference rewards (reward-weighted fine-tuning / RLHF-style). “Unaligned” = likelihood-trained baselines. Core claims to verify later: alignment-tuned diffusion yields smoother but more stereotyped/temporally persistent portrayals; preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generated videos; QX2 supports multi-granular measurement including within-video persistence; curating attribute distributions and counter-biased rewards can control downstream representations.
From Related Work (new): existing T2V benchmarks (VBench, EvalCrafter, T2V-CompBench) use metrics like Fréchet Video Distance, CLIP-Score, and object consistency but do not audit depicted identities or portrayal demographics. GRiT-based measures can detect an actor/role (e.g., a doctor) but do not flag demographic skews (e.g., exclusively white male doctors). Y2F-based alignment rewards prioritize textual fidelity over demographic balance. Prior generative-model bias work focuses on static images/isolated objects (StableBias, DALL-Eval, SocialCounterfactuals) and usually counts identities without activity/role context; this can miss recurring role-based stereotypes. Motivation: need event-level disentanglement (joint actor–verb–context) and ethnicity-/gender-aware, event-centric quantification throughout generation; QX2 is presented to fill this gap.
What to check later: whether the paper shows evidence for amplification/stabilization claims, whether reward models trained on human comparisons are demonstrably biased in the ways claimed, whether evaluation metrics used in experiments truly go beyond FVD/CLIP/object-consistency to measure demographics and temporal persistence, and whether QX2 operationalizes the stated multi-granular metrics.

final_notes: Paper argues reward-based alignment often inherits/amplifies biases and requires auditing across video-generation pipeline. Key summary stats (Sec.5.1): 69.23% of HPDv2 verbs favor men; 61.11% of Pick-a-Pic verbs favor women. Table 4 avg PBSG: HPSv2.0 = 0.6039; PickScore = -0.1157. Image-level (Table 7, avg over 42 verbs): CLIP = -0.0726; RMM = 1.5280; RMW = -0.7448 (noted table subscript/label inconsistency). Video-level (Table 8, avg): VCM-VC2 = 0.8034; +RMM = 0.9584 (+0.155); +RMW = 0.3082 (−0.495). Per-ethnicity examples: White base 0.7925 → +RMM 0.9595, +RMW 0.3341; East Asian base 0.7115 → +RMW 0.1008. Broader Impact: alignment can stabilize/amplify bias (cites Table 5 & Table 6); controllable preference modeling is dual-use (cites Table 7 RMM 1.5280, RMW -0.7448 and Table 8 +RMM 0.9584, +RMW 0.3082); recommends continuous auditing and careful preference-data curation. Limitations: use of U.S. Census categories; human-validated VLM evaluators operate at image-level; only single-step latent consistency distillation & limited reward models tested; controllable preference experiments use synthetic gender manipulations; fixed set of 42 actions may limit generalization. Outstanding flagged inconsistency: text/columns claim RMW is negative for every ethnicity but Table 8 per-ethnicity +RMW entries appear positive; Table 7 subscript/label issue remains.

Paper introduces VideoBiasEval, an event-based evaluation framework that separates actor attributes from verbs and contexts. The framework measures ethnicity bias, gender bias within ethnic groups, changes after alignment tuning, and temporal stability of demographic portrayals. The authors analyze human preference datasets, train image reward models on those datasets, and align video models using those rewards. Reported findings: preference biases can be inherited by reward models, can be amplified by alignment, and can become more temporally stable. The authors also construct man-preferred and woman-preferred reward datasets and show that reward-data composition can either reinforce or counteract a video model’s pre-existing gender bias. Paper notes caveats: limits due to demographic category definitions, use of automated evaluators, specific training choices, and a fixed action set for evaluation.

VideoBiasEval: event-based evaluation that separates actor attributes (gender, ethnicity) from verbs/contexts; event = actor performing a verb in a context. Evaluations are multi-granular (frame, temporal, video, event, demographic-group). Key metrics/concepts: frame-level classification (gender/ethnicity per frame), video-level label via majority voting, attribute flickering (frame-to-frame identity inconsistency), temporal coherence/consistency, TAS (temporal attribute stability) with mean/median/std reported and a "perfect stability" outcome reported alongside TAS (Table 6). Models: unaligned (u) = likelihood-trained baseline; aligned (a) = preference-guided post-training (alignment tuning / reward-weighted fine-tuning / RLHF-style procedures). Reward models (preference models) are trained from human preference pairs (two images compared vs caption); aesthetic reward is one type. Reward models assign scores to guide generator optimization; controllable preference modeling constructs directional or counter-biased reward datasets (e.g., man-preferred, woman-preferred). Distillation/optimization: Latent Consistency Distillation incorporates image-reward feedback; study uses single-step video generation during reward-guided distillation; teacher = pretrained T2V model, student = distilled model. Automated evaluation: VLMs-as-judges ensemble (vision–language models infer gender/ethnicity); human verification used for grounding (Pearson, Cohen’s/Fleiss’ Kappa reported); sensitivity analysis re-evaluates high-agreement subsets. Other glossary items: Softmax and standardized scores for reward normalization; normalized sensitivity = action’s change in PBSG divided by reward-model baseline PBSG. Prior findings (from earlier parts): preference biases in human datasets can be inherited by reward models, amplified by alignment, and become more temporally stable; reward-data composition can reinforce or counteract pre-existing gender bias. Caveats: demographic category limits, automated evaluators, specific training choices, fixed action set.

Related work (this part): prior T2V benchmarks (VBench, EvalCrafter, T2V-CompBench) use FVD, CLIP-Score, object consistency and overlook who appears/how identities are portrayed; GRiT-based metrics can detect roles but not demographic homogeneity; CLIP-based alignment rewards textual fidelity but ignores demographic balance. The paper positions its event-level audit as separating actor attributes from verbs/environments to catch role stereotypes and temporal narrative bias.

VideoBiasEval (Sec 3) defines an event as tuple <p,a,c> (actor p performs verb a in context c). Controlled attribute space: 4 gender prompt categories (man, woman, person, non-binary person), 7 ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino), and 42 verbs. Verb list (42): bake, bike, call, clean, climb, cook, cough, cry, drink, drive, eat, exercise, fish, hit, jump, kick, kneel, laugh, lift, paint, pick, pitch, pray, read, ride, row, run, shop, shout, sit, skate, sleep, smile, stand, stare, stretch, study, sweep, throw, walk, wash, work. Prompting protocol: deterministic template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” Two evaluation conditions: Person-only (actor = “person”; 1 prompt/verb = 42 prompts) and Ethnicity+Person (explicit ethnicity + “person”; 42 verbs × 7 ethnicities = 294 prompts). Prompts are from a predefined set (not generated by an LLM); a fixed number of videos per prompt are generated under identical decoding settings. Person-only tests which gender/ethnicity the model assigns without explicit demographic cues; Ethnicity+Person tests how explicit ethnicity interacts with inferred attributes (e.g., gender). Keep in mind earlier-section empirical results to check consistency later: datasets (Sec 5.1) — HPDv2: 18/26 verbs man-preferred (69.23%), reported White preference 43.34% (paper claimed dataset favors White — flagged earlier as inconsistent since 43.34%<50%); Pick-a-Pic: 11/18 verbs woman-preferred (61.11%), reported White preference 40.08%. TAS (Table 6): gender TAS mean 0.9763->0.9967 after alignment; ethnicity TAS: VCM-VC2 0.8904; +HPSv2.0 0.9305; +HPSv2.1 0.9632; +PickScore 0.9406. Controlled reward (Table 8): baseline 0.8034; +RMM 0.9584; +RMW 0.3082.

errors.claim: "A value of 0.5 means men occur twice as often as women: N_{man}=3N_{woman}."
errors.evidence: "\mathrm{PBS}_G=\frac{N_{\text{man}}-N_{\text{woman}}}{N_{\text{total}}}\in[-1,1]." and the sentence "A value of 0.5 means men occur twice as often as women: N_{\text{man}}=3N_{\text{woman}}."
errors.explanation: The numeric equality N_man = 3 N_woman implies men occur three times as often as women, not twice. Plugging N_man=3N_woman into the PBS_G formula gives (3N - 1N)/(4N) = 0.5, so the textual phrase 'twice as often' is incorrect (men twice as often would yield PBS_G = 1/3 ≈ 0.333).

steps.notes_before: Section 3.3: multi-granular event-centric bias evaluation. VLM judges: Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B. Uniformly sample 16 frames/video. Each judge assigns gender g in G={man, woman} and ethnicity e in E={White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino}. Per-model majority vote over frames → video-level labels; then fuse across models. TAS = % of frames matching final majority-voted label (temporal stability). PBS_G = (N_man - N_woman)/N_total ∈ [-1,1] (note: paper's example misstates that PBS_G=0.5 means 'twice as often' — given N_man=3 N_woman it actually means 3x; 2x would give PBS≈0.333). RDS_e: P_e = N_e/N_total; RDS_e = P_e - 1/|E| (uniform ref 1/7 ≈14.3%); example RDS 0.769 → P_e ≈91.2%. SDI = 1 - Σ_e P_e^2. Bias shift Δ metrics: ΔPBSG, ΔRDSe, ΔSDI used to compare unaligned vs aligned. Footnote: gender-bias excluded in some analyses because person-only prompts mostly yield White individuals (Figures 14,30). Retain earlier empirical numbers from notes for cross-checking (dataset preferences, Tables 4,5,6,8).

final_notes: Dataset & models: Built man-/woman-preferred image reward datasets (2.94M Ethnicity+Gender preference pairs; 537,660 HPDv2 pairs). Male images labeled 1 (man-preferred), female 0. Fine-tuned two CLIP-based reward models: RMM (man-preferred) and RMW (woman-preferred). Reported reward scores (Table 7, avg across 42 verbs): CLIP avg = -0.0726; RMM avg ≈ 1.5280 (example White 1.6300); RMW avg ≈ -0.7448 (example White -0.6318). PBSG results (Table 8): baseline VCM-VC2 PBSG = 0.8034; +RMM -> 0.9584 (+0.1550 reported); +RMW -> 0.3082 (-0.4952 reported). Sensitivity analysis across 42 actions: normalized sensitivity = ΔPBSG / baseline PBSG. Top-sensitive actions include sleep, stretch, read; RMM amplifies exercise/row/cook; RMW shifts bake/sleep/sweep. Conclusions: VideoBiasEval can decouple identity from content semantics; reward-model alignment often inherits/amplifies biases; recommend auditing/mitigation across the pipeline. Section 7 (controllable preference modeling) shows dual-use: curated preference datasets can amplify or suppress social attributes. Broader Impact: alignment tuning (e.g., RLHF as example) can act as a “bias stabilizer”; controllable preference modeling is dual-use; recommend multi-granular, event-centric auditing (VideoBiasEval) and rigorous preference dataset curation. Limitations: analysis limited to two social dimensions (gender, ethnicity using U.S. Census categories); VLM evaluators validated vs human judgments but operate at image-frame level and may be biased; authors ensemble evaluators and call for larger ground-truth video annotations; alignment study used a specific training protocol (single-step latent consistency distillation) and limited reward models; controllable preference experiments are synthetic gender manipulations only; benchmark limited to 42 socially associated actions. Title: From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models. Authors: Zefan Cai et al. (footnote marker †† appears used twice in title block — inconsistent). Key claim/goal: introduce VideoBiasEval, a diagnostic framework to analyze social bias in text-to-video generation and to trace effects of alignment tuning. Definitions: 'aligned models' = video diffusion models undergoing post-training optimization to better match human preferences (via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style procedures using learned reward/preference models trained on human comparisons). Pipeline: base video diffusion model → preference/reward model → post-training optimization. 'Unaligned counterparts' = models trained only with likelihood-based objectives, used as baselines. Motivation: alignment improves perceptual quality and temporal coherence but may encode/reinforce human preference biases, affecting representation (who is generated, roles, frequency). VideoBiasEval methods: event-based prompting to separate verb/context (semantic content) from actor identity attributes; uses established social bias taxonomies; focuses on gender and ethnicity. Metrics: multi-granular metrics to assess (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) shifts in social attribute distributions across models, and (4) temporal persistence of bias within videos. Paper promises an end-to-end analysis tracing how social attribute distributions evolve through the alignment tuning pipeline. Existing eval gaps listed (limited identity coverage in prompts; lack of specific metrics; lack of methods to track pre/post alignment shifts).

Goal: introduce VideoBiasEval to diagnose social bias in text-to-video generation and trace effects of alignment tuning. Pipeline: base video diffusion model → human preference dataset → image reward model (e.g., HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore) → post-training alignment tuning (reward-weighted fine-tuning) producing an 'aligned' video diffusion model; compare to unaligned (likelihood-trained) baselines. Data & models examined: human preference datasets HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic; reward models HPSv2.0/HPSv2.1 and PickScore; a video consistency model distilled from VideoCrafter-2 is fine-tuned for experiments. Key empirical claims: (1) HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic show non-neutral gender preferences and a strong imbalance favoring White representations; (2) reward models inherit and amplify these biases; (3) alignment-tuned video models propagate biases—alignment with male- or female-preferred reward models systematically shifts gender portrayals while ethnic representation stays uneven; (4) Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS): alignment improves temporal consistency of social attribute portrayals but can make biased portrayals more persistent and visually stable. They also explore constructing controllable image reward datasets (Section 7) and report analyses across 42 events, claiming controllable/counter-biased reward modeling as a mitigation strategy. Contributions summarized: VideoBiasEval framework, first end-to-end analysis linking datasets→reward models→aligned video models, and experiments showing alignment improves quality/coherence while reshaping/reinforcing social composition.

Goal: introduce VideoBiasEval to diagnose social bias in text-to-video generation and trace effects of alignment tuning. Pipeline: base video diffusion model → human preference dataset → image reward model (HPSv2.0/HPSv2.1, PickScore) → reward-weighted fine-tuning producing 'aligned' video diffusion model; compare to unaligned (likelihood-trained) baselines. Also explore constructing controllable image reward datasets and claim controllable/counter-biased reward modeling as mitigation. Related work: existing T2V benchmarks (VBench, EvalCrafter, T2V-CompBench) use metrics like Fréchet Video Distance, CLIP-Score, object consistency but overlook who is depicted and demographic balance; GRiT/CLIP-based metrics verify presence/faithfulness of entities but fail to audit demographic representation or event-level role/verb/context joint patterns. This work proposes an event-centric, actor-verb-environment audit for gender and ethnicity-aware biases across the T2V pipeline.

VideoBiasEval: event-based framework for evaluating social biases in video diffusion models. Use structured prompts varying actor gender/ethnicity across real-world events; generate videos and extract social attributes via a VLM-based evaluation (Sec. 3.3). Events modeled as tuple <p,a,c> (actor p performs verb a in context c). Controlled attribute space: 4 gender categories (man, woman, the neutral term “person,” non-binary person) per Luccioni et al.; 7 ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino) per Karkkainen & Joo / US Census conventions. Verb set: 42 visually distinctive verbs (bake; bike; call; clean; climb; cook; cough; cry; drink; drive; eat; exercise; fish; hit; jump; kick; kneel; laugh; lift; paint; pick; pitch; pray; read; ride; row; run; shop; shout; sit; skate; sleep; smile; stand; stare; stretch; study; sweep; throw; walk; wash; work). Section 3.2 begins Event-Based Prompting Protocol (Settings) but details not shown in this part. Framing emphasizes reproducibility and bounded scope to trace bias propagation; connects to earlier claims about actor-verb-environment audit and later analyses (e.g., temporal consistency/TAS).

Prompt conditions: Person-only (actor='person', 42 prompts) and Ethnicity+Person (7 ethnic descriptors × 42 = 294 prompts). Videos generated under identical decoding; uniformly sample 16 frames per video. Three VLMs (Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B) infer frame-wise gender and ethnicity; frame predictions majority-voted per model then ensembled to get per-video labels. Reported VLM outputs: gender g∈{man, woman} and ethnicity e∈{White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino} (note earlier text had a conflicting 4-category gender space). TAS (Temporal Attribute Stability): percent of frames matching the video's final majority-voted label. Ethnicity-aware gender metric: PBS_G = (N_man - N_woman)/N_total ∈ [-1,1]; computed under the ethnicity+gender condition to probe stereotype amplification (0.5 corresponds to N_man = 3 N_woman). Ethnicity bias metrics (part 8): for each group e, P_e = N_e / N_total where N_total counts outputs with an identifiable ethnicity. Representation Deviation Score RDS_e = P_e - 1/|E| (with |E|=7, 1/7≈14.3%); example: RDS_e=0.769 → P_e≈0.912 (≈91.2%). Simpson's Diversity Index SDI = 1 - Σ_e P_e^2 (probability two random outputs are from different groups). Bias shift between unaligned and aligned models is measured via ΔPBS_G, ΔRDS_e, and ΔSDI (directional changes toward zero RDS, zero PBS_G, or higher SDI indicate improvements). final_notes: Metrics: L2V gender-preference metric; ethnicity metrics via fixed-verb softmax → P_e → F6N = (P_e - 1/7); W3H = 1 - sum_e P_e^2 (max ≈ 6/7 ≈ 0.857). Labels: man-preferred male = 1; woman-preferred flips. Reward models (Table 7): Y2F avg L2V = -0.0726; Z6B (avg man-pref) = 1.5280; P3L (avg woman-pref) = -0.7448. Limitations: single-step latent distillation, limited rewards; VLM judges are biased image-level classifiers (ensembling mitigates but does not eliminate); US-census categories and fixed action taxonomy; need diverse annotation and intersectional groups. Broader impact: alignment can stabilize/entrench bias; dual-use risks; aesthetic metrics insufficient—recommend multi-granular, event-centric audits (QX2). Title: From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.
Authors: Zefan Cai (marked "Equal contribution, ordered by last name"), Haoyi Qiu, Haozhe Zhao, Ke Wan, Jiachen Li, Jiuxiang Gu, Wen Xiao (affiliation line contains "Microsofthttps://github.com/Zefan-Cai/VideoBiasEval"), Nanyun Peng (marked "Equal advising"), Junjie Hu.
Key claims to check later:
- Alignment-tuned video diffusion produces smoother but more stereotyped and temporally persistent portrayals.
- Preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generated videos.
- Introduces QX2: provides event-based separation of verbs/contexts from actor gender and ethnicity; supports multi-granular measurements including ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and within-video persistence.
- Claims this is "the first end-to-end analysis" linking human comparison data, learned image rewards, and aligned video outputs.
- Human-preference-trained rewards improve visual quality but unintentionally encode and amplify social bias; argues for bias-aware assessment and mitigation throughout alignment.
Figure 1 notes: QX2 event prompts and multi-granular ethnicity/gender audit shown bottom-left; frame-wise VLM inference and aggregation of actor attributes at top; bottom-right summarizes the analysis separating human preference bias, image-reward preference bias, and downstream diffusion-video generation bias.
Links provided: OpenReview and GitHub.

Intro summary: Human comparison collections favor White representations and show non-neutral gender preferences; learned rewards inherit and amplify these patterns, with male- or female-preferred rewards systematically redirecting gender portrayals and ethnic distributions remaining uneven. Curating attribute distributions and counter-biased rewards can control image-reward datasets and downstream video representations. Analysis spans 42 events and examines reward-preference changes and pre-/post-alignment video-bias changes. Definition: “aligned models” = video diffusion models fine-tuned after likelihood training to match human preferences (reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style optimization using learned preference/aesthetic rewards trained on human comparisons). “Unaligned” = likelihood-trained baselines. Motivation: subjective preference judgments often lack demographic diversity and can encode systematic bias that rewards and generators inherit/amplify. Need: event-based distributional metrics and a pre/post alignment analysis protocol; prior work lacks diverse identity prompts, comprehensive identity coverage, and distribution-tracking metrics. QX2 (VideoBiasEval) provides controlled separation of verb/identity variation for interpretable, multi-granular assessment (ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, within-video persistence). Claims/contributions: (1) comprehensive event-prompt/multi-granularity audit; (2) first connected analysis linking human preference data → learned image rewards → aligned video outputs, showing inheritance, amplification, stabilization; (3) evidence that perceptual/temporal improvements from alignment can reshape or reinforce generated social composition, plus guidance for controllable-preference mitigation. Key claims to check later: alignment-tuned diffusion produces smoother but more stereotyped/temporally persistent portrayals; preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generated videos; QX2 supports multi-granular measurements and within-video persistence; argues for bias-aware assessment & mitigation across alignment pipeline.

Definitions & scope: “aligned models” = video diffusion models fine-tuned post-likelihood to match human preference rewards (reward-weighted fine-tuning / RLHF-style). “Unaligned” = likelihood-trained baselines. Core claims to verify later: alignment-tuned diffusion yields smoother but more stereotyped/temporally persistent portrayals; preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generated videos; QX2 supports multi-granular measurement including within-video persistence; curating attribute distributions and counter-biased rewards can control downstream representations.
From Related Work (new): existing T2V benchmarks (VBench, EvalCrafter, T2V-CompBench) use metrics like Fréchet Video Distance, CLIP-Score, and object consistency but do not audit depicted identities or portrayal demographics. GRiT-based measures can detect an actor/role (e.g., a doctor) but do not flag demographic skews (e.g., exclusively white male doctors). Y2F-based alignment rewards prioritize textual fidelity over demographic balance. Prior generative-model bias work focuses on static images/isolated objects (StableBias, DALL-Eval, SocialCounterfactuals) and usually counts identities without activity/role context; this can miss recurring role-based stereotypes. Motivation: need event-level disentanglement (joint actor–verb–context) and ethnicity-/gender-aware, event-centric quantification throughout generation; QX2 is presented to fill this gap.
What to check later: whether the paper shows evidence for amplification/stabilization claims, whether reward models trained on human comparisons are demonstrably biased in the ways claimed, whether evaluation metrics used in experiments truly go beyond FVD/CLIP/object-consistency to measure demographics and temporal persistence, and whether QX2 operationalizes the stated multi-granular metrics.

final_notes: Data & labels: Built man-/woman-preferred image-pair datasets — 2.94M same-action/same-ethnicity pairs each from Ethnicity+Gender; +537,660 HPDv2 face-free pairs. Labeling: man-preferred = male:1/female:0; woman-preferred = reversed. Fine-tuned CLIP reward models: RMM (man) and RMW (woman). Key reported results: Table 5 (PBSG, avg over 42 verbs): VCM-VC2 0.8034; +HPSv2.0 0.9116; +HPSv2.1 0.2267; +PickScore 0.3714. Table 7 (reward-model avg PBSG): CLIP -0.0726; RMM 1.5280; RMW -0.7448. Table 8 (video PBSG ablation avg): VCM-VC2 0.8034; +RMM 0.9584 (+~0.155); +RMW 0.3082 (-~0.495). Fig.6: per-action ΔPBSG sensitivities (sleep/stretch/read among highest). Conclusion-level counts: HPDv2: 18/26 favor men (69.23%); Pick-a-Pic: 11/18 favor women (61.11%). Limitations: five items (limited identity categories; VLM evaluators image-level classification bias; only one tuning strategy; synthetic gender manipulations; VideoBiasEval fixed 42 actions). Broader impact: warns alignment can stabilize/amplify bias; preference control dual-use; urges auditing/data curation; cites Tables 5–8 to support claims. Acknowledgment: funding from AFOSR MURI (#FA9550-22-1-0380), ONR (#N00014-23-1-2780), NSF (IIS-2449768), NVIDIA cloud credits, Coefficient Giving (Technical AI Safety Research Program); views are authors' own. Flagged internal contradiction to follow up: paper's Conclusion/Table 4 reportedly gives conflicting average PBSG values (e.g., HPSv2.0=0.6039 and PickScore=-0.1157) that contradict Table 5 values (HPSv2.0=0.9116; PickScore=0.3714).

steps.notes_before: (none yet: this is the first part)

Paper introduces VideoBiasEval, an event-based evaluation framework that separates actor attributes from verbs and contexts. The framework measures ethnicity bias, gender bias within ethnic groups, changes after alignment tuning, and temporal stability of demographic portrayals. The authors analyze human preference datasets, train image reward models on those datasets, and align video models using those rewards. Reported findings: preference biases can be inherited by reward models, can be amplified by alignment, and can become more temporally stable. The authors also construct man-preferred and woman-preferred reward datasets and show that reward-data composition can either reinforce or counteract a video model’s pre-existing gender bias. Paper notes caveats: limits due to demographic category definitions, use of automated evaluators, specific training choices, and a fixed action set for evaluation.

VideoBiasEval: event-based evaluation that separates actor attributes (gender, ethnicity) from verbs/contexts; event = actor performing a verb in a context. Evaluations are multi-granular (frame, temporal, video, event, demographic-group). Key metrics/concepts: frame-level classification (gender/ethnicity per frame), video-level label via majority voting, attribute flickering (frame-to-frame identity inconsistency), temporal coherence/consistency, TAS (temporal attribute stability) with mean/median/std reported and a "perfect stability" outcome reported alongside TAS (Table 6). Models: unaligned (u) = likelihood-trained baseline; aligned (a) = preference-guided post-training (alignment tuning / reward-weighted fine-tuning / RLHF-style procedures). Reward models (preference models) are trained from human preference pairs (two images compared vs caption); aesthetic reward is one type. Reward models assign scores to guide generator optimization; controllable preference modeling constructs directional or counter-biased reward datasets (e.g., man-preferred, woman-preferred). Distillation/optimization: Latent Consistency Distillation incorporates image-reward feedback; study uses single-step video generation during reward-guided distillation; teacher = pretrained T2V model, student = distilled model. Automated evaluation: VLMs-as-judges ensemble (vision–language models infer gender/ethnicity); human verification used for grounding (Pearson, Cohen’s/Fleiss’ Kappa reported); sensitivity analysis re-evaluates high-agreement subsets. Other glossary items: Softmax and standardized scores for reward normalization; normalized sensitivity = action’s change in PBSG divided by reward-model baseline PBSG. Prior findings (from earlier parts): preference biases in human datasets can be inherited by reward models, amplified by alignment, and become more temporally stable; reward-data composition can reinforce or counteract pre-existing gender bias. Caveats: demographic category limits, automated evaluators, specific training choices, fixed action set.

VideoBiasEval (Sec 3) defines an event as tuple <p,a,c> (actor p performs verb a in context c). Controlled attribute space: 4 gender prompt categories (man, woman, person, non-binary person), 7 ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino), and 42 verbs. Verb list (42): bake, bike, call, clean, climb, cook, cough, cry, drink, drive, eat, exercise, fish, hit, jump, kick, kneel, laugh, lift, paint, pick, pitch, pray, read, ride, row, run, shop, shout, sit, skate, sleep, smile, stand, stare, stretch, study, sweep, throw, walk, wash, work. Prompting protocol: deterministic template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” Two evaluation conditions: Person-only (actor = “person”; 1 prompt/verb = 42 prompts) and Ethnicity+Person (explicit ethnicity + “person”; 42 verbs × 7 ethnicities = 294 prompts). Prompts are from a predefined set (not generated by an LLM); a fixed number of videos per prompt are generated under identical decoding settings. Person-only tests which gender/ethnicity the model assigns without explicit demographic cues; Ethnicity+Person tests how explicit ethnicity interacts with inferred attributes (e.g., gender). Keep in mind earlier-section empirical results to check consistency later: datasets (Sec 5.1) — HPDv2: 18/26 verbs man-preferred (69.23%), reported White preference 43.34% (paper claimed dataset favors White — flagged earlier as inconsistent since 43.34%<50%); Pick-a-Pic: 11/18 verbs woman-preferred (61.11%), reported White preference 40.08%. TAS (Table 6): gender TAS mean 0.9763->0.9967 after alignment; ethnicity TAS: VCM-VC2 0.8904; +HPSv2.0 0.9305; +HPSv2.1 0.9632; +PickScore 0.9406. errors.explanation: The Broader Impact asserts controllable preference modeling can correct underrepresentation, but Section 7's empirical results show the woman-preference reward model (RMW) did not eliminate male-leaning bias in generated videos: +RMW PBSG remained positive overall and across ethnicities, contradicting the claim that it successfully corrects skewed portrayals.

final_notes: Section 7 (controllable preference modeling): reward datasets comprised ~2.94M Ethnicity+Gender preference pairs and 537,660 HPDv2 pairs. Fine-tuned CLIP reward models: RMM (man-preferred) and RMW (woman-preferred). Table 7: CLIP avg -0.0726; RMM avg 1.5280 (per-ethnicity ≈1.43–1.63); RMW avg -0.7448 (per-ethnicity ≈-0.63 to -0.88). Table 8 (generation PBSG, 42 verbs): baseline VCM-VC2 = 0.8034; +RMM = 0.9584 (amplifies male preference); +RMW = 0.3082 (reduced but still >0, i.e., still male-leaning). Per-ethnicity +RMW PBSG values remained positive (examples: 0.3341, 0.3913, 0.3314, 0.1008, 0.2639, 0.3446, 0.3894). Figures 39–43 show per-action PBSG shifts; some actions flagged sensitive. Paper earlier framed RMW as a corrective/steering tool but generation results show it did not reach gender equilibrium — an internal tension noted. Conclusions/broader impact: reward-model alignment can inherit/amplify biases and may stabilize them; controllable preference modeling is dual-use and showed limited corrective effect here; recommended mitigations: multi-granular, event-centric auditing (VideoBiasEval) and careful preference-dataset curation. Limitations: only gender & census ethnicity categories; VLM-based evaluators are image-level and biased (ensemble used); single-step LCD training; controllable preference modeling limited to synthetic gender manipulations; benchmark limited to 42 socially associated actions. steps.notes_before: Title: From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models. Authors: Zefan Cai (UW–Madison), Haoyi Qiu, Haozhe Zhao, Ke Wan (UCSD), Jiachen Li (UCSB), Jiuxiang Gu, Wen Xiao (Microsoft; GitHub link noted), Nanyun Peng (UCLA), Junjie Hu (UIUC). Note: footnote marker †† is used twice with different meanings (equal contribution and equal advising) — inconsistent. Abstract: introduce VideoBiasEval, a diagnostic framework for social bias in text-to-video generation. Key methods: event-based prompting to separate semantic content (verbs/contexts) from actor attributes (gender/ethnicity); multi-granular metrics for (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) distributional shifts across model variants, (4) temporal persistence of bias in videos. Analysis: end-to-end trace from human preference datasets → reward models → alignment-tuned video diffusion models; claim this is the first such end-to-end analysis. Findings: alignment tuning amplifies representational biases and makes them temporally stable, producing smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Figure 1 caption references Sections 3, 3.3, 5.1, 5.2, and 6 and mentions VLMs inferring actor attributes across frames and aggregating for bias quantification.

Title: From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models. Authors: Zefan Cai et al. (footnote marker †† appears used twice in title block — inconsistent). Key claim/goal: introduce VideoBiasEval, a diagnostic framework to analyze social bias in text-to-video generation and to trace effects of alignment tuning. Definitions: 'aligned models' = video diffusion models undergoing post-training optimization to better match human preferences (via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style procedures using learned reward/preference models trained on human comparisons). Pipeline: base video diffusion model → preference/reward model → post-training optimization. 'Unaligned counterparts' = models trained only with likelihood-based objectives, used as baselines. Motivation: alignment improves perceptual quality and temporal coherence but may encode/reinforce human preference biases, affecting representation (who is generated, roles, frequency). VideoBiasEval methods: event-based prompting to separate verb/context (semantic content) from actor identity attributes; uses established social bias taxonomies; focuses on gender and ethnicity. Metrics: multi-granular metrics to assess (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) shifts in social attribute distributions across models, and (4) temporal persistence of bias within videos. Paper promises an end-to-end analysis tracing how social attribute distributions evolve through the alignment tuning pipeline. Existing eval gaps listed (limited identity coverage in prompts; lack of specific metrics; lack of methods to track pre/post alignment shifts).

Goal: introduce VideoBiasEval to diagnose social bias in text-to-video generation and trace effects of alignment tuning. Pipeline: base video diffusion model → human preference dataset → image reward model (e.g., HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore) → post-training alignment tuning (reward-weighted fine-tuning) producing an 'aligned' video diffusion model; compare to unaligned (likelihood-trained) baselines. Data & models examined: human preference datasets HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic; reward models HPSv2.0/HPSv2.1 and PickScore; a video consistency model distilled from VideoCrafter-2 is fine-tuned for experiments. Key empirical claims: (1) HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic show non-neutral gender preferences and a strong imbalance favoring White representations; (2) reward models inherit and amplify these biases; (3) alignment-tuned video models propagate biases—alignment with male- or female-preferred reward models systematically shifts gender portrayals while ethnic representation stays uneven; (4) Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS): alignment improves temporal consistency of social attribute portrayals but can make biased portrayals more persistent and visually stable. They also explore constructing controllable image reward datasets (Section 7) and report analyses across 42 events, claiming controllable/counter-biased reward modeling as a mitigation strategy. Contributions summarized: VideoBiasEval framework, first end-to-end analysis linking datasets→reward models→aligned video models, and experiments showing alignment improves quality/coherence while reshaping/reinforcing social composition.

Goal: introduce VideoBiasEval to diagnose social bias in text-to-video generation and trace effects of alignment tuning. Pipeline: base video diffusion model → human preference dataset → image reward model (HPSv2.0/HPSv2.1, PickScore) → reward-weighted fine-tuning producing 'aligned' video diffusion model; compare to unaligned (likelihood-trained) baselines. Key empirical claims: (1) HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic show non-neutral gender preferences and a strong imbalance favoring White representations; (2) reward models inherit and amplify these biases; (3) alignment-tuned video models propagate biases—alignment with male- or female-preferred reward models systematically shifts gender portrayals while ethnic representation stays uneven; (4) Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS): alignment improves temporal consistency of social attribute portrayals but can make biased portrayals more persistent. Also explore constructing controllable image reward datasets and claim controllable/counter-biased reward modeling as mitigation. Related work: existing T2V benchmarks (VBench, EvalCrafter, T2V-CompBench) use metrics like Fréchet Video Distance, CLIP-Score, object consistency but overlook who is depicted and demographic balance; GRiT/CLIP-based metrics verify presence/faithfulness of entities but fail to audit demographic representation or event-level role/verb/context joint patterns. This work proposes an event-centric, actor-verb-environment audit for gender and ethnicity-aware biases across the T2V pipeline.

VideoBiasEval: event-based framework for evaluating social biases in video diffusion models. Use structured prompts varying actor gender/ethnicity across real-world events; generate videos and extract social attributes via a VLM-based evaluation (Sec. 3.3). Events modeled as tuple <p,a,c> (actor p performs verb a in context c). Controlled attribute space: 4 gender categories (man, woman, the neutral term “person,” non-binary person) per Luccioni et al.; 7 ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino) per Karkkainen & Joo / US Census conventions. Verb set: 42 visually distinctive verbs (bake; bike; call; clean; climb; cook; cough; cry; drink; drive; eat; exercise; fish; hit; jump; kick; kneel; laugh; lift; paint; pick; pitch; pray; read; ride; row; run; shop; shout; sit; skate; sleep; smile; stand; stare; stretch; study; sweep; throw; walk; wash; work). Section 3.2 begins Event-Based Prompting Protocol (Settings) but details not shown in this part. Framing emphasizes reproducibility and bounded scope to trace bias propagation; connects to earlier claims about actor-verb-environment audit and later analyses (e.g., temporal consistency/TAS).

VideoBiasEval: deterministic template "A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context]"; 42 verbs. Prompt conditions: Person-only (actor='person', 42 prompts) and Ethnicity+Person (7 ethnic descriptors × 42 = 294 prompts). Videos generated under identical decoding; uniformly sample 16 frames per video. Three VLMs (Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B) infer frame-wise gender and ethnicity; frame predictions majority-voted per model then ensembled to get per-video labels. Reported VLM outputs: gender g∈{man, woman} and ethnicity e∈{White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino} (note earlier text had a conflicting 4-category gender space). TAS (Temporal Attribute Stability): percent of frames matching the video's final majority-voted label. Ethnicity-aware gender metric: PBS_G = (N_man - N_woman)/N_total ∈ [-1,1]; computed under the ethnicity+gender condition to probe stereotype amplification (0.5 corresponds to N_man = 3 N_woman). Ethnicity bias metrics (part 8): for each group e, P_e = N_e / N_total where N_total counts outputs with an identifiable ethnicity. Representation Deviation Score RDS_e = P_e - 1/|E| (with |E|=7, 1/7≈14.3%); example: RDS_e=0.769 → P_e≈0.912 (≈91.2%). Simpson's Diversity Index SDI = 1 - Σ_e P_e^2 (probability two random outputs are from different groups). Bias shift between unaligned and aligned models is measured via ΔPBS_G, ΔRDS_e, and ΔSDI (directional changes toward zero RDS, zero PBS_G, or higher SDI indicate improvements). Human–model correlation analyses deferred to Section 4.

Reward scores standardized (mean/std), averaged over 100 images per generation prompt. PBSG = (avg standardized score for men) - (avg for women), computed per (ethnicity, verb). Sign: positive → preference for men. Reported avg PBSG: CLIP -0.0726 (slight woman-pref), HPSv2.0 +0.6039 (strong man-pref), HPSv2.1 -0.0984 (woman-pref), PickScore -0.1157 (woman-pref). Ethnicity bias (RDS_e, SDI): evaluation prompts = "A person is [verb]-ing [context]" (omits ethnicity); generation prompts = "A/An [ethnicity] person is ..." Scores standardized and averaged over 100 images. Paper says to fix verb and apply softmax to normalize scores per ethnicity, then compute RDSe and SDI; claims positive RDSe = overrep, negative = underrep, and higher SDI = more balanced. Reported: CLIP RDS=0.0182, SDI=0.8495 (highest); HPSv2.0 RDS=0.0315 (Middle Eastern); HPSv2.1 RDS=0.0382 (Latino); PickScore RDS=0.0352 (East Asian); all show reduced SDI after fine-tuning. Inconsistencies flagged: (1) SDI scale/definition conflict across the paper — earlier Table 2 had SDI ~0.0267–0.1252 and a sensitivity change ~0.745→0.761, but here SDI ≈0.8495 (unreconciled); (2) methodological contradiction: softmax outputs cannot be negative, yet text says RDSe can be negative; (3) claim that shifts "align with each model's training data" conflicts with statement that HPSv2.1's training data is undisclosed.

final_notes: Models/datasets: baseline G4S = Video Consistency Model (VCM-VC2). Prior aligned rewards: +A3J (HPSv2.0), +U8D (HPSv2.1), +E5W (PickScore). Table 5 (42-verb averages): G4S 0.8034; +A3J 0.9116; +U8D 0.2267; +E5W 0.3714. Per-ethnicity: G4S underrepresents Black / East Asian / Middle Eastern (F6N negative). Note persistent ambiguity in L2V numeric scale/interpretation across tables (negative values, >1, and 0–1 ranges appear). Gender-controlled preference modeling: two image-preference collections (each 2.94M pairs from C4Z) plus 537,660 R9C face‑free pairs; prompts: "A/An [ethnicity] person is [action]-ing [context]." Man-preferred labels: male=1/female=0; woman-preferred reversed. Pretrained Y2F encoder fine-tuned into two reward models: Z6B (Man-Preferred RMM) and P3L (Woman-Preferred RMW). Table 7 (reward-model L2V preference bias, 42 verbs): Y2F avg -0.0726; Z6B avg 1.5280 (+1.60); P3L avg -0.7448 (-2.27). Table 8 (aligned-video-model L2V social bias, 42 verbs): G4S 0.8034; +Z6B 0.9584 (+0.16); +P3L 0.3082 (-0.50). Z6B raises L2V (reinforces male preference); P3L lowers L2V substantially but remains positive overall. Action sensitivity (Fig.6): ΔL2V normalized by baseline L2V; sleep/stretch/read most sensitive. Broader impact: alignment can stabilize and polish biases, dual-use risks (reward engineering can amplify or suppress social attributes), aesthetic metrics insufficient; recommend continual multi-granular/event-centric audits (e.g., QX2) and rigorous preference-data curation. Supplementary inventory: per-verb gender/ethnicity analyses, training-data effects, implementation/training details and many numbered gender/ethnicity plots (items A, Dataset item #10, C, D, F, G and plot numbers listed). Title: From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.
Authors: Zefan Cai (marked "Equal contribution, ordered by last name"), Haoyi Qiu, Haozhe Zhao, Ke Wan, Jiachen Li, Jiuxiang Gu, Wen Xiao (affiliation line contains "Microsofthttps://github.com/Zefan-Cai/VideoBiasEval"), Nanyun Peng (marked "Equal advising"), Junjie Hu.
Key claims to check later:
- Alignment-tuned video diffusion produces smoother but more stereotyped and temporally persistent portrayals.
- Preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generated videos.
- Introduces QX2: provides event-based separation of verbs/contexts from actor gender and ethnicity; supports multi-granular measurements including ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and within-video persistence.
- Claims this is "the first end-to-end analysis" linking human comparison data, learned image rewards, and aligned video outputs.
- Human-preference-trained rewards improve visual quality but unintentionally encode and amplify social bias; argues for bias-aware assessment and mitigation throughout alignment.
Figure 1 notes: QX2 event prompts and multi-granular ethnicity/gender audit shown bottom-left; frame-wise VLM inference and aggregation of actor attributes at top; bottom-right summarizes the analysis separating human preference bias, image-reward preference bias, and downstream diffusion-video generation bias.
Links provided: OpenReview and GitHub.

Intro summary: Human comparison collections favor White representations and show non-neutral gender preferences; learned rewards inherit and amplify these patterns, with male- or female-preferred rewards systematically redirecting gender portrayals and ethnic distributions remaining uneven. Curating attribute distributions and counter-biased rewards can control image-reward datasets and downstream video representations. Analysis spans 42 events and examines reward-preference changes and pre-/post-alignment video-bias changes. Definition: “aligned models” = video diffusion models fine-tuned after likelihood training to match human preferences (reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style optimization using learned preference/aesthetic rewards trained on human comparisons). “Unaligned” = likelihood-trained baselines. Motivation: subjective preference judgments often lack demographic diversity and can encode systematic bias that rewards and generators inherit/amplify. Need: event-based distributional metrics and a pre/post alignment analysis protocol; prior work lacks diverse identity prompts, comprehensive identity coverage, and distribution-tracking metrics. QX2 (VideoBiasEval) provides controlled separation of verb/identity variation for interpretable, multi-granular assessment (ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, within-video persistence). Claims/contributions: (1) comprehensive event-prompt/multi-granularity audit; (2) first connected analysis linking human preference data → learned image rewards → aligned video outputs, showing inheritance, amplification, stabilization; (3) evidence that perceptual/temporal improvements from alignment can reshape or reinforce generated social composition, plus guidance for controllable-preference mitigation. Key claims to check later: alignment-tuned diffusion produces smoother but more stereotyped/temporally persistent portrayals; preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generated videos; QX2 supports multi-granular measurements and within-video persistence; argues for bias-aware assessment & mitigation across alignment pipeline.

Definitions & scope: “aligned models” = video diffusion models fine-tuned post-likelihood to match human preference rewards (reward-weighted fine-tuning / RLHF-style). “Unaligned” = likelihood-trained baselines. Core claims to verify later: alignment-tuned diffusion yields smoother but more stereotyped/temporally persistent portrayals; preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generated videos; QX2 supports multi-granular measurement including within-video persistence; curating attribute distributions and counter-biased rewards can control downstream representations.
From Related Work (new): existing T2V benchmarks (VBench, EvalCrafter, T2V-CompBench) use metrics like Fréchet Video Distance, CLIP-Score, and object consistency but do not audit depicted identities or portrayal demographics. GRiT-based measures can detect an actor/role (e.g., a doctor) but do not flag demographic skews (e.g., exclusively white male doctors). Y2F-based alignment rewards prioritize textual fidelity over demographic balance. Prior generative-model bias work focuses on static images/isolated objects (StableBias, DALL-Eval, SocialCounterfactuals) and usually counts identities without activity/role context; this can miss recurring role-based stereotypes. Motivation: need event-level disentanglement (joint actor–verb–context) and ethnicity-/gender-aware, event-centric quantification throughout generation; QX2 is presented to fill this gap.
What to check later: whether the paper shows evidence for amplification/stabilization claims, whether reward models trained on human comparisons are demonstrably biased in the ways claimed, whether evaluation metrics used in experiments truly go beyond FVD/CLIP/object-consistency to measure demographics and temporal persistence, and whether QX2 operationalizes the stated multi-granular metrics.

steps.notes_before: QX2: event-centric audit using diffusion models. Event = <actor, verb, context>. Claimed bounded attribute space: 4 gender categories (man, woman, neutral person, non-binary), 7 ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino), 42 verbs (listed). Prompt template: "A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context]." Two prompt regimes: J7K (Person-only, 42 prompts) and V9R (Ethnicity+Person, 294 prompts = 42 verbs * 7 ethnicities). Deterministic prepending of ethnicity for V9R. Attribute extraction: ensemble of Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B; sample 16 frames per video; per-frame labels majority-voted per video and fused across models. Declared extraction outputs: gender G={man,woman} and ethnicity E=7 groups. Temporal metric T8Q / TAS = percent of frames matching the video majority-voted attribute (within-video stability). Notes to check later: (1) inconsistency between claimed four gender categories and classifier G={man,woman}; how 'person' prompts and non-binary/neutral actors are handled; (2) contradiction between statement that demographics are not introduced during generation and explicit ethnicity prepending in V9R; (3) ensure downstream analyses actually use the stated attribute sets and clarify protocol for underspecified prompts.

steps.notes_before: Event-centric audit with diffusion models. Prompts: 'A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context]'. Two regimes: J7K (person-only, 42 prompts) and V9R (ethnicity+person, 42*7=294 prompts; ethnicity prepended deterministically). Extraction: ensemble of Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B; sample 16 frames/video; per-frame labels majority-voted per video and fused across models. Temporal metric T8Q/TAS = percent frames matching video's majority-voted attribute. Note: paper earlier claimed a 4-category gender space (man, woman, neutral person, non-binary) but classifier outputs/metrics here use only G={man,woman} (inconsistency flagged). Gender diagnostic L2V = (N_man - N_woman)/(N_man + N_woman) computed per verb and ethnicity (ethnicity+gender condition); gender-only analysis excluded because unspecified-ethnicity prompts yield predominantly White individuals. Ethnic measures: P_e = N_e / N_total (N_total here = outputs with identifiable ethnicity), F6N_e (RDS) = P_e - 1/7 (example F6N_e=0.769 → P_e≈0.912), W3H = 1 - Σ_e P_e^2 (Simpson). Shift metrics ΔL2V, ΔF6N_e, ΔW3H measure alignment-induced changes. Outstanding issues: reconcile 4-category gender claim with two-category operationalization; clarify/avoid reusing N_total with different meanings.

Pretrained Y2F encoder fine-tuned into two reward models: Z6B (Man-Preferred RMM) and P3L (Woman-Preferred RMW).

Table 7 (reward-model L2V preference bias, 42 verbs): Y2F avg -0.0726; Z6B avg 1.5280 (subscript +1.60); P3L avg -0.7448 (subscript -2.27). Per-ethnicity entries reported (Z6B high positive; P3L strongly negative). Subscripts appear to be effect-size/stat statistics relative to Y2F.

Conclusion/Limitations (new): calls for bias auditing/mitigation at every generation stage; notes predefined gender/ethnicity categories are socially constructed; VLM judges are image-level classifiers with biases (ensembling helps but not solves); larger diverse video annotation needed; alignment used single-step latent consistency distillation and limited rewards (RL/multi-turn may differ); synthetic gender-preference modulation is targeted but not full value alignment; fixed action taxonomy limits generalization.

final_notes: Paper aim: VideoBiasEval separates identity attributes from content semantics to track how alignment changes representations; main claim that reward-based alignment often inherits and can amplify biases, but reward design can sometimes counter bias. Key quantitative findings: counts — HPDv2: 69.23% (18/26) qualifying verbs favor men; Pick-a-Pic: 61.11% (11/18) favor women. Image-level averages (Table 4): HPSv2.0 PBSG = 0.6039; PickScore = -0.1157. Video-level baseline (VCM-VC2) PBSG = 0.8034. Video-level alignment effects: +HPSv2.0 -> 0.9116 (Δ +0.1082 vs baseline); +RMM -> 0.9584 (Δ +0.1550 vs baseline); +RMW -> 0.3082 (Δ −0.4952 vs baseline). Action-/image-level (Table 7, across 42 verbs): CLIP -0.0726; RMM 1.5280; RMW -0.7448. Gender stability (Table 6): mean TAS 0.9763 → 0.9967; perfect stability 0.8850 → 0.9830. Broader impact: alignment can stabilize/amplify bias by removing artifacts, making stereotypes appear coherent; controllable preference modeling is dual-use; recommendations include continuous auditing and rigorous preference-data curation. Limits: (1) identity categories per U.S. Census conventions, (2) VLM evaluators operate image-level and may be biased/inaccurate, (3) tested mainly single-step latent consistency distillation with limited reward models, (4) controllable-preference experiments use synthetic manipulations only, (5) fixed set of 42 actions limits generalization. Open/uncertain items: Table 7 baseline/subscript ambiguity; PickScore vs Pick-a-Pic label consistency. Paper introduces VideoBiasEval, an event-based evaluation framework that separates actor attributes from verbs and contexts. The framework measures ethnicity bias, gender bias within ethnic groups, changes after alignment tuning, and temporal stability of demographic portrayals. The authors analyze human preference datasets, train image reward models on those datasets, and align video models using those rewards. Reported findings: preference biases can be inherited by reward models, can be amplified by alignment, and can become more temporally stable. The authors also construct man-preferred and woman-preferred reward datasets and show that reward-data composition can either reinforce or counteract a video model’s pre-existing gender bias. Paper notes caveats: limits due to demographic category definitions, use of automated evaluators, specific training choices, and a fixed action set for evaluation.

VideoBiasEval: event-based evaluation that separates actor attributes (gender, ethnicity) from verbs/contexts; event = actor performing a verb in a context. Evaluations are multi-granular (frame, temporal, video, event, demographic-group). Key metrics/concepts: frame-level classification (gender/ethnicity per frame), video-level label via majority voting, attribute flickering (frame-to-frame identity inconsistency), temporal coherence/consistency, TAS (temporal attribute stability) with mean/median/std reported and a "perfect stability" outcome reported alongside TAS (Table 6). Models: unaligned (u) = likelihood-trained baseline; aligned (a) = preference-guided post-training (alignment tuning / reward-weighted fine-tuning / RLHF-style procedures). Reward models (preference models) are trained from human preference pairs (two images compared vs caption); aesthetic reward is one type. Reward models assign scores to guide generator optimization; controllable preference modeling constructs directional or counter-biased reward datasets (e.g., man-preferred, woman-preferred). Distillation/optimization: Latent Consistency Distillation incorporates image-reward feedback; study uses single-step video generation during reward-guided distillation; teacher = pretrained T2V model, student = distilled model. Automated evaluation: VLMs-as-judges ensemble (vision–language models infer gender/ethnicity); human verification used for grounding (Pearson, Cohen’s/Fleiss’ Kappa reported); sensitivity analysis re-evaluates high-agreement subsets. Other glossary items: Softmax and standardized scores for reward normalization; normalized sensitivity = action’s change in PBSG divided by reward-model baseline PBSG. Prior findings (from earlier parts): preference biases in human datasets can be inherited by reward models, amplified by alignment, and become more temporally stable; reward-data composition can reinforce or counteract pre-existing gender bias. Caveats: demographic category limits, automated evaluators, specific training choices, fixed action set.

Related work (this part): prior T2V benchmarks (VBench, EvalCrafter, T2V-CompBench) use FVD, CLIP-Score, object consistency and overlook who appears/how identities are portrayed; GRiT-based metrics can detect roles but not demographic homogeneity; CLIP-based alignment rewards textual fidelity but ignores demographic balance. The paper positions its event-level audit as separating actor attributes from verbs/environments to catch role stereotypes and temporal narrative bias.

VideoBiasEval (Sec 3) defines an event as tuple <p,a,c> (actor p performs verb a in context c). Controlled attribute space: 4 gender prompt categories (man, woman, person, non-binary person), 7 ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino), and 42 verbs. Verb list (42): bake, bike, call, clean, climb, cook, cough, cry, drink, drive, eat, exercise, fish, hit, jump, kick, kneel, laugh, lift, paint, pick, pitch, pray, read, ride, row, run, shop, shout, sit, skate, sleep, smile, stand, stare, stretch, study, sweep, throw, walk, wash, work. Prompting protocol: deterministic template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” Two evaluation conditions: Person-only (actor = “person”; 1 prompt/verb = 42 prompts) and Ethnicity+Person (explicit ethnicity + “person”; 42 verbs × 7 ethnicities = 294 prompts). Prompts are from a predefined set (not generated by an LLM); a fixed number of videos per prompt are generated under identical decoding settings. Person-only tests which gender/ethnicity the model assigns without explicit demographic cues; Ethnicity+Person tests how explicit ethnicity interacts with inferred attributes (e.g., gender). Keep in mind earlier-section empirical results to check consistency later: datasets (Sec 5.1) — HPDv2: 18/26 verbs man-preferred (69.23%), reported White preference 43.34% (paper claimed dataset favors White — flagged earlier as inconsistent since 43.34%<50%); Pick-a-Pic: 11/18 verbs woman-preferred (61.11%), reported White preference 40.08%. Reward models (Table 4): HPSv2.0 PBSG=0.6039; PickScore=-0.1157. Video alignment effects (Table 5): baseline VCM-VC2 PBSG=0.8034; +HPSv2.0=0.9116; +HPSv2.1=0.2267; +PickScore=0.3714. TAS (Table 6): gender TAS mean 0.9763->0.9967 after alignment; ethnicity TAS: VCM-VC2 0.8904; +HPSv2.0 0.9305; +HPSv2.1 0.9632; +PickScore 0.9406. Controlled reward (Table 8): baseline 0.8034; +RMM 0.9584; +RMW 0.3082.

final_notes: VideoBiasEval: framework to decouple identity attributes from content semantics and track how alignment tuning reshapes social representations. Datasets: 2.94M Ethnicity+Gender pairs; 537,660 HPDv2 pairs. Reward models: CLIP-based RMM (man-preferred) and RMW (woman-preferred); other image reward-models HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore. Image-level PBSG (avg over 42 verbs): CLIP -0.0726 (by-ethnicity: White +0.0343, Black -0.1198, Latino -0.0934, E Asian -0.1315, SE Asian -0.0865, India -0.0508, Middle E -0.0607); RMM +1.5280; RMW -0.7448; HPSv2.0 +0.6039; HPSv2.1 -0.0984; PickScore -0.1157. Video alignment (VCM-VC2) baseline PBSG 0.8034 (per-ethnicity W 0.7925, B 0.7758, L 0.8690, EA 0.7115, SE 0.7945, India 0.8634, ME 0.8071); +RMM -> 0.9584 (+0.155); +RMW -> 0.3082 (-0.495). Table 5: +HPSv2.0 0.9116; +HPSv2.1 0.2267; +PickScore 0.3714. Video SDI: baseline 0.1433; +HPSv2.0 0.1257; +HPSv2.1 0.0976; +PickScore 0.1467. TAS baseline: Ethnicity 0.8904; Gender 0.9763; HPSv2.1 improved ethnicity TAS to 0.9632. Controllable trade-offs: mixtures of man-/woman-preferred data offer continuous trade-offs between bias mitigation and aesthetic coherence. Action-level sensitivity: RMM amplifies male-preferred activities (exercise, row, cook); RMW shifts toward woman-preferred (bake, sleep, sweep); top normalized-sensitive actions include sleep, stretch, read. Broader impact: alignment tuning can act as a "bias stabilizer" by removing artifacts and smoothing flicker, making stereotyped representations appear polished and harder to detect; controllable preference modeling has dual-use. Mitigation recommendation: adopt multi-granular, event-centric auditing frameworks; treat preference dataset curation with rigor. Limitations: focus on two social dimensions (gender, ethnicity) with U.S.-style categories; VLM evaluators are image-level classifiers and may carry biases; primary training used single-step latent consistency distillation with limited reward models; controllable preference experiments used synthetic manipulations; benchmark limited to 42 actions. Acknowledgments: supported by AFOSR MURI #FA9550-22-1-0380, ONR #N00014-23-1-2780, NSF #IIS-2449768, NVIDIA cloud credits, and Coefficient Giving; views are authors' own.

Title: From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models. Authors: Zefan Cai et al. (footnote marker †† appears used twice in title block — inconsistent). Key claim/goal: introduce VideoBiasEval, a diagnostic framework to analyze social bias in text-to-video generation and to trace effects of alignment tuning. Definitions: 'aligned models' = video diffusion models undergoing post-training optimization to better match human preferences (via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style procedures using learned reward/preference models trained on human comparisons). Pipeline: base video diffusion model → preference/reward model → post-training optimization. 'Unaligned counterparts' = models trained only with likelihood-based objectives, used as baselines. Motivation: alignment improves perceptual quality and temporal coherence but may encode/reinforce human preference biases, affecting representation (who is generated, roles, frequency). VideoBiasEval methods: event-based prompting to separate verb/context (semantic content) from actor identity attributes; uses established social bias taxonomies; focuses on gender and ethnicity. Metrics: multi-granular metrics to assess (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) shifts in social attribute distributions across models, and (4) temporal persistence of bias within videos. Paper promises an end-to-end analysis tracing how social attribute distributions evolve through the alignment tuning pipeline. Existing eval gaps listed (limited identity coverage in prompts; lack of specific metrics; lack of methods to track pre/post alignment shifts).

Goal: introduce VideoBiasEval to diagnose social bias in text-to-video generation and trace effects of alignment tuning. Pipeline: base video diffusion model → human preference dataset → image reward model (e.g., HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore) → post-training alignment tuning (reward-weighted fine-tuning) producing an 'aligned' video diffusion model; compare to unaligned (likelihood-trained) baselines. Data & models examined: human preference datasets HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic; reward models HPSv2.0/HPSv2.1 and PickScore; a video consistency model distilled from VideoCrafter-2 is fine-tuned for experiments. Key empirical claims: (1) HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic show non-neutral gender preferences and a strong imbalance favoring White representations; (2) reward models inherit and amplify these biases; (3) alignment-tuned video models propagate biases—alignment with male- or female-preferred reward models systematically shifts gender portrayals while ethnic representation stays uneven; (4) Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS): alignment improves temporal consistency of social attribute portrayals but can make biased portrayals more persistent and visually stable. They also explore constructing controllable image reward datasets (Section 7) and report analyses across 42 events, claiming controllable/counter-biased reward modeling as a mitigation strategy. Contributions summarized: VideoBiasEval framework, first end-to-end analysis linking datasets→reward models→aligned video models, and experiments showing alignment improves quality/coherence while reshaping/reinforcing social composition.

This work proposes an event-centric, actor-verb-environment audit for gender and ethnicity-aware biases across the T2V pipeline.

VideoBiasEval: event-based framework for evaluating social biases in video diffusion models. Use structured prompts varying actor gender/ethnicity across real-world events; generate videos and extract social attributes via a VLM-based evaluation (Sec. 3.3). Events modeled as tuple <p,a,c> (actor p performs verb a in context c). Controlled attribute space: 4 gender categories (man, woman, the neutral term “person,” non-binary person) per Luccioni et al.; 7 ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino) per Karkkainen & Joo / US Census conventions. Verb set: 42 visually distinctive verbs (bake; bike; call; clean; climb; cook; cough; cry; drink; drive; eat; exercise; fish; hit; jump; kick; kneel; laugh; lift; paint; pick; pitch; pray; read; ride; row; run; shop; shout; sit; skate; sleep; smile; stand; stare; stretch; study; sweep; throw; walk; wash; work). Ethnicity bias metrics (part 8): for each group e, P_e = N_e / N_total where N_total counts outputs with an identifiable ethnicity. Simpson's Diversity Index SDI = 1 - Σ_e P_e^2 (probability two random outputs are from different groups). Bias shift between unaligned and aligned models is measured via ΔPBS_G, ΔRDS_e, and ΔSDI (directional changes toward zero RDS, zero PBS_G, or higher SDI indicate improvements).
