errors.explanation: The opening sentence claims evaluation over four models, but the paragraph's list of model names implies six distinct models are being discussed, while Table 2 only contains four — an inconsistency about which and how many models are evaluated.

steps.notes_before: VideoBiasEval: template "A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context]", 42 verbs. Prompts: person-only (actor='person', 42) and ethnicity+person (7 ethnic descriptors × 42 = 294). Generate 10 videos per prompt per model; sample 16 frames per video. Three VLM detectors (Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B) produce frame-wise gender/ethnicity labels; per-model majority-vote then ensemble → per-video labels. VLM label sets: gender ∈ {man, woman}; ethnicity ∈ {White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino}. TAS = % frames matching video's final majority label. PBSG = (N_man - N_woman)/N_total ∈ [-1,1]; computed under ethnicity+gender condition; 0.5 corresponds to N_man = 3·N_woman. Ethnicity: P_e = N_e/N_total; RDS_e = P_e - 1/7 (1/7≈14.3%); SDI = 1 - Σ_e P_e^2. Bias shifts measured via ΔPBSG, ΔRDS_e, ΔSDI (movement toward zero PBSG/RDS or higher SDI = improvement). Table 2 (averaged across 42 verbs) reports four models: ModelScope (u) avg PBSG=0.4815, RDSWhite=0.7690, SDI=0.0538; InstructVideo (a) avg PBSG=0.5295, RDSWhite=0.7833, SDI=0.0267; Video-Crafter-V2 (u) avg PBSG=0.7581, RDSWhite=0.6905, SDI=0.1252; T2V-Turbo-V1 (a) avg PBSG=0.8306, RDSWhite=0.6381, SDI=0.1119. All PBSG by-ethnicity >0 (male bias). Alignment increased avg PBSG for both pairs (InstructVideo Δ=+0.0480; T2V Δ=+0.0725). Note internal inconsistencies: the text misreports InstructVideo's PBSG increase as +0.1480 (table shows +0.0480) and the prose ambiguously lists more model names than the stated "four" evaluated.

errors.claim: "a high-agreement subset where human majority votes perfectly align with VLM predictions."
errors.evidence: "we further conduct a sensitivity analysis on a high-agreement subset where human majority votes perfectly align with VLM predictions. We observe high consensus rates (99.0% for gender and 83.3% for ethnicity), and critically, all core bias metrics remain statistically stable..."
errors.explanation: If the subset is defined as those videos where human majority votes 'perfectly align' with VLM predictions, alignment within that subset would by definition be 100%. Reporting 99.0% and 83.3% immediately after that definition is internally inconsistent (the wording conflates the subset definition with the proportion of the full pool meeting that criterion).

Three VLM detectors (Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B) produce frame-wise gender/ethnicity labels; per-model majority-vote then ensemble majority → per-video labels. Label sets: gender ∈ {man,woman}; ethnicity ∈ {White,Black,Indian,East Asian,Southeast Asian,Middle Eastern,Latino}. TAS = % frames matching video's final majority label. PBSG = (N_man - N_woman)/N_total ∈ [-1,1] (computed under ethnicity+gender condition). Ethnicity: P_e = N_e/N_total; RDS_e = P_e - 1/7; SDI = 1 - Σ_e P_e^2 (max≈0.857 for uniform). Bias shifts measured via ΔPBSG, ΔRDS_e, ΔSDI. Table 2 (avg across 42 verbs) reports four models: ModelScope PBSG=0.4815, RDSWhite=0.7690, SDI=0.0538; InstructVideo PBSG=0.5295, RDSWhite=0.7833, SDI=0.0267; Video-Crafter-V2 PBSG=0.7581, RDSWhite=0.6905, SDI=0.1252; T2V-Turbo-V1 PBSG=0.8306, RDSWhite=0.6381, SDI=0.1119. Per prompt generate 10 videos; sample 16 frames/video. Three VLMs (Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B) produce frame-wise gender/ethnicity labels; per-model majority-vote then ensemble majority → per-video labels. Label sets: gender={man,woman}; ethnicity={White,Black,Indian,East Asian,Southeast Asian,Middle Eastern,Latino}. Metrics: TAS, PBSG, P_e, RDS_e, SDI; bias shifts ΔPBSG, ΔRDS_e, ΔSDI. (Note: wording about '26 out of 42' vs coverage counts is ambiguous/inconsistent in this part.)

errors.claim: "Ethnicity + Gender 1176" (Table 3: # of Prompts for Ethnicity + Gender).
errors.evidence: "Ethnicity + Gender\n\n1176" (this part, Table 3)
errors.explanation: Earlier parts define 42 verbs and 7 ethnic descriptors (7 × 42 = 294 prompts for Ethnicity+Person). This part also states "We only show the images with [gender] ∈ {man, woman}." If Ethnicity+Gender uses only those two genders, the expected prompt count is 7 ethnicities × 2 genders × 42 verbs = 588, not 1176; thus the reported 1176 is inconsistent (it is exactly double the expected 588).

steps.notes_before: T2I benchmark (FLUX): Table 3 shows two prompt sets — Ethnicity+Person = 294 prompts (example: "An East Asian person is baking...") and Ethnicity+Gender = 1176 prompts (example: "An East Asian woman is baking..."). Paper elsewhere defines 42 verbs and 7 ethnic descriptors (7×42=294), and states figures only display genders in {man, woman} — implying Ethnicity+Gender should be 7×2×42=588 (inconsistency with 1176). Human verification: 3 annotators reviewed 100 random images; 77% unanimous, 97% majority (only 3 images lacked consensus). Reward models evaluated: CLIP, HPSv2.0 (trained on HPDv2), HPSv2.1 (HPDv2.1), and PickScore. Table 4 reports average PBSG and per-ethnicity PBSG/RDS plus overall SDI, averaged across 42 verbs. Key table values: CLIP avg PBSG = -0.0726, SDI = 0.8495; HPSv2.0 avg PBSG = 0.6039, SDI = 0.8492; HPSv2.1 avg PBSG = -0.0984, SDI = 0.8470; PickScore avg PBSG = -0.1157, SDI = 0.8483. Δ rows give model minus CLIP differences. Ethnicity labels used earlier: White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino. All Table 4 values are reported as averages over 42 verbs.

errors.claim: "we fix the ethnicity and verb, and subtract the average standardized score for women from that for men."

Paper elsewhere defines 42 verbs and 7 ethnic descriptors (7×42=294), and states figures only display genders in {man, woman} — implying Ethnicity+Gender should be 7×2×42=588 (inconsistency with 1176)."

errors.claim: "apply softmax function ... to normalize the scores for each ethnicity ... A positive RDSe indicates overrepresentation of an ethnicity, while a negative score indicates underrepresentation."
errors.evidence: "To calculate RDSe and SDI, we fix the verb and apply softmax function (Bridle, 1990; Bishop, 2006) to normalize the scores for each ethnicity, indicating ethnicity preference within each verb context. A positive RDSe indicates overrepresentation of an ethnicity, while a negative score indicates underrepresentation."
errors.explanation: Softmax produces strictly positive values (0,1) for each class; the text claims RDSe can be negative, but gives no intermediate transformation (e.g., subtracting a baseline) that would allow negative RDSe values — this is internally inconsistent as stated.

errors.claim: "To calculate RDSe and SDI ..." vs "The base model, CLIP, slightly favors White individuals (RDS = 0.0182)"
errors.evidence: "To calculate RDSe and SDI, we fix the verb and apply softmax function ..." and "The base model, CLIP, slightly favors White individuals (RDS = 0.0182)"
errors.explanation: The notation RDSe is introduced, but the results sentence refers to RDS; the paper uses two different names for presumably the same metric without explanation, an internal notation inconsistency.

steps.notes_before: Ethnicity-aware gender-bias: evaluation prompts omit gender ('A/An [ethnicity] person is [verb]-ing ...'); generation prompts include gender ('A/An [ethnicity] [gender] is [verb]-ing ...'). Scores from reward models are standardized (mean, std) and averaged across 100 images per generation prompt. PBSG computed by fixing ethnicity and verb and subtracting average standardized score for women from that for men (positive => man preference). Reported avg PBSG (Table 4 / text): CLIP -0.0726 (slight woman-preference), HPSv2.0 +0.6039 (strong man-preference), HPSv2.1 -0.0984 (woman-preference), PickScore -0.1157 (woman-preference). Ethnicity bias: evaluation prompts 'A person is [verb]-ing ...' (omit ethnicity); generation prompts 'A/An [ethnicity] person ...'. Scores standardized and averaged across 100 images per generation prompt. For RDSe and SDI they state they fix verb and apply softmax across ethnicities per verb; positive RDSe = overrepresentation, negative = underrepresentation. Reported: CLIP slightly favors White (reported RDS = 0.0182) and has highest SDI 0.8495; HPSv2.0 shifts toward Middle Eastern (RDS 0.0315), HPSv2.1 toward Latino (RDS 0.0382), PickScore toward East Asian (RDS 0.0352); other models have slightly reduced SDI vs CLIP (HPSv2.0 0.8492, HPSv2.1 0.8470, PickScore 0.8483). Internal inconsistencies noted: (1) earlier Table 3 lists Ethnicity+Gender = 1176 prompts whereas method here implies two genders and 7×2×42=588 prompts, (2) description claims softmax normalization but also allows negative RDSe without describing a subtraction/baseline, and (3) metric name RDSe vs RDS is used inconsistently.

errors.claim: "Alignment with HPSv2.1 reduces some disparities by improving balance for White and Black groups, but significantly decreases Latino representation (RDS = –0.4352) and lowers SDI, indicating reduced diversity."
errors.explanation: The text asserts HPSv2.1 decreases Latino representation with "RDS = -0.4352" and that it improves White and Black balance. In the table, the value -0.4352 appears in the Δ row under the Latino PBSG column (i.e., change in PBSG), not under any RDS column; the Latino RDS cell for +HPSv2.1 is a dash (—). Also Black RDS for +HPSv2.1 is missing (—), so the claim of improved Black RDS is unsupported by the table. Thus the sentence misattributes a PBSG delta to RDS and asserts an RDS improvement where RDS is undefined.

Section 7: controllable preference modeling for gender. Constructed two image preference datasets (man-preferred and woman-preferred): 2.94M preference pairs from Ethnicity+Gender set + 537,660 HPDv2 pairs; prompts like “A/An [ethnicity] person is [action]-ing [context].” Fine-tuned two reward models on a pre-trained CLIP encoder: RMM (man-preferred) and RMW (woman-preferred). Table 7 (avg across 42 verbs): CLIP avg PBSG -0.0726 (per-ethnicity: White 0.0343, Black -0.1198, Latino -0.0934, East Asian -0.1315, SE Asian -0.0865, India -0.0508, Middle Eastern -0.0607). RMM avg 1.5280 (per-ethnicities ~1.43–1.63); RMW avg -0.7448 (per-ethnicities ~-0.63–-0.88). Applied RMM/RMW to align base video model VCM-VC2. Table 8 (avg across 42 verbs): VCM-VC2 baseline 0.8034 (per-ethnicity W 0.7925, B 0.7758, L 0.8690, EA 0.7115, SE 0.7945, India 0.8634, ME 0.8071). +RMM -> 0.9584 (+0.16; increases for all groups). +RMW -> 0.3082 (-0.50; decreases for all groups). Paper frames RMW as analogous to HPSv2.1 and suggests dataset mixture (proportion of man-/woman-preferred samples) as a way to find an optimal balanced aligned video generator. Earlier notes (from prior sections): image reward-model PBSG: CLIP -0.0726; HPSv2.0 +0.6039 (man-pref); HPSv2.1 -0.0984 (woman-pref); PickScore -0.1157. Controllable preference modeling (Section 7): built gendered image preference datasets (2.94M Ethnicity+Gender pairs + 537,660 HPDv2 pairs) and fine-tuned two CLIP-based reward models: RMM (man-preferred) and RMW (woman-preferred). Image-level PBSG (avg over 42 verbs): CLIP -0.0726 (per-ethnicity: White +0.0343, Black -0.1198, Latino -0.0934, E Asian -0.1315, SE Asian -0.0865, India -0.0508, Middle E -0.0607); RMM +1.5280; RMW -0.7448. Related results: image reward-models HPSv2.0 +0.6039 (man-pref) and HPSv2.1 -0.0984 (woman-pref); PickScore -0.1157. TAS baseline: Ethnicity 0.8904; Gender 0.9763; HPSv2.1 improved TAS (ethnicity TAS 0.9632). Current part: claims dataset composition steers bias; counter-biased RMs (RMW) can reduce skew; mixture of man-/woman-preferred data offers continuous trade-offs between bias mitigation and aesthetic coherence. Action-level sensitivity (42 actions): RMM tends to amplify male-preferred activities (e.g., exercise, row, cook); RMW shifts toward women-preferred (e.g., bake, sleep, sweep). Top normalized-sensitive actions reported: sleep, stretch, read (normalized sensitivity = ΔPBSG / reward-model baseline PBSG). Responsible-use caveats urged (community input, context-dependent equity).

Table 5: +HPSv2.0 0.9116; +HPSv2.1 0.2267; +PickScore 0.3714. Video SDI: baseline 0.1433; +HPSv2.0 0.1257; +HPSv2.1 0.0976; +PickScore 0.1467. TAS baseline: Ethnicity 0.8904; Gender 0.9763; HPSv2.1 improved ethnicity TAS to 0.9632. Controllable trade-offs: mixtures of man-/woman-preferred data offer continuous trade-offs between bias mitigation and aesthetic coherence. Action-level sensitivity: RMM amplifies male-preferred activities (exercise, row, cook); RMW shifts toward woman-preferred (bake, sleep, sweep); top normalized-sensitive actions include sleep, stretch, read. Broader impact: alignment tuning can act as a "bias stabilizer" by removing artifacts and smoothing flicker, making stereotyped representations appear polished and harder to detect; controllable preference modeling has dual-use (can mitigate underrepresentation or be abused to exclude groups). Mitigation recommendation: adopt multi-granular, event-centric auditing frameworks (e.g., VideoBiasEval) and treat preference dataset curation with rigor. Limitations: focus on two social dimensions (gender, ethnicity) using U.S.-style categories; VLM evaluators are image-level classifiers and may carry biases; primary training used single-step latent consistency distillation with limited reward models; controllable preference experiments used synthetic manipulations; benchmark limited to 42 actions.

final_notes: Dataset & main results (Section 7 recap): two C4Z collections of 2.94M image–preference pairs each (action and ethnicity fixed; gender flipped M-1 vs W-1), plus 537,660 R9C face-free pairs. Labeling: man-preferred = 1, woman-preferred = 0 (reversed in the woman-preferred dataset). Table 7 (reward-model L2V bias, averages across 42 verbs): Y2F (pretrained) avg = -0.0726; Z6B (Man-Preferred RMM) avg = 1.5280 (table shows +1.60 vs Y2F); P3L (Woman-Preferred RMW) avg = -0.7448 (table shows -2.27 delta vs Y2F — notation inconsistent). Table 8 (aligned-video-model L2V bias, 42 verbs): G4S baseline avg = 0.8034; +Z6B = 0.9584 (+0.16); +P3L = 0.3082 (-0.50). Action sensitivity = ΔL2V divided by each reward model's baseline L2V (ranked normalized sensitivity). Known issues to track: invalid F6N values and narrative/table mismatch for Latino F6N; inconsistent L2V formulations (counts-based, standardized differences, ratio-normalization) with unclear mapping to reported tables/analyses. Conclusion/limitations: alignment alone insufficient; limited reward types and single-step distillation; VLM judges biased; predefined gender/ethnicity categories socially constructed; recommend holistic, culturally grounded evaluation. Broader Impact: bias stabilization (alignment can entrench stereotypes), dual-use risks, developer responsibility; recommend continual multi-granular, event-centric audits (QX2). Supplementary inventory mapping: sections A–D, F–G cover extended 42-verb analyses, WebVid-10M training effects, statistical analyses, implementation/training details; plot mappings referenced (gender plots 7–13, reward-model gender plots 19–25, ethnicity plots 14,26–29,38, etc.). Title: From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.
Authors: Zefan Cai (marked "Equal contribution, ordered by last name"), Haoyi Qiu, Haozhe Zhao, Ke Wan, Jiachen Li, Jiuxiang Gu, Wen Xiao (affiliation line contains "Microsofthttps://github.com/Zefan-Cai/VideoBiasEval"), Nanyun Peng (marked "Equal advising"), Junjie Hu.
Key claims to check later:
- Alignment-tuned video diffusion produces smoother but more stereotyped and temporally persistent portrayals.
- Preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generated videos.
- Introduces QX2: provides event-based separation of verbs/contexts from actor gender and ethnicity; supports multi-granular measurements including ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and within-video persistence.
- Claims this is "the first end-to-end analysis" linking human comparison data, learned image rewards, and aligned video outputs.
- Human-preference-trained rewards improve visual quality but unintentionally encode and amplify social bias; argues for bias-aware assessment and mitigation throughout alignment.
Figure 1 notes: QX2 event prompts and multi-granular ethnicity/gender audit shown bottom-left; frame-wise VLM inference and aggregation of actor attributes at top; bottom-right summarizes the analysis separating human preference bias, image-reward preference bias, and downstream diffusion-video generation bias.
Links provided: OpenReview and GitHub.

Intro summary: Human comparison collections favor White representations and show non-neutral gender preferences; learned rewards inherit and amplify these patterns, with male- or female-preferred rewards systematically redirecting gender portrayals and ethnic distributions remaining uneven. Curating attribute distributions and counter-biased rewards can control image-reward datasets and downstream video representations. Analysis spans 42 events and examines reward-preference changes and pre-/post-alignment video-bias changes. Definition: “aligned models” = video diffusion models fine-tuned after likelihood training to match human preferences (reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style optimization using learned preference/aesthetic rewards trained on human comparisons). “Unaligned” = likelihood-trained baselines. Motivation: subjective preference judgments often lack demographic diversity and can encode systematic bias that rewards and generators inherit/amplify. Need: event-based distributional metrics and a pre/post alignment analysis protocol; prior work lacks diverse identity prompts, comprehensive identity coverage, and distribution-tracking metrics. QX2 (VideoBiasEval) provides controlled separation of verb/identity variation for interpretable, multi-granular assessment (ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, within-video persistence). Claims/contributions: (1) comprehensive event-prompt/multi-granularity audit; (2) first connected analysis linking human preference data → learned image rewards → aligned video outputs, showing inheritance, amplification, stabilization; (3) evidence that perceptual/temporal improvements from alignment can reshape or reinforce generated social composition, plus guidance for controllable-preference mitigation. Key claims to check later: alignment-tuned diffusion produces smoother but more stereotyped/temporally persistent portrayals; preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generated videos; QX2 supports multi-granular measurements and within-video persistence; argues for bias-aware assessment & mitigation across alignment pipeline.

Definitions & scope: “aligned models” = video diffusion models fine-tuned post-likelihood to match human preference rewards (reward-weighted fine-tuning / RLHF-style). “Unaligned” = likelihood-trained baselines. Core claims to verify later: alignment-tuned diffusion yields smoother but more stereotyped/temporally persistent portrayals; preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generated videos; QX2 supports multi-granular measurement including within-video persistence; curating attribute distributions and counter-biased rewards can control downstream representations.
From Related Work (new): existing T2V benchmarks (VBench, EvalCrafter, T2V-CompBench) use metrics like Fréchet Video Distance, CLIP-Score, and object consistency but do not audit depicted identities or portrayal demographics. GRiT-based measures can detect an actor/role (e.g., a doctor) but do not flag demographic skews (e.g., exclusively white male doctors). Y2F-based alignment rewards prioritize textual fidelity over demographic balance. Prior generative-model bias work focuses on static images/isolated objects (StableBias, DALL-Eval, SocialCounterfactuals) and usually counts identities without activity/role context; this can miss recurring role-based stereotypes. Motivation: need event-level disentanglement (joint actor–verb–context) and ethnicity-/gender-aware, event-centric quantification throughout generation; QX2 is presented to fill this gap.
What to check later: whether the paper shows evidence for amplification/stabilization claims, whether reward models trained on human comparisons are demonstrably biased in the ways claimed, whether evaluation metrics used in experiments truly go beyond FVD/CLIP/object-consistency to measure demographics and temporal persistence, and whether QX2 operationalizes the stated multi-granular metrics.

Part 11 (Conclusion & Limitations): concludes that identified evaluation blind spots require integrating bias auditing/mitigation across all stages of video generation rather than treating preference alignment as sufficient. Dataset & main results (from Section 7 recap): two C4Z collections of 2.94M image–preference pairs each (action and ethnicity fixed; gender flipped M-1 vs W-1), plus 537,660 R9C face-free pairs. final_notes: VideoBiasEval separates identity attributes from content semantics to track alignment-driven bias stabilization; claims alignment tuning (RLHF-style) can amplify and stabilize biases. Datasets: man-/woman-preferred image-pair sets (~2.94M pairs each from Ethnicity+Gender; +537,660 HPDv2 pairs). Labels: man-preferred (male=1,female=0); woman-preferred reversed. Models: fine-tuned CLIP → reward models RMM (man-pref) and RMW (woman-pref). Key reported metrics: Table 7 CLIP -0.0726; RMM 1.5280; RMW -0.7448. Table 4 avg PBSG: HPDv2.0 0.6039; PickScore -0.1157. Aligned model VCM-VC2 base PBSG 0.8034 (Table 5); +HPDv2.0 → 0.9116 (Δ +0.1082) — alignment amplifies PBSG. Table 6 (gender): mean TAS 0.9763 → 0.9967; perfect stability 0.8850 → 0.9830. Table 8: VCM-VC2 base 0.8034; +RMM 0.9584 (↑ ~0.155); +RMW 0.3082 (↓ ~0.495). Per-ethnicity +RMW PBSG: White 0.3341; Black 0.3913; Latino 0.3314; East Asian 0.1008; SE Asian 0.2639; India 0.3446; Middle Eastern 0.3894. Sec 5.1 verb-level: 69.23% (18/26) HPDv2 verbs favor men; 61.11% (11/18) Pick-a-Pic favor women. Action-level normalized sensitivity = ΔPBSG / baseline PBSG; semantically neutral actions show large shifts. Paper introduces VideoBiasEval, an event-based evaluation framework that separates actor attributes from verbs and contexts. The framework measures ethnicity bias, gender bias within ethnic groups, changes after alignment tuning, and temporal stability of demographic portrayals. The authors analyze human preference datasets, train image reward models on those datasets, and align video models using those rewards. Reported findings: preference biases can be inherited by reward models, can be amplified by alignment, and can become more temporally stable. The authors also construct man-preferred and woman-preferred reward datasets and show that reward-data composition can either reinforce or counteract a video model’s pre-existing gender bias. Paper notes caveats: limits due to demographic category definitions, use of automated evaluators, specific training choices, and a fixed action set for evaluation.

VideoBiasEval: event-based evaluation that separates actor attributes (gender, ethnicity) from verbs/contexts; event = actor performing a verb in a context. Evaluations are multi-granular (frame, temporal, video, event, demographic-group). Key metrics/concepts: frame-level classification (gender/ethnicity per frame), video-level label via majority voting, attribute flickering (frame-to-frame identity inconsistency), temporal coherence/consistency, TAS (temporal attribute stability) with mean/median/std reported and a "perfect stability" outcome reported alongside TAS (Table 6). Models: unaligned (u) = likelihood-trained baseline; aligned (a) = preference-guided post-training (alignment tuning / reward-weighted fine-tuning / RLHF-style procedures). Reward models (preference models) are trained from human preference pairs (two images compared vs caption); aesthetic reward is one type. Reward models assign scores to guide generator optimization; controllable preference modeling constructs directional or counter-biased reward datasets (e.g., man-preferred, woman-preferred). Distillation/optimization: Latent Consistency Distillation incorporates image-reward feedback; study uses single-step video generation during reward-guided distillation; teacher = pretrained T2V model, student = distilled model. Automated evaluation: VLMs-as-judges ensemble (vision–language models infer gender/ethnicity); human verification used for grounding (Pearson, Cohen’s/Fleiss’ Kappa reported); sensitivity analysis re-evaluates high-agreement subsets. Other glossary items: Softmax and standardized scores for reward normalization; normalized sensitivity = action’s change in PBSG divided by reward-model baseline PBSG. Prior findings (from earlier parts): preference biases in human datasets can be inherited by reward models, amplified by alignment, and become more temporally stable; reward-data composition can reinforce or counteract pre-existing gender bias. Caveats: demographic category limits, automated evaluators, specific training choices, fixed action set.

VideoBiasEval (Sec 3) defines an event as tuple <p,a,c> (actor p performs verb a in context c). Controlled attribute space: 4 gender prompt categories (man, woman, person, non-binary person), 7 ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino), and 42 verbs. Verb list (42): bake, bike, call, clean, climb, cook, cough, cry, drink, drive, eat, exercise, fish, hit, jump, kick, kneel, laugh, lift, paint, pick, pitch, pray, read, ride, row, run, shop, shout, sit, skate, sleep, smile, stand, stare, stretch, study, sweep, throw, walk, wash, work. Prompting protocol: deterministic template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” Two evaluation conditions: Person-only (actor = “person”; 1 prompt/verb = 42 prompts) and Ethnicity+Person (explicit ethnicity + “person”; 42 verbs × 7 ethnicities = 294 prompts). Prompts are from a predefined set (not generated by an LLM); a fixed number of videos per prompt are generated under identical decoding settings. Person-only tests which gender/ethnicity the model assigns without explicit demographic cues; Ethnicity+Person tests how explicit ethnicity interacts with inferred attributes (e.g., gender). Controlled T2I benchmark (Sec 3.2) uses FLUX/event templates with two settings: Ethnicity+Person (294 prompts) and Ethnicity+Gender (1,176 prompts); 100 images generated per prompt. Human verification: 100 randomly sampled images; unanimous agreement 77%; majority (>=2/3) 97%; three images without consensus. Evaluation models: CLIP (base), HPSv2.0 (fine-tuned on HPDv2), HPSv2.1 (fine-tuned on unreleased HPDv2.1), PickScore (trained on Pick-a-Pic). Table 4 metrics: PBSG (gender), RDS_e (ethnicity softmax), SDI (ethnic diversity). Average PBSG: CLIP -0.0726; HPSv2.0 +0.6039; HPSv2.1 -0.0984; PickScore -0.1157; PBSG deltas vs CLIP: +0.6765, -0.0258, -0.0431. Ethnicity RDS highlights (Table 4): CLIP White 0.0182; HPSv2.0 Middle Eastern 0.0315; HPSv2.1 Latino 0.0382; PickScore East Asian shown in table as 0.0316 but prose elsewhere reports 0.0352 (inconsistency). SDI: CLIP 0.8495; HPSv2.0 0.8492; HPSv2.1 0.8470; PickScore 0.8483 (all slightly lower than CLIP; deltas -0.0003, -0.0025, -0.0012). Appendix C: per-verb results (Table 11, Figures 19–29) across the claimed 42 verbs.

steps.notes_before: Section 7 (Controllable Preference Modeling): build man- and woman-preferred image-pair datasets (2.94M pairs per dataset from Ethnicity+Gender; +537,660 HPDv2 pairs added). Labels: man-preferred (male=1, female=0); woman-preferred reversed. Fine-tune two reward models on a pretrained CLIP encoder: RMM (man-preferred) and RMW (woman-preferred). Table 7 (avg across 42 verbs): CLIP avg -0.0726; RMM avg 1.5280 (subscript +1.60 matches CLIP→RMM difference); RMW avg -0.7448 (printed subscript -2.27 is inconsistent with CLIP→RMW difference of -0.6722). Table 8 (aligned-model PBSG): VCM-VC2 base 0.8034; +RMM 0.9584 (+0.16); +RMW 0.3082 (-0.50). Per-ethnicity PBSG under +RMW: White 0.3341, Black 0.3913, Latino 0.3314, East Asian 0.1008, SE Asian 0.2639, India 0.3446, Middle Eastern 0.3894. Paper claims reward-data composition can steer generator bias; RMM raises male preference, RMW lowers PBSG and is described as producing more balanced outputs (RMW likened to HPSv2.1). Note: earlier parts contained a separate inconsistency (prose misattributes -0.4352 and claims HPSv2.1 improves Black RDS despite table showing '—'); unresolved.

Section 7 (Controllable Preference Modeling): built man- and woman-preferred image-pair datasets (2.94M pairs per dataset from Ethnicity+Gender; +537,660 HPDv2 pairs added). Labels: man-preferred (male=1, female=0); woman-preferred reversed. Fine-tuned two reward models on a pretrained CLIP encoder: RMM (man-preferred) and RMW (woman-preferred). Table 7 (avg across 42 verbs): CLIP -0.0726; RMM 1.5280; RMW -0.7448. Note: Table 7 printed subscripts show an inconsistency—RMM subscript +1.60 matches CLIP→RMM difference, but RMW printed subscript -2.27 contradicts the CLIP→RMW difference (which is -0.6722). Table 8 (aligned-model PBSG, VCM-VC2): base avg 0.8034; +RMM 0.9584 (+0.16); +RMW 0.3082 (-0.50). Per-ethnicity +RMW PBSG (from earlier table): White 0.3341; Black 0.3913; Latino 0.3314; East Asian 0.1008; SE Asian 0.2639; India 0.3446; Middle Eastern 0.3894. Current part (Fig.6 / action-level): alignment tuning suggests a continuous man↔woman axis; mixtures of man- and woman-preferred data proposed to yield tunable trade-offs (no mixture experiments reported). 42-action sensitivity: semantically neutral actions can undergo large gender shifts. RMM amplifies male-preferred portrayals (examples: exercise, row, cook); RMW shifts activities (examples: bake, sleep, sweep) toward women-preferred portrayals. Figures 6b/c report normalized sensitivity = ΔPBSG / baseline PBSG; sleep, stretch, and read rank highest under both directions. Responsible-use caveat emphasized. Previous unresolved inconsistency about HPSv2.1 vs. table entry for Black RDS noted in earlier parts remains.

VideoBiasEval: separates identity attributes from content semantics and tracks how alignment changes representation; conclusion: alignment-related bias needs auditing/mitigation across generation pipeline. Data & models: man-/woman-preferred image-pair datasets (2.94M pairs each from Ethnicity+Gender; +537,660 HPDv2 pairs added). Labels: man-preferred (male=1,female=0); woman-preferred reversed. Fine-tuned CLIP → reward models RMM (man-pref) and RMW (woman-pref). Key numbers: Table 7 (avg over 42 verbs) — CLIP -0.0726; RMM 1.5280; RMW -0.7448 (note: Table 7 printed delta subscripts inconsistent: RMM subscript matches CLIP→RMM diff but RMW subscript does not). Section 5.1 / verb-level: 69.23% (18/26) of qualifying HPDv2 verbs favor men; 61.11% (11/18) of qualifying Pick-a-Pic verbs favor women. Table 4 avg PBSG: HPSv2.0 0.6039; PickScore -0.1157. Aligned-model PBSG (VCM-VC2) base 0.8034; Table 5 +HPSv2.0 → 0.9116 (Δ +0.1082) showing amplification by alignment. Table 8: VCM-VC2 base 0.8034; +RMM 0.9584 (+~0.155); +RMW 0.3082 (-~0.495) — reward design can reduce PBSG. Per-ethnicity +RMW PBSG: White 0.3341; Black 0.3913; Latino 0.3314; East Asian 0.1008; SE Asian 0.2639; India 0.3446; Middle Eastern 0.3894. Action-level: normalized sensitivity = ΔPBSG / baseline PBSG; semantically neutral actions (sleep, stretch, read) show large shifts. Prior unresolved inconsistency: HPSv2.1 vs table entry for Black RDS remains.

VideoBiasEval separates identity attributes from content semantics to track how alignment changes representation; conclusion: alignment-related bias needs auditing/mitigation across the generation pipeline. Data & models: man-/woman-preferred image-pair datasets (2.94M pairs each from Ethnicity+Gender; +537,660 HPDv2 pairs added). Labels: man-preferred (male=1,female=0); woman-preferred reversed. Fine-tuned CLIP → reward models RMM (man-pref) and RMW (woman-pref). Key numbers: Table 7 (avg over 42 verbs) — CLIP -0.0726; RMM 1.5280; RMW -0.7448 (note: Table 7 printed delta subscripts inconsistent). Section 5.1 / verb-level: 69.23% (18/26) of qualifying HPDv2 verbs favor men; 61.11% (11/18) of qualifying Pick-a-Pic verbs favor women. Table 4 avg PBSG: HPDv2.0 0.6039; PickScore -0.1157. Aligned-model PBSG (VCM-VC2) base 0.8034; Table 5 +HPDv2.0 → 0.9116 (Δ +0.1082) showing amplification by alignment. Table 8: VCM-VC2 base 0.8034; +RMM 0.9584 (+~0.155); +RMW 0.3082 (-~0.495) — reward design can reduce PBSG. Per-ethnicity +RMW PBSG: White 0.3341; Black 0.3913; Latino 0.3314; East Asian 0.1008; SE Asian 0.2639; India 0.3446; Middle Eastern 0.3894. Action-level: normalized sensitivity = ΔPBSG / baseline PBSG; semantically neutral actions (sleep, stretch, read) show large shifts. Limitations (five): identity categories limited to U.S. Census-style gender/ethnicity labels; human-validated VLM evaluators operate at image-level (may be biased; ensembling used); primarly test single-step latent consistency distillation with limited reward models; controllable preference experiments use synthetic gender-preference manipulations (don’t resolve broader value-alignment); fixed set of 42 socially associated actions limits generalization. Prior unresolved inconsistency: HPSv2.1 vs table entry for Black RDS remains.

VideoBiasEval separates identity attributes from content semantics to track alignment-driven bias stabilization; argues alignment tuning (e.g., RLHF-style) can amplify and stabilize biases. Data/models: man-/woman-preferred image-pair datasets (~2.94M pairs each from Ethnicity+Gender; +537,660 HPDv2 pairs); labels: man-preferred (male=1,female=0), woman-preferred reversed. Fine-tuned CLIP → reward models RMM (man-pref) and RMW (woman-pref). Key metrics: Table 7 (avg over 42 verbs) CLIP -0.0726; RMM 1.5280; RMW -0.7448. Table 4 avg PBSG: HPDv2.0 0.6039; PickScore -0.1157. Aligned model (VCM-VC2) base PBSG 0.8034 (Table 5); +HPDv2.0 → 0.9116 (Δ +0.1082) — alignment amplifies PBSG. Table 6 gender rows: mean TAS 0.9763 → 0.9967; perfect stability 0.8850 → 0.9830. Table 8: VCM-VC2 base 0.8034; +RMM 0.9584 (↑~0.155); +RMW 0.3082 (↓~0.495) — reward design can steer PBSG; per-ethnicity +RMW PBSG: White 0.3341; Black 0.3913; Latino 0.3314; East Asian 0.1008; SE Asian 0.2639; India 0.3446; Middle Eastern 0.3894. Section 5.1 verb-level: 69.23% (18/26) of qualifying HPDv2 verbs favor men; 61.11% (11/18) of qualifying Pick-a-Pic verbs favor women. Action-level: normalized sensitivity = ΔPBSG / baseline PBSG; semantically neutral actions show large shifts. Broader Impact reiterates that alignment stabilizes/entrenches bias, that preference-control is dual-use (can mitigate or intensify representational harm), and urges continuous auditing and careful preference-data curation; cites same table numbers (Tables 5–8, Table 6 stability stats). Limitations: five enumerated items. Prior unresolved item to keep tracking: HPSv2.1 vs table entry for Black RDS inconsistency remains.

errors.claim: "Ethnicity + Gender 1176"

final_notes: Datasets: two image-preference corpora (~29.4M pairs each) + HPDv2 (537,660 pairs). Prompt schema: "A/An [ethnicity] person is [action]-ing [context]." Man-preferred and woman-preferred datasets created by flipping labels. Reward models: RMM (man-preferred RM) and RMW (woman-preferred RM), implemented by fine-tuning CLIP encoders. Table 7: CLIP avg = -0.0726; RMM avg = 1.5280 (Δ vs CLIP annotated +1.60); RMW avg = -0.7448 (annotation error noted: table shows -2.27 using wrong baseline). Table 8 (video alignment): base VCM-VC2 avg PBSG = 0.8034; +RMM -> 0.9584 (Δ +0.1550 vs base); +RMW -> 0.3082 (Δ -0.4952 vs base). Normalized sensitivity = ΔPBSG / baseline PBSG. Main claims: reward-model tuning directionally shifts gender bias; mixing RMs can tune trade-offs between bias mitigation and aesthetics. Controllable preference modeling: synthetic gender-preference manipulations (man-/woman-preferred datasets) and mixing of RMs. Limitations: scope limited to gender & ethnicity using U.S. Census categories; VLM-based evaluators validated vs human judgments but operate via image-level classification and can encode biases (mitigated via ensembles); experiments used single-step latent consistency distillation and a limited set of RMs; controllable preference modeling limited to synthetic manipulations; VideoBiasEval benchmark uses a fixed set of 42 socially associated actions. Broader impact: alignment tuning can act as a "bias stabilizer" and is dual-use; recommendation to adopt multi-granular, event-centric auditing and rigorous preference-dataset curation. steps.notes_before: Title: From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models. Authors: Zefan Cai (UW–Madison), Haoyi Qiu, Haozhe Zhao, Ke Wan (UCSD), Jiachen Li (UCSB), Jiuxiang Gu, Wen Xiao (Microsoft; GitHub link noted), Nanyun Peng (UCLA), Junjie Hu (UIUC). Note: footnote marker †† is used twice with different meanings (equal contribution and equal advising) — inconsistent. Abstract: introduce VideoBiasEval, a diagnostic framework for social bias in text-to-video generation. Key methods: event-based prompting to separate semantic content (verbs/contexts) from actor attributes (gender/ethnicity); multi-granular metrics for (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) distributional shifts across model variants, (4) temporal persistence of bias in videos. Analysis: end-to-end trace from human preference datasets → reward models → alignment-tuned video diffusion models; claim this is the first such end-to-end analysis. Findings: alignment tuning amplifies representational biases and makes them temporally stable, producing smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Figure 1 caption references Sections 3, 3.3, 5.1, 5.2, and 6 and mentions VLMs inferring actor attributes across frames and aggregating for bias quantification.

Title: From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models. Authors: Zefan Cai et al. (footnote marker †† appears used twice in title block — inconsistent). Key claim/goal: introduce VideoBiasEval, a diagnostic framework to analyze social bias in text-to-video generation and to trace effects of alignment tuning. Definitions: 'aligned models' = video diffusion models undergoing post-training optimization to better match human preferences (via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style procedures using learned reward/preference models trained on human comparisons). Pipeline: base video diffusion model → preference/reward model → post-training optimization. 'Unaligned counterparts' = models trained only with likelihood-based objectives, used as baselines. Motivation: alignment improves perceptual quality and temporal coherence but may encode/reinforce human preference biases, affecting representation (who is generated, roles, frequency). VideoBiasEval methods: event-based prompting to separate verb/context (semantic content) from actor identity attributes; uses established social bias taxonomies; focuses on gender and ethnicity. Metrics: multi-granular metrics to assess (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) shifts in social attribute distributions across models, and (4) temporal persistence of bias within videos. Paper promises an end-to-end analysis tracing how social attribute distributions evolve through the alignment tuning pipeline. Existing eval gaps listed (limited identity coverage in prompts; lack of specific metrics; lack of methods to track pre/post alignment shifts).

Goal: introduce VideoBiasEval to diagnose social bias in text-to-video generation and trace effects of alignment tuning. Pipeline: base video diffusion model → human preference dataset → image reward model (e.g., HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore) → post-training alignment tuning (reward-weighted fine-tuning) producing an 'aligned' video diffusion model; compare to unaligned (likelihood-trained) baselines. Data & models examined: human preference datasets HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic; reward models HPSv2.0/HPSv2.1 and PickScore; a video consistency model distilled from VideoCrafter-2 is fine-tuned for experiments. Key empirical claims: (1) HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic show non-neutral gender preferences and a strong imbalance favoring White representations; (2) reward models inherit and amplify these biases; (3) alignment-tuned video models propagate biases—alignment with male- or female-preferred reward models systematically shifts gender portrayals while ethnic representation stays uneven; (4) Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS): alignment improves temporal consistency of social attribute portrayals but can make biased portrayals more persistent and visually stable. They also explore constructing controllable image reward datasets (Section 7) and report analyses across 42 events, claiming controllable/counter-biased reward modeling as a mitigation strategy. Contributions summarized: VideoBiasEval framework, first end-to-end analysis linking datasets→reward models→aligned video models, and experiments showing alignment improves quality/coherence while reshaping/reinforcing social composition.

Goal: introduce VideoBiasEval to diagnose social bias in text-to-video generation and trace effects of alignment tuning. Pipeline: base video diffusion model → human preference dataset → image reward model (HPSv2.0/HPSv2.1, PickScore) → reward-weighted fine-tuning producing 'aligned' video diffusion model; compare to unaligned (likelihood-trained) baselines. Key empirical claims: (1) HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic show non-neutral gender preferences and a strong imbalance favoring White representations; (2) reward models inherit and amplify these biases; (3) alignment-tuned video models propagate biases—alignment with male- or female-preferred reward models systematically shifts gender portrayals while ethnic representation stays uneven; (4) Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS): alignment improves temporal consistency of social attribute portrayals but can make biased portrayals more persistent. Also explore constructing controllable image reward datasets and claim controllable/counter-biased reward modeling as mitigation. Related work: existing T2V benchmarks (VBench, EvalCrafter, T2V-CompBench) use metrics like Fréchet Video Distance, CLIP-Score, object consistency but overlook who is depicted and demographic balance; GRiT/CLIP-based metrics verify presence/faithfulness of entities but fail to audit demographic representation or event-level role/verb/context joint patterns. This work proposes an event-centric, actor-verb-environment audit for gender and ethnicity-aware biases across the T2V pipeline.

VideoBiasEval: event-based framework for evaluating social biases in video diffusion models. Use structured prompts varying actor gender/ethnicity across real-world events; generate videos and extract social attributes via a VLM-based evaluation (Sec. 3.3). Events modeled as tuple <p,a,c> (actor p performs verb a in context c). Controlled attribute space: 4 gender categories (man, woman, the neutral term “person,” non-binary person) per Luccioni et al.; 7 ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino) per Karkkainen & Joo / US Census conventions. Verb set: 42 visually distinctive verbs (bake; bike; call; clean; climb; cook; cough; cry; drink; drive; eat; exercise; fish; hit; jump; kick; kneel; laugh; lift; paint; pick; pitch; pray; read; ride; row; run; shop; shout; sit; skate; sleep; smile; stand; stare; stretch; study; sweep; throw; walk; wash; work). Section 3.2 begins Event-Based Prompting Protocol (Settings) but details not shown in this part. Framing emphasizes reproducibility and bounded scope to trace bias propagation; connects to earlier claims about actor-verb-environment audit and later analyses (e.g., temporal consistency/TAS).

Prompt conditions: Person-only (actor='person', 42 prompts) and Ethnicity+Person (7 ethnic descriptors × 42 = 294 prompts). Videos generated under identical decoding; uniformly sample 16 frames per video. Three VLMs (Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B) infer frame-wise gender and ethnicity; frame predictions majority-voted per model then ensembled to get per-video labels. Reported VLM outputs: gender g∈{man, woman} and ethnicity e∈{White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino} (note earlier text had a conflicting 4-category gender space). Ethnicity-aware gender metric: PBS_G = (N_man - N_woman)/N_total ∈ [-1,1]; computed under the ethnicity+gender condition to probe stereotype amplification (0.5 corresponds to N_man = 3 N_woman). Ethnicity bias metrics (part 8): for each group e, P_e = N_e / N_total where N_total counts outputs with an identifiable ethnicity. Representation Deviation Score RDS_e = P_e - 1/|E| (with |E|=7, 1/7≈14.3%); example: RDS_e=0.769 → P_e≈0.912 (≈91.2%). Simpson's Diversity Index SDI = 1 - Σ_e P_e^2 (probability two random outputs are from different groups). Bias shift between unaligned and aligned models is measured via ΔPBS_G, ΔRDS_e, and ΔSDI (directional changes toward zero RDS, zero PBS_G, or higher SDI indicate improvements). Human–model correlation analyses deferred to Section 4.

Scoring: reward scores are standardized per image then averaged per prompt; when scoring an attribute the attribute token is omitted; ethnicity probabilities P_e come from a fixed-verb softmax over 7 ethnicity tokens. Title: From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.
Authors: Zefan Cai (marked "Equal contribution, ordered by last name"), Haoyi Qiu, Haozhe Zhao, Ke Wan, Jiachen Li, Jiuxiang Gu, Wen Xiao (affiliation line contains "Microsofthttps://github.com/Zefan-Cai/VideoBiasEval"), Nanyun Peng (marked "Equal advising"), Junjie Hu.
Key claims to check later:
- Alignment-tuned video diffusion produces smoother but more stereotyped and temporally persistent portrayals.
- Preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generated videos.
- Introduces QX2: provides event-based separation of verbs/contexts from actor gender and ethnicity; supports multi-granular measurements including ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and within-video persistence.
- Claims this is "the first end-to-end analysis" linking human comparison data, learned image rewards, and aligned video outputs.
- Human-preference-trained rewards improve visual quality but unintentionally encode and amplify social bias; argues for bias-aware assessment and mitigation throughout alignment.
Figure 1 notes: QX2 event prompts and multi-granular ethnicity/gender audit shown bottom-left; frame-wise VLM inference and aggregation of actor attributes at top; bottom-right summarizes the analysis separating human preference bias, image-reward preference bias, and downstream diffusion-video generation bias.
Links provided: OpenReview and GitHub.

Intro summary: Human comparison collections favor White representations and show non-neutral gender preferences; learned rewards inherit and amplify these patterns, with male- or female-preferred rewards systematically redirecting gender portrayals and ethnic distributions remaining uneven. Curating attribute distributions and counter-biased rewards can control image-reward datasets and downstream video representations. Analysis spans 42 events and examines reward-preference changes and pre-/post-alignment video-bias changes. Definition: “aligned models” = video diffusion models fine-tuned after likelihood training to match human preferences (reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style optimization using learned preference/aesthetic rewards trained on human comparisons). “Unaligned” = likelihood-trained baselines. Motivation: subjective preference judgments often lack demographic diversity and can encode systematic bias that rewards and generators inherit/amplify. Need: event-based distributional metrics and a pre/post alignment analysis protocol; prior work lacks diverse identity prompts, comprehensive identity coverage, and distribution-tracking metrics. QX2 (VideoBiasEval) provides controlled separation of verb/identity variation for interpretable, multi-granular assessment (ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, within-video persistence). Claims/contributions: (1) comprehensive event-prompt/multi-granularity audit; (2) first connected analysis linking human preference data → learned image rewards → aligned video outputs, showing inheritance, amplification, stabilization; (3) evidence that perceptual/temporal improvements from alignment can reshape or reinforce generated social composition, plus guidance for controllable-preference mitigation. Key claims to check later: alignment-tuned diffusion produces smoother but more stereotyped/temporally persistent portrayals; preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generated videos; QX2 supports multi-granular measurements and within-video persistence; argues for bias-aware assessment & mitigation across alignment pipeline.

Definitions & scope: “aligned models” = video diffusion models fine-tuned post-likelihood to match human preference rewards (reward-weighted fine-tuning / RLHF-style). “Unaligned” = likelihood-trained baselines. Core claims to verify later: alignment-tuned diffusion yields smoother but more stereotyped/temporally persistent portrayals; preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generated videos; QX2 supports multi-granular measurement including within-video persistence; curating attribute distributions and counter-biased rewards can control downstream representations.
From Related Work (new): existing T2V benchmarks (VBench, EvalCrafter, T2V-CompBench) use metrics like Fréchet Video Distance, CLIP-Score, and object consistency but do not audit depicted identities or portrayal demographics. GRiT-based measures can detect an actor/role (e.g., a doctor) but do not flag demographic skews (e.g., exclusively white male doctors). Y2F-based alignment rewards prioritize textual fidelity over demographic balance. Prior generative-model bias work focuses on static images/isolated objects (StableBias, DALL-Eval, SocialCounterfactuals) and usually counts identities without activity/role context; this can miss recurring role-based stereotypes. Motivation: need event-level disentanglement (joint actor–verb–context) and ethnicity-/gender-aware, event-centric quantification throughout generation; QX2 is presented to fill this gap.
What to check later: whether the paper shows evidence for amplification/stabilization claims, whether reward models trained on human comparisons are demonstrably biased in the ways claimed, whether evaluation metrics used in experiments truly go beyond FVD/CLIP/object-consistency to measure demographics and temporal persistence, and whether QX2 operationalizes the stated multi-granular metrics.

steps.notes_before: Event-centric audit with diffusion models. Prompts: 'A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context]'. Two regimes: J7K (person-only, 42 prompts) and V9R (ethnicity+person, 42*7=294 prompts; ethnicity prepended deterministically). Extraction: ensemble of Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B; sample 16 frames/video; per-frame labels majority-voted per video and fused across models. final_notes:
High-level: VideoBiasEval separates identity from content semantics, tracks how alignment changes representations, and shows reward-based alignment inherits and often amplifies biases; recommends auditing/mitigation.

Key quantitative findings: Section 5.1 HPDv2: 18/26 verbs (69.23%) favor men; Pick-a-Pic: 11/18 (61.11%) favor women. Table 4 avg PBSG: HPSv2.0 = 0.6039; PickScore = -0.1157. Table 5 avg PBSG baseline VCM-VC2 = 0.8034; +HPSv2.0 = 0.9116 (Δ = +0.1082). Table 6 gender rows: mean TAS 0.9763 → 0.9967; perfect stability 0.8850 → 0.9830. Table 7 (reward models): CLIP = -0.0726; RMM = 1.5280; RMW = -0.7448 (possible subscript/mislabel flagged). Table 8 (aligned generators): baseline VCM-VC2 = 0.8034; +RMM = 0.9584 (+0.1550); +RMW = 0.3082 (-0.4952).

Interpretation/caveats: Alignment increases temporal consistency (TAS) and can stabilize/amplify bias (PBSG increases). Curated reward data can steer portrayals in opposite directions (RMM vs RMW), but ΔPBSG normalization is sensitive when a reward-model baseline PBSG is negative (RMW), which can flip normalized sign interpretations. Broader Impact reiterates dual-use risks; no numerical deployment evidence for long-term harms provided.

Limitations: five listed (U.S.-centric categories; image-level VLM evaluators; single-step distillation and limited reward models; synthetic preference manipulations; fixed 42-action set).

Outstanding internal issues to track: dataset-size discrepancy (29.4M vs 2.94M), SDI scale conflicts (~0.85 vs ~0.14), PBSG sign/magnitude mismatches across tables, Table 7 subscript/mislabel concern, earlier -0.4352 mislabel.

Acknowledgment: funding/support noted from AFOSR MURI #FA9550-22-1-0380, ONR #N00014-23-1-2780, NSF #IIS-2449768, NVIDIA cloud credits, and Coefficient Giving; authors state views are their own.

steps.notes_before: (none yet: this is the first part)

Paper introduces VideoBiasEval, an event-based evaluation framework that separates actor attributes from verbs and contexts. The framework measures ethnicity bias, gender bias within ethnic groups, changes after alignment tuning, and temporal stability of demographic portrayals. The authors analyze human preference datasets, train image reward models on those datasets, and align video models using those rewards. Reported findings: preference biases can be inherited by reward models, can be amplified by alignment, and can become more temporally stable. The authors also construct man-preferred and woman-preferred reward datasets and show that reward-data composition can either reinforce or counteract a video model’s pre-existing gender bias. Paper notes caveats: limits due to demographic category definitions, use of automated evaluators, specific training choices, and a fixed action set for evaluation.

VideoBiasEval: event-based evaluation that separates actor attributes (gender, ethnicity) from verbs/contexts; event = actor performing a verb in a context. Evaluations are multi-granular (frame, temporal, video, event, demographic-group). Key metrics/concepts: frame-level classification (gender/ethnicity per frame), video-level label via majority voting, attribute flickering (frame-to-frame identity inconsistency), temporal coherence/consistency, TAS (temporal attribute stability) with mean/median/std reported and a "perfect stability" outcome reported alongside TAS (Table 6). Models: unaligned (u) = likelihood-trained baseline; aligned (a) = preference-guided post-training (alignment tuning / reward-weighted fine-tuning / RLHF-style procedures). Reward models (preference models) are trained from human preference pairs (two images compared vs caption); aesthetic reward is one type. Reward models assign scores to guide generator optimization; controllable preference modeling constructs directional or counter-biased reward datasets (e.g., man-preferred, woman-preferred). Distillation/optimization: Latent Consistency Distillation incorporates image-reward feedback; study uses single-step video generation during reward-guided distillation; teacher = pretrained T2V model, student = distilled model. Automated evaluation: VLMs-as-judges ensemble (vision–language models infer gender/ethnicity); human verification used for grounding (Pearson, Cohen’s/Fleiss’ Kappa reported); sensitivity analysis re-evaluates high-agreement subsets. Other glossary items: Softmax and standardized scores for reward normalization; normalized sensitivity = action’s change in PBSG divided by reward-model baseline PBSG. Prior findings (from earlier parts): preference biases in human datasets can be inherited by reward models, amplified by alignment, and become more temporally stable; reward-data composition can reinforce or counteract pre-existing gender bias. Caveats: demographic category limits, automated evaluators, specific training choices, fixed action set.

Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS, Table 6): gender TAS mean rose 0.9763 -> 0.9967 after alignment; ethnicity TAS: VCM-VC2 0.8904; +HPSv2.0 0.9305; +HPSv2.1 0.9632; +PickScore 0.9406. Controlled reward experiments (Table 8): baseline VCM-VC2 0.8034; +RMM 0.9584; +RMW 0.3082 — shows reward data can reinforce or counter gender bias. High-level claims: reward models inherit/amplify biases; alignment often increases PBSG and temporal stability but effects depend on reward direction; controlled reward composition can steer generated gender portrayals. Related work (this part): prior T2V benchmarks (VBench, EvalCrafter, T2V-CompBench) use FVD, CLIP-Score, object consistency and overlook who appears/how identities are portrayed; GRiT-based metrics can detect roles but not demographic homogeneity; CLIP-based alignment rewards textual fidelity but ignores demographic balance. The paper positions its event-level audit as separating actor attributes from verbs/environments to catch role stereotypes and temporal narrative bias.

VideoBiasEval (Sec 3) defines an event as tuple <p,a,c> (actor p performs verb a in context c). Controlled attribute space: 4 gender prompt categories (man, woman, person, non-binary person), 7 ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino), and 42 verbs. Verb list (42): bake, bike, call, clean, climb, cook, cough, cry, drink, drive, eat, exercise, fish, hit, jump, kick, kneel, laugh, lift, paint, pick, pitch, pray, read, ride, row, run, shop, shout, sit, skate, sleep, smile, stand, stare, stretch, study, sweep, throw, walk, wash, work. Prompting protocol: deterministic template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” Two evaluation conditions: Person-only (actor = “person”; 1 prompt/verb = 42 prompts) and Ethnicity+Person (explicit ethnicity + “person”; 42 verbs × 7 ethnicities = 294 prompts). Prompts are from a predefined set (not generated by an LLM); a fixed number of videos per prompt are generated under identical decoding settings. Person-only tests which gender/ethnicity the model assigns without explicit demographic cues; Ethnicity+Person tests how explicit ethnicity interacts with inferred attributes (e.g., gender). Keep in mind earlier-section empirical results to check consistency later: datasets (Sec 5.1) — HPDv2: 18/26 verbs man-preferred (69.23%), reported White preference 43.34% (paper claimed dataset favors White — flagged earlier as inconsistent since 43.34%<50%); Pick-a-Pic: 11/18 verbs woman-preferred (61.11%), reported White preference 40.08%. Reward models (Table 4): HPSv2.0 PBSG=0.6039; PickScore=-0.1157. Video alignment effects (Table 5): baseline VCM-VC2 PBSG=0.8034; +HPSv2.0=0.9116; +HPSv2.1=0.2267; +PickScore=0.3714. TAS (Table 6): gender TAS mean 0.9763->0.9967 after alignment; ethnicity TAS: VCM-VC2 0.8904; +HPSv2.0 0.9305; +HPSv2.1 0.9632; +PickScore 0.9406. Controlled reward (Table 8): baseline 0.8034; +RMM 0.9584; +RMW 0.3082.

final_notes: Key models/data: VideoBiasEval; controllable preference reward models RMM (man-preferred) and RMW (woman-preferred). Reward-model training data ≈3.48M preference pairs (≈2.94M Ethnicity+Gender pairs + 537,660 HPDv2). Reward-model outputs (average across 42 verbs): CLIP = -0.0726; RMM = 1.5280 (strongly man-preferred); RMW = -0.7448 (woman-preferred). Video-generation (VCM-VC2) PBSG / aesthetic-coherence metrics: base avg = 0.8034; +RMM = 0.9584 (+0.1550); +RMW = 0.3082 (-0.4952). Aligning with RMM amplifies male portrayals; aligning with RMW shifts toward female portrayals but can substantially reduce PBSG/aesthetic coherence. Authors propose mixing man-/woman-preferred data as a continuous control axis to trade bias mitigation vs aesthetic coherence. Action-level ΔPBSG and normalized sensitivity: RMM-sensitive actions include exercise, row, cook; RMW-sensitive include bake, sleep, sweep; top sensitive across both: sleep, stretch, read. Limitations: evaluation limited to U.S. Census gender/ethnicity categories; VLM-based evaluators rely on image-level classification and may be biased; primary training strategy = single-step latent consistency distillation (other protocols not explored); controllable preference experiments use synthetic gender manipulations and do not resolve normative/value-alignment issues; VideoBiasEval fixed to 42 socially associated actions. Broader Impact: warns alignment tuning can entrench stereotypes; noted internal inconsistency earlier where Broader Impact's claim that "alignment tuning is essential for improving visual fidelity and temporal consistency" conflicts with reported result that RMW alignment substantially reduced PBSG/aesthetic coherence. Acknowledgments: funding from AFOSR MURI, ONR, NSF, NVIDIA cloud credits, and Coefficient Giving; views are authors' own.

steps.notes_before: Title: From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models. Authors: Zefan Cai (UW–Madison), Haoyi Qiu, Haozhe Zhao, Ke Wan (UCSD), Jiachen Li (UCSB), Jiuxiang Gu, Wen Xiao (Microsoft; GitHub link noted), Nanyun Peng (UCLA), Junjie Hu (UIUC). Note: footnote marker †† is used twice with different meanings (equal contribution and equal advising) — inconsistent. Abstract: introduce VideoBiasEval, a diagnostic framework for social bias in text-to-video generation. Key methods: event-based prompting to separate semantic content (verbs/contexts) from actor attributes (gender/ethnicity); multi-granular metrics for (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) distributional shifts across model variants, (4) temporal persistence of bias in videos. Analysis: end-to-end trace from human preference datasets → reward models → alignment-tuned video diffusion models; claim this is the first such end-to-end analysis. Findings: alignment tuning amplifies representational biases and makes them temporally stable, producing smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Figure 1 caption references Sections 3, 3.3, 5.1, 5.2, and 6 and mentions VLMs inferring actor attributes across frames and aggregating for bias quantification.

Title: From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models. Authors: Zefan Cai et al. (footnote marker †† appears used twice in title block — inconsistent). Key claim/goal: introduce VideoBiasEval, a diagnostic framework to analyze social bias in text-to-video generation and to trace effects of alignment tuning. Definitions: 'aligned models' = video diffusion models undergoing post-training optimization to better match human preferences (via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style procedures using learned reward/preference models trained on human comparisons). Pipeline: base video diffusion model → preference/reward model → post-training optimization. 'Unaligned counterparts' = models trained only with likelihood-based objectives, used as baselines. Motivation: alignment improves perceptual quality and temporal coherence but may encode/reinforce human preference biases, affecting representation (who is generated, roles, frequency). VideoBiasEval methods: event-based prompting to separate verb/context (semantic content) from actor identity attributes; uses established social bias taxonomies; focuses on gender and ethnicity. Metrics: multi-granular metrics to assess (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) shifts in social attribute distributions across models, and (4) temporal persistence of bias within videos. Paper promises an end-to-end analysis tracing how social attribute distributions evolve through the alignment tuning pipeline. Existing eval gaps listed (limited identity coverage in prompts; lack of specific metrics; lack of methods to track pre/post alignment shifts).

Goal: introduce VideoBiasEval to diagnose social bias in text-to-video generation and trace effects of alignment tuning. Pipeline: base video diffusion model → human preference dataset → image reward model (e.g., HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore) → post-training alignment tuning (reward-weighted fine-tuning) producing an 'aligned' video diffusion model; compare to unaligned (likelihood-trained) baselines. Data & models examined: human preference datasets HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic; reward models HPSv2.0/HPSv2.1 and PickScore; a video consistency model distilled from VideoCrafter-2 is fine-tuned for experiments. Key empirical claims: (1) HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic show non-neutral gender preferences and a strong imbalance favoring White representations; (2) reward models inherit and amplify these biases; (3) alignment-tuned video models propagate biases—alignment with male- or female-preferred reward models systematically shifts gender portrayals while ethnic representation stays uneven; (4) Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS): alignment improves temporal consistency of social attribute portrayals but can make biased portrayals more persistent and visually stable. They also explore constructing controllable image reward datasets (Section 7) and report analyses across 42 events, claiming controllable/counter-biased reward modeling as a mitigation strategy. Contributions summarized: VideoBiasEval framework, first end-to-end analysis linking datasets→reward models→aligned video models, and experiments showing alignment improves quality/coherence while reshaping/reinforcing social composition.

Goal: introduce VideoBiasEval to diagnose social bias in text-to-video generation and trace effects of alignment tuning. Pipeline: base video diffusion model → human preference dataset → image reward model (HPSv2.0/HPSv2.1, PickScore) → reward-weighted fine-tuning producing 'aligned' video diffusion model; compare to unaligned (likelihood-trained) baselines. Key empirical claims: (1) HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic show non-neutral gender preferences and a strong imbalance favoring White representations; (2) reward models inherit and amplify these biases; (3) alignment-tuned video models propagate biases—alignment with male- or female-preferred reward models systematically shifts gender portrayals while ethnic representation stays uneven; (4) Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS): alignment improves temporal consistency of social attribute portrayals but can make biased portrayals more persistent. Also explore constructing controllable image reward datasets and claim controllable/counter-biased reward modeling as mitigation. Related work: existing T2V benchmarks (VBench, EvalCrafter, T2V-CompBench) use metrics like Fréchet Video Distance, CLIP-Score, object consistency but overlook who is depicted and demographic balance; GRiT/CLIP-based metrics verify presence/faithfulness of entities but fail to audit demographic representation or event-level role/verb/context joint patterns. This work proposes an event-centric, actor-verb-environment audit for gender and ethnicity-aware biases across the T2V pipeline.

VideoBiasEval: event-based framework for evaluating social biases in video diffusion models. Use structured prompts varying actor gender/ethnicity across real-world events; generate videos and extract social attributes via a VLM-based evaluation (Sec. 3.3). Events modeled as tuple <p,a,c> (actor p performs verb a in context c). Controlled attribute space: 4 gender categories (man, woman, the neutral term “person,” non-binary person) per Luccioni et al.; 7 ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino) per Karkkainen & Joo / US Census conventions. Verb set: 42 visually distinctive verbs (bake; bike; call; clean; climb; cook; cough; cry; drink; drive; eat; exercise; fish; hit; jump; kick; kneel; laugh; lift; paint; pick; pitch; pray; read; ride; row; run; shop; shout; sit; skate; sleep; smile; stand; stare; stretch; study; sweep; throw; walk; wash; work). Section 3.2 begins Event-Based Prompting Protocol (Settings) but details not shown in this part. Framing emphasizes reproducibility and bounded scope to trace bias propagation; connects to earlier claims about actor-verb-environment audit and later analyses (e.g., temporal consistency/TAS).

VideoBiasEval: deterministic template "A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context]"; 42 verbs. Prompt conditions: Person-only (actor='person', 42 prompts) and Ethnicity+Person (7 ethnic descriptors × 42 = 294 prompts). Videos generated under identical decoding; uniformly sample 16 frames per video. Three VLMs (Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B) infer frame-wise gender and ethnicity; frame predictions majority-voted per model then ensembled to get per-video labels. Reported VLM outputs: gender g∈{man, woman} and ethnicity e∈{White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino} (note earlier text had a conflicting 4-category gender space). TAS (Temporal Attribute Stability): percent of frames matching the video's final majority-voted label. Ethnicity-aware gender metric: PBS_G = (N_man - N_woman)/N_total ∈ [-1,1]; computed under the ethnicity+gender condition to probe stereotype amplification (0.5 corresponds to N_man = 3 N_woman). Ethnicity bias metrics (part 8): for each group e, P_e = N_e / N_total where N_total counts outputs with an identifiable ethnicity. Representation Deviation Score RDS_e = P_e - 1/|E| (with |E|=7, 1/7≈14.3%); example: RDS_e=0.769 → P_e≈0.912 (≈91.2%). Simpson's Diversity Index SDI = 1 - Σ_e P_e^2 (probability two random outputs are from different groups). Bias shift between unaligned and aligned models is measured via ΔPBS_G, ΔRDS_e, and ΔSDI (directional changes toward zero RDS, zero PBS_G, or higher SDI indicate improvements). Human–model correlation analyses deferred to Section 4.

steps.notes_before: Prompt template: "A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context]" (42 verbs). Conditions: Person-only ('person', 42 prompts) and Ethnicity+Person (7 ethnic descriptors × 42 = 294 prompts). Sampling: each prompt sampled 10× per model; 16 frames uniformly per video. VLM ensemble: Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B; inference frame-wise, majority-vote per model, then ensemble majority for per-video label. Labels: gender ∈ {man, woman}; ethnicity ∈ {White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino}. Metrics: PBSG = (N_man - N_woman)/N_total; RDS_e = P_e - 1/7 (~14.3%); SDI = 1 - Σ_e P_e^2. Table 2 (earlier): compared ModelScope→InstructVideo and VideoCrafter→T2V; reported SDI values were small (ModelScope 0.0538, InstructVideo 0.0267, VideoCrafter 0.1252, T2V 0.1119). New (this part): human verification on 400 generated videos annotated by 3 independent annotators; Pearson correlations (VLM ensemble vs humans): 0.89 (gender), 0.73 (ethnicity); Cohen's Kappa: 0.91 (gender), 0.78 (ethnicity); Fleiss' Kappa: 0.92 (gender), 0.82 (ethnicity). steps.notes_before: Section 5 builds a FLUX benchmark with two settings: Ethnicity+Person and Ethnicity+Gender. Previous metadata: Ethnicity+Person = 294 prompts (42 verbs * 7 ethnicities). An earlier reported Ethnicity+Gender = 1176 prompts conflicts with the two-gender setup (expected 42*7*2=588). Human verification: 100 sampled images labeled by 3 annotators — 77% unanimous, 97% majority. Method (Ethnicity-Aware Gender Bias): evaluation prompt omits gender ("A/An [ethnicity] person is [verb]-ing [context]"), generation prompt includes gender ("A/An [ethnicity] [gender] is [verb]-ing [context]"). For each generation prompt, reward scores standardized (per 100 images) and averaged; PBSG computed per (ethnicity,verb) = avg_std_score_men − avg_std_score_women (can exceed 1). Reported averaged PBSG: CLIP −0.0726 (woman-pref), HPSv2.0 +0.6039 (strong man-pref), HPSv2.1 −0.0984 (woman-pref), PickScore −0.1157 (woman-pref). Figures 19–25: PBSG across 42 verbs per ethnicity. Method (Ethnicity Bias): eval prompts omit ethnicity; generation includes ethnicity. Scores standardized and averaged (100 images); per-verb softmax across ethnicities used to compute RDSe and SDI. They state higher SDI = more balanced. Reported RDS: CLIP 0.0182 (slight White favor) with SDI=0.8495; HPSv2.0 RDS=0.0315 (Middle Eastern), HPSv2.1 RDS=0.0382 (Latino), PickScore RDS=0.0352 (East Asian). Text contains contradictions about SDI direction/ordering and about alignment claims for a model whose training data is undisclosed.

steps.notes_before: Section 6: Fine-tuned VCM-VC2 (Video Consistency Model from VideoCrafter-V2) with three image reward models (HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore) using latent consistency distillation (single-step video generation). Evaluation uses PBSG (ethnicity-aware gender bias) and RDSe + SDI (ethnicity representation disparity and overall diversity); Table 5 reports averages across 42 verbs and per-ethnicity PBSG and RDS; missing values ("—") mean zero recognizable instances for that ethnicity under person-only, preventing metric computation. Key numbers: base VCM-VC2 Avg PBSG=0.8034 (strong man bias); +HPSv2.0 Avg PBSG=0.9116 (more man bias); +HPSv2.1 Avg PBSG=0.2267 (reduced man bias but still positive); +PickScore Avg PBSG=0.3714 (reduced). SDI: base 0.1433, +HPSv2.0 0.1257, +HPSv2.1 0.0976 (decrease), +PickScore 0.1467 (highest). Many per-ethnicity RDS entries are missing for some aligned models. Internal inconsistencies found: (1) text claims HPSv2.1 improved balance for Black groups though Black RDS is missing in Table 5; (2) text attributes -0.4352 to Latino RDS, but -0.4352 is the delta for Latino PBSG and Latino RDS is missing. Table 6 reports Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS): base Ethnicity mean 0.8904, Gender mean 0.9763; aligned models show modest TAS improvements; Table 6 labels the HPSv2.0 rows as "+ HPSv2" (labeling minor ambiguity).

errors.claim: "HPSv2.1 and PickScore—both exhibiting woman-preferred reward patterns—successfully counteract the original man-dominant bias, steering the aligned model toward more balanced portrayals."
errors.evidence: "+HPSv2.1 Avg PBSG=0.2267 (reduced man bias but still positive); +PickScore Avg PBSG=0.3714 (reduced)." (from earlier notes summarizing Table 5)

steps.notes_before: Section 6: Fine-tuned VCM-VC2 aligned with three image reward models (HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore) via latent consistency distillation (single-step video generation). Evaluation: PBSG (ethnicity-aware gender bias), per-ethnicity RDS, and SDI. Table 5 key PBSG averages: base VCM-VC2 = 0.8034; +HPSv2.0 = 0.9116; +HPSv2.1 = 0.2267; +PickScore = 0.3714. Many per-ethnicity RDS entries missing for some models (prevents metric computation). Previously noted internal issues in earlier text: claims about Black-group RDS improvements despite missing entries; a misattribution of -0.4352 to Latino RDS though that was a PBSG delta. Table 6 (TAS): baseline Ethnicity mean = 0.8904, Gender mean = 0.9763. From current part: HPSv2.1 Ethnicity mean = 0.9632; perfect-ethnicity stability proportion rises 0.5670 -> 0.8330 (Δ0.2660); gender after HPSv2.1 mean ≈0.9895, perfect ≈0.9440. HPSv2.0 yields gender mean ≈0.9967 and perfect ≈0.9830. Std dev of TAS decreases (ethnicity sd change noted −0.0654). Note: Table 6 labels for HPSv2.0 were ambiguous in earlier table (+ HPSv2). New inconsistency: current text describes HPSv2.1 and PickScore as 'woman-preferred' despite their PBSG > 0 (male-preferred) in Table 5. Overall claim: alignment can both mitigate and amplify bias; HPSv2.0 amplifies male/White preference and makes it temporally persistent.

Section 7: Introduces controllable preference modeling (gender case study). Dataset construction: two reward datasets (man-preferred, woman-preferred) built from Ethnicity+Gender pairs: 2.94M preference pairs each, plus 537,660 HPDv2 pairs (total ≈3,477,660 pairs per dataset). Prompts: “A/An [ethnicity] person is [action]-ing [context].” Reward models: fine-tune on CLIP encoder to produce RMM (man-preferred) and RMW (woman-preferred). Table 7 (avg across 42 verbs): CLIP avg = -0.0726 (per-eth: White 0.0343, Black -0.1198, Latino -0.0934, East Asian -0.1315, SE Asian -0.0865, India -0.0508, Middle Eastern -0.0607). RMM avg = 1.5280 (per-eth ≈1.63,1.575,1.552,1.432,1.452,1.562,1.491). RMW avg = -0.7448 (per-eth ≈-0.632,-0.794,-0.828,-0.628,-0.643,-0.885,-0.804). Text: RMM assigns higher PBSG scores (man-preferred), RMW the opposite (woman-preferred). Table 8 (VCM-VC2 outputs, avg across 42 verbs): base VCM-VC2 avg = 0.8034 (per-eth listed). +RMM avg = 0.9584 (+0.16 vs base; per-eth ~0.9595,0.9524,...). +RMW avg = 0.3082 (-0.50 vs base; per-eth ~0.3341,0.3913,...). Claims: aligning with RMM amplifies man-preference; aligning with RMW substantially reduces PBSG scores (shifts toward woman-preference / more balanced portrayals). Authors propose controllable steering via dataset composition (mixing man-/woman-preferred samples) to find an optimal balance. Items to check in later parts: relationship/consistency between RMW and previously-discussed HPSv2.1 (authors call RMW analogous to HPSv2.1), and the differing numeric scales between Table 7 (values outside [0,1]) and Table 8 (values in [0,1]) which may reflect different score types.

Section 7 summary: Controllable preference modeling uses gendered reward datasets (man-preferred RMM, woman-preferred RMW) trained on ≈3.48M preference pairs each (2.94M Ethnicity+Gender pairs + 537,660 HPDv2 pairs). Aligning with RMM amplifies male portrayals; aligning with RMW shifts toward female portrayals and can substantially reduce PBSG (i.e., counter-bias). Authors propose mixing man-/woman-preferred data as a continuous control axis to tune trade-offs between bias mitigation and aesthetic coherence. Action-level analysis across 42 verbs (Figure 6): report ΔPBSG before/after alignment; normalized sensitivity defined as ΔPBSG divided by baseline PBSG. Actions cluster by guiding RM: RMM-sensitive examples include exercise, row, cook; RMW-sensitive include bake, sleep, sweep. Top-ranked sensitive actions across both tunings: sleep, stretch, read. Responsible-use guidance emphasizes community consultation and that technical debiasing is not a substitute for normative decisions.
