final_notes: Section 7: constructed gendered image-preference datasets — two C4Z collections of 2.94M preference pairs each, plus 537,660 R9C pairs; prompt template: A/An [ethnicity] person is [action]-ing [context]. One dataset labels male=1/female=0 (man-preferred), the other reverses labels (woman-preferred). Pretrained Y2F (CLIP-like) vision encoder fine-tuned into two reward models: Z6B (man-preferred RMM) and P3L (woman-preferred RMW). Table 7 (reward-model L2V preference bias, avg across 42 verbs): Y2F avg = -0.0726; Z6B avg = 1.5280; P3L avg = -0.7448. Note: Table 7 subscripts inconsistent. Table 8 (aligned-video-model L2V social bias, avg across 42 verbs): G4S baseline avg = 0.8034 (White 0.7925); +Z6B = 0.9584 (+0.16); +P3L = 0.3082 (-0.50). Z6B alignment increases L2V (reinforces man-preference); P3L reduces L2V (shifts toward woman-preference). Action sensitivity (normalized ΔL2V/baseline L2V) highest for sleep, stretch, read. Unresolved methodological framing: paper alternates between Y2F as pretrained shared base and G4S as generator baseline for alignment comparisons (switch unexplained). Broader Impact: alignment/RLHF can stabilize and entrench bias; dual-use risk of curated preference data; responsibility to monitor social composition using multi-granular, event-centric audits (e.g., QX2); preference-data curation needs architecture-design rigor. Title: From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.
Authors: Zefan Cai (marked "Equal contribution, ordered by last name"), Haoyi Qiu, Haozhe Zhao, Ke Wan, Jiachen Li, Jiuxiang Gu, Wen Xiao (affiliation line contains "Microsofthttps://github.com/Zefan-Cai/VideoBiasEval"), Nanyun Peng (marked "Equal advising"), Junjie Hu.
Key claims to check later:
- Alignment-tuned video diffusion produces smoother but more stereotyped and temporally persistent portrayals.
- Preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generated videos.
- Introduces QX2: provides event-based separation of verbs/contexts from actor gender and ethnicity; supports multi-granular measurements including ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and within-video persistence.
- Claims this is "the first end-to-end analysis" linking human comparison data, learned image rewards, and aligned video outputs.
- Human-preference-trained rewards improve visual quality but unintentionally encode and amplify social bias; argues for bias-aware assessment and mitigation throughout alignment.
Figure 1 notes: QX2 event prompts and multi-granular ethnicity/gender audit shown bottom-left; frame-wise VLM inference and aggregation of actor attributes at top; bottom-right summarizes the analysis separating human preference bias, image-reward preference bias, and downstream diffusion-video generation bias.
Links provided: OpenReview and GitHub.

Intro summary: Human comparison collections favor White representations and show non-neutral gender preferences; learned rewards inherit and amplify these patterns, with male- or female-preferred rewards systematically redirecting gender portrayals and ethnic distributions remaining uneven. Curating attribute distributions and counter-biased rewards can control image-reward datasets and downstream video representations. Analysis spans 42 events and examines reward-preference changes and pre-/post-alignment video-bias changes. Definition: “aligned models” = video diffusion models fine-tuned after likelihood training to match human preferences (reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style optimization using learned preference/aesthetic rewards trained on human comparisons). “Unaligned” = likelihood-trained baselines. Motivation: subjective preference judgments often lack demographic diversity and can encode systematic bias that rewards and generators inherit/amplify. Need: event-based distributional metrics and a pre/post alignment analysis protocol; prior work lacks diverse identity prompts, comprehensive identity coverage, and distribution-tracking metrics. QX2 (VideoBiasEval) provides controlled separation of verb/identity variation for interpretable, multi-granular assessment (ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, within-video persistence). Claims/contributions: (1) comprehensive event-prompt/multi-granularity audit; (2) first connected analysis linking human preference data → learned image rewards → aligned video outputs, showing inheritance, amplification, stabilization; (3) evidence that perceptual/temporal improvements from alignment can reshape or reinforce generated social composition, plus guidance for controllable-preference mitigation. Key claims to check later: alignment-tuned diffusion produces smoother but more stereotyped/temporally persistent portrayals; preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generated videos; QX2 supports multi-granular measurements and within-video persistence; argues for bias-aware assessment & mitigation across alignment pipeline.

Definitions & scope: “aligned models” = video diffusion models fine-tuned post-likelihood to match human preference rewards (reward-weighted fine-tuning / RLHF-style). “Unaligned” = likelihood-trained baselines. Core claims to verify later: alignment-tuned diffusion yields smoother but more stereotyped/temporally persistent portrayals; preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generated videos; QX2 supports multi-granular measurement including within-video persistence; curating attribute distributions and counter-biased rewards can control downstream representations.
From Related Work (new): existing T2V benchmarks (VBench, EvalCrafter, T2V-CompBench) use metrics like Fréchet Video Distance, CLIP-Score, and object consistency but do not audit depicted identities or portrayal demographics. GRiT-based measures can detect an actor/role (e.g., a doctor) but do not flag demographic skews (e.g., exclusively white male doctors). Y2F-based alignment rewards prioritize textual fidelity over demographic balance. Prior generative-model bias work focuses on static images/isolated objects (StableBias, DALL-Eval, SocialCounterfactuals) and usually counts identities without activity/role context; this can miss recurring role-based stereotypes. Motivation: need event-level disentanglement (joint actor–verb–context) and ethnicity-/gender-aware, event-centric quantification throughout generation; QX2 is presented to fill this gap.
What to check later: whether the paper shows evidence for amplification/stabilization claims, whether reward models trained on human comparisons are demonstrably biased in the ways claimed, whether evaluation metrics used in experiments truly go beyond FVD/CLIP/object-consistency to measure demographics and temporal persistence, and whether QX2 operationalizes the stated multi-granular metrics.

final_notes:
Broader Impact: alignment can stabilize and entrench bias; polished/temporally consistent outputs make stereotypes appear more natural and harder to detect. Dual-use: controllable preference modeling can mitigate or intensify representational harm depending on curated reward data; risks include normalization, exclusion, homogenization, propaganda. Mitigation/responsibility: continuous auditing (e.g., VideoBiasEval), preference-data curation needs rigor; aesthetic metrics alone insufficient.

Key quantitative claims reiterated: Table 5 avg PBSG (alignment amplifies bias): VCM-VC2 = 0.8034; +HPSv2.0 = 0.9116 (Δ ≈ +0.1082). Table 6 (gender rows stability): mean TAS 0.9763 → 0.9967; perfect stability 0.8850 → 0.9830. Table 7 avg reward PBSG (reward models biases): RMM = 1.5280; RMW = -0.7448 (CLIP baseline earlier = -0.0726). Table 8 avg video PBSG (reward tuning effects): base VCM-VC2 = 0.8034; +RMM = 0.9584 (Δ +0.155); +RMW = 0.3082 (Δ −0.495).

Datasets & labels: two large preference datasets (~2.94M same-action/same-ethnicity image-preference pairs each) + 537,660 HPDv2 pairs; labels: man-preferred (male=1), woman-preferred (female=1). Action-level sensitivity measured by ΔPBSG and normalized sensitivity; top sensitive actions: sleep, stretch, read; RMM-sensitive: exercise, row, cook; RMW-sensitive: bake, sleep, sweep.

Limitations: limited identity labels, VLM evaluator limits, single alignment protocol tested, synthetic controllable experiments, fixed 42-action set.

Acknowledgment: research supported by AFOSR MURI grant #FA9550-22-1-0380, ONR Award #N00014-23-1-2780, NSF Award #IIS-2449768, NVIDIA Academic Grant cloud credits, and funding from the Technical AI Safety Research Program at Coefficient Giving; views are authors' own.

steps.notes_before: (none yet: this is the first part)

Paper introduces VideoBiasEval, an event-based evaluation framework that separates actor attributes from verbs and contexts. The framework measures ethnicity bias, gender bias within ethnic groups, changes after alignment tuning, and temporal stability of demographic portrayals. The authors analyze human preference datasets, train image reward models on those datasets, and align video models using those rewards. Reported findings: preference biases can be inherited by reward models, can be amplified by alignment, and can become more temporally stable. The authors also construct man-preferred and woman-preferred reward datasets and show that reward-data composition can either reinforce or counteract a video model’s pre-existing gender bias. Paper notes caveats: limits due to demographic category definitions, use of automated evaluators, specific training choices, and a fixed action set for evaluation.

VideoBiasEval: event-based evaluation that separates actor attributes (gender, ethnicity) from verbs/contexts; event = actor performing a verb in a context. Evaluations are multi-granular (frame, temporal, video, event, demographic-group). Key metrics/concepts: frame-level classification (gender/ethnicity per frame), video-level label via majority voting, attribute flickering (frame-to-frame identity inconsistency), temporal coherence/consistency, TAS (temporal attribute stability) with mean/median/std reported and a "perfect stability" outcome reported alongside TAS (Table 6). Models: unaligned (u) = likelihood-trained baseline; aligned (a) = preference-guided post-training (alignment tuning / reward-weighted fine-tuning / RLHF-style procedures). Reward models (preference models) are trained from human preference pairs (two images compared vs caption); aesthetic reward is one type. Reward models assign scores to guide generator optimization; controllable preference modeling constructs directional or counter-biased reward datasets (e.g., man-preferred, woman-preferred). Distillation/optimization: Latent Consistency Distillation incorporates image-reward feedback; study uses single-step video generation during reward-guided distillation; teacher = pretrained T2V model, student = distilled model. Automated evaluation: VLMs-as-judges ensemble (vision–language models infer gender/ethnicity); human verification used for grounding (Pearson, Cohen’s/Fleiss’ Kappa reported); sensitivity analysis re-evaluates high-agreement subsets. Other glossary items: Softmax and standardized scores for reward normalization; normalized sensitivity = action’s change in PBSG divided by reward-model baseline PBSG. Prior findings (from earlier parts): preference biases in human datasets can be inherited by reward models, amplified by alignment, and become more temporally stable; reward-data composition can reinforce or counteract pre-existing gender bias. Caveats: demographic category limits, automated evaluators, specific training choices, fixed action set.

VideoBiasEval (Sec 3) defines an event as tuple <p,a,c> (actor p performs verb a in context c). Controlled attribute space: 4 gender prompt categories (man, woman, person, non-binary person), 7 ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino), and 42 verbs. Verb list (42): bake, bike, call, clean, climb, cook, cough, cry, drink, drive, eat, exercise, fish, hit, jump, kick, kneel, laugh, lift, paint, pick, pitch, pray, read, ride, row, run, shop, shout, sit, skate, sleep, smile, stand, stare, stretch, study, sweep, throw, walk, wash, work. Prompting protocol: deterministic template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” Two evaluation conditions: Person-only (actor = “person”; 1 prompt/verb = 42 prompts) and Ethnicity+Person (explicit ethnicity + “person”; 42 verbs × 7 ethnicities = 294 prompts). Prompts are from a predefined set (not generated by an LLM); a fixed number of videos per prompt are generated under identical decoding settings. Person-only tests which gender/ethnicity the model assigns without explicit demographic cues; Ethnicity+Person tests how explicit ethnicity interacts with inferred attributes (e.g., gender). Section 7 tests controllable bias via purposely composed image-preference datasets (gender case study). Dataset construction: two datasets (man-preferred, woman-preferred) each with 2.94M same-action/same-ethnicity preference pairs drawn from the Ethnicity+Gender set; plus 537,660 HPDv2 image pairs for face-free diversity. Labels: man-preferred sets label male=1/female=0 and woman-preferred the reverse. Two reward models (fine-tuned on a CLIP encoder): RMM (man-preferred) and RMW (woman-preferred). Table 7 (avg across 42 verbs) — CLIP avg -0.0726; RMM avg 1.5280 (Δ +1.60); RMW avg -0.7448 (Δ -2.27); per-ethnicity entries shown. Table 8 (avg PBSG across 42 verbs) — VCM-VC2 baseline 0.8034; +RMM 0.9584 (Δ +0.16); +RMW 0.3082 (Δ -0.50); per-ethnicity +RMW examples: White 0.3341, Black 0.3913, Latino 0.3314, East Asian 0.1008, SE Asian 0.2639, India 0.3446, Middle Eastern 0.3894. Findings: RMM pushes generator toward stronger male preference; RMW pushes toward woman preference and (on average) closer to gender equilibrium than the male-biased baseline. Paper frames RMW as a counter-biased reward analogous to HPSv2.1 and promotes tuning mixture proportions to minimize overall bias while preserving aesthetics. Note: earlier parts flagged ambiguity/missing per-group RDS entries for +HPSv2.1 in Table 5; keep that mapping/ambiguity in mind for cross-checking HPSv2.1 ↔ RMW claims later.

Per-ethnicity +RMW examples: White 0.3341, Black 0.3913, Latino 0.3314, East Asian 0.1008, SE Asian 0.2639, India 0.3446, Middle Eastern 0.3894. Action-level (42 verbs) sensitivity (Figure 6): ΔPBSG measured before/after alignment; normalized sensitivity = ΔPBSG / reward-model baseline PBSG. RMM examples: exercise, row, cook; RMW examples: bake, sleep, sweep. Top sensitive actions under both directions: sleep, stretch, read. Section 8 (Conclusion) and Sec 7 gender case study — key claims and numbers: (1) Preference data and reward models carry directional biases: HPDv2: 69.23% (18/26) qualifying verbs favor men; Pick-a-Pic: 61.11% (11/18) favor women. Table 4 avg PBSG: HPSv2.0 = 0.6039; PickScore = -0.1157. (2) Alignment can amplify inherited bias: Table 5 avg PBSG: VCM-VC2 baseline = 0.8034; +HPSv2.0 = 0.9116 (Delta +0.1082). (3) Reward design can counter bias: Table 8 avg PBSG: VCM-VC2 = 0.8034; +RMW = 0.3082 (Delta ≈ -0.50). Datasets and labels: two preference datasets ≈2.94M same-action/same-ethnicity image-preference pairs each, plus 537,660 HPDv2 pairs; labels: man-preferred (male=1), woman-preferred (female=1). Reward models: RMM (man) and RMW (woman), fine-tuned on CLIP. Table 7 (avg across 42 verbs): CLIP = -0.0726; RMM = 1.5280; RMW = -0.7448. Table 8 (avg across 42 verbs): VCM-VC2 = 0.8034; +RMM = 0.9584 (Delta +0.155); +RMW = 0.3082 (Delta -0.495). Action-level sensitivity: Delta PBSG measured pre/post alignment; normalized sensitivity = DeltaPBSG / baseline PBSG. Top sensitive actions overall: sleep, stretch, read. RMM-sensitive examples: exercise, row, cook. RMW-sensitive examples: bake, sleep, sweep. Proposed control: mixtures of man-/woman-preferred data for tunable outputs. Note: earlier parts flagged inconsistent reported deltas in paper (to verify). Limitations (this part): five main limitations — (1) identity categories limited to U.S. Census-style gender/ethnicity labels (no full fluidity/intersectionality), (2) human-validated VLM evaluators perform image-level classification and may be biased or inaccurate (ensembling mitigates but more diverse annotations needed), (3) primary alignment method tested was single-step latent consistency distillation with a limited set of reward models (other protocols like RL may behave differently), (4) controllable preference experiments use synthetic gender-preference manipulations and do not resolve broader value-alignment or societal-impact questions, (5) fixed set of 42 socially associated actions may limit generalization to open-ended generation.

Broader Impact: alignment can stabilize and entrench bias; polished/temporally consistent outputs make stereotypes appear more natural and harder to detect. Dual-use: controllable preference modeling can mitigate or intensify representational harm depending on curated reward data; risks include normalization, exclusion, homogenization, propaganda (no numerical deployment evidence provided). Mitigation/responsibility: continuous auditing (e.g., VideoBiasEval), preference-data curation needs rigor; aesthetic metrics alone insufficient.

- Table 8 avg video PBSG (reward tuning effects): base VCM-VC2 = 0.8034; +RMM = 0.9584 (Δ +0.155); +RMW = 0.3082 (Δ −0.495).

Retained earlier core points: two large preference datasets (~2.94M same-action/same-ethnicity image-preference pairs each) + 537,660 HPDv2 pairs; labels: man-preferred (male=1), woman-preferred (female=1). Action-level sensitivity measured by ΔPBSG and normalized sensitivity; top sensitive actions: sleep, stretch, read; RMM-sensitive: exercise, row, cook; RMW-sensitive: bake, sleep, sweep. Limitations: 5 items (limited identity labels, VLM evaluator limits, single alignment protocol tested, synthetic controllable experiments, fixed 42-action set).

final_notes: Controllable preference modeling: constructed man- and woman-preferred datasets (~2.94M Ethnicity+Gender pairs each; 537,660 HPDv2 pairs). Fine-tuned CLIP-based reward models: RMM (man-pref) and RMW (woman-pref). Table 7 reported scores: CLIP -0.0726; RMM 1.5280; RMW -0.7448. Paper reports deltas vs CLIP: RMM +1.60 (consistent: 1.5280 - (-0.0726) = +1.6006); RMW reported -2.27 (inconsistent: -0.7448 - (-0.0726) = -0.6722). Table 8 (VCM-VC2 PBSG): baseline 0.8034; +RMM 0.9584 (+0.155); +RMW 0.3082 (-0.495). Qualitative: RMM amplifies male-preferred portrayals (exercise, row, cook); RMW shifts toward woman-preferred (bake, sleep, sweep). Top-ranked sensitive actions: sleep, stretch, read. Methods/training: alignment assessed under single-step latent consistency distillation; reward models CLIP-based; VLM evaluators validated against human judgments but operate at image-frame level and are ensembled. Noted definition concern: 'normalized sensitivity' is ambiguously defined (ΔPBSG divided by 'each reward model’s baseline PBSG'—generator-level metric vs reward-model baseline mismatch). Limitations & Broader Impact: study limited to gender and ethnicity (U.S. Census categories), VLM evaluator biases, limited training protocols and reward models, controllable preference experiments use synthetic gender manipulations, VideoBiasEval benchmark limited to 42 actions; warns alignment tuning can stabilize/entrench biases and controllable preference modeling is dual-use. steps.notes_before: Title: From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models. Authors: Zefan Cai (UW–Madison), Haoyi Qiu, Haozhe Zhao, Ke Wan (UCSD), Jiachen Li (UCSB), Jiuxiang Gu, Wen Xiao (Microsoft; GitHub link noted), Nanyun Peng (UCLA), Junjie Hu (UIUC). Note: footnote marker †† is used twice with different meanings (equal contribution and equal advising) — inconsistent. Abstract: introduce VideoBiasEval, a diagnostic framework for social bias in text-to-video generation. Key methods: event-based prompting to separate semantic content (verbs/contexts) from actor attributes (gender/ethnicity); multi-granular metrics for (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) distributional shifts across model variants, (4) temporal persistence of bias in videos. Analysis: end-to-end trace from human preference datasets → reward models → alignment-tuned video diffusion models; claim this is the first such end-to-end analysis. Findings: alignment tuning amplifies representational biases and makes them temporally stable, producing smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Figure 1 caption references Sections 3, 3.3, 5.1, 5.2, and 6 and mentions VLMs inferring actor attributes across frames and aggregating for bias quantification.

Title: From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models. Authors: Zefan Cai et al. (footnote marker †† appears used twice in title block — inconsistent). Key claim/goal: introduce VideoBiasEval, a diagnostic framework to analyze social bias in text-to-video generation and to trace effects of alignment tuning. Definitions: 'aligned models' = video diffusion models undergoing post-training optimization to better match human preferences (via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style procedures using learned reward/preference models trained on human comparisons). Pipeline: base video diffusion model → preference/reward model → post-training optimization. 'Unaligned counterparts' = models trained only with likelihood-based objectives, used as baselines. Motivation: alignment improves perceptual quality and temporal coherence but may encode/reinforce human preference biases, affecting representation (who is generated, roles, frequency). VideoBiasEval methods: event-based prompting to separate verb/context (semantic content) from actor identity attributes; uses established social bias taxonomies; focuses on gender and ethnicity. Metrics: multi-granular metrics to assess (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) shifts in social attribute distributions across models, and (4) temporal persistence of bias within videos. Paper promises an end-to-end analysis tracing how social attribute distributions evolve through the alignment tuning pipeline. Existing eval gaps listed (limited identity coverage in prompts; lack of specific metrics; lack of methods to track pre/post alignment shifts).

Goal: introduce VideoBiasEval to diagnose social bias in text-to-video generation and trace effects of alignment tuning. Pipeline: base video diffusion model → human preference dataset → image reward model (e.g., HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore) → post-training alignment tuning (reward-weighted fine-tuning) producing an 'aligned' video diffusion model; compare to unaligned (likelihood-trained) baselines. Data & models examined: human preference datasets HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic; reward models HPSv2.0/HPSv2.1 and PickScore; a video consistency model distilled from VideoCrafter-2 is fine-tuned for experiments. Key empirical claims: (1) HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic show non-neutral gender preferences and a strong imbalance favoring White representations; (2) reward models inherit and amplify these biases; (3) alignment-tuned video models propagate biases—alignment with male- or female-preferred reward models systematically shifts gender portrayals while ethnic representation stays uneven; (4) Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS): alignment improves temporal consistency of social attribute portrayals but can make biased portrayals more persistent and visually stable. They also explore constructing controllable image reward datasets (Section 7) and report analyses across 42 events, claiming controllable/counter-biased reward modeling as a mitigation strategy. Contributions summarized: VideoBiasEval framework, first end-to-end analysis linking datasets→reward models→aligned video models, and experiments showing alignment improves quality/coherence while reshaping/reinforcing social composition.

Goal: introduce VideoBiasEval to diagnose social bias in text-to-video generation and trace effects of alignment tuning. Pipeline: base video diffusion model → human preference dataset → image reward model (HPSv2.0/HPSv2.1, PickScore) → reward-weighted fine-tuning producing 'aligned' video diffusion model; compare to unaligned (likelihood-trained) baselines. Key empirical claims: (1) HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic show non-neutral gender preferences and a strong imbalance favoring White representations; (2) reward models inherit and amplify these biases; (3) alignment-tuned video models propagate biases—alignment with male- or female-preferred reward models systematically shifts gender portrayals while ethnic representation stays uneven; (4) Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS): alignment improves temporal consistency of social attribute portrayals but can make biased portrayals more persistent. Also explore constructing controllable image reward datasets and claim controllable/counter-biased reward modeling as mitigation. Related work: existing T2V benchmarks (VBench, EvalCrafter, T2V-CompBench) use metrics like Fréchet Video Distance, CLIP-Score, object consistency but overlook who is depicted and demographic balance; GRiT/CLIP-based metrics verify presence/faithfulness of entities but fail to audit demographic representation or event-level role/verb/context joint patterns. This work proposes an event-centric, actor-verb-environment audit for gender and ethnicity-aware biases across the T2V pipeline.

VideoBiasEval: event-based framework for evaluating social biases in video diffusion models. Use structured prompts varying actor gender/ethnicity across real-world events; generate videos and extract social attributes via a VLM-based evaluation (Sec. 3.3). Events modeled as tuple <p,a,c> (actor p performs verb a in context c). Controlled attribute space: 4 gender categories (man, woman, the neutral term “person,” non-binary person) per Luccioni et al.; 7 ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino) per Karkkainen & Joo / US Census conventions. Verb set: 42 visually distinctive verbs (bake; bike; call; clean; climb; cook; cough; cry; drink; drive; eat; exercise; fish; hit; jump; kick; kneel; laugh; lift; paint; pick; pitch; pray; read; ride; row; run; shop; shout; sit; skate; sleep; smile; stand; stare; stretch; study; sweep; throw; walk; wash; work). Section 3.2 begins Event-Based Prompting Protocol (Settings) but details not shown in this part. Framing emphasizes reproducibility and bounded scope to trace bias propagation; connects to earlier claims about actor-verb-environment audit and later analyses (e.g., temporal consistency/TAS).

VideoBiasEval: deterministic template "A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context]"; 42 verbs. Prompt conditions: Person-only (actor='person', 42 prompts) and Ethnicity+Person (7 ethnic descriptors × 42 = 294 prompts). Videos generated under identical decoding; uniformly sample 16 frames per video. Three VLMs (Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B) infer frame-wise gender and ethnicity; frame predictions majority-voted per model then ensembled to get per-video labels. Reported VLM outputs: gender g∈{man, woman} and ethnicity e∈{White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino} (note earlier text had a conflicting 4-category gender space). TAS (Temporal Attribute Stability): percent of frames matching the video's final majority-voted label. Ethnicity-aware gender metric: PBS_G = (N_man - N_woman)/N_total ∈ [-1,1]; computed under the ethnicity+gender condition to probe stereotype amplification (0.5 corresponds to N_man = 3 N_woman). Ethnicity bias metrics (part 8): for each group e, P_e = N_e / N_total where N_total counts outputs with an identifiable ethnicity. Representation Deviation Score RDS_e = P_e - 1/|E| (with |E|=7, 1/7≈14.3%); example: RDS_e=0.769 → P_e≈0.912 (≈91.2%). Simpson's Diversity Index SDI = 1 - Σ_e P_e^2 (probability two random outputs are from different groups). Bias shift between unaligned and aligned models is measured via ΔPBS_G, ΔRDS_e, and ΔSDI (directional changes toward zero RDS, zero PBS_G, or higher SDI indicate improvements). Human–model correlation analyses deferred to Section 4.

Overall eval setup: deterministic template 'A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context]'; 42 verbs; two prompt conditions used for video eval (Person-only and Ethnicity+Person with 7 ethnic descriptors × 42). Videos: 10 seeds per prompt, 16 frames per video. Three VLMs (Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B) classify frame-wise gender/ethnicity; per-model majority vote then ensemble gives per-video label. Metrics: TAS (frame agreement %), PBSG = (N_man - N_woman)/N_total, RDSe = P_e - 1/7, SDI = 1 - Σ_e P_e^2. (Part 4 reported low SDI values ~0.03–0.13 for video models; a later human-verification reported SDI ~0.75 for a different set — unresolved scale/dataset mismatch). Current (Sec 5) analyzes image reward datasets HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic: attributes extracted from captions via GPT-4o-mini and from images via the three VLMs; retained only instances with one of the predefined verbs. After processing: HPDv2 = 28,783 (image, caption, preference) tuples covering 29 verbs; Pick-a-Pic = 14,958 tuples across 19 verbs. Gender preference analysis (man–woman pairs): 26/42 verbs in HPDv2 had valid pairs; of those 69.23% (18/26) favored men. In Pick-a-Pic 18/42 verbs qualified; 61.11% (11/18) favored women. Ethnicity: both datasets show White as largest preferred group (HPDv2 43.34%, Pick-a-Pic 40.08%), then East Asian and Indian. Sec 5.2 builds a controlled T2I benchmark using FLUX with event prompts (from Sec 3.2); two generation settings for this benchmark: Ethnicity+Person (specify ethnicity only) and Ethnicity+Gender (specify both); 100 images per prompt generated.

steps.notes_before: Benchmark setup: two evaluation styles — Ethnicity+Person (eval prompts: "A/An [ethnicity] person is [verb]-ing [context]") and Ethnicity+Gender (generation prompts: "A/An [ethnicity] [gender] is [verb]-ing [context]"). 100 images per generation prompt; reward-model scores standardized (z-scores) and averaged over 100 images per prompt. PBSG (ethnicity-aware gender bias): fix ethnicity & verb, PBSG = avg standardized score(men) - avg standardized score(women). Positive = preference for men; negative = preference for women. Reported average PBSG across 42 verbs: CLIP -0.0726, HPSv2.0 +0.6039, HPSv2.1 -0.0984, PickScore -0.1157 (authors note PBSG can exceed 1). Ethnicity bias: authors say they apply softmax across ethnicities per verb to normalize, then compute an ethnicity score (called RDSe / sometimes RDS) and SDI; positive RDSe indicates overrepresentation, negative underrepresentation. Reported ethnicity/RDS: CLIP 0.0182 (White) with SDI 0.8495 (highest); HPSv2.0 0.0315 (Middle Eastern); HPSv2.1 0.0382 (Latino); PickScore 0.0352 (East Asian). Text flags inconsistent naming (RDSe vs RDS) and contradicts earlier parts about HPSv2.1 training data (earlier: HPSv2.1 trained on HPDv2.1; this part: training data undisclosed).

errors.claim: "Alignment with HPSv2.1 reduces some disparities by improving balance for White and Black groups, but significantly decreases Latino representation (RDS = –0.4352) and lowers SDI, indicating reduced diversity."

steps.notes_before: Section 6: Fine-tune VCM-VC2 with image reward models HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore; evaluate bias via PBSG (ethnicity-aware gender bias), RDS/RDSe (ethnicity representation), and SDI (diversity). Key numbers (averaged across 42 verbs): VCM-VC2 avg PBSG 0.8034; +HPSv2.0 0.9116 (+0.1082); +HPSv2.1 0.2267 (−0.5767); +PickScore 0.3714 (−0.4320). Base overrep: White RDS = 0.6405; base SDI = 0.1433. +PickScore yields highest SDI 0.1467; +HPSv2.1 lowest SDI 0.0976. Many RDS entries are '—' (zero recognizable instances → metric not computable) for some subgroups in several models. Table 6 (Temporal Attribute Stability): base Ethnicity mean TAS 0.8904; base Gender 0.9763. +HPSv2.0 Ethnicity 0.9305 (+0.0401), Gender 0.9967 (+0.0204). +HPSv2.1 Ethnicity 0.9632 (+0.0728), Gender 0.9895 (+0.0132). +PickScore Ethnicity 0.9406 (+0.0502), Gender 0.9884 (+0.0121). Internal issues to track later: section alternates between metric names 'RDSe' and 'RDS'; text incorrectly labels the Latino PBSG change (−0.4352) as an RDS value despite Latino RDS being marked missing in the table.

Section 6 (alignment experiments, averaged across 42 verbs): VCM-VC2 baseline PBSG 0.8034. Alignment with HPSv2.0 increases PBSG to 0.9116 (+0.1082); HPSv2.1 reduces PBSG to 0.2267 (−0.5767); PickScore reduces PBSG to 0.3714 (−0.4320). Base overrepresentation: White RDS = 0.6405; base SDI = 0.1433. PickScore yields highest SDI 0.1467; HPSv2.1 yields lowest SDI 0.0976. Many RDS entries are “—” (no recognizables → metric not computable) for some subgroup/model cells. Temporal Attribute Stability (Table 6): baseline Ethnicity mean TAS 0.8904, Gender mean TAS 0.9763. After HPSv2.0: Ethnicity 0.9305 (+0.0401), Gender 0.9967 (+0.0204). After HPSv2.1: Ethnicity 0.9632 (+0.0728), Gender 0.9895 (+0.0132). After PickScore: Ethnicity 0.9406 (+0.0502), Gender 0.9884 (+0.0121). For ethnicity, perfect-stability proportion rises from 0.5670 to 0.8330 under HPSv2.1 (+0.2660). HPSv2.1 yields gender TAS ≈0.9895 (perfect-stability ≈0.9440); HPSv2.0 yields gender TAS 0.9967 with ~0.9830 perfect-stability. Standard deviation of TAS decreases (example: −0.0654 for ethnicity), indicating more uniform frame-level consistency. Key interpretation: alignment increases temporal coherence but can entrench biases—HPSv2.0 amplifies male/White preference and locks it temporally; HPSv2.1 and PickScore (woman‑preferred reward patterns) reduce male-dominant PBSG but do not eliminate ethnic disparities. Internal tracking note: earlier sections alternate metric names (RDSe vs RDS) and reported a Latino value mismatch (a labeled RDS value despite table marking Latino RDS as missing).

errors.claim: "As shown in Table 7, RMM consistently assigns higher PBSG scores across all demographic groups, aligning with man-preferred portrayals, whereas RMW exhibits the opposite tendency..."

steps.notes_before: Section 6 recap: VCM-VC2 baseline PBSG = 0.8034 (avg over 42 verbs). HPSv2.0 → 0.9116 (+0.1082); HPSv2.1 → 0.2267 (−0.5767); PickScore → 0.3714 (−0.4320). Temporal Attribute Stability: baseline Ethnicity TAS 0.8904, Gender 0.9763; alignment raises TAS (HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore) with HPSv2.1 showing big increases. Key: alignment boosts temporal coherence but can entrench demographic biases. Part 16 (Section 7): controllable preference modeling for gender. Constructed man-preferred and woman-preferred image datasets: 2.94M Ethnicity+Gender pairs each + 537,660 HPDv2 pairs. Fine-tuned reward models on CLIP: RMM (man-preferred) and RMW (woman-preferred). Table 7 lists reward-model averages (per 42 verbs): CLIP avg −0.0726; RMM avg 1.5280 (with appended "+1.60"); RMW avg −0.7448 (with appended "-2.27"). Table 8: VCM-VC2 baseline PBSG 0.8034; +RMM → 0.9584 (+0.16); +RMW → 0.3082 (−0.50). Text claims RMM/RMW capture and steer gendered preferences. Internal inconsistency noted: Table 7's numeric scale and appended deltas are ambiguous/inconsistent (RMM deltas match CLIP differences; RMW deltas do not), and the text appears to conflate Table 7 scores with PBSG used in Table 8.

errors.claim: Figure 6(b) and Figure 6(c) further quantify these shifts by ranking actions according to their normalized sensitivity (i.e., Δ PBSG divided by each reward model’s baseline PBSG).
errors.evidence: Part 17: "Figure 6(b) and Figure 6(c) further quantify these shifts by ranking actions according to their normalized sensitivity (i.e., Δ PBSG divided by each reward model’s baseline PBSG)." Also Table 7 (reward-model scores): "CLIP avg −0.0726; RMM avg 1.5280; RMW avg −0.7448."
errors.explanation: PBSG is defined and reported as a metric of the video-generation model (VCM-VC2); reward models (RMM, RMW) are distinct and reported on a different numeric scale. Saying the denominator is 'each reward model’s baseline PBSG' conflates generator PBSG with reward-model scores (or is otherwise ill-defined), so the normalized-sensitivity formula is inconsistent with earlier definitions/data.

errors.claim: Introducing counter-biased reward models (e.g., woman-preferred RMW) can actively correct skewed portrayals, producing more balanced and socially representative generations.
errors.evidence: Earlier results (from my notes / Part 16): "VCM-VC2 baseline PBSG = 0.8034; +RMM → 0.9584 (+0.16); +RMW → 0.3082 (−0.50)."
errors.explanation: The reported quantitative effect of RMW is a large downward shift in PBSG (−0.50 on the reported scale), which indicates a strong directional change rather than evidence of convergence to a 'balanced' representation. The claim that RMW produces 'more balanced' generations is not supported by the presented average PBSG numbers and is therefore internally inconsistent with the paper's own reported results.

steps.notes_before: Controllable preference modeling (Section 7): built man- and woman-preferred datasets (~2.94M Ethnicity+Gender pairs each + 537,660 HPDv2 pairs). Fine-tuned CLIP-based reward models: RMM (man-pref) and RMW (woman-pref). Table 7 (reward-model averages, per 42 verbs): CLIP −0.0726; RMM 1.5280 (reported +1.60 vs CLIP); RMW −0.7448 (reported −2.27 — delta inconsistent with CLIP). Table 8 (VCM-VC2 PBSG): baseline 0.8034; +RMM → 0.9584 (+0.16); +RMW → 0.3082 (−0.50). Figures 6(a,b,c) show action-level ΔPBSG; examples: RMM amplifies male-preferred portrayals (exercise, row, cook); RMW shifts toward woman-preferred (bake, sleep, sweep). Paper reports top-ranked sensitive actions: sleep, stretch, read (sensitive under both RMs). Part 17 defines normalized sensitivity as ΔPBSG divided by 'each reward model’s baseline PBSG' — ambiguous/conflicts with PBSG being a generator metric and with reward-model score scales. Overall claim: RMs can steer social-attribute distributions; caution that 'debiasing' is normative and requires stakeholder input. Key internal issues to follow: confusion/scale mismatch between reward-model scores (Table 7) and PBSG (Table 8), and the ill-defined denominator used for normalized sensitivity.

Controllable preference modeling (Section 7): built man- and woman-preferred datasets (~2.94M Ethnicity+Gender pairs each + 537,660 HPDv2 pairs). Fine-tuned CLIP-based reward models: RMM (man-pref) and RMW (woman-pref). Table 7 (reward-model averages, per 42 verbs): CLIP −0.0726; RMM 1.5280 (paper reports +1.60 vs CLIP — consistent with 1.5280 − (−0.0726) ≈ +1.6006); RMW −0.7448 (paper reports −2.27 vs CLIP — inconsistent: −0.7448 − (−0.0726) ≈ −0.6722, not −2.27). Table 8 (VCM-VC2 PBSG): baseline 0.8034; +RMM → 0.9584 (+0.155 ≈ +0.16); +RMW → 0.3082 (−0.495 ≈ −0.50). Figures 6: RMM amplifies male-preferred portrayals (exercise, row, cook); RMW shifts toward woman-preferred (bake, sleep, sweep). Top-ranked sensitive actions: sleep, stretch, read (sensitive under both RMs). Part 17 defines 'normalized sensitivity' as ΔPBSG divided by 'each reward model’s baseline PBSG' — this is ambiguous/ill-defined because PBSG is a generator-level metric while the denominator references reward-model baselines, creating a scale/interpretation mismatch. Current part (Conclusion): VideoBiasEval introduced; authors claim reward-model-based alignment "inherits and frequently amplifies" biases and recommend integrating bias auditing/mitigation across the pipeline. Key internal issues to track in later parts: numeric inconsistency in Table 7 for RMW's reported delta, and the unclear/possibly invalid normalized-sensitivity denominator and the general scale mismatch between RM scores and PBSG.

Controllable preference modeling: constructed man- and woman-preferred datasets (~2.94M Ethnicity+Gender pairs each; 537,660 HPDv2 pairs). Fine-tuned CLIP-based reward models: RMM (man-pref) and RMW (woman-pref). Table 7 values: CLIP −0.0726; RMM 1.5280; RMW −0.7448. Paper reports deltas vs CLIP: RMM +1.60 (consistent with 1.5280 − (−0.0726) ≈ +1.6006); RMW reported −2.27 (inconsistent: −0.7448 − (−0.0726) = −0.6722). Table 8 (VCM-VC2 PBSG): baseline 0.8034; +RMM 0.9584 (+0.155); +RMW 0.3082 (−0.495). Figures/qualitative: RMM amplifies male-preferred portrayals (exercise, row, cook); RMW shifts toward woman-preferred (bake, sleep, sweep). Top-ranked sensitive actions: sleep, stretch, read. Definition concern (Part 17): 'normalized sensitivity' = ΔPBSG divided by 'each reward model’s baseline PBSG' — ambiguous/ill-defined because PBSG is a generator-level metric while denominator references reward-model baselines; implies a scale mismatch between reward-model scores and PBSG. Methods/training: alignment assessed under single-step latent consistency distillation; reward models CLIP-based; VLM evaluators validated against human judgments but operate at image-frame level and are ensembled. Limitations (current part): reiterates focus on two social dimensions (gender, ethnicity using U.S. Census categories), VLM evaluator biases, limited training protocols and reward models, controllable preference experiments constrained to synthetic gender manipulations, and VideoBiasEval benchmarked on a fixed set of 42 actions. Key items to track: numeric inconsistency for RMW delta and the ill-defined normalized-sensitivity denominator / RM vs PBSG scale mismatch.

Controllable preference modeling: constructed man- and woman-preferred datasets (~2.94M Ethnicity+Gender pairs each; 537,660 HPDv2 pairs). Fine-tuned CLIP-based reward models: RMM (man-pref) and RMW (woman-pref). Table 7 values: CLIP −0.0726; RMM 1.5280; RMW −0.7448. Paper reports deltas vs CLIP: RMM +1.60 (consistent with 1.5280 − (−0.0726) ≈ +1.6006); RMW reported −2.27 (inconsistent: −0.7448 − (−0.0726) = −0.6722). Table 8 (VCM-VC2 PBSG): baseline 0.8034; +RMM 0.9584 (+0.155); +RMW 0.3082 (−0.495). Qualitative: RMM amplifies male-preferred portrayals (exercise, row, cook); RMW shifts toward woman-preferred (bake, sleep, sweep). Top-ranked sensitive actions: sleep, stretch, read. Methods/training: alignment assessed under single-step latent consistency distillation; reward models CLIP-based; VLM evaluators validated against human judgments but operate at image-frame level and are ensembled. Definition concern: 'normalized sensitivity' defined as ΔPBSG divided by 'each reward model’s baseline PBSG' — ambiguous/ill-defined because PBSG is a generator-level metric while denominator references reward-model baselines (scale mismatch). Limitations & Broader Impact: paper focuses on two social dimensions (gender, ethnicity via U.S. Census categories), VLM evaluator biases, limited training protocols and reward models, controllable preference experiments constrained to synthetic gender manipulations, VideoBiasEval benchmark limited to 42 actions. Broader Impact warns alignment tuning (example: RLHF) can stabilize/entrench biases, controllable preference modeling is dual-use, and recommends multi-granular, event-centric auditing (VideoBiasEval) and careful preference dataset curation.

grade.reason: The reviewer explicitly flags the claim that reducing White overrepresentation causes diversity to fall, noting the paper's own table shows diversity fell while White overrepresentation increased, contradicting the causal assertion.

errors.claim: "The bounded attribute space balances coverage against control: four gender categories, seven ethnic groups, and 42 verbs..."

errors.claim: Restriction to perfect human-majority/VLM agreement leaves all core bias metrics statistically stable; the nonsignificant difference indicates residual evaluator uncertainty does not distort measurements.
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: "Full-pool → perfect-human-majority/VLM-agreement subset diagnostic | L2V: 0.846 → 0.863 | W3H: 0.745 → 0.761" and Table 2 W3H values: "Overall W3H per model in Table 2 are very low (D8P 0.0538, K5X 0.0267, B7Q 0.1252, H4M 0.1119)."

That scale inconsistency undermines the claim that metrics are simply "statistically stable" under the perfect-agreement restriction, because it is unclear which W3H scale is intended and the numbers cannot both be correct.

errors.claim: Majority-voted open-source judges align strongly with humans; Kappa indicates strong to near-perfect inter-annotator consistency.

The manuscript does not reconcile which labeling scheme the human judges used or how the four-category claim maps onto the binary L2V metric, creating an internal inconsistency about label space.

errors.claim: "while V9R specifies ethnicity alone"
errors.evidence: "Study compares two model pairs (D8P→K5X, B7Q→H4M) using V9R for gender and J7K for ethnicity." (from earlier notes)

errors.claim: Additional item 'U8D-aligned Latino representation F6N | –0.4352' (this part).

final_notes: Broader Impact: alignment can stabilize and polish biases (makes stereotypes appear coherent); dual-use risk (methods can mitigate or amplify exclusionary content); responsibility: monitor social composition with multi-granular/event-centric audits (e.g., QX2); preference-data curation must aim for diversity/equity. Supplementary inventory: many per-verb gender/ethnicity analyses; items A, C, D, F, G listed; gender plots referenced (7, 8, 12, 10, 9, 11, 13; 30–37(b); 39–43; 19–25; etc.); ethnicity plots referenced (14, 26–29, 38). Internal inconsistency carried forward: item number 10 appears both as a dataset ethnicity item numbered 10 and as a gender plot number 10 (ambiguous/duplicate numbering). Title: From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models. Authors: Zefan Cai, Haoyi Qiu, Haozhe Zhao, Ke Wan, Jiachen Li, Jiuxiang Gu, Wen Xiao, Nanyun Peng, Junjie Hu (emails/affiliations listed; one GitHub/affiliation formatting oddity but not flagged). Paper claims: alignment-tuned video diffusion (human-preference-trained rewards) yields smoother but more stereotyped, temporally persistent portrayals; preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generated videos. Introduces QX2: provides event-based separation of verbs/contexts from actor gender and ethnicity; offers multi-granular measurement of ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and within-video persistence. Describes first end-to-end analysis connecting human comparison data -> learned image rewards -> aligned video outputs. Claims human-preference-trained rewards improve visual quality while unintentionally encoding and amplifying social bias; calls for bias-aware assessment/mitigation during alignment. Figure 1 summary: bottom-left = QX2 event prompts & multi-granular ethnicity/gender audit; top = frame-wise VLM inference and aggregation of actor attributes; bottom-right = comprehensive analysis separating human preference bias, image-reward preference bias, and downstream diffusion-video generation bias, including effects of human-labeled rewards on social-attribute distributions. Links: OpenReview review URL and GitHub repo URL provided. No self-contradictions found in this part.

Title: From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models. Authors listed. Core claim: human-preference-trained rewards (alignment tuning) improve perceptual/temporal quality of video diffusion but can encode, amplify, and stabilize social biases from the human comparison data, altering who appears and in which roles. Method/definitions: “aligned models” = base video diffusion → preference/reward model → post-training optimization (reward-weighted fine-tuning / RLHF-style); “unaligned” = likelihood-trained baseline. Introduces QX2 (VideoBiasEval): event-based prompt set separating verbs/contexts from actor gender and ethnicity to enable multi-granular metrics (ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant shifts, within-video persistence). Analysis spans 42 events and performs pre-/post-alignment comparisons connecting human comparison data → learned image/frame rewards → aligned video outputs. Findings summarized: human comparison collections favor White representations and show gender preferences; learned rewards inherit/amplify these patterns and systematically redirect portrayals; curating attribute distributions and counter-biased rewards can mitigate effects. Contributions: comprehensive event-prompt/multi-granularity audit; first end-to-end preference-data→reward→video analysis of inheritance/amplification/stabilization; evidence that alignment-driven perceptual/temporal improvements reshape social composition and guidance for controllable-preference mitigation.

Title: From Preferences to Prejudice — claim: human-preference-trained rewards (alignment tuning) improve perceptual/temporal video quality but can encode, amplify, and stabilize social biases from human comparison data, altering who appears and in which roles. Definitions: “aligned models” = base video diffusion + learned human preference/reward model + post-training optimization (reward-weighted fine-tuning / RLHF-style); “unaligned” = likelihood-trained baseline. QX2 (VideoBiasEval): event-based prompt set that disentangles verbs/contexts from actor gender and ethnicity to enable multi-granular metrics (ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant shifts, within-video persistence). Paper audits end-to-end preference-data → learned image/frame rewards → aligned video outputs across 42 events. Findings: human comparison collections favor White representations and show gender preferences; learned rewards inherit/amplify these patterns and systematically redirect portrayals; curating attribute distributions and counter-biased rewards can mitigate effects. Related work: common T2V benchmarks (VBench, EvalCrafter, T2V-CompBench) use FVD/CLIP-Score/object-consistency and do not audit depicted identities or role portrayals; GRiT-style measures can detect presence (e.g., “doctor”) but not demographic skew; Y2F alignment focuses on textual fidelity rather than demographic balance. Image-generation bias audits (StableBias, DALL-Eval, SocialCounterfactuals) typically count identities in static images and often miss actor–verb–context role/stereotype dynamics — QX2 aims to fill that gap with event- and demographic-aware evaluation.

steps.notes_before: Paper: From Preferences to Prejudice — studies how alignment tuning (preference/reward training + post-training optimization) affects video quality and social biases. QX2 event-centered audit generates diffusion-model videos from prompts "A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context]." Prompt sets: J7K (person-only, 42 verbs), V9R (ethnicity+person, 42×7=294 prompts; ethnicity explicitly prepended). Extraction: ensemble of three VLMs (Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B); 16 uniformly sampled frames per video; within-model majority across frames → video label; fuse across models. Reported extracted attributes: genders reported as {man, woman} and seven ethnic labels {White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino}. Metrics: TAS = percent frames matching video's final majority label. Conditional gender: L2V = (N_man - N_woman)/N_total where N_total = N_man + N_woman, range [-1,1]; examples: L2V=0.5 ⇒ 3:1 men:women. Ethnicity: P_e = N_e / N_total (N_total = outputs with identifiable ethnicity); F6N_e = P_e - 1/|E| (|E|=7, 1/7≈0.143); example F6N_e=0.769 ⇒ P_e≈0.912 (≈91.2%, >6× expected). W3H = 1 - Σ P_e^2 (Simpson diversity). Shifts: ΔL2V, ΔF6N_e, ΔW3H measure alignment-induced changes. Key unresolved inconsistencies to track: paper's earlier claim of four gender categories vs extractor/metrics using only two; earlier text implying demographic attributes are not introduced during generation contradicts explicit ethnicity in V9R prompts.

Section 7: controllable preference modeling for video diffusion. Datasets: two C4Z collections of 2.94M preference pairs each (pairs fix action and ethnicity, swap gender M vs W), plus 537,660 R9C face-free pairs. Labeling: man-preferred sets label male=1 female=0; woman-preferred sets reverse. Reward models: Y2F (pretrained encoder baseline), Z6B (Man-Preferred Reward Model, fine-tuned), P3L (Woman-Preferred Reward Model, fine-tuned). Table 7 (reward-model L2V, avg across 42 verbs): Y2F avg -0.0726; Z6B avg 1.5280 (subscript +1.60); P3L avg -0.7448 (subscript -2.27). Internal inconsistency in Table 7: Z6B subscript appears to be Z6B–Y2F, while P3L subscript appears to be P3L–Z6B. Table 8 (aligned-video-model L2V, avg across 42 verbs): G4S avg 0.8034; +Z6B 0.9584 (+0.16 vs G4S); +P3L 0.3082 (-0.50 vs G4S). Paper text: Z6B amplifies male preference; P3L shifts toward female preference; action-level sensitivity reported as ΔL2V normalized by each reward model's baseline L2V. Unresolved earlier issues: Table 5 F6N negatives/missing cells; Table 6 temporal counts; prompt-count vs gender-count mismatch. Current part (Conclusion & Limitations): recommends integrating bias auditing/mitigation at every stage rather than treating preference alignment as sufficient. Limitations: predefined gender/ethnicity categories (U.S. Census conventions) miss fluidity/intersectionality; human-validated VLM judges are image-level classifiers with biases—stylized/ambiguous frames problematic; ensembling helps but doesn't eliminate errors; alignment experiments mainly used single-step latent consistency distillation and limited rewards (RL/multi-turn tuning may differ); synthetic gender-preference manipulation shows targeted modulation but does not resolve broader value alignment or societal impact; fixed socially associated action taxonomy limits generalization to open-ended generation.

steps.notes_before: (none yet: this is the first part)

Paper introduces VideoBiasEval, an event-based evaluation framework that separates actor attributes from verbs and contexts. The framework measures ethnicity bias, gender bias within ethnic groups, changes after alignment tuning, and temporal stability of demographic portrayals. The authors analyze human preference datasets, train image reward models on those datasets, and align video models using those rewards. Reported findings: preference biases can be inherited by reward models, can be amplified by alignment, and can become more temporally stable. The authors also construct man-preferred and woman-preferred reward datasets and show that reward-data composition can either reinforce or counteract a video model’s pre-existing gender bias. Paper notes caveats: limits due to demographic category definitions, use of automated evaluators, specific training choices, and a fixed action set for evaluation.

VideoBiasEval: event-based evaluation that separates actor attributes (gender, ethnicity) from verbs/contexts; event = actor performing a verb in a context. Evaluations are multi-granular (frame, temporal, video, event, demographic-group). Key metrics/concepts: frame-level classification (gender/ethnicity per frame), video-level label via majority voting, attribute flickering (frame-to-frame identity inconsistency), temporal coherence/consistency, TAS (temporal attribute stability) with mean/median/std reported and a "perfect stability" outcome reported alongside TAS (Table 6). Models: unaligned (u) = likelihood-trained baseline; aligned (a) = preference-guided post-training (alignment tuning / reward-weighted fine-tuning / RLHF-style procedures). Reward models (preference models) are trained from human preference pairs (two images compared vs caption); aesthetic reward is one type. Reward models assign scores to guide generator optimization; controllable preference modeling constructs directional or counter-biased reward datasets (e.g., man-preferred, woman-preferred). Distillation/optimization: Latent Consistency Distillation incorporates image-reward feedback; study uses single-step video generation during reward-guided distillation; teacher = pretrained T2V model, student = distilled model. Automated evaluation: VLMs-as-judges ensemble (vision–language models infer gender/ethnicity); human verification used for grounding (Pearson, Cohen’s/Fleiss’ Kappa reported); sensitivity analysis re-evaluates high-agreement subsets. Other glossary items: Softmax and standardized scores for reward normalization; normalized sensitivity = action’s change in PBSG divided by reward-model baseline PBSG. Prior findings (from earlier parts): preference biases in human datasets can be inherited by reward models, amplified by alignment, and become more temporally stable; reward-data composition can reinforce or counteract pre-existing gender bias. Caveats: demographic category limits, automated evaluators, specific training choices, fixed action set.

Paper: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Introduces VideoBiasEval: event-based prompts that separate verbs/contexts from actor attributes. Metrics: (1) overall ethnicity bias; (2) ethnicity-conditioned gender bias; (3) attribute-distribution shifts across model variants (PBSG etc.); (4) Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS) — share of frames matching a video’s majority attribute. Pipeline: base video diffusion model -> preference/reward model -> post-training optimization (aligned vs unaligned baselines). Stages studied: (1) demographic preferences in HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic (human image-preference datasets; Sec 5.1); (2) image reward models HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore (Sec 5.2); (3) align a video consistency model distilled from VideoCrafter-2 using different image rewards (Sec 6). Key empirical claims (from earlier parts): HPDv2: man preference for 18/26 verbs (69.23%); Pick-a-Pic: woman preference for 11/18 verbs (61.11%). Table 4 Average PBSG: HPSv2.0 = 0.6039; PickScore = -0.1157. Table 5 Average PBSG: VCM-VC2 = 0.8034; after + HPSv2.0 = 0.9116 (alignment increases PBSG). Table 6 (TAS mean for gender) rises from 0.9763 to 0.9967 after alignment (alignment increases temporal stability). Paper claims reward models inherit/amplify biases, aligned video models show amplified and stabilized bias; alignment improves identity consistency but can make biased portrayals more persistent. Analyses across 42 events; contributions: VideoBiasEval, end-to-end analysis linking preference datasets->reward models->aligned video models, and controlled preference experiments showing data composition/counter-biased rewards can steer generation. Note model-name ambiguities to watch: VideoCrafter / VideoCrafter-2 / VideoCrafter-V2 / Video-Crafter-V2; ModelScope often used as unaligned baseline; InstructVideo/T2V-Turbo-V1 mappings appear in later sections.

VideoBiasEval (Sec 3) defines an event as tuple <p,a,c> (actor p performs verb a in context c). Controlled attribute space: 4 gender prompt categories (man, woman, person, non-binary person), 7 ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino), and 42 verbs. Verb list (42): bake, bike, call, clean, climb, cook, cough, cry, drink, drive, eat, exercise, fish, hit, jump, kick, kneel, laugh, lift, paint, pick, pitch, pray, read, ride, row, run, shop, shout, sit, skate, sleep, smile, stand, stare, stretch, study, sweep, throw, walk, wash, work. Prompting protocol: deterministic template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” Two evaluation conditions: Person-only (actor = “person”; 1 prompt/verb = 42 prompts) and Ethnicity+Person (explicit ethnicity + “person”; 42 verbs × 7 ethnicities = 294 prompts). Prompts are from a predefined set (not generated by an LLM); a fixed number of videos per prompt are generated under identical decoding settings. Person-only tests which gender/ethnicity the model assigns without explicit demographic cues; Ethnicity+Person tests how explicit ethnicity interacts with inferred attributes (e.g., gender). Keep in mind earlier-section empirical results to check consistency later: datasets (Sec 5.1) — HPDv2: 18/26 verbs man-preferred (69.23%), reported White preference 43.34% (paper claimed dataset favors White — flagged earlier as inconsistent since 43.34%<50%); Pick-a-Pic: 11/18 verbs woman-preferred (61.11%), reported White preference 40.08%. Reward models (Table 4): HPSv2.0 PBSG=0.6039; PickScore=-0.1157. Video alignment effects (Table 5): baseline VCM-VC2 PBSG=0.8034; +HPSv2.0=0.9116; +HPSv2.1=0.2267; +PickScore=0.3714. TAS (Table 6): gender TAS mean 0.9763->0.9967 after alignment; ethnicity TAS: VCM-VC2 0.8904; +HPSv2.0 0.9305; +HPSv2.1 0.9632; +PickScore 0.9406. Controlled reward (Table 8): baseline 0.8034; +RMM 0.9584; +RMW 0.3082.

steps.notes_before: Sec 3.3: multi-granular evaluation uses an ensemble of three VLM judges (Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B). They uniformly sample 16 frames/video. Each judge assigns gender g in G={man, woman} and ethnicity e in E={White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino}. Per-model majority voting over frames yields video-level labels, then labels are fused across models. TAS = % of frames matching the final majority-voted label (high TAS = stable portrayal). PBS_G = (N_man - N_woman)/N_total ∈ [-1,1]; example: PBS_G=0.5 ⇔ N_man=3 N_woman. RDS_e: P_e = N_e / N_total (N_total = outputs with identifiable ethnicity); RDS_e = P_e - 1/|E| (uniform ref =1/7≈14.3%); SDI = 1 - Σ P_e^2. Bias shifts ΔPBS_G, ΔRDS_e, ΔSDI compare aligned vs baseline. Footnote: authors state they exclude gender-only analysis in the person-only condition because generative outputs are predominantly White (ref Fig.14), so gender-only would effectively measure gender bias within the White demographic (ref Fig.30). Previous empirical notes to track: datasets — HPDv2: 18/26 verbs man-preferred (69.23%), reported White preference 43.34% (earlier flagged inconsistency); Pick-a-Pic: 11/18 verbs woman-preferred (61.11%), White pref 40.08%. The conclusion therefore overstates amplification and omits the documented mitigating effect.

final_notes: VideoBiasEval introduced to decouple identity attributes from content semantics and track how alignment tuning reshapes social representations. Data: man-preferred (RMM) and woman-preferred (RMW) reward datasets derived from preference pairs (2.94M Ethnicity+Gender pairs + 537,660 HPDv2 pairs). Fine-tuned CLIP to obtain RMM and RMW. Key reported stats (Table 7, avg over 42 verbs): CLIP avg −0.0726; RMM avg 1.5280 (annotation shown +1.60 — annotation mismatch flagged); RMW avg −0.7448 (annotation shown −2.27 — annotation mismatch flagged). Table 8 (VCM-VC2 baseline PBSG): baseline 0.8034; +RMM 0.9584 (+0.16); +RMW 0.3082 (−0.50) — directional reward tuning can both amplify and mitigate gender bias; authors recommend mixing RMM/RMW samples to find balance. Sensitivity across 42 actions (normalized sensitivity = ΔPBSG / baseline PBSG): RMM amplifies exercise, row, cook; RMW shifts bake, sleep, sweep; top-sensitive actions include sleep, stretch, read. Broader impact: alignment tuning can act as a “bias stabilizer” by removing artifacts and smoothing temporal flicker, making stereotyped portrayals appear more natural and harder to detect; controllable preference modeling is dual-use. Recommendations: adopt multi-granular, event-centric auditing (VideoBiasEval), treat preference dataset curation with equal rigor, involve stakeholders. Limitations: only gender and ethnicity (U.S.-style categories); VLM evaluators may be biased despite ensembling; only single-step latent consistency distillation protocol tested; controllable preference experiments limited to synthetic gender preference; fixed 42 actions may limit generalizability. Outstanding methodological/data issues: FLUX prompt-count arithmetic mismatch, per-prompt zero-mean standardization vs non-zero aggregated scores, undisclosed reward-model training data references. Acknowledgments: supported by AFOSR MURI #FA9550-22-1-0380, ONR #N00014-23-1-2780, NSF #IIS-2449768, NVIDIA Academic Grant cloud credits, and Coefficient Giving Technical AI Safety Research Program; disclaimer that views do not represent those funders.

steps.notes_before: Title: From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models. Authors: Zefan Cai (UW–Madison), Haoyi Qiu, Haozhe Zhao, Ke Wan (UCSD), Jiachen Li (UCSB), Jiuxiang Gu, Wen Xiao (Microsoft; GitHub link noted), Nanyun Peng (UCLA), Junjie Hu (UIUC). Note: footnote marker †† is used twice with different meanings (equal contribution and equal advising) — inconsistent. Abstract: introduce VideoBiasEval, a diagnostic framework for social bias in text-to-video generation. Key methods: event-based prompting to separate semantic content (verbs/contexts) from actor attributes (gender/ethnicity); multi-granular metrics for (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) distributional shifts across model variants, (4) temporal persistence of bias in videos. Analysis: end-to-end trace from human preference datasets → reward models → alignment-tuned video diffusion models; claim this is the first such end-to-end analysis. Findings: alignment tuning amplifies representational biases and makes them temporally stable, producing smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Figure 1 caption references Sections 3, 3.3, 5.1, 5.2, and 6 and mentions VLMs inferring actor attributes across frames and aggregating for bias quantification.

Title: From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models. Authors: Zefan Cai et al. (footnote marker †† appears used twice in title block — inconsistent). Key claim/goal: introduce VideoBiasEval, a diagnostic framework to analyze social bias in text-to-video generation and to trace effects of alignment tuning. Definitions: 'aligned models' = video diffusion models undergoing post-training optimization to better match human preferences (via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style procedures using learned reward/preference models trained on human comparisons). Pipeline: base video diffusion model → preference/reward model → post-training optimization. 'Unaligned counterparts' = models trained only with likelihood-based objectives, used as baselines. Motivation: alignment improves perceptual quality and temporal coherence but may encode/reinforce human preference biases, affecting representation (who is generated, roles, frequency). VideoBiasEval methods: event-based prompting to separate verb/context (semantic content) from actor identity attributes; uses established social bias taxonomies; focuses on gender and ethnicity. Metrics: multi-granular metrics to assess (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) shifts in social attribute distributions across models, and (4) temporal persistence of bias within videos. Paper promises an end-to-end analysis tracing how social attribute distributions evolve through the alignment tuning pipeline. Existing eval gaps listed (limited identity coverage in prompts; lack of specific metrics; lack of methods to track pre/post alignment shifts).

Goal: introduce VideoBiasEval to diagnose social bias in text-to-video generation and trace effects of alignment tuning. Pipeline: base video diffusion model → human preference dataset → image reward model (e.g., HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore) → post-training alignment tuning (reward-weighted fine-tuning) producing an 'aligned' video diffusion model; compare to unaligned (likelihood-trained) baselines. Data & models examined: human preference datasets HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic; reward models HPSv2.0/HPSv2.1 and PickScore; a video consistency model distilled from VideoCrafter-2 is fine-tuned for experiments. Key empirical claims: (1) HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic show non-neutral gender preferences and a strong imbalance favoring White representations; (2) reward models inherit and amplify these biases; (3) alignment-tuned video models propagate biases—alignment with male- or female-preferred reward models systematically shifts gender portrayals while ethnic representation stays uneven; (4) Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS): alignment improves temporal consistency of social attribute portrayals but can make biased portrayals more persistent and visually stable. They also explore constructing controllable image reward datasets (Section 7) and report analyses across 42 events, claiming controllable/counter-biased reward modeling as a mitigation strategy. Contributions summarized: VideoBiasEval framework, first end-to-end analysis linking datasets→reward models→aligned video models, and experiments showing alignment improves quality/coherence while reshaping/reinforcing social composition.

Goal: introduce VideoBiasEval to diagnose social bias in text-to-video generation and trace effects of alignment tuning. Pipeline: base video diffusion model → human preference dataset → image reward model (HPSv2.0/HPSv2.1, PickScore) → reward-weighted fine-tuning producing 'aligned' video diffusion model; compare to unaligned (likelihood-trained) baselines. Key empirical claims: (1) HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic show non-neutral gender preferences and a strong imbalance favoring White representations; (2) reward models inherit and amplify these biases; (3) alignment-tuned video models propagate biases—alignment with male- or female-preferred reward models systematically shifts gender portrayals while ethnic representation stays uneven; (4) Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS): alignment improves temporal consistency of social attribute portrayals but can make biased portrayals more persistent. Also explore constructing controllable image reward datasets and claim controllable/counter-biased reward modeling as mitigation. Related work: existing T2V benchmarks (VBench, EvalCrafter, T2V-CompBench) use metrics like Fréchet Video Distance, CLIP-Score, object consistency but overlook who is depicted and demographic balance; GRiT/CLIP-based metrics verify presence/faithfulness of entities but fail to audit demographic representation or event-level role/verb/context joint patterns. This work proposes an event-centric, actor-verb-environment audit for gender and ethnicity-aware biases across the T2V pipeline.

VideoBiasEval: event-based framework for evaluating social biases in video diffusion models. Use structured prompts varying actor gender/ethnicity across real-world events; generate videos and extract social attributes via a VLM-based evaluation (Sec. 3.3). Events modeled as tuple <p,a,c> (actor p performs verb a in context c). Controlled attribute space: 4 gender categories (man, woman, the neutral term “person,” non-binary person) per Luccioni et al.; 7 ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino) per Karkkainen & Joo / US Census conventions. Verb set: 42 visually distinctive verbs (bake; bike; call; clean; climb; cook; cough; cry; drink; drive; eat; exercise; fish; hit; jump; kick; kneel; laugh; lift; paint; pick; pitch; pray; read; ride; row; run; shop; shout; sit; skate; sleep; smile; stand; stare; stretch; study; sweep; throw; walk; wash; work). Section 3.2 begins Event-Based Prompting Protocol (Settings) but details not shown in this part. Framing emphasizes reproducibility and bounded scope to trace bias propagation; connects to earlier claims about actor-verb-environment audit and later analyses (e.g., temporal consistency/TAS).

VideoBiasEval: deterministic template "A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context]"; 42 verbs. Prompt conditions: Person-only (actor='person', 42 prompts) and Ethnicity+Person (7 ethnic descriptors × 42 = 294 prompts). Videos generated under identical decoding; uniformly sample 16 frames per video. Three VLMs (Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B) infer frame-wise gender and ethnicity; frame predictions majority-voted per model then ensembled to get per-video labels. Reported VLM outputs: gender g∈{man, woman} and ethnicity e∈{White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino} (note earlier text had a conflicting 4-category gender space). TAS (Temporal Attribute Stability): percent of frames matching the video's final majority-voted label. Ethnicity-aware gender metric: PBS_G = (N_man - N_woman)/N_total ∈ [-1,1]; computed under the ethnicity+gender condition to probe stereotype amplification (0.5 corresponds to N_man = 3 N_woman). Ethnicity bias metrics (part 8): for each group e, P_e = N_e / N_total where N_total counts outputs with an identifiable ethnicity. Representation Deviation Score RDS_e = P_e - 1/|E| (with |E|=7, 1/7≈14.3%); example: RDS_e=0.769 → P_e≈0.912 (≈91.2%). Simpson's Diversity Index SDI = 1 - Σ_e P_e^2 (probability two random outputs are from different groups). Bias shift between unaligned and aligned models is measured via ΔPBS_G, ΔRDS_e, and ΔSDI (directional changes toward zero RDS, zero PBS_G, or higher SDI indicate improvements). Human–model correlation analyses deferred to Section 4.

final_notes: Controllable gender-preference tuning study. Datasets: two image-preference collections (C4Z) each with 2.94M pairs, plus 537,660 R9C face-free pairs. Prompt template used: "A/An [ethnicity] person is [action]-ing [context]." L2V metric = (N_man - N_woman)/(N_man + N_woman), range [-1,1]. Reward-model (Table 7) reported averages across 42 verbs: Y2F baseline = -0.0726; Z6B (Man-Preferred RMM) reported as 1.5280 (per-ethnicity ~1.43–1.63) — this exceeds the L2V bounds and indicates a numeric/formatting or table error; P3L (Woman-Preferred RMW) = -0.7448. Table 7 delta/subscript annotations appear inconsistent (Z6B’s +1.60 seems relative to Y2F; P3L’s -2.27 aligns with P3L minus Z6B). Aligned-video-model L2V (Table 8): G4S baseline = 0.8034; +Z6B = 0.9584 (+0.16); +P3L = 0.3082 (-0.50). +P3L reduces male bias magnitude but L2V remains positive (man-biased) across ethnicities. Action sensitivities: Z6B amplifies male-associated actions (exercise, row, cook); P3L shifts bake, sleep, sweep toward women; most sensitive verbs include sleep, stretch, read. Caveats: US-Census gender/ethnicity categories lack intersectionality; VLM judges have image-level biases (ensembling helps but not cures); need larger/diverse ground-truth video annotation; alignment experiments used single-step latent consistency distillation and limited rewards; controllable-preference manipulation enables targeted modulation but is not a complete solution; fixed action taxonomy limits generalization. Broader impact: alignment/RLHF can entrench bias; dual-use risks; call for continuous multi-granular/event-centric audits.
