Title: From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.
Authors: Zefan Cai (marked "Equal contribution, ordered by last name"), Haoyi Qiu, Haozhe Zhao, Ke Wan, Jiachen Li, Jiuxiang Gu, Wen Xiao (affiliation line contains "Microsofthttps://github.com/Zefan-Cai/VideoBiasEval"), Nanyun Peng (marked "Equal advising"), Junjie Hu.
Key claims to check later:
- Alignment-tuned video diffusion produces smoother but more stereotyped and temporally persistent portrayals.
- Preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generated videos.
- Introduces QX2: provides event-based separation of verbs/contexts from actor gender and ethnicity; supports multi-granular measurements including ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and within-video persistence.
- Claims this is "the first end-to-end analysis" linking human comparison data, learned image rewards, and aligned video outputs.
- Human-preference-trained rewards improve visual quality but unintentionally encode and amplify social bias; argues for bias-aware assessment and mitigation throughout alignment.
Figure 1 notes: QX2 event prompts and multi-granular ethnicity/gender audit shown bottom-left; frame-wise VLM inference and aggregation of actor attributes at top; bottom-right summarizes the analysis separating human preference bias, image-reward preference bias, and downstream diffusion-video generation bias.
Links provided: OpenReview and GitHub.

Intro summary: Human comparison collections favor White representations and show non-neutral gender preferences; learned rewards inherit and amplify these patterns, with male- or female-preferred rewards systematically redirecting gender portrayals and ethnic distributions remaining uneven. Curating attribute distributions and counter-biased rewards can control image-reward datasets and downstream video representations. Analysis spans 42 events and examines reward-preference changes and pre-/post-alignment video-bias changes. Definition: “aligned models” = video diffusion models fine-tuned after likelihood training to match human preferences (reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style optimization using learned preference/aesthetic rewards trained on human comparisons). “Unaligned” = likelihood-trained baselines. Motivation: subjective preference judgments often lack demographic diversity and can encode systematic bias that rewards and generators inherit/amplify. Need: event-based distributional metrics and a pre/post alignment analysis protocol; prior work lacks diverse identity prompts, comprehensive identity coverage, and distribution-tracking metrics. QX2 (VideoBiasEval) provides controlled separation of verb/identity variation for interpretable, multi-granular assessment (ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, within-video persistence). Claims/contributions: (1) comprehensive event-prompt/multi-granularity audit; (2) first connected analysis linking human preference data → learned image rewards → aligned video outputs, showing inheritance, amplification, stabilization; (3) evidence that perceptual/temporal improvements from alignment can reshape or reinforce generated social composition, plus guidance for controllable-preference mitigation. Key claims to check later: alignment-tuned diffusion produces smoother but more stereotyped/temporally persistent portrayals; preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generated videos; QX2 supports multi-granular measurements and within-video persistence; argues for bias-aware assessment & mitigation across alignment pipeline.

Definitions & scope: “aligned models” = video diffusion models fine-tuned post-likelihood to match human preference rewards (reward-weighted fine-tuning / RLHF-style). “Unaligned” = likelihood-trained baselines. Core claims to verify later: alignment-tuned diffusion yields smoother but more stereotyped/temporally persistent portrayals; preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generated videos; QX2 supports multi-granular measurement including within-video persistence; curating attribute distributions and counter-biased rewards can control downstream representations.
From Related Work (new): existing T2V benchmarks (VBench, EvalCrafter, T2V-CompBench) use metrics like Fréchet Video Distance, CLIP-Score, and object consistency but do not audit depicted identities or portrayal demographics. GRiT-based measures can detect an actor/role (e.g., a doctor) but do not flag demographic skews (e.g., exclusively white male doctors). Y2F-based alignment rewards prioritize textual fidelity over demographic balance. Prior generative-model bias work focuses on static images/isolated objects (StableBias, DALL-Eval, SocialCounterfactuals) and usually counts identities without activity/role context; this can miss recurring role-based stereotypes. Motivation: need event-level disentanglement (joint actor–verb–context) and ethnicity-/gender-aware, event-centric quantification throughout generation; QX2 is presented to fill this gap.
What to check later: whether the paper shows evidence for amplification/stabilization claims, whether reward models trained on human comparisons are demonstrably biased in the ways claimed, whether evaluation metrics used in experiments truly go beyond FVD/CLIP/object-consistency to measure demographics and temporal persistence, and whether QX2 operationalizes the stated multi-granular metrics.

Section: controllable gender preference tuning. Datasets: two image-preference collections (C4Z), each 2.94M pairs; plus 537,660 R9C face-free pairs. Prompt template: "A/An [ethnicity] person is [action]-ing [context]." L2V defined as (N_man - N_woman)/(N_man + N_woman), range [-1,1]. Reward-models (Table 7, averages across 42 verbs) reported: Y2F baseline -0.0726; Z6B (Man-Preferred RMM) 1.5280 (per-ethnicity ~1.43–1.63) — this exceeds L2V bounds and signals a table inconsistency; P3L (Woman-Preferred RMW) -0.7448. Table 7 delta/subscript notations are inconsistent: Z6B's +1.60 appears relative to Y2F, while P3L's -2.27 corresponds to P3L minus Z6B. Aligned-video-model L2V (Table 8): G4S baseline 0.8034; +Z6B 0.9584 (+0.16); +P3L 0.3082 (-0.50). +P3L reduces male bias but L2V remains positive across ethnicities (still man-biased). Action sensitivity: Z6B amplifies male-associated actions (exercise, row, cook); P3L shifts bake, sleep, sweep toward women; most sensitive actions: sleep, stretch, read. Caveat: numeric/formatting inconsistencies in Table 7 must be resolved before trusting magnitudes. Conclusion: integrate bias auditing and mitigation across video-generation pipeline. Limitations: US-Census-based gender/ethnicity categories (lack intersectionality); VLM judges are image-level classifiers with biases; ensembling mitigates but does not eliminate errors; larger, more diverse ground-truth video annotation needed; alignment experiments used single-step latent consistency distillation and limited rewards (RL/multi-turn tuning may behave differently); synthetic gender-preference manipulation shows targeted modulation but does not solve broader value alignment; fixed action taxonomy limits generalization.

Controllable gender-preference tuning: datasets include two image-preference collections (C4Z) each with 2.94M pairs, plus 537,660 R9C face-free pairs. Prompt template: "A/An [ethnicity] person is [action]-ing [context]." L2V = (N_man - N_woman)/(N_man + N_woman), range [-1,1]. Reward-model (Table 7) reported averages across 42 verbs: Y2F baseline = -0.0726; Z6B (Man-Preferred RMM) = 1.5280 (per-ethnicity ~1.43–1.63) — this exceeds L2V bounds, indicating a numeric/formatting inconsistency in Table 7; P3L (Woman-Preferred RMW) = -0.7448. Table 7 delta/subscript annotations appear inconsistent: Z6B’s +1.60 looks relative to Y2F, while P3L’s -2.27 corresponds to P3L minus Z6B. Aligned-video-model L2V (Table 8): G4S baseline = 0.8034; +Z6B = 0.9584 (+0.16); +P3L = 0.3082 (-0.50). +P3L reduces male bias but L2V remains positive (man-biased) across ethnicities. Action sensitivities: Z6B amplifies male-associated actions (exercise, row, cook); P3L shifts bake, sleep, sweep toward women; most sensitive actions include sleep, stretch, read. Caveats/limitations: US-Census-based gender/ethnicity categories lack intersectionality; VLM judges are image-level classifiers with biases (ensembling mitigates but doesn't eliminate errors); need larger/diverse ground-truth video annotation; alignment experiments used single-step latent consistency distillation and limited rewards (RL/multi-turn tuning may differ); controllable-preference manipulation enables targeted modulation but doesn't solve broader alignment; fixed action taxonomy limits generalization. Broader Impact: alignment (incl. RLHF) can stabilize/entrench bias; dual-use risk (same methods can mitigate or enable exclusionary propaganda); responsibility calls for continual multi-granular, event-centric audits (e.g., QX2) and careful preference-data curation. Supplementary inventory (per-verb gender/ethnicity analyses, training-data effects, stats, implementation): items A, dataset ethnicity item #10, C, D, F, G; gender/ethnicity plot groups: 7–13 (four-model), 14 (four-model ethnicity), 19–25 (reward-model), 26–29 (reward-model ethnicity), 30–37(b) (reward-aligned video), 38 (reward-aligned ethnicity), 39–43 (controllable-preference L2V).

final_notes: Broader impact: alignment can stabilize/polish/entrench bias; controllable preference modeling is dual-use; developers should audit social composition and curate preference data. Key quantitative findings: Table 5 avg PBSG — baseline generator VCM-VC2 = 0.8034; + HPSv2.0 = 0.9116. Table 6 (gender rows): mean TAS increases 0.9763 → 0.9967; perfect-stability 0.8850 → 0.9830. Action-level patterns: RMM amplifies male portrayals (exercise, row, cook); RMW shifts bake, sleep, sweep toward women; highest normalized sensitivity for sleep, stretch, read. Unresolved/flagged internal issues to verify: label inconsistencies in tables (Table 7 deltas), a possible mislabeling (-0.4352 labeled Latino RDS), and a textual claim that HPSv2.0 "reinforces White preference" that may conflict with Table 5 White RDS behavior. Limitations: U.S.-centric demographics, VLM evaluators are image-level, single-step tuning, synthetic preference manipulations, limited 42-action set. Paper introduces VideoBiasEval, an event-based evaluation framework that separates actor attributes from verbs and contexts. The framework measures ethnicity bias, gender bias within ethnic groups, changes after alignment tuning, and temporal stability of demographic portrayals. The authors analyze human preference datasets, train image reward models on those datasets, and align video models using those rewards. Reported findings: preference biases can be inherited by reward models, can be amplified by alignment, and can become more temporally stable. The authors also construct man-preferred and woman-preferred reward datasets and show that reward-data composition can either reinforce or counteract a video model’s pre-existing gender bias. Paper notes caveats: limits due to demographic category definitions, use of automated evaluators, specific training choices, and a fixed action set for evaluation.

VideoBiasEval: event-based evaluation that separates actor attributes (gender, ethnicity) from verbs/contexts; event = actor performing a verb in a context. Evaluations are multi-granular (frame, temporal, video, event, demographic-group). Key metrics/concepts: frame-level classification (gender/ethnicity per frame), video-level label via majority voting, attribute flickering (frame-to-frame identity inconsistency), temporal coherence/consistency, TAS (temporal attribute stability) with mean/median/std reported and a "perfect stability" outcome reported alongside TAS (Table 6). Models: unaligned (u) = likelihood-trained baseline; aligned (a) = preference-guided post-training (alignment tuning / reward-weighted fine-tuning / RLHF-style procedures). Reward models (preference models) are trained from human preference pairs (two images compared vs caption); aesthetic reward is one type. Reward models assign scores to guide generator optimization; controllable preference modeling constructs directional or counter-biased reward datasets (e.g., man-preferred, woman-preferred). Distillation/optimization: Latent Consistency Distillation incorporates image-reward feedback; study uses single-step video generation during reward-guided distillation; teacher = pretrained T2V model, student = distilled model. Automated evaluation: VLMs-as-judges ensemble (vision–language models infer gender/ethnicity); human verification used for grounding (Pearson, Cohen’s/Fleiss’ Kappa reported); sensitivity analysis re-evaluates high-agreement subsets. Other glossary items: Softmax and standardized scores for reward normalization; normalized sensitivity = action’s change in PBSG divided by reward-model baseline PBSG. Prior findings (from earlier parts): preference biases in human datasets can be inherited by reward models, amplified by alignment, and become more temporally stable; reward-data composition can reinforce or counteract pre-existing gender bias. Caveats: demographic category limits, automated evaluators, specific training choices, fixed action set.

VideoBiasEval (Sec 3) defines an event as tuple <p,a,c> (actor p performs verb a in context c). Controlled attribute space: 4 gender prompt categories (man, woman, person, non-binary person), 7 ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino), and 42 verbs. Verb list (42): bake, bike, call, clean, climb, cook, cough, cry, drink, drive, eat, exercise, fish, hit, jump, kick, kneel, laugh, lift, paint, pick, pitch, pray, read, ride, row, run, shop, shout, sit, skate, sleep, smile, stand, stare, stretch, study, sweep, throw, walk, wash, work. Prompting protocol: deterministic template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” Two evaluation conditions: Person-only (actor = “person”; 1 prompt/verb = 42 prompts) and Ethnicity+Person (explicit ethnicity + “person”; 42 verbs × 7 ethnicities = 294 prompts). Prompts are from a predefined set (not generated by an LLM); a fixed number of videos per prompt are generated under identical decoding settings. Person-only tests which gender/ethnicity the model assigns without explicit demographic cues; Ethnicity+Person tests how explicit ethnicity interacts with inferred attributes (e.g., gender). Section 7: controllable gender bias via curated reward datasets. Data: man- and woman-preferred image-pair datasets (2.94M same-action/same-ethnicity pairs per dataset + 537,660 HPDv2 pairs). Reward models trained on CLIP encoder: RMM (man-preferred) and RMW (woman-preferred). Table 7 (avg over 42 verbs): CLIP -0.0726; RMM 1.5280; RMW -0.7448. Note: Table 7 delta-subscript annotations are inconsistent (earlier observed: subscripts appear to use CLIP as baseline for RMM but RMM as baseline for RMW). Table 8 (generator PBSG, avg over 42 verbs): VCM-VC2 0.8034; +RMM 0.9584 (+0.16); +RMW 0.3082 (-0.50). Textual claims: RMM increases PBSG (reinforces male preference) across ethnicity columns; RMW decreases PBSG (counteracts male bias) across ethnicity columns. Action-level (Figure 6): RMM amplifies male portrayals for activities like exercise, row, cook; RMW shifts activities like bake, sleep, sweep toward women; normalized sensitivity (ΔPBSG / baseline PBSG) ranks sleep, stretch, read highest under both directions. Mixtures of preference data proposed as tunable control (no mixture experiments reported). Carry-forward unresolved inconsistencies from earlier parts: mislabeling of -0.4352 as Latino RDS, and a textual claim that HPSv2.0 "reinforces White preference" that contradicts Table 5's White RDS decrease.

Paper conclusion (Sec. 8): alignment-related bias requires auditing/mitigation across generation pipeline; VideoBiasEval separates identity attributes from content semantics and tracks how alignment changes representation; reward-based alignment inherits and often amplifies biases in human preference data. Key quantitative points to carry forward: Preference-data directional bias (Sec. 5.1) — 69.23% (18/26) of qualifying HPDv2 verbs favor men; 61.11% (11/18) of qualifying Pick-a-Pic verbs favor women. Table 4 avg PBSG: HPSv2.0 0.6039; PickScore -0.1157. Generator baseline (VCM-VC2) avg PBSG 0.8034. Alignment amplification example (Table 5): + HPSv2.0 -> 0.9116 (Δ +0.1082). Reward-design can counter bias (Table 8): + RMW -> 0.3082 (from baseline 0.8034). Reward-model experiments (curated datasets): Table 7 (avg over 42 verbs) — CLIP -0.0726; RMM 1.5280; RMW -0.7448. Action-level findings: RMM amplifies male portrayals for activities (exercise, row, cook); RMW shifts bake, sleep, sweep toward women; normalized sensitivity (ΔPBSG / baseline PBSG) ranks sleep, stretch, read highest. Proposed tunable mixtures of preference data (no mixtures tested). Carry-forward unresolved issues noted earlier: some table/label inconsistencies (e.g., Table 7 delta-subscript baselines inconsistent), a previously observed mislabeling of -0.4352 as Latino RDS, and a textual claim that HPSv2.0 "reinforces White preference" that appears to contradict Table 5's White RDS decrease. Keep these numbers/claims handy for checking later parts.

Conclusion summary: alignment-related bias requires auditing/mitigation across generation pipeline; VideoBiasEval separates identity attributes from content semantics and tracks how alignment changes representation; reward-based alignment inherits and often amplifies biases in human preference data. Key quantitative points: Preference-data directional bias — 69.23% (18/26) of qualifying HPDv2 verbs favor men; 61.11% (11/18) of qualifying Pick-a-Pic verbs favor women. Table 4 avg PBSG: HPSv2.0 0.6039; PickScore -0.1157. Generator baseline (VCM-VC2) avg PBSG 0.8034. Alignment amplification example (Table 5): + HPSv2.0 -> 0.9116 (Δ +0.1082). Reward-design can counter bias (Table 8): + RMW -> 0.3082 (from baseline 0.8034). Reward-model experiments (avg over 42 verbs, Table 7): CLIP -0.0726; RMM 1.5280; RMW -0.7448. Action-level: RMM amplifies male portrayals (exercise, row, cook); RMW shifts bake, sleep, sweep toward women; normalized sensitivity (ΔPBSG / baseline PBSG) ranks sleep, stretch, read highest. Proposed tunable mixtures of preference data mentioned but not tested. Unresolved/inconsistent items to watch: table/label inconsistencies (delta-subscript baselines in Table 7), mislabeling of -0.4352 as Latino RDS earlier, and textual claim that HPSv2.0 "reinforces White preference" which appears to contradict Table 5's reported White RDS decrease. New from Limitations (Part 21): study uses U.S. Census-style gender/ethnicity categories; VLM evaluators are image-level and may be biased (ensembling used); primary tuning strategy is single-step latent consistency distillation with limited reward models (other protocols not tested); controllable experiments use synthetic gender-preference manipulations; VideoBiasEval uses fixed set of 42 actions, limiting generalization.

Broader Impact: alignment stabilizes and can polish/entrench bias; controllable preference modeling is dual-use (can mitigate or intensify representational harms); developers should audit social composition and curate preference data. Claims & reported numbers in this part: Table 5 avg PBSG — VCM-VC2 (baseline) 0.8034; + HPSv2.0 0.9116. Table 6 (gender rows): mean TAS 0.9763 → 0.9967; perfect-stability 0.8850 → 0.9830. Table 7 (reward-model averages over 42 verbs): RMM 1.5280; RMW -0.7448 (CLIP -0.0726 per earlier notes). Table 8 (avg video PBSG after tuning): + RMM 0.9584; + RMW 0.3082. These support statements that alignment can stabilize amplified biases and that curated reward data can steer portrayals. Keep prior key results: preference-data directional bias — HPDv2: 69.23% (18/26) verbs favor men; Pick-a-Pic: 61.11% (11/18) verbs favor women. Table 4 avg PBSG: HPSv2.0 0.6039; PickScore -0.1157. Baseline generator (VCM-VC2) avg PBSG 0.8034. Action-level: RMM amplifies male portrayals (exercise,row,cook); RMW shifts bake,sleep,sweep toward women; normalized sensitivity highest for sleep,stretch,read. Unresolved/flagged items from earlier parts remain: table/label inconsistencies (Table 7 deltas), a possible mislabeling (-0.4352 labeled Latino RDS), and a prior textual claim that HPSv2.0 "reinforces White preference" which may conflict with Table 5's White RDS behavior. Limitations noted: U.S.-centric demographic categories; VLM evaluators are image-level; single-step tuning protocol; synthetic preference manipulations; 42-action set limits generalization.

final_notes: Dataset & eval: VideoBiasEval — 42 verbs × 7 ethnicities = 294 ethnicity+person conditions. Image reward-model means: CLIP -0.0726 (woman-preferred), HPSv2.0 +0.6039 (man-preferred), HPSv2.1 -0.0984 (woman-preferred), PickScore -0.1157 (woman-preferred). Temporal stability: baseline Ethnicity TAS = 0.8904, Gender TAS = 0.9763; HPSv2.1 raises Ethnicity TAS to 0.9632 and increases perfect-stability proportion by +0.2660. Constructed controllable-preference datasets: 2.94M Ethnicity+Gender preference pairs and 537,660 HPDv2 pairs; fine-tuned CLIP reward models RMM (man-preferred) and RMW (woman-preferred). Reported reward-model effects include RMM ≈ +1.5280 and RMW ≈ -0.7448, though elsewhere the paper claims magnitude-matched opposites (flagged internal inconsistency). Base VCM-VC2 PBSG = 0.8034; after alignment: +RMM = 0.9584 (+0.155), +RMW = 0.3082 (−0.495) — showing a large asymmetric effect where RMW produces a much larger negative shift. High-level inconsistency: some text says RMW can 'actively correct' skew while other conclusions state reward-model-based alignment 'frequently amplifies' biases. Limitations: focus on binary/US-style gender and ethnicity categories; VLM-based evaluators validated vs human judgments but may err on stylized/ambiguous frames; single-step latent consistency distillation used (other protocols like RL may differ); controllable-preference experiments are synthetic and limited; VideoBiasEval covers only 42 actions. Broader impacts: alignment tuning can act as a 'bias stabilizer'; controllable-preference modeling is dual-use; recommends multi-granular, event-centric auditing and rigorous preference-dataset curation. Title: From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models. Authors: Zefan Cai et al. (footnote marker †† appears used twice in title block — inconsistent). Key claim/goal: introduce VideoBiasEval, a diagnostic framework to analyze social bias in text-to-video generation and to trace effects of alignment tuning. Definitions: 'aligned models' = video diffusion models undergoing post-training optimization to better match human preferences (via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style procedures using learned reward/preference models trained on human comparisons). Pipeline: base video diffusion model → preference/reward model → post-training optimization. 'Unaligned counterparts' = models trained only with likelihood-based objectives, used as baselines. Motivation: alignment improves perceptual quality and temporal coherence but may encode/reinforce human preference biases, affecting representation (who is generated, roles, frequency). VideoBiasEval methods: event-based prompting to separate verb/context (semantic content) from actor identity attributes; uses established social bias taxonomies; focuses on gender and ethnicity. Metrics: multi-granular metrics to assess (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) shifts in social attribute distributions across models, and (4) temporal persistence of bias within videos. Paper promises an end-to-end analysis tracing how social attribute distributions evolve through the alignment tuning pipeline. Existing eval gaps listed (limited identity coverage in prompts; lack of specific metrics; lack of methods to track pre/post alignment shifts).

Goal: introduce VideoBiasEval to diagnose social bias in text-to-video generation and trace effects of alignment tuning. Pipeline: base video diffusion model → human preference dataset → image reward model (e.g., HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore) → post-training alignment tuning (reward-weighted fine-tuning) producing an 'aligned' video diffusion model; compare to unaligned (likelihood-trained) baselines. Data & models examined: human preference datasets HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic; reward models HPSv2.0/HPSv2.1 and PickScore; a video consistency model distilled from VideoCrafter-2 is fine-tuned for experiments. Key empirical claims: (1) HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic show non-neutral gender preferences and a strong imbalance favoring White representations; (2) reward models inherit and amplify these biases; (3) alignment-tuned video models propagate biases—alignment with male- or female-preferred reward models systematically shifts gender portrayals while ethnic representation stays uneven; (4) Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS): alignment improves temporal consistency of social attribute portrayals but can make biased portrayals more persistent and visually stable. They also explore constructing controllable image reward datasets (Section 7) and report analyses across 42 events, claiming controllable/counter-biased reward modeling as a mitigation strategy. Contributions summarized: VideoBiasEval framework, first end-to-end analysis linking datasets→reward models→aligned video models, and experiments showing alignment improves quality/coherence while reshaping/reinforcing social composition.

Goal: introduce VideoBiasEval to diagnose social bias in text-to-video generation and trace effects of alignment tuning. Pipeline: base video diffusion model → human preference dataset → image reward model (HPSv2.0/HPSv2.1, PickScore) → reward-weighted fine-tuning producing 'aligned' video diffusion model; compare to unaligned (likelihood-trained) baselines. Key empirical claims: (1) HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic show non-neutral gender preferences and a strong imbalance favoring White representations; (2) reward models inherit and amplify these biases; (3) alignment-tuned video models propagate biases—alignment with male- or female-preferred reward models systematically shifts gender portrayals while ethnic representation stays uneven; (4) Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS): alignment improves temporal consistency of social attribute portrayals but can make biased portrayals more persistent. Also explore constructing controllable image reward datasets and claim controllable/counter-biased reward modeling as mitigation. Related work: existing T2V benchmarks (VBench, EvalCrafter, T2V-CompBench) use metrics like Fréchet Video Distance, CLIP-Score, object consistency but overlook who is depicted and demographic balance; GRiT/CLIP-based metrics verify presence/faithfulness of entities but fail to audit demographic representation or event-level role/verb/context joint patterns. This work proposes an event-centric, actor-verb-environment audit for gender and ethnicity-aware biases across the T2V pipeline.

VideoBiasEval: event-based framework for evaluating social biases in video diffusion models. Use structured prompts varying actor gender/ethnicity across real-world events; generate videos and extract social attributes via a VLM-based evaluation (Sec. 3.3). Events modeled as tuple <p,a,c> (actor p performs verb a in context c). Controlled attribute space: 4 gender categories (man, woman, the neutral term “person,” non-binary person) per Luccioni et al.; 7 ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino) per Karkkainen & Joo / US Census conventions. Verb set: 42 visually distinctive verbs (bake; bike; call; clean; climb; cook; cough; cry; drink; drive; eat; exercise; fish; hit; jump; kick; kneel; laugh; lift; paint; pick; pitch; pray; read; ride; row; run; shop; shout; sit; skate; sleep; smile; stand; stare; stretch; study; sweep; throw; walk; wash; work). Section 3.2 begins Event-Based Prompting Protocol (Settings) but details not shown in this part. Framing emphasizes reproducibility and bounded scope to trace bias propagation; connects to earlier claims about actor-verb-environment audit and later analyses (e.g., temporal consistency/TAS).

steps.notes_before: Prompt template: "A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context]" (42 verbs). Conditions: Person-only ('person', 42 prompts) and Ethnicity+Person (7 ethnic descriptors × 42 = 294 prompts). Sampling: each prompt sampled 10× per model; 16 frames uniformly per video. VLM ensemble: Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B; inference frame-wise, majority-vote per model, then ensemble majority for per-video label. Labels: gender ∈ {man, woman}; ethnicity ∈ {White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino}. Metrics: PBSG = (N_man - N_woman)/N_total; RDS_e = P_e - 1/7 (~14.3%); SDI = 1 - Σ_e P_e^2. Table 2 (earlier): compared ModelScope→InstructVideo and VideoCrafter→T2V; reported SDI values were small (ModelScope 0.0538, InstructVideo 0.0267, VideoCrafter 0.1252, T2V 0.1119). New (this part): human verification on 400 generated videos annotated by 3 independent annotators; Pearson correlations (VLM ensemble vs humans): 0.89 (gender), 0.73 (ethnicity); Cohen's Kappa: 0.91 (gender), 0.78 (ethnicity); Fleiss' Kappa: 0.92 (gender), 0.82 (ethnicity). Internal inconsistencies: (1) the SDI scale/values here (~0.75) conflict with SDI values shown in Table 2 (~0.03–0.13); (2) the wording 'perfectly align' conflicts with reported consensus rates <100% (99.0%, 83.3%). final_notes: Broader impact: alignment can stabilize/entrench bias (removing artifacts/temporal flicker makes stereotypes appear natural); dual-use risk; responsibility to monitor generated social composition with multi-granular, event-centric audits (e.g., QX2). Supplementary inventory: A (42-verb video analysis; WebVid-10M training-data effects; stat analysis #9); dataset ethnicity item #10 (human image-reward-dataset ethnicity preference distributions); C (reward-model implementation; 42-verb analysis; stat #11); D (42-verb aligned-video analysis; stat #12); F (reward-model training/inference); G (video post-training/inference). Many numbered plots (7–43) map gender/ethnicity across 42 verbs for different models/settings; ethnicity plot #38 for reward-aligned video. Key datasets: two collections each 2.94M preference pairs (fixed action+ethnicity; M-1 vs W-1) plus 537,660 R9C face-free pairs. Reward models: Y2F (pretrained encoder), Z6B (Man-preferred RMM), P3L (Woman-preferred RMW). L2V (Table 7, avg 42 verbs): Y2F -0.0726; Z6B 1.5280; P3L -0.7448. Title: From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.
Authors: Zefan Cai (marked "Equal contribution, ordered by last name"), Haoyi Qiu, Haozhe Zhao, Ke Wan, Jiachen Li, Jiuxiang Gu, Wen Xiao (affiliation line contains "Microsofthttps://github.com/Zefan-Cai/VideoBiasEval"), Nanyun Peng (marked "Equal advising"), Junjie Hu.
Key claims to check later:
- Alignment-tuned video diffusion produces smoother but more stereotyped and temporally persistent portrayals.
- Preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generated videos.
- Introduces QX2: provides event-based separation of verbs/contexts from actor gender and ethnicity; supports multi-granular measurements including ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and within-video persistence.
- Claims this is "the first end-to-end analysis" linking human comparison data, learned image rewards, and aligned video outputs.
- Human-preference-trained rewards improve visual quality but unintentionally encode and amplify social bias; argues for bias-aware assessment and mitigation throughout alignment.
Figure 1 notes: QX2 event prompts and multi-granular ethnicity/gender audit shown bottom-left; frame-wise VLM inference and aggregation of actor attributes at top; bottom-right summarizes the analysis separating human preference bias, image-reward preference bias, and downstream diffusion-video generation bias.
Links provided: OpenReview and GitHub.

Intro summary: Human comparison collections favor White representations and show non-neutral gender preferences; learned rewards inherit and amplify these patterns, with male- or female-preferred rewards systematically redirecting gender portrayals and ethnic distributions remaining uneven. Curating attribute distributions and counter-biased rewards can control image-reward datasets and downstream video representations. Analysis spans 42 events and examines reward-preference changes and pre-/post-alignment video-bias changes. Definition: “aligned models” = video diffusion models fine-tuned after likelihood training to match human preferences (reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style optimization using learned preference/aesthetic rewards trained on human comparisons). “Unaligned” = likelihood-trained baselines. Motivation: subjective preference judgments often lack demographic diversity and can encode systematic bias that rewards and generators inherit/amplify. Need: event-based distributional metrics and a pre/post alignment analysis protocol; prior work lacks diverse identity prompts, comprehensive identity coverage, and distribution-tracking metrics. QX2 (VideoBiasEval) provides controlled separation of verb/identity variation for interpretable, multi-granular assessment (ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, within-video persistence). Claims/contributions: (1) comprehensive event-prompt/multi-granularity audit; (2) first connected analysis linking human preference data → learned image rewards → aligned video outputs, showing inheritance, amplification, stabilization; (3) evidence that perceptual/temporal improvements from alignment can reshape or reinforce generated social composition, plus guidance for controllable-preference mitigation. Key claims to check later: alignment-tuned diffusion produces smoother but more stereotyped/temporally persistent portrayals; preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generated videos; QX2 supports multi-granular measurements and within-video persistence; argues for bias-aware assessment & mitigation across alignment pipeline.

Definitions & scope: “aligned models” = video diffusion models fine-tuned post-likelihood to match human preference rewards (reward-weighted fine-tuning / RLHF-style). “Unaligned” = likelihood-trained baselines. Core claims to verify later: alignment-tuned diffusion yields smoother but more stereotyped/temporally persistent portrayals; preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generated videos; QX2 supports multi-granular measurement including within-video persistence; curating attribute distributions and counter-biased rewards can control downstream representations.
From Related Work (new): existing T2V benchmarks (VBench, EvalCrafter, T2V-CompBench) use metrics like Fréchet Video Distance, CLIP-Score, and object consistency but do not audit depicted identities or portrayal demographics. GRiT-based measures can detect an actor/role (e.g., a doctor) but do not flag demographic skews (e.g., exclusively white male doctors). Y2F-based alignment rewards prioritize textual fidelity over demographic balance. Prior generative-model bias work focuses on static images/isolated objects (StableBias, DALL-Eval, SocialCounterfactuals) and usually counts identities without activity/role context; this can miss recurring role-based stereotypes. Motivation: need event-level disentanglement (joint actor–verb–context) and ethnicity-/gender-aware, event-centric quantification throughout generation; QX2 is presented to fill this gap.
What to check later: whether the paper shows evidence for amplification/stabilization claims, whether reward models trained on human comparisons are demonstrably biased in the ways claimed, whether evaluation metrics used in experiments truly go beyond FVD/CLIP/object-consistency to measure demographics and temporal persistence, and whether QX2 operationalizes the stated multi-granular metrics.

final_notes: Metrics: PBSG = (N_man - N_woman)/N_total; RDSe = P_e - 1/7; SDI = 1 - ΣP_e^2. TAS reported (mean, std, perfect-stability share). Human validation: 100 images → 77% unanimous, 97% majority. Dataset: 42 socially associated actions/verbs. Key numbers: Table 4 (avg across 42 verbs): CLIP -0.0726; HPSv2.0 0.6039; HPSv2.1 -0.0984; PickScore -0.1157. Table4 SDI ≈ 0.85. Section 5.1 counts: HPDv2 18/26 (69.23%) verbs favor men; Pick-a-Pic 11/18 (61.11%) favor women. Aligned generators (Table 5): baseline VCM-VC2 0.8034; +HPSv2.0 0.9116 (+0.1082); +HPSv2.1 0.2267 (-0.5767); +PickScore 0.3714 (-0.4320). Table5 SDI baseline ~0.1433. Reward-model alignment (Table 7): CLIP -0.0726; RMM 1.5280; RMW -0.7448 (asymmetric magnitudes). Per-ethnicity RMM ≈1.43–1.63; RMW ≈-0.63–-0.88. Table 8 (generators): VCM-VC2 0.8034; +RMM 0.9584 (+0.1550); +RMW 0.3082 (-0.4952). Action-level effects: RMM amplifies male-leaning actions (exercise, row, cook); RMW shifts bake, sleep, sweep toward women. Normalized sensitivity = ΔPBSG / baseline PBSG; sleep, stretch, read rank highest. Conclusions: preference/reward data carry directional biases and alignment often amplifies them; reward design can counter biases. Limitations: U.S. Census categories only; VLM evaluators are image-level classifiers with biases; single-step latent distillation; synthetic manipulations for controllable preference; fixed 42-action set. Broader impact: alignment can stabilize/amplify bias; curated preference data can steer portrayals; risks include normalization/exclusion/homogenization/propaganda; no deployment evidence. steps.notes_before: (none yet: this is the first part)

Paper introduces VideoBiasEval, an event-based evaluation framework that separates actor attributes from verbs and contexts. The framework measures ethnicity bias, gender bias within ethnic groups, changes after alignment tuning, and temporal stability of demographic portrayals. The authors analyze human preference datasets, train image reward models on those datasets, and align video models using those rewards. Reported findings: preference biases can be inherited by reward models, can be amplified by alignment, and can become more temporally stable. The authors also construct man-preferred and woman-preferred reward datasets and show that reward-data composition can either reinforce or counteract a video model’s pre-existing gender bias. Paper notes caveats: limits due to demographic category definitions, use of automated evaluators, specific training choices, and a fixed action set for evaluation.

VideoBiasEval: event-based evaluation that separates actor attributes (gender, ethnicity) from verbs/contexts; event = actor performing a verb in a context. Evaluations are multi-granular (frame, temporal, video, event, demographic-group). Key metrics/concepts: frame-level classification (gender/ethnicity per frame), video-level label via majority voting, attribute flickering (frame-to-frame identity inconsistency), temporal coherence/consistency, TAS (temporal attribute stability) with mean/median/std reported and a "perfect stability" outcome reported alongside TAS (Table 6). Models: unaligned (u) = likelihood-trained baseline; aligned (a) = preference-guided post-training (alignment tuning / reward-weighted fine-tuning / RLHF-style procedures). Reward models (preference models) are trained from human preference pairs (two images compared vs caption); aesthetic reward is one type. Reward models assign scores to guide generator optimization; controllable preference modeling constructs directional or counter-biased reward datasets (e.g., man-preferred, woman-preferred). Distillation/optimization: Latent Consistency Distillation incorporates image-reward feedback; study uses single-step video generation during reward-guided distillation; teacher = pretrained T2V model, student = distilled model. Automated evaluation: VLMs-as-judges ensemble (vision–language models infer gender/ethnicity); human verification used for grounding (Pearson, Cohen’s/Fleiss’ Kappa reported); sensitivity analysis re-evaluates high-agreement subsets. Other glossary items: Softmax and standardized scores for reward normalization; normalized sensitivity = action’s change in PBSG divided by reward-model baseline PBSG. Prior findings (from earlier parts): preference biases in human datasets can be inherited by reward models, amplified by alignment, and become more temporally stable; reward-data composition can reinforce or counteract pre-existing gender bias. Caveats: demographic category limits, automated evaluators, specific training choices, fixed action set.

VideoBiasEval (Sec 3) defines an event as tuple <p,a,c> (actor p performs verb a in context c). Controlled attribute space: 4 gender prompt categories (man, woman, person, non-binary person), 7 ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino), and 42 verbs. Verb list (42): bake, bike, call, clean, climb, cook, cough, cry, drink, drive, eat, exercise, fish, hit, jump, kick, kneel, laugh, lift, paint, pick, pitch, pray, read, ride, row, run, shop, shout, sit, skate, sleep, smile, stand, stare, stretch, study, sweep, throw, walk, wash, work. Prompting protocol: deterministic template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” Two evaluation conditions: Person-only (actor = “person”; 1 prompt/verb = 42 prompts) and Ethnicity+Person (explicit ethnicity + “person”; 42 verbs × 7 ethnicities = 294 prompts). Prompts are from a predefined set (not generated by an LLM); a fixed number of videos per prompt are generated under identical decoding settings. Person-only tests which gender/ethnicity the model assigns without explicit demographic cues; Ethnicity+Person tests how explicit ethnicity interacts with inferred attributes (e.g., gender). Keep in mind earlier-section empirical results to check consistency later: datasets (Sec 5.1) — HPDv2: 18/26 verbs man-preferred (69.23%), reported White preference 43.34% (paper claimed dataset favors White — flagged earlier as inconsistent since 43.34%<50%); Pick-a-Pic: 11/18 verbs woman-preferred (61.11%), reported White preference 40.08%. "We exclude gender bias from this analysis because, in the absence of explicit ethnicity specifications, generative models predominantly produce representations of White individuals (Figure 14). Consequently, analyzing gender alone effectively reduces to examining gender bias within the White demographic (Figure 30)."
errors.explanation: The paragraph both states that it will assess gender across ethnic groups using PBSG and immediately states that it "excludes gender bias from this analysis," which is a direct internal contradiction about whether gender bias is being analyzed.

errors.claim: Definition of PBSG uses only N_man and N_woman (and defines N_total as their sum)
errors.evidence: This part: "PBSG is defined as (N_man - N_woman)/N_total ... where N_man and N_woman denote the number of representations depicting men and women, respectively, and N_total is their sum." Earlier notes: "Controlled-attribute claim earlier: 4 gender categories (man, woman, neutral 'person', non-binary)"
errors.explanation: The PBSG formula ignores the earlier-declared additional gender categories (neutral 'person' and non-binary). The paper thus appears to both claim four gender categories exist and then compute a gender-bias score that only counts 'man' and 'woman', without explaining how other categories are treated.

errors.claim: 'RDS_e = P_e - 1/|E|; for |E|=7 the uniform baseline is 1/7 ≈14.3%.' (definition from earlier part/notes)
errors.evidence: Table 2 in this part reports RDSe entries smaller than -0.142857 (e.g. ModelScope (u) shows Black RDS = -0.1952 and Latino RDS = -0.1952; ModelScope Middle Eastern RDS = -0.1976; InstructVideo Black RDS = -0.1976, etc.).
errors.explanation: By the stated definition RDS_e = P_e - 1/7, the minimum possible RDS_e is -1/7 ≈ -0.142857 (when P_e = 0). Values like -0.1952 < -0.142857 imply P_e < 0 (e.g. P_black = -0.1952 + 0.142857 ≈ -0.0523), which is impossible. Thus the RDSe numbers in Table 2 contradict the earlier RDSe definition and the nonnegativity of proportions.

final_notes: Paper studies steering bias in video generation by fine-tuning a CLIP-based VLM into two reward models (RMM = man-preferred, RMW = woman-preferred) using synthetic preference datasets. Data: synthetic man-/woman-preferred preference data (≈2.94M Ethnicity+Gender pairs) plus 537,660 HPDv2 pairs. Key metrics: baseline VCM-VC2 avg PBSG = 0.8034; RMM PBSG = 0.9584 (Δ ≈ +0.155); RMW PBSG = 0.3082 (Δ ≈ -0.495). Reported raw score means (Table 7): CLIP avg = -0.0726, RMM avg = 1.5280, RMW avg = -0.7448 (noted earlier as a potential inconsistency to verify). Main findings: varying gender composition of preference data steers generator bias; counter-biased RM (RMW) can correct baseline male-skew; mixing preference data gives a tunable alignment axis. Action-level analysis: reports ΔPBSG and normalized sensitivity metrics; RMM amplifies male-preferred actions (exercise, row, cook); RMW shifts toward woman-preferred (bake, sleep, sweep); top sensitive actions include sleep, stretch, read. Limitations and caveats: focus limited to gender and ethnicity using U.S. Census categories; evaluation used single-step latent consistency distillation and a small set of RMs; controllable-preference experiments limited to synthetic gender manipulations; VideoBiasEval covers a fixed set of 42 socially associated actions. Evaluation validation: VLM evaluators were validated against humans but paper also contains inconsistent language about evaluator biases/inaccuracies vs exact human agreement. Broader impacts: alignment tuning can stabilize/entrench biases; controllable preference modeling is dual-use; authors recommend multi-granular, event-centric auditing (VideoBiasEval) and stakeholder-informed preference dataset curation.

steps.notes_before: Title: From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models. Authors: Zefan Cai (UW–Madison), Haoyi Qiu, Haozhe Zhao, Ke Wan (UCSD), Jiachen Li (UCSB), Jiuxiang Gu, Wen Xiao (Microsoft; GitHub link noted), Nanyun Peng (UCLA), Junjie Hu (UIUC). Note: footnote marker †† is used twice with different meanings (equal contribution and equal advising) — inconsistent. Abstract: introduce VideoBiasEval, a diagnostic framework for social bias in text-to-video generation. Key methods: event-based prompting to separate semantic content (verbs/contexts) from actor attributes (gender/ethnicity); multi-granular metrics for (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) distributional shifts across model variants, (4) temporal persistence of bias in videos. Analysis: end-to-end trace from human preference datasets → reward models → alignment-tuned video diffusion models; claim this is the first such end-to-end analysis. Findings: alignment tuning amplifies representational biases and makes them temporally stable, producing smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Figure 1 caption references Sections 3, 3.3, 5.1, 5.2, and 6 and mentions VLMs inferring actor attributes across frames and aggregating for bias quantification.

Title: From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models. Authors: Zefan Cai et al. (footnote marker †† appears used twice in title block — inconsistent). Key claim/goal: introduce VideoBiasEval, a diagnostic framework to analyze social bias in text-to-video generation and to trace effects of alignment tuning. Definitions: 'aligned models' = video diffusion models undergoing post-training optimization to better match human preferences (via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style procedures using learned reward/preference models trained on human comparisons). Pipeline: base video diffusion model → preference/reward model → post-training optimization. 'Unaligned counterparts' = models trained only with likelihood-based objectives, used as baselines. Motivation: alignment improves perceptual quality and temporal coherence but may encode/reinforce human preference biases, affecting representation (who is generated, roles, frequency). VideoBiasEval methods: event-based prompting to separate verb/context (semantic content) from actor identity attributes; uses established social bias taxonomies; focuses on gender and ethnicity. Metrics: multi-granular metrics to assess (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) shifts in social attribute distributions across models, and (4) temporal persistence of bias within videos. Paper promises an end-to-end analysis tracing how social attribute distributions evolve through the alignment tuning pipeline. Existing eval gaps listed (limited identity coverage in prompts; lack of specific metrics; lack of methods to track pre/post alignment shifts).

Goal: introduce VideoBiasEval to diagnose social bias in text-to-video generation and trace effects of alignment tuning. Pipeline: base video diffusion model → human preference dataset → image reward model (e.g., HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore) → post-training alignment tuning (reward-weighted fine-tuning) producing an 'aligned' video diffusion model; compare to unaligned (likelihood-trained) baselines. Data & models examined: human preference datasets HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic; reward models HPSv2.0/HPSv2.1 and PickScore; a video consistency model distilled from VideoCrafter-2 is fine-tuned for experiments. Key empirical claims: (1) HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic show non-neutral gender preferences and a strong imbalance favoring White representations; (2) reward models inherit and amplify these biases; (3) alignment-tuned video models propagate biases—alignment with male- or female-preferred reward models systematically shifts gender portrayals while ethnic representation stays uneven; (4) Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS): alignment improves temporal consistency of social attribute portrayals but can make biased portrayals more persistent and visually stable. They also explore constructing controllable image reward datasets (Section 7) and report analyses across 42 events, claiming controllable/counter-biased reward modeling as a mitigation strategy. Contributions summarized: VideoBiasEval framework, first end-to-end analysis linking datasets→reward models→aligned video models, and experiments showing alignment improves quality/coherence while reshaping/reinforcing social composition.

Goal: introduce VideoBiasEval to diagnose social bias in text-to-video generation and trace effects of alignment tuning. Pipeline: base video diffusion model → human preference dataset → image reward model (HPSv2.0/HPSv2.1, PickScore) → reward-weighted fine-tuning producing 'aligned' video diffusion model; compare to unaligned (likelihood-trained) baselines. Key empirical claims: (1) HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic show non-neutral gender preferences and a strong imbalance favoring White representations; (2) reward models inherit and amplify these biases; (3) alignment-tuned video models propagate biases—alignment with male- or female-preferred reward models systematically shifts gender portrayals while ethnic representation stays uneven; (4) Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS): alignment improves temporal consistency of social attribute portrayals but can make biased portrayals more persistent. Also explore constructing controllable image reward datasets and claim controllable/counter-biased reward modeling as mitigation. Related work: existing T2V benchmarks (VBench, EvalCrafter, T2V-CompBench) use metrics like Fréchet Video Distance, CLIP-Score, object consistency but overlook who is depicted and demographic balance; GRiT/CLIP-based metrics verify presence/faithfulness of entities but fail to audit demographic representation or event-level role/verb/context joint patterns. This work proposes an event-centric, actor-verb-environment audit for gender and ethnicity-aware biases across the T2V pipeline.

VideoBiasEval: event-based framework for evaluating social biases in video diffusion models. Use structured prompts varying actor gender/ethnicity across real-world events; generate videos and extract social attributes via a VLM-based evaluation (Sec. 3.3). Events modeled as tuple <p,a,c> (actor p performs verb a in context c). Controlled attribute space: 4 gender categories (man, woman, the neutral term “person,” non-binary person) per Luccioni et al.; 7 ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino) per Karkkainen & Joo / US Census conventions. Verb set: 42 visually distinctive verbs (bake; bike; call; clean; climb; cook; cough; cry; drink; drive; eat; exercise; fish; hit; jump; kick; kneel; laugh; lift; paint; pick; pitch; pray; read; ride; row; run; shop; shout; sit; skate; sleep; smile; stand; stare; stretch; study; sweep; throw; walk; wash; work). Section 3.2 begins Event-Based Prompting Protocol (Settings) but details not shown in this part. Framing emphasizes reproducibility and bounded scope to trace bias propagation; connects to earlier claims about actor-verb-environment audit and later analyses (e.g., temporal consistency/TAS).

TAS (Temporal Attribute Stability): % of frames whose classified attributes match the final majority-voted video label. Evaluation setup: two prompting conditions (Person-only / Ethnicity+Person), 16 frames sampled per video, 3 VLM judges, per-frame gender/ethnicity predictions aggregated by majority vote to a video label. PBSG (Proportion Bias Score for Gender) was introduced earlier as (N_man - N_woman)/N_total ∈ [-1,1] with N_total = N_man + N_woman; PBSG=0.5 interpreted as men occur 3× women. Notes: earlier text contained contradictions about gender analysis (one paragraph said it would assess gender across ethnic groups with PBSG then immediately said it "excludes gender bias from this analysis") and ambiguity about gender categories (earlier parts mentioned 4 gender categories but PBSG uses only man/woman; unclear handling of 'person' and non-binary labels). Current part (Ethnicity Bias): defines P_e = N_e / N_total where N_total counts outputs with an identifiable ethnicity. RDS_e = P_e - 1/|E|; for |E|=7 the uniform baseline is 1/7 ≈14.3%. Example: RDS_e = 0.769 → P_e ≈0.769+0.143 ≈91.2% (noted as >6× expected). SDI = 1 - Σ_e P_e^2 (higher = more diverse). Authors frame the uniform baseline as a diagnostic under the neutral person-only setting. Bias Shift: compute ΔPBSG, ΔRDSe, ΔSDI between unaligned and aligned models; improvement = shifts toward balanced gender ratios, reduced ethnic skew, or higher diversity.

final_notes: Datasets: two image-preference datasets (each 2.94M pairs from C4Z) controlling action+ethnicity while varying gender (M-1 vs W-1); plus 537,660 face-free pairs. Methods: pretrained vision encoder Y2F fine-tuned into two reward models: Z6B (man-preferred / RMM) and P3L (woman-preferred / RMW). Reward-model L2V (Table 7) averages: Y2F avg -0.0726; Z6B avg 1.5280; P3L avg -0.7448. Note: Table 7 uses inconsistent baselines for subscripts (Z6B deltas vs Y2F; P3L deltas vs Z6B) — ambiguous. Aligned-video-model L2V (Table 8): baseline G4S avg 0.8034 (by group: White 0.7925, Black 0.7758, Latino 0.8690, East Asian 0.7115, SE Asian 0.7945, India 0.8634, Middle Eastern 0.8071). Adding Z6B → avg 0.9584 (+0.16). Adding P3L → avg 0.3082 (-0.50); e.g., East Asian 0.7115 → 0.1008 (Δ -0.61). Earlier mislabeling: a -0.4352 figure was misattributed as Latino F6N; actually a Δ for Latino L2V and the F6N entry was missing. Conclusions & limitations: recommend bias auditing/mitigation at every video-generation stage; limitations include U.S.-centric demographic categories, VLM judge biases, problematic claim that "Exact human agreement on every attribute makes larger, more diverse ground-truth video annotation redundant", single-step distillation/limited reward signals, and fixed action taxonomy. Broader impact: warns of bias stabilization by alignment, dual-use risk of curated preference rewards, and responsibility to monitor social composition (e.g., QX2). Supplementary inventory: many sections (A, C, D, F, G) and numbered plots; note conflict reusing item number 10 for two different entries. Title: From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.
Authors: Zefan Cai (marked "Equal contribution, ordered by last name"), Haoyi Qiu, Haozhe Zhao, Ke Wan, Jiachen Li, Jiuxiang Gu, Wen Xiao (affiliation line contains "Microsofthttps://github.com/Zefan-Cai/VideoBiasEval"), Nanyun Peng (marked "Equal advising"), Junjie Hu.
Key claims to check later:
- Alignment-tuned video diffusion produces smoother but more stereotyped and temporally persistent portrayals.
- Preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generated videos.
- Introduces QX2: provides event-based separation of verbs/contexts from actor gender and ethnicity; supports multi-granular measurements including ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and within-video persistence.
- Claims this is "the first end-to-end analysis" linking human comparison data, learned image rewards, and aligned video outputs.
- Human-preference-trained rewards improve visual quality but unintentionally encode and amplify social bias; argues for bias-aware assessment and mitigation throughout alignment.
Figure 1 notes: QX2 event prompts and multi-granular ethnicity/gender audit shown bottom-left; frame-wise VLM inference and aggregation of actor attributes at top; bottom-right summarizes the analysis separating human preference bias, image-reward preference bias, and downstream diffusion-video generation bias.
Links provided: OpenReview and GitHub.

Intro summary: Human comparison collections favor White representations and show non-neutral gender preferences; learned rewards inherit and amplify these patterns, with male- or female-preferred rewards systematically redirecting gender portrayals and ethnic distributions remaining uneven. Curating attribute distributions and counter-biased rewards can control image-reward datasets and downstream video representations. Analysis spans 42 events and examines reward-preference changes and pre-/post-alignment video-bias changes. Definition: “aligned models” = video diffusion models fine-tuned after likelihood training to match human preferences (reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style optimization using learned preference/aesthetic rewards trained on human comparisons). “Unaligned” = likelihood-trained baselines. Motivation: subjective preference judgments often lack demographic diversity and can encode systematic bias that rewards and generators inherit/amplify. Need: event-based distributional metrics and a pre/post alignment analysis protocol; prior work lacks diverse identity prompts, comprehensive identity coverage, and distribution-tracking metrics. QX2 (VideoBiasEval) provides controlled separation of verb/identity variation for interpretable, multi-granular assessment (ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, within-video persistence). Claims/contributions: (1) comprehensive event-prompt/multi-granularity audit; (2) first connected analysis linking human preference data → learned image rewards → aligned video outputs, showing inheritance, amplification, stabilization; (3) evidence that perceptual/temporal improvements from alignment can reshape or reinforce generated social composition, plus guidance for controllable-preference mitigation. Key claims to check later: alignment-tuned diffusion produces smoother but more stereotyped/temporally persistent portrayals; preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generated videos; QX2 supports multi-granular measurements and within-video persistence; argues for bias-aware assessment & mitigation across alignment pipeline.

Definitions & scope: “aligned models” = video diffusion models fine-tuned post-likelihood to match human preference rewards (reward-weighted fine-tuning / RLHF-style). “Unaligned” = likelihood-trained baselines. Core claims to verify later: alignment-tuned diffusion yields smoother but more stereotyped/temporally persistent portrayals; preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generated videos; QX2 supports multi-granular measurement including within-video persistence; curating attribute distributions and counter-biased rewards can control downstream representations.
From Related Work (new): existing T2V benchmarks (VBench, EvalCrafter, T2V-CompBench) use metrics like Fréchet Video Distance, CLIP-Score, and object consistency but do not audit depicted identities or portrayal demographics. GRiT-based measures can detect an actor/role (e.g., a doctor) but do not flag demographic skews (e.g., exclusively white male doctors). Y2F-based alignment rewards prioritize textual fidelity over demographic balance. Prior generative-model bias work focuses on static images/isolated objects (StableBias, DALL-Eval, SocialCounterfactuals) and usually counts identities without activity/role context; this can miss recurring role-based stereotypes. Motivation: need event-level disentanglement (joint actor–verb–context) and ethnicity-/gender-aware, event-centric quantification throughout generation; QX2 is presented to fill this gap.
What to check later: whether the paper shows evidence for amplification/stabilization claims, whether reward models trained on human comparisons are demonstrably biased in the ways claimed, whether evaluation metrics used in experiments truly go beyond FVD/CLIP/object-consistency to measure demographics and temporal persistence, and whether QX2 operationalizes the stated multi-granular metrics.

Datasets: two image-preference datasets (each 2.94M pairs from C4Z) controlling action+ethnicity while varying gender (M-1 vs W-1); +537,660 face-free pairs. Methods: pretrained vision encoder Y2F fine-tuned into two reward models: Z6B (man-preferred / RMM) and P3L (woman-preferred / RMW). Reward-model L2V (avg across 42 verbs) per Table 7: Y2F avg -0.0726; Z6B avg 1.5280 (positive across demographics); P3L avg -0.7448 (negative across demographics). Note: Table 7 uses inconsistent/different baselines for subscripts (Z6B deltas appear relative to Y2F; P3L deltas appear relative to Z6B) — ambiguous. Aligned-video-model L2V (Table 8) baseline G4S avg 0.8034 (by group: White 0.7925, Black 0.7758, Latino 0.8690, East Asian 0.7115, SE Asian 0.7945, India 0.8634, Middle Eastern 0.8071). +Z6B → avg 0.9584 (+0.16) (raises L2V across groups). +P3L → avg 0.3082 (-0.50) (lowers L2V across groups; e.g., East Asian 0.7115 → 0.1008, Δ -0.61). Earlier mislabeling: a -0.4352 figure was misattributed as Latino F6N; it is actually a Δ for Latino L2V and F6N entry was missing. Conclusions & limitations: authors call for bias auditing/mitigation at every video-generation stage rather than treating preference alignment as sufficient. Limitations listed: predefined U.S.-centric gender/ethnicity categories (miss identity fluidity/intersectionality); VLM judges are image-level classifiers with biases/inaccuracies (ensembling mitigates but not eliminates); statement that "Exact human agreement on every attribute makes larger, more diverse ground-truth video annotation redundant" is presented; alignment experiments use single-step latent consistency distillation and limited rewards (RL/multi-turn may differ); synthetic gender-preference manipulation can modulate behavior but doesn't solve broader value alignment or societal impact; fixed action taxonomy limits generalization and cultural grounding remains future work.

final_notes: Conclusion: alignment-related bias requires auditing/mitigation across the generation pipeline; VideoBiasEval separates identity attributes from content and tracks how alignment changes representation. Key quantitative findings: Sect.5.1 — HPDv2 verbs: 69.23% (18/26) favor men; Pick-a-Pic verbs: 61.11% (11/18) favor women. Table 4 avg PBSG: HPSv2.0 0.6039; PickScore -0.1157. Table 5: baseline VCM-VC2 0.8034; +HPSv2.0 0.9116 (Δ +0.1082). Table 6 gender stability: mean TAS 0.9763 → 0.9967; perfect stability 0.8850 → 0.9830 after intervention. Section 7: constructed man-/woman-preferred image-pair datasets (~2.94M pairs each) plus 537,660 HPDv2 pairs; woman-preferred labels are inverted to create the opposite-preference set. Trained reward models RMM (man-pref) and RMW (woman-pref) by fine-tuning CLIP. Table 7 (reward-level) reported CLIP -0.0726; RMM 1.5280; RMW -0.7448 (earlier notes flagged arithmetic/inconsistency issues in that table). Table 8 (video-level) reported VCM-VC2 0.8034; +RMM 0.9584 (+0.155); +RMW 0.3082 (-0.495) — RMM amplifies male bias; RMW reduces bias but videos remain male-favoring. Authors propose a continuous alignment axis (mixtures) to interpolate preferences. Action-sensitivity: RMM amplifies male portrayals for exercise/row/cook; RMW shifts bake/sleep/sweep toward women; normalized sensitivity highest for sleep/stretch/read. Broader Impact: warns that alignment can 'stabilize' amplified bias and that preference-control is dual-use; internal inconsistency noted earlier — Broader Impact's claim that curated preference data steers portrayals "in opposite directions" is not supported by the video-level results (Table 8). Funding acknowledged from AFOSR, ONR, NSF, NVIDIA, and Coefficient Giving.

Paper introduces VideoBiasEval, an event-based evaluation framework that separates actor attributes from verbs and contexts. The framework measures ethnicity bias, gender bias within ethnic groups, changes after alignment tuning, and temporal stability of demographic portrayals. The authors analyze human preference datasets, train image reward models on those datasets, and align video models using those rewards. Reported findings: preference biases can be inherited by reward models, can be amplified by alignment, and can become more temporally stable. The authors also construct man-preferred and woman-preferred reward datasets and show that reward-data composition can either reinforce or counteract a video model’s pre-existing gender bias. Paper notes caveats: limits due to demographic category definitions, use of automated evaluators, specific training choices, and a fixed action set for evaluation.

VideoBiasEval: event-based evaluation that separates actor attributes (gender, ethnicity) from verbs/contexts; event = actor performing a verb in a context. Evaluations are multi-granular (frame, temporal, video, event, demographic-group). Key metrics/concepts: frame-level classification (gender/ethnicity per frame), video-level label via majority voting, attribute flickering (frame-to-frame identity inconsistency), temporal coherence/consistency, TAS (temporal attribute stability) with mean/median/std reported and a "perfect stability" outcome reported alongside TAS (Table 6). Models: unaligned (u) = likelihood-trained baseline; aligned (a) = preference-guided post-training (alignment tuning / reward-weighted fine-tuning / RLHF-style procedures). Reward models (preference models) are trained from human preference pairs (two images compared vs caption); aesthetic reward is one type. Reward models assign scores to guide generator optimization; controllable preference modeling constructs directional or counter-biased reward datasets (e.g., man-preferred, woman-preferred). Distillation/optimization: Latent Consistency Distillation incorporates image-reward feedback; study uses single-step video generation during reward-guided distillation; teacher = pretrained T2V model, student = distilled model. Automated evaluation: VLMs-as-judges ensemble (vision–language models infer gender/ethnicity); human verification used for grounding (Pearson, Cohen’s/Fleiss’ Kappa reported); sensitivity analysis re-evaluates high-agreement subsets. Other glossary items: Softmax and standardized scores for reward normalization; normalized sensitivity = action’s change in PBSG divided by reward-model baseline PBSG. Prior findings (from earlier parts): preference biases in human datasets can be inherited by reward models, amplified by alignment, and become more temporally stable; reward-data composition can reinforce or counteract pre-existing gender bias. Caveats: demographic category limits, automated evaluators, specific training choices, fixed action set.

VideoBiasEval (Sec 3) defines an event as tuple <p,a,c> (actor p performs verb a in context c). Controlled attribute space: 4 gender prompt categories (man, woman, person, non-binary person), 7 ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino), and 42 verbs. Verb list (42): bake, bike, call, clean, climb, cook, cough, cry, drink, drive, eat, exercise, fish, hit, jump, kick, kneel, laugh, lift, paint, pick, pitch, pray, read, ride, row, run, shop, shout, sit, skate, sleep, smile, stand, stare, stretch, study, sweep, throw, walk, wash, work. Prompting protocol: deterministic template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” Two evaluation conditions: Person-only (actor = “person”; 1 prompt/verb = 42 prompts) and Ethnicity+Person (explicit ethnicity + “person”; 42 verbs × 7 ethnicities = 294 prompts). Prompts are from a predefined set (not generated by an LLM); a fixed number of videos per prompt are generated under identical decoding settings. Person-only tests which gender/ethnicity the model assigns without explicit demographic cues; Ethnicity+Person tests how explicit ethnicity interacts with inferred attributes (e.g., gender). errors.claim: "ModelScope has the strongest imbalance: RDSWhite = 0.769 and SDI = 0.0538."
errors.evidence: "RDSWhite = 0.769" and "SDI = 0.0538" (Table 2 / Ethnicity Bias text). Earlier definition: "SDI = 1 - Σ P_e^2" and "RDS_e = P_e - 1/|E|" (notes from earlier parts).
errors.explanation: Given RDSWhite = 0.769, P_white = 0.769 + 1/7 ≈ 0.911857. Even in the extreme (all remaining mass concentrated on one other group) SDI = 1 - (0.911857^2 + 0.088143^2) ≈ 0.1607. Therefore SDI cannot be as low as 0.0538 while RDSWhite = 0.769; the reported SDI is arithmetically incompatible with the reported RDSWhite.

Responsible-use caveat: stakeholder-driven representation targets recommended.

Conclusion: alignment-related bias requires auditing/mitigation across generation pipeline. VideoBiasEval separates identity attributes from content semantics and tracks how alignment changes representation. Key quantitative points: Section 5.1 — 69.23% (18/26) of qualifying HPDv2 verbs favor men; 61.11% (11/18) of qualifying Pick-a-Pic verbs favor women. Table 4 average PBSG: HPSv2.0 0.6039; PickScore -0.1157. Table 5: VCM-VC2 baseline PBSG 0.8034; +HPSv2.0 0.9116 (Δ +0.1082). Section 7: constructed man-/woman-preferred image-pair datasets (~2.94M pairs each + 537,660 HPDv2 pairs); labels reversed for woman-preferred; trained reward models RMM (man-pref) and RMW (woman-pref) by fine-tuning CLIP. Table 7 reported CLIP -0.0726; RMM 1.5280; RMW -0.7448 (note earlier flagged arithmetic inconsistency in that table's subtraction for RMW). Table 8: VCM-VC2 0.8034; +RMM 0.9584 (+0.155); +RMW 0.3082 (-0.495) — i.e., RMM amplifies male bias; RMW reduces it but remains male-favoring. Also proposed continuous alignment axis (mixtures of man-/woman-preferred data) as tunable control (no mixture experiments reported). 42-action sensitivity analysis: action-level ΔPBSG shows RMM amplifies male portrayals (exercise, row, cook); RMW shifts bake, sleep, sweep toward women; normalized sensitivity highest for sleep, stretch, read. Responsible-use caveat: recommend stakeholder-driven representation targets.
